t: Chapter 2 · 2.1  Introduction: The Architecture of Principle
x: Insurance contracts are, in one sense, ordinary commercial contracts: they require offer, acceptance, consideration, and legal capacity. But they are simultaneously extraordinary contracts — extraordinary because of the informational asymmetry between the parties, because of the nature of what is being exchanged, and because their entire commercial logic depends on the parties behaving with a degree of honesty and good faith that the law does not require in most other commercial contexts. It is this unusual character that generated, over centuries of English and Nigerian common law development, a set of principles specific to insurance. These principles are not merely academic formulations. They are operative doctrines that determine whether a policy is valid, whether a claim is payable, and whether a third party can be held responsible for a loss that an insurer has already met. Every insurance practitioner — underwriter, claims handler, broker, or agent — makes decisions daily that are, consciously or not, applications of these principles. This chapter examines the six fundamental principles: utmost good faith, insurable interest, indemnity, subrogation, contribution, and proximate cause. Each principle is treated in its theoretical, legal, and practical dimensions. The chapter concludes with an analysis of warranties and conditions, and with a review of the reforms to these principles introduced by the Nigerian Insurance Industry Reform Act (NIIRA) 2025 — the most significant legislative overhaul of the legal framework for insurance in Nigeria in two decades.

2.2.1 The Basis and Rationale of the Duty Of all the principles of insurance law, none is more foundational, more litigated, or more consequential in the Nigerian market than the duty of utmost good faith — expressed in the Latin maxim uberrimae fidei, meaning 'of the utmost good faith.' It is a duty that elevates insurance contracts above ordinary commercial agreements and imposes on both parties an obligation of transparency that has no parallel in the general law of contract. The principle was articulated with enduring clarity by Lord Mansfield in Carter v Boehm (1766):[1] "Insurance is a contract upon speculation. The special facts, upon which the contingent chance is to be computed, lie most commonly in the knowledge of the insured only: the underwriter trusts to his representation, and proceeds upon the confidence that he does not keep back any circumstance in his knowledge, to mislead the underwriter into a belief that the circumstance does not exist, and to induce him to estimate the risk, as if it did not exist." This rationale remains compelling today. An underwriter assessing a life insurance proposal cannot personally examine the life assured's medical records, attend the doctor's surgery, or inspect the applicant's family history. The underwriter is entirely dependent on the accuracy of what the proposer declares. If the proposer withholds material information — that he has a family history of heart disease, that he has been declined cover elsewhere, that he engages in hazardous pursuits — the underwriter is pricing a risk materially different from the one she believes she is accepting. The informational asymmetry is structural, and the principle of utmost good faith is the law's corrective mechanism. Utmost Good Faith (Uberrimae Fidei) The principle that both parties to an insurance contract are required to act with the utmost honesty towards one another: to disclose all facts material to the risk, not to misrepresent any material fact, and not to actively conceal information that a prudent underwriter would consider significant in deciding whether to accept the risk and on what terms. Breach of this duty by the insured entitles the insurer to avoid the contract ab initio (from the beginning), subject to the proportionate remedies introduced under NIIRA 2025. Derived from: Carter v Boehm (1766); codified in Marine Insurance Act 1961 (now repealed); preserved under NIIRA 2025. 2.2.2 The Three Branches of the Duty (a) Duty of Disclosure The duty of disclosure requires the proposer, before the contract is formed, to voluntarily disclose all facts that are material to the risk being insured — without waiting to be asked. This is the feature of insurance that most distinguishes it from ordinary contracts: in general contract law, a party is not ordinarily obliged to volunteer information; silence is not misrepresentation. In insurance, silence about a material fact is a breach of duty. A fact is material if it would influence the judgment of a prudent underwriter in deciding whether to accept the risk, and if so, at what premium and on what conditions. This is known as the prudent underwriter test or the materiality test. It is objective — the question is not whether this particular underwriter would have been influenced, but whether a hypothetical prudent underwriter in the same market would have been. Examples of facts material in life assurance proposals include: Current and past medical conditions, diagnoses, and treatment; Family medical history relevant to hereditary conditions; Hazardous occupations or avocations (racing, mountaineering, aviation as a non-commercial pilot); Existing life policies, including previous declinatures and special terms imposed by other insurers; Lifestyle factors: smoking, alcohol consumption above typical thresholds, narcotics use; Financial circumstances relevant to the sum assured requested (to detect over-insurance); Planned foreign travel or residence in high-risk territories. The duty of disclosure extends to facts within the proposer's knowledge, to facts that a person in the proposer's position ought to know (constructive knowledge), and — controversially — to facts that a reasonable person would realise are material even if the proposer personally did not. It does not extend to facts of common knowledge, facts the insurer knows or ought to know from its market expertise, or facts the insurer has expressly or impliedly waived. (b) Duty Not to Misrepresent The duty not to misrepresent is the negative counterpart of the duty of disclosure. Where the proposer makes a positive statement about the risk — whether in the proposal form, in correspondence, or in conversation with an agent — that statement must be accurate. A misrepresentation is a false statement of fact made before or at the time of contracting which induces the insurer to enter the contract. Three categories of misrepresentation are recognised in Nigerian insurance law, each with distinct legal consequences: Fraudulent misrepresentation: A statement made knowing it to be false, or recklessly as to its truth. This is the most serious category and entitles the insurer to avoid the contract and potentially claim damages in tort for deceit. Negligent misrepresentation: A statement made without reasonable grounds for believing it to be true. The insurer may avoid the policy, and under NIIRA 2025's reformed framework, the remedy is now calibrated to the gravity of the breach. Innocent misrepresentation: A false statement made honestly and reasonably, without fault. Under the pre-NIIRA 2025 common law position, even an innocent misrepresentation entitled the insurer to avoid the policy entirely. NIIRA 2025 modifies this harsh outcome — an important reform discussed in Section 2.2.5. In practice, the most frequently litigated misrepresentations in Nigerian life insurance involve health history. The proposer who states 'No' to a question about pre-existing medical conditions, knowing that she has been treated for diabetes, commits a fraudulent misrepresentation. The proposer who states 'No' because he forgot about a minor operation five years ago may be making an innocent misrepresentation. The legal treatment of these two cases was, until NIIRA 2025, identical: both entitled the insurer to avoid the policy. (c) Duty Not to Conceal Concealment is the active suppression of a material fact — not a mere failure to volunteer it (which is non-disclosure) but a deliberate act to keep it from the insurer's attention. An insured who, when completing a proposal form, notices that a question asks about 'hospital admissions' and deliberately construes the question narrowly to exclude a recent clinic visit is not merely failing to disclose; she may be concealing. Concealment is treated as equivalent to fraudulent misrepresentation and gives the insurer the right to avoid the policy. 2.2.3 Nigerian Case Law on Utmost Good Faith Nigerian courts have, consistent with the English common law tradition, applied the duty of utmost good faith strictly. Several cases warrant examination for their doctrinal importance and their practical lessons for practitioners. Case Note — Leadway Assurance Co Ltd v Zeco Nigeria Ltd (2004) 11 NWLR (Pt 884) 316 (SC) The Supreme Court of Nigeria held that the insured's failure to disclose previous losses entitled Leadway Assurance to void the policy. The Court applied the prudent underwriter test and confirmed that the insurer need not demonstrate a causal link between the undisclosed fact and the actual loss claimed. The non-disclosure alone was sufficient to trigger the right of avoidance. This case is the leading Nigerian Supreme Court authority on utmost good faith and is regularly cited in subsequent decisions. Lesson for practitioners: Previous insurance history — especially losses and claims — is invariably material. A proposer who conceals prior motor accidents when applying for motor insurance, or prior hospitalisations when applying for life insurance, faces the prospect of a voided policy at the point of claiming. Case Note — NICON v Power & Industrial Engineering Co Ltd (1986) 1 NWLR (Pt 20) 1 (SC) The respondent failed to disclose material facts relating to the risk of a vessel. The Supreme Court affirmed the insurer's right to void the policy. Significantly, the Court held that the insurer did not need to prove that the undisclosed facts would have changed the decision to insure; it was sufficient that a prudent underwriter would have found the facts material.[3] Lesson for practitioners: The materiality test is objective and applies to the class of risk, not to the specific underwriter's decision-making process. Underwriters should document the material facts on which they rely in risk assessment. Case Note — Akpata v African Alliance Insurance Company Limited In this case, the insured had applied for a life policy and answered questions about his health in the negative. The insurer sought to void the policy on death, arguing non-disclosure of a medical condition. The court found for the policyholder's estate, holding that at the time of contracting, the insured was not in a position to know or appreciate the critical nature of his health status, as he was neither medically trained nor in possession of a diagnosis.[5] Lesson for practitioners: An insured cannot disclose what he does not know. Where a proposer reasonably did not know of a medical condition at the time of proposal, the insurer's avoidance defence may fail. Careful medical underwriting — including thorough medical questionnaires and, where appropriate, requiring medical examinations — is the underwriter's protection against this scenario. Case Note — Joseph Irukwu v Trinity Mills Insurance Broker (CA/L/145/90, 1992) A life policy was set aside by the Court of Appeal because the life assured had not disclosed his medical history at the proposal stage. The Court restated that insurance contracts of every class are uberrimae fidei contracts, and that this duty is most powerfully operative at the moment the contract is formed.[4] Lesson for practitioners: The duty of utmost good faith applies at the pre-contractual proposal stage. Its observance or breach is crystallised at the moment the contract is formed; subsequent disclosures do not retroactively cure an earlier non-disclosure, though they may affect the insurer's election to continue or void a policy. 2.2.4 Exceptions to the Duty of Disclosure The duty of disclosure is not unlimited. A number of recognised exceptions reduce its scope: Facts of common knowledge: Information publicly known and available to the market does not require individual disclosure. An underwriter is presumed to know the general conditions of the market in which she operates. Facts the insurer knows or ought to know: If the insurer's own inspection or enquiry would have revealed the relevant fact, it cannot invoke the proposer's non-disclosure as grounds for avoidance. Facts that diminish the risk: A proposer is not required to disclose facts that would reduce the premium she is charged. Facts waived by the insurer: If the insurer, through its proposal form or conduct, impliedly waives disclosure of a particular class of information — by asking incomplete questions or accepting answers without further enquiry — it cannot later claim avoidance on the grounds of non-disclosure in that waived area. Facts protected by legal privilege: Information protected by lawyer-client privilege or equivalent legal immunities is exempt from disclosure. 2.2.5 NIIRA 2025: Reform of the Utmost Good Faith Regime Regulatory Spotlight — NIIRA 2025 — Reforming the Duty of Utmost Good Faith The harshest feature of the pre-NIIRA 2025 regime was the all-or-nothing remedy of avoidance: regardless of the nature of the non-disclosure — fraudulent, negligent, or entirely innocent — the insurer's remedy was to void the policy ab initio, leaving the policyholder with no claim payment and frequently no premium refund. This outcome, while legally coherent, generated enormous public mistrust in the Nigerian insurance industry. NIIRA 2025 moves significantly in the direction of the UK Insurance Act 2015, introducing two material reforms: Fair Presentation of Risk: NIIRA 2025 replaces the harsh common law duty with a more balanced obligation of fair presentation. The insured must disclose information that a reasonable insured in their position would have disclosed, and must do so in a reasonably clear and accessible manner. This formulation is more workable than the abstract 'prudent underwriter' test and is better aligned with the practical reality of consumer insurance transactions. Proportionate Remedies: NIIRA 2025 limits the insurer's right to avoid the contract solely on the ground that utmost good faith was not observed in circumstances where the breach was innocent and unconnected to the loss. Where the non-disclosure was careless but not fraudulent, the remedy is calibrated — the insurer may adjust the claim proportionately to the premium it would have charged had it known the true facts, rather than voiding the policy entirely. These reforms are significant steps forward for consumer protection. However, the pre-2025 cases — including Leadway v Zeco and NICON v Power & Industrial — remain binding authority for policies issued before NIIRA 2025 came into force. Policies issued under NIIRA 2025 operate under the reformed, more favourable policyholder regime. Practitioners must distinguish which regime applies based on the policy inception date.[15][16]

2.3.1 Definition and Rationale Insurable interest is the legally recognised relationship between the insured and the subject matter of the insurance such that the insured would suffer a genuine financial loss if the insured event occurred. It is the answer to the question: why does this person have the right to insure this risk? Without insurable interest, an insurance policy is not merely unenforceable — it is legally void, and in some cases constitutes an illegal wagering contract. The requirement of insurable interest serves two vital functions. First, it prevents insurance from being used as a wagering instrument — a concern that predates modern regulation. The Life Assurance Act 1774 (England), which established the insurable interest requirement for life assurance, was enacted precisely because life policies were being written by strangers who had no connection to the life assured other than a desire to speculate on when they would die. Second, insurable interest reduces moral hazard: a person who stands to benefit financially from a loss has a reduced incentive to prevent it. Insurable interest ensures that the insured has a pre-existing financial stake in the preservation of the subject matter. Insurable Interest A legally recognised financial relationship between the insured and the subject matter of the insurance, such that the insured would suffer a quantifiable financial loss if the insured event occurred, or would have a legal liability to another party. In life insurance, insurable interest is the basis upon which a person may validly insure the life of another. Without insurable interest, a policy of insurance is void ab initio. See: Life Assurance Act 1774 (England); NIIRA 2025; Macaura v Northern Assurance Co Ltd [1925] AC 619. 2.3.2 Insurable Interest in Life Assurance In life assurance, the rules on insurable interest differ materially from those applying in property and liability insurance. Several categories are established at common law and confirmed in Nigerian practice: Category of Insurable Interest Basis Required at What Point? Own life Every person has an unlimited insurable interest in their own life; the sum assured is unrestricted. At inception only — an own-life policy remains valid even if the financial circumstances change. Spouse's life Recognised by statute and common law; unlimited (not capped at financial loss). At inception — no ongoing proof required. Employer in key employee (Keyman) Financial interest in the employee's continued contribution to the business; capped at demonstrable economic value. At inception; sum assured must be justifiable. Creditor in debtor's life The creditor has insurable interest to the extent of the debt owed. At inception; interest is capped at the debt amount, not unlimited. Business partners (cross-option arrangements) Partners may insure each other's lives to fund buy-out on death. At inception; the policy must be structured on insurable interest principles. Parent in child's life Recognised in Nigerian practice to the extent of financial dependency. At inception of the dependency relationship. Endorsement and nomination situations The life assured nominates a beneficiary; the beneficiary need not have insurable interest — interest belongs to the proposer. Proposer's interest at inception; beneficiary's beneficial interest governed by nomination provisions. The celebrated English authority on insurable interest in property insurance is Macaura v Northern Assurance Co Ltd [1925] AC 619 (House of Lords), in which the sole shareholder of a company purported to insure company-owned timber in his own name. The House of Lords held that he had no insurable interest: his interest was in the company as a separate legal entity, not in its assets directly. This case, though a property decision, is routinely applied in Nigerian courts as the touchstone for what constitutes a legally recognised interest. The principle from Macaura is that insurable interest requires a right recognised at law — not a mere expectancy, not a moral hope, not a relationship of affection. The debtor-creditor relationship, the employer-employee relationship, the partner-partner relationship — these are legally cognisable interests that support valid insurance. A stranger's interest in another's continued good health, however strongly felt, is not a legally recognised interest.[7] 2.3.3 Timing of Insurable Interest In life assurance, the established rule is that insurable interest need exist only at the time the policy is taken out — not at the time of the claim. A wife who insures her husband's life retains a valid claim even if they subsequently divorce, provided she held insurable interest when the policy was incepted. This rule distinguishes life assurance from non-life insurance, where insurable interest is generally required at the time of loss. This distinction has practical implications in the Nigerian context. Credit life policies, which insure the life of a debtor to repay a loan on death, are valid only for the duration of the debt: once the debt is repaid, the creditor's insurable interest is extinguished, and the policy should not continue in the same form. Group life master policies under the Pension Reform Act 2014 require that the insured employee be in active employment at the time of claim — a form of ongoing insurable interest requirement for group schemes. Advisory — Structuring Life Proposals to Demonstrate Insurable Interest Underwriters and brokers should adopt the practice of documenting insurable interest at the proposal stage, particularly for large sums assured and third-party life proposals. In Keyman insurance, the employer should be required to provide a financial justification — typically a multiple of the employee's salary or an estimate of the economic cost of replacement — to support the sum assured. For cross-option business protection arrangements, legal agreements should be in place before the policy is incepted. Poor insurable interest documentation is a common source of claim disputes and is a finding in NAICOM examination reports.

2.4.1 The Principle The principle of indemnity holds that insurance should restore the insured, as nearly as possible, to the financial position they occupied immediately before the loss — neither better nor worse. The classic statement is that of Brett LJ in Castellain v Preston (1883): [8] "The very foundation of every rule which has been applied to insurance law is this, namely that the contract of insurance contained in a marine or fire policy is a contract of indemnity, and of indemnity only, and that this contract means that the assured, in case of a loss against which the policy has been made, shall be fully indemnified, but shall never be more than fully indemnified." The indemnity principle prevents insurance from becoming a source of profit for the insured. If a policyholder could recover more than her actual loss, she would have a financial incentive to allow losses to occur — or worse, to cause them. The principle is therefore both a legal constraint and a moral safeguard. Indemnity The contractual obligation of the insurer to restore the insured, upon the occurrence of an insured loss, to the same financial position as was occupied immediately before the loss — no more and no less. The indemnity principle underlies all non-life insurance and operates in life assurance only in modified form, since the value of a human life cannot be precisely quantified. Note: Indemnity does not apply in its strict form to life assurance, where the benefit is typically a pre-agreed fixed sum (the 'sum assured') rather than a measure of the actual financial loss. 2.4.2 Methods of Providing Indemnity In practice, insurers discharge the indemnity obligation in one of four ways, depending on the class of insurance and the nature of the loss: Cash payment: The insurer pays a sum of money representing the financial loss. This is the most common method in Nigerian insurance practice across all classes. Repair: For property damage, the insurer arranges and pays for reinstatement to the pre-loss condition. Motor insurers routinely use authorised repair panels. Replacement: The insurer replaces the lost or destroyed property with a new or equivalent item. Typically used for total loss of personal property. Reinstatement: Used in commercial property insurance. The insurer rebuilds or reconstructs a damaged building. A specialised method with specific valuation considerations. 2.4.3 Indemnity Measurement: The Sum Insured, Underinsurance, and Averaging The measure of indemnity is constrained by the sum insured stated in the policy. The sum insured represents the maximum the insurer will pay — it is a ceiling, not a guarantee. Three scenarios are common in practice: Adequately insured: Sum insured equals or exceeds the value at risk. Full indemnity is available up to the sum insured. Over-insured: Sum insured exceeds the value at risk. The insurer pays only the actual loss — the indemnity principle prevents recovery of the excess. Over-insurance may also trigger moral hazard concerns and investigation. Under-insured: Sum insured is less than the value at risk. Where an averaging (or co-insurance) clause applies, the insurer will pay only the proportion that the sum insured bears to the full value. Example: a building worth ₦50 million insured for ₦25 million (50% of value) suffers a ₦10 million partial loss. With an averaging clause, the insurer pays 50% of the loss = ₦5 million. The insured is her own insurer for the balance. Underinsurance is a systemic problem in the Nigerian insurance market. Commercial properties are routinely under-declared in value, either through ignorance of the averaging clause or through a deliberate strategy to reduce premium. Practitioners have a professional responsibility to advise clients on adequate sums insured and to document that advice. 2.4.4 Indemnity in Life Assurance The strict indemnity principle does not apply to life assurance. The reasons are compelling: human life cannot be valued with the precision required for indemnity measurement; the loss on death is partly a financial loss, but it is also a personal and emotional loss that money can only imperfectly address; and the sum assured is, in any case, agreed between the parties at inception. Life assurance policies pay a pre-agreed sum assured on the occurrence of the specified event — death, survival to maturity, critical illness diagnosis. This sum is payable regardless of the precise financial consequence of the event. The widow who claims on her late husband's term assurance will receive the full sum assured even if her financial loss is less than that sum (she has other income) or greater than that sum (her financial need exceeds the policy benefit). This distinction between indemnity and life assurance is why insurable interest in life policies is not measured with reference to financial loss: it would be impossible to do so precisely, and the policy is not designed to indemnify in the strict sense but to provide a financial benefit on a contingent event. The sum assured is therefore a measure of benefit, not of loss.

2.5.1 The Basis of Subrogation Subrogation is the doctrine by which, having indemnified the insured for a loss caused by a third party's wrongful act or negligence, the insurer steps into the shoes of the insured and acquires the right to pursue the responsible third party for recovery of the sum paid. It is the law's mechanism for ensuring that the wrongdoer — not the insurer — ultimately bears the cost of the loss, and that the insured does not receive double compensation. The classic authority is again Castellain v Preston (1883), in which the insurer, having paid for fire damage to a property, claimed the benefit of the sale price (which included a sum representing the fire damage) that the seller-insured subsequently received from a purchaser. The Court of Appeal upheld the insurer's claim: to allow the insured to retain both the insurance payment and the sale price would breach the indemnity principle by allowing profit from the loss.[11] Subrogation The right of an insurer, after indemnifying an insured for a loss caused by a third party's wrongful act or default, to stand in the place of the insured and exercise all rights, remedies, and actions that the insured could have exercised against the third party to recover the amount of the indemnity paid. Subrogation is a corollary of indemnity and does not apply in life assurance. See: Castellain v Preston (1883) 11 QBD 380; Yorkshire Insurance Co v Nisbet Shipping Co [1962] 2 QB 330. 2.5.2 Conditions for Subrogation Three conditions must be met before subrogation can arise: The contract must be one of indemnity. Subrogation does not apply to life assurance, personal accident insurance paying a fixed sum, or critical illness policies — because these are not indemnity contracts. An insurer who pays a ₦20 million death benefit cannot subrogate against the party who caused the death: the payment was not an indemnity against a measurable financial loss. The insurer must have paid the claim. Subrogation does not arise before the insurer has discharged its indemnity obligation. An insurer cannot sue the third party in advance of paying the insured. The insured must have a right of action against the third party. If no such right exists — because the loss was caused by a non-negligent act, for example — there is nothing for the insurer to subrogate to. 2.5.3 Practical Application and Limits The insurer's right in subrogation is limited to the amount it has paid as indemnity. If the insurer paid ₦5 million and the third party is found liable for ₦8 million, the insured is entitled to the excess ₦3 million: the insurer recovers only what it paid, no more. This principle was confirmed in Yorkshire Insurance Co v Nisbet Shipping Co [1962] 2 QB 330.[10] In practice, Nigerian insurers — particularly in the motor and property lines — frequently neglect subrogation recovery, citing the high cost of litigation relative to the likely recovery. This tendency is not merely a missed financial opportunity; it distorts the loss cost experience of the portfolio, because claims that should ultimately be recovered from third parties are charged permanently to the insurer's claims account. NAICOM has issued circulars urging transparency in salvage and subrogation handling; NIIRA 2025 provides for subrogation rights in insurance claims after settlement. Subrogation can be modified by contractual agreement. 'Waiver of subrogation' clauses in commercial policies — common in construction, engineering, and logistics contracts — preclude the insurer from pursuing the third party. Practitioners must be alert to such clauses when advising commercial clients, as they affect the premium pricing and the insurer's loss cost expectations.

2.6.1 Double Insurance and the Contribution Doctrine Contribution arises in the context of double insurance — where the same insured has insured the same interest against the same risk with two or more insurers. Without a contribution doctrine, the insured could claim the full indemnity from each insurer, receiving a windfall that would violate the indemnity principle. Contribution ensures that where multiple policies cover the same loss, the total indemnity received does not exceed the actual loss, and that the multiple insurers share the loss equitably among themselves. Contribution The right of an insurer who has paid more than its fair share of a loss covered by two or more policies to recover the excess from the other insurers. Contribution operates between co-insurers of the same risk and ensures that no insured can profit from double insurance. It is the inter-insurer complement of the indemnity principle. Note: Contribution applies only where both policies cover the same insured, the same interest, and the same risk. It does not arise where one policy is life assurance or a fixed-benefit policy. 2.6.2 Conditions for Contribution Four conditions must be satisfied before contribution rights arise between insurers: Both policies must cover the same insured: Contribution requires that the same person holds both policies, or that the same interest is insured (as in the case of a co-assured). Both policies must cover the same subject matter and interest: A building contents policy and a building structure policy covering the same address are separate interests; contribution would not apply between them in respect of a claim that relates only to the structure. Both policies must cover the same risk or peril: If one policy excludes the very peril that caused the loss, it is not a co-insurer of that loss, and contribution does not arise. Both policies must be valid and enforceable: A policy voidable for non-disclosure, if actually avoided, cannot be called upon to contribute. 2.6.3 Methods of Apportionment Where contribution does arise, the sharing of the loss between co-insurers is determined by one of two methods: Independent liability method (preferred): Each insurer calculates the maximum it would pay if it were the only insurer, and the actual loss is shared in proportion to those independent liabilities. This is the method most consistent with the terms of each individual policy and is the approach generally favoured by Nigerian and English courts. Rateable proportion method (older approach): Each insurer pays the proportion that its policy's sum insured bears to the aggregate of all sums insured. A simpler calculation but one that can produce inequitable outcomes where policies have different limits or conditions. In practice, most commercial policies contain a contribution clause that addresses this expressly, frequently providing that the insurer will pay no more than its rateable proportion of any loss that is covered by two or more policies. Practitioners must identify and disclose double insurance at proposal stage, as failure to do so may itself constitute a breach of the duty of utmost good faith.

2.7.1 The Rule and Its Purpose Insurance policies are written in terms of covered perils — fire, death, theft, flood, accident. A loss does not arise in isolation: it has a chain of causation, sometimes simple (fire caused by an electrical fault), sometimes complex (a sequence of events involving multiple contributing factors). The proximate cause principle provides the legal rule for identifying which cause is legally relevant to the determination of policy response. The rule is: an insurer is liable for a loss if the proximate cause of that loss is a covered peril, and is not liable if the proximate cause is an excluded peril. The proximate cause is the efficient, dominant, and effective cause of the loss — the cause without which the loss would not have occurred. It need not be the immediate, final, or last cause in time. Proximate Cause (Causa Proxima) The dominant, efficient, and operative cause of a loss — the cause without which the loss would not have occurred. Where a chain of events leads to a loss, the proximate cause is identified by asking: which cause set the whole sequence in motion, remained operative throughout, and was the effective cause of the final outcome? It is not necessarily the last event in time, but the cause that most directly produced the loss. Latin maxim: Causa proxima non remota spectatur — the proximate, not the remote, cause is to be looked at. 2.7.2 The Leading Case Case Note — Leyland Shipping Co Ltd v Norwich Union Fire Insurance Society Ltd [1918] AC 350 (HL) A ship insured under a marine policy 'against perils of the seas' but excluding 'war risks' was struck by an enemy torpedo during the First World War. The ship reached port in a damaged state and continued to deteriorate. She was eventually moved to the harbour entrance where she sank in heavy seas. The House of Lords held that the torpedo — not the storm — was the proximate cause of the loss. The torpedo's effect was continuous and unbroken throughout the sequence of events: it was the efficient cause, and the storm at the harbour entrance was merely an additional circumstance. The war risks exclusion applied.[13] Principle extracted: The proximate cause need not be the last event in time. It is the cause that was dominant and operative throughout the chain of events leading to the loss. This principle has been adopted in Nigerian insurance litigation. 2.7.3 Applying Proximate Cause in Practice: Scenarios Scenario Proximate Cause Policy Response Insured has a heart attack while driving; the vehicle collides with a wall and catches fire. The heart attack. The fire is consequential. Life policy responds to the death (natural causes or accidental, depending on terms). Motor policy may not respond if driver error is the operative event. A fire damages a wall; the wall is demolished by the municipal authority; the demolition injures a pedestrian. The fire — its effects are continuous throughout. Fire policy should respond to the pedestrian injury claim (liability section), because the fire was the proximate cause. Insured is injured in an accident and, while recovering in hospital, contracts a hospital-acquired infection and dies. The accident — the infection is a direct and foreseeable consequence of the hospitalisation caused by the accident. Personal accident policy likely responds; the infection does not break the chain of causation. A flood damages a warehouse; the insured's goods are looted during the evacuation. The flood and the theft are independent causes. The theft (excluded peril) is a separate intervening cause, not a consequence of the flood. Flood damage covered; theft loss not covered (absent a theft cover extension). The insured commits suicide within the contestability period stated in a life policy. Suicide — a deliberate act of the insured. Most Nigerian life policies exclude suicide within 12–24 months of inception; death benefit not payable in that period. 2.7.4 Concurrent Causes The most difficult proximate cause scenarios arise when two perils operate simultaneously or in close succession to produce a single loss — one peril covered, one excluded. The courts have developed a pragmatic approach: if the concurrent causes are inseparably mixed and cannot be disaggregated, the proximate cause is determined by which cause was the dominant or most effective operative force. If one covered cause and one excluded cause are truly concurrent and of equal weight, some authorities support a denial of the claim; others support pro-rata recovery. Nigerian practitioners should be alert to the specificity of policy wording in concurrent cause scenarios — clear anti-concurrent causation clauses are increasingly used in commercial policies to address this ambiguity.

t: Chapter 2 · 2.8  Warranties and Conditions in Insurance Contracts
x: 2.8.1 Warranties A warranty in insurance law is a term of the insurance contract that the insured promises to fulfil or to keep true throughout the policy. Unlike a condition, a warranty is a strict undertaking: if the insured breaches a warranty — even innocently, and even where the breach has no connection to the subsequent loss — the insurer is automatically discharged from liability from the moment of breach. There is no requirement for the insurer to show prejudice. Two types of warranty are recognised: Promissory warranties: A promise as to future conduct. 'The insured warrants that a burglar alarm will be maintained in operational condition.' Breach of this warranty at any point during the policy period discharges the insurer's liability from that moment. Affirmative warranties: An assurance that a stated fact is true at the time of the contract. 'The insured warrants that the vessel is seaworthy at the date of commencement.' If the vessel is not seaworthy at inception, the warranty is breached and the insurer is discharged. The severity of the warranty regime — automatic discharge without proof of prejudice or causal connection — has long been criticised as commercially harsh. The UK Insurance Act 2015 substantially reformed the English position, replacing the automatic discharge rule with a more nuanced framework. NIIRA 2025 signals a similar evolution in Nigerian law, though the extent of the warranty reform under NIIRA 2025 remains subject to interpretive development as cases arise under the new Act. 2.8.2 Conditions A condition is a term of the policy that, if breached, gives the insurer the right to avoid a specific claim or, in the case of a fundamental condition, the entire contract. Conditions are less severe than warranties in their effect on a single breach, but they are equally important in the daily management of insurance contracts. Two categories are essential to distinguish: Conditions precedent: Terms that must be fulfilled before the insurer's liability arises or before a claim can be made. Examples include the requirement to notify a loss within a specified time, to provide documentary evidence of loss within a stated period, or to obtain the insurer's consent before incurring expenses. Failure to comply with a condition precedent suspends or forfeits the right to claim. Conditions subsequent: Terms whose breach does not affect the formation of the contract or the right to claim, but may give the insurer grounds to terminate the policy prospectively. An obligation to maintain fire extinguishers in working order, for example, is typically a condition subsequent rather than a warranty. Case Note — Tab Assurance Co Ltd v Akwuzie Industries Nigeria Limited The court held that the insured was not entitled to be paid on a claim where the elements of utmost good faith — including compliance with policy conditions — had been breached. The case illustrates the Nigerian courts' willingness to enforce condition precedent clauses strictly, particularly where the breach undermines the insurer's ability to investigate the loss or manage the claim.[6] Practical implication: Claims management staff must be trained to identify breaches of condition precedent at the notification stage and to document their investigation consistently. Applying a condition precedent defence without legal advice, however, creates the risk of a bad faith complaint under NIIRA 2025's enhanced consumer protection provisions. 2.8.3 Distinguishing Warranties from Conditions: Practical Consequences Feature Warranty Condition Precedent Basis of obligation Absolute and strict Must be reasonably observed Effect of breach Automatic discharge of insurer from time of breach Insurer may decline the specific claim or entire contract depending on materiality Causal link required? No — breach discharges irrespective of connection to loss Generally no, but courts increasingly require materiality Insurer must prove prejudice? No Increasingly required under NIIRA 2025's consumer protection framework Example in life insurance 'The insured warrants that annual premiums will be paid on the due date.' 'Notice of claim must be given in writing within 30 days of death.'

t: Chapter 2 · 2.9  NIIRA 2025: Consumer Protection and the Reform of Fundamental Principles
x: Regulatory Spotlight — NIIRA 2025 — Summary of Reforms to Insurance Contract Principles NIIRA 2025 represents the most significant legislative reform of insurance contract principles in Nigeria since the colonial era. The following reforms are directly relevant to the doctrines covered in this chapter: Duty of utmost good faith — reformed: The all-or-nothing avoidance remedy is qualified. NIIRA 2025 introduces the concept of fair presentation and limits the insurer's right to avoid solely on grounds of breach of utmost good faith where the breach is innocent and unconnected to the loss. Proportionate remedies apply. Claims settlement timelines — mandatory: Section 210 of NIIRA 2025 requires all claims to be settled in writing within 60 days of notification or such period as specified in NAICOM regulations. Failure to comply attracts fines and licence sanctions — a powerful enforcement tool against the 'claim delay, deny, defend' practices that have historically characterised the market. Consumer Protection Fund (Section 212): The Act establishes an Insurance Policyholders' Protection Fund to compensate policyholders if an insurer becomes insolvent. This is a structural safeguard that addresses one of the sector's most damaging trust failures — policyholders left uncompensated when small, under-capitalised insurers failed. Proportionate remedies for misrepresentation: Aligning with the UK Insurance Act 2015 model, NIIRA 2025 allows courts to award proportionate relief where a misrepresentation was careless rather than deliberate, rather than requiring the stark choice between full avoidance and no remedy at all. Enhanced disclosure obligations on insurers: The Act imposes clearer obligations on insurers and brokers to ask relevant questions, thereby sharing the disclosure burden with policyholders who may be unaware of what is material. Transition note: Policies incepted before NIIRA 2025 are governed by the old regime. The pre-2025 cases — Leadway v Zeco, NICON v Power & Industrial — remain binding for those policies. Practitioners must maintain dual fluency in the old and new frameworks for the duration of the run-off of legacy portfolios.[17]

This chapter has examined the six fundamental principles that govern insurance contracts in Nigeria and across the common law world. Utmost good faith (uberrimae fidei) imposes on both parties a duty of full and honest disclosure of material facts, a duty not to misrepresent, and a duty not to actively conceal. Under the pre-NIIRA 2025 common law regime, breach of this duty entitled the insurer to void the contract ab initio regardless of the nature of the breach. NIIRA 2025 introduces proportionate remedies and a duty of fair presentation, significantly improving consumer protection. Insurable interest is the legally recognised financial relationship between the insured and the subject matter of the insurance. In life assurance, every person has unlimited insurable interest in their own life; third-party life insurance requires a legally cognisable interest, established at inception. Indemnity requires the insurer to restore the insured to the pre-loss financial position, no more and no less. It is the foundational principle of non-life insurance but does not apply in its strict form to life assurance, where a pre-agreed fixed sum is payable regardless of the precise financial loss. Subrogation is the right of the insurer, having indemnified the insured, to exercise the insured's rights against the responsible third party. It is limited to the amount paid as indemnity and does not apply to life assurance or fixed-benefit policies. Contribution arises in double insurance and ensures that co-insurers share the loss equitably, preventing the insured from profiting by receiving more than full indemnity in aggregate. Proximate cause requires that for an insurer to be liable, the covered peril must be the efficient, dominant, and operative cause of the loss — not merely a remote or sequential cause. The principle operates to resolve complex causation chains, concurrent causes, and scenarios involving covered and excluded perils. Warranties and conditions are policy terms whose breach has significant legal consequences. Warranties operate strictly: breach automatically discharges the insurer regardless of causal connection to the loss. Conditions precedent require fulfilment before a claim can be made. NIIRA 2025 is developing a more nuanced approach that balances strict enforcement with consumer fairness.

Uberrimae Fidei Of the utmost good faith. The maxim governing insurance contracts, requiring both parties to act with the highest standard of honesty and to disclose all material facts. Material Fact Any fact that would influence the judgment of a prudent underwriter in deciding whether to accept a risk or in fixing the premium and conditions. Non-disclosure of a material fact entitles the insurer to avoid the contract. Prudent Underwriter Test The objective test of materiality: would a hypothetical prudent underwriter in the same market consider the fact material to the risk? The test is objective, not assessed by reference to this particular underwriter's decision. Misrepresentation A false statement of fact made by the insured before or at the time of contracting, upon which the insurer relies in accepting the risk. Insurable Interest A legally recognised financial relationship between the insured and the subject matter of insurance, such that the insured would suffer a quantifiable loss if the insured event occurred. Indemnity The obligation to restore the insured to the pre-loss financial position. The amount recoverable is the lesser of the actual financial loss and the sum insured. Subrogation The right of an insurer, after paying an indemnity, to exercise the insured's rights against the third party responsible for the loss. Contribution The right of one co-insurer, after paying more than its fair share of a doubly-insured loss, to recover the excess from the other co-insurer(s). Double Insurance The situation where the same insured has insured the same interest against the same risk with two or more insurers. Proximate Cause The dominant, efficient, and operative cause of an insured loss — the cause without which the loss would not have occurred. Warranty A strict term of the insurance contract whose breach automatically discharges the insurer from liability from the date of breach, irrespective of any causal link to the loss. Condition Precedent A policy term that must be fulfilled before the insurer's liability to pay a claim arises. Failure to comply may forfeit the right to claim. Avoidance Ab Initio The insurer's remedy for breach of utmost good faith: treating the contract as void from the beginning, as if it had never existed. Modified under NIIRA 2025. Fair Presentation The reformed obligation under NIIRA 2025 requiring the insured to make a fair, clear, and accessible disclosure of all material information known to it — replacing the harsher common law duty of strict disclosure.

The principle of utmost good faith requires the proposer to: Disclose only the facts specifically asked about in the proposal form. Disclose all facts material to the risk whether asked for or not. Disclose only facts that are in the public domain. Disclose only facts that have caused a loss in the previous five years. (B) Disclose all facts material to the risk whether asked for or not. Why (B) is Correct The duty of utmost good faith (uberrimae fidei), established in Carter v Boehm (1766) and confirmed repeatedly in Nigerian courts (Leadway Assurance v Zeco [2004]), requires the proposer to volunteer all information a prudent insurer would consider material in assessing the risk — even if the proposal form does not specifically ask for it. The duty is proactive and extends beyond answering the questions posed. Why the Others Are Wrong (A) is the ‘specific questions only’ position — it fundamentally underestimates the scope of the disclosure duty. An insured who answers all specific questions truthfully but omits a material fact not asked about has still breached utmost good faith.(C) is incorrect — the test for materiality is what a prudent insurer would consider important, not whether the information is publicly available. Many material facts (a medical diagnosis, a criminal conviction) are not public.(D) is incorrect — there is no five-year historical loss limitation on the disclosure obligation. A health condition from twelve years ago may still be highly material to a life insurance application.

Insurable interest in a life assurance policy taken on one’s own life: Is limited to the financial loss that would arise from the insured’s death. Must be re-proved at the time of each claim. Is unlimited in amount and need only exist at the time of contracting. Requires a third party to confirm the financial relationship. (C) Is unlimited in amount and need only exist at the time of contracting. Why (C) is Correct A person has an unlimited insurable interest in their own life. The law presumes this without any requirement to quantify it. Insurable interest in a life policy need only exist at the time of contracting — not at the date of claim (unlike most indemnity policies). Once the policy is validly formed, its continuity does not depend on re-establishing interest. Why the Others Are Wrong (A) applies the creditor-debtor rule: a creditor’s interest in a debtor’s life is limited to the outstanding debt. This rule does not apply to a person’s own life, where interest is unlimited.(B) is false — re-proving insurable interest at the date of claim is a rule for indemnity insurance (property insurance), where the insured must demonstrate they still own the insured property at the date of loss. Life assurance does not require this.(D) has no basis in law. No third-party confirmation is required for a person’s interest in their own life.

The principle of indemnity is MOST accurately described as: The right of the insured to be paid the full sum insured regardless of actual loss. The obligation to restore the insured to the same financial position as before the loss, no more and no less. A requirement that the insurer must always accept all claims presented. A guarantee that the insured will profit from an insurance policy. (B) The obligation to restore the insured to the same financial position as before the loss, no more and no less. Why (B) is Correct Indemnity means making the insured whole — precisely compensating the actual financial loss suffered, no more and no less. The insured must not be better off after a loss than before it (which would create moral hazard — an incentive to generate insured events). The insured must not be worse off either (which would defeat the purpose of insurance). The principle is stated in Castellain v Preston (1883): ‘The contract of insurance... is a contract of indemnity, and... the indemnity means that [the insured] shall be fully indemnified, but shall never be more than fully indemnified.’ Why the Others Are Wrong (A) contradicts indemnity — the sum insured is the maximum payable but not the guaranteed amount. Payment is limited to actual loss, which may be below the sum insured.(C) is incorrect — the insurer has the right to apply exclusions, conditions, and policy defences. Indemnity governs the measure of payment, not the right to refuse.(D) is the opposite of indemnity. The principle expressly prohibits profit from insurance. An insured who profits from an insura

Which ONE of the following is a CORRECT statement about subrogation? Subrogation applies to life assurance policies. The insurer may subrogate before paying the claim. The insurer can recover from the third party only up to the amount it has paid as indemnity. Subrogation gives the insurer the right to take over the insured’s entire business. (C) The insurer can recover from the third party only up to the amount it has paid as indemnity. Why (C) is Correct Subrogation prevents unjust enrichment of both the insurer and the insured. The insurer steps into the insured’s shoes to pursue the party responsible for the loss, but its recovery is capped at the amount it paid in indemnity. If the insurer paid ₦8 million in settlement of a ₦10 million claim, it can recover at most ₦8 million from the tortfeasor. Any recovery above the amount paid goes to the insured to cover any shortfall (Yorkshire Insurance v Nisbet Shipping [1962]). Why the Others Are Wrong (A) is false — subrogation is a corollary of indemnity. Because life assurance is a contract of financial provision (not indemnity), subrogation does not arise. A life insurer that pays a death benefit cannot sue the party responsible for the death to recover the sum paid.(B) reverses the correct sequence — subrogation can only arise after the insurer has fulfilled its obligation by paying the claim. It is not available as a pre-payment remedy.(D) exaggerates the right entirely. Subrogation is a specific right to recover the particular loss for which indemnity was paid, not a general transfer of the insured’s commercial interest

A warranty in an insurance contract: Can be breached without any consequence if the breach is minor. Automatically discharges the insurer from liability on breach, regardless of any causal link to the loss. Is a term that the insurer must satisfy before the policyholder can make a claim. Is equivalent to a condition subsequent in its legal effect. (B) Automatically discharges the insurer from liability on breach, regardless of any causal link to the loss. Why (B) is Correct A warranty is a fundamental term of the insurance contract at common law. Any breach, however minor and however unrelated to the eventual loss, discharges the insurer from further liability from the date of breach. This is the strict common law position confirmed in Bank of Nova Scotia v Hellenic Mutual [1992] and applied in Nigerian courts. An insured who warrants their vessel will not sail beyond certain waters, and then briefly exceeds those limits before returning — and later suffers a fire at port — may find the insurer discharged by the warranty breach, even though the breach had no connection to the fire. Why the Others Are Wrong (A) is false — there is no de minimis exception to warranty breach at common law. Even a trivial breach technically discharges the insurer.(C) inverts the position. Warranties are obligations of the insured, not of the insurer. The insured warrants the truth of certain statements or undertakes to do (or not do) certain things.(D) is incorrect. Nnamdi applies for a life insurance policy. On the proposal form he answers 'No' to a question asking whether he has been diagnosed with any serious illness in the last five years. In fact, Nnamdi had been treated for hypertension eighteen months earlier but had forgotten about it. Nnamdi dies two years after the policy is incepted. The insurer discovers the undisclosed hypertension treatment and seeks to void the policy.

(b) Explain how NIIRA 2025 modifies the analysis, and what remedy would be proportionate in these circumstances.   Part (a) — Common Law Position To void the policy for non-disclosure, the insurer must establish three elements: (i) materiality — would a prudent insurer consider the fact material in assessing the risk? (ii) non-disclosure or misrepresentation — did the insured fail to disclose the material fact? (iii) inducement — was the insurer induced to enter the contract by the non-disclosure?(i) Materiality: Treated hypertension is unquestionably material. A life insurer assessing a standard life application would significantly elevate the risk assessment if it knew the applicant was being treated for cardiovascular hypertension. Explain the doctrine of proximate cause with reference to the decision in Leyland Shipping Co Ltd v Norwich Union [1918]. Apply the doctrine to the following scenario: an insured warehouse is damaged by flood, and during the flooding, thieves enter and steal goods. The fire and special perils policy covers flood but excludes theft. The insured claims for both flood damage and theft. Advise the insurer.   The Doctrine of Proximate Cause The proximate cause doctrine holds that the insured event must be the proximate — dominant, effective, and real — cause of the loss, not merely the first event in a chain or the most recent event before the loss. Identifying the proximate cause cuts through the factual sequence to identify the root cause that set the chain in motion. Leyland Shipping Co Ltd v Norwich Union [1918] AC 350: The Leyland vessel was torpedoed in World War I (a wartime exclusion). It was towed to a harbour of refuge at Le Havre, where it was grounded at a safe berth. Tidal action over several days caused it to sink. The insurer argued the proximate cause was the grounding at Le Havre (not an excluded event). The House of Lords held that the torpedo was the proximate cause throughout — it set the irreversible chain in motion. The tidal sinking was a manifestation of the torpedo’s original injury, not an independent new cause. Application to the Warehouse Scenario Flood causes structural damage to the warehouse — covered. During the flooding, thieves enter and steal goods — excluded.The proximate cause analysis must determine whether the theft has the flood as its pro

Distinguish between a warranty and a condition precedent in an insurance contract. Explain the legal consequences of breach of each, and discuss whether NIIRA 2025 modifies the traditional strict approach to breach of warranty in Nigerian insurance law.   Warranties: Definition and Consequences of Breach A warranty is a fundamental term of the insurance contract, breach of which automatically discharges the insurer from all further liability, regardless of any causal connection between the breach and the loss. The insured may have warranted: the truth of a statement at inception (affirmative warranty); or a course of future conduct (promissory warranty). At common law, even a minor technical breach, entirely unrelated to the eventual loss, discharges the insurer. The insurer need not prove the breach contributed to the claim. Conditions Precedent: Definition and Consequences of Breach A condition precedent is a condition that must be fulfilled before a specific contractual right arises. In insurance, conditions precedent to the right to claim require the insured to take specific steps (e.g., notify the insurer within a defined period; provide documents; co-operate with investigations) before the claim becomes enforceable. Breach prevents the specific right from arising but does not, of itself, discharge the insurer from all future liability under the policy.Key distinction: A warranty breach affects the entire contract from the date of breach. A condition precedent breach affects the specific claim to which the condition attaches — the policy continues for future claims. NI

Critically evaluate the doctrine of utmost good faith as applied in Nigerian insurance law prior to NIIRA 2025, with particular reference to the decisions in Leadway Assurance Co Ltd v Zeco Nigeria Ltd (2004) and NICON v Power & Industrial Engineering Co Ltd (1986). Assess the extent to which NIIRA 2025 achieves a fair balance between insurer security and policyholder protection.   Essay Framework Thesis The pre-NIIRA 2025 doctrine of utmost good faith in Nigerian insurance law was robust in its theoretical foundation but disproportionate and commercially damaging in its primary remedy: automatic avoidance for any material non-disclosure, regardless of the insured’s good faith, the severity of the breach, or its connection to the claimed loss. NIIRA 2025 represents a genuine improvement through proportionality, but falls short of the standard set by the UK Insurance Act 2015.
