Discuss this proposition, explaining how each principle reinforces the other, and evaluate the practical challenges of enforcing subrogation rights in the Nigerian insurance market.   Essay Framework Thesis Indemnity and subrogation are not merely related but are logically interdependent. Subrogation is the mechanism that gives effect to indemnity where a third party is responsible for the loss. Without indemnity, subrogation has no purpose; without subrogation in applicable cases, indemnity would be routinely breached by double recovery. The Conceptual Link Indemnity prohibits profit from insurance: the insured must not receive more than their actual financial loss. Where a third party caused the loss, the insured could potentially recover twice: once from the insurer (under the policy) and once from the tortfeasor (in the courts). Double recovery constitutes profit from misfortune, which violates indemnity.Subrogation prevents this: once the insurer has paid the claim, it acquires the insured’s rights against the responsible third party. The insured is fully restored (indemnity satisfied). The insurer recovers from the party who caused the loss (the economic burden of the loss falls on its originator). The insured cannot pursue the tortfeasor independently — their interest has been extinguished by the insurance payment.Castellain v Preston (1883): ‘The contract of insurance... is a contract of indemnity... The assured shall not recover more than a full indemnity. If... the same part

Learning Objectives On completing this chapter, the reader should be able to: Identify and apply the essential elements of a valid contract of insurance: offer, acceptance, consideration, legal capacity, and legality. Explain the legal status of the proposal form and describe how the offer-acceptance sequence operates in insurance contracts. Define a cover note and describe its legal nature, duration, and the circumstances in which it creates binding temporary insurance. Describe the structure and main components of an insurance policy document and explain the legal rules for policy interpretation. Apply the contra proferentem rule to ambiguous insurance policy terms and explain its rationale in the insurance context. Distinguish between conditions precedent and conditions subsequent and explain the legal consequences of breach of each. Explain the function of endorsements and riders and describe the procedure for altering an insurance contract. Describe the legal requirements for assignment and nomination of life assurance policies under Nigerian law and NIIRA 2025. Distinguish between void, voidable, and unenforceable insurance contracts and give examples of each in the Nigerian context. Summarise NIIRA 2025's provisions on consumer rights, claims settlement timelines, the Policyholders' Protection Fund, and NAICOM's complaints redress framework.

t: Chapter 3 · 3.1  Introduction: The Insurance Contract as a Legal Instrument
x: An insurance policy is, at its foundation, a contract. This may seem self-evident, but its implications are profound and pervasive. Because insurance is a contract, all of the general principles of Nigerian contract law apply to its formation, interpretation, performance, and enforcement. And yet, because it is an insurance contract, it is subject to additional rules, doctrines, and statutory requirements that have no parallel in the ordinary law of commerce. It is this layered nature — general contract law as foundation, insurance-specific rules as superstructure — that gives insurance contract law its distinctive and sometimes surprising character. This chapter examines the life of an insurance contract from its formation to its termination. It proceeds through the stages that a practitioner encounters in practice: the proposal, the cover note, the policy document, the mid-term alteration, the assignment, and — when things go wrong — the questions of voidness, voidability, and unenforceability. It then turns to the consumer protection regime introduced by NIIRA 2025 and to the NAICOM complaints redress framework that gives that regime its enforcement teeth. The chapter is structured to be read as a complete treatment of insurance contract law for the CIIN candidate, but it is equally relevant to the practitioner — the claims handler who must assess whether a notification condition has been satisfied, the underwriter who must decide whether a counter-proposal has been accepted, the compliance officer who must ensure that policy wordings meet NAICOM's disclosure requirements, and the broker who must advise a client on the effect of assigning a life policy as security for a mortgage.

t: Chapter 3 · 3.2  Formation of a Valid Contract of Insurance
x: 3.2.1 The Essential Elements For any contract to be valid and enforceable under Nigerian law — and insurance contracts are no exception — five elements must be present: Offer: A clear and definite proposal by one party to enter into a contract on specific terms, made with the intention that it will be binding on acceptance. Acceptance: An unconditional agreement by the offeree to all the terms of the offer. A conditional or qualified acceptance is not an acceptance but a counter-offer which, in turn, requires acceptance by the original offeror. Consideration: Something of value given by each party in exchange for the other's promise. In insurance, the insured's consideration is the premium; the insurer's consideration is the assumption of the risk and the promise to pay on the occurrence of the specified event. Legal capacity: Both parties must have the legal capacity to contract. For the insured, this means being of full age (18 years), of sound mind, and not under any legal disability. For the insurer, this means being duly licensed under NIIRA 2025. Legal purpose: The contract must not be for an illegal or immoral purpose. An insurance contract taken out to cover the financial consequences of the insured's own criminal act — arson, fraud, murder — is void as contrary to public policy. Two additional elements are sometimes listed: intention to create legal relations (present in all commercial contracts as a matter of presumption) and certainty of terms (the contract must be sufficiently definite to be enforceable). Both are relevant to insurance but rarely generate difficulty in practice because insurance policies are prepared by commercial institutions with legal expertise. Contract of Insurance A legally binding agreement, constituted by offer, acceptance, consideration, legal capacity, and a legal purpose, whereby the insurer undertakes to pay a sum of money or provide a benefit to the insured or a named beneficiary upon the occurrence of a specified uncertain event, in exchange for the payment of a premium. An insurance contract is characterised by the element of risk transfer and is subject, in addition to the general law of contract, to the doctrine of utmost good faith and the specific requirements of NIIRA 2025. See also: Chapter 2 (Fundamental Principles); NIIRA 2025 (Act No. 2, 2025). 3.2.2 Who Makes the Offer? The Proposal Form Analysis In insurance, there is an important and sometimes misunderstood question: who makes the offer? In most commercial contracts, it is clear — the seller offers goods at a price, and the buyer accepts. In insurance, the sequence depends on how the transaction is initiated. The dominant view in Nigerian and English insurance law is that the proposer (the person seeking insurance) makes the offer by completing and submitting the proposal form to the insurer. The insurer then has the option to accept the offer (by issuing a policy or cover note), to reject it (by written notification), or to counter-offer (by offering to insure on different terms — perhaps at a higher premium, with an exclusion, or with a loading). The proposer must then accept the counter-offer for a contract to be formed. However, the position is not always so straightforward. Where the insurer first issues a quotation or a standard rate card and the proposer accepts it by returning the proposal form and paying the premium, the insurer may be the offeror and the proposer the acceptor. The correct analysis depends on the commercial context and the specific sequence of communications. Case Note — Rust v Abbey Life Assurance Co Ltd [1979] 2 Lloyd's Rep 334 (CA) Rust completed a proposal form for a property bond insurance policy and returned it to the insurer, who issued a policy document. Rust later sought to reject the policy and recover her premium, arguing she had never formally accepted the insurer's offer. The Court of Appeal held that by completing and returning the proposal form, Rust had herself made the offer which the insurer accepted by issuing the policy. There was a binding contract from the moment of acceptance by the insurer.[1] Practical lesson: The proposal form is the pivotal document in the formation of an insurance contract. Once returned by the proposer, it constitutes either an offer or an acceptance depending on the sequence. The insurer's act of issuing a policy, cover note, or written acceptance closes the contract. Practitioners should ensure that no cover is treated as incepted unless a formal acceptance has been communicated. 3.2.3 Acceptance: Conditional and Unconditional The law requires that acceptance be unconditional and mirror the offer in all material respects. In life assurance practice, this principle generates a specific and frequently tested scenario: the conditional acceptance pending medical examination. Case Note — Canning v Farquhar (1886) 16 QBD 727 (CA) A proposer applied for life assurance. The insurer accepted his application by letter but expressly stated that cover would not attach until the first premium was paid and that it was 'a condition of this offer that you are in good health.' After sending the acceptance letter but before the proposer paid the first premium, he fell off a cliff and was seriously injured. When he subsequently paid the premium and claimed cover, the insurer refused. The Court of Appeal upheld the insurer: the acceptance was conditional on the proposer's good health at the time of premium payment, and as he was not in good health, no contract had been formed.[2] Practical lesson: In life assurance, acceptance is commonly conditional on the proposer remaining in good health between the date of submission and the date of policy inception. Underwriters and agents must be explicit about the conditions attached to any acceptance, particularly where there is a gap between submission and the first premium payment. Digital onboarding processes that combine submission and payment in a single session reduce this risk. 3.2.4 Consideration: The Premium and the Assumption of Risk The consideration moving from the insured is the premium — the monetary sum paid in exchange for the insurer's assumption of the specified risk. The consideration moving from the insurer is not merely the promise to pay on the occurrence of the specified event but the assumption of the risk itself — the insured's peace of mind and security during the policy period. This analysis has practical importance: it explains why a policyholder who suffers no loss during a policy term has still received value (the insurer's risk assumption) and is not entitled to a refund of premium on the ground of 'no claims.' Premium payment under Nigerian insurance law and NIIRA 2025 is governed by the 'no premium, no cover' rule, which provides that no insurance risk shall attach and no cover shall be effective unless and until the premium has been paid and received by the insurer or its authorised agent. This rule, introduced in the original Insurance Act 2003 and strengthened in NIIRA 2025, was a response to the widespread practice of credit insurance — where policies were issued against the promise of future premium payment — which contributed significantly to premium debts, insurer insolvency, and claims disputes. Regulatory Spotlight — NIIRA 2025 — The 'No Premium, No Cover' Rule NIIRA 2025 preserves and reinforces the 'no premium, no cover' principle as a cardinal rule of Nigerian insurance practice. The Act provides that an insurer shall not accept a risk without the prior payment of the premium except in the case of renewals and such other cases as the Commission may by regulation permit. The consequence of this rule is that: A policy issued in advance of premium receipt is unenforceable in respect of any loss occurring before the premium is paid. An agent who purports to grant cover without premium authority binds neither the insurer (without actual or ostensible authority) nor the insured (who has not paid). Brokers who receive premiums from clients are required to remit them to the insurer within prescribed timelines; failure to do so creates personal liability for the broker and potentially leaves the client uninsured. NIIRA 2025 provides that an insurance agent shall not collect premium for an insurer: premium is paid directly to the insurer (s.38(2)). An agent who fails to pay over premium collected is liable to a penalty of up to 5% of the premium plus ₦100,000 for each day of default, and may not be engaged as an agent or employee by any insurance operator for 12 months (s.38(3)). Brokers may collect premium, which is deemed paid to the insurer (s.60(2)), and must pay it over within 20 working days or 30 calendar days (s.61); the penalty is ₦500,000 or twice the commission earned, whichever is higher, plus interest. Issuing a receipt for every premium received is good practice. [8]

t: Chapter 3 · 3.3  The Proposal Form: Legal Status and Practical Role
x: 3.3.1 Nature and Function The proposal form is a standardised questionnaire prepared by the insurer and presented to the prospective insured to complete. It serves simultaneously as the vehicle for the insured's offer (or acceptance), as the primary instrument through which the insurer gathers material facts for underwriting, and as a legal document whose contents may determine the validity of the policy. Its importance in insurance practice cannot be overstated. The form typically requests information in the following categories: Personal particulars: Full name, date of birth, occupation, residential address, contact details. Risk particulars: The nature of the risk to be insured — for life assurance, this includes the sum assured requested, the policy type, beneficiary details, and payment frequency. Health and medical history: For life and health insurance, a detailed medical questionnaire covering existing conditions, past illnesses and treatment, hospitalisations, family medical history, and lifestyle factors. Existing insurance: Details of all current insurance policies and any previous declinatures, special terms, or cancellations imposed by other insurers. Declaration: A signed declaration by the proposer that the information provided is true and complete, and an agreement that the proposal shall form the basis of any contract entered into. 3.3.2 The 'Basis of Contract' Clause and Its Consequences A feature common to many Nigerian insurance proposal forms — and one with significant legal consequences — is the 'basis of contract' clause. This clause, inserted in the declaration at the foot of the proposal form, provides that the information given in the proposal form shall be the basis of the contract between the insurer and the insured. The legal effect of such a clause is dramatic: it converts every answer on the proposal form into a promissory warranty, such that any inaccuracy — however innocent, however immaterial — entitles the insurer to avoid the policy entirely. Case Note — Condogianis v Guardian Assurance Co [1921] 2 AC 125 (Privy Council) The proposer stated in a fire insurance proposal that he had not been the subject of insurance losses within the preceding five years. In fact, he had made one small claim two years earlier. The Privy Council held that the 'basis of contract' clause in the proposal form converted this statement into a warranty; as the statement was inaccurate, the insurer was entitled to avoid the policy, even though the loss claimed bore no relationship to the undisclosed previous claim.[15] Practical lesson: The 'basis of contract' clause remains a feature of many Nigerian insurance proposal forms. Its effect is harsh and is frequently unknown to proposers. NIIRA 2025's movement towards a fair presentation framework limits, but does not entirely eliminate, the clause's impact for post-2025 contracts. Practitioners should advise proposers to answer all questions with meticulous accuracy, and should advise insurers reviewing pre-2025 portfolio wordings to consider whether the clause produces outcomes consistent with NIIRA 2025's consumer protection objectives. 3.3.3 The Agent-Completion Problem A recurring problem in the Nigerian market — particularly where literacy rates are lower or where the distribution model relies on agents completing forms on behalf of clients — is the legal consequence when the agent inserts incorrect information without the proposer's knowledge or consent. The general legal rule, applied in Nigerian courts, is that an agent who assists a proposer in completing a proposal form is in that capacity the agent of the proposer, not the insurer. The insurer is therefore not bound by incorrect answers inserted by its own agent where the proposer failed to read, question, or correct the form before signing. However, if the agent inserted incorrect information based on fraudulent instructions from his principal (the insurer), or if the insurer had represented to the proposer that the agent had authority to fill in the form on its behalf, the analysis may differ. Advisory — Agent-Completion Best Practices The agent-completion problem is among the most damaging and litigated sources of claims dispute in the Nigerian market. Insurers and brokers should implement the following controls: Require all completed proposal forms to be reviewed aloud with the proposer before signing, with each question confirmed verbally. Where an agent completes the form on behalf of an illiterate or semi-literate proposer, use an independent witness (not connected to the insurer or agent) to confirm that the contents were explained and agreed. Implement digital proposal forms with the proposer's own submission (via mobile app or USSD) that do not pass through agent intermediaries. Train agents on the legal consequence of 'basis of contract' clauses and the duty of utmost good faith — this is a required component of the CIIN Certificate of Proficiency curriculum. Maintain a clean audit trail: date-stamp, IP-address-log, or biometric authentication of all digital proposals.

t: Chapter 3 · 3.4  Cover Notes and Temporary Cover
x: 3.4.1 Nature and Legal Character of a Cover Note A cover note is a temporary document issued by an insurer or its authorised agent to provide evidence of insurance for a defined period, pending the issue of the formal policy document. It is not the policy; it is a temporary contract of insurance in its own right, binding on the insurer for the period and in respect of the risks specified within it. The cover note serves a practical function in the time gap that exists between the submission of a proposal and the insurer's formal underwriting decision. The insured may need immediate evidence of insurance — for example, a vehicle owner seeking a road licence, an employer required to demonstrate Group Life cover, or an importer needing marine cover to release goods from port. The cover note provides that evidence without waiting for the full policy to be prepared, reviewed, and issued. Cover Note A temporary document issued by an insurer or authorised agent providing evidence of insurance for a specified period pending the issue of a formal policy. A cover note is itself a binding contract of insurance for the period and risks stated within it; it is not merely a receipt or acknowledgement. Upon issue of the formal policy, the cover note is superseded, but its validity for the period it covered is not retroactively affected. See: General Accident Fire & Life Assurance Corp Ltd v Midland Bank Ltd [1940] 2 KB 388; NIIRA 2025. 3.4.2 Duration and Termination of a Cover Note The key principle established in General Accident Fire & Life Assurance Corporation Ltd v Midland Bank Ltd [1940] 2 KB 388 is that a cover note creates a temporary and separate contract that operates until the main policy is issued, the proposal is declined, or the stated period expires — whichever occurs first.[3] In practice, NAICOM regulations and NIIRA 2025 impose the following requirements on cover notes in the Nigerian market: A cover note must bear the actual date and time of issue — backdating is prohibited under NIIRA 2025 and under long-standing NAICOM circulars. A cover note must specify the period of cover, the insured, the subject matter, the sum insured or limit of indemnity, and the premium (or premium basis) applicable. Cover notes for motor third party insurance must be issued in compliance with the specific format and period requirements applicable to that compulsory class under NIIRA 2025. A cover note does not automatically import all the terms of the main policy that is subsequently issued; its terms are determined by its own wording. Case Note — Stockton v Mason [1978] 2 Lloyd's Rep 430 (CA) An insured sought to extend his cover by asking his agent to make an endorsement to his motor policy. A cover note was issued for a transitional period. The Court of Appeal held that the cover note constituted a separate and self-contained contract, and that its terms did not necessarily incorporate all the conditions of the main policy. Where there was ambiguity about the terms of the temporary cover, the court construed the cover note strictly and in favour of the insured.[4] Practical lesson: Cover notes should be drafted with precision. Insurers who issue cover notes by reference to an anticipated policy ('cover as per policy to be issued') must ensure that the anticipated policy terms are clearly identified and that the insured is aware of any conditions that attach to the temporary cover. Ambiguities in cover notes are resolved against the insurer under the contra proferentem doctrine.

t: Chapter 3 · 3.5  The Policy Document: Structure and Legal Effect
x: 3.5.1 The Policy as Evidence of the Contract A common misconception — sometimes held even by practitioners — is that the insurance policy is the contract. It is not. The contract of insurance is formed at the point of offer and acceptance, which may occur before the policy document is prepared or issued. The policy document is the written evidence of the contract — its formal embodiment — rather than the contract itself. This distinction matters in practice: if a loss occurs after the contract is formed but before the policy is issued, the insured can still claim, because the contract exists independently of the document that records it. The policy document serves several essential functions. It is the primary reference document for determining the scope of cover, the exclusions, the conditions, and the procedures for making a claim. It is admissible in evidence before a court or before NAICOM in any dispute between insurer and insured. And it is the document that regulators — in the form of NAICOM under NIIRA 2025 — require to be filed, approved, and maintained in a form accessible to policyholders. 3.5.2 Standard Sections of a Life Assurance Policy While policy wordings differ between insurers and product types, a standard Nigerian life assurance policy typically comprises the following components: Section Content Legal Significance Schedule Identifies the policy: policyholder's name, policy number, date of inception, sum assured, premium amount and frequency, policy term, beneficiary details. The schedule is the personalised component; ambiguities between the schedule and the general conditions are usually resolved in favour of the schedule wording. Recitals States the basis on which the policy was issued, typically incorporating the proposal form by reference. May include the 'basis of contract' declaration. Incorporation of the proposal by reference makes the proposal's contents part of the policy. Inaccuracies in the proposal become policy breaches. Operative (Insuring) Clause The core promise: 'The Company hereby agrees to pay the Sum Assured upon the death of the Life Assured' or 'upon the first occurrence of…' The insuring clause defines the trigger event and the benefit. Courts interpret insuring clauses broadly in favour of the insured; exclusions are interpreted narrowly. Exclusions Events or circumstances for which the insurer will not pay: suicide within the contestability period, death from pre-existing conditions not disclosed, death from war or terrorism. Exclusion clauses are interpreted strictly and construed against the insurer. NAICOM must approve standard exclusions in filed products. Conditions Obligations of the insured (premium payment, claims notification, policy maintenance) and the insurer (claims payment timelines, policy review rights). Conditions precedent must be strictly observed; conditions subsequent give rise to prospective termination rights rather than automatic forfeiture. Definitions Defines key terms used throughout the policy: 'Life Assured,' 'Sum Assured,' 'Policy Anniversary,' 'Total and Permanent Disability,' etc. Definitions control meaning throughout the policy. Courts apply defined terms consistently; undefined terms are given their natural and ordinary meaning. General Provisions Miscellaneous provisions: currency of payment, governing law (Nigerian law), jurisdiction (Nigerian courts), policy loans, assignment procedure. Governing law clauses confirm Nigerian law applies and Nigerian courts have jurisdiction — relevant where the insurer has international parents. 3.5.3 Rules of Policy Interpretation Where a dispute arises about the meaning of a policy term, Nigerian courts apply a structured set of interpretive rules, drawn from the general law of contract and the specific jurisprudence of insurance law. Plain and ordinary meaning: The court first gives words their natural and ordinary meaning in the context of the policy as a whole. Technical or legal terms are given their technical or legal meaning; everyday terms are given their everyday meaning. The policy as a whole: A provision in one part of the policy must be read in the context of the policy as a whole. Apparent conflicts between provisions may be resolved by reading them harmoniously. Contra proferentem: Where a term remains genuinely ambiguous after the application of the above rules, the court applies contra proferentem — the ambiguity is resolved against the party that drafted the policy, which is invariably the insurer. The ejusdem generis rule: Where a general term follows a list of specific items, the general term is confined to the same genus or category as the specific items. Commercial purpose: Courts are reluctant to adopt an interpretation that would produce an absurd or commercially impractical result; an interpretation that gives effect to the commercial purpose of the contract is preferred. Contra Proferentem A rule of contractual interpretation providing that, where a term in a contract is ambiguous and cannot be resolved by the application of ordinary interpretive rules, it shall be construed against the party who drafted or introduced it. In insurance, this invariably means construing ambiguous terms in favour of the insured, since the insurer drafts the standard-form policy. The doctrine reflects the inequality of bargaining power between insurer and individual policyholder, and incentivises the insurer to draft clear and unambiguous policy language. Latin: verba chartarum fortius accipiuntur contra proferentem — the words of a document are to be construed most strongly against the party who drew them up. The contra proferentem rule is of particular practical importance in Nigerian insurance litigation because policy wordings have historically been ambiguous, outdated, or prepared by reference to English standard forms that may not accurately reflect Nigerian practice or regulatory requirements. NIIRA 2025's product filing and approval regime — which requires NAICOM to review and approve all new and substantially amended insurance products — is designed, in part, to improve the clarity and fairness of policy wordings across the market. 3.5.4 NAICOM Product Filing Requirements under NIIRA 2025 Regulatory Spotlight — NIIRA 2025 — Policy Wording Approval and Consumer Disclosure NIIRA 2025 strengthens the product filing regime. Key requirements include: All new life insurance products, and any material amendment to existing products, must be filed with and approved by NAICOM before launch. NAICOM reviews the product terms, conditions, exclusions, and premium rates for fairness and compliance with the Act. Policy documents must be provided to policyholders at the time of inception, in plain and accessible language. The use of archaic or unnecessarily technical language in consumer-facing policies is inconsistent with NAICOM's transparency requirements. Insurers must provide a summary of key terms — including the main benefits, exclusions, premium payment obligations, and claims procedure — in a format suitable for a retail policyholder. Digital policies must meet the same content and disclosure standards as paper policies; electronic delivery is permitted but must be capable of being retained and reproduced by the policyholder. NAICOM has the power to direct any insurer to amend policy wordings that are ambiguous, unfair, or inconsistent with NIIRA 2025. An insurer that markets a product without prior NAICOM approval faces administrative sanctions including fines and the suspension of the product.[9]

t: Chapter 3 · 3.6  Conditions Precedent and Conditions Subsequent
x: Chapter 2 introduced the distinction between warranties and conditions in insurance contracts. This section focuses specifically on the two main categories of conditions and their practical operation in Nigerian insurance practice, with particular reference to claims notification requirements — the most frequently litigated category of conditions in the country's courts. 3.6.1 Conditions Precedent to the Contract Certain conditions in a policy are precedent to the existence or validity of the contract itself — they must be satisfied before any binding insurance comes into being. Examples in life assurance include the requirement that the first premium be paid in full, and the requirement that the life assured submit to a medical examination where the sum assured exceeds the non-medical limit. Failure to satisfy these conditions means no contract comes into existence. 3.6.2 Conditions Precedent to Liability The most commercially important category of conditions precedent are those that must be satisfied before the insurer's liability to pay a specific claim arises. Claims notification clauses — which require the insured to notify the insurer of a loss within a specified period after the occurrence — are the archetype. The legal consequence of failing to comply with a notification condition precedent is forfeiture of the right to claim, even if the loss itself is unquestionably covered. Case Note — CIIN Court Judgements Aide Memoirs — Claims Notification Conditions (Nigeria) The CIIN digest of Nigerian insurance decisions records that Nigerian courts have consistently applied the condition precedent rule to claims notification clauses. In one fire insurance case (Suit No. O/304/86), the policy required the insured to give written notice of loss 'forthwith' and to deliver a formal claim within 30 days. The insured delayed notification by several weeks and the formal claim was submitted late. The court upheld the insurer's refusal to pay, confirming that the 30-day clause was a condition precedent to the right to claim, and that the insured's failure to observe it forfeited the claim entirely, regardless of the merits of the underlying loss.[5] Lancashire and Yorkshire Accident Insurance Co's Arbitration (1902) 19 TLR 82 — applied in Nigerian courts: A delay of nearly two months in notification was held fatal to the claim. The principle is applied regardless of the reason for delay, unless the insured can demonstrate that compliance was impossible.[6] Practical lesson: Claims handlers must identify and apply notification conditions precedent at the earliest stage. However, NIIRA 2025's enhanced consumer protection provisions and proportionate remedies approach suggest that a slavish application of notification conditions to deny meritorious claims — without evidence of genuine prejudice to the insurer — will attract increasing scrutiny from NAICOM under its complaints redress jurisdiction. 3.6.3 Conditions Subsequent A condition subsequent is a policy obligation whose breach does not forfeit the right to a specific claim but may, depending on the gravity of the breach, give the insurer the right to terminate the policy going forward. The obligation to cooperate with the insurer's claims investigation, to maintain risk improvements required as a condition of cover, and to report changes in the nature of the risk are typically conditions subsequent. The distinction between a condition precedent and a condition subsequent is not always clearly labelled in Nigerian policy wordings. Where a condition is expressed in general terms ('The insured shall take all reasonable precautions to prevent loss'), it is more likely to be a condition subsequent than a condition precedent; where it is expressed as a prerequisite to a specific right ('The insured shall notify the insurer within 30 days; failure to do so shall relieve the insurer of liability'), it is more clearly a condition precedent. Advisory — Drafting Clear Conditions in Life Policy Documents Many disputes about conditions precedent versus subsequent arise because policy wordings are ambiguous. Nigerian practitioners involved in policy drafting or review should: Expressly label conditions as 'conditions precedent to the right to claim' where that is the intended legal effect. State clearly the period for compliance and the consequence of non-compliance in the same clause. Avoid general 'housekeeping' conditions that list multiple obligations without distinguishing their legal character. Review all policy conditions against NIIRA 2025's consumer protection requirements before filing with NAICOM for approval — the Act's proportionate remedies framework makes it harder to sustain a condition precedent defence where the breach is trivial and the insurer has suffered no prejudice.

t: Chapter 3 · 3.7  Endorsements, Riders, and Policy Alterations
x: 3.7.1 Endorsements An endorsement is a written amendment to an insurance policy that modifies, adds to, or removes a term from the original policy document. Endorsements may be issued at inception (to record a special condition agreed during underwriting), at mid-term (to reflect a change in the risk or the insured's circumstances), or at renewal (to record changes in cover or premium from the previous period). Endorsements must be signed or authenticated by an authorised officer of the insurer and must be attached to or referenced in the policy to form part of the contract. A verbal agreement to amend a policy is unenforceable in Nigerian law as it lacks the formal written evidence required for insurance contracts. Endorsements operate prospectively — they take effect from the date specified — unless the parties expressly agree to retroactive effect. 3.7.2 Riders A rider is an additional benefit or cover attached to a life assurance policy, expanding its scope beyond the base cover. Common life assurance riders available in the Nigerian market include: Critical illness rider: Provides a lump-sum benefit if the life assured is diagnosed with a specified serious illness (cancer, heart attack, stroke, kidney failure) during the policy term. Total and permanent disability (TPD) rider: Pays the sum assured (or a specified benefit) if the life assured becomes permanently unable to perform their occupation or any occupation. Waiver of premium rider: Waives all future premiums if the life assured becomes disabled, ensuring the policy remains in force without the insured needing to pay. Accidental death benefit (ADB) rider: Doubles (or increases by a multiple) the death benefit if death is caused by an accident. Hospital cash rider: Pays a daily benefit for each day the life assured is hospitalised. Riders are subject to their own terms, conditions, and exclusions, which may differ from those of the base policy. Premium loadings for riders must be approved by NAICOM as part of the product filing process. Advisers recommending riders must assess their suitability for the specific insured's needs and document that assessment. 3.7.3 The Effect of Alterations on Utmost Good Faith A material alteration to the risk — whether the insured changes occupation, engages in a hazardous activity not disclosed at inception, or substantially increases the sum assured — may amount to a new proposal, triggering the duty of utmost good faith afresh. In life assurance, any alteration that increases the risk to the insurer (an increase in sum assured, the addition of a TPD rider, the extension of the policy term) is typically treated as a fresh underwriting decision, requiring updated medical information. Practitioners must be aware that failure to disclose a change in health status when making a mid-term alteration may give the insurer grounds to decline the enhanced benefit.

t: Chapter 3 · 3.8  Assignment and Nomination of Life Policies
x: 3.8.1 Assignment Assignment is the legal transfer of the rights and benefits under a life assurance policy from the current policyholder (the assignor) to a third party (the assignee). Assignment is a common mechanism in two contexts in the Nigerian market: as collateral for a bank loan or mortgage (the policyholder assigns the policy to the bank as security for the debt), and as part of estate and trust planning (the policyholder assigns the policy to a trust for the benefit of named beneficiaries). Assignment of a life policy in Nigeria requires the following: The assignment must be in writing — oral assignments are unenforceable. The assignee must have notice of the assignment given to the insurer, which is typically effected by endorsing the assignment on the policy and notifying the insurer in writing. Once notified, the insurer will record the assignee's interest and will direct all future communications and payments to the assignee. The assignor must have the legal capacity to assign — minors and persons under legal disability cannot validly assign. Assignment cannot take place after a claim has been filed: the insured's right to claim is a chose in action that vests at the date of the insured event; subsequent attempts to assign the claim to a third party are void. An absolute assignment transfers all rights under the policy to the assignee, including the right to receive the benefit, to surrender the policy, and to alter the terms. A conditional assignment (also known as a collateral or mortgage assignment) transfers the policy to the assignee only as security for a specific obligation; once that obligation is discharged, the policy reverts to the assignor. 3.8.2 Nomination Nomination is a simpler mechanism by which the policyholder designates one or more persons (nominees) to receive the policy proceeds on the death of the life assured. Unlike assignment, nomination does not transfer ownership of the policy during the life of the policyholder: the policyholder retains full policy rights, including the right to revoke or change the nomination at any time before death. In Nigerian life assurance practice, nomination is the most common method of directing the death benefit to intended beneficiaries. The nominee receives the proceeds as the policyholder's representative, but this does not necessarily mean that the nominee is the beneficial owner — the proceeds may form part of the deceased's estate and be subject to the claims of creditors and other beneficiaries under a will or the laws of intestacy. t: Chapter 3 · 3.9  Void, Voidable, and Unenforceable Insurance Contracts
x: 3.9.1 Void Contracts A void insurance contract is one that has no legal existence at all — it is treated as never having been made. It cannot be enforced by either party, and any premiums paid under it may be recoverable on the basis of total failure of consideration, provided the proposer was not aware of the vitiating factor at the time of contracting. Void contracts in insurance arise principally in the following circumstances: Absence of insurable interest: A policy written without any legally recognised insurable interest is void ab initio, not merely voidable. The absence of insurable interest is not a defect the parties can waive. Wagering or gaming contracts: A policy taken out as a bet on the life of a stranger — with no insurable interest — is void as a wager under the general law. It is also illegal under Nigerian insurance law. Illegality of subject matter: A policy on property that is the subject of criminal activity, or a policy that is itself entered into for fraudulent purposes, is void as contrary to public policy. Fundamental mistake: A contract based on a fundamental common mistake of fact — for example, where both parties are unaware that the life assured has already died at the moment the policy is purportedly taken out — is void for impossibility. 3.9.2 Voidable Contracts A voidable insurance contract is one that is valid and subsisting unless and until one party elects to avoid it. The right to avoid is a legal remedy, not a legal consequence that operates automatically. The most common basis for avoidance in insurance is breach of the duty of utmost good faith — material non-disclosure or misrepresentation — discussed fully in Chapter 2. Avoidance is effected by the insurer communicating its election to treat the contract as if it had never existed, typically by written notice to the policyholder returning any premiums paid. The right to avoid may be lost — it may be 'waived' — if the insurer continues to accept premiums, continues to correspond as though the contract is valid, or takes any action inconsistent with an intention to avoid. Under NIIRA 2025, the remedy of avoidance is qualified for consumer insurance contracts: where the non-disclosure was innocent and unconnected to the loss, the insurer is not entitled to avoid the contract entirely but must offer a proportionate remedy. This is a significant departure from the pre-2025 common law position. Avoidance Ab Initio The remedy available to an insurer for breach of the duty of utmost good faith. The insurer elects to treat the contract as void from the beginning — as if it had never been made — and returns the premiums paid. The effect of avoidance is retrospective: any claims paid under the avoided policy may be recoverable by the insurer. Under NIIRA 2025, avoidance must be proportionate to the nature of the breach; innocent non-disclosure unconnected to the loss does not entitle the insurer to full avoidance. See: Chapter 2; NIIRA 2025, reformed utmost good faith provisions. 3.9.3 Unenforceable Contracts An unenforceable contract is one that is valid in substance but cannot be enforced through the courts because of a procedural or evidential defect. In insurance practice in Nigeria, the most common category of unenforceable contract is one where the insurer is not duly licensed under NIIRA 2025 to transact the business in question. The policy may be 'valid' in the sense that a risk transfer was agreed, but it is unenforceable because the insurer lacks the legal authority to carry on insurance business in Nigeria. NIIRA 2025 imposes strict liability on both insurers and intermediaries who transact unlicensed insurance business. Policyholders who knowingly transact with unlicensed insurers may find their policies unenforceable and their claims unsatisfied — a powerful consumer protection argument for verifying the licence status of any insurer before committing a premium. The practical rule for the Nigerian practitioner is straightforward: before placing any risk, verify the insurer's current licence status on the NAICOM public register. NAICOM maintains a publicly accessible list of licensed insurers, reinsurers, brokers, and agents on its website (naicom.gov.ng). Placing risks with unlicensed entities is both a breach of professional duty and a potential criminal offence under NIIRA 2025.

t: Chapter 3 · 3.10  Consumer Rights, Claims Settlement, and NAICOM's Redress Framework under NIIRA 2025
x: 3.10.1 The Consumer Protection Imperative If one theme runs through NIIRA 2025 more consistently than any other, it is consumer protection. The Act was enacted in a context where Nigerian policyholders — having paid premiums faithfully for years — repeatedly encountered insurers who contested, delayed, or denied legitimate claims. The public perception that 'insurance companies don't pay' is not entirely without foundation; research by NAICOM and the NIA has repeatedly identified claims disputes as the primary driver of the sector's trust deficit. NIIRA 2025's consumer protection provisions are a legislative response to this trust deficit. 3.10.2 Claims Settlement Timelines Regulatory Spotlight — NIIRA 2025 — Claims Settlement: The 60-Day Mandate Section 210 of NIIRA 2025 establishes mandatory claims settlement timelines as a cornerstone of the Act's consumer protection framework: All claims must be settled within 60 days of notification or such shorter period as may be prescribed in NAICOM regulations. The 60-day period represents the outer limit; NAICOM's implementing regulations may prescribe shorter periods for specific product classes. An insurer that fails to settle a valid claim within the prescribed period is liable for compound interest on the outstanding amount for each month of delay, calculated at a rate prescribed by NAICOM. This penalty provision is designed to make delay financially painful for insurers rather than financially advantageous. Where an insurer disputes a claim, it must notify the claimant in writing within the settlement period, stating the grounds of the dispute with specificity. A general denial without stated grounds is not a valid dispute for the purposes of the Act. Fraudulent claims: An insurer who suspects fraud must notify the claimant in writing within the settlement period and may refer the matter to the police or to NAICOM's fraud investigation unit without making payment. The fraud exception cannot be used as a pretext to delay legitimate claims. The compound interest penalty for late payment is a significant innovation. Under the pre-NIIRA 2025 regime, delayed claims settlement imposed almost no cost on the insurer — the interest cost of holding unpaid claims was typically less than the investment return earned on the float. NIIRA 2025 inverts this calculus: compound interest at NAICOM-prescribed rates is designed to exceed the investment return, making prompt payment the financially rational choice.[8][14] 3.10.3 The Insurance Policyholders' Protection Fund A major structural innovation in NIIRA 2025 is the Insurance Policyholders' Protection Fund (IPPF), established under Section 212. The IPPF is financed by a contribution from every insurer and reinsurer of 0.25% of gross premium income (plus 0.25% of the balance of the Security and Insurance Development Fund), creating a pooled fund managed by NAICOM to compensate policyholders of insolvent insurers. This is the insurance sector's equivalent of the bank deposit guarantee scheme administered by the Nigeria Deposit Insurance Corporation (NDIC). Prior to the IPPF, a policyholder whose insurer became insolvent — and there have been several such cases in the Nigerian market's history — was an unsecured creditor in the insolvency, ranking behind the insurer's secured creditors and employees in the distribution of assets. In practice, this meant that policyholders frequently recovered little or nothing. The IPPF provides a dedicated compensation mechanism that is independent of the general insolvency estate, giving policyholders meaningful protection for the first time. 3.10.4 The NAICOM Complaints Redress Framework NIIRA 2025 substantially strengthens NAICOM's jurisdiction over consumer complaints. The Act establishes a formal complaints redress mechanism through which any policyholder, beneficiary, or other affected party may refer a dispute with an insurer or intermediary to NAICOM for resolution. Process — NAICOM Complaints Redress: Step-by-Step Process The complaints process under NIIRA 2025 and NAICOM's Complaints Bureau operates as follows: Step 1 — Internal complaint: The policyholder must first lodge a formal complaint in writing with the insurer's internal complaints department. The insurer is required under NIIRA 2025 to maintain and publicise a customer complaints procedure and to respond within a specified period (currently 15 working days per NAICOM's implementing guidance). Step 2 — NAICOM referral: If the complaint is not resolved within the insurer's internal process to the complainant's satisfaction, the complainant may refer the matter to NAICOM's Consumer Complaints Bureau in writing, attaching evidence of the internal complaint and the insurer's response (or failure to respond within the deadline). Step 3 — NAICOM investigation: NAICOM investigates the complaint, requiring documents, information, and oral representations from both parties. NAICOM has the power to summon officers of the insurer, inspect records, and impose interim measures (including requiring provisional payment) pending the outcome of the investigation. Step 4 — NAICOM determination: NAICOM issues a written determination upholding, dismissing, or partially upholding the complaint. The determination may require the insurer to pay a claim, compensate the complainant, or amend its practices. NAICOM may also impose administrative sanctions including fines and licence suspension. Step 5 — Court proceedings: If either party is dissatisfied with NAICOM's determination, they may seek judicial review in the Federal High Court. The court treats NAICOM's determination as a relevant but not conclusive factor in its own assessment. NAICOM's Complaints Bureau operates a dedicated online complaints portal at naicom.gov.ng. Complaints may also be submitted by email or in person at NAICOM's head office in Abuja or any state liaison office. NAICOM has committed to acknowledging all complaints within 5 working days under its Service Charter published under NIIRA 2025.[10][17] 3.10.5 Cooling-Off Period NAICOM regulation and market practice provide a right of cancellation — commonly known as a cooling-off period — for certain classes of personal insurance contracts, consistent with international best practice for consumer financial products (the Act itself contains no cooling-off provision). During the cooling-off period, which is prescribed by NAICOM regulations (typically 15 to 30 days from the date of inception or policy delivery, whichever is later), the policyholder may cancel the policy and receive a full refund of premiums paid, less any pro-rata premium for cover already provided. The cooling-off right reflects the regulatory recognition that insurance is a complex product sold in circumstances where the policyholder may not fully understand what they have purchased. The period gives the policyholder time to review the policy document, assess its terms against their needs, and exit if the product does not suit — without financial penalty beyond the cost of the cover already consumed. Advisory — Implementing the Cooling-Off Right — Operational Requirements for Insurers The cooling-off obligation (a NAICOM regulatory requirement, not a provision of the Act) has operational implications for all life insurers: Policy documents must prominently state the cooling-off period, the deadline for exercise, and the process for cancellation (the 'how to cancel' disclosure). Digital platforms must provide a clearly labelled 'Cancel Policy' function accessible without navigating through multiple screens. Refund processing must occur within the period prescribed by NAICOM — typically 14 days of receiving the cancellation notice. Delay in refunding premiums attracts the same compound interest penalty as late claims settlement. Insurers' CRM systems must flag policies within the cooling-off window and route any communication from such policyholders to trained service staff who can address concerns before the cancellation is exercised. Where a claim has been paid during the cooling-off period (unusual but not impossible), the insurer is entitled to deduct the claim amount from any refund due.

This chapter has traced the insurance contract from its formation through the documents that evidence it, the modifications that may alter it, and the circumstances that may vitiate or terminate it. The following are the chapter's essential propositions. A valid insurance contract requires offer, acceptance, consideration, legal capacity, and legal purpose. In most insurance transactions, the completed proposal form constitutes the offer by the proposer; the insurer's issue of a cover note or policy document constitutes the acceptance. The proposal form is the foundational underwriting document. Its 'basis of contract' clause — where present — converts all answers into promissory warranties, entitling the insurer to avoid for any inaccuracy. NIIRA 2025's fair presentation regime moderates, but does not eliminate, this harsh effect for post-2025 contracts. The 'no premium, no cover' rule under NIIRA 2025 is absolute: no insurance risk attaches before the premium is paid. Agents and brokers who grant cover without premium authority incur personal liability. A cover note is a temporary contract of insurance, binding on the insurer for the period specified. It is not the policy and does not automatically import all the terms of the subsequent policy. Cover notes must not be backdated and must specify date, time, period, subject matter, and sum insured. The policy document is evidence of the contract, not the contract itself. It is interpreted by the rules of plain meaning, reading the policy as a whole, and — for genuine ambiguities — contra proferentem: against the drafter, invariably the insurer. Conditions precedent to the right to claim must be strictly observed; failure to comply forfeits the claim. Conditions subsequent give the insurer prospective termination rights, not retrospective forfeiture. Labelling conditions correctly in policy wordings is a key drafting obligation under NIIRA 2025's product approval regime. Endorsements and riders alter the policy by agreement; endorsements are mid-term amendments, riders are additional benefit modules. Material alterations re-trigger the duty of utmost good faith. Assignment transfers ownership of the policy; nomination designates the recipient of proceeds without transferring ownership. Assignment requires written notice to the insurer; nomination requires a written nomination form lodged with the insurer. Void contracts have no legal existence (typically due to absence of insurable interest or illegality). Voidable contracts are valid until the insurer elects to avoid (typically for breach of utmost good faith). Unenforceable contracts cannot be enforced in court due to procedural defects, principally the insurer's unlicensed status. NIIRA 2025's consumer protections are structural: a mandatory 60-day claims settlement timeline with compound interest for delay; the Insurance Policyholders' Protection Fund (IPPF); a NAICOM complaints redress process (set by the Service Charter and NAICOM procedures, not detailed in the Act); a cooling-off right under NAICOM regulation; and NAICOM product approval to ensure fair and clear policy wordings.

Proposal Form The standardised questionnaire completed by the prospective insured providing the insurer with material information about the risk. The proposer's completion and submission of the form typically constitutes the offer in an insurance contract. Basis of Contract Clause A clause in the declaration of a proposal form that converts all answers given by the proposer into promissory warranties, entitling the insurer to avoid the policy for any inaccuracy, however innocent or immaterial to the loss. Cover Note A temporary insurance document issued by an insurer or authorised agent providing interim evidence of insurance for a stated period pending the issue of the formal policy. A cover note is itself a binding contract of insurance for the period specified. Policy Document The written evidence of the insurance contract, comprising the schedule, recitals, insuring clause, exclusions, conditions, definitions, and general provisions. It is not the contract itself — the contract is formed at the point of offer and acceptance. Contra Proferentem A rule of contractual interpretation resolving ambiguous contract terms against the party that drafted them; in insurance, always the insurer. Applied as a last resort after ordinary interpretive methods have failed. Condition Precedent A policy term that must be strictly observed before the insurer's obligation to pay a claim arises. Failure to observe a condition precedent typically forfeits the right to claim entirely. Condition Subsequent A policy term whose breach does not automatically forfeit a claim but may entitle the insurer to terminate the policy going forward or reduce the claim proportionately. Endorsement A written amendment to an insurance policy, effected with the insurer's authority, modifying, adding to, or removing a term from the original policy. Rider An additional benefit or cover module attached to a base life assurance policy, providing supplementary protection (critical illness, TPD, waiver of premium, ADB) for an additional premium. Assignment (Life Policy) The legal transfer of all rights under a life assurance policy from the policyholder (assignor) to a third party (assignee), effected in writing with notice to the insurer. Used as mortgage collateral, loan security, and in trust planning. Nomination The policyholder's designation of one or more persons to receive the policy proceeds on the death of the life assured. Does not transfer ownership. Revocable at any time by the policyholder during their lifetime. Void Contract A contract that has no legal existence, treated as if it had never been made. Neither party can enforce it. Common causes in insurance: absence of insurable interest; illegality of subject matter. Voidable Contract A contract that is valid and subsisting unless and until one party elects to avoid it. In insurance, the insurer's right to avoid typically arises from breach of utmost good faith. Under NIIRA 2025, avoidance must be proportionate to the nature of the breach. No Premium, No Cover Rule The Nigerian statutory rule under NIIRA 2025 that no insurance risk shall attach and no cover shall be effective unless and until the premium has been paid and received by the insurer or its authorised agent. Insurance Policyholders' Protection Fund (IPPF) The compensation fund established under Section 212 of NIIRA 2025, financed by a 0.25% levy on the gross premium income of every insurer and reinsurer, to compensate policyholders of insolvent insurers. The insurance sector's equivalent of the NDIC bank deposit guarantee scheme. Cooling-Off Period The statutory right under NIIRA 2025 for policyholders to cancel a personal insurance policy within a prescribed period of inception (typically 15–30 days) and receive a full refund of premiums less any pro-rata cover already consumed.

Which one of the following BEST describes the legal status of an insurance policy document? It is the contract of insurance itself. It is an offer made by the insurer to the insured. It is written evidence of a contract formed at the point of offer and acceptance. It is only binding once signed by both parties. (C) It is written evidence of a contract formed at the point of offer and acceptance. Why (C) is Correct The insurance contract is formed at the moment of offer and acceptance — typically when the insurer communicates its acceptance of the proposer’s application. The policy document is issued subsequently and records the agreed terms. It is evidence of the pre-existing contract, not the contract itself. Crucially, if the policy document is lost or destroyed, the underlying contract remains legally enforceable — its existence can be proved by other means. Why the Others Are Wrong (A) The contract exists independently of any written document. At common law, insurance contracts can be oral or evidenced by correspondence. The policy formalises an already-formed agreement.(B) The policy is not a fresh offer. By the time the policy is issued, the contract has already been concluded. The insurer cannot withdraw the policy as if it were a standing offer.(D) Insurance contracts do not generally require both parties’ signatures to be binding. The insurer’s signed policy schedule and the insured’s acceptance of the policy terms create a binding contract without any requirement for a separately signed agreement.

The ‘no premium, no cover’ rule under NIIRA 2025 means that: An insurer may refuse to pay a claim if the insured missed a single premium payment after inception. No insurance risk attaches and no cover is effective unless and until the premium has been paid and received by the insurer. Premiums must be paid annually. The insurer may deduct unpaid premiums from a claim settlement. (B) No insurance risk attaches and no cover is effective unless and until the premium has been paid and received by the insurer. Why (B) is Correct NIIRA 2025 codifies the no-premium-no-cover rule as a statutory principle applicable to all new policies: coverage does not commence until the insurer actually receives the premium. This prevents the longstanding practice of agents issuing cover notes or confirming coverage before collecting premium, which exposed insurers to unfinanced liabilities. The rule applies to policy inception — not to ongoing premium payments after the policy has commenced. Why the Others Are Wrong (A) describes the different (and incorrect) reading that missing one renewal premium immediately voids the policy. After inception, most policies allow a grace period (commonly 30 days) under the policy conditions before the policy lapses for non-payment; the Act sets no statutory minimum.(C) No annual payment frequency is mandated by the no-premium-no-cover rule. Policies may be paid monthly, quarterly, or annually — the rule requires that whichever frequency is chosen, the first premium must be received before cover begins.(D) describes an entirely separate provision applicable to

A cover note is BEST described as: A formal policy document issued immediately on payment of premium. A quotation from the insurer setting out the proposed premium. A temporary contract of insurance binding on the insurer for a stated period pending the issue of the formal policy. An endorsement to an existing policy adding a new risk. (C) A temporary contract of insurance binding on the insurer for a stated period pending the issue of the formal policy. Why (C) is Correct A cover note is an immediate, temporary insurance contract. It provides legally binding coverage from the moment of issuance for a stated period (typically 30-60 days) while the formal policy is being prepared, underwritten, and delivered to the insured. The insurer is bound by the cover note from the moment of issue — a claim arising during the cover note period is a valid claim. General Accident v Midland Bank [1940] established the legal status of the cover note as a binding temporary contract. Why the Others Are Wrong (A) The formal policy is the permanent insurance document; a cover note is explicitly temporary and must be superseded by the formal policy before expiry.(B) A quotation is a pre-contractual communication conveying proposed premium terms. It is not a contract and creates no binding obligations on the insurer. An insurer may withdraw a quotation before it is accepted.(D) An endorsement amends or extends an existing policy that has already been issued. A cover note precedes the formal policy — there is nothing to endorse yet.

The contra proferentem rule provides that: The insured must prove the proximate cause of a loss. Any ambiguous policy term shall be construed against the party that drafted it, normally the insurer. A condition precedent must be strictly complied with by the insured. The insurer may avoid a policy for any breach of warranty, however minor. (B) Any ambiguous policy term shall be construed against the party that drafted it, normally the insurer. Why (B) is Correct Contra proferentem (‘against the one who proffers’) is a rule of contractual interpretation: where a contract term is genuinely ambiguous — capable of bearing more than one reasonable meaning — the ambiguity is resolved against the party who drafted the document, because that party was in the best position to make the meaning clear and chose not to. In insurance, the insurer drafts the policy, so ambiguous exclusions, conditions, and limitations are construed in favour of the policyholder. Confirmed in Nigeria by Leadway Assurance v Zeco [2005] CA. Why the Others Are Wrong (A) describes the burden of proof rules for claims — a separate procedural matter. The insured must generally prove an insured event occurred; the insurer must prove exclusions apply.(C) describes the strict compliance rule for conditions precedent — a distinct substantive rule about the consequences of non-compliance, not an interpretation rule.(D) describes the warranty breach doctrine — again a substantive rule about the consequences of breach, not about how ambiguous terms are read.

Under NIIRA 2025, an insurer that fails to settle a valid claim within the prescribed 60-day period is liable to pay the claimant: A fixed administrative fine, payable to the claimant. Compound interest on the outstanding claim for each month of delay. Criminal prosecution only if the delay exceeds six months. No additional liability beyond the original claim amount. (B) Compound interest on the outstanding claim for each month of delay. Why (B) is Correct Section 210 of NIIRA 2025 requires valid claims to be settled within 60 days of notification (or any shorter period NAICOM prescribes). An insurer that fails to do so is liable to a ₦500,000 penalty and must pay compound interest on the outstanding amount for each month of delay, so the claimant is compensated for the delay in addition to the claim itself. Why the Others Are Wrong (A) The ₦500,000 penalty in s.210(7) is a sanction on the insurer, not an amount payable to the claimant; the claimant’s entitlement is the claim plus monthly compound interest.(C) Criminal prosecution is not the remedy for late settlement; criminal provisions target fraud and wilful misconduct.(D) No additional liability was the position before NIIRA 2025; the reform was designed to change it.

Adewale completed an insurance proposal form with the help of an agent of the insurer who filled in answers without reading each question to Adewale and without Adewale's specific instruction. The form contains errors that Adewale says he was unaware of. The insurer seeks to avoid the policy on the ground of misrepresentation.
(a) Analyse who is legally responsible for the errors in the proposal form, applying the relevant principles of insurance contract law.
(b) Explain how NIIRA 2025's provisions on fair presentation affect the insurer's right to avoid in these circumstances.   Part (a) — Legal Responsibility for Errors Under agency law, an agent acts on behalf of and binds the principal. When an insurer’s agent completes a proposal form on behalf of the insurer (performing an administrative function connected with the insurance business), errors made in that process are attributable to the insurer, not the proposer.The key principle: a proposer who relies in good faith on an agent’s handling of the proposal process is not responsible for errors they did not instruct and were not asked about. The insurer cannot rely on errors created by its own agent as a ground for avoiding the policy against an innocent insured.This principle has been applied in numerous common law and Nigerian cases. The proposition is straightforward: the insurer created the flawed record; it cannot now weaponise that record against the insured.Additional point: if Adewale signed the form without reading it, the insurer might argue he adopted the form’s contents. Distinguish between an assignment and a nomination in the context of a Nigerian life assurance policy. Ngozi has assigned her life policy to Zenith Bank as collateral for a business loan. She has also nominated her two children as beneficiaries. The bank loan has been fully repaid. Advise Ngozi on the current state of her policy, the effect of the repayment on the assignment, and the status of the nomination. The assignee becomes the party entitled to receive benefits. A legal assignment (by deed) must be in writing and notified to the insurer to be effective under the Policies of Assurance Act (applicable in Nigeria through received English law).Nomination designates the person to receive policy proceeds on the policyholder’s death without transferring ownership of the policy. The policyholder retains ownership; the nominee acquires an expectation, not a vested right. A nomination can be changed at any time by the policyholder. Current State of Ngozi’s Policy Currently, Zenith Bank holds a legal assignment over the policy as security for the business loan. The bank’s interest is paramount — it takes priority over the children’s nomination. Until the assignment is discharged, if Ngozi dies, the bank is legally entitled to receive the policy proceeds first (up to any outstanding debt), with any surplus going to the nominated beneficiaries. (a) Classify this clause as either a condition precedent or a condition subsequent and explain the legal consequences of breach.
(b) A policyholder's husband died suddenly while working in an offshore oil facility, and communication difficulties meant that the insurer was not notified for 45 days. Advise the insurer on whether it may lawfully rely on this clause to decline the claim under NIIRA 2025.   Part (a) — Classification and Consequences This is a condition precedent to the right to claim. The telltale indicator is the words ‘failure to comply shall relieve the Company of all liability under this policy’ — imposing an obligation on the insured that must be performed before the right to claim arises, with a stated consequence (loss of all liability) for non-compliance.Condition precedent vs condition subsequent: A condition subsequent is one whose breach terminates a right that has already arisen. Critically evaluate the extent to which NIIRA 2025's consumer protection provisions — including the mandatory claims settlement timeline, the Insurance Policyholders' Protection Fund, the cooling-off right, and NAICOM's complaints redress framework — are adequate to address the trust deficit that has historically limited insurance penetration in Nigeria. In your answer, identify any gaps in the legislation that remain to be addressed.   Essay Framework Thesis NIIRA 2025’s consumer protection framework is the most comprehensive in Nigeria’s insurance history and directly targets the specific mechanisms through which the trust deficit was created. However, framework quality and enforcement quality are different dimensions, and several structural gaps remain. Evaluating Each Provision 1. Mandatory 60-day claims settlement timeline: This addresses the primary trust-building action the industry needs. Financial penalties for non-compliance create genuine consequences.
