t: Chapter 8 · 8.1  Introduction: The Problem Annuities Solve
x: Every working person faces two fundamental financial risks in retirement. The first — dying too soon — is the risk that life assurance addresses: it pays a lump sum to dependants if the breadwinner dies before financial obligations are met. The second — living too long — is the mirror risk, and in many respects the more insidious of the two. A person who retires at 60 with sufficient savings to last until an expected death at 75 is exposed to serious financial jeopardy if they live to 85 or 90. They will outlive their savings. An annuity solves this problem by reversing the mortality risk. Instead of paying when the insured dies (as life assurance does), an annuity pays for as long as the insured lives. The annuity contract transfers longevity risk — the risk of unexpectedly long survival — from the individual to the insurer. The insurer, pooling thousands of annuitants, predicts aggregate mortality experience with actuarial confidence and prices its payments accordingly. Those who die early in effect subsidise those who live long — the same pooling mechanism that underlies all insurance, but applied to survival rather than death. In Nigeria, the annuity market is inextricably linked to the Contributory Pension Scheme (CPS) established by the Pension Reform Act 2014. The CPS mandates that retiring employees either purchase a Retiree Life Annuity (RLA) from a NAICOM-licensed life insurer or remain under Programmed Withdrawal (PW) administered by their Pension Fund Administrator (PFA). The choice between these two modes is one of the most consequential financial decisions a Nigerian worker will ever make. This chapter equips the practitioner with the theoretical, actuarial, regulatory, and advisory foundations needed to understand, explain, and advise on annuities and retirement income products in Nigeria. It begins with a systematic taxonomy of annuity types, proceeds through the actuarial basis of annuity pricing, maps the Nigerian CPS framework in detail, and provides the comparative analysis of PW and RLA that every practitioner serving retirees must master.

8.2.1 Definition Annuity A financial contract under which an insurer undertakes to make a series of periodic payments to an individual (the annuitant) either immediately or from a specified future date. Life annuities are contingent on the survival of the annuitant — payments continue for as long as the annuitant lives and cease on death, unless a guaranteed payment period applies. An annuity transforms a lump sum of capital into a guaranteed income stream, transferring longevity risk from the individual to the pooling institution. Cf: Life assurance (pays a lump sum on death). An annuity is the economic and actuarial complement of life assurance. 8.2.2 Classification by Commencement (a) Immediate Annuity An immediate annuity begins making payments within one payment period of the premium being paid. The annuitant makes a single lump-sum payment to the insurer and receives the first annuity payment almost immediately — typically within one month for monthly annuities. This is the structure used for the Retiree Life Annuity (RLA) in Nigeria: the retiree transfers their RSA balance as a single premium, and the insurer begins making monthly or quarterly payments within the same period. (b) Deferred Annuity A deferred annuity postpones the payment commencement to a specified future date — the annuity commencement date (ACD) — which may be years after the premium is paid. During the deferral period, the fund grows at a guaranteed rate or in a linked investment account. At the ACD, the accumulated fund converts to an income stream. The Contributory Pension Scheme itself functions as a mandatory national deferred annuity system: contributions accumulate during the working years (the accumulation phase) and the fund is accessed at retirement (the income phase). Annuity Type When Payments Begin Primary Application in Nigeria Immediate annuity Within one payment period of premium payment RLA purchased with RSA balance at retirement Deferred annuity At a specified future date — years after accumulation The CPS is a deferred annuity accumulation mechanism; also sold as savings-to-retirement plans Variable deferred annuity At a future date; accumulation linked to investment fund performance Investment-linked retirement plans: AXA Mansard Wealth Plus, Leadway Smart Life, ARM Life 8.2.3 Classification by Duration and Guarantee (a) Whole Life Annuity A whole life annuity pays an income for the entire remaining lifetime of the annuitant. Payments cease on death. This provides the highest possible income per unit of premium — the insurer has no obligation after death — but leaves no estate benefit if the annuitant dies shortly after purchase. (b) Life Annuity with Guaranteed Period To address the perceived unfairness of early death under a pure life annuity, most annuity products include a guaranteed payment period — in Nigeria, 10 years. The insurer guarantees payments for at least the guaranteed period regardless of whether the annuitant dies within it. If the annuitant dies before the end of the guaranteed period, the remaining guaranteed payments are paid to the named beneficiary. After the guaranteed period, payments continue for life. PenCom's CPS framework stipulates the 10-year guarantee for the Nigerian RLA. (c) Annuity-Certain An annuity-certain pays for a fixed period regardless of survival. If the annuitant dies before the end of the period, payments continue to the estate or beneficiary. No mortality contingency applies — it is a fixed series of payments with no longevity protection. (d) Temporary Life Annuity A temporary life annuity pays for a specified period but only while the annuitant survives. If the annuitant dies before the end of the period, payments cease. Useful for matching a specific finite obligation. 8.2.4 Classification by Number of Lives (a) Single-Life Annuity Written on one life only. Payments contingent on the annuitant's survival. Provides the highest monthly income per unit of premium but leaves a surviving spouse with no continuing income after death. (b) Joint-Life Annuity Written on two lives — typically a married couple — paying while both are alive. Payments cease on the first death. Lower income than single-life for the same premium because payments extend until the first of two deaths. (c) Last-Survivor (Reversionary) Annuity The most practical structure for couples. Pays a full income while both lives are alive, then a reduced continuation rate (typically 50–66% of the original payment) to the surviving annuitant after the first death, continuing until the survivor's death. The continuation rate is agreed at inception and affects the annuity price. Last-Survivor Annuity A joint annuity that pays a full income while both lives are alive and a reduced income (the continuation rate, typically 50–66%) to the surviving annuitant after the first death. Payments continue until the death of the last survivor. The continuation rate determines the price: higher continuation rate = higher annuity premium for the same initial income. Primary application: Married couples in retirement seeking income continuity for both partners across both lifetimes.

t: Chapter 8 · 8.3  The Actuarial Basis of Annuity Pricing
x: 8.3.1 The Pricing Problem Pricing a life annuity requires the insurer to answer one complex question: given a single premium received today, how large a periodic payment can the insurer guarantee to make for the remainder of the annuitant's life while remaining financially solvent? The answer depends on: the mortality table (how long the annuitant is expected to live), the investment return assumption (the rate the insurer expects to earn on the premium fund), and the expense and profit loading. The mortality table used for annuity pricing uses lighter (lower) mortality rates than life assurance tables — annuity mortality tables assume annuitants will live longer than the general population. This is because of adverse selection: a person who chooses to purchase an annuity has implicitly bet on living a long time. People who expect to die soon are less likely to buy life annuities. The insurer must price for this self-selected, longer-lived population. Critically, life assurance and annuity portfolios provide a natural hedge to each other: a year of lower-than-expected mortality (fewer deaths) is good news for annuity portfolios (fewer death claims, more annuity payments required) but bad news for life assurance portfolios. This natural inverse relationship is one reason life insurance companies are the natural and regulatory home for annuity products. Annuity Factor The present value of a periodic payment of ₦1 to a life aged x at an assumed interest rate i, representing the lump sum needed today to fund all expected future payments to the annuitant. In standard actuarial notation, a_x denotes the whole life annuity-immediate factor; ä_x denotes the annuity-due (beginning-of-period payments). The single annuity premium = Desired annual income × Annuity factor. The factor falls as the interest rate rises (higher returns require a smaller fund to support the same income) and rises as the mortality table becomes lighter (longer expected survival requires a larger fund). See: Dickson, Hardy and Waters, Actuarial Mathematics for Life Contingent Risks (3rd edn, Cambridge, 2020); EFU Life Table (Nigerian standard). Illustration — Annuity Pricing — A Simplified Worked Example Scenario: A 60-year-old male Nigerian retiree has an RSA balance of ₦15 million after his lump sum withdrawal, to be used as a single premium for an RLA with a 10-year guarantee. Actuarial assumptions used by the RLA provider: Male life expectancy at age 60 (Nigerian EFU Life Table): approximately 20 additional years Investment return assumption: 12% per annum Expense and profit loading: 5% of annual annuity payment 10-year guaranteed period built into the product Simplified annuity factor ≈ 7.5 (present value of ₦1 per year for the expected lifetime at 12% p.a., incorporating both time value and mortality probability — a simplified figure for illustration). Estimated annual annuity = Premium ÷ Annuity Factor ÷ (1 + expense loading) = ₦15,000,000 ÷ 7.5 ÷ 1.05 = ₦1,904,762 per year → approximately ₦158,730 per month. This ₦158,730 per month is guaranteed for at least 10 years. If the retiree dies before age 70, the present value of remaining guaranteed payments is paid as a lump sum to the beneficiary. If the retiree survives to 88 (28 years of payments), total payments received = ₦53.4 million against a ₦15 million premium — the pool funded by those who died early. 8.3.2 Interest Rate Sensitivity Annuity prices are highly sensitive to the assumed investment rate. Higher assumed returns produce higher annuity payments for the same premium; lower returns produce lower payments. This sensitivity creates a market dynamic in Nigeria: during periods of high interest rates — as experienced in recent years with Nigerian government bond yields above 18% — annuity income rates are relatively favourable. When yields fall, annuity rates deteriorate. This also creates a key actuarial risk for the insurer: if actual investment returns fall below the pricing assumption, reserves may be inadequate for all future payments — precisely why NIIRA 2025 requires full actuarial reserving and excludes annuity business from the lower-capitalised Standalone Insurtech category.

t: Chapter 8 · 8.4  The Contributory Pension Scheme: Nigeria's Retirement Income Architecture
x: 8.4.1 Overview The Contributory Pension Scheme (CPS) was established by the Pension Reform Act 2004 and re-enacted by the Pension Reform Act 2014. It replaced Nigeria's defined-benefit (DB) pension system — which had accumulated massive unfunded liabilities and failed to pay many retirees — with a privately managed, individually funded defined-contribution (DC) system. Each employee holds their own Retirement Savings Account (RSA), contributed to by both employer and employee throughout the working career. The accumulated fund belongs to the employee and is portable across employers. Contributory Pension Scheme (CPS) Nigeria's mandatory national pension system under the PRA 2014, under which employers (minimum 10%) and employees (minimum 8%) contribute to individual Retirement Savings Accounts (RSAs) managed by licensed Pension Fund Administrators (PFAs). The accumulated RSA balance plus investment returns forms the retirement corpus used to fund post-retirement income either through Programmed Withdrawal or a Retiree Life Annuity. Minimum contributions: 10% employer + 8% employee = minimum 18% of monthly emoluments (basic salary + housing + transport). 8.4.2 Key Institutions of the CPS Institution Role Regulatory Oversight National Pension Commission (PenCom) Apex regulator. Licenses PFAs and PFCs. Sets investment guidelines. Administers the Revised Regulation on Retirement Benefits. Issues joint circulars with NAICOM on RLA products. Autonomous commission under PRA 2014. Pension Fund Administrator (PFA) Manages and invests RSA balances. Processes retirement benefit claims. Administers PW. Provides performance reports. ~25 licensed PFAs including ARM, Stanbic IBTC, Leadway Pensure, Crusader Sterling. Licensed and supervised by PenCom. Fiduciary duty to contributors. Pension Fund Custodian (PFC) Holds and safeguards pension assets — ring-fenced from the PFA's balance sheet. Executes investment instructions from the PFA. Key PFCs: Access Bank Pension Custody and FBN Quest Trustees. Licensed by PenCom. NAICOM-licensed Life Insurers (RLA Providers) Receive RSA balance transfer as single annuity premium. Pay monthly/quarterly RLA income for life (10-year guarantee). RLA product terms approved by NAICOM. NAICOM (financial soundness, product approval) and PenCom (benefit administration compliance). Data & Statistics — The CPS in Numbers — Cumulative Data to End-2022 Metric Cumulative Data (Inception to 31 December 2022) Registered contributors Over 10 million RSA holders Total pension assets under management Over ₦14 trillion Retirees on Programmed Withdrawal 319,833 approved; ₦908.04 billion lump sums; ₦14.18 billion monthly pensions Retirees on Retiree Life Annuity 105,047 retirees; ₦201.43 billion lump sums; ₦615.78 billion in RLA premiums transferred; ₦6.24 billion monthly annuities PW vs RLA ratio ~3:1 in favour of PW Death benefits paid ₦328.05 billion to beneficiaries of 86,610 deceased contributors En-bloc payments (small balances) ₦38.71 billion to 145,313 retirees

t: Chapter 8 · 8.5  Accessing Retirement Benefits Under the CPS
x: 8.5.1 The Retirement Trigger and Lump Sum Under Section 7(1) of PRA 2014, an RSA holder accesses retirement benefits upon retirement or attaining age 50, whichever is later. At retirement, the holder may withdraw a lump sum from the RSA, provided that the residual amount is sufficient to fund PW or RLA income of not less than 50% of the retiree's last monthly salary.[1] In December 2024, PenCom issued a revised PW template that removed the previous restriction capping lump sum access at 50% of the RSA balance. Retirees may now access any lump sum amount provided the residual balance still funds the 50% minimum pension threshold. This liberalisation allows retirees with large RSA balances to access more capital for specific needs — home purchase, business investment, debt settlement — while maintaining their minimum ongoing income.[8] 8.5.2 The Two Modes of Retirement Income After any lump sum withdrawal, the retiree must choose between two income modes:[3] Programmed Withdrawal (PW): The residual RSA balance remains with the PFA, which calculates and pays monthly or quarterly pension from the RSA over the retiree's expected lifespan. Retiree Life Annuity (RLA): The residual RSA balance is transferred to a NAICOM-licensed life insurer as a single annuity premium. The insurer pays monthly or quarterly income for life with a 10-year guarantee. PenCom's regulations require that PFAs provide the CPS Retirement Pack to employees at least three months before their expected retirement date. No party — employer, PFA, RLA provider, or broker — may compel a retiree to choose either option.

8.6.1 Mechanics Under PW, the retiree's residual RSA balance remains with the PFA and is transferred to the Retiree Fund (Fund IV) — a dedicated, conservatively allocated investment fund. The PFA calculates the monthly or quarterly pension using PenCom's standardised PW template, taking into account the RSA balance, the retiree's actuarial life expectancy, and projected investment returns.[12] The key feature of PW is that the RSA balance is not transferred to a third party — it remains the property of the retiree, managed by the PFA. This means: The RSA balance continues to earn investment returns, which may enhance future PW payments if the PFA's Retiree Fund performs well. If the retiree dies, whatever balance remains is paid in full to the named beneficiary — no forfeiture, no time limit. The retiree may switch from PW to RLA at any time. The reverse is not permitted. PW payment levels may be periodically revised — upward if the fund performs well; downward if the fund is depleted faster than expected. 8.6.2 Risks in PW Fund depletion risk: If the retiree lives significantly longer than actuarial expectation, the RSA may be exhausted. PenCom's Guaranteed Minimum Pension (GMP) provides a floor for retirees whose PW falls below one-third of the national minimum wage, but this does not replicate the lifetime income guarantee of an RLA. Investment risk: PW payments are linked to Retiree Fund performance. A sequence of poor returns shortly after retirement can permanently reduce PW income. PFA operational risk: If the PFA encounters financial or operational difficulties, PenCom oversight and the PFC's ring-fenced custody structure reduce but do not fully eliminate the risk.

8.7.1 Core Features The RLA is a contract between the retiree and a NAICOM-licensed life insurer. The retiree transfers the residual RSA balance as a single premium; the insurer guarantees a fixed monthly or quarterly income for the remainder of the retiree's life, with a minimum 10-year guarantee.[2] Income for life: Payments continue regardless of how long the annuitant lives. The insurer bears longevity risk. 10-year minimum guarantee: If the retiree dies within 10 years, the present value of remaining guaranteed payments is paid to the named beneficiary as a lump sum. Fixed nominal amount: Income does not fluctuate with investment performance — it is a guaranteed contractual obligation. Generally irrevocable: The decision cannot normally be reversed. The retiree may transfer to a different RLA provider after at least two years. NAICOM product approval required: All RLA products must be filed with and approved by NAICOM. Standalone Insurtechs may not write RLA business under NIIRA 2025. Retiree Life Annuity (RLA) A contract under which a NAICOM-licensed life insurer receives the residual RSA balance of a CPS retiree as a single premium and undertakes to pay a fixed monthly or quarterly income for life, guaranteed for a minimum of 10 years. If the retiree dies within the guaranteed period, the present value of remaining guaranteed payments is paid as a lump sum to the named beneficiary. Generally irrevocable — transfers longevity risk from the retiree to the insurer. Regulatory basis: PRA 2014, Section 7(1)(c); PenCom Revised Regulation on Retirement Benefits (2022); NAICOM product approval; NIIRA 2025 (annuity excluded from Standalone Insurtech licences). 8.7.2 The RLA Purchase Process The RLA purchase involves a structured workflow between the retiree, PFA, and RLA provider:[9] Pre-retirement (3 months before): PFA provides the CPS Retirement Pack with SRBC template showing estimated RSA balance, lump sum options, and projected monthly income under both PW and RLA. Retiree decision: Retiree studies both options and selects voluntarily. Independent financial advice is recommended. RLA provider selection: Retiree chooses an approved life insurer from NAICOM's register and obtains a provisional RLA agreement showing the monthly income, guarantee terms, and beneficiary designation. PFA submission: Signed provisional RLA agreement submitted to PFA with required documentation: retirement letter from employer; evidence of age; RSA statement. Fund transfer: PFA verifies documentation, confirms with PenCom, and transfers the designated RSA balance to the RLA provider as a single premium. Annuity commencement: RLA provider confirms receipt of premium and commences monthly/quarterly payments — typically within one month of premium transfer. Illustration — The 10-Year Guarantee — Two Scenarios Scenario 1 — Early death (within guarantee): Retired at 60. Monthly annuity: ₦150,000. Died March 2027 — 25 months into the annuity. Remaining guaranteed payments: 95 months. Present value of 95 × ₦150,000 at the prevailing discount rate is paid as a lump sum to the named beneficiary. The family still receives significant capital despite the early death. Scenario 2 — Long life (beyond guarantee): Retired at 60. Monthly annuity: ₦150,000. Lives to 88 — 28 years of payments totalling ₦50.4 million against a ₦15 million single premium. The insurer meets this obligation from the pooling effect: those who died early in the guaranteed period funded the long-lived annuitants. After death in 2053, the beneficiary receives nothing — the annuity is fully exhausted.

t: Chapter 8 · 8.8  Programmed Withdrawal vs RLA: Comparative Analysis
x: The PW-RLA choice is one of the most consequential financial decisions a Nigerian retiree will ever make. PenCom's own data shows a persistent 3:1 preference for PW. The following table provides a structured comparison across seven key dimensions. Dimension Programmed Withdrawal (PW) Retiree Life Annuity (RLA) Income certainty Variable — may change with fund performance and PW recalculations Fixed — monthly payment guaranteed for life at the contracted rate Longevity risk Borne by the retiree — RSA may be exhausted if retiree lives longer than expected Transferred to the insurer — payments continue for life regardless Investment risk Borne by the retiree — linked to Retiree Fund (Fund IV) performance Borne by the insurer — monthly income fixed regardless of investment performance Estate benefit on death Generous — full RSA balance paid to beneficiary whenever death occurs Limited — only the 10-year guarantee period; after year 10, no estate benefit Flexibility High — retiree can switch to RLA at any time; monthly or quarterly withdrawals Very low — generally irrevocable; can only transfer to another RLA provider after 2 years Inflation protection Partial — if Retiree Fund earns real returns, PW may keep pace with inflation (not guaranteed) None for standard RLA — fixed nominal payment loses purchasing power over decades Regulatory oversight PenCom and the PFA are the primary counterparties and regulators Dual: NAICOM (product and insurer solvency) + PenCom (benefit administration) From inception to end-2022, approximately 319,833 retirees chose PW vs 105,047 choosing RLA — a 3:1 preference for PW. This persistent preference is driven by: cultural weight placed on estate inheritance (PW leaves the full RSA balance to beneficiaries at death); limited trust in life insurance institutions; and inadequate financial education about the longevity risk the PW retiree bears. Advisory — PW vs RLA — A Decision Framework for Practitioners Practitioners advising retirees on the PW-RLA choice should apply the following structured framework: Health and life expectancy: Excellent health and family longevity favours RLA (the lifetime income guarantee is valuable). Serious health conditions favouring short life expectancy favour PW (preserving the RSA balance for beneficiaries). Other income sources: A retiree with reliable other income (rental, business) can bear PW's longevity risk. A retiree whose CPS pension is their primary income source should consider RLA's certainty carefully. Beneficiary needs: Substantial dependants (young children, disabled spouse) increase the value of PW's full estate benefit. A retiree with no dependants has less reason to sacrifice the RLA's certainty. Inflation risk: In Nigeria's high-inflation environment, the fixed nominal RLA income may be inadequate in 15–20 years. Explore whether the chosen RLA provider offers indexed or escalating annuity options. Insurer creditworthiness: The RLA is only as good as the insurer's financial solvency over 20–30 years. Assess NIIRA 2025 recapitalisation compliance, Agusto & Co. or GCR rating, and claims settlement record before recommending a specific provider. Legal note: 'The law does not favour either option but preserves retirees' right to make an informed election. The choice should be made deliberately, knowledgeably, and with full appreciation of its legal implications.' — Ivo Takor, VP NBA Epe Branch, February 2026.[7]

t: Chapter 8 · 8.9  NIIRA 2025: The Regulatory Framework for Annuity Business
x: 8.9.1 The Annuity Licence Class Under NIIRA 2025, annuity is one of the four statutory classes of life insurance business. A life insurer must hold specific annuity class authorisation to write RLA products. NAICOM reviews and approves all RLA product terms, pricing structures, and guarantee features before they may be offered to retirees.[13] 8.9.2 Standalone Insurtech Exclusion Regulatory Spotlight — NIIRA 2025 — Annuity Business Excluded from Standalone Insurtech Licences NIIRA 2025 specifically excludes Retirement Life Annuity business from the scope of the Standalone Insurtech licence. Only conventional life insurance companies with full NAICOM life insurance licences and annuity class authorisation may write RLA products. The regulatory rationale is compelling: Long duration: RLA obligations extend over 20–30 years. The ₦10 billion minimum capital for conventional life insurers reflects this; Standalone Insurtechs (minimum ₦1 billion) are not capitalised for decades of guaranteed annuity payments. Actuarial complexity: RLA pricing requires mortality modelling, long-term investment return assumptions, and sophisticated reserving — only feasible with a full actuarial function that conventional life insurers maintain. Longevity risk pooling: Financial sustainability of the RLA depends on pooling a large annuitant population. A new Insurtech with a small book lacks actuarial credibility. Irrevocability: The retiree cannot exit the RLA if the provider becomes insolvent. The higher capital requirements and supervision of full life insurers are the primary consumer protection. Implication: Insurtechs may participate in the RLA distribution chain as comparison platforms, digital onboarding facilitators, or customer service interfaces — but may not underwrite any annuity risk. Any attempt to do so would constitute unlicensed insurance under NIIRA 2025.[17] 8.9.3 Joint PenCom-NAICOM Oversight The administration of RLA products sits at the intersection of pension regulation (PenCom) and insurance regulation (NAICOM). This is managed through joint circulars and agreed protocols: NAICOM: supervises the financial soundness of the RLA provider (capital, investment, reserving, solvency) and approves RLA product terms and rates. PenCom: supervises the retirement benefit administration process — fund transfer from RSA to RLA provider, documentation requirements, and the protection of retirees' rights during benefit election. A dissatisfied RLA retiree should first complain to the provider, then escalate to NAICOM (product and financial complaints) or PenCom (benefit administration complaints).

t: Chapter 8 · 8.10  Disability Income Insurance and the Retirement Lifecycle
x: 8.10.1 Disability Income Insurance A disability income insurance policy pays a regular monthly income if the policyholder becomes unable to work due to illness or injury. Unlike the death benefit of a life policy or the Retiree Life Annuity, disability income insurance is designed for the working years — it replaces income lost due to a disability that prevents earnings. Key structural features: Benefit: Typically 60–75% of pre-disability monthly income. Waiting (deferred) period: 30, 60, or 90 days before benefits begin. Longer waiting period = lower premium. Benefit period: To age 60 (retirement) or for a specified number of years. Definition of disability: 'Own occupation' (more favourable to policyholder) or 'any occupation' (more restrictive). Own-occupation definition pays if the policyholder cannot perform their specific duties; any-occupation pays only if they cannot perform any reasonable work. 8.10.2 The Full Retirement Lifecycle Understanding annuities in context requires understanding the full retirement lifecycle: Accumulation phase (working years): CPS contributions accumulate in the RSA. Voluntary Contributions (VCs) may boost the retirement corpus. PFA investment management compounds returns over 30 years. Pre-retirement phase (3–5 years before retirement): RSA consolidated. CPS Retirement Pack provided. Lump sum, PW, and RLA options evaluated. Estate planning and beneficiary nominations completed. Retirement access phase: Lump sum accessed (subject to 50% minimum pension floor). PW or RLA selected and implemented. Income phase: Monthly income received from PFA (PW) or RLA provider. Supplemented by any other income sources. Advanced age phase: If PW balance is exhausted, GMP and en-bloc payment provisions apply. RLA retirees continue receiving guaranteed income for life — the product delivers as designed.

An annuity solves the longevity risk problem — the risk of outliving savings — by guaranteeing periodic income for the annuitant's entire lifetime. It is the economic complement of life assurance: where life assurance pays on death, an annuity pays on survival. Annuities are classified by commencement (immediate vs deferred), by duration and guarantee (whole life, life with guaranteed period, annuity-certain, temporary), and by the number of lives covered (single life, joint-life, last-survivor/reversionary). Annuity pricing uses lighter mortality tables than life assurance (annuitants self-select for longer lives), a discount rate reflecting investment returns, and expense/profit loadings. The annuity factor is the present value of ₦1 per period for a life aged x at interest rate i. Life assurance and annuity portfolios provide a natural mortality hedge. The CPS under PRA 2014 is Nigeria's mandatory national retirement system: minimum contributions of 10% employer + 8% employee to individual RSAs managed by PFAs. PenCom supervises; PFCs hold assets; licensed life insurers provide RLA products. At retirement, RSA holders may withdraw a lump sum (provided the residual funds the 50% minimum pension floor), then choose PW (income from PFA, variable, full estate benefit) or RLA (guaranteed lifetime income from insurer, fixed, 10-year beneficiary guarantee). From inception to end-2022: 319,833 retirees on PW vs 105,047 on RLA — a 3:1 preference for PW. This reflects estate benefit preferences, limited insurer trust, and inadequate financial literacy about longevity risk. The RLA is generally irrevocable once executed. A retiree can switch from PW to RLA at any time; cannot reverse from RLA to PW; can transfer to a different RLA provider after 2 years. NIIRA 2025 excludes annuity business from Standalone Insurtech licences. Only full life insurance licensees with annuity class authorisation may write RLA products. Insurtechs may distribute but may not underwrite annuity risk. The PW-RLA advisory decision framework considers: health status, other income sources, beneficiary needs, inflation risk tolerance, and the financial strength of the chosen RLA provider.

Annuity A contract providing periodic payments to an annuitant for as long as they live (life annuity) or for a specified period. Converts a lump sum into a guaranteed income stream, transferring longevity risk to the pooling institution. Longevity Risk The risk of outliving one's savings. Transferred to the insurer under an RLA; borne by the retiree under PW. Immediate Annuity Annuity beginning payments within one payment period of premium receipt. Structure of the Nigerian RLA. Deferred Annuity Annuity whose payment commencement is postponed to a future date. The CPS accumulation phase is a mandatory deferred annuity structure. Life Annuity with Guaranteed Period Whole life annuity guaranteeing payments for a minimum period (10 years for Nigerian RLA) even if the annuitant dies earlier. Last-Survivor Annuity Joint annuity paying full income while both lives are alive and a reduced continuation rate to the survivor after the first death. Annuity Factor The present value of ₦1 per period payable to a life aged x at interest rate i. Single annuity premium = Desired annual income × Annuity factor. Contributory Pension Scheme (CPS) Nigeria's mandatory pension system under PRA 2014. Employer (min. 10%) and employee (min. 8%) contribute to individual RSAs managed by PFAs. Retirement Savings Account (RSA) Individual pension savings account held in the contributor's name, managed by their chosen PFA. Portable across employers. Pension Fund Administrator (PFA) PenCom-licensed institution managing and investing RSA balances; administers Programmed Withdrawal. Programmed Withdrawal (PW) CPS retirement income mode where the RSA balance remains with the PFA and is paid out monthly/quarterly over expected lifespan. Variable; full balance paid to beneficiaries on death. Retiree Life Annuity (RLA) NAICOM-regulated contract under which a life insurer receives the RSA balance as a single premium in exchange for guaranteed monthly lifetime income with a 10-year beneficiary guarantee. An annuity PRIMARILY addresses which financial risk? The risk of the breadwinner dying prematurely. The risk of outliving one's savings. The risk of property loss from fire. The risk of the employer failing to pay wages. (B) The risk of outliving one's savings — receiving income for longer than savings can sustain. Why (B) is Correct Longevity risk — the risk of outliving accumulated financial resources — is the defining risk that annuities are designed to eliminate. By converting a lump sum into a guaranteed lifetime income, the annuity ensures the annuitant receives income for as long as they live. The insurer pooling the longevity risk across many annuitants achieves the same statistical predictability that underpins all insurance. Why the Others Are Wrong (A) Premature death risk is addressed by life assurance — the product category designed to provide a lump sum or income to dependants in the event of the breadwinner's early death. Annuities protect against the opposite risk (living too long). (C) Property fire risk is a general insurance exposure — wholly separate from the retirement income risk that annuities address. (D) Employer wage default risk (non-payment of contractual wages) is an employment law matter, addressed through the labour courts, not an insurable retirement income risk.

Under PRA 2014, minimum total CPS contributions are: 8% from employee only. 10% from employer only. 18% aggregate: minimum 10% employer + 8% employee. 25%, all from employer. (C) 18% in aggregate: minimum 10% employer + minimum 8% employee. Why (C) is Correct PRA 2014 Section 7 establishes two separate contribution obligations: the employer must contribute at least 10% of monthly emoluments and the employee at least 8%, giving a combined minimum of 18%. Both amounts are credited to the employee's individual RSA. Employers may voluntarily contribute above 10% (many larger employers contribute 12–15%), but neither may go below the statutory minimum. Why the Others Are Wrong (A) 8% from the employee alone ignores the employer's mandatory 10% contribution — it describes only half the obligation.(B) 10% from the employer alone ignores the employee's mandatory 8% contribution.(D) 25% all from the employer has no basis in PRA 2014 — the combined rate is 18%, split between employer and employee.

The RLA in Nigeria is regulated by: PenCom only. CBN only. NAICOM (financial soundness and product) jointly with PenCom (benefit administration). Federal Ministry of Finance. (C) NAICOM (financial soundness and product) jointly with PenCom (benefit administration). Why (C) is Correct The RLA sits at the intersection of insurance and pension regulation. NAICOM regulates the life insurer writing the annuity — its capital adequacy, RBC compliance, NIIRA 2025 product approval, and actuarial solvency. PenCom regulates the RSA transfer process (the mechanics of moving funds from the PFA to the insurer), the PenCom Approved RLA Insurer Register, and the overall benefit adequacy framework that ensures the annuity meets the 50% minimum pension threshold. Both regulators' requirements must be met for a valid RLA to be issued. Why the Others Are Wrong (A) PenCom alone cannot regulate life insurance products — it has no NIIRA 2025 mandate over insurer solvency or product pricing.(B) CBN regulates banking and monetary policy — it has no direct role in life insurance or annuity products (though it regulates bank treasury functions that may hold RSA assets).(D) The Federal Ministry of Finance sets fiscal policy but does not directly regulate insurance or pension products.

Under the Nigerian RLA, the 10-year guaranteed period means: The retiree pays premiums for 10 years before receiving income. If the retiree dies within 10 years, the present value of remaining guaranteed payments is paid to the named beneficiary. The monthly payment is fixed for 10 years only. The annuity income increases 10% annually for the first decade. (B) If the retiree dies within 10 years, the present value of remaining guaranteed payments is paid to the named beneficiary. Why (B) is Correct A guaranteed payment period means the annuity is paid for a minimum of a defined number of years regardless of the annuitant's survival. If the annuitant dies within the 10-year guarantee window, the insurer pays the present value of the remaining guaranteed payments (or continues the payment stream, depending on the policy design) to the designated beneficiary. This protects against the 'bad luck' scenario of dying very shortly after purchasing an annuity and receiving almost nothing for a large purchase price. Why the Others Are Wrong (A) Describes a premium payment period before income begins — the opposite of what a guarantee period means. The RLA pays income from inception; there is no waiting period for premium accumulation.(C) The annuity continues for the lifetime of the annuitant after the 10-year period — it does not stop at 10 years.(D) A 10% annual income increase describes an escalation feature — a separate and optional product add-on, not the guaranteed period concept.

NIIRA 2025 specifically excludes RLA business from which licence category? Full conventional life licence. Non-life licence. Standalone Insurtech licence. Partnering Insurtech licence. (D) Partnering Insurtech licence. Why (D) is Correct NIIRA 2025 expressly excludes Retirement Life Annuity business from the Partnering Insurtech licence because Partnering Insurtechs are technology/distribution companies — they cannot assume insurance risk on their own account. The long-duration, actuarially complex nature of annuity liabilities requires the full capital adequacy, actuarial governance, and solvency framework applicable to conventional licensed life insurers. Allowing under-capitalised Partnering Insurtechs to assume annuity risk would create material policyholder protection risk for retirees who have converted their lifetime savings. Why the Others Are Wrong (A) Conventional life insurance licence holders are expressly permitted to write RLA business — they have the required capital, governance, and actuarial framework.(B) Non-life licences cannot write any life or annuity business at all — the exclusion of RLA from non-life is automatic and obvious.(C) Standalone Insurtech licensees at the life capital level (₦1bn minimum) may write life insurance and are generally permitted to write RLA business, subject to meeting NAICOM's specific RLA requirements.

A CPS retiree who chooses an RLA: Can switch back to PW at any time. Can only transfer to another RLA provider after at least 2 years; cannot return to PW. Receives variable monthly payments linked to fund performance. Must wait 12 months for the first payment. (B) Can only transfer to another RLA provider after at least 2 years; cannot return to PW. Why (B) is Correct The RLA is an irrevocable purchase. Once the RSA has been transferred to the life insurer and the annuity has commenced, the retiree cannot return to Programmed Withdrawal. The decision is final. A transfer between RLA providers (if dissatisfied with service) is possible but requires PenCom and NAICOM approval and is subject to a minimum holding period of approximately 2 years. This irrevocability is the product's primary protection design feature — the insurer can only price and guarantee lifetime income if it can reliably match long-duration assets against the lifetime liability. Why the Others Are Wrong (A) The RLA cannot be switched back to PW at any time — this is precisely why the PW-RLA decision requires careful financial guidance.(C) RLA income is fixed (or escalating at a defined rate) — it is not variable or fund-linked. Variability is the characteristic of Programmed Withdrawal (which depends on fund performance), not the RLA.(D) The first monthly payment typically commences within 30 days of fund receipt — not after a 12-month waiting period.

Ngozi, aged 62, has an RSA balance of ₦25 million at retirement. Her last monthly salary was ₦480,000. Use an annuity factor of 8.0 and an expense loading of 5%.
(a) Calculate the minimum residual RSA balance required after the lump sum withdrawal, based on the 50% minimum pension threshold.
(b) Calculate:
(i) the maximum lump sum;

(c) If Ngozi instead chooses PW with the full ₦25 million, explain the key risks she bears relative to the RLA option. Distinguish between an immediate and a deferred annuity. Explain how the CPS functions as a deferred annuity system during the working years. Describe PW and RLA as modes of accessing CPS retirement benefits and compare them across income certainty, investment risk, longevity risk, and estate benefit.   Immediate vs Deferred Annuity Immediate annuity: Income commences immediately (or within one payment period) following the purchase. The RLA is an immediate annuity — the retiree purchases with their RSA funds and the first payment arrives within 30 days.Deferred annuity: The benefit purchase or funding occurs now, but income commences at a future date (typically retirement age). During the deferral period, contributions accumulate at an agreed rate or in an investment fund, growing into a larger pot that will eventually produce income. The CPS as a Deferred Annuity System Throughout an employee's working life (typically 20–35 years of RSA contributions), the CPS functions economically as a deferred annuity accumulation system:• Each monthly contribution (18% of emoluments) is invested in the RSA by the PFA.• The fund grows through investment returns over the accumulation phase.• At retirement, the accumulated RSA balance represents the deferred annuity purchase price.• The retiree then 'annuitises' — converting the accumulated RSA into either an RLA (guaranteed lifetime income) or PW (managed drawdown).This two-phase structure (accumulation then decumulation) precisely mirrors the economic structure of a deferred annuity, though administered through separate regulated insti

The Annuity Factor The annuity factor (a_x) is the present value of a series of future payments of ₦1 per year (or per month) payable from a given age x until death. It combines two variables:1. Mortality: The probability of surviving to each future age (derived from the annuity mortality table, which shows how long annuitants are expected to live).2. PenCom data shows a persistent 3:1 preference for Programmed Withdrawal over the RLA. Critically evaluate the factors driving this preference and assess whether it represents an informed financial choice or a failure of consumer protection. Discuss steps that PenCom and the insurance industry should take to improve the quality of the PW-RLA decision for Nigerian retirees. The combination produces a systematic under-annuitisation that leaves a significant proportion of Nigerian retirees with material longevity risk they have not adequately priced. t: Chapter 9 · 9.1  Introduction: Insurance Through the Lens of Faith
x: In any market where religious conviction shapes economic behaviour, the structure of financial products matters as much as their function. For Nigeria's approximately 100 million Muslims — representing roughly 48% of the country's population, the largest Muslim population in sub-Saharan Africa — conventional insurance presents a theological problem. Insurance, as traditionally structured, involves elements that Islamic jurisprudence identifies as prohibited: the exchange of money for a contingent payment resembles gharar (excessive uncertainty); the premium paid to an insurer who may never pay a claim resembles maysir (gambling); and the investment of insurance premiums in interest-bearing instruments involves riba (interest). These are not merely technical objections — they represent a sincere religious position that prevents many Nigerian Muslims from participating in the conventional insurance market. The consequence is significant: a substantial fraction of Nigeria's uninsured population is uninsured not for reasons of affordability or awareness alone, but for reasons of conviction. Takaful — the Islamic cooperative risk-sharing framework — was developed precisely to provide a Shariah-compliant alternative: the financial security of insurance, structured in a way that is permissible under Islamic law. As Nigeria's Takaful market leader Noor Takaful observed at its October 2025 Partnership Event, Takaful has 'reached a turning point, shifting from a niche product to a mainstream, inclusion-driven growth engine' — and NIIRA 2025's recognition of non-interest insurance as a formally regulated category provides the structural legislative support to fulfil that potential.[4] This chapter treats Takaful not as an exotic speciality but as a co-equal member of Nigeria's life insurance product universe, warranting the same rigorous understanding that any CIIN candidate or insurance professional must bring to conventional life products. The chapter proceeds from the philosophical foundations through the practical mechanics — models, products, surplus distribution, governance — to the Nigerian market's current state and its regulatory framework under NIIRA 2025.

t: Chapter 9 · 9.2  The Philosophical and Religious Basis of Takaful
x: 9.2.1 Islamic Commercial Law and the Three Prohibitions The foundation of Takaful lies in Islamic commercial law (fiqh al-muamalat) and specifically in the Shariah principles governing permissible financial transactions. Three elements render conventional insurance impermissible under classical Islamic jurisprudence: Riba (Prohibition of Interest) Riba is the Arabic term for interest or usury — the predetermined, guaranteed return on a loan or investment regardless of the outcome of the transaction. Islamic commercial law prohibits Riba in all its forms, based on Quranic injunctions (Q 2:275–279; Q 3:130) and Hadith. Conventional insurance engages Riba by investing policyholders' premium funds in interest-bearing instruments (government bonds, fixed deposits, corporate debt). Takaful addresses this by investing all participant and operator funds exclusively in Shariah-compliant assets — sukuk (Islamic bonds), Murabaha contracts, equity in halal businesses, real estate — that generate returns without interest. Source: IFSB-8, Guiding Principles on Governance for Takaful Undertakings (2009). Gharar (Prohibition of Excessive Uncertainty) Gharar refers to excessive uncertainty, ambiguity, or risk in a contractual transaction — a contract whose terms, outcomes, or subject matter are insufficiently defined. Classical scholars identified Gharar in conventional insurance because the insured pays a premium (certain outflow) in exchange for a contingent payment that may never materialise. The exchange is characterised by radical uncertainty about what, if anything, the insured will receive. Takaful addresses Gharar by replacing the exchange contract with a donation (Tabarru') contract: the participant donates to a mutual pool to help other participants; there is no expectation of a personal return, and therefore no unconscionable uncertainty. Note: Not all uncertainty is prohibited — only excessive or deceptive uncertainty that leads to injustice between parties. Maysir (Prohibition of Gambling) Maysir is the Arabic term for gambling or speculation — a zero-sum transaction where one party's gain is another's loss, based on chance rather than productive activity. The Quran explicitly prohibits Maysir (Q 5:90). Conventional insurance has been characterised by some Islamic scholars as resembling Maysir because the insured 'bets' on suffering a loss (if the loss occurs, the insured receives much more than the premium; if it does not, the insured loses the premium entirely). Takaful eliminates the gambling character by treating all contributions as donations (Tabarru') and by ensuring that no individual participant 'wins' at the expense of another — the pool supports all members jointly. See also: Gharar above. In practice, Riba, Gharar, and Maysir often appear together in scholarly analysis of conventional insurance's Shariah concerns. 9.2.2 The Takaful Concept: Mutual Cooperative Risk-Sharing Takaful resolves the Shariah concerns of conventional insurance by replacing the bilateral exchange contract (premium for contingent payment) with a multilateral cooperative arrangement founded on three Islamic principles: Ta'awun (Mutual Cooperation): Members of the Takaful pool agree to support and assist one another in times of need. The Quranic injunction to 'cooperate in righteousness and piety' (Q 5:2) is the scriptural foundation for the cooperative insurance concept. Tabarru' (Donation/Contribution): Each participant donates a portion of their contribution to the mutual pool, specifically intending to assist other participants who suffer losses. The donation character eliminates Gharar — the participant is not exchanging money for an uncertain return but donating to a communal pool. Crucially, the participant retains no proprietary interest in the amount donated; it belongs to the pool and its beneficiaries. Wakalah or Mudarabah (Agency or Profit-Sharing): The Takaful operator — the company that manages the pool — does so under one of the Shariah-compliant management contracts discussed in Section 9.4. The operator receives compensation for its management services in a structured, predetermined, and Shariah-compliant manner. Takaful A Shariah-compliant insurance model based on the principles of mutual cooperation (Ta'awun) and voluntary donation (Tabarru'), under which participants contribute to a communal pool from which claims are paid to those who suffer losses. The Takaful operator manages the pool as an agent (Wakeel) or entrepreneur (Mudarib) and receives a fee or profit share for its services. Unlike conventional insurance, the Takaful fund belongs to the participants, not to the operator. The operator's profit comes from management fees and/or investment profit-sharing, not from the underwriting surplus. NAICOM definition (Operational Guidelines 2013): Takaful is 'a scheme based on brotherhood, solidarity, and mutual assistance which provides for mutual financial aid and assistance to the participants in case of need whereby the participants mutually agree to contribute for that purpose.' 9.2.3 The Structural Difference from Conventional Insurance Feature Conventional Insurance Takaful Legal basis of contribution Premium: a contractual payment for risk transfer. Certain outflow, uncertain return. Tabarru': a donation to the mutual pool. No expectation of return — contribution is an act of charity and cooperation. Ownership of the fund Belongs to the insurer (policyholder has only a contractual right to claim) Belongs to the participants (the Takaful operator manages it as agent or entrepreneur) Source of operator profit Underwriting profit (premium surplus after claims and expenses) + investment income on policyholder funds Management fees (Wakalah) and/or share of investment profit (Mudarabah) — NOT the underwriting surplus, which belongs to participants Treatment of underwriting surplus Insurer's profit — retained or distributed to shareholders Participants' surplus — returned to participants (those who did not claim) after reserves and the operator's agreed share are deducted Investment of funds Conventional instruments including interest-bearing securities Shariah-compliant only: Sukuk, Murabaha, halal equity, real estate — no Riba-bearing instruments Governance Board of Directors + external auditors Board of Directors + Shariah Advisory Council (Advisory Council of Experts) — Shariah compliance is a parallel governance requirement NAICOM categorisation Life insurance or non-life insurance Non-interest insurance (statutory term under NIIRA 2025); formerly categorised under Takaful Insurance Operations Guidelines (2013)

t: Chapter 9 · 9.3  Family Takaful and General Takaful
x: 9.3.1 The Two Branches of Takaful Like conventional insurance, Takaful divides into two broad product categories that mirror the life/non-life distinction: Family Takaful (the Shariah-compliant equivalent of life assurance and related products) and General Takaful (the Shariah-compliant equivalent of property, motor, marine, and other general insurance products). In Nigeria, NAICOM licenses Takaful operators as composite operators — authorised to write both Family and General Takaful under a single licence — reflecting the NAICOM 2013 Guidelines' composite structure. 9.3.2 Family Takaful Family Takaful provides Shariah-compliant protection and savings products for individual participants and their families. A Family Takaful plan is analogous to a participating (with-profit) life assurance product: the participant's contribution is divided into two components. The first is the Tabarru' donation — credited to the Participants' Risk Fund (PRF) and used to pay death and disability claims to participants who suffer losses. The second is the savings/investment component — credited to the Participants' Investment Fund (PIF) and invested in Shariah-compliant instruments on behalf of the participant.[9] At the end of the Family Takaful plan (maturity or earlier death), the participant or their beneficiary receives the Tabarru'-funded benefit (from the PRF) and the accumulated investment value (from the PIF) — the Takaful equivalent of a with-profit endowment maturity or death claim. If the participant survives the plan term, no Tabarru' claim is made and the full investment fund is returned — an important structural difference from term assurance where no benefit is payable on survival. Family Takaful The Shariah-compliant equivalent of life assurance. A Family Takaful plan provides death and disability cover (funded from the Participants' Risk Fund via Tabarru' donations) and a savings/investment component (accumulated in the Participants' Investment Fund) in a single product. At maturity or on death, the participant or beneficiary receives both the risk fund benefit and the accumulated investment. Family Takaful plans are available for protection, education funding, retirement savings, mortgage cover, and critical illness. Note: The investment component of Family Takaful is invested only in Shariah-compliant instruments. Investment returns are earned on the Mudarabah or Wakalah basis depending on the model used. Family Takaful product types available in the Nigerian market include: Protection plans (Term Takaful): Provides a death benefit for a specified period funded entirely from the Tabarru' donation. Analogous to term assurance. On survival to the end of the term, no benefit is payable — this is the purest protection product. Savings and protection plans (Investment-linked Family Takaful): Combines a Tabarru'-funded death benefit with a Shariah-compliant investment fund. Analogous to a whole life or endowment plan. The most common Family Takaful product type in Nigeria. Education Takaful: Designed to fund a child's education. Structured as a savings plan with death cover and a premium waiver feature — if the participant (parent) dies, the plan continues funded from the pool. Retirement/Pension Takaful: A deferred savings plan accumulating a retirement fund in Shariah-compliant assets, with death and disability protection during the accumulation phase. Mortgage Takaful (Home Finance Takaful): Provides Tabarru'-funded cover to settle the outstanding Islamic home finance balance on the participant's death or total disability — the Takaful equivalent of decreasing term mortgage protection. Critical Illness Takaful: Pays a lump-sum benefit from the PRF if the participant is diagnosed with a specified critical illness. Increasingly offered by Nigerian Takaful operators as a rider to the basic savings plan. 9.3.3 General Takaful General Takaful provides Shariah-compliant cover for material assets, liabilities, and other non-life risks. The Tabarru' mechanism operates in the same way as for Family Takaful: participants donate to a mutual pool, and the pool pays claims to participants who suffer covered losses. General Takaful products include: Motor Takaful: The Shariah-compliant equivalent of motor insurance, covering damage to the participant's vehicle and liability to third parties from road traffic accidents. In Nigeria, Motor Takaful satisfies the compulsory motor third party liability requirement under NIIRA 2025. Property/Fire Takaful: Covers damage to buildings and contents from fire, flood, and other specified perils. Analogous to property/fire insurance. Marine Takaful: Covers goods in transit and marine hulls on a Shariah-compliant basis. Relevant to Nigeria's import/export sector. Engineering Takaful: Covers construction, plant, and machinery risks on an Islamic basis. Liability Takaful: Covers public liability, employers' liability, and professional indemnity on a Shariah-compliant basis — including the compulsory employers' liability and public building liability classes under NIIRA 2025. Health Takaful: Provides Shariah-compliant medical expense cover and hospitalisation benefits. Noor Takaful's Noor Health product, launched in 2024, is the leading Nigerian example.

NAICOM's Operational Guidelines 2013 permit three models for Takaful operations in Nigeria: the Mudarabah model, the Wakalah model, and the Wakalah-Mudarabah hybrid. The Waqf model — permitted in some jurisdictions — is not explicitly authorised under the 2013 Guidelines but is discussed here for its theoretical importance and its presence in international Takaful markets. Each model defines how the Takaful operator is compensated, how the participants' fund is managed, and how the underwriting surplus is distributed.[2][7] 9.4.1 The Mudarabah Model Under the Mudarabah model, the Takaful operator acts as the Mudarib — the entrepreneur who manages both the underwriting operations and the investment of the participants' fund on a profit-sharing basis. The participants are the Rab al-Mal (capital providers). The operator receives no fixed fee; instead, it shares in the underwriting surplus and the investment profit according to a pre-agreed ratio (e.g. 60:40 between participants and operator, or 70:30).[12] The Mudarabah model has the advantage of aligning the operator's interests with participants' welfare — if the fund performs poorly, the operator earns nothing. However, it creates ambiguity about the operator's remuneration from the underwriting (risk fund) versus the investment fund, and the AAOIFI (Accounting and Auditing Organisation for Islamic Financial Institutions) and IFSB standards note that applying Mudarabah to the underwriting fund is technically complex, since the underwriting surplus is not purely an investment return. Concept in Practice — Mudarabah Takaful — A Simplified Flow 1. Participant pays contribution → a portion goes to the Participants' Risk Fund (PRF) as Tabarru'. 2. The remaining portion goes to the Participants' Investment Fund (PIF). 3. The Takaful operator (Mudarib) manages both the PRF and the PIF. Claims are paid from the PRF. 4. At year-end: PRF surplus (if any) is shared between participants and the operator per the pre-agreed Mudarabah ratio (e.g. 70% participants, 30% operator). 5. PIF investment returns are similarly distributed between the participants (as capital providers) and the operator (as entrepreneur) per the pre-agreed ratio. 6. If the PRF is in deficit, the operator may provide a Qard (interest-free loan) to the fund, repayable from future surpluses. 9.4.2 The Wakalah Model Under the Wakalah model, the Takaful operator acts purely as the Wakeel — the agent of the participants — managing the Takaful fund for a fixed management fee (the Wakalah fee). The Wakalah fee is charged as a percentage of the total contribution, agreed at the outset and approved by the Shariah Advisory Council. The operator does not share in the underwriting surplus or the investment returns; these belong entirely to the participants. However, the operator meets its own management expenses from the Wakalah fee.[11] The Wakalah model is structurally cleaner than the Mudarabah model because the operator's remuneration (the fixed fee) is clearly separated from the participants' fund. The operator's profit is predictable and does not fluctuate with the fund's performance — which removes the incentive to take excessive risk to generate a higher surplus share. The Wakalah model is the dominant model internationally and the most common model in NAICOM-licensed Nigerian Takaful operators. Wakalah Fee The fixed fee charged by a Takaful operator acting as Wakeel (agent) for managing the Takaful fund, expressed as a percentage of the total contribution received. The fee rate is fixed annually in advance and approved by the Shariah Advisory Council. It compensates the operator for underwriting operations management, administration, and regulatory compliance. In the pure Wakalah model, the operator's remuneration is limited to the Wakalah fee; it does not participate in underwriting surplus or investment returns. Typical Wakalah fee: 15–30% of gross contribution, depending on the product type and the operator's cost structure. Approval of the Shariah Advisory Council required. 9.4.3 The Hybrid (Wakalah-Mudarabah) Model The hybrid Wakalah-Mudarabah model combines the two pure models: the operator charges a Wakalah fee for managing the underwriting operations (the risk fund) and also participates as Mudarib in the investment profit generated from the Participants' Investment Fund. This is the most commercially sophisticated model: the operator earns a fixed fee for the technical insurance work and an additional profit-sharing return if investment performance is strong.[8] The hybrid model is permitted under NAICOM's 2013 Takaful Guidelines and is used by several Nigerian operators. Its advantage is that it incentivises the operator to generate strong investment returns (because it participates in investment profit) while maintaining transparency about the underwriting management fee (the fixed Wakalah component). The key requirement is that the basis for both components — the Wakalah fee rate and the Mudarabah profit-sharing ratio — must be disclosed to participants and approved by the Shariah Advisory Council before any contribution period begins. 9.4.4 The Waqf Model The Waqf model is a more advanced Takaful structure in which the risk fund is established as a Waqf — an Islamic endowment under which an asset is dedicated permanently to a charitable or specified purpose and cannot be withdrawn or distributed to the donor. Under this model, the Takaful operator (or the initial founders) establish the Waqf fund by donating a seed amount, which is permanently dedicated to the Takaful risk pool. Participants' Tabarru' donations augment the Waqf fund, which is used to pay claims. The operator manages the Waqf fund as Wakeel and invests it on a Mudarabah basis.[13] The Waqf model has the cleanest Shariah structure — the risk fund is formally a charitable endowment rather than a commercial fund — but it is the most complex to implement and the least common in practice. Pakistan's Takaful market has adopted the Waqf model widely; it is rare in West Africa. The NAICOM 2013 Guidelines do not explicitly permit or prohibit the Waqf model; it would require a specific product filing and Shariah Council certification to be offered in Nigeria. Model Operator Compensation Surplus Distribution Nigerian Status Mudarabah Pre-agreed share of underwriting surplus and investment profit. No fixed fee. Shared between participants and operator per agreed ratio. Operator bears reputational risk of zero earnings in deficit years. Permitted under NAICOM 2013 Guidelines; less common in practice. Wakalah Fixed Wakalah fee (% of contributions). No share of surplus or investment returns. Underwriting surplus belongs entirely to participants. Operator earns only the fixed fee. Permitted and most commonly used by Nigerian Takaful operators. Hybrid (Wakalah-Mudarabah) Fixed Wakalah fee for underwriting management + Mudarabah share of investment profit.
