Not explicitly permitted in NAICOM 2013; requires case-by-case NAICOM and Shariah approval.

9.5.1 Separation of Funds A fundamental structural requirement of Takaful — whether under the Mudarabah, Wakalah, or hybrid model — is the strict separation of the Takaful participants' funds from the Takaful operator's shareholders' fund. This separation is not merely a governance preference; it is a Shariah necessity. The participants' Tabarru' donations belong to the pool, not to the operator's shareholders. Commingling the funds would transform the Takaful structure into something equivalent to conventional insurance, where the insurer owns the premium. NAICOM's 2013 Takaful Guidelines require every licensed Takaful operator to maintain separate accounting and investment records for: The Participants' Risk Fund (PRF): Also called the Participants' Takaful Fund or the Tabarru' Pool. Funded by participants' Tabarru' donations. Used to pay claims. Subject to a separate Shariah-compliant investment policy. Any surplus at the end of the period is available for distribution to participants. The Participants' Investment Fund (PIF): The savings/investment component of the contribution for Family Takaful plans. Belongs to each individual participant. Invested in Shariah-compliant assets on Mudarabah or Wakalah basis. Returned to the participant at maturity, on earlier withdrawal, or on death. The Shareholders' Fund (SF): The operator's own capital and retained earnings. Funded by Wakalah fees, Mudarabah profit shares, and equity contributions. Shareholder dividends are paid from the SF, not from the participants' funds. 9.5.2 The Qard (Interest-Free Loan) Mechanism A critical structural feature of the PRF is the Qard — the interest-free loan mechanism for managing fund deficits. If the PRF is in deficit at the end of any period (because claims and expenses exceeded contributions), the Takaful operator is required to provide an interest-free loan (Qard) from the Shareholders' Fund to the PRF to restore solvency. The Qard is repayable from future surpluses of the PRF — not from participants' future contributions. This mechanism ensures that participants' claims are always paid even when the PRF is temporarily in deficit, while maintaining the prohibition on interest: the loan is provided at zero interest. The Qard mechanism is a significant protection for participants — it ensures that a run of bad claims experience does not result in the fund being unable to pay benefits. It is also a significant financial obligation for the operator's Shareholders' Fund, and it is one reason why NAICOM's minimum capital requirements for Takaful operators must be sufficient to absorb Qard obligations in adverse years.

The distribution of the underwriting surplus — the amount remaining in the PRF after all claims, reserves, and the operator's agreed share are deducted — is one of the most commercially important and Shariah-sensitive aspects of Takaful operations. It is the feature that most visibly differentiates Takaful from conventional insurance (where the premium surplus belongs to shareholders) and the feature most valued by participants. 9.6.1 The Basis for Surplus Distribution In conventional insurance, the relationship between the premium collected and the claims paid is straightforward: if premiums exceed claims and expenses, the surplus is the insurer's profit. In Takaful, the Tabarru' donations paid to the PRF belong to the participants. If fewer claims are made than expected — if the pool has a surplus — the Islamic principle of equitable treatment requires that the surplus be returned to those who contributed it, subject to the deduction of the operator's agreed share and the maintenance of adequate reserves. The Shariah basis for this distribution lies in the non-commercial character of the Tabarru' donation: the participant donated to help others, not to enrich the operator. If the donation was not needed in full, the residual is returned — subject to Shariah supervision to ensure the distribution methodology is fair and transparent. 9.6.2 Mechanics of Surplus Distribution in Nigeria NAICOM's 2013 Takaful Guidelines require that the surplus distribution methodology be approved by the Shariah Advisory Council before the scheme year begins and be disclosed to participants. The standard Nigerian practice is: Claims and IBNR reserves are deducted from the PRF for the period. Retakaful recoverables are added back to the PRF. The operator's agreed share of surplus (under the Mudarabah or hybrid model) is deducted. A reserve for future contingencies (typically 10–30% of gross surplus) is retained in the PRF. The remaining surplus is distributed to participants who did not make claims during the year, on a pro-rata basis relative to their Tabarru' contributions. Illustration — Surplus Distribution — A Worked Example PRF Item Amount (₦) Total Tabarru' contributions received 50,000,000 Claims paid during the year (18,000,000) IBNR reserves maintained (4,000,000) Retakaful recoveries 2,000,000 Gross underwriting surplus 30,000,000 Less: Operator's Mudarabah share (30%) (9,000,000) Less: Contingency reserve (15% of gross surplus) (4,500,000) Distributable surplus to participants 16,500,000 Number of non-claiming participants 1,000 Average surplus distribution per participant ₦16,500 This ₦16,500 surplus distribution is returned to each non-claiming participant — reducing the net cost of their Takaful cover for the year. A participant who paid ₦50,000 in Tabarru' and received ₦16,500 in surplus has an effective net cost of ₦33,500 for the year's risk protection. This surplus return is what the Noor Takaful Chairman described as 'demonstrating commitment to encouraging Nigerian participation in ethical insurance' when announcing surplus distributions of ₦12 million (2018) and ₦15 million (2019).

t: Chapter 9 · 9.7  The Shariah Advisory Council (Advisory Council of Experts)
x: 9.7.1 The Governance Requirement Every NAICOM-licensed Takaful operator is required by the 2013 Takaful Guidelines to establish a Shariah Advisory Council — also referred to in Nigerian practice as the Advisory Council of Experts (ACE). The Shariah Advisory Council is a body of qualified Islamic scholars who are responsible for all Shariah decisions, opinions, and views relating to the Takaful operation. It is the equivalent of an independent governance and compliance function specifically for Shariah matters — analogous to the audit committee for financial integrity but focused on religious compliance.[2] The Shariah Advisory Council's mandate includes: Approving all product designs, contribution structures, investment policies, surplus distribution methodologies, and marketing materials for Shariah compliance before they are used or marketed. Issuing Fatwa (Shariah rulings) on specific operational questions that arise in the course of business. Reviewing and approving the Wakalah fee rate, Mudarabah profit-sharing ratio, and Qard terms annually. Certifying the insurer's annual financial statements as Shariah-compliant. Reporting to the Board of Directors on Shariah compliance matters and recommending corrective action where deviations are identified. 9.7.2 Composition and Independence Requirements The Shariah Advisory Council must comprise qualified scholars — persons with recognised expertise in Islamic jurisprudence (fiqh) and specifically in Islamic finance and muamalat (commercial transactions). NAICOM requires a minimum of three scholars, with at least one holding academic qualifications in Shariah and at least one with practical expertise in Islamic finance. The scholars must be independent of the operator's management — they cannot hold executive positions, be shareholders, or have material commercial relationships with the operator that might compromise their independence. A practical challenge noted in NAICOM's own communications is the scarcity of qualified Shariah scholars with both religious and commercial finance expertise in Nigeria. The 2013 Guidelines recognised this by permitting operators in their initial stages to rely on NAICOM's own Takaful Advisory Council for Shariah decisions while building their independent councils. As the Nigerian Takaful market has matured, this transitional arrangement has been progressively replaced by independently constituted Advisory Councils. The international benchmark for Shariah governance in Takaful is the IFSB-8 standard (Guiding Principles on Governance for Takaful Undertakings, 2009), which requires that Shariah scholars serving on Takaful Advisory Councils have no conflicts of interest, rotate on a defined schedule, and report directly to the board rather than to management.

Re-Takaful is the Shariah-compliant equivalent of reinsurance — a mechanism by which a Takaful operator cedes a portion of the participants' risk to a specialised Re-Takaful entity, in exchange for a portion of the Tabarru' contributions. The Re-Takaful entity manages the ceded risks on the same Takaful principles (mutual cooperation, Tabarru', Shariah-compliant investment) as the primary Takaful operator. The rationale for Re-Takaful is identical to conventional reinsurance: a primary Takaful operator with a limited participants' pool needs to spread catastrophic risks beyond its own fund's capacity. A single large claim — a major fire, a ship loss, a catastrophic health event — could deplete the PRF if the primary operator bears it alone. Re-Takaful provides capacity and stability. Re-Takaful The Shariah-compliant equivalent of conventional reinsurance, under which a primary Takaful operator cedes a portion of the participants' risk to a Re-Takaful entity in exchange for a pro-rata share of the Tabarru' contributions. The Re-Takaful entity manages the ceded risk on Islamic cooperative principles, with a separate Shariah Advisory Council and Shariah-compliant investment of funds. Re-Takaful is essential for Takaful operators writing large or catastrophic risks. Note: In the absence of adequate Re-Takaful capacity (a persistent challenge globally), some Shariah Advisory Councils have issued conditional Fatwa permitting temporary use of conventional reinsurance where no Shariah-compliant alternative is available — subject to review as Re-Takaful capacity develops. Re-Takaful capacity in West Africa and specifically in Nigeria is limited. The principal global Re-Takaful entities — including Swiss Re Takaful, Munich Re Takaful, and a small number of specialised Islamic Re-Takaful companies — are the primary sources of capacity. NAICOM's 2013 Guidelines permit Nigerian Takaful operators to use conventional reinsurance as a temporary measure where Re-Takaful capacity is unavailable, subject to a specific ruling from the operator's Shariah Advisory Council on the permissibility of this approach in the specific circumstances. NIIRA 2025's domestic cession requirements apply to Takaful operators as well as conventional insurers — a portion of the risk must be ceded to domestic reinsurers before any international cession.

t: Chapter 9 · 9.9  The Nigerian Takaful Market: History and Current State
x: 9.9.1 Historical Development The history of Takaful in Nigeria follows a pattern of gradual regulatory development and progressive market entry. The timeline is as follows:[1][3] Year/Period Development 2003 The Halal Mutual Concept is introduced — the first Takaful-style offering in Nigeria, structured informally by a cooperative group. It offered family Takaful-style protection with a savings component. 2004–2012 Niger Insurance introduces Niger Mutual Halal Plus — the first named Takaful-style product from a licensed insurer. Cornerstone Insurance establishes Halal Takaful Nigeria, a Takaful window operation offering both Family and General Takaful. 2013 NAICOM issues the Operational Guidelines 2013 Takaful — Insurance Operation — the first formal national Takaful regulatory framework. Three models permitted: Mudarabah, Wakalah, Wakalah-Mudarabah. Shariah Advisory Council (ACE) requirement introduced. Cornerstone becomes the first licensed composite Takaful operator. 2016 NAICOM licenses the first two full standalone Takaful companies: Noor Takaful Insurance Limited (April 2016 — first full-fledged composite Takaful operator with 100% Nigerian shareholding) and Jaiz Takaful Insurance Plc. 2019 NAICOM grants Approval in Principle to two more Takaful operators: Cornerstone Takaful Insurance Company Limited and Salam Takaful Insurance Company Limited — bringing the total to four licensed standalone Takaful companies. 2020–2022 The four operators build their portfolios. Jaiz Takaful achieves 85% contribution growth (2018–2019). Noor Takaful declares surplus distributions. NAICOM receives additional Takaful licence applications. 2024 Noor Takaful launches Noor Health — Nigeria's first Shariah-compliant health insurance product targeting both Muslims and non-Muslims. 2025 (August) NIIRA 2025 signed. Non-interest insurance (Takaful) is formally recognised as a statutory insurance category. NAICOM's authority to regulate Takaful is preserved and strengthened. Industry expects the Act to attract further capital into the Takaful space. 9.9.2 The Four Licensed Takaful Operators Institution Profile — Noor Takaful Insurance Limited Established: April 2016 — first full-fledged standalone composite Takaful operator in Nigeria Shareholding: 100% indigenous Nigerian ownership Position: Pioneer and market leader in Nigerian Takaful; works closely with NAICOM on Takaful structure and promotion Products: Family Takaful (protection, savings, education); General Takaful (motor, property, marine, engineering, liability); Noor Health (Shariah-compliant health insurance, launched 2024) Surplus distributions: ₦12 million (2018) and ₦15 million (2019) — first public surplus distributions in Nigeria International partnership: Partners with International Shariah Research Academy for Islamic Finance (ISRA), Malaysia, for officer training NIIRA 2025 statement: 'Signing and implementing the NIIRA Act will strengthen participants' confidence and trust in fund safety, encourage stronger capital bases and create better insurance penetration.' Institution Profile — Jaiz Takaful Insurance Plc Established: 2016 (full operating licence) Parent: Related to Jaiz Bank Plc — Nigeria's first non-interest bank, providing synergy between Islamic banking and Takaful distribution Growth: Gross contributions: >₦408 million (2018) → >₦753 million (2019) — 85% growth; 80%+ retention of existing participants Position: Strong positioning in the northern Nigerian market where Jaiz Bank's branch network provides distribution reach Products: Family Takaful (savings and protection); General Takaful (motor, property, marine); group medical Takaful Institution Profile — Cornerstone Takaful Insurance Company Limited Background: Subsidiary of Cornerstone Insurance plc — a conventional insurer that operated a Takaful window (Halal Takaful Nigeria) since 2013 before hiving off to a standalone entity Approval in Principle: September 2019 Composite status: Licensed to write both Family Takaful and General Takaful Significance: First conventional insurer to transition from window to standalone Takaful — a model for other conventional insurers with Takaful ambitions Institution Profile — Salam Takaful Insurance Company Limited Approval in Principle: September 2019 Composite status: Licensed for both Family and General Takaful Position: Newer entrant; building product portfolio and distribution network Significance: Part of the second wave of Takaful licensing that doubled the number of operators in 2019 9.9.3 Market Size, Potential, and Challenges As of 2024, Nigeria's Takaful penetration stood at approximately 0.3% — even lower than the already low general insurance penetration rate of 0.4% of GDP. However, the industry's growth trajectory is encouraging: Jaiz Takaful's 85% contribution growth and Noor Takaful's surplus distributions demonstrate that Takaful products can achieve commercial viability. The industry projects penetration reaching 1.5% by 2030, driven by digital distribution, growing awareness of ethical finance, and the tailwinds of NIIRA 2025.[4] The structural opportunity is enormous: Nigeria's 100 million Muslims represent the world's sixth-largest Muslim population. If even 5% of Nigerian Muslim adults held a basic Family Takaful plan, the resulting portfolio would be several times larger than the current entire Takaful market. The barriers to capturing this opportunity include: Limited distribution reach into northern Nigeria where most of the Muslim population is concentrated. The conventional insurance distribution network is primarily urban and southern-focused. Low financial literacy and awareness of Takaful as a concept. Many northern Nigerian Muslims are unaware that Shariah-compliant insurance products exist. Capital limitations: the four licensed Takaful operators are small relative to the leading conventional insurers. NIIRA 2025's recapitalisation requirement (minimum ₦10 billion for life insurers, and the equivalent for composite Takaful operators) will require the Takaful sector to attract significant additional investment. Limited Shariah expertise for Advisory Councils. The supply of qualified Shariah scholars with financial expertise remains constrained. Re-Takaful capacity: limited domestic Re-Takaful capacity requires reliance on international markets, adding cost and complexity to large risk management. Advisory — Strategic Opportunities in Nigerian Takaful — For Practitioners and Operators The Nigerian Takaful market in 2025 presents one of the most compelling untapped opportunities in the African insurance landscape. Practitioners and operators should consider the following strategic imperatives: Bancatakaful: The partnership between Jaiz Bank and Jaiz Takaful illustrates the power of the bancatakaful distribution model. The 25+ branches of Jaiz Bank provide a pre-qualified Muslim customer base. Conventional banks with Islamic banking windows (CBN-licensed Non-Interest Banking products) represent an additional distribution channel for Family Takaful. Digital Takaful (Takatech): NAICOM's Insurtech licensing framework (Partnering Insurtech model at ₦10 million capital) creates a low-barrier entry point for digital Takaful distribution platforms. A Partnering Insurtech could build a USSD or mobile app interface for Takaful contributions and claims, partnering with a licensed Takaful operator to carry the risk. Employer-sponsored Family Takaful: The mandatory Group Life Insurance under PRA 2014 requires life cover but does not specify conventional insurance. Employers with predominantly Muslim workforces in northern Nigeria could satisfy their PRA 2014 group life obligation through a Group Family Takaful scheme — meeting both the legal requirement and the employees' religious preferences. Microinsurance integration: NAICOM's Microinsurance Guidelines permit low-ticket Takaful products (below the minimum ticket for conventional microinsurance). This creates a pathway to serve the mass market with Shariah-compliant protection at premium points accessible to the informal sector. NIIRA 2025 as catalyst: The Takaful industry should actively engage NAICOM in developing implementing regulations for non-interest insurance under NIIRA 2025, including specific capital requirements, investment guidelines, and consumer disclosure standards calibrated to the Takaful structural model.

t: Chapter 9 · 9.10  NIIRA 2025 and the Regulatory Framework for Non-Interest Insurance
x: 9.10.1 NIIRA 2025: Takaful as Non-Interest Insurance NIIRA 2025 uses the term 'non-interest insurance' as the statutory equivalent of Takaful — a neutral and inclusive formulation that encompasses all Shariah-compliant insurance models without requiring the specific theological label of 'Takaful' in primary legislation. This terminological choice reflects Nigeria's constitutional requirement for religious neutrality in legislation: calling the product 'Islamic insurance' would raise questions about the state's relationship with a specific religion.[17] The practical effect of NIIRA 2025's non-interest insurance provisions is: Legal recognition: Non-interest insurance is a formal statutory insurance category. This gives Takaful operators the same legal standing as conventional insurers and provides a clear legislative basis for NAICOM's Takaful-specific regulations. Preserved NAICOM authority: NAICOM's power to issue guidelines, approve products, license operators, and supervise non-interest insurance operations is preserved and strengthened under NIIRA 2025. Consumer protection: Takaful participants benefit from the same consumer protection framework as conventional insurance policyholders — including NIIRA 2025's mandatory 60-day claims settlement timeline, the Insurance Policyholders' Protection Fund (IPPF), and NAICOM's complaints redress mechanism. Recapitalisation: Takaful operators are subject to NIIRA 2025's recapitalisation requirements. A composite Takaful operator (writing both Family and General Takaful) is categorised as a composite insurer for capital purposes (minimum ₦25 billion by 30 July 2026), while a Family-only Takaful operator is categorised as a life insurer (minimum ₦10 billion). Regulatory Spotlight — NIIRA 2025 — Non-Interest Insurance: Key Implications for Takaful Operators NIIRA 2025's treatment of non-interest (Takaful) insurance has the following direct operational implications: Capital adequacy: Composite Takaful operators must meet the ₦25 billion composite minimum capital by 30 July 2026. Given the current scale of Nigerian Takaful operators, this may necessitate mergers, capital injections from Islamic investors, or strategic partnerships with conventional insurers. Product approval: All Takaful products must be filed with and approved by NAICOM — including the Shariah Advisory Council's certification of compliance. NAICOM will not approve any product that has not been certified as Shariah-compliant by a qualified ACE. Consumer disclosure: Takaful operators must provide the same minimum disclosures to participants as conventional insurers to policyholders: summary of benefits, exclusions, contribution obligations, surplus distribution methodology, and the cooling-off right. Claims settlement: The 60-day claims settlement mandate applies to Takaful operators. Surplus distribution must occur within the period specified in the Takaful product terms and approved by the Shariah Advisory Council. IPPF contributions: Takaful operators are required to contribute to the Insurance Policyholders' Protection Fund (IPPF) — the Act sets the levy at 0.25% of the gross premium income of every insurer and reinsurer (s.212); its application to Family Takaful contributions follows NAICOM regulation. This provides a safety net for Takaful participants if an operator becomes insolvent. Industry perspective: Noor Takaful's leadership publicly welcomed NIIRA 2025, stating that the Act 'will strengthen participants' confidence and trust in fund safety, encourage stronger capital bases to underwrite larger risks, and create better insurance penetration.' This positive reception reflects the industry's view that stronger regulation — not weaker — is what the Takaful market needs to build the trust and scale that its enormous demographic opportunity demands.[18]

Takaful is a Shariah-compliant insurance model based on the Islamic principles of Ta'awun (mutual cooperation), Tabarru' (donation to the risk pool), and either Wakalah (agency) or Mudarabah (profit-sharing) for the operator's compensation. It avoids the three elements of Riba (interest), Gharar (excessive uncertainty), and Maysir (gambling) that Islamic jurisprudence identifies as rendering conventional insurance impermissible. Family Takaful (the equivalent of life assurance) and General Takaful (the equivalent of non-life insurance) are the two branches of the Takaful product universe. Family Takaful plans combine a Tabarru'-funded death and disability benefit (from the Participants' Risk Fund) with a Shariah-compliant savings component (in the Participants' Investment Fund). NAICOM's 2013 Takaful Operational Guidelines permit three models: the Mudarabah model (operator shares in surplus and investment profit), the Wakalah model (operator charges a fixed agency fee only), and the Hybrid Wakalah-Mudarabah model (fixed Wakalah fee plus Mudarabah investment profit share). The Wakalah model is the most common in Nigeria. The Waqf model is not currently permitted under NAICOM's guidelines. The underwriting surplus of the Participants' Risk Fund belongs to the participants, not the operator. NAICOM requires surplus distribution methodology to be approved by the Shariah Advisory Council before each year begins. Noor Takaful distributed ₦12 million (2018) and ₦15 million (2019) as surplus to participants — tangible proof of the Takaful model's differentiation from conventional insurance. Every NAICOM-licensed Takaful operator must establish a Shariah Advisory Council (Advisory Council of Experts) comprising qualified Islamic scholars responsible for all Shariah decisions. The Council must be independent of management, and its approval is required for all products, investment policies, fee structures, and financial statements. The Qard (interest-free loan) mechanism ensures that the PRF can pay claims even in deficit years — the operator provides a zero-interest loan from the Shareholders' Fund, repayable from future surpluses. Nigeria currently has four NAICOM-licensed standalone Takaful operators: Noor Takaful Insurance Limited (first, 2016; 100% Nigerian-owned; market leader), Jaiz Takaful Insurance Plc (2016; Jaiz Bank affiliate), Cornerstone Takaful Insurance Company Limited (AIP 2019; conventional insurer subsidiary), and Salam Takaful Insurance Company Limited (AIP 2019). Re-Takaful is the Shariah-compliant equivalent of reinsurance, providing capacity management for Takaful operators. Domestic Re-Takaful capacity in Nigeria is limited; operators rely primarily on international Re-Takaful entities. NIIRA 2025's domestic cession requirements apply. NIIRA 2025 uses the term 'non-interest insurance' as the statutory category encompassing Takaful, giving it full legal recognition alongside conventional insurance. All NIIRA 2025 consumer protection provisions apply: 60-day claims settlement, IPPF contributions, product approval, and consumer disclosure requirements.

Takaful A Shariah-compliant cooperative insurance model based on mutual cooperation (Ta'awun) and voluntary donation (Tabarru'). The participants' fund belongs to the participants; the operator earns a management fee (Wakalah) or profit share (Mudarabah), not the underwriting surplus. Riba Arabic for interest or usury — the predetermined guaranteed return on a loan or investment. Prohibited in Islamic commercial law. Avoided in Takaful by investing exclusively in Shariah-compliant, non-interest-bearing instruments. Gharar Excessive uncertainty or ambiguity in a contractual transaction. A basis for the Islamic objection to conventional insurance. Avoided in Takaful by replacing the exchange contract with a Tabarru' donation. Maysir Gambling or speculation — a zero-sum transaction based on chance. A basis for the Islamic objection to conventional insurance. Avoided in Takaful because participants donate cooperatively rather than betting on outcomes. Tabarru' A voluntary donation to the Takaful risk pool with the charitable intention of assisting fellow participants who suffer losses. The legal basis for Shariah-compliant risk-sharing. Replaces the conventional insurance premium. Family Takaful The Shariah-compliant equivalent of life assurance. Combines a Tabarru'-funded death and disability benefit (PRF) with a Shariah-compliant savings component (PIF) in a single product. General Takaful The Shariah-compliant equivalent of non-life insurance, covering material assets, liabilities, motor, marine, engineering, and health on cooperative risk-sharing principles. Participants' Risk Fund (PRF) The mutual pool funded by participants' Tabarru' donations. Used to pay claims. Any surplus at the end of the year is distributable to participants. Belongs to the participants, not the operator. Participants' Investment Fund (PIF) The savings/investment component of a Family Takaful plan. Belongs to the individual participant. Invested in Shariah-compliant instruments. Returned at maturity, withdrawal, or death. Shareholders' Fund (SF) The Takaful operator's own capital and retained earnings. Funded by Wakalah fees, Mudarabah profit shares, and equity. Source of the Qard (interest-free loan) facility for the PRF. Mudarabah Model Takaful operational model under which the operator acts as Mudarib (entrepreneur), sharing the underwriting surplus and investment profit with participants per a pre-agreed ratio. No fixed fee. Wakalah Model Takaful operational model under which the operator acts as Wakeel (agent), charging a fixed fee (Wakalah fee) for managing the fund. Does not share in underwriting surplus or investment returns. Hybrid (Wakalah-Mudarabah) Model Takaful model combining a Wakalah fee for underwriting management and a Mudarabah profit-sharing arrangement for investment management. Qard An interest-free loan from the Takaful operator's Shareholders' Fund to the Participants' Risk Fund in the event of a PRF deficit. Repayable from future PRF surpluses. Ensures claims can always be paid. Shariah Advisory Council (ACE) The Advisory Council of Experts — the body of qualified Islamic scholars required in every NAICOM-licensed Takaful operator. Responsible for all Shariah compliance decisions. Must be independent of management. Surplus Distribution The return to participants of the underwriting surplus remaining in the PRF after claims, reserves, and the operator's agreed share. The feature that most visibly differentiates Takaful from conventional insurance. Re-Takaful The Shariah-compliant equivalent of conventional reinsurance. Takaful operators cede portions of participants' risks to Re-Takaful entities operating on Islamic cooperative principles. Non-Interest Insurance The statutory term used in NIIRA 2025 for Shariah-compliant (Takaful) insurance, providing formal legal recognition as an insurance category under Nigerian law.

The Shariah prohibition Takaful addresses by investing only in non-interest-bearing assets is: Gharar (excessive uncertainty). Maysir (gambling). Riba (interest or usury). Qard (interest-free loan). (C) Riba (interest or usury). Why (C) is Correct Riba is the Shariah prohibition on receiving or paying interest. Conventional life insurance invests premium funds in interest-bearing instruments (bonds, bank deposits, treasury bills) — all of which involve Riba and are therefore prohibited for observant Muslims. Takaful operators invest exclusively in Shariah-compliant assets (FGN Sukuk, Shariah-screened equities, commodity Murabaha, Musharakah-structured real estate) to ensure no investment income derived from interest flows through the product. Why the Others Are Wrong (A) Gharar (excessive uncertainty) is a separate Shariah prohibition addressed by the Tabarru' donation structure — participants donate to a mutual pool rather than paying premiums in exchange for a specific personal uncertain benefit, reducing the uncertainty element.(B) Maysir (gambling) is addressed by the cooperative, non-profit orientation of the Participants' Risk Fund — participants are not 'betting' on their death but mutually assisting each other.(D) Qard is an interest-free loan — it is a Shariah-compliant financing mechanism that Takaful operators may use to address PRF deficits, not the prohibition the investment policy is designed to avoid.

Under the Wakalah Takaful model, the Takaful operator's compensation is: A share of the underwriting surplus of the PRF. A fixed fee (the Wakalah fee) as a percentage of contributions. A share of investment returns from the Participants' Investment Fund. Both a Wakalah fee and a share of investment returns. (B) A fixed fee (the Wakalah fee) as a percentage of contributions. Why (B) is Correct Under the Wakalah (agency) model, the operator acts as agent (Wakil) for the participants in managing the PRF. The compensation is a pre-agreed fixed fee — the Wakalah fee — expressed as a percentage of contributions (typically 15–35%). This fee is earned regardless of underwriting outcome: the operator receives the Wakalah fee whether the PRF generates a surplus or a deficit. The entire underwriting surplus (if any) belongs to the participants. Why the Others Are Wrong (A) describes the Mudarabah model where the operator shares in the PRF underwriting surplus — a separate and distinct compensation structure.(C) A share of investment returns from the PIF is the investment management fee — a separate charge under both Mudarabah and Wakalah models for managing the savings/investment component of Family Takaful contributions.(D) describes the hybrid Wakalah-Mudarabah model used by some operators where a Wakalah fee is charged on contributions AND an investment profit share is taken on PIF returns — a third, distinct model.

Family Takaful is BEST described as: The Shariah-compliant equivalent of general (non-life) insurance. A cooperative savings scheme without any protection element. The Shariah-compliant equivalent of life assurance, combining a risk fund benefit with a savings component. A government-run pension scheme for public sector employees. (C) The Shariah-compliant equivalent of life assurance, combining a risk fund benefit with a savings component. Why (C) is Correct Family Takaful mirrors the structure of conventional life assurance but using Shariah-compliant mechanisms throughout. Each participant's contribution is split: (a) Tabarru' — a charitable donation to the Participants' Risk Fund that funds death and disability claims; (b) the balance is invested in the Participants' Investment Fund (PIF) for long-term savings accumulation. On death, the participant's family receives both the PRF death benefit and the accumulated PIF balance. This dual protection + savings structure is the direct Islamic equivalent of a conventional with-profit life policy. Why the Others Are Wrong (A) General Takaful is the Shariah-compliant equivalent of non-life (general) insurance — covering motor, property, marine, and liability risks. Family Takaful corresponds to life assurance.(B) A savings-only scheme with no risk fund has no mutual protection element and is not Takaful. Takaful is fundamentally defined by its mutual risk-sharing component.(D) Government pension schemes are State-sponsored defined benefit or defined contribution arrangements. Takaful is commercially operated by NAICOM-licensed

The Participants' Risk Fund (PRF) in a Takaful scheme: Belongs to the Takaful operator's shareholders. Is funded by participants' Tabarru' donations and belongs to the participants. Is managed entirely by NAICOM. Cannot be used to pay claims in the first year. (B) Is funded by participants' Tabarru' donations and belongs to the participants. Why (B) is Correct The PRF is funded exclusively by the Tabarru' donations from participating members. These donations are unconditional gifts to the mutual pool — they do not belong to the operator's shareholders, and the operator has no proprietary claim on the PRF balance except as permitted by the agreed Mudarabah surplus share (under the Mudarabah model). The PRF belongs legally and beneficially to the participants collectively. This collective ownership is the foundation of Takaful's Shariah compliance. Why the Others Are Wrong (A) The operator's shareholders own the shareholders' fund — entirely separate from the PRF. Commingling of the PRF and shareholders' funds would violate NAICOM's Takaful window segregation requirements and NIIRA 2025's Takaful provisions.(C) NAICOM supervises the operator but does not own or manage the PRF — regulatory oversight does not constitute ownership or management of the insurance fund.(D) The PRF must be operational and funded from inception to pay claims as they arise. There is no first-year moratorium; the PRF must be capable of paying valid claims from day one.

How many full-fledged standalone Takaful operators are currently licensed by NAICOM in Nigeria? Two. Three. Four. Six. (B) Three. Several conventional insurers additionally operate Takaful windows within their existing composite or life licences.
