t: Chapter 10 · 10.1  Introduction: Why Product Design Matters
x: A life insurance product is not a commodity. Unlike a bank deposit, whose terms are fixed by the interest rate, or a government bond, whose coupon is set by the issuing authority, a life insurance product is an entirely constructed financial instrument. Every element — the benefit trigger, the premium rate, the policy term, the exclusion clauses, the bonus basis, the surrender value table — is a deliberate design decision made by the insurer's product development team. The quality of those decisions determines whether the product is actuarially sound, commercially viable, legally compliant, and genuinely suitable for the intended market. In Nigeria, the product development function carries a further dimension of importance: the country's insurance penetration rate of 0.4% of GDP reflects, among other things, a market that has historically been ill-served by poorly designed, inappropriately priced, or insufficiently accessible products. Policies that lapse at high rates in the first two years, products whose benefit illustrations set unrealistic expectations, and premium structures that are incompatible with monthly income cycles have all contributed to a pattern of policyholder disappointment that erodes trust across the market. Good product design is therefore not merely a technical function — it is a market-building function. This chapter examines the complete product development lifecycle for a Nigerian life insurance company, with emphasis on the actuarial pricing discipline, the NAICOM regulatory approval process under NIIRA 2025, the product governance framework, and the specific design challenges of credit life and health rider products — two of the most commercially significant product categories in the current market.

10.2.1 Overview The product development lifecycle (PDL) is the end-to-end process through which an insurance company transforms a business opportunity or consumer need into a market-ready, actuarially sound, and regulatorily approved product. Globally, the average time from concept to market for a life insurance risk product is approximately 7.1 months; for savings and living benefits products, the average is somewhat longer due to their actuarial complexity.[2] In the Nigerian market, NAICOM's product filing and approval requirement adds a mandatory regulatory phase to the timeline. A product that might be launched in a less regulated market within three months requires a minimum of four to five months in Nigeria when the filing and approval window is factored in. Organisations that build the regulatory timeline into their product development plan from the outset — rather than treating it as an afterthought — consistently achieve faster and smoother launches. Process — The Product Development Lifecycle — Seven Stages Stage 1: Strategic Concept: The product development committee or strategy function identifies a market opportunity, competitive gap, or regulatory requirement that warrants a new product or revision of an existing one. Questions addressed: What customer need is being met? What is the target segment? What is the expected volume? How does this product complement the existing portfolio? Stage 2: Market Research and Consumer Insight: Consumer research — including focus groups, agent surveys, and analysis of competitor offerings — refines the product concept. In Nigeria, field research in target markets (urban formal sector, northern Nigeria for Takaful, rural cooperatives for microinsurance) is essential for affordability and benefit design calibration. Stage 3: Technical Design: The actuarial team designs the product structure: benefit triggers, premium payment modes, policy term options, sum assured levels, riders available, surrender value basis, bonus basis (if participating), and exclusion clauses. A preliminary pricing model is constructed and first-pass premiums are calculated. Stage 4: Actuarial Pricing and Profit Testing: Full actuarial pricing is conducted (see Section 10.3). Best-estimate and loaded assumptions are set for all pricing variables. A profit-testing model projects the product's expected profitability over its lifetime under base, stress, and lapse scenarios. The statutory actuary reviews and signs off on the pricing basis. Stage 5: NAICOM Filing and Approval: The product filing document — including the actuarial pricing report, proposed policy wording, benefit illustration templates, and marketing materials — is submitted to NAICOM for approval. The 30-day deemed-approval clock begins on receipt. Stage 6: Systems, Operations, and Distribution Readiness: Policy Administration System (PAS) configuration, agent training, branch readiness, digital onboarding flows, and customer service scripts are prepared during the approval period. Marketing materials are aligned with the approved product wording. Stage 7: Launch and Post-Launch Monitoring: The product is launched. New business volumes, premium income, early lapse rates, and claims experience are monitored monthly in the first year. Actual experience is compared to pricing assumptions; material deviations trigger a product review. 10.2.2 The Product Development Steering Committee Best practice product development — as documented in RGA's global survey of life insurers — is governed by a dedicated Product Development Steering Committee (PDSC). The PDSC sets the company's annual product development agenda, manages the pipeline of products in development, provides cross-functional governance, and ensures that each product's business case is reviewed against the company's strategic objectives before significant development resources are committed.[2] The PDSC typically comprises: the Chief Executive Officer (or Chief Life Officer), the Chief Actuary/Head of Actuarial, the Head of Product Development, the Chief Underwriting Officer, the Head of Marketing, the Head of Sales/Distribution, the Chief Compliance Officer, and the Chief Financial Officer. Its mandate includes approving the product roadmap, reviewing profit test results, approving regulatory filing submissions, and signing off on launch authorisation. For NAICOM purposes, the PDSC's approval is part of the governance evidence required in the product filing package. 10.2.3 Time-to-Market Benchmarks Product Type Global Average (Concept to Launch) Nigerian Target (Including NAICOM Filing) Term assurance (pure risk) 5–7 months 7–10 months Endowment / savings plan 7–10 months 10–14 months Investment-linked (unit-linked) 9–12 months 12–18 months (additional SEC coordination) Group life scheme 3–4 months 5–6 months Credit life (bank/fintech partnership) 2–4 months 4–6 months Rider (on existing approved base policy) 2–3 months 3–5 months Microinsurance product 3–5 months 5–8 months (NAICOM microinsurance guidelines apply)

10.3.1 The Pricing Objective The objective of actuarial pricing is to calculate a premium rate that: (a) is sufficient to pay all expected claims, expenses, and taxes; (b) provides an adequate return on the capital committed to the product; and (c) is competitive in the market. These three objectives are frequently in tension — a premium that fully meets the first two may not be competitive; a premium competitive in the market may be inadequate for the first two. The actuary's role is to quantify the trade-offs and advise management on the risks associated with each pricing decision.[3] A critical feature of life insurance pricing is the long-term commitment required. When an insurer issues a 20-year endowment policy, it commits to specific premium and benefit terms for the full 20 years. The premium set today must be adequate to meet claims and expenses in years 15–20, when the actuary has no direct visibility of future mortality rates, investment returns, expense inflation, or policyholder behaviour. This long-term commitment to pre-determined terms is what makes life insurance pricing fundamentally different from general insurance pricing — and what makes the quality of actuarial assumptions so critically important. Profit Testing A prospective financial modelling technique used in life insurance product pricing to project the expected profitability of a product over its entire lifetime. A profit test projects all expected cash flows (premiums, claims, expenses, commissions, investment income, reserves, taxes) on a year-by-year basis under a set of pricing assumptions. The output shows the expected profit or loss in each year and key profitability metrics including the Internal Rate of Return (IRR), the net present value (NPV) of profits, and the payback period. Products that fail to meet the company's minimum profitability threshold at the pricing assumptions are redesigned or repriced before filing. See: Dickson, Hardy and Waters, Actuarial Mathematics for Life Contingent Risks (3rd edn, Cambridge, 2020). 10.3.2 The Five Pricing Assumptions Actuarial pricing for a life insurance product requires the actuary to set assumptions for five principal risk drivers. Each assumption is set on a best-estimate basis (reflecting the actuary's expectation of future experience) and a loaded basis (adding a margin for adverse deviation above the best estimate to ensure that the premium is adequate even if experience is somewhat worse than expected). (a) Mortality Assumption The mortality assumption specifies the probability of death for a policyholder of a given age, sex, smoking status, and occupational class in each future year of the policy. In Nigeria, the EFU Life Table is the standard actuarial mortality table — it was developed from the experience of Nigerian life insurers and provides age- and sex-specific mortality rates (qx values) for the Nigerian population.[4] The pricing actuary selects a mortality basis — the starting table, any adjustments for the specific product target market, and any trend assumptions for future mortality improvements — and loads it with a margin for adverse deviation. The mortality margin is typically expressed as a percentage of the base table rates: if the EFU table qx for a 35-year-old male is 0.0028, the loaded pricing assumption might be 0.0028 × 110% = 0.00308 (a 10% loading). The margin is calibrated based on the credibility of the base experience data, the degree of anti-selection risk in the target market, and the insurer's own claims experience on its in-force portfolio. For new products targeting demographics or distribution channels for which the insurer has no prior experience — rural microinsurance, USSD-distributed term plans, credit life through fintech platforms — the mortality assumption carries a higher uncertainty margin. Actuaries in this situation may use a combination of the EFU table, published research on the target population's health profile, and reinsurer input (reinsurers bring global and regional experience on new markets). (b) Investment Return Assumption The investment return assumption specifies the rate of return the insurer expects to earn on the premium reserves invested during the policy term. It reflects the expected yield on the insurer's admissible asset portfolio — typically a mix of FGN bonds, Treasury bills, money market instruments, equities, and real estate — and the expected reinvestment rates for future cash flows. Because life insurance liabilities are long-duration, the investment return assumption is particularly sensitive: a 1% reduction in the assumed return over a 20-year endowment can significantly reduce the projected maturity benefit.[5] In the Nigerian context, the investment return assumption is unusually complex due to the high-interest-rate environment and its volatility. The 12-month Treasury bill rate in Nigeria exceeded 22% in 2024 — a rate that, if used as the pricing assumption, would produce extremely generous benefit projections. However, prudent actuarial practice requires the assumption to reflect a long-term normalised rate rather than the current elevated level. An endowment product priced assuming 22% investment returns will be unable to deliver its projected maturity benefits if rates revert to single digits over the policy term. NAICOM's product approval process scrutinises investment return assumptions carefully; NAICOM expects assumptions to be defensible, documented, and stress-tested. (c) Persistency / Lapse Assumption The persistency assumption specifies the proportion of policyholders expected to keep their policies in force (paying premiums) in each year of the product lifecycle. Its complement — the lapse rate — is the proportion expected to stop paying and allow the policy to lapse, surrender, or convert to paid-up. Persistency is one of the most commercially sensitive assumptions in life insurance pricing: For term assurance: if lapse rates are higher than expected, the insurer collects less premium and retains a higher-risk pool (policyholders with health conditions who cannot get other cover tend to persist; healthy ones who find alternatives tend to lapse). This can produce adverse mortality experience and pricing losses. For endowments and whole life: early lapses release back-end loaded profits but increase the per-policy expense ratio. Late lapses in the profitable later years remove the insurer's expected profitability from those years. For participating policies: high lapse rates reduce the size of the with-profit fund, reducing the investment returns that underpin the bonus declarations that are the product's key commercial promise. In Nigeria, lapse rates are historically high — driven by premium affordability constraints, economic volatility, and inadequate policyholder servicing. Actuaries pricing Nigerian products must use lapse assumptions that reflect local market experience, which typically shows heavy lapses in years 1 and 2 (often 15–30% of policies issued lapse in the first year) and declining lapse rates in later years. A product priced on the assumption that 90% of policies persist to maturity in a market where 30% lapse in year 1 will be significantly under-reserved and potentially unprofitable.[11] (d) Expense Assumption The expense assumption allocates the insurer's total operating costs to individual product lines and policy transactions. Expenses in life insurance divide into three categories: Initial (first-year) expenses: All costs incurred to acquire a new policy — agent commission (first-year), underwriting costs, policy issue costs, marketing expenses, and a proportion of head office overhead. These are front-loaded and are the primary reason why surrender values are low in the early policy years. Renewal expenses: The per-policy costs of administering an in-force policy in each year after the first — processing premium payments, maintaining the policy record, generating annual statements, and responding to policyholder queries. Expressed as a cost per policy per year or as a percentage of renewal premium. Claim expenses: The cost of processing a claim — claims assessment, medical evidence review, legal review (for contested claims), and benefit payment processing. Expressed as a cost per claim settled. The expense loading in the premium is designed to recover all these costs over the policy's lifetime, with an appropriate margin. Under-estimating expenses — a common failing in early-stage life companies — means the premium is insufficient to recover actual costs, destroying profitability. Overestimating expenses makes the product uncompetitive. The discipline of maintaining a detailed and accurate unit cost study — typically updated annually for the management expense ratio (MER) — is the foundation of sound expense loading. (e) Policyholder Behaviour Assumptions Beyond lapse rates, actuaries model additional policyholder behaviour assumptions that can materially affect product profitability: Policy loan utilisation: The proportion of eligible policyholders expected to take policy loans in each year, the average loan balance, and the interest charged. High loan utilisation reduces the insurer's investment income on the policy reserve. Paid-up conversions: The proportion expected to convert to paid-up policies rather than fully lapsing. Paid-up conversions reduce premium income but retain some future liability. Claim acceleration: For critical illness and disability products, assumptions about the rate at which acceleration (early payment) of the sum assured will be triggered. Partial withdrawals: For investment-linked products, assumptions about the frequency and size of partial withdrawals from the policyholder's fund account. 10.3.3 Best-Estimate, Loaded, and Stressed Assumptions Assumption Type Definition Used In Best-estimate The actuary's most likely expectation of future experience, without any margin for adverse deviation. Based on the insurer's own historical data, supplemented by industry data where own data is insufficient. Reporting actual profit vs expected profit; IFRS 17 financial reporting; management information Loaded (pricing basis) Best-estimate assumptions plus a margin (loading) for adverse deviation. The standard basis for setting premium rates. Ensures the product is financially resilient even if experience is somewhat worse than best estimate. Premium rate calculation; profit testing; product pricing submissions to NAICOM Stressed Extreme adverse assumptions applied to test whether the product remains solvent and able to pay claims under worst-case scenarios. Not expected to materialise, but must not produce insolvency. Solvency capital calculations; Risk-Based Capital (RBC) framework; ORSA; NAICOM stress testing requirements under NIIRA 2025

t: Chapter 10 · 10.4  Profit Testing and the Financial Viability Assessment
x: 10.4.1 What Profit Testing Does Profit testing is the prospective financial modelling technique that determines, before a product is launched, whether it is likely to be profitable under the pricing assumptions, and how sensitive that profitability is to changes in experience. A profit test model takes the proposed premium rate, benefit structure, and pricing assumptions as inputs, and projects the expected cash flows, reserves, and profits year by year over the full lifetime of a hypothetical cohort of policies. The key outputs of a profit test are: Annual profit vector: The expected profit or loss in each year of the product's lifetime. Early years are typically loss-making (due to high initial expenses and the cost of building reserves); later years become profitable as expenses are amortised and the invested reserve generates returns. Net Present Value (NPV) of profits: The present value of the entire profit stream, discounted at the company's required return on capital. A positive NPV indicates that the product is expected to create value for shareholders at the pricing assumptions. Internal Rate of Return (IRR): The discount rate at which the NPV of profits equals zero. The product's IRR must exceed the company's cost of capital (hurdle rate) for the product to be financially viable. Payback period: The number of years before the product's cumulative profit turns positive. A long payback period increases the company's exposure to adverse experience before the product becomes profitable. Illustration — Profit Test — Simplified Illustration for a 20-Year Endowment Metric Value Product 20-year participating endowment; sum assured ₦5 million; annual premium ₦150,000 Investment return assumption 11% per annum Mortality assumption EFU Life Table × 110% Lapse assumption Year 1: 20%; Year 2: 15%; Years 3–5: 8%; Years 6+: 4% Expense assumption First year: ₦40,000 per policy; Renewal: ₦8,000 per policy Expected profit: Year 1 (₦25,000) — loss due to initial expenses and commission Expected profit: Year 5 ₦3,200 — break-even approaching Expected profit: Year 10 ₦12,500 — growing investment income margin Expected profit: Year 20 ₦38,000 — mature policy in profitable phase NPV of profits (at 15% hurdle rate) ₦85,000 per policy IRR 19.3% — exceeds 15% hurdle rate; product is viable Payback period 5.5 years Key insight: The early-year losses are a function of the front-loaded expense structure — the insurer incurs significant costs to acquire and issue the policy before the investment income on the growing reserve compensates. A policy that lapses in year 2 is almost certainly unprofitable. This explains why persistency — keeping policyholders in force — is so central to life insurance economics.

t: Chapter 10 · 10.5  NAICOM Product Filing and Approval Under NIIRA 2025
x: 10.5.1 The Legal Obligation Under NIIRA 2025, no insurer may introduce a new insurance product or make a material amendment to an existing product without prior approval from NAICOM. This requirement applies to all four classes of life insurance business — individual life assurance, group life assurance, annuity, and health insurance — and extends to all riders and supplementary benefit modules attached to base policies. A product launched without prior NAICOM approval is in breach of NIIRA 2025 and attracts a penalty of ₦500,000 per day until the breach is remediated. Regulatory Spotlight — NIIRA 2025 — Product Filing: Key Requirements and Timelines The product filing and approval framework under NIIRA 2025 operates as follows: Filing requirement: All new products and material amendments must be submitted to NAICOM before marketing. A 'material amendment' includes any change to the benefit structure, premium rate, exclusion clauses, or consumer disclosure documents. Filing document: The submission must include: the proposed policy wording (in consumer-accessible language); the actuarial pricing report (prepared and certified by the company's statutory actuary); the benefit illustration template (showing guaranteed and non-guaranteed elements separately); the marketing materials (brochures, agent training guides, digital content); and a consumer disclosure summary meeting NIIRA 2025's minimum disclosure requirements. The 30-day deemed-approval window: NAICOM has 30 days from receipt of the filing to respond. If NAICOM does not respond within 30 days, the product is deemed approved. This provision prevents indefinite regulatory delay from blocking time-sensitive product launches. Penalty for non-compliance: An insurer that markets a product without NAICOM approval (or after a disapproval notice) is liable to a fine of ₦500,000 per day for each day the unapproved product is marketed. Policy delivery: Under NIIRA 2025, the policy document must be delivered to the policyholder on or before the policy start date. Electronic delivery is permitted but requires confirmation of receipt from the policyholder. This replaces the previous five-working-day delivery window. Regulatory sandbox: NAICOM operates a regulatory sandbox under which innovative new products or distribution models may be tested in a controlled environment before full market launch. The sandbox is particularly relevant for Insurtech-driven product innovations and for products targeting previously unserved demographics. Sources: NIIRA 2025 (Act No. 2, 2025); NAICOM Regulatory Guidelines (August 2025); 1914 Reader analysis of NIIRA 2025 provisions.[7][8][9] 10.5.2 The Actuarial Pricing Report The actuarial pricing report is the cornerstone of the product filing document. It is prepared by the company's statutory actuary (or a suitably qualified actuary under the statutory actuary's supervision) and must: Describe the product design in actuarial terms: the benefit structure, payment modes, policy term options, surrender value basis, and any embedded guarantees. Set out all pricing assumptions with their justification: the mortality table used, loading factors, investment return assumption (and the reasoning for its level relative to current market rates), lapse assumption (and its basis in the insurer's experience data or market data), and expense assumption. Present the profit test results: the annual profit vector, NPV, IRR, and sensitivity analysis showing how profitability changes if mortality is 20% worse than expected, if lapses are 30% higher than expected, or if investment returns are 300 basis points lower than assumed. Confirm that the premium rates are actuarially adequate: that the expected premium income, net of claims, expenses, and the cost of reserves, is sufficient to provide the company's required return on capital. Certify compliance with NAICOM's pricing standards: that the assumptions and methods are consistent with NAICOM's guidelines and with the actuarial profession's standards of practice. NAICOM has been progressively strengthening its actuarial oversight of product pricing since the issuance of new annuity guidelines requiring ALM analysis, and the NIIRA 2025 mandate for annual actuarial investigations. Pricing reports that lack rigour, use assumptions inconsistent with experience data, or fail to present sensitivity analysis will be returned with queries — adding time and cost to the approval process. 10.5.3 Benefit Illustrations and Consumer Disclosure Every life insurance product sold in Nigeria must be supported by a benefit illustration — a document showing the policyholder the projected financial outcomes of the policy under defined scenarios. NAICOM's product approval process reviews benefit illustrations to ensure they:[15] Clearly distinguish between guaranteed benefits (e.g. the basic sum assured) and non-guaranteed elements (e.g. projected bonuses or investment returns). Use investment return projections that are consistent with the pricing assumptions submitted to NAICOM — illustrations may not show higher returns than those supported by the actuarial pricing report. Present at least two scenarios: a base case (using pricing assumptions) and a stress case (using materially lower investment returns or bonus rates) so that policyholders understand the range of possible outcomes. State clearly on the face of the illustration that projected values are not guaranteed and that actual results may differ. The prohibition of misleading benefit illustrations is one of NAICOM's most actively enforced market conduct standards. Historically, the Nigerian market has seen benefit illustrations that showed maturity values at historically high bonus rates without any downside scenario — creating expectations that could never be met and generating complaints and lapse when actual maturities fell short. NIIRA 2025's product approval and consumer disclosure requirements are designed to eliminate this practice.

t: Chapter 10 · 10.6  Product Governance: Suitability, Target Market, and Review Cycles
x: 10.6.1 Target Market Definition Product governance begins with a clear definition of the target market — the category of customers for whom the product is designed and to whom it is appropriate to sell. NIIRA 2025's consumer protection framework, aligned with international best practice, requires every product to be designed for and distributed to a defined target market whose characteristics are understood at inception. A target market definition for a life insurance product typically addresses: Demographics: Age range, income level, employment status, educational level, family circumstances. Financial needs: What specific protection or savings need does the product serve? Risk profile: The customer's tolerance for investment risk, premium volatility, and liquidity constraints. Distribution channel fit: Is the product designed to be sold by agents, through bancassurance, digitally, or through employer group schemes? Negative target market: Categories of customers for whom the product is NOT appropriate — e.g. a long-term endowment plan is not appropriate for a customer who needs liquidity within three years. Target Market The specific category of customers for whom a life insurance product is designed, based on their demographic characteristics, financial needs, risk profile, and distribution channel preferences. Every NAICOM-approved product must have a defined target market, and the product's distribution network must be configured to ensure it is sold only to customers within the target market. Marketing and selling a product to customers outside the target market constitutes mis-selling. NIIRA 2025: Consumer protection provisions require that product design, pricing, and distribution are aligned with the target market. NAICOM may sanction insurers whose distribution practices result in systematic sales to customers outside the intended target market. 10.6.2 The Product Review Cycle A launched product does not manage itself. Every life insurance product requires a structured annual review that compares actual experience against the pricing assumptions and assesses whether the product continues to be commercially viable, actuarially adequate, and market-appropriate. The annual review covers: Mortality experience study: Actual deaths vs expected deaths (as a proportion of the pricing assumption). A significant excess of actual over expected deaths triggers a mortality review and potentially a repricing. Persistency experience study: Actual lapse rates vs pricing assumption. Persistency worse than assumed accelerates the amortisation of initial expenses and reduces the long-term profitability of the portfolio. Investment return review: The actual investment yield on the product's reserve fund vs the pricing assumption. An adverse investment return gap — sustained yield below the pricing assumption — requires either repricing or a reduction in non-guaranteed bonus rates. Expense review: Actual unit costs vs the expense loading in the premium. Rising unit costs without a corresponding premium adjustment produce an expense overrun. Competitive benchmarking: The product's premium rates, benefit levels, and features relative to the current market. A product that was competitively priced at launch may become uncompetitive as the market evolves. The statutory actuary is responsible for presenting the annual product experience study to the board and for recommending any changes required. Significant experience deviations — where actual experience is materially worse than the pricing basis — require either repricing, product withdrawal, or a reinsurance arrangement to stabilise the liability. 10.6.3 Repricing Repricing is the formal process of adjusting the premium rates, benefit levels, or terms of an existing product to reflect updated experience. Repricing is typically applied only to new business from the repricing date — existing policies continue on their original terms (they are guaranteed). A repricing event requires: Board approval of the repricing decision and the proposed new premium rates. Actuarial certification of the new premium rates as actuarially adequate. NAICOM notification (and potentially filing): a material change to the premium rates of an approved product constitutes a material amendment requiring NAICOM filing under NIIRA 2025. Distribution communication: agents and distribution partners must be notified of the rate change and provided with updated illustration templates. Customer communication: policyholders who are within the guaranteed renewable period must be notified of the new rates for renewals. Clear, timely communication prevents complaints and regulatory sanction. 10.6.4 Product Withdrawal A product may need to be withdrawn from new business sale when it is no longer commercially viable, when it fails to meet NAICOM's updated standards, or when it has been superseded by a newer design. Product withdrawal requires NAICOM notification; the product cannot be withdrawn from new business without informing the regulator. Existing in-force policies continue on their original terms until maturity, claim, or lapse — withdrawal from new business does not affect policyholders who already hold the product. Run-off management of a withdrawn product remains an actuarial responsibility until the last policy has been discharged.

t: Chapter 10 · 10.7  Advisory: Product Design Best Practices for the Nigerian Market
x: Advisory — Designing Life Insurance Products for Nigerian Market Realities The following design principles reflect the specific characteristics of the Nigerian market — its income structure, inflation environment, digital infrastructure, and cultural attitudes to financial products. They should guide product design decisions from the earliest concept stage. Premium Affordability and Entry Points Premium affordability is the single most binding constraint on retail life insurance penetration in Nigeria. The practical implication for product design: Monthly minimum premiums should be accessible at the ₦2,000–₦5,000 per month level for standard products, and below ₦1,000 per month for microinsurance and mobile-first products. Single-premium options for credit life and investment-linked products allow lump-sum funding that aligns with irregular income patterns. Regular premium products should be priced with realistic lapse assumptions for the target market; unrealistic persistency assumptions produce profit tests that look attractive but deliver losses in practice. Payment Frequency Flexibility Nigerian consumers — particularly in the informal sector — have irregular, unpredictable income flows. Product designs that allow: Daily or weekly micro-premiums via USSD (consistent with the Insurtech Guidelines' digital distribution framework) Salary-deduction-at-source for formal sector employees (partnering with HR and payroll systems) Flexi-payment features that allow contributions above and below the standard premium within specified limits ...substantially improve persistency by matching the product's payment structure to the customer's actual cash flow reality. Digital-First Structuring Products that are designed from the outset for digital onboarding — not retrofitted with a digital wrapper on top of a paper-based design — achieve significantly better acquisition economics. Digital-first design includes: Simplified underwriting for low-sum-assured products (no medical examination, self-declaration only, auto-acceptance below the non-medical limit) API-enabled policy issuance: policy number, certificate, and premium receipt generated and delivered digitally within 60 seconds of completed application Self-service policy management: policyholders can view their policy, make contributions, update beneficiaries, and request policy loans through a mobile app or USSD without agent involvement Digital benefit illustrations: generated in real time based on the customer's inputted age and desired sum assured, compliant with NAICOM's disclosure requirements Financial Inclusion Imperatives NAICOM's financial inclusion mandate and NIIRA 2025's provisions on miscellaneous insurance business create both a regulatory expectation and a commercial opportunity for products that serve under-served populations. Design considerations include: Simplified terms and conditions: policy documents of 2–4 pages maximum, using plain English (or local language versions where appropriate), with key terms explained in everyday language Group-based distribution: structuring products for distribution through cooperatives, trade associations, SACCO groups, and informal savings circles (Ajo/Esusu) Index-based or parametric triggers: for agricultural and weather-linked products, parametric triggers (e.g. payment if rainfall below threshold) eliminate claims assessment costs and enable faster payment

t: Chapter 10 · 10.8  Credit Life Insurance: Structuring for Bank and Fintech Partnerships
x: 10.8.1 The NIIRA 2025 Mandate and Its Market Implications As detailed in Chapter 6, NIIRA 2025, Section 91(3) mandates credit life insurance for all loans exceeding ₦10 million. The lender must require the borrower to obtain credit life insurance before loan disbursement; the lender is the named beneficiary up to the outstanding loan balance. This mandate creates the largest single regulatory-driven expansion of the Nigerian life insurance market since the Pension Reform Act 2014's Group Life Insurance obligation.[14] The credit life mandate has a transformative distribution implication: the primary distribution channel for credit life is not the insurance agent or broker but the lender — the bank, microfinance bank, digital lender, or fintech platform that disburses the loan. The insurer's commercial challenge is to position its product as the lender's preferred credit life solution and to deliver it in a way that is seamlessly embedded in the lending transaction. 10.8.2 Product Design Principles for Credit Life Credit life insurance differs from retail individual life assurance in its design in five important ways: Reducing sum assured: The sum assured mirrors the outstanding loan balance, which reduces over the loan term as repayments are made. For fixed-term amortising loans, the sum assured follows the loan's amortisation schedule exactly, ensuring that the benefit at any point equals the outstanding balance. Single-premium or annual-premium structure: Credit life is most commonly priced as a single premium paid at loan inception, funded as part of the loan disbursement. This eliminates the premium collection problem — the insurer is paid upfront and the loan is larger by the amount of the insurance premium. Alternatively, annual renewable term structures are used for revolving credit facilities. Simplified underwriting: A key commercial requirement for fintech and digital lender partnerships is near-instant policy issuance with no underwriting delay. Credit life products for mass-market loans below a specified sum (typically ₦25–50 million) should be underwritten on a simplified basis: age limits, evidence of the loan, and a simple health declaration without medical examination. Lender as policyholder, borrower as life assured: The lender holds the master credit life policy; individual borrowers are covered as lives assured under the scheme. Individual policy certificates are issued to borrowers. The lender processes claims as they arise. Beneficiary structure: The lender is the first beneficiary up to the outstanding loan balance. Any excess benefit (where the sum assured exceeds the outstanding debt at the time of claim) is paid to the borrower's estate or named beneficiary. This 'assignment to lender' structure must be disclosed to the borrower clearly — NIIRA 2025 prohibits hidden insurance charges bundled into loan fees. Concept in Practice — API-Enabled Credit Life — How a Fintech Partnership Works A digital lending platform (the Fintech) disburses personal loans of ₦500,000 to ₦15 million through a mobile app. All loans above ₦10 million must be covered by credit life insurance under NIIRA 2025. The Fintech enters a credit life partnership with a licensed life insurer: Loan application: The borrower applies for a ₦12 million business loan through the Fintech app. The app identifies that the loan exceeds the ₦10 million threshold and triggers the credit life module. Instant underwriting: The insurer's API receives the borrower's age, loan amount, and loan term from the Fintech. For a 40-year-old borrower with a 36-month ₦12 million loan, the API returns a single-premium quote of ₦60,000 (calculated as 0.5% of the loan amount × term adjustment factor) within 2 seconds. Borrower disclosure: The app presents the insurance cost transparently: 'Your loan includes a credit life insurance premium of ₦60,000, payable as part of your loan facility fee. This insurance will repay your loan balance if you die or become permanently disabled before the loan is fully repaid. You are being covered by [Insurer Name], licensed by NAICOM. The insurer's contact details are: [contact].' Policy issuance: On loan acceptance, the insurer's API issues the credit life policy instantaneously. The borrower receives a digital policy certificate within 60 seconds. The Fintech's risk department receives confirmation. The ₦60,000 single premium is transferred to the insurer from the loan disbursement. Claims: If the borrower dies during the loan term, the Fintech notifies the insurer with the death certificate and the outstanding loan balance. The insurer settles the claim within 60 days (targeting best-practice performance well within the 60-day NIIRA 2025 maximum). The commercial benefit to the insurer: high-volume, low-cost distribution through the Fintech's existing customer base with no agent commission. The commercial benefit to the Fintech: reduced credit risk on loans above ₦10 million, a differentiated responsible lending proposition, and a potential fee income share. The benefit to the borrower: their family does not inherit the debt if they die.

t: Chapter 10 · 10.9  Health Riders and Critical Illness Product Design
x: 10.9.1 Health Riders on Life Policies A health rider is an additional benefit module attached to a base life assurance policy that provides coverage for health-related events — hospitalisation, critical illness, disability, or specified medical procedures. Health riders serve the dual commercial purpose of increasing the policy's total premium (and therefore the insurer's revenue per policy) and deepening the customer relationship by providing cover that addresses multiple risks under one product relationship. The design of health riders in Nigeria must balance three competing objectives: the benefit must be meaningful enough to justify the additional premium; the definition of covered events must be clear and unambiguous to avoid claims disputes; and the pricing must be actuarially adequate based on Nigerian health utilisation data — which is limited in quality and coverage relative to developed markets. 10.9.2 Critical Illness Product Design Critical illness (CI) insurance pays a lump sum on the first diagnosis of a specified covered illness. Unlike health insurance (which reimburses medical expenses), CI insurance pays regardless of what the proceeds are used for — the policyholder may use the benefit for medical treatment, income replacement, home adaptation, or debt repayment. This fixed-benefit, event-triggered structure makes CI insurance simpler to administer and less subject to medical expense inflation than indemnity health cover. The key product design decisions for a CI product are: Disease list: The 'dread disease' definitions. Standard CI products in Nigeria cover a core list of high-incidence, high-impact conditions: cancer (all malignant tumours), heart attack, stroke, kidney failure, major organ transplant, and coronary artery bypass surgery. More comprehensive products add conditions such as blindness, major burns, HIV (where contracted through blood transfusion or occupational accident), and permanent total disability. Trigger definition: The clinical criteria that must be satisfied for a claim to be valid. 'Cancer' must be defined precisely — typically as a histologically confirmed malignant tumour; benign tumours, pre-cancerous lesions, and early-stage carcinoma in situ may be excluded. The definition of 'heart attack' requires specific clinical evidence (raised cardiac enzymes, ECG changes, wall motion abnormality). Vague or outdated definitions generate claims disputes. Survival period: Most CI products impose a minimum survival period of 14–30 days after diagnosis before the benefit is payable. This prevents claims on behalf of patients who die immediately from a newly diagnosed condition — a design feature that reduces the insurer's exposure to very early claims where the condition may pre-date the policy. Exclusions: Conditions that were known or ought to have been known to the proposer at the time of application are excluded. Pre-existing conditions not disclosed at proposal — consistent with the utmost good faith principle in Chapter 2 — are a common basis for CI claim denial. Clear, consumer-accessible exclusion language is a NAICOM requirement. Integration with the base policy: When a CI rider is attached to a life policy, the typical design is that a CI claim reduces the life policy's sum assured by the CI benefit paid (an 'accelerated benefit' structure) and the policy continues for the residual sum. Alternatively, the CI benefit can be structured as an 'additional benefit' paid on top of the life policy sum, which leaves the life cover intact — but at a higher premium. Advisory — CI Product Design — Advisory for Nigerian Product Development Teams Critical illness products are among the most litigated life insurance products globally. The following design standards reduce claims disputes and regulatory risk: Use internationally standardised definitions: The Critical Illness Working Group of the International Association of Insurance and Financial Advisors (IAIFA) and the Global Taskforce on CI definitions provide benchmark disease definitions that have been refined through claims experience in multiple markets. Start with these standards rather than developing bespoke Nigerian definitions without reference to global experience. Clarity over comprehensiveness: A policy covering 10 conditions with clear, clinically precise definitions is superior to one covering 30 conditions with vague or overlapping definitions. The latter generates more sales but produces more disputes. Align CI definitions with Nigerian disease burden: Nigeria's leading causes of premature death and disability include cerebrovascular disease (stroke), coronary artery disease, cancer (particularly breast, cervical, and prostate), HIV/AIDS, and kidney disease. Product designs that cover conditions with low Nigerian prevalence at the expense of high-prevalence conditions serve policyholders poorly. Disclosure of waiting periods: All CI products have a waiting period — typically 90 days from policy inception — before any benefit is claimable (to prevent the insured from applying immediately after a diagnosis). This waiting period must be prominently disclosed in the policy document, the benefit illustration, and the sales conversation.

The product development lifecycle for a life insurance product spans seven stages: strategic concept, market research, technical design, actuarial pricing and profit testing, NAICOM filing and approval, systems and distribution readiness, and launch with post-launch monitoring. The global average from concept to launch is 6–12 months; the Nigerian process adds 2–4 months for the NAICOM approval stage. The five actuarial pricing assumptions are mortality, investment return, persistency/lapse, expense, and policyholder behaviour. Each is set on a best-estimate basis for management reporting and a loaded basis for premium-setting. Stressed assumptions are used for solvency capital calculations under the NIIRA 2025 Risk-Based Capital framework. Profit testing projects the product's expected cash flows, reserves, and profitability over its full lifetime. Key outputs are the annual profit vector, NPV, IRR, and payback period. Products that fail to meet the company's hurdle rate must be redesigned or repriced before filing with NAICOM. NIIRA 2025 requires NAICOM approval for all new products and material amendments. The filing includes the actuarial pricing report, proposed policy wording, benefit illustration templates, and marketing materials. NAICOM has 30 days (or the period set in its Service Charter) to respond; silence equals deemed approval (s.18). The penalty for marketing without approval is ₦500,000 per day (s.18(3)). Policy documents must be delivered to policyholders on or before the policy start date. Product governance requires target market definition, annual experience studies (mortality, persistency, investment, expense), repricing when experience deviates materially from pricing assumptions, and product withdrawal notification to NAICOM when a product ceases new business writing. Best practices for the Nigerian market include affordable entry-point premiums (₦2,000–₦5,000/month minimum), payment frequency flexibility (daily/weekly micro-premiums via USSD; salary deduction at source), digital-first structuring (simplified underwriting, API-enabled issuance, self-service management), and community-based distribution for financial inclusion products. Credit life insurance under the NIIRA 2025 mandate (mandatory for loans exceeding ₦10 million) requires reducing sum assured structures, single-premium or annual-renewable-term pricing, simplified underwriting for mass-market lending, and API-enabled integration with banking and fintech loan origination platforms. Transparent disclosure of the insurance cost to the borrower is required by NIIRA 2025. Critical illness product design requires clinically precise 'dread disease' definitions, a survival period (typically 14–30 days), clear exclusions for pre-existing conditions, and a disclosed waiting period (typically 90 days from inception). CI product designs aligned with Nigerian disease burden (stroke, heart disease, cancer, kidney failure) serve policyholders better than designs imported from other markets without local calibration.

Product Development Lifecycle (PDL) The end-to-end process transforming a business opportunity into a market-ready, actuarially priced, and regulatorily approved insurance product. Spans concept, research, technical design, pricing, filing, readiness, and post-launch monitoring. Product Development Steering Committee (PDSC) A cross-functional governance body responsible for setting the company's product development agenda, reviewing profit test results, approving NAICOM filing submissions, and authorising product launches. Profit Testing A prospective financial modelling technique projecting the expected cash flows, reserves, and profitability of a proposed life insurance product over its full lifetime. Key outputs: annual profit vector, NPV, IRR, payback period. Internal Rate of Return (IRR) The discount rate at which the NPV of a product's expected profit stream equals zero. The product's IRR must exceed the company's hurdle rate (cost of capital) for the product to be commercially viable. Best-Estimate Assumption The actuary's most likely expectation of future experience, without any margin for adverse deviation. Used for IFRS 17 reporting and management information. Loaded Assumption A best-estimate assumption plus a margin for adverse deviation. The standard basis for setting premium rates. Ensures financial resilience if experience is worse than expected. Stressed Assumption Extreme adverse assumptions used to test product solvency under worst-case scenarios. Used in the RBC framework and ORSA under NIIRA 2025. Mortality Assumption The age- and sex-specific probability of death in each future policy year, derived from the EFU Life Table for Nigeria plus loading factors. Persistency / Lapse Assumption The proportion of policyholders expected to maintain their policies in each year (persistency), and the proportion expected to lapse or surrender (lapse rate). Target Market The specific category of customers for whom a product is designed. NAICOM requires all approved products to have a defined target market; selling outside the target market constitutes mis-selling. Material Amendment Any change to a product's benefit structure, premium rate, exclusions, or consumer disclosures that requires a fresh NAICOM filing and approval. Deemed Approval The legal status of a product filing after 30 days if NAICOM has not responded to the submission. The product is treated as approved and may be marketed. Credit Life Insurance Life insurance covering an outstanding loan balance against the borrower's death or permanent disability. Mandatory under NIIRA 2025 for loans exceeding ₦10 million. Survival Period (CI) The minimum period (14–30 days) a policyholder must survive after a CI diagnosis before the benefit is payable. Prevents claims on behalf of patients who die immediately after a newly identified condition. Dread Disease Definition The clinical criteria that must be satisfied for a critical illness claim to be valid. Precision of definition is critical to managing claims disputes and NAICOM market conduct compliance.

The penalty under NIIRA 2025 for marketing a life insurance product without prior NAICOM approval is: ₦250,000 per policy sold. ₦500,000 per day for each day the unapproved product is marketed. Suspension of the company's licence with immediate effect. A written warning for the first offence only. (B) ₦500,000 per day for each day the unapproved product is marketed. Why (B) is Correct NIIRA 2025 establishes a per-day penalty for marketing life insurance products without prior NAICOM approval. The daily accrual structure creates an escalating financial consequence proportional to the duration of non-compliance — an insurer marketing an unapproved product for 60 days accumulates ₦30 million in fines. This structure is a stronger deterrent than a fixed per-policy or one-time penalty, which might be treated as a cost of doing business. Why the Others Are Wrong (A) A per-policy fine would create minimal deterrent for a high-volume product launch but excessive liability for a specialist product — the per-day model is more consistently calibrated.(C) Immediate licence suspension as the first-instance penalty for product approval non-compliance would be disproportionate; NIIRA 2025 reserves suspension for more serious or repeated violations.(D) A written warning with no financial consequence is the pre-NIIRA 2025 approach that the Act's strengthened enforcement philosophy was designed to replace.

Under NIIRA 2025, the policy document must be delivered to the policyholder: Within 5 working days of the policy start date. Within 30 days of premium receipt. On or before the policy start date; electronic delivery requires confirmation of receipt. At the insurer's discretion within the first policy month. (C) On or before the policy start date; electronic delivery requires confirmation of receipt. Why (C) is Correct NIIRA 2025 requires the policy document to be in the policyholder's hands no later than the commencement date of coverage. For electronic delivery (email, WhatsApp, online portal), delivery is deemed effective only when the insurer has confirmation of actual receipt — a read receipt, an affirmative response, or logged portal access. This prevents the gap where coverage has commenced but the policyholder has not yet seen the terms governing their coverage. Why the Others Are Wrong (A) 5 working days post-commencement would mean coverage is in force before the policyholder knows the policy terms — directly contrary to NIIRA 2025's consumer protection objective.(B) 60 days is the claims settlement deadline, not the document delivery requirement. Conflating the two is a common examination error.(D) 'At the insurer's discretion' describes the pre-NIIRA 2025 practice that the mandatory delivery requirement was introduced to eliminate.

The 'deemed approval' provision in NAICOM's product filing process means: NAICOM automatically approves all products without review. If NAICOM does not respond within 30 days, the product is treated as approved. Products may be marketed while under review, subject to later approval. Only new products require NAICOM approval; amendments are exempt. (B) If NAICOM does not respond to a product filing within 30 days, the product is treated as approved. Why (B) is Correct The deemed approval provision prevents NAICOM's processing backlog from indefinitely delaying new product launches. If NAICOM does not issue an approval, rejection, or request for further information within 30 days of receiving a complete product filing, the filing is deemed approved and the insurer may market the product. This creates an incentive for NAICOM to review promptly while also protecting insurers from indefinite regulatory silence. Why the Others Are Wrong (A) NAICOM does review all filings — the deemed approval applies only after the 30-day window expires without a NAICOM decision on a complete filing.(C) Marketing before approval (even while under review) is prohibited under NIIRA 2025. The 30-day deemed approval only activates after the window passes without a decision.(D) Material product amendments require NAICOM notification or formal resubmission; they are not categorically exempt from the approval process.

The persistency assumption in a life insurance pricing model specifies: The probability of a policyholder dying in each future policy year. The rate at which the insurer expects to earn investment returns. The proportion of policyholders expected to keep their policies in force in each year. The fixed annual cost of administering each in-force policy. (C) The proportion of policyholders expected to keep their policies in force in each year. Why (C) is Correct The persistency assumption models the lapse behaviour of the in-force portfolio — what percentage of policies are expected to remain in force in each future policy year. It is the complement of the lapse rate: if persistency is 82% in year 3, the lapse rate is 18% in year 3. Persistency affects the insurer's future premium income stream, the expected claims cost profile (lapses remove policies from the risk pool), and the expense amortisation calculation. Getting persistency assumptions right is critical to pricing profitability. Why the Others Are Wrong (A) The probability of dying in each policy year is the mortality assumption (qx from the EFU Nigerian life table) — a separate and distinct actuarial input.(B) Expected investment returns are the yield assumption — the projected return on the insurer's investment of premium funds. A separate actuarial input.(D) The fixed annual administration cost per policy is the per-policy renewal expense loading — another separate pricing element from the persistency assumption.

A credit life insurance policy under NIIRA 2025 typically has: A fixed sum assured for the entire loan term. A reducing sum assured mirroring the outstanding loan balance over the loan term. A sum assured written by a bank and not an insurance company. An optional sum assured for all loans regardless of amount. (B) A reducing sum assured mirroring the outstanding loan balance over the loan term. Why (B) is Correct Credit life insurance is specifically designed to match the risk profile of a repayment loan: as the borrower repays principal each period, the outstanding balance falls, and so does the required coverage amount. A reducing sum assured (the structure of decreasing term assurance) precisely matches this profile — the insurer's maximum exposure at any point equals the outstanding loan balance. This matching eliminates over-insurance (which would burden the borrower with higher premiums than necessary) and under-insurance (which would leave a residual debt uncovered). Why the Others Are Wrong (A) A fixed sum assured would over-insure in the later stages of a repayment loan when the outstanding balance is low, imposing unnecessary premium cost.(C) Credit life must be underwritten by a NAICOM-licensed life insurer — banks cannot underwrite insurance risk on their own account without a separate insurance licence.(D) NIIRA 2025 makes credit life mandatory (not optional) for qualifying loans above ₦10 million.
