t: Chapter 14 · 14.1 Introduction: The Purpose and Functions of Reinsurance
x: Reinsurance is insurance for insurers. It is the contractual arrangement under which a direct insurer (the cedant) transfers a defined portion of the risks it has accepted from policyholders to one or more reinsurers, in exchange for a proportionate share of the premium. The reinsurer assumes the transferred risk and, in the event of a claim that triggers the reinsurance cover, pays its share of the claim to the cedant. The existence of reinsurance is what makes it economically feasible for a relatively small life insurance company to issue a ₦500 million policy on the life of a corporate executive, or to insure the entire workforce of a large employer under a group life scheme with an aggregate potential liability running into billions of naira. Without reinsurance, an insurer could only write risks up to the limit its own capital can absorb. With reinsurance, the insurer accesses the global capacity of the reinsurance market, spreading its risks across a far larger capital base. Reinsurance serves six distinct functions in life insurance: Capacity expansion Enables the direct insurer to accept sums assured that would exceed its own capital’s ability to absorb a single large death claim. Without reinsurance, the maximum insurable life would be constrained by the insurer’s retention limit. Mortality risk transfer Transfers the statistical uncertainty of mortality experience — the risk that more policyholders die than the pricing assumptions expected — from the cedant to the reinsurer. This smooths the cedant’s claims experience and reduces the volatility of its annual results. Portfolio stabilisation Limits the impact of catastrophic mortality events (pandemics, mass casualty accidents, industrial disasters) that could generate a surge of simultaneous claims on the in-force portfolio. Stop loss and excess of loss treaties provide this protection. New business strain management In the first year of a new policy, the insurer pays heavy acquisition costs (commissions, underwriting, system setup) while collecting only the first premium. This creates a cash flow deficit: ‘new business strain’. Co-insurance and YRT reinsurance provide fronted cash flows that reduce this strain. Actuarial expertise Reinsurers bring global mortality data, underwriting manuals, claims statistics, and product design experience that most direct insurers — particularly smaller Nigerian companies — cannot generate internally. Access to reinsurer expertise is a material benefit of the reinsurance relationship. Capital management Under the NIIRA 2025 Risk-Based Capital framework, transferring mortality risk to a reinsurer reduces the direct insurer’s insurance risk charge (C1) and therefore reduces the total capital required. Reinsurance is thus a tool for optimising the RBC solvency ratio.

14.2.1 Proportional Reinsurance In a proportional reinsurance arrangement, the cedant and the reinsurer share both the premium and the risk in defined proportions. If the cedant cedes 60% of the risk to the reinsurer, the reinsurer receives 60% of the premium and pays 60% of any claim. The sharing ratio is defined at the outset of the treaty and applies to every risk ceded under it. Proportional reinsurance is the dominant form in the Nigerian life market, where the most common structures are the quota share and the surplus treaty. 14.2.2 Quota Share Treaty Quota Share Treaty A proportional reinsurance treaty under which the cedant cedes a fixed percentage of every risk accepted within the treaty’s scope to the reinsurer. The same percentage applies to premiums and claims: if the cession rate is 40%, the reinsurer receives 40% of every premium and pays 40% of every claim, regardless of the size of the individual risk. The cedant retains the remaining 60% for its own account. Quota share treaties are the simplest reinsurance structure and are widely used in the Nigerian market, particularly for: group life schemes (where a fixed percentage of the entire scheme’s liability is ceded); new product lines where the insurer has limited mortality experience and wishes to share the risk broadly until experience data accumulates; and smaller insurers with limited capital capacity that need to cede a high proportion of all risks to remain within their retention capability. Worked Example 14.1 — Quota Share Premium and Claims A life insurer has a 40% quota share treaty with its reinsurer. In a given year, the insurer writes new group life business with total annual premiums of ₦120,000,000 and total sum assured of ₦10,000,000,000. Three death claims arise, with sum assureds of ₦50m, ₦200m, and ₦50m respectively. Reinsurer receives: 40% × ₦120m = ₦48m premiumReinsurer pays: 40% × (₦50m + ₦200m + ₦50m) = 40% × ₦300m = ₦120m in claimsCedant net position: Retains ₦72m premium; pays ₦180m claims net of recovery. Note: The cedant paid out ₦300m in claims, recovered ₦120m from the reinsurer, and retained net claims cost of ₦180m against net premium income of ₦72m — a bad year. But without the reinsurer, the cedant would have paid the full ₦300m against ₦120m premium — a far worse outcome. Quota share smooths and distributes the experience. 14.2.3 Surplus Treaty Surplus Treaty A proportional reinsurance treaty under which the cedant retains risks up to its defined retention limit and cedes to the reinsurer only the amount by which any individual risk’s sum assured exceeds the retention. The cession ratio therefore varies from policy to policy depending on the relationship between the sum assured and the retention limit. The reinsurer accepts risks proportional to their excess over the retention, with a defined maximum multiple of the retention (expressed in ‘lines’). The surplus treaty is more selective than the quota share: the cedant retains 100% of small risks (below the retention limit) and only cedes the excess on larger risks. This means the cedant retains more premium income from the smaller policy segment while passing the capacity challenge of large policies to the reinsurer. The surplus treaty is the more common structure for individual life business in the Nigerian market. Worked Example 14.2 — Surplus Treaty Mechanics An insurer has a surplus treaty with a retention limit of ₦50,000,000 and a reinsurer capacity of 10 lines (i.e., the reinsurer accepts up to 10 × ₦50m = ₦500m in surplus capacity). Three policies are issued: Policy Sum Assured Cedant Retention Ceded to Reinsurer Cession % Policy A ₦30,000,000 ₦30,000,000 (100%) ₦nil (below retention) 0% Policy B ₦150,000,000 ₦50,000,000 (33.3%) ₦100,000,000 (66.7%) 66.7% Policy C ₦400,000,000 ₦50,000,000 (12.5%) ₦350,000,000 (87.5%) 87.5% On Policy C: a death claim of ₦400m triggers a cedant payment of ₦50m (12.5%) and a reinsurer payment of ₦350m (87.5%). Premium sharing follows the same percentages. Policy A (below the retention) generates no reinsurance involvement; the cedant bears the full risk and keeps the full premium. 14.2.4 Excess of Loss Reinsurance Excess of Loss (XL) Reinsurance A non-proportional reinsurance arrangement under which the reinsurer pays the amount of a claim (or aggregate claims) that exceeds a defined threshold (the ‘priority’ or ‘deductible’), up to a defined maximum. Unlike proportional treaties, premiums are not shared: the cedant pays a fixed reinsurance premium and the reinsurer only responds when claims breach the priority level. In life insurance, excess of loss can be structured on a per-life basis (individual XL) or on an aggregate basis (aggregate XL or stop loss). Per-life excess of loss: Protects against a single very large death claim. Example: the cedant pays the first ₦100m of any individual death claim; the reinsurer pays the excess above ₦100m up to a maximum of ₦500m. This is particularly relevant for individual life policies with very high sums assured, where the insurer’s net retention after a surplus treaty cession still creates a per-life exposure it wishes to limit. Aggregate excess of loss: Protects against an unexpectedly large total claims experience across the entire portfolio in a year. Example: the cedant retains the first 105% of expected claims; the reinsurer pays any excess above 105% up to 130% of expected claims. This limits the downside risk from a mortality shock year (pandemic, catastrophe). 14.2.5 Stop Loss Reinsurance Stop Loss Reinsurance A non-proportional reinsurance arrangement that protects the cedant against an aggregate claims experience that exceeds a defined percentage of total premium income (or a fixed monetary threshold) in a given year. Once total claims breach the stop loss attachment point, the reinsurer bears all or a defined share of the excess. Stop loss is the purest form of catastrophe protection: it converts an open-ended mortality risk into a capped financial exposure. Stop loss reinsurance is expensive relative to proportional covers because the reinsurer is bearing tail risk — the risk of extreme adverse outcomes that occur rarely but severely. Its primary application in the Nigerian market is for group life schemes, where a single employer accident, industrial disaster, or epidemic could generate a large number of simultaneous claims, and for microinsurance portfolios where the insurer may have limited capital to absorb a bad mortality year.

t: Chapter 14 · 14.3 Facultative Reinsurance and Treaty Reinsurance
x: 14.3.1 Treaty Reinsurance A reinsurance treaty is a standing agreement between the cedant and one or more reinsurers under which defined categories of risk are automatically ceded and accepted without the need for individual case referral or negotiation. Treaty reinsurance provides the cedant with the assurance that every policy falling within the treaty’s terms will be automatically reinsured. The treaty is typically negotiated annually (on the renewal date), at which point the cedant and reinsurer agree on: the scope of risks covered; the retention limit and capacity; the premium basis; the underwriting guidelines embedded in the treaty; the reporting and accounting schedule; and the treaty’s territorial scope. Once the treaty is in force, new policies that fall within its terms are automatically ceded as they are issued, without further individual negotiation. The treaty also typically includes an ‘automatic binding limit’ — the maximum sum assured the reinsurer will automatically accept under the treaty without individual case review. Risks above the automatic binding limit require facultative placement. 14.3.2 Facultative Reinsurance Facultative reinsurance involves the placement of individual risks with one or more reinsurers, case by case. The cedant submits a risk to the reinsurer with full details; the reinsurer is free (has the ‘faculty’) to accept, decline, or offer modified terms; and the cedant is free to accept or reject the offer. There is no standing obligation on either party. Facultative placement is used for: risks that exceed the automatic binding limit of the treaty; risks with medical or occupational characteristics that fall outside the treaty’s underwriting guidelines; large individual life policies where the cedant wants firm reinsurer commitment before issuing the policy; and risks for which multiple reinsurer quotations are sought to achieve competitive pricing. Facultative reinsurance is slower and more expensive per unit of capacity than treaty reinsurance, but it provides underwriting flexibility for risks that the automatic treaty cannot accommodate. The facultative underwriting process is described in Chapter 11 (Section 11.10). 14.3.3 Facultative-Obligatory (Fac-Ob) Treaty Facultative-Obligatory (Fac-Ob) A hybrid reinsurance arrangement under which the cedant has the option (the ‘facultative’ element) to cede any risk within a defined class to the treaty or not, at its own discretion; but the reinsurer is obliged (the ‘obligatory’ element) to accept whatever the cedant chooses to cede. Fac-ob arrangements are less common in the Nigerian market but provide cedants with flexibility to cede selectively, subject to the anti-selection risk that the reinsurer faces from this asymmetry.

t: Chapter 14 · 14.4 Life Reinsurance Methods: Co-insurance, Modco, and YRT
x: The distinction between reinsurance ‘types’ (quota share, surplus, XL) describes how risk is shared between cedant and reinsurer. The reinsurance ‘method’ describes the specific cash flow and reserve arrangement under which the sharing operates. Life reinsurance has three principal methods: co-insurance, modified co-insurance (Modco), and Yearly Renewable Term (YRT). Each has distinct implications for the cedant’s cash flow, reserves, and balance sheet. 14.4.1 Co-insurance Co-insurance (Life Reinsurance) A life reinsurance method under which the reinsurer assumes a proportionate share of the policy’s full economics: it receives its share of the gross premium, holds its share of the policy reserve, and pays its share of all claims and expenses. The reinsurer effectively owns a defined proportion of the policy for the full duration of the in-force period. The cedant cedes the reinsurer’s share of the gross premium net of a ceding commission (a reimbursement to the cedant for its initial acquisition costs). Under co-insurance, the reinsurer is a true proportionate partner in the policy. If the cedant holds a reserve of ₦10m on a policy and the cession ratio is 60%, the reinsurer holds a corresponding reserve of ₦6m. The reinsurer’s financial position is therefore exposed to the full actuarial risk of the policy, including investment return risk on the reserves it holds. This makes co-insurance favourable for the cedant’s balance sheet (reserves are shared) but creates investment risk management complexity for the reinsurer. Co-insurance is well-suited to long-duration savings and endowment products, where the reserve-sharing feature provides meaningful balance sheet relief to the cedant from the first year of the policy. 14.4.2 Modified Co-insurance (Modco) Modified Co-insurance (Modco) A variant of co-insurance under which the reinsurer assumes its share of the policy risk and reserve liability, but the cedant retains the physical assets backing the reserve. The reinsurer’s share of the reserve remains on the cedant’s balance sheet, but the reinsurer receives an interest credit from the cedant equal to the investment return earned on the assets backing the ceded reserve. This allows the cedant to maintain direct control over its investment portfolio while still sharing the risk and reserve liability with the reinsurer. Modco is the preferred reinsurance method where: the cedant’s investment portfolio contains assets (property, infrastructure bonds, illiquid instruments) that cannot be physically transferred; the cedant wishes to maintain a unified investment strategy across its entire portfolio; or the regulatory framework (as in Nigeria) restricts the transfer of certain classes of admitted assets to foreign reinsurers. The Modco interest credit — the yield paid by the cedant to the reinsurer on the retained reserve — is the defining financial feature of the method. If the cedant earns 14% on the assets backing the reserve and the Modco credit rate is 12%, the cedant profits from the 2% spread; if investment returns fall below the credit rate, the cedant faces a loss on the Modco arrangement. 14.4.3 Yearly Renewable Term (YRT) Yearly Renewable Term (YRT) Reinsurance A life reinsurance method under which the reinsurer provides mortality cover only — specifically, cover for the Net Amount at Risk (the difference between the sum assured and the policy reserve) — for one policy year at a time, renewable annually for the duration of the policy. The cedant retains the full policy reserve and the investment risk. The YRT premium is calculated each year as: Net Amount at Risk × qx (the insured’s current-year mortality rate from the reinsurance treaty’s agreed mortality table) × the reinsurer’s mortality rate factor. YRT Annual Reinsurance Premium YRT Premium (year t) = NAR(t) × q(x+t) × Rate Factor Where: NAR(t) = Net Amount at Risk at duration t = Sum Assured − Policy Reserve at duration t; q(x+t) = the probability of death for a life aged x+t from the treaty mortality table; Rate Factor = the reinsurer’s pricing factor as a percentage of the treaty mortality rate. Key insight: As the policy reserve builds up over time (for endowments and savings products), the NAR decreases — so the YRT premium falls over the policy term, even as the insured ages and qx increases. For pure term assurance (which has no reserve build-up), the NAR equals the full sum assured throughout the term, and the YRT premium increases each year as qx rises with age. Worked Example 14.3 — YRT Net Amount at Risk and Premium A 20-year endowment policy on a life aged 40 has a sum assured of ₦10,000,000. The insurer has a 50% YRT surplus treaty with the reinsurer. Using illustrative values: Policy Year Sum Assured Policy Reserve NAR (SA − Reserve) Reinsurer’s 50% NAR Approx. YRT Premium Year 1 ₦10,000,000 ₦200,000 ₦9,800,000 ₦4,900,000 ₦47,000 Year 5 ₦10,000,000 ₦1,500,000 ₦8,500,000 ₦4,250,000 ₦42,000 Year 10 ₦10,000,000 ₦4,000,000 ₦6,000,000 ₦3,000,000 ₦33,000 Year 15 ₦10,000,000 ₦6,800,000 ₦3,200,000 ₦1,600,000 ₦22,000 Year 19 ₦10,000,000 ₦9,200,000 ₦800,000 ₦400,000 ₦7,000 Observation: Despite the insured aging from 40 to 59 over the term (increasing mortality risk), the YRT premium falls dramatically because the NAR shrinks as the reserve builds up. In year 19, the reinsurer’s exposure is only ₦400,000 — reflecting that the reserve covers almost the full sum assured and the reinsurer is providing very little additional mortality cover. YRT is the most widely used life reinsurance method in the Nigerian market. Its attractions are: simplicity of administration (annual premium recalculation); alignment of the reinsurance premium with actual mortality exposure; and the cedant’s retention of full control over policy reserves and investment assets. Its limitation is that the reinsurer can reprice (reset the rate factor) at each treaty renewal, introducing a risk that reinsurance costs increase if the industry’s mortality experience deteriorates. 14.4.4 Comparison of Life Reinsurance Methods Feature Co-insurance Modco YRT What is ceded Proportionate share of gross premium, reserve, and all benefits Same as co-insurance, but reserve physically stays with cedant Net Amount at Risk only (mortality risk). No reserve transfer. Reserve held by Reinsurer holds its proportionate share Cedant holds full reserve; reinsurer receives interest credit Cedant holds 100% of reserve Investment risk Shared between cedant and reinsurer Cedant bears investment risk; reinsurer bears credit risk on interest credit Cedant bears all investment risk Cash flow to reinsurer Share of gross premium, less ceding commission Share of gross premium, less ceding commission, plus/minus reserve interest Annual YRT mortality premium only Balance sheet impact for cedant Significant liability relief (reserve partially transferred to reinsurer) Same as co-insurance for risk; assets stay with cedant Minimal balance sheet impact; only reduces mortality risk component Best suited for Long-duration savings/endowment products with large reserves Savings products where cedant must retain assets for regulatory or investment reasons Pure risk (term assurance, group life); any product for straightforward mortality risk transfer Administrative complexity Moderate: reserve sharing requires treaty-level actuarial reconciliation High: ongoing interest credit calculation and cash settlement required Low to moderate: annual NAR-based premium recalculation Treaty repricing risk Lower: premium sharing tied to in-force policy terms Lower: same as co-insurance Higher: rate factor re-negotiated at each treaty renewal

t: Chapter 14 · 14.5 Retention Limits and Automatic Binding Authority
x: 14.5.1 Setting the Retention Limit The retention limit is the maximum Net Amount at Risk (or sum assured, for term products with no reserve) that the direct insurer retains on any single life for its own account, net of all reinsurance. Amounts above the retention limit are ceded to the reinsurer(s) under the treaty or facultatively. Setting the retention limit is a critical actuarial and capital management decision. The key considerations are: Capital capacity: The retention must be proportionate to the insurer’s available capital. A standard actuarial guideline is that the maximum single-life retention should not exceed 1% of the insurer’s total available capital. For a Nigerian life insurer with ₦15bn of available capital, a retention limit of ₦100–150m per life is consistent with this guideline. Portfolio experience: If the insurer’s in-force portfolio has a high concentration of large sum assured policies, a higher retention is needed to retain meaningful premium income; if the portfolio is predominantly small policies, a lower retention can be set without losing material premium. Reinsurer requirements: Reinsurers prefer cedants to retain a meaningful proportion of every risk (to maintain aligned incentives and avoid anti-selection). Treaty terms often specify minimum retention requirements — e.g., the cedant must retain at least 10–15% of every ceded risk. RBC impact: A higher retention means more mortality risk on the cedant’s own account, increasing the C1 (insurance risk) component of the RBC calculation and requiring more capital. The actuary models the RBC impact of different retention scenarios as part of the annual capital management review. 14.5.2 Automatic Binding Limit The automatic binding limit (ABL) is the maximum sum assured that the reinsurer will accept automatically under the treaty, without individual case review. It is typically set at a multiple of the retention limit — for example, if the retention limit is ₦50m and the treaty has 10 lines of surplus capacity, the ABL might be ₦550m (retention of ₦50m plus 10 lines of ₦50m = ₦500m ceded capacity). Risks with sum assureds above the ABL require facultative placement. The ABL therefore defines the boundary between automatic treaty processing and individual negotiation. For a Nigerian life insurer writing significant large case individual life business (high-net-worth individuals, keyman insurance for senior executives), managing the volume of facultative cases above the ABL is a significant underwriting operations function. 14.5.3 Net Amount at Risk Net Amount at Risk (NAR) The portion of the sum assured that the insurer (or reinsurer) is genuinely ‘at risk’ for in any given policy year. It equals the sum assured minus the policy reserve at that duration. The NAR represents the additional amount that must be paid from new funds (not from accumulated reserve) if the insured dies in that year. For term assurance (which carries no reserve build-up), the NAR equals the full sum assured. For endowments and whole life policies, the NAR declines as the reserve builds up. The NAR concept is important beyond reinsurance pricing. It is also the basis for:the mortality risk component of the RBC capital calculation (C1 charge); the actuarial assessment of catastrophe risk exposure across the portfolio; and the calculation of excess of loss reinsurance trigger amounts for per-life XL treaties.

t: Chapter 14 · 14.6 The Reinsurance Treaty: Structure and Key Provisions
x: A life reinsurance treaty is a legal contract between the cedant and the reinsurer that defines every aspect of their relationship for the duration of the treaty. Nigerian life insurers dealing with domestic and international reinsurers should understand the key components of this document, as treaty terms directly affect the insurer’s operational obligations, financial exposure, and claims recovery rights. Parties and Scope Identifies the cedant and reinsurer; defines the classes of business covered (individual life, group life, credit life), the territory (Nigeria only or including diaspora risks), and the policy types included. Retention and Capacity The retention limit; number of lines of surplus capacity (for surplus treaties); the ABL; and any per-group or aggregate capacity limits for group life treaties. Underwriting Guidelines The mortality table(s) applicable to the treaty; medical evidence requirements (NML schedule); occupational hazard schedule; exclusions (risks the reinsurer will not automatically cover, such as aviation, certain occupational hazards, or — pre-NIIRA 2025 — HIV-positive lives); and any age or sum assured restrictions. Premium Basis For YRT: the treaty mortality rates (expressed as a percentage of the standard table), the rate guarantee period, and renewal pricing provisions. For co-insurance/Modco: the ceding commission basis and the interest credit calculation methodology. Claims Provisions The cedant’s obligation to notify the reinsurer of claims above defined thresholds; the documentation required for a recovery claim; the reinsurer’s payment timeline after receipt of complete claims documentation; provisions for disputed claims. Accounting and Reporting The quarterly or annual premium accounting schedule; the format and timing of experience reports required by the reinsurer; any experience refund or profit commission provisions. Duration and Termination The treaty term (usually annual with tacit renewal); notice periods for termination; run-off provisions for in-force policies after termination (policies issued during the treaty period continue to be covered under the treaty’s terms until they expire, even if the treaty terminates). Insolvency and Security The reinsurer’s obligations if the cedant becomes insolvent; any letter of credit or funds withheld arrangements that enhance the cedant’s security over the reinsurer’s obligations; applicable law and dispute resolution jurisdiction.

t: Chapter 14 · 14.7 The Nigerian Domestic Reinsurance Market
x: 14.7.1 Nigerian Reinsurance Corporation (NRC) The Nigerian Reinsurance Corporation (NRC) is the state-owned reinsurance company of the Federal Government of Nigeria, established by decree in 1977 and subsequently incorporated under the Companies and Allied Matters Act. NRC is the market leader in the domestic Nigerian reinsurance market and receives statutory preferential cessions from Nigerian direct insurers under the domestic cession obligations imposed by Nigerian insurance law. NRC provides reinsurance capacity across all classes of insurance business, including life reinsurance. Its life reinsurance operations cover: group life schemes for employers and government entities; individual life surplus treaties; and credit life reinsurance for bank-led lending products. NRC’s market position is reinforced by the compulsory cession requirements discussed in Section 14.9.2, which require Nigerian insurers to offer a defined minimum proportion of every reinsurance placement to domestic reinsurers before ceding internationally. Under NIIRA 2025, NRC is required to comply with the ₦35 billion minimum capital requirement applicable to all Nigerian reinsurers. This requirement, which represents a significant increase from the previous capital level, is intended to strengthen the domestic reinsurance market’s capacity and financial resilience, enabling it to retain a larger proportion of Nigerian risk domestically rather than ceding to the international market. 14.7.2 Continental Reinsurance Plc Continental Reinsurance Plc (Continental Re) is a pan-African specialist reinsurer headquartered in Lagos, operating across multiple African markets through offices in Abuja, Nairobi, Tunis, Douala, and Abidjan, as well as a London office. Continental Re is the leading private-sector African reinsurer and a significant provider of life reinsurance capacity to Nigerian life insurers. Continental Re’s life reinsurance offering includes: YRT and co-insurance treaty structures for individual and group life; facultative capacity for large individual life risks; credit life reinsurance programs for bank and microfinance partnerships; and actuarial and underwriting advisory services for cedant insurers seeking to develop new life products. Continental Re is rated by international rating agencies, providing cedant insurers with counterparty security assurance that is increasingly important for NIIRA 2025 compliance and IFRS 17 credit risk assessment of reinsurance assets. 14.7.3 Africa Re and Other Domestic Reinsurers The African Reinsurance Corporation (Africa Re), headquartered in Lagos, is a multilateral development finance institution owned by African Development Bank member states, including Nigeria. Africa Re provides life reinsurance capacity across the continent and operates a dedicated Africa-specific life reinsurance programme. Nigerian life insurers are shareholder-members of Africa Re and have preferred access to its capacity. Other domestic reinsurers operating in the Nigerian market include: Waica Reinsurance Corporation (West Africa-focused); NSIA Reinsurance (formerly Colina Re); and several smaller reinsurance companies. The domestic reinsurance market’s capacity for large life risks remains limited relative to international market capacity, which is why Nigerian life insurers continue to access international reinsurers — primarily European and Asian companies — for capacity above what the domestic market can absorb. 14.7.4 International Reinsurers in the Nigerian Life Market The international reinsurance market provides the majority of large-case life reinsurance capacity for Nigerian direct insurers. The primary international life reinsurers active in Nigeria are: Munich Re (Germany), Swiss Re (Switzerland), General Re (a Berkshire Hathaway company), RGA Reinsurance (USA), Hannover Re (Germany), and several Lloyd’s of London syndicates for specialist risks. International reinsurers bring three capabilities that domestic reinsurers cannot yet fully replicate at scale: global mortality data from diverse populations and markets; technical underwriting expertise, particularly for complex medical conditions and specialist occupations; and deep balance sheet capacity for very large individual life risks and catastrophe covers. The relationship between Nigerian life insurers and their international reinsurers is therefore not merely transactional — it is a substantive technical partnership. NIIRA 2025’s domestic cession requirements (Section 14.9.2) regulate the proportion of reinsurance premiums that may be ceded internationally, ensuring that the domestic reinsurance market receives a minimum volume of business. This protects the domestic market’s economic viability while still permitting access to international capacity for risks that exceed domestic limits.

t: Chapter 14 · 14.8 Reinsurance as a Capital Management Tool
x: 14.8.1 New Business Strain and Reinsurance Finance New business strain is the cash flow deficit created in the first year of a new life insurance policy. In a typical long-term savings or whole life product, the insurer pays commission to the agent (which may equal 30–70% of the first-year premium), incurs underwriting and policy issue costs, and begins building the policy reserve — all in the same year it collects only the first annual premium. The result is a first-year loss on virtually every new policy, even if the policy will eventually be highly profitable over its full term. Reinsurance — particularly co-insurance and Modco — provides a partial solution to new business strain. Under co-insurance, the reinsurer takes its share of the first-year premium and simultaneously assumes its share of the first-year reserve. The ceding commission paid by the reinsurer to the cedant represents a cash transfer that offsets a portion of the cedant’s initial acquisition costs. This ‘fronting’ of the reserve by the reinsurer is, in economic terms, a form of financing: the reinsurer is advancing cash against the future stream of reinsurance premiums it will receive over the policy’s lifetime. 14.8.2 Mortality Risk Transfer and Earnings Volatility Life insurance profits are volatile because mortality experience varies from year to year. In a good year, fewer people die than expected and the insurer earns surplus; in a bad year (a pandemic, a series of high-value deaths, or a cluster of group life claims from an industrial accident), claims exceed expectations and the insurer reports a loss on its life book. Reinsurance — particularly YRT — converts this volatile mortality risk into a more stable cost. The insurer pays a predictable annual reinsurance premium and recovers a proportionate share of actual claims from the reinsurer. The net effect is to smooth annual earnings: the reinsurer absorbs the peaks of bad mortality years, and the cedant gives up a share of the profits from good years. From a shareholder and board perspective, this trade-off is typically worthwhile — predictable earnings are valued more highly than volatile earnings. 14.8.3 RBC Capital Optimisation Under NIIRA 2025’s Risk-Based Capital framework, the amount of capital a life insurer must hold is directly linked to the mortality risk it retains. By transferring mortality risk to reinsurers through YRT or proportional treaties, the insurer reduces its net NAR exposure and therefore reduces the C1 (insurance risk) component of its RBC Total Risk Charge. The capital relief benefit of reinsurance can be quantified precisely by the actuary: if a reinsurance programme reduces the net portfolio NAR by ₦100 billion and the C1 risk factor for the relevant product category is 0.5% of NAR, the reinsurance programme releases ₦500 million of required capital. This released capital can be deployed for new business growth, returned to shareholders, or held as a buffer above the RBC minimum. Capital Relief from Reinsurance — Simplified Capital Relief = Reduction in Net NAR × C1 Risk Factor This simplification illustrates the mechanism. The actual RBC calculation involves more complex diversification adjustments. The key principle is that every naira of mortality risk transferred to a reinsurer is a naira of NAR removed from the denominator of the C1 capital charge — directly reducing the minimum capital requirement.

t: Chapter 14 · 14.9 NIIRA 2025: Reinsurer Capital Requirements and Domestic Cession Obligations
x: 14.9.1 Minimum Capital for Reinsurers NIIRA 2025: ₦35 Billion Minimum Capital for Reinsurers NIIRA 2025 establishes a minimum paid-up capital requirement of ₦35,000,000,000 (Thirty-Five Billion Naira; s.15(1)(c), or risk-based capital if higher) for reinsurance companies operating in Nigeria. This requirement applies to: Nigerian Reinsurance Corporation (NRC) and all domestic reinsurers licenced by NAICOM. International reinsurers operating branches or representative offices in Nigeria. Any entity seeking a new reinsurance licence under NIIRA 2025. The ₦35 bn threshold is substantially higher than the previous minimum, reflecting NAICOM’s objective of creating a domestic reinsurance market with genuine capital depth — capable of retaining larger proportions of Nigerian insurance risk without exhausting its capacity. Reinsurers that fail to meet the minimum capital requirement within the NIIRA 2025 transition period are required to either: (a) raise capital to the required level; (b) merge with another domestic reinsurer to achieve the combined threshold; or (c) surrender their reinsurance licence. The capital consolidation this requirement incentivises is intended to produce a smaller number of better-capitalised, more credible domestic reinsurers — matching the model of reinsurance markets in South Africa and Kenya, where a concentrated domestic reinsurance industry has enabled significantly higher domestic risk retention. 14.9.2 Domestic Cession Obligations Nigerian insurance law has historically required direct insurers to offer a minimum proportion of all reinsurance placements to the domestic market before accessing international capacity. This domestic cession obligation has two purposes: to develop and sustain the domestic reinsurance industry by guaranteeing it a minimum premium volume, and to reduce the outflow of insurance premium to foreign reinsurers (which represents an outflow of foreign exchange from the Nigerian economy). Under the framework that NIIRA 2025 builds on and reinforces, Nigerian life insurers are required to offer their domestic reinsurance treaties to domestic reinsurers (NRC, Continental Re, Africa Re) before placing internationally. The domestic market must be given the first right of refusal on a defined percentage of every placement. Placements that exceed domestic capacity — which is common for very large individual life risks and catastrophe covers — may then proceed to international reinsurers for the excess. The practical implication for life insurance companies is that the broking of reinsurance programmes — typically done through specialist reinsurance brokers — must be structured to document compliance with the domestic cession requirement. NAICOM may request evidence of domestic market approach as part of its annual supervisory review of reinsurance arrangements. 14.9.3 NAICOM Oversight of Reinsurance Arrangements NIIRA 2025 extends NAICOM’s supervisory powers over reinsurance arrangements. Key provisions relevant to life insurers include: Treaty approval: NAICOM may require life insurers to submit their primary reinsurance treaty terms for review as part of the licensing and annual reporting process. Where NAICOM considers that a treaty’s terms create an unacceptable risk transfer structure or reduce the insurer’s solvency margin below required levels, it may direct the insurer to modify the treaty. Reinsurer credit quality: NAICOM expects direct insurers to assess the credit quality of their reinsurance counterparties. Ceding risk to an insolvent or financially weak reinsurer provides no genuine risk transfer; the cedant remains exposed if the reinsurer cannot pay claims. Under IFRS 17, reinsurance recoverables must be assessed for credit risk and the expected credit loss provision must be reflected in the financial statements. Actuarial certification: The Statutory Actuary’s annual report must confirm that the reinsurance programme is consistent with the pricing and reserving bases used in the annual valuation — i.e., that the reinsurer’s share of the reserve and premium, as recorded in the treaty, matches the reinsurance asset recognised in the insurer’s financial statements. Reporting of material changes: Material changes to the reinsurance programme — including termination of a treaty, a significant reduction in capacity, or a change in the key reinsurance counterparty — must be notified to NAICOM promptly.

t: Chapter 14 · 14.10 Advisory: Building and Managing a Life Reinsurance Programme
x: A well-constructed reinsurance programme is a strategic asset for a Nigerian life insurer. A poorly structured one is a source of operational risk, financial leakage, and potential solvency pressure. This advisory section addresses the design, negotiation, governance, and review of a best-practice programme. 14.10.1 Programme Design Principles The design of the reinsurance programme begins with the insurer’s risk appetite and capital strategy. The reinsurance structure should answer four questions precisely: What is the maximum net mortality exposure the insurer is prepared to carry on any single life, and how does this relate to available capital? What is the maximum tolerable annual claims volatility from mortality experience, and what aggregate cover is needed to cap adverse years? What cash flow relief (ceding commissions from co-insurance) is needed to manage new business strain in the current business plan? What proportion of the programme must be placed domestically for regulatory compliance, and what capacity exists in the domestic market? These four questions map to the programme’s four components: surplus/quota share treaty (capacity and proportional risk sharing); excess of loss or stop loss cover (volatility cap); co-insurance (new business strain); and domestic market allocation (regulatory compliance). 14.10.2 Treaty Negotiation and Reinsurer Selection Reinsurance treaty negotiation is a technical commercial process conducted either directly or through a specialist reinsurance broker. Nigerian life insurers — particularly those without large in-house actuarial teams — are well advised to engage a qualified reinsurance broker for annual treaty renewals. The broker brings: market access to multiple reinsurers simultaneously; benchmarking data on market rates and terms; negotiating experience; and claims support when recoveries need to be pursued. Reinsurer selection criteria should include: Financial strength: International credit ratings (minimum A- from Standard & Poor’s, A.M. Best, or equivalent). An unrated reinsurer should be approached with caution. Under IFRS 17, higher credit risk means a larger expected credit loss provision against the reinsurance asset. Market commitment: Reinsurers who have maintained continuous presence in the Nigerian market through cycles of premium growth and economic stress are preferred to those who enter during profitable years and exit when conditions deteriorate. Technical support: Reinsurers who provide underwriting manuals, medical officer consultations, experience analysis, and product development support add value beyond the pure risk transfer function. Claims responsiveness: The reinsurer’s track record in paying claims promptly and without unnecessary disputation is a critical selection criterion, assessed through reference checks with other Nigerian cedants. 14.10.3 Treaty Administration and Recoveries Management A signed treaty is only the beginning of the reinsurance relationship. The operational value of the treaty depends entirely on how well it is administered. Key treaty administration obligations include: Quarterly/annual accounts: Premium accounting statements are submitted to the reinsurer on the schedule defined in the treaty. Late or incomplete accounts are a common operational failure in the Nigerian market and can create disputes about the calculation of recoveries. Loss notifications: Large claims (typically those exceeding 50–75% of the retention limit) must be notified to the reinsurer promptly. Failure to notify within the treaty’s prescribed window can give the reinsurer grounds to dispute or delay recovery. Faculty bordereau: A regular submission listing all facultative placements made under the treaty’s facultative capacity, confirming that each risk accepted by the reinsurer is within the treaty’s underwriting guidelines. Experience reporting: Many treaties include provisions for annual experience reporting by the cedant, showing the actual claims experience on the ceded portfolio. This data supports the reinsurer’s renewal pricing assessment. Advisory: Building an Internal Reinsurance Administration Capability Many Nigerian life insurers manage reinsurance administration through informal processes — spreadsheets, email exchanges, and ad-hoc premium settlements. This creates significant operational risk: late or erroneous premium accounting exposes the insurer to treaty termination; failure to track facultative placements leaves uninsured gaps; and unreconciled recovery claims mean the insurer may be holding less reinsurance protection than its treaty provides. Recommended minimum operational standards: Reinsurance module in the PAS: Every policy ceded under the treaty should be recorded in the Policy Administration System with the reinsured proportion and the reinsurer’s reference number, enabling automatic premium and claims accounting. Dedicated reinsurance accounting function: At least one senior finance officer should have primary responsibility for reinsurance accounting and recovery management, with clear KPIs for account settlement timeliness and outstanding recovery tracking. Actuarial review of reinsurance assets: The Statutory Actuary’s annual valuation should include an explicit reconciliation of the reinsurance asset recognised in the financial statements against the treaty records and outstanding recovery amounts. Annual programme review: Before each treaty renewal, the actuary should model the RBC capital impact of the current and alternative programme structures, and the CFO should review the net cost of reinsurance (premiums paid less recoveries received) as a percentage of gross premium income.

Reinsurance A contract under which a direct insurer (the cedant) transfers a defined portion of the insurance risks it has accepted from policyholders to one or more reinsurers, in exchange for a proportionate share of the premium. Cedant The direct insurance company that transfers (cedes) a portion of its insurance risk to a reinsurer. Also called the ceding company or the direct insurer. Proportional Reinsurance A reinsurance arrangement in which the cedant and the reinsurer share both the premium and the risk in defined proportions. Premium and claims are allocated in the same ratio. Includes quota share and surplus treaties. Non-Proportional Reinsurance A reinsurance arrangement in which the reinsurer’s obligation is triggered only when claims exceed a defined threshold (priority or attachment point). The reinsurer does not receive a proportionate share of premium. Includes excess of loss and stop loss. Quota Share Treaty A proportional reinsurance treaty under which a fixed percentage of every risk within the treaty scope is ceded to the reinsurer. The same percentage applies to premiums and claims on every ceded policy. Surplus Treaty A proportional reinsurance treaty under which the cedant retains risks up to the retention limit and cedes only the excess. The cession ratio varies by policy size. Excess of Loss (XL) A non-proportional reinsurance arrangement under which the reinsurer pays claims (or aggregate claims) exceeding a defined priority level, up to a maximum. Structured per-life or in aggregate. Stop Loss A non-proportional reinsurance arrangement that limits the cedant’s aggregate claims experience in a year to a defined percentage of premium income. The reinsurer pays the excess above the attachment point. Treaty Reinsurance A standing reinsurance agreement covering all risks of a defined class automatically, without individual case negotiation. Every qualifying risk is automatically ceded and accepted under the treaty terms. Facultative Reinsurance Individual-case reinsurance in which the cedant offers a specific risk to the reinsurer, who is free to accept, decline, or quote modified terms. Used for risks above the treaty ABL or outside the treaty guidelines. Co-insurance (Reinsurance Method) A life reinsurance method in which the reinsurer assumes a proportionate share of the full policy economics — premium, reserve, and benefits. The reinsurer holds its share of the policy reserve. Modified Co-insurance (Modco) A variant of co-insurance in which the reinsurer assumes its share of risk but the cedant retains the physical reserve assets, paying the reinsurer an interest credit on the retained reserve amount. Yearly Renewable Term (YRT) A life reinsurance method providing annual mortality cover only, on the Net Amount at Risk. The YRT premium is recalculated each year based on the current NAR and the insured’s age-specific mortality rate. No reserve is ceded. Net Amount at Risk (NAR) The difference between the sum assured and the policy reserve at any given duration. Represents the amount the insurer must pay from current funds (not from the accumulated reserve) if the insured dies in that year. Retention Limit The maximum net amount at risk that the direct insurer retains on any single life for its own account, net of reinsurance. Amounts above the retention are ceded to the reinsurer. Automatic Binding Limit (ABL) The maximum sum assured the reinsurer will automatically accept under the treaty without individual case review. Risks above the ABL require facultative placement. Ceding Commission A payment by the reinsurer to the cedant under a proportional treaty (particularly co-insurance), representing a reimbursement of the cedant’s initial acquisition costs on the ceded business. New Business Strain The first-year cash flow deficit arising when the initial expenses of a new life insurance policy (commission, underwriting, issue costs) exceed the first-year premium. Co-insurance reinsurance partially addresses new business strain through the ceding commission. Domestic Cession Obligation The regulatory requirement under Nigerian insurance law for direct insurers to offer a defined minimum proportion of all reinsurance placements to domestic reinsurers before accessing international capacity. Nigerian Reinsurance Corporation (NRC) The state-owned domestic reinsurance company of the Federal Republic of Nigeria. Receives preferential domestic cessions from Nigerian direct insurers. Continental Reinsurance Plc A pan-African private-sector reinsurer headquartered in Lagos. The leading private domestic reinsurer in Nigeria, with operations across multiple African markets.

Under a 30% quota share reinsurance treaty, the insurer accepts a group life scheme with annual premium of ₦60m and sum assured of ₦6bn. Three death claims total ₦450m. The reinsurer is required to pay: ₦18m. ₦135m. ₦315m. ₦450m. (B) ₦135,000,000. Why (B) is Correct Under a quota share treaty, the reinsurer shares a fixed percentage of all premiums and all claims. At 30% quota share:• Reinsurer's share of premium: 30% × ₦60m = ₦18m (received by reinsurer)• Reinsurer's share of claims: 30% × ₦450m = ₦135m (paid by reinsurer) The reinsurer pays ₦135m and the cedant retains 70% of the claims (₦315m net). Why the Others Are Wrong (A) ₦18m is the reinsurer's share of premium income, not its claims liability.(C) ₦315m is the cedant's 70% retention of the claims — the cedant's net liability, not the reinsurer's payment.(D) ₦450m is the total gross claims liability before reinsurance — the reinsurer pays only its quota share proportion.

Yearly Renewable Term (YRT) reinsurance provides the cedant insurer with: A proportionate share of the reinsurer's entire premium income and reserve. Annual mortality cover on the Net Amount at Risk only, with the reserve retained by the cedant. A guarantee that the reinsurer will accept all risks ceded without individual review. Coverage for aggregate claims exceeding a defined percentage of premium income in any year. (B) Annual mortality cover on the Net Amount at Risk only, with the reserve retained by the cedant. Why (B) is Correct YRT (Yearly Renewable Term) reinsurance is a non-proportional mortality cover: the cedant cedes only the pure mortality risk (the Net Amount at Risk — the excess of the sum assured over the policy reserve) to the reinsurer. The cedant retains the full policy reserve on its balance sheet and continues to collect the full gross premium. The reinsurer charges an annual risk premium based on the NAR and the applicable mortality rate. The YRT premium is renegotiated annually at renewal, hence 'yearly renewable.' Why the Others Are Wrong (A) describes co-insurance (proportional reinsurance) — where a fixed share of premium and reserve is ceded to the reinsurer. This is the opposite of YRT, which cedes no reserve.(C) No reinsurance treaty guarantees automatic acceptance of all ceded risks without review. Facultative reinsurance is individually assessed; treaty reinsurance accepts within agreed parameters but does not guarantee individual case acceptance.(D) describes a stop-loss (aggregate excess of loss) cover — triggered when total claims exceed

The minimum paid-up capital requirement for reinsurance companies under NIIRA 2025 is: ₦10 billion. ₦18 billion. ₦35 billion. ₦100 billion. (C) ₦35 billion. Why (C) is Correct Section 15(1)(c) of NIIRA 2025 sets the minimum capital for reinsurance business at ₦35 billion, or the risk-based capital determined by the Commission if higher. This represents a large increase from the prior ₦10 billion minimum and is intended to transform the domestic reinsurance market into a credible first-line capacity provider capable of retaining a materially larger proportion of Nigerian insurance risk. Why the Others Are Wrong (A) ₦10 billion is the minimum for life insurance companies — not reinsurers.(B) ₦18 billion is not a NIIRA 2025 threshold: the Act sets no composite capital figure, and composite licences are no longer issued to insurers (s.6).(D) ₦100 billion is not a NIIRA 2025 capital threshold for any licence category.

The Net Amount at Risk (NAR) on a life insurance policy is best defined as: The total sum assured payable on death. The difference between the sum assured and the policy reserve at a given policy duration. The reinsurer's maximum liability under the treaty in any single year. The amount the insurer retains after paying all claims and expenses. (B) The difference between the sum assured and the policy reserve at a given policy duration. Why (B) is Correct The NAR is the portion of the death benefit that the insurer is at risk of paying from current assets (not from accumulated reserves). If a policy has a sum assured of ₦10m and a policy reserve of ₦2.5m, the NAR is ₦10m − ₦2.5m = ₦7.5m. On death, the insurer would pay ₦10m total: ₦2.5m from the policy reserve (already set aside) and ₦7.5m from current assets. The YRT reinsurance covers the NAR because that is the additional risk the insurer bears beyond its accumulated reserve. Why the Others Are Wrong (A) The sum assured is the total death benefit — the NAR is a subset of the sum assured (the portion above the reserve).(C) The reinsurer's maximum treaty liability is determined by treaty capacity limits — related to NAR but not the same concept.(D) The net retained amount after claims and expenses is an accounting concept, not the actuarial NAR definition.

A reinsurance treaty under which the cedant retains all risks below ₦50 million and cedes only the amount of individual policy sum assured above ₦50 million is: A quota share treaty. A stop loss treaty. A surplus treaty. An excess of loss treaty. (C) A surplus treaty. Why (C) is Correct A surplus treaty is a proportional reinsurance arrangement in which the cedant retains a defined amount per risk (the 'retention' — ₦50m in this case) and cedes only the surplus above the retention. The surplus is distributed across the reinsurer's lines of capacity. Unlike quota share (which cedes a fixed percentage regardless of size), the surplus treaty cedes different amounts from different risks — a ₦100m policy cedes ₦50m (100%); a ₦60m policy cedes ₦10m (17%). Why the Others Are Wrong (A) A quota share treaty cedes a fixed percentage of every risk — e.g., 30% of all risks regardless of size. It does not have a retention threshold below which nothing is ceded.(B) A stop loss (aggregate excess of loss) treaty is triggered when total claims in a period exceed a defined percentage of premium income. It is an aggregate cover, not a per-risk excess-of-retention arrangement.(D) An excess of loss treaty in life insurance is typically a per-life XL cover — attaching at a defined net retained amount per individual life (not the same as the surplus mechanism, which is proportional above the retention).

A Nigerian life insurer has the following reinsurance programme: a YRT surplus treaty with a retention limit of ₦60m and 8 lines of capacity (₦480m maximum cession); and a per-life excess of loss cover attaching at ₦200m per life (net of treaty) with a maximum of ₦300m. An individual life policy for ₦700m is applied for.
(a) Show how the ₦700m risk is distributed among the cedant, the YRT reinsurer, and the XL reinsurer.
(b) Calculate the cedant’s net retained position after all reinsurance.
(c) Explain the purpose of combining a YRT surplus treaty with a per-life XL cover in this way.
(d) If the individual dies and the full ₦700m benefit falls due, calculate the recovery the cedant receives from each reinsurance layer.   Part (a) — Risk Distribution The ₦700m risk is distributed as follows:Cedant retention: ₦60m (the first layer — the surplus treaty's retention limit)YRT surplus treaty cession: The surplus treaty has 8 lines of capacity. Each 'line' equals the retention (₦60m). Total surplus capacity: 8 × ₦60m = ₦480m. The surplus above the ₦60m retention is ceded: ₦700m − ₦60m = ₦640m. However, the treaty capacity is only ₦480m. So the surplus cession is capped at ₦480m.Net of treaty (before XL): Cedant's position after surplus cession: ₦700m − ₦60m (retention) − ₦480m (surplus ceded) = ₦160m. But we specified the XL attaches at ₦200m net — since the net is ₦160m which is below the XL attachment, the XL does not attach on this risk. The remaining ₦160m net must either be retained by the cedant or individually reinsured (facultative placement).Note for candidates: This str

A life insurer’s YRT treaty with its reinsurer is approaching renewal. The reinsurer has indicated it will increase the rate factor (the multiple of the treaty mortality table) from 85% to 110% for the coming year, citing adverse mortality experience on the cedant’s group life portfolio over the past three years.
(a) Explain the financial impact of this rate increase on the insurer’s claims costs and profitability.
(b) Describe the negotiating options available to the cedant.
(c) Explain why the domestic cession obligations under NIIRA 2025 both constrain and assist the cedant in this negotiation.
(d) If the cedant cannot negotiate an acceptable rate, describe the capital and risk management implications of reducing reinsurance coverage or increasing its retention limit instead.   Part (a) — Financial Impact of the Rate Increase The rate factor is the multiple applied to the treaty's standard mortality table to calculate the annual YRT risk premium. An increase from 85% to 110% represents a 29.4% increase in the YRT risk premium cost.Financial impact example: If the current YRT risk premium is ₦500m per annum (at 85% of table), the new premium at 110% is:₦500m × (110/85) = ₦500m × 1.294 = ₦647m per annumAdditional annual cost: ₦147m — a direct hit to the insurer's underwriting profit. t: Chapter 15 · Enterprise Risk Management for Life Insurance Companies
x: Learning Objectives On completing this chapter, the reader should be able to: Explain the purpose and scope of Enterprise Risk Management (ERM) in the context of a life insurance company and describe the principal international ERM frameworks — ISO 31000, COSO, and the IAIS Insurance Core Principles — and how they are applied in the Nigerian regulatory context. Identify and describe the eight principal categories of risk faced by Nigerian life insurers — insurance risk, market risk, credit risk, operational risk, liquidity risk, regulatory risk, reputational risk, and cyber risk — and explain the specific drivers of each in the Nigerian operating environment. Define risk appetite and risk tolerance, explain how Boards of Directors set and monitor risk limits, and describe the components of a Board-approved risk appetite statement for a life insurance company. Describe the structure and purpose of the risk register and explain how Key Risk Indicators (KRIs) are selected, monitored, and reported as part of the ongoing risk management cycle. Explain the Own Risk and Solvency Assessment (ORSA), describe its mandatory requirements under NIIRA 2025, and outline the process for conducting and reporting the ORSA to the Board and NAICOM. Describe the three-lines-of-defence model as applied to life insurance risk governance, explain the roles of the Chief Risk Officer and the Board Risk Committee, and identify the governance failures that commonly undermine effective ERM in practice.
