t: Chapter 17 · 17.1 Introduction: The Agency as a Business Within a Business
x: Each distribution channel that a life insurance company operates is, in effect, a business within a business. It has its own customer base, its own cost structure, its own productivity drivers, its own compliance obligations, and its own talent management challenges. The insurer that treats its distribution channels as passive conduits for premium collection — rather than as actively managed commercial operations — will find that they underperform, generate compliance risks, and produce the high early-lapse rates that erode the profitability of even a well-priced product. Chapter 16 examined the landscape of distribution channels available to Nigerian life insurers. This chapter goes deeper: it addresses the operational design, management disciplines, incentive structures, and governance frameworks required to build each major channel into a high-performing, sustainable distribution asset. It draws on the specific commercial realities of the Nigerian market — the informal economy’s impact on prospecting, the employer-as-gateway for corporate distribution, the regulatory architecture of bancassurance, the untapped potential of fintech and agritech partnerships — to offer management-level guidance that goes beyond regulatory compliance into genuine operational excellence. The chapter is structured around five agency types: the retail agency, the bancassurance agency, the corporate and worksite sales operation, the annuity distribution channel, and the alternative partnership model. For each, the chapter addresses: structure, management disciplines, incentive design, KPIs, compliance oversight, and digital integration.

17.2.1 Overview and Strategic Role The retail agency is the foundational distribution channel for individual life insurance in Nigeria. Retail agents — whether called financial advisers, life assurance consultants, marketing associates, or simply agents — form the human interface between the insurer’s products and the individual consumer. Their work is fundamentally relational: they build trust with potential policyholders, understand their financial circumstances and protection needs, present products, manage the underwriting process, collect the first premium, and maintain the ongoing service relationship. The retail agency channel is well-suited to products that require explanation and personalisation: whole life, endowments, participating policies, health riders, and larger individual term assurance plans. Its limitation is cost: a retail agent requires recruitment, training, supervision, and ongoing incentive management — costs that are only justified by the premium income generated. This makes the retail agency channel commercially viable for policies of meaningful premium size and duration, and less viable for the low-premium, high-volume products better suited to digital or cooperative distribution. 17.2.2 The Agency Hierarchy Level Title (typical) Responsibility Typical Team Size Primary KPI Level 1 — Field Agent Agent / Life Assurance Consultant / FA Direct client prospecting, presentation, and policy acquisition. Manages their own client portfolio. Reports to a Unit Manager. Individual Annualised First-Year Premium (AFYP) per month; cases per month. Level 2 — Unit Manager (UM) Unit Manager / Team Leader Recruits, trains, and supervises a team of 8–15 agents. Personally produces (retains own client portfolio). Earns overrider on team production. 8–15 agents Team AFYP; agent retention rate; new agent activation rate (% of new recruits who make first sale within 90 days). Level 3 — Branch Manager (BM) Branch Manager / Agency Manager Manages 3–8 unit managers and their teams. Oversees branch compliance, training, and operations. Does not personally sell; focused entirely on management and coaching. 30–100+ agents Branch AFYP; 13-month persistency rate; agent headcount growth; compliance audit score. Level 4 — Regional Director (RD) Regional Director / Regional Manager Manages 3‒6 branches across a geographic region. Sets regional strategy, manages branch managers, oversees regional compliance. Multiple branches Regional AFYP growth; market share in region; regional persistency; expense ratio. Level 5 — Agency Director / Distribution Head Chief Agency Officer / Director of Sales National leadership of the entire retail agency channel. Reports to CEO. Sets channel strategy, budget, and performance standards. Interface with NAICOM on agency matters. Entire national agency National AFYP; total active agent count; channel expense ratio; national persistency rate. 17.2.3 Pyramid vs. Flat Agency Models The agency hierarchy described above is the traditional pyramid model: a large base of individual agents, managed through progressively fewer layers of supervision, each layer earning override commissions on the production of the layer below. The pyramid model’s commercial logic is that it finances supervision through override rather than salary, keeping the fixed cost base low. Feature Pyramid Model Flat Model Structure Multiple layers (agent → unit manager → branch manager → regional director → director of sales) Fewer layers; agents report to a branch manager or directly to regional management with limited intermediate supervision. Override cost Higher: multiple layers of overrider commissions reduce the net revenue per policy to the insurer. Lower: fewer override layers; more commission reaches the individual agent, but less supports supervisory infrastructure. Supervision depth High: unit managers are hands-on coaches with small teams; daily activity tracking is feasible. Lower: branch managers supervise more agents directly; individual attention is diluted. New agent support Strong: unit manager is directly incentivised (through overrider) to develop their agents’ productivity. Weaker: flat model provides less personalised coaching for new agents, increasing early attrition risk. Scalability Easily scalable: adding a new unit manager creates a platform for 8–15 new agents. Less scalable: branch manager span of control limits growth without expanding management. Best suited for Large, geographically diverse retail agency forces; markets where new agent training is a significant challenge; companies targeting aggressive headcount growth. Experienced, self-managing agent forces; companies with strong digital productivity tools that reduce the need for hands-on supervision; lean-cost distribution strategies. 17.2.4 Productivity Management Retail agent productivity is the ratio of premium income generated to the resources (time, cost, management attention) invested in the agent. Productivity management is the systematic discipline of tracking, analysing, and improving this ratio at the individual, unit, and branch levels. The productivity cascade for a retail agent runs as follows: The Agent Productivity Cascade ACTIVITY (inputs) → PIPELINE (intermediate outputs) → PRODUCTION (results) ACTIVITY: The number of prospecting contacts made per week (calls, referral requests, community events attended, LinkedIn outreach for professional-market agents). Activity is the one variable that agents fully control. A low-activity agent cannot achieve high production regardless of skill. PIPELINE: The number of qualified appointments set from prospecting activity; proposals presented; applications submitted. The pipeline converts activity into visible prospective business. Pipeline management reveals where the sales process is breaking down: if an agent has high activity but few appointments, their prospecting script is failing. If they have appointments but few proposals, their approach-to-presentation conversion needs work. PRODUCTION: New annualised first-year premium (AFYP) submitted and issued. Cases submitted per month. Average case size. Persistency of the in-force book (the quality dimension of production). AFYP is the headline productivity metric; average case size is the margin quality indicator; persistency is the durability indicator. Productivity Metric Definition Frequency Nigerian Market Benchmark (Indicative) Annualised First-Year Premium (AFYP) Total new business premium submitted in the period, annualised (monthly premium × 12 for monthly-pay policies). Monthly Active agent: ₦1.5m–3m AFYP per month. Top performer: ₦6m+ per month. Cases per Month Number of new policies submitted. Monthly Active agent: 3–6 cases per month. Top performer: 10+ cases per month. Average Case Size AFYP ÷ Cases submitted. Monthly ₦300,000–₦700,000 per case (varies significantly by market segment). Activity Ratio Prospecting contacts per week. Weekly Minimum 20 contacts/week for an active agent. Appointment Conversion Appointments set ÷ Contacts made. Weekly Target: 20–30% conversion from contact to appointment. Presentation Conversion Proposals presented ÷ Appointments attended. Monthly Target: 60–80% of appointments resulting in a presentation. Close Rate Applications submitted ÷ Proposals presented. Monthly Target: 30–50% of presentations resulting in an application. 13-Month Persistency Policies in force at month 13 ÷ Policies issued 13 months ago. Quarterly Target: 70%+. Below 60% requires performance management. Agent Income Total commission (FYC + renewal + bonus) earned. Monthly Active agent target income: ₦150,000–₦350,000 per month. 17.2.5 Incentive Design for the Retail Agency Incentive design is one of the most consequential management decisions in running a retail agency. A poorly designed incentive structure can: drive agents to sell unsuitable products; encourage manipulation of the underwriting process; create pressure to submit policies that lapse before the 13-month mark; and generate NAICOM market conduct concerns. A well-designed incentive structure rewards productive, quality business while filtering out the behavioural patterns that harm policyholders and the insurer’s in-force book. The principles of sound incentive design for a retail insurance agency are: Reward quality, not just volume: A persistency bonus that pays out only when the agent’s 13-month persistency exceeds 70% creates a direct financial incentive for quality business. An agent who submits 20 policies a month but lapses 15 of them within a year is a compliance risk and a financial drain, not an asset. Structure commission to reward long-term relationships: Renewal commission (paid in year 2 and beyond on each in-force policy) gives every agent a growing book of renewal income that creates financial stability independent of new business production. This ‘trailing income’ provides security in lean months and creates an incentive to service the in-force book. Reward professional development: A qualification bonus (a one-time payment when an agent completes the CIIN Cert. COP, Diploma, or Associateship) rewards the professional development the insurer wants to encourage without distorting the sales incentive. Make the incentive structure transparent: Agents who do not understand how their commission is calculated cannot optimise their behaviour toward the insurer’s objectives. Full transparency in commission calculation — a monthly detailed commission statement — is both a compliance requirement and a productivity enabler. Avoid gaming incentives: Annual production contests with prizes for top producers — particularly when the contest period end coincides with heightened pressure to submit incomplete or marginal cases — are a documented driver of poor-quality business submission in the final weeks of the contest. Contest design should include a quality gate (persistency threshold or underwriting quality score) that must be met to qualify for the prize. Illustrative Retail Agent Incentive Structure The following is an illustrative incentive structure for a tied retail agent selling individual life products. All percentages are applied to the annualised first-year premium of the policy: Component Basis Rate Condition First-Year Commission Annualised FY premium of each issued policy 35–40% (varies by product) Policy issued and first premium paid. Renewal Commission Renewal premium received in years 2+ 7.5% Policy in force and premium paid. Persistency Bonus Calculated on agent’s AFYP for the relevant cohort 5% bonus on cohort AFYP if 13-month persistency ≥ 75% Paid quarterly, 13 months after the submission cohort. Qualification Bonus One-time payment ₦25,000 (Cert. COP); ₦75,000 (Dip. CIIN); ₦150,000 (AIIN) On passing CIIN examination and NAICOM registration update. Production Club Annual AFYP total Tiered recognition + non-cash reward (travel, tablet, etc.) Must achieve minimum 70% 13-month persistency to qualify. Unit Manager Overrider Team AFYP (UM only) 5–8% on team AFYP Paid on issued policies from supervised agents. Note: These rates are illustrative and must comply with NAICOM maximum commission guidelines as outlined in Chapter 16. The specific rates for each product line are set in the insurer’s commission schedule. 17.2.6 Persistency Tracking and Conservation Persistency is the single most important quality metric in retail agency management. A policy that lapses in year 1 or year 2 destroys the insurer’s profitability on that policy (the acquisition cost has already been paid in commission; the reserve has already been established; the lapse releases only a fraction of the invested cost). High early lapse rates are simultaneously a financial problem, a compliance risk (NAICOM monitors persistency as a market conduct indicator), and a customer harm indicator. A well-managed retail agency tracks persistency at three levels: Policy-level tracking: Each policy’s premium payment status is monitored by the PAS. When a premium falls due and is not received, an automated alert is generated to the agent whose code is on the policy. The agent has a defined window (typically 30 days) to contact the policyholder, identify the cause of non-payment, and either collect the overdue premium or initiate a paid-up conversion or revival application. Agent-level tracking: The insurer calculates each agent’s 13-month and 25-month persistency rate monthly. Agents falling below the target persistency rate receive a performance alert from their unit manager. Persistency below 60% at 13 months triggers a formal performance improvement process. Branch-level tracking: Branch managers receive monthly persistency reports for their entire portfolio, allowing them to identify whether persistency problems are concentrated in specific agents, specific product lines, or specific geographic areas.

17.3.1 Bank-Insurer Agreement Structures A bancassurance relationship is governed by a Master Distribution Agreement (MDA) — a commercial contract that defines every aspect of the partnership between the insurer and the bank. Unlike a standard agent appointment letter, the MDA is a complex, negotiated document that must address the commercial interests of two regulated entities operating under different regulatory frameworks (CBN and NAICOM). The key commercial and operational elements of a well-structured MDA include: Exclusivity arrangement Whether the bank is an exclusive or non-exclusive distributor of the insurer’s products. Exclusive arrangements give the insurer protected distribution through the bank but limit the bank’s flexibility to offer competitive alternatives to customers. Non-exclusive arrangements allow the bank to distribute products from multiple insurers (subject to NAICOM approval) but expose the insurer to competitive displacement. Product shelf The specific products the bank is authorised to distribute, their approved benefit illustrations, and the process for adding new products or modifying existing ones. The product shelf must be approved by NAICOM for bancassurance distribution. Distribution territories Which branches, digital channels, and customer segments are in scope. Large banks with national networks require specific provisions for regional variation in product suitability and regulatory compliance. Commission and fee structure The commission rates, fee arrangements, and any performance bonuses payable to the bank. These must comply with NAICOM maximum commission guidelines. Premium remittance The timeline and mechanism for the bank to remit collected premiums to the insurer. NAICOM requires remittance within a defined period (typically 3–5 business days); delays constitute a breach by the corporate agent. Data sharing and privacy The basis on which customer data is shared between the bank and the insurer, and the consent mechanisms required under the NDPA 2023. Data sharing must be limited to what is necessary for the insurance transaction and must not be used for any purpose not disclosed to the customer. Compliance and audit rights The insurer’s right to audit the bank’s bancassurance operations, review sales recordings, inspect agent qualifications, and review customer complaint records. Essential for the insurer to discharge its regulatory responsibility for the bank’s conduct in selling its products. Performance targets and review Minimum production targets (if any), the mechanism for quarterly performance reviews, and the process for terminating the arrangement if performance consistently falls below agreed levels. 17.3.2 Product Shelf Architecture for Bancassurance The product shelf is the curated range of insurance products that the bank is authorised to offer through its distribution channels. Designing the right product shelf is the most commercially critical element of the bancassurance arrangement. A well-designed bancassurance product shelf follows three principles: Simplicity: Bank staff are not insurance specialists. Products on the shelf must be explainable in under three minutes without reference to an actuarial pricing report. The simpler the benefit structure, the higher the conversion rate at teller and relationship manager level. Alignment with the bank’s customer journeys: Each product on the shelf should be attached to a specific customer interaction at the bank — a loan application triggers a credit life conversation; an account opening triggers a savings plan conversation; a salary account servicing call triggers a term assurance conversation. Products that have no natural moment of insertion in the bank’s customer journey will not be sold, regardless of their quality. Regulatory pre-clearance: Every product on the bancassurance shelf must have NAICOM product approval (or deemed approval under NIIRA 2025’s 30-day provision). Products that have not been filed with NAICOM cannot be marketed through any channel, including bancassurance. Customer Journey Moment Natural Product Insertion Key Selling Point Duration of Conversation Loan origination (mortgage, auto, SME) Credit life insurance ‘Your loan balance is covered if you die or become permanently disabled before repayment’ 2–3 minutes; integrated into loan documentation signing. Salary account opening / activation Simple term assurance or accidental death cover ‘From ₦1,500/month, your family receives ₦5 million if you die’ 3–5 minutes; offered as part of the account welcome package. Fixed deposit or investment discussion Endowment or savings plan ‘Add an insurance savings plan that also protects your family’ 10–15 minutes; relationship manager conversation. SME business loan discussion Keyman life / credit life ‘Protect your business and your loan against the death of the key person who runs it’ 10–20 minutes; business banking relationship manager. Retirement planning inquiry Retirement annuity quotation (referral to specialist) ‘Let me connect you to our retirement specialist’ Referral; specialist follow-up within 48 hours. Child education savings inquiry Children’s education endowment plan ‘Build your child’s university fund with guaranteed coverage’ 10–20 minutes; relationship manager or digital self-service. 17.3.3 Training Tellers and Relationship Managers The quality of the bancassurance channel depends entirely on the willingness and competence of bank staff to have insurance conversations with customers. Bank staff who are uncomfortable with, uninformed about, or uninterested in insurance will not sell it — regardless of the quality of the MDA or the product shelf. Training is the investment that converts the partnership from a signed contract into a functioning revenue stream. Training for bancassurance staff must address four dimensions: Product knowledge: The specific products on the shelf, their benefits, premiums, and exclusions. Training should use real-life scenarios relevant to the bank’s customer base, not generic insurance theory. A mortgage banker needs to understand credit life; a retail teller needs to understand term assurance and accidental death cover. Sales skills: How to introduce the insurance product naturally in a banking conversation; how to handle common objections (‘I already have insurance’, ‘I’ll think about it’, ‘I can’t afford it’); how to complete the application form and premium debit authorisation. Regulatory compliance: The CIIN Cert. COP curriculum; the duty not to misrepresent insurance products as bank deposit products; the disclosure obligations under NIIRA 2025; and the correct handling of premium remittance. Systems and process: How to enter the application into the bank’s insurance platform (whether a standalone portal or an integrated banking system); how to handle a customer who wants to make a claim; who to escalate unusual queries to. Training should be delivered through a combination of initial certification (a mandatory pre-launch training programme before any bancassurance selling), refresher training (quarterly product knowledge updates), and digital microlearning (short video modules, 3–5 minutes each, accessible on the bank staff’s mobile phone for just-in-time reference). The insurer’s bancassurance manager is responsible for designing, delivering, and tracking the training programme.

17.4.1 The Employee Benefit Consultant The corporate and worksite sales channel is built around a specialist sales role: the Employee Benefit Consultant (EBC) or Corporate Sales Executive. Unlike the retail agent (who sells to individuals) or the bancassurance relationship manager (who works within a bank’s existing customer interaction), the EBC sells to organisations — specifically to the HR directors, CFOs, and senior management of Nigerian employers who make decisions about employee benefit packages. The EBC’s role requires a fundamentally different skill set from the retail agent. Where the retail agent’s primary skill is personal relationship-building with individuals, the EBC must: Understand and speak to the employer’s financial objectives — staff retention, tax efficiency of benefit packages, compliance with mandatory insurance requirements, total cost of employment. Present group life, pension, and healthcare benefit packages in the language of HR strategy and cost management, not insurance products. Navigate the procurement process of large organisations — which may involve formal tender submissions, committee presentations, and multi-stage approval processes — with professionalism and persistence. Manage a smaller number of larger accounts (20–50 corporate clients vs. 200–500 individual policyholders for the retail agent) at a higher average premium value. 17.4.2 HR-Facing Distribution Mechanics The typical corporate sales process for a Nigerian life insurer proceeds through six stages: Prospect identification: Identifying organisations with 50+ employees as primary targets; cross-referencing with existing bancassurance or retail relationships to identify warm entry points. Industry associations, employer databases (LCCI, MAN, organized private sector), and LinkedIn are the primary prospecting sources. Initial approach and needs assessment: The EBC seeks an introduction to the HR Director or CFO. The initial meeting is a needs assessment — the EBC asks questions about the current employee benefit structure, identifies gaps, and positions the insurer as a problem-solver rather than a product seller. Scheme design and quotation: Based on the needs assessment, the EBC works with the insurer’s group underwriting and actuarial teams to design a benefit structure and produce a competitive quotation. For large schemes (500+ employees), the quotation may require reinsurer input. Presentation and negotiation: The EBC presents the scheme design to the employer’s decision-making committee. Price, benefit breadth, claims service standards, and financial strength are all negotiating points. The EBC must be equipped to defend the insurer’s position on each. Scheme implementation: Following acceptance, the EBC coordinates the member enrolment process (data collection from HR, medical evidence where required, scheme booklets for members, payroll deduction instructions), the master policy issuance, and the scheme account setup. Ongoing account management: Annual scheme renewal (re-underwriting, premium review, benefit update), claims service support, and member communication. Well-managed corporate accounts renew automatically year after year; poorly managed ones are lost at first renewal. 17.4.3 Group Life and Pension Cross-Selling The most commercially powerful dynamic in corporate distribution is the cross-selling opportunity between group life insurance and occupational pension schemes. Under the Pension Reform Act 2014, every employer with 15 or more employees must enroll them in the Contributory Pension Scheme (CPS). The same employers who buy group life insurance are also responsible for their employees’ pension contributions — creating a natural opportunity to serve as the employer’s integrated employee benefit partner for both group life and pension. An insurer with group life expertise can partner with a Pension Fund Administrator (PFA) to offer an integrated employee benefit solution: the insurer provides the group life and credit life cover; the PFA provides the CPS pension management; the two products are presented together in a unified employee benefit package that addresses the employer’s statutory obligations under both the Insurance Act and the Pension Reform Act in a single conversation. This integrated approach is more compelling to the HR director than a standalone group life pitch, and more defensible at renewal.

17.5.1 The Annuity Distribution Challenge Life annuities — contracts that convert a lump sum into a guaranteed income for life — are the most technically complex life insurance product in terms of both the actuarial risk they create (longevity risk: the insurer must pay for as long as the annuitant lives) and the distribution challenge they present. The annuity customer is typically a retiree converting their retirement savings into income. They are often making the largest single financial decision of their lives; they are making it once; and the decision is irreversible. The stakes of poor advice or poor product design are correspondingly high. The Nigerian annuity market is structured primarily around the Retirement Life Annuity (RLA), which is the mandatory conversion option for Retirement Savings Account (RSA) holders under the Pension Reform Act 2014 who have accumulated sufficient pension savings. The RLA market is therefore driven by the pension system’s accumulated savings and the retirement rate of the formal sector workforce. 17.5.2 PFA Referral Pipelines Pension Fund Administrators (PFAs) are the natural first point of contact for an RSA holder approaching retirement. The PFA knows when the member will retire (it is recorded in the RSA), knows the fund balance, and is the entity that provides the retirement benefit counselling at the pre-retirement stage. This makes the PFA the single most important referral source for the RLA market. A well-structured PFA referral pipeline works as follows: the life insurer’s annuity sales team establishes formal referral agreements with multiple PFAs; for each RSA holder approaching retirement (typically 12–18 months before retirement date), the PFA notifies the insurer and provides the member’s contact details and approximate fund balance (with the member’s consent); the insurer’s retirement specialist contacts the member to discuss their annuity options, presents a quotation, and, if accepted, coordinates the fund transfer from the PFA to the insurer. The insurer pays the PFA a referral fee for completed annuity conversions. The fee structure and the PFA’s fiduciary obligation to recommend the most suitable annuity provider for the member must be managed carefully: a PFA that recommends only the insurer that pays the highest referral fee, regardless of product quality or financial strength, is in breach of its fiduciary duty to the pensioner. 17.5.3 The Retirement Specialist Role Given the complexity and irreversibility of the annuity purchase decision, annuity distribution requires a specialist sales and advice function distinct from the retail agency. The Retirement Specialist (or Retirement Planning Consultant) is a senior, highly qualified member of the annuity sales team whose role is: Retirement income planning: Conducting a comprehensive review of the retiree’s financial position — RSA balance, other savings, expected expenditure, family obligations — to determine the appropriate annuity structure (single life or joint life; fixed or escalating; with or without guarantee period). Multi-product comparison: Presenting quotes from multiple insurers (in the independent advisory model) or the insurer’s own product range (in the tied model), with clear explanation of the differences. The retiree must understand why they are being recommended a specific product. Documentation and compliance: Completing the PenCom-required Retirement Benefits Computation Form, the annuity application, the anti-money laundering checks, and the consent documentation for fund transfer. Post-retirement service: Maintaining contact with the annuitant after the annuity commences: confirming monthly payment receipt, updating the annuitant on any product changes, and being available for queries about payment variations, estate planning, and beneficiary nominations.

17.6.1 Telecommunications Companies (Telcos) Nigeria’s major telecommunications companies — MTN Nigeria, Airtel Africa, Glo, and 9mobile — collectively serve over 200 million subscriber lines and operate extensive airtime, data, and mobile money platforms. Their distribution reach into every corner of Nigeria, including rural areas with no bank branch or insurance agent, makes them potentially the most powerful distribution partners for micro-insurance and low-premium life products. The telco-insurer partnership model works at two levels. At the platform level, the telco embeds insurance into its mobile app or USSD menu — the insurer’s product is presented to the telco’s subscriber base as a value-added service, and premiums are charged to the airtime wallet or mobile money account. At the data level, anonymised and consented subscriber data (spending patterns, geographic location, tenure) can help the insurer segment the telco’s user base for targeted product offers. Key commercial and regulatory requirements for a telco-insurer partnership: the telco must hold or operate under a NAICOM corporate agent licence (or partner under the Insurtech framework); the premium and claims transaction must comply with CBN mobile payment regulations; consumer disclosure must meet NIIRA 2025 standards at the USSD or app interface; and the data sharing arrangement must comply with the NDPA 2023 (specifically, the telco’s subscriber data cannot be used for insurance marketing without the subscriber’s explicit consent or another lawful basis under the NDPA). 17.6.2 Fintech Platforms Nigeria’s fintech ecosystem — including digital lenders (Carbon, FairMoney, Branch), savings platforms (Piggyvest, Cowrywise), payment processors (Flutterwave, Paystack), and neobanks (Kuda, ALAT) — serves millions of digitally-active Nigerians who have financial services relationships outside the traditional banking sector. These platforms collect behavioural data, have transaction histories, and have demonstrated ability to acquire and retain customers at scale. The most natural fintech-insurance partnership is credit life embedded in digital lending: when a fintech platform disburses a loan, a credit life insurance policy is automatically issued, covering the outstanding balance in the event of the borrower’s death or permanent disability. NIIRA 2025’s mandatory credit life requirement for loans above ₦10 million (and the commercial logic for extending this to smaller loans) makes this partnership structure almost obligatory for digital lenders. Beyond credit life, savings platforms and neobanks are natural distribution partners for: term assurance (complementary to an emergency savings fund); children’s education savings plans (aligned with Piggyvest-style goal-based saving); and hospital cash / critical illness covers (aligned with the health and financial wellbeing positioning of platforms like FairMoney). The insurer provides the risk product; the fintech provides the distribution reach and the customer relationship. 17.6.3 Agritech Platforms Agriculture employs approximately 35–40% of Nigeria’s working population, yet the agricultural community is among the most underinsured. Agritech platforms — companies like Babban Gona, Farmcrowdy, ThriveAgric, and Hello Tractor — are building agricultural value chains that provide smallholder farmers with inputs (seeds, fertilisers), training, market access, and financing. These platforms have direct relationships with farmers, farmer cooperatives, and agricultural aggregators across Nigeria’s rural belt. For life insurance distribution, the agritech platform is a gateway to the agricultural community that the retail agency model cannot efficiently penetrate. Products appropriate for agritech-based distribution include: simple term assurance for farmers (protecting the family from the loss of the primary income earner); group credit life for farmers participating in platform-financed input loans; and, where parametric insurance is available, index-based coverage that pays out based on rainfall or temperature data without requiring a farm-level loss assessment. The commercial structure of an agritech distribution partnership typically involves: a data-sharing agreement (with farmer consent) enabling the insurer to enrol platform participants; a group policy structure covering all participating farmers under a master policy with individual certificates; premium collection through the agritech platform’s own payment system; and claims reporting and payment through the platform’s communication channel. 17.6.4 Real Estate Developers and Mortgage Partners Real estate developers and mortgage finance institutions are natural distribution partners for mortgage protection insurance — life cover that ensures the outstanding mortgage balance is paid in the event of the borrower’s death, so the family retains the property. The developer or mortgage institution has a direct financial interest in the property being insured against the death of the mortgagor: without mortgage protection, the default on the outstanding balance falls on the lender. In the Nigerian market, where the mortgage market is nascent but growing (driven by the Federal Mortgage Bank, primary mortgage banks, and developers offering instalment payment plans), embedded mortgage protection insurance is both a product development opportunity and a risk management tool for the developer. The distribution mechanic is straightforward: at the point of mortgage documentation signing, the developer’s relationship manager presents the mortgage protection insurance as a condition or strong recommendation of the financing arrangement, and the first premium is included in the closing costs or the first instalment.

x: 17.7.1 Organisational Design Principles by Agency Type The optimal organisational structure for each agency type reflects the nature of the sales process, the customer interaction model, and the compliance oversight requirement. The following frameworks represent best-practice structures adapted for the Nigerian life insurance market. Centralised support for complex scheme design. Supported by IT integration, legal/compliance, and actuarial product design. Partnership Manager; Commercial Analyst; Integration Coordinator 1:5 (Manager:active partnerships) Head of Partnerships → Chief Distribution Officer 17.7.2 KPI Frameworks by Agency Type KPIs must be designed to drive the behaviours that create sustainable business — not just volume metrics that encourage short-term submission at the expense of quality. Each agency type requires a balanced KPI framework that covers volume (new business), quality (persistency and compliance), and capability (people development and customer satisfaction). Agency Type Volume KPI Quality KPI Capability KPI Retail Agency Monthly AFYP; cases per agent per month 13-month persistency rate (≥ 70%); mis-selling complaint rate % agents with CIIN qualification; agent retention rate (>12 months) Bancassurance Premium income per branch per month; product penetration rate (policies per 1,000 active accounts) Sales call recording compliance (%); premium remittance timeliness (% within SLA) % bancassurance staff CIIN-certified; mystery shopping score Corporate / Worksite Number of new schemes implemented; total group premium written Scheme renewal rate (≥ 85%); claims turnaround time (days to settlement) EBC pipeline coverage ratio (prospects / annual target); scheme implementation cycle time Annuity Number of annuity conversions; total single premium volume Annuity persistency (% of annuitants current on payments); retiree satisfaction score PFA referral pipeline size; retirement counselling completion rate Alternative Partnerships Premium income per active partnership; new partners onboarded per quarter Partner compliance audit score; NDPA breach incidents (target: 0) Partnership revenue diversification ratio; API integration uptime (%) 17.7.3 Compliance Oversight in Agency Management Compliance is not the exclusive responsibility of the compliance department — it is a first-line management obligation. Every level of the agency hierarchy carries compliance accountability: Individual agents: Must hold current CIIN qualifications; complete required CPD; submit only products for which they are authorised; complete suitability assessments for every client; not misrepresent product terms. Unit managers: Must supervise agent compliance; review proposal forms for completeness and accuracy before submission; conduct monthly one-on-one reviews with each agent to assess suitability practices; report agent misconduct to the branch compliance officer. Branch compliance officers: A dedicated compliance role at each branch (or shared across a cluster of smaller branches). Responsible for: monthly compliance audits of a random sample of applications; maintaining the branch agent register and qualification records; escalating conduct concerns to the regional compliance team. Regional directors: Accountable for the regional compliance score as a KPI. Must ensure that compliance findings are remediated within prescribed timelines and that repeat findings trigger escalated management action. A compliance score dashboard — tracking qualification rates, proposal form accuracy rates, complaint rates, and persistency rates by agent, unit, and branch — should be reviewed by agency management monthly and by the Board’s Audit and Risk Committee quarterly. NAICOM may request any element of this data in its market conduct supervision activities. 17.7.4 Digital Integration in Agency Management Advisory: Digital Tools That Transform Agency Productivity and Compliance The following digital investments, in order of priority, deliver the most significant productivity and compliance improvements for Nigerian life insurance agency management: 1. DIGITAL PROPOSAL FORM (Agent App): Replace paper proposal forms with a smartphone app that guides the agent through the proposal form, validates field entries in real time, automatically calculates the premium, and submits the proposal electronically. Eliminates the lag between sale and underwriting; eliminates data entry errors; creates an automatic audit trail for each application. Estimated productivity gain: 20–30% reduction in application processing time; 40–60% reduction in ‘not in good order’ (NIGO) returns. 2. CRM SYSTEM (Customer Relationship Management): A mobile-first CRM that enables each agent to manage their prospect pipeline, record client interactions, set follow-up reminders, and view their in-force book’s persistency status. The CRM converts the agent’s activity management from a paper diary into a measurable, manageable, supervisable data feed. Unit managers can see each agent’s pipeline in real time. Estimated productivity gain: 15–25% improvement in appointment conversion rates. 3. DIGITAL BENEFIT ILLUSTRATION TOOL: A compliance-approved tool that generates personalised benefit illustrations for every product, using the client’s age, sum assured, and premium amount. Replaces printed projection tables that quickly become outdated. Ensures that every illustration presented to a customer is the currently approved illustration. Critical for NAICOM market conduct compliance. 4. VIRTUAL TRAINING PLATFORM: An online learning management system (LMS) delivering product training, CIIN exam preparation, compliance modules, and sales skills content. Reduces the cost and logistical complexity of centralised training; enables just-in-time learning; enables automated tracking of CPD completion for NAICOM compliance purposes. 5. PERSISTENCY ALERT SYSTEM: An automated system that generates alerts to agents (via app notification or SMS) when any policy in their book misses a premium payment. The alert is generated at the premium due date, not 30 days later when the policy is already approaching lapse. First-day contact by the agent converts a missed payment into a late payment at far higher rates than contact at day 30.

Retail Agency The distribution channel in which individual agents build personal relationships with prospective policyholders to sell individual life insurance products, typically organised in a pyramid hierarchy of agents, unit managers, branch managers, and regional directors. Agency Hierarchy The management structure of a retail agency force, defining roles, spans of control, and reporting lines from individual agents through unit managers and branch managers to the agency director. Unit Manager (UM) A supervisory role in the retail agency hierarchy who recruits, trains, and supervises a team of 8–15 agents and earns an overrider commission on the team’s production. Pyramid Agency Model An agency structure with multiple management layers, each earning override commission on the production of the layer below. Provides intensive supervision and coaching but carries higher override cost. Flat Agency Model An agency structure with fewer management layers. Agents report directly to branch or regional management. Lower override cost but reduced supervision intensity. Annualised First-Year Premium (AFYP) The standard metric for measuring new business production, expressing the first-year premium on each policy in annual terms (monthly premium × 12). Persistency Rate The proportion of policies issued in a defined cohort that remain in force at a subsequent duration (13 months or 25 months). A key quality indicator for all distribution channels. Employee Benefit Consultant (EBC) A specialist sales executive who manages the insurer’s corporate relationships with employers, selling group life schemes, worksite products, and pension-linked benefits to HR directors and CFOs. Master Distribution Agreement (MDA) The commercial contract governing a bancassurance partnership between a bank and an insurer, covering exclusivity, product shelf, commission structure, premium remittance, compliance obligations, and data sharing. Product Shelf (Bancassurance) The curated range of insurance products approved for distribution through a specific bancassurance channel, designed for simplicity and alignment with the bank’s customer interaction moments. Retirement Life Annuity (RLA) The annuity product available under the Nigerian Contributory Pension Scheme, converting an RSA holder’s retirement savings into a guaranteed income for life or a defined period. Pension Fund Administrator (PFA) A PenCom-licensed entity that manages Retirement Savings Accounts under the Contributory Pension Scheme. A critical referral source for annuity distribution. PFA Referral Pipeline A structured commercial arrangement between a life insurer and one or more PFAs, under which the PFA refers RSA holders approaching retirement to the insurer for annuity quotation and conversion. Retirement Specialist A senior, highly qualified member of the annuity sales team who advises retirees on annuity options, conducts retirement income planning, and manages the fund transfer process from the PFA to the insurer. Bancassurance Coordinator The insurer’s representative embedded at a bank branch level to support bancassurance product sales, training, and compliance. Reports to the Bancassurance Manager. Not in Good Order (NIGO) An application or proposal form that is returned to the agent or sales team by the underwriting function because it is incomplete, contains errors, or lacks required supporting documentation.
