Post impressions, connections, lead form submissions, profile views. 19.6.1 WhatsApp Business: The Most Powerful Insurance Channel in Nigeria WhatsApp deserves special attention because it is uniquely positioned in the Nigerian insurance marketing landscape. It is the primary communication tool for the majority of Nigerians across all income segments; it is a high-trust, private channel that consumers use with people they know; and it enables insurance transactions (policy explanations, document delivery, premium reminders, claims notifications) that no other social platform can match. A WhatsApp Business insurance programme has three components: the broadcast list (a list of opted-in policyholders and prospects who receive periodic educational and marketing messages); the agent business profile (each agent has their own WhatsApp Business account, serving as their personal client communication and lead management tool); and the catalogue (the insurer’s product range available for browsing within the WhatsApp interface). WhatsApp marketing compliance under the NDPA 2023 is critical: broadcast messages may only be sent to individuals who have explicitly opted in to receive them. Sending unsolicited marketing via WhatsApp to contacts obtained without consent is a data protection breach. The insurer’s opt-in mechanism must be clearly documented and auditable.

t: Chapter 19 · 19.7 Content Marketing and Financial Literacy
x: 19.7.1 The Educational Content Strategy Content marketing is the creation and distribution of useful, educational content that builds the insurer’s reputation as a trusted financial authority — without directly selling a product in every piece of content. The commercial logic is that a consumer who has learned about insurance, who understands why it matters, and who has come to trust the insurer as a source of reliable financial information is far easier to convert to a customer than a consumer who encounters the insurer for the first time in a product advertisement. For Nigerian life insurance, educational content serves two simultaneous functions: it builds the insurer’s brand authority; and it develops the overall market by raising the population’s general understanding of insurance. Market development content — ‘What is life insurance?’, ‘Why do Nigerians avoid insurance?’, ‘What really happens when you make a claim?’ — benefits the entire industry, not just the insurer who creates it. But the insurer who is consistently the most trusted voice on these topics earns a market share premium that justifies the investment. 19.7.2 Financial Literacy as Market Development Financial literacy programming — educating Nigerians about savings, debt management, retirement planning, and risk protection — is both a genuine corporate social responsibility obligation and one of the most commercially intelligent long-term marketing investments a life insurer can make. The most financially literate consumers are also the most likely to buy and retain life insurance. Nigerian life insurers that have invested in sustained financial literacy programmes — through school curricula partnerships, workplace financial wellness programmes, radio shows, and YouTube series — report measurable improvements in brand awareness, product understanding, and new business leads generated from educated audiences. The investment horizon is 18–36 months: financial literacy work rarely produces immediate sales, but it builds a market where more people are ready to buy when they encounter a distribution channel. 19.7.3 Content Calendar and Format Mix Content Type Format Frequency Platform Purpose Financial education ‘Did you know?’ carousel posts; explainer Reels; YouTube shorts 3–5× per week Instagram, TikTok, YouTube Awareness; market education; brand authority Claims stories Video testimony (real claimants with consent); written case study 1–2× per month YouTube, Instagram, Facebook Trust building; rebutting the claim denial narrative Product feature posts Benefit highlight carousel; premium calculator tool 1–2× per week Instagram, Facebook, WhatsApp Consideration; lead generation Behind-the-scenes Office culture; team profiles; actuary/agent day-in-the-life 1× per week Instagram, LinkedIn Humanising the brand; talent attraction Thought leadership CEO article; actuarial market commentary; NIIRA 2025 explainer 2–4× per month LinkedIn, website blog B2B credibility; intermediary engagement Community content Local language posts; event coverage; partner testimonials 2–3× per week WhatsApp, Facebook Community engagement; mass market reach Interactive/user-generated Premium calculator; polls; quizzes; ‘tag a friend’ campaigns 1–2× per week Instagram, TikTok Engagement; viral reach; list building

19.8.1 The Role of Influencers in Insurance Marketing Influencer marketing — partnering with individuals who have built trusted audiences on social media platforms to create and distribute content on the insurer’s behalf — is a fast-growing channel for Nigerian insurance marketing. Influencers have an advantage that traditional advertising does not: their audience trusts them as individuals, not as brands. A personal finance influencer who says ‘I recently took out life insurance with XYZ Life and here is why’ is more persuasive to their audience than the same insurer’s own advertisement, because the audience has a pre-existing trust relationship with the influencer. The categories of influencer most effective for insurance marketing include: personal finance creators (who educate their audience about money management and are natural insurance advocates); family and lifestyle creators (who speak to the same protection motivations that drive insurance purchase); business and entrepreneurship creators (who reach the small business owner and employer market); and community leaders with large WhatsApp broadcast lists or local radio audiences (whose reach into offline communities complements the digital channel). 19.8.2 Selection Criteria and Compliance The selection of influencer partners for insurance marketing requires more rigour than for most consumer goods, because the regulatory and reputational risks of influencer content errors are higher. A food influencer who misstates a recipe creates no regulatory liability; an influencer who makes a false claim about an insurance product’s returns or coverage scope may create NAICOM compliance exposure for the insurer. Selection criteria for insurance influencer partners: Audience alignment: The influencer’s audience must overlap with the insurer’s target segment. A micro-influencer with 30,000 highly engaged personal finance followers is more valuable for insurance marketing than a lifestyle macro-influencer with 2 million followers who have no particular financial awareness. Credibility and authenticity: The influencer’s personal positioning must be consistent with insurance as a relevant product. A personal finance creator who genuinely talks about savings and investment planning is a more credible insurance advocate than a fashion or entertainment creator. Compliance capability: The influencer must be willing and able to follow the insurer’s content guidelines: using only approved product claims, including mandatory disclosures, and not making representations about investment returns that exceed the NAICOM-approved benefit illustration. Disclosure obligation: All sponsored insurance content must be clearly labelled as a paid partnership (‘#ad’, ‘#sponsored’, or equivalent disclosure) in compliance with advertising standards. The insurer is responsible for ensuring its influencer partners make appropriate disclosures.

t: Chapter 19 · 19.9 Employer-Market and HNI Segment Marketing
x: 19.9.1 The Employer Market The employer market — marketing insurance benefits to companies for their employees — operates entirely differently from consumer marketing. The HR director or CFO who makes the group life insurance decision is not swayed by an Instagram Reel or a WhatsApp broadcast. They respond to: verified evidence of the insurer’s financial strength and claims payment performance; competitive premium pricing with transparent benefit illustrations; and service quality commitments backed by SLA documentation. Effective employer-market marketing relies on three channels: thought leadership content distributed through LinkedIn and industry events (establishing the insurer as a knowledgeable partner in employee benefit design); direct B2B marketing by Employee Benefit Consultants who build personal relationships with HR directors (addressed in Chapter 17); and broker relationships — the majority of large employer group life placements are broker-intermediated, making the insurer’s investment in broker relationship marketing (seminars, technical updates, insurer-sponsored CPD events) a core employer-market strategy. 19.9.2 High-Net-Worth Individual (HNI) Marketing The HNI segment — entrepreneurs, executives, professionals, and inheritors with investable assets above ₦50 million — requires the most personalised and relationship-intensive marketing approach. HNI clients do not respond to mass advertising. They respond to referrals from trusted advisers (lawyers, accountants, private bankers) and to private, invitation-only engagement opportunities that signal the insurer’s understanding of their specific financial situation. HNI insurance marketing strategies in Nigeria: Estate planning seminars: Private, invitation-only events (dinner or afternoon session format) focused on estate planning, succession, and wealth transfer — framed as educational events rather than sales presentations. The insurance conversation emerges naturally from the financial planning context. Referral network cultivation: Systematic relationships with the lawyers, accountants, and private bankers who advise HNI clients. A solicitor drafting a will who is aware of the client’s uninsured life risk is a natural insurance referral source. Bespoke product positioning: HNI clients are interested in large-sum life covers (keyman, personal protection, estate equalization), offshore placement options (where permitted), and products designed for their specific planning objectives — not off-the-shelf endowments. Private client manager: A dedicated relationship manager who understands HNI financial planning, maintains the relationship proactively, and coordinates the insurer’s service delivery for the HNI’s full insurance programme.

Below-the-line (BTL) marketing — direct, targeted, non-mass-media marketing activities — is essential for reaching the majority of Nigerians who are not accessible through digital channels or formal insurance distribution. BTL activities include branch activations, community events, religious community partnerships, and integration with informal savings structures. 19.10.1 Branch Activation Branch activation is a marketing event held at an insurance company branch, bank branch (for bancassurance products), or mobile activation van at a high-traffic public location (a market, a transport hub, a shopping complex). The activation creates an interactive, experiential encounter with the brand: staff are present to answer questions, demonstrate the product, and initiate the application process for interested individuals. Effective branch activations in the Nigerian insurance market combine entertainment (music, games, promotional gifts) with education (a short presentation on the product benefit, live demonstration of the USSD enrolment process) and transaction (the ability to complete an application and pay a first premium on the spot). The goal is not just footfall; it is enrolments. 19.10.2 Church and Mosque Partnerships Nigeria’s religious communities are among the most powerful social institutions in the country. Megachurches in Lagos, Abuja, and Enugu have congregations of tens of thousands of members who gather weekly; the Jumu’ah (Friday) mosque congregations in Kano, Kaduna, and Sokoto bring together hundreds of thousands of Muslims who share deep bonds of community and mutual obligation. Religious leaders are uniquely trusted authorities on financial decisions: their endorsement of a product — particularly one framed as responsible financial stewardship and care for one’s family — is more persuasive than any advertisement. Church and mosque partnerships for insurance marketing typically involve: a formal partnership with the religious institution’s leadership; educational sessions during mid-week services or post-Jumu’ah meetings; a tailored product offering for congregation members (potentially at group rates); and premium collection through the religious community’s own financial administration channels. Takaful products (Shari’ah-compliant insurance) are particularly relevant for mosque partnerships in Muslim-majority communities. 19.10.3 Ajo/Esusu Integration Ajo (Yoruba) and Esusu (broader West African) are traditional rotating savings groups in which members contribute a fixed amount at regular intervals, and each member receives the total pool in rotation. These groups are ubiquitous across Nigeria — market traders, transport workers, teachers, and urban professionals all participate in Ajo/Esusu groups. They represent pre-existing financial discipline, regular savings behaviour, and strong community trust bonds — all characteristics that make them ideal entry points for insurance. Insurance integration with Ajo/Esusu groups can take several forms: the group collectively purchases a life cover that protects all members’ contributions in the event of a member’s death; individual members within the group are offered insurance products at group rates; or the Ajo/Esusu platform evolves into a savings-plus-insurance hybrid product (where the savings component generates the traditional rotating pool and the insurance component protects the contributors). The group leader’s endorsement is the key to adoption: an Ajo leader who champions the insurance product to their group will achieve far higher penetration than any external marketing.

t: Chapter 19 · 19.11 SEO, Email Funnels, and Performance Marketing
x: 19.11.1 Search Engine Optimisation (SEO) for Insurance SEO is the discipline of ensuring that when a potential insurance buyer searches on Google (or Bing, or YouTube) for insurance-related information, the insurer’s website and content appears prominently in the results. For insurance, SEO is particularly valuable because the highest-intent prospective buyers — those who are already considering purchasing insurance — frequently search for answers before they contact a company. High-value SEO content categories for Nigerian life insurance: ‘best life insurance Nigeria’; ‘how much does term assurance cost in Nigeria’; ‘what is credit life insurance’; ‘life insurance for children Nigeria’; ‘group life scheme for SMEs Nigeria’. An insurer that creates comprehensive, accurate, well-structured content on these topics will attract organic traffic from high-intent prospects at zero media cost per click. Technical SEO requirements: a fast-loading, mobile-responsive website (most Nigerian users browse on mobile devices); structured content with clear headings; local SEO optimisation for Nigerian search (Google.com.ng targeting); and a backlink strategy that builds the website’s authority through citations from reputable financial and news sources. 19.11.2 Email Marketing and Nurture Funnels Email marketing remains one of the highest-ROI digital marketing channels for financial services in Nigeria, particularly for the formal sector and employer market. An email list of opted-in prospects and customers is a direct, low-cost communication channel that enables personalised messaging, product education, and conversion nurturing over time. A life insurance email nurture funnel works in stages: the prospect provides their email address in exchange for a useful resource (a financial planning guide, a premium calculator, a webinar registration); they receive a series of educational emails over 4–12 weeks that build their understanding of insurance and the insurer’s trustworthiness; a call to action to get a personalised quotation is introduced at the point where the prospect has received enough education to be in a genuine consideration mindset; and the lead is passed to a sales agent or broker for follow-up. 19.11.3 Performance Marketing (Paid Digital Advertising) Performance marketing — paid digital advertising on Meta (Facebook/Instagram), Google, TikTok, and YouTube — enables the insurer to reach defined audiences at scale, with measurable cost-per-lead and cost-per-acquisition metrics. Unlike brand advertising, performance marketing is designed to generate direct responses: form submissions, phone calls, USSD interactions, or website visits that can be tracked to an eventual policy sale. Key principles for effective insurance performance marketing in Nigeria: Audience targeting precision: Meta’s targeting allows the insurer to reach salaried employees in Lagos aged 30–45, or small business owners in Abuja, or recent university graduates nationally. Segment-specific targeting dramatically improves lead quality compared to broad audience campaigns. Lead form optimisation: Insurance lead forms should be as short as possible: name, phone number, email, and one qualifying question (product interest or income bracket). Every additional field reduces completion rate. Rapid lead follow-up: Digital leads have a very short shelf life: a lead contacted within 5 minutes of submission converts at 5–10 times the rate of a lead contacted 24 hours later. Performance marketing investment is wasted without a same-day lead follow-up protocol. NDPA 2023 compliance: Lead forms must include clear consent statements for the use of the prospect’s data for insurance marketing and sales follow-up. The consent must meet the NDPA 2023’s requirements for informed, specific, and freely given consent.

Marketing compliance in Nigerian insurance sits at the intersection of NAICOM’s advertising standards, the NDPA 2023’s data marketing obligations, and the general commercial law prohibition on false and misleading statements. A well-designed compliance framework does not constrain effective marketing — it channels creativity within boundaries that protect the insurer and the consumer simultaneously. Compliance Area Requirement Risk of Non-Compliance Product claim accuracy All specific product claims (return rates, sum assured, premium levels) must match the NAICOM-approved product filing. Any deviation requires a fresh filing. Penalty set by the Commission (s.208(5)); amendment or withdrawal of the advertisement; reputational damage. Benefit illustration format Benefit illustrations must follow NAICOM’s prescribed format, including a clear disclaimer that projections are not guaranteed where relevant. Claims dispute; potential mis-selling liability; NAICOM sanction. Influencer disclosure Sponsored content must be labelled as paid partnership. The insurer is responsible for ensuring influencer compliance. Advertising Standards Council sanction; NAICOM market conduct finding; reputational damage if undisclosed partnership is exposed. Data consent Digital lead capture and email/WhatsApp marketing require NDPA 2023-compliant opt-in consent. NDPC enforcement action; potential NAICOM cross-referral; data subject claims. Testimonials Client testimonials used in advertising must be genuine, not fabricated; must not make specific return or benefit claims that could not be replicated; and must be accompanied by the client’s consent to publication. NAICOM market conduct finding; legal liability for false representation. No-premium, no-cover Marketing that implies coverage exists before the first premium is paid and the policy is formally issued is misleading. The ‘no premium, no cover’ principle must be respected in all marketing communications. Claims dispute; regulatory finding; policyholder harm.

19.13.1 Customer Acquisition Cost (CAC) Customer Acquisition Cost Formula CAC = Total Marketing + Sales Cost for Period ÷ New Customers Acquired in Period CAC should be calculated by channel (agency CAC vs. digital CAC vs. bancassurance CAC) to identify the most cost-efficient acquisition routes. CAC is only meaningful when compared to the Lifetime Value (LTV) of the acquired customer: a channel with a high CAC but producing highly persistent, high-premium policies may be more commercially valuable than a low-CAC channel that produces high-lapse, low-premium policies. Channel Typical CAC Range (Nigerian Market, Indicative) LTV Consideration Retail agent (individual life) ₦25,000–₦120,000 per policy High LTV if persistency > 70%; low LTV if high lapse. Commission front-loads CAC. Bancassurance (credit life) ₦5,000–₦15,000 per policy Single-premium credit life has lower LTV; high volume compensates. Digital (performance marketing) ₦8,000–₦40,000 per converted lead CAC declines with audience targeting optimisation; LTV depends on product and persistency. Cooperative / community channel ₦2,000–₦8,000 per policy Low CAC due to group enrolment efficiency; LTV moderate (lower premiums but payroll/dues deduction supports persistency). Worksite / employer market ₦5,000–₦20,000 per employee enrolled Strong LTV: payroll deduction persistency; employer renewal relationship. 19.13.2 Key Marketing Metrics Dashboard Reach metrics Total impressions; unique reach by channel; frequency per audience; brand awareness score (unaided recall %) Engagement metrics Social media engagement rate (likes + comments + shares ÷ reach); video completion rate; email open rate; WhatsApp broadcast read rate Lead generation metrics Total leads generated by channel; cost per lead (CPL); lead quality score (% of leads that meet qualification criteria); lead-to-appointment conversion rate Conversion metrics Application submission rate; policy issuance rate; first premium collection rate; time from lead to issued policy (days) Retention metrics 13-month persistency rate by acquisition channel; 25-month persistency rate; renewal rate for group and corporate accounts Brand health metrics Unaided brand awareness (%); net promoter score (NPS); brand trust score (survey); share of online conversation (social listening) ROI metrics CAC by channel; revenue per marketing naira spent; return on ad spend (ROAS) for performance campaigns; lifetime value to CAC ratio (LTV:CAC)

t: Chapter 19 · 19.14 Advisory: Building a Marketing Function for a Nigerian Life Insurer
x: Most Nigerian life insurance companies are significantly under-invested in marketing relative to the commercial opportunity that effective marketing represents. The following advisory section addresses the structural, talent, and technology investments required to build a marketing function capable of driving sustained premium growth. Advisory: The Five Investments That Transform Insurance Marketing in Nigeria INVESTMENT 1: A CHIEF MARKETING OFFICER WHO UNDERSTANDS BOTH INSURANCE AND DIGITAL. The most common marketing failure in Nigerian insurance is appointing a brand-marketing generalist with no insurance knowledge, or an insurance professional with no marketing expertise. The CMO role requires a rare combination: deep understanding of the trust deficit, the regulatory environment, and the distribution system; and genuine digital marketing capability. This person is hard to find and worth paying for. INVESTMENT 2: A CONTENT STUDIO. Nigerian insurance brands that are winning on social media in 2025 have invested in in-house content production capability: a videographer, a graphic designer, a copywriter, and a social media manager. External agencies are too slow and too expensive for the cadence of content required to build an engaged digital audience. A modest in-house studio (₦10–25 million annual cost) can produce daily content across all platforms. INVESTMENT 3: A MARKETING TECHNOLOGY STACK. At minimum: a CRM system that captures lead source and tracks conversion through to policy issuance; an email marketing platform (Mailchimp, ActiveCampaign, or equivalent) for nurture funnel management; a social media management tool (Buffer, Hootsuite, or equivalent) for scheduling and analytics; and a website analytics platform (Google Analytics) with conversion tracking. Without attribution data, it is impossible to know which marketing spend is working. INVESTMENT 4: CLAIMS STORYTELLING. The most underutilised marketing asset in Nigerian insurance is the paid claim. Every time the insurer pays a death benefit that protects a family, a critical illness benefit that enables a policyholder to receive treatment, or a group life claim that supports a deceased employee’s family, there is a genuine human story available — with appropriate consent — that directly addresses the trust deficit. Insurers that systematically collect and publish verified claims stories, with the claimants’ consent, will build brand trust faster than any other marketing activity. INVESTMENT 5: A MARKETING COMPLIANCE FRAMEWORK. NIIRA 2025’s tighter advertising standards mean that the cost of a marketing compliance failure — financial penalty, product withdrawal, reputational damage — can far exceed the cost of investing in a proper pre-publication review process. A marketing compliance policy, a trained compliance reviewer embedded in the marketing team, and a content approval workflow documented in the company’s quality management system are non-negotiable for a CMO operating in the post-NIIRA 2025 regulatory environment.

Trust Deficit The deeply embedded consumer scepticism about insurance companies in Nigeria, rooted in historical claims payment failures and the perception that insurers will find reasons not to pay valid claims. Awareness Gap The proportion of the Nigerian population that lacks knowledge of what insurance is, what it covers, how much it costs, or how to access it. Brand Positioning The deliberate process of establishing a specific, distinct, and credible place for the insurer’s brand in the consumer’s mind, relative to competitors and the consumer’s own values. Monolithic Brand Architecture A brand structure in which all products are marketed under a single corporate brand identity. All marketing investment reinforces the same brand. Content Marketing The creation and distribution of educational or informative content that builds the insurer’s authority and trust, without directly selling a product in every piece of content. Financial Literacy The knowledge and skills required to make informed financial decisions. For insurance marketers, building financial literacy in the target population is a market development strategy. Below-the-Line (BTL) Marketing Direct, targeted, non-mass-media marketing activities including branch activation, community events, religious community partnerships, and Ajo/Esusu group integration. Ajo/Esusu Traditional Nigerian rotating savings groups in which members contribute at regular intervals and each member receives the pool in rotation. A powerful entry point for community-level insurance marketing. Customer Acquisition Cost (CAC) The total marketing and sales expenditure required to acquire one new customer, calculated as total marketing + sales cost divided by new customers acquired in the same period. Performance Marketing Paid digital advertising designed to generate measurable direct responses (leads, applications, sign-ups) with trackable cost-per-acquisition metrics. Includes paid social media ads and search engine ads. Nurture Funnel A sequenced series of marketing communications (typically email or WhatsApp) that guide a prospect from initial awareness through education to a purchase decision over a defined period. Search Engine Optimisation (SEO) The discipline of optimising website content and structure so that relevant pages rank prominently in search engine results, generating organic (unpaid) traffic from high-intent users. Influencer Marketing Partnering with individuals who have built trusted social media audiences to create and distribute content about the insurer’s brand or products to those audiences. Culturally Resonant Messaging Marketing communications that use culturally familiar concepts, language, metaphors, and values to make the message more relatable and persuasive to the target audience. Brand Health Tracking The ongoing measurement of brand awareness, brand perception, and net promoter score through consumer surveys and social listening, used to assess the impact of marketing investment on brand strength. Lead Quality Score A metric that assesses the likelihood of a marketing-generated lead converting to a policy, based on qualification criteria such as income, intent level, and product fit. Return on Ad Spend (ROAS) The revenue generated per naira spent on paid digital advertising. ROAS = Revenue from Ads ÷ Cost of Ads.

t: Chapter 20 · 20.1 Introduction: The Customer Experience Imperative
x: Customer experience (CX) is every interaction a policyholder has with an insurance company — from the first advertisement they encounter, through the sales conversation, the policy issuance, the premium payment, the annual anniversary statement, and ultimately the claims experience. Each of these interactions either strengthens or weakens the policyholder’s trust in the insurer, their likelihood of maintaining the policy, and their willingness to recommend the company to family and friends. In most consumer industries, CX management is primarily a commercial function: companies invest in service quality because satisfied customers buy more and stay longer. In Nigerian life insurance, the commercial argument for CX excellence is even stronger — but the urgency is different. Here, CX is a trust-repair function as much as a commercial one. Every policy serviced promptly, every query answered clearly, every claim paid fairly represents a counter-narrative to the industry’s dominant negative perception. An insurer that delivers consistently excellent CX is not merely retaining customers; it is actively rebuilding public trust in the institution of insurance itself. The CX imperative is also intensified by NIIRA 2025. The Act’s consumer protection provisions create enforceable obligations around service response times, complaint handling, claims settlement, and the treatment of vulnerable customers. CX failure is no longer merely a commercial risk — it is a regulatory risk, with NAICOM’s expanded enforcement arsenal available to respond to systemic service quality failures. This chapter addresses the full scope of the CX and customer acquisition agenda for a Nigerian life insurer: the tools to measure and understand the customer experience, the service standards required to deliver it, the retention programmes that protect the existing portfolio, the acquisition strategies that grow it, and the regulatory framework that governs both.

20.2.1 What is a Customer Journey Map? A customer journey map is a structured visual representation of every significant interaction a customer has with an organisation, from the first moment of awareness through to the end of the relationship. It documents: the sequence of interactions (touchpoints); what the customer is trying to do at each stage (their goal); how the customer feels at each stage (their emotional state); and where the company is currently succeeding or failing to meet the customer’s needs (moments of truth and pain points). For life insurance, journey mapping reveals the reality of the customer’s experience as they live it — not as the insurer designs it on paper. A sales process that looks smooth from the inside (agent contacts prospect, presents product, completes application, submits to underwriting, policy is issued, premium direct debit is set up) may look very different from the customer’s perspective: the agent took three weeks to follow up; the underwriting request for medical evidence was confusing; the direct debit instruction was not processed correctly; the policy document arrived six weeks after the first premium was deducted. 20.2.2 The Life Insurance Customer Journey: Five Stages Stage Customer Goal Key Touchpoints Typical Pain Points Moment of Truth 1. Awareness Understand that insurance exists, what it does, and whether it’s relevant to them. Advertisement; social media content; word of mouth; agent cold call. Confusing jargon; irrelevant messaging; distrust from past experiences. First impression of the insurer’s brand — does it feel trustworthy and relevant? 2. Consideration Evaluate whether this specific insurer and product is right for them. Agent presentation; broker comparison; online calculator; website; peer recommendation. Aggressive sales tactics; benefit illustrations that are hard to understand; pressure to decide quickly. The agent’s ability to explain clearly and honestly, without pressure. 3. Purchase and Onboarding Complete the application, provide required information, and receive a policy they understand. Proposal form; underwriting process; medical examination; policy issuance; premium setup. Lengthy and complex proposal form; slow underwriting; medical evidence collection friction; confusing policy document. First premium collected; policy document received — does the customer feel confident about what they’ve bought? 4. In-Force Servicing Maintain the policy, receive regular information, make alterations if needed. Annual statement; premium receipts; alterations (address change, beneficiary update); query handling via phone, WhatsApp, or branch. No proactive communication from the insurer; difficulty reaching customer service; errors in annual statements; slowness in processing requests. Annual statement receipt — does the customer feel valued and informed? 5. Claim or Maturity Receive the benefit they paid for, when they need it, without excessive procedural burden. Claims notification; documentation request; assessment; settlement payment. Extensive documentation requirements; slow settlement; disputed coverage; no communication during assessment period. Claim payment — the ultimate moment of truth: was the promise kept? 20.2.3 Moments of Truth The term ‘moment of truth’ — coined by Jan Carlzon of SAS Airlines and extensively applied in service management — refers to the specific interaction at which the customer forms a definitive impression of the organisation that either builds or destroys their trust. For life insurance, the moments of truth are fewer than in a high-frequency transaction service, but they are disproportionately important because they occur at emotionally significant junctures: when the customer is making a major financial commitment (purchase), when they need help urgently (a service failure), or when they are at their most vulnerable (a death in the family, a critical illness diagnosis). The claim payment is universally recognised as the ultimate moment of truth in insurance. But the policy onboarding experience, the first annual statement, and the response to the customer’s first query are also critical: they set the tone for the entire in-force relationship. An insurer that handles the first three months of a new policyholder’s experience with clarity, warmth, and speed will retain that policyholder at a materially higher rate than an insurer that loses contact with the customer after the first premium is collected.

20.3.1 The Contact Centre The contact centre (whether a physical call centre or a virtual team) is the primary human-to-human service channel for most Nigerian life insurers. It is the first point of contact for policyholders with queries, complaints, claims notifications, and premium payment issues. The quality of the contact centre experience is often the primary determinant of the policyholder’s overall satisfaction with their insurer. Key design principles for a best-practice Nigerian insurance contact centre: Omnichannel capability: The contact centre must handle queries across all channels the customer uses: inbound telephone; WhatsApp text and voice; email; and, for digital-native products, in-app chat. Customers who have to switch channels to resolve a query — ‘call us on this number’ when they have sent a WhatsApp message — experience friction that reduces satisfaction. Policy information at first contact: Contact centre agents must have real-time access to the customer’s complete policy record — premium status, sum assured, beneficiary, outstanding loans, claims history. A customer who has to repeat their policy details, spell out their name multiple times, or be transferred three times before their query is addressed will not renew. Empathy-first scripting: Particularly for claims-related calls and hardship-driven lapse inquiries, contact centre agents must be trained to acknowledge the customer’s emotional state before moving to procedural responses. A recently bereaved family calling to start the claims process needs empathy before documentation. First Contact Resolution (FCR) discipline: Every query should be resolved in the first interaction wherever possible. Queries that require escalation should be tracked to resolution with a proactive callback commitment: ‘We will call you back within 48 hours.’ Failure to meet the callback commitment is a service failure. 20.3.2 Digital Self-Service Digital self-service channels — the insurer’s mobile app, customer portal, USSD interface, and WhatsApp chatbot — enable policyholders to access information and complete routine transactions without contacting a human agent. For the policyholder, self-service offers 24/7 access and instant response. For the insurer, it reduces contact centre volume and cost while increasing policyholder engagement frequency. Core capabilities that Nigerian life insurance digital self-service should provide: premium payment confirmation and receipt; policy summary and benefit details; beneficiary information; premium payment via card, bank transfer, or mobile money; alteration requests (name change, address update, beneficiary update) with document upload; loan application (where policy loans are available); claims notification initiation; and the ability to escalate to a human agent without loss of context. The design of self-service interfaces for a Nigerian audience must account for the diversity of the user base: screen interfaces designed for high-literacy, smartphone-proficient users will fail the significant proportion of policyholders on low-literacy, basic smartphone, or feature phone devices. A ‘mobile-first, simple-first’ design philosophy — prioritising clarity, minimal text, visual cues, and USSD fallback for critical transactions — is essential for inclusive service design. 20.3.3 Field Operations Despite the growth of digital channels, the field operations function — the agent who visits the policyholder at home, the branch that is physically accessible — remains critical for several categories of customer interaction: complex queries that require human explanation; in-person conservation visits when a policy is at risk of lapse; and communities where digital literacy or connectivity is insufficient for self-service. The field operations model in Nigeria must be designed for the country’s geographic and infrastructure realities: traffic congestion in Lagos, poor road conditions in some rural areas, and the concentration of policyholders in locations where branches are not economically viable. The ‘phygital’ model — a hybrid of physical field presence and digital enablement — is the most practical for many Nigerian life insurers. Agents equipped with smartphones and the insurer’s agent app can conduct policy reviews, update beneficiary details, collect premium payments, and submit alteration requests remotely, reducing the need for physical branch visits for routine servicing while maintaining the human relationship for higher-stakes interactions. 20.3.4 Claims Handling as a CX Moment Every aspect of claims handling is addressed in Chapter 12. From a CX management perspective, the additional dimension is that claims handling must be designed not merely to settle valid claims correctly — that is the minimum standard — but to make the claimant feel cared for, informed, and respected throughout what is often the most stressful financial and personal experience of their life. Best-practice CX elements of claims handling: a dedicated claims relationship manager for every open claim above a defined threshold; a guaranteed maximum of 48 hours between any documentation submission and acknowledgement of receipt; a proactive status update (by phone or WhatsApp) every five business days while the claim is open; a compassionate, plain-language declination letter that explains the specific reason for non-payment and the available recourse options; and a post-claims survey to collect feedback on the claimant’s experience.

20.4.1 The Purpose of SLAs in Insurance A Service Level Agreement (SLA) is a commitment by the insurer to deliver a defined standard of service within a defined timeframe. SLAs convert the subjective concept of ‘good service’ into measurable, manageable, and enforceable performance targets. They are the operational expression of the insurer’s customer promise and the measurement framework against which CX performance is assessed. Under NIIRA 2025, some service standards are no longer discretionary. The 60-day maximum claims settlement timeline (Chapter 12, s.210) is a regulatory SLA: late settlement attracts compound interest, administrative sanctions and possible compensation. A 5-business-day claims acknowledgement is recommended practice, although no statutory acknowledgement period has been confirmed. An insurer’s internal SLA framework should be set at standards more stringent than the regulatory minimum, creating a management buffer that prevents regulatory breaches. 20.4.2 SLA Standards by Interaction Type Interaction Type Internal SLA Target NIIRA 2025 Requirement Consequence of Breach Inbound call answer time 80% of calls answered within 30 seconds; 95% within 90 seconds. Not specifically mandated; subject to general consumer protection duty. Policyholder abandonment; increased complaint rate; negative social media. WhatsApp/email query response First response within 4 business hours; full resolution within 2 business days. Not specifically mandated. Customer dissatisfaction; escalation to branch; complaints. Policy alteration request processing Processed and confirmed within 5 business days of complete documentation. Not specifically mandated. Incorrect records; potential claims disputes. Claims notification acknowledgement Within 24 business hours (internal target). Within 5 business days (mandatory). Regulatory breach if statutory SLA exceeded; financial penalty. Claims documentation checklist delivery Same day as notification acknowledgement. Must accompany acknowledgement (NIIRA 2025). Regulatory finding; extended claims cycle. Claims settlement (individual life) Within 20 business days of complete documentation (internal target). Within 60 days of notification (mandatory). Compound interest for each month of delay (NIIRA 2025 s.210); NAICOM enforcement; reputational damage. Complaint acknowledgement Within 24 business hours. Prompt acknowledgement (NAICOM guidelines). NAICOM consumer protection finding. Complaint resolution Within 10 business days for standard complaints; 20 for complex. NAICOM specifies reasonable timeframes. Escalation to NAICOM Consumer Protection Department. Policy document delivery Within 5 business days of policy issuance. On or before policy start date (NIIRA 2025). Regulatory breach; potential voiding of exclusion clauses if not delivered. 20.4.3 SLA Monitoring and Escalation SLA compliance must be monitored in real time through the insurer’s CRM and case management systems. Every open customer interaction should have a due date (the SLA deadline) visible to the handling agent and their supervisor. Interactions approaching the SLA deadline should trigger an automated alert; interactions that breach the SLA should trigger an automatic escalation to the supervisor and a notification to the quality assurance team. Monthly SLA compliance reporting should be presented to the Customer Experience Director and the COO. Any metric consistently below target requires a root cause investigation: Is the SLA breach due to inadequate staffing? Process complexity? Technology failure? Policy information quality? Each root cause requires a different remediation. An insurer that monitors SLA compliance but does not investigate root causes will produce the same compliance report month after month without improvement.

t: Chapter 20 · 20.5 CX Measurement: NPS and Other Metrics
x: 20.5.1 Net Promoter Score (NPS) Net Promoter Score (NPS) A customer loyalty metric that measures the likelihood of a customer recommending the insurer to a friend or colleague. Customers are asked: ‘On a scale of 0–10, how likely are you to recommend [insurer] to a friend or colleague?’ Respondents scoring 9–10 are Promoters; 7–8 are Passives; 0–6 are Detractors. NPS = % Promoters − % Detractors. Scores range from −100 to +100. A positive score indicates more promoters than detractors. NPS Formula NPS = (% Promoters) − (% Detractors) Example: 400 customers surveyed. 160 score 9–10 (Promoters = 40%). 80 score 0–6 (Detractors = 20%). 160 score 7–8 (Passives). NPS = 40 − 20 = +20. Benchmarks: NPS > 0 = more promoters than detractors (acceptable). NPS > 30 = strong loyalty. NPS > 50 = excellent. NPS < 0 = more detractors than promoters (crisis level in most markets). Nigerian insurance industry average NPS is estimated in the −5 to +10 range, reflecting the sector’s trust challenges. NPS is a leading indicator of growth: companies with high NPS grow faster because promoters actively refer new customers. For a Nigerian life insurer, building a promoter base is particularly valuable because peer recommendation is the most trusted source of insurance information in a market where advertising scepticism is high. A policyholder who received a prompt, fair claim settlement and tells their colleagues is worth more than a full-page newspaper advertisement. 20.5.2 Customer Satisfaction Score (CSAT) CSAT measures satisfaction with a specific interaction — ‘How satisfied were you with your claims experience today?’ (scored 1–5 or 1–10). Unlike NPS, which measures relationship-level loyalty, CSAT measures transaction-level satisfaction. It is best used immediately after a specific service interaction (post-call, post-claim, post-policy issuance) to capture the customer’s reaction to that specific touchpoint. CSAT by touchpoint enables the insurer to identify which specific interactions are generating dissatisfaction. A high post-sales CSAT but a low post-underwriting CSAT reveals that the underwriting process (medical evidence collection, turnaround time) is the friction point. A high CSAT at policy issuance but a low CSAT at first annual statement indicates a gap in the ongoing communication experience. 20.5.3 Customer Effort Score (CES) CES measures how easy it was for the customer to complete an interaction: ‘The insurance company made it easy for me to handle my issue.’ (Strongly agree = 7 to Strongly disagree = 1). Research consistently shows that reducing customer effort — making it easier to interact with the insurer — has a stronger impact on loyalty than delight. A policyholder who finds it effortless to pay their premium, update their address, or submit a claim will maintain their policy far longer than one who has to struggle with every routine interaction. In the Nigerian insurance context, the highest-effort interactions are typically: obtaining a policy document after payment; getting through to a contact centre agent; and submitting a claim — particularly gathering the required documentation. CES data on these interactions provides a direct improvement roadmap: reduce the effort at these specific points and retention will improve. 20.5.4 First Contact Resolution (FCR) FCR measures the proportion of customer queries or complaints resolved in the first interaction, without the customer needing to call back or escalate. FCR is both a service quality metric and an operational efficiency metric: every repeat contact to resolve the same issue represents a cost to the insurer and a frustration to the customer. Target FCR rate for a Nigerian insurance contact centre: 70%+ for standard queries (premium payment confirmation, policy balance, basic alteration requests). Complex queries (claims disputes, non-disclosure investigations, policy reinstatement) are unlikely to be resolved at first contact and should not distort the FCR metric for simple queries. FCR is best tracked by query category to identify where process improvement or agent training can increase first-contact resolution rates.

t: Chapter 20 · 20.6 Customer Retention: Lapse Management, Conservation, and Revival
x: Customer retention in life insurance is not a passive function — it is an active, structured commercial discipline. A policy that lapses represents a destroyed premium stream, a wasted acquisition cost, a policyholder left without protection, and a potential claims dispute (if the lapse was not the customer’s free choice). The financial mathematics of lapse prevention are straightforward: preventing one lapse is worth far more than acquiring one new policy, because the acquisition cost on the new policy must be paid again. 20.6.1 Lapse Management Lapse management is the systematic effort to prevent policies from lapsing — to identify at-risk policies early, diagnose the cause, and intervene before the policy moves from active to lapsed. The earlier in the lapse process an intervention occurs, the higher the success rate: a policyholder who has missed one premium is far easier to retain than one who has missed three. A best-practice lapse management programme has four components: Early warning system: An automated alert generated on the premium due date when the premium has not been received. The alert is sent simultaneously to the policyholder (SMS or WhatsApp reminder) and to the responsible agent. This is the first-day contact principle: reach the policyholder before they have consciously decided to lapse. Cause diagnosis: When the agent or contact centre contacts the policyholder, the conversation must identify the reason for non-payment: affordability (the premium is too high for current income); forgotten (the debit mandate was not set up or failed); dissatisfaction (the customer intends to cancel); or administrative (a bank account change or payment routing error). Each cause requires a different response. Tailored intervention: Affordability issues: offer to reduce the sum assured or convert to a lower-premium plan; facilitate a payment plan for arrears; explain the paid-up conversion option. Forgotten payment: resend the debit instruction; set up WhatsApp payment reminder. Dissatisfaction: route to a senior agent or customer experience manager for a conservation conversation. Grace period management: Most Nigerian life policies provide a 30-day grace period after the premium due date during which the policy remains in force. Every intervention attempt within the grace period should be documented. If the grace period expires without payment, the lapse is recorded but the policyholder should continue to receive communication for a defined period about revival options. 20.6.2 Conservation Programmes A conservation programme is a structured set of interventions designed to retain policyholders who are considering or have initiated a surrender or cancellation. Unlike lapse management (which focuses on missed premiums), conservation programmes address the policyholder who has actively decided they want out. Conservation interventions require a different skill set from standard agent interaction: the conservation specialist must understand the policyholder’s concerns, address misconceptions about the policy’s value, present alternatives to surrender, and — where surrender is genuinely in the policyholder’s interest — process it efficiently and with goodwill. Conservation is not about persuading policyholders to stay against their financial interest; it is about ensuring they have all the information they need to make a genuinely informed decision. Common alternatives presented in conservation conversations: premium reduction through sum assured adjustment; conversion to paid-up status; policy loan to fund a short-term cash need without surrendering; alteration to a more affordable premium payment frequency; and, where available, reduction riders or product switching. 20.6.3 Revival Campaigns A policy revival campaign targets lapsed policyholders — those whose policies have already passed the grace period and are technically in lapsed status — with an invitation to reinstate their coverage. Revival is commercially attractive: the original policyholder has already been underwritten and has demonstrated willingness to pay for insurance; the cost of reactivating them is significantly lower than acquiring a new customer. A well-designed revival campaign includes: a targeted segment of lapsed policyholders (typically those who lapsed within the past 12–24 months, before the coverage gap becomes a major underwriting concern); a compelling reactivation offer (reduced reinstatement medical requirements for policyholders who lapsed recently; waiver of interest on missed premiums for policyholders who reinstate within a defined window; a revised lower premium on reinstatement); and personalised outreach through the original agent plus direct insurer communication (SMS, WhatsApp, email). From a NAICOM regulatory perspective, reinstated policies may be subject to a new suicide clause period from the reinstatement date. This must be clearly disclosed to the reinstating policyholder as part of the revival documentation.

20.7.1 The Cross-Sell Opportunity Map An existing policyholder is the easiest customer to sell to: the trust barrier has been overcome, the KYC process has been completed, and the customer’s financial profile is partially known. Cross-selling (selling a different product to an existing customer) and upselling (increasing the coverage or value of the existing product) generate premium income at a fraction of the Customer Acquisition Cost of new customer acquisition. Existing Policy Cross-Sell Opportunity Trigger Moment Value Proposition Individual term assurance Endowment or savings plan Premium anniversary; life event (marriage, new child) ‘Your term assurance protects your family. An endowment plan also builds savings for their future.’ Group life (employer) Group health insurance; critical illness extension; EBC retainer Scheme renewal; HR strategy review ‘Extend your employee benefit package beyond mandatory life cover to attract and retain talent.’ Individual endowment (maturing) Retirement Life Annuity 12–18 months before maturity date ‘Your endowment matures soon. Convert the proceeds into a guaranteed income for life.’ Credit life (borrower) Stand-alone term assurance; family protection plan Loan repayment milestone; loan renewal ‘Your credit life covers your loan balance. This plan protects your family’s entire income, not just the debt.’ Children’s education plan Waiver of premium rider; critical illness rider Policy review conversation ‘If you are unable to pay premiums due to illness or disability, the waiver rider keeps your child’s plan going.’ Term assurance (breadwinner) Income protection / disability cover Agent annual review ‘Your family is protected if you die. What happens if you become disabled and cannot work for two years?’ 20.7.2 Cross-Sell Compliance Obligations Cross-selling to existing customers is subject to the same suitability obligations as any new insurance sale. An insurer that uses the data it holds about an existing policyholder to target them with an unsuitable product — for example, marketing an investment-linked product to a policyholder whose financial profile suggests they have no risk tolerance or investable surplus — is engaging in potential mis-selling. The insurer’s cross-sell protocols must include: a suitability assessment before any cross-sell approach (using the policyholder’s known financial profile to identify appropriate products); clear separation between service interactions (a premium collection call should not become a cross-sell pitch without the policyholder’s knowledge); and compliance review of any cross-sell scripts or materials used by contact centre agents or field agents. NIIRA 2025’s treating customers fairly obligation applies to cross-selling as fully as it applies to new customer acquisition.

20.8.1 Referral Programmes A referral programme is a structured incentive that rewards existing policyholders for introducing new customers to the insurer. Referrals from satisfied policyholders are the highest-quality leads in insurance: they arrive with a level of social proof and predisposition to purchase that cold leads lack; they convert at higher rates; and they tend to have higher average premium values because the referrer has pre-qualified the prospect. A well-designed referral programme: offers a reward that is genuinely valuable to the referrer (a premium discount, a gift, or a donation to a named charity in the referrer’s name rather than a cash payment, which can create regulatory complications); makes the referral process frictionless (a simple WhatsApp share, an app referral link, or a verbal introduction at the next policy review); tracks referral outcomes systematically so the referring policyholder can see when their referral has converted; and complies with the NDPA 2023 requirements on data use (the referred prospect must consent to contact before they are reached by the insurer). 20.8.2 Affinity Groups An affinity group is a defined population of people who share a common characteristic, institutional relationship, or membership — alumni of a university, members of a professional body, employees of a single employer, members of a trade association — to whom the insurer offers tailored insurance products at group rates or with simplified underwriting. Affinity marketing is one of the most efficient acquisition models in insurance: the insurer reaches a defined, pre-qualified population through a trusted intermediary (the alumni association, the professional body’s membership communications, the employer’s HR portal); the group discount or simplified access creates a compelling offer; and the institutional endorsement reduces the trust barrier. Nigerian professional associations — ICAN (accountants), NMA (medical doctors), NBA (lawyers), CIIN (insurance professionals) — are natural affinity group partners for life insurance with occupational income protection and group life products. 20.8.3 Employer Portals An employer portal is a digital platform through which an employer’s workforce can access, enrol in, and manage the insurance benefits available to them. It sits at the intersection of worksite marketing (the distribution approach described in Chapter 17) and digital self-service: it gives employees 24/7 access to their benefit elections, coverage details, and enrolment options without requiring a dedicated HR or benefits administration team to process each transaction manually. A well-designed employer portal enables: online enrolment for new employees; digital beneficiary nomination; coverage summary and policy certificate download; premium contribution statement (for payroll deduction schemes); and integration with the employer’s payroll system for seamless deduction management. The portal reduces the employer’s administrative burden and increases employee engagement with their benefits — employees who actively manage their benefits are more likely to value them and less likely to lapse their individual add-on covers. 20.8.4 Digital Funnels A digital acquisition funnel is the end-to-end digital pathway through which a prospective customer moves from first awareness of the insurer’s brand to a completed policy application. Digital funnels convert the investment made in marketing (Chapter 19) into measurable policy issuances by managing the prospect’s journey through defined stages: awareness (reached via social media, search, or display advertising); interest (captured via a lead magnet, premium calculator, or educational content); consideration (nurtured via email sequences or WhatsApp conversations); and decision (converted via a simplified online application or agent handoff). The critical success factors for Nigerian insurance digital funnels: speed of response after lead capture (same-day contact); simplicity of the application process (mobile-optimised, minimal fields); transparent benefit illustrations (presented in consumer-friendly format before the application); and a clear, trusted payment mechanism (integration with major mobile money platforms and bank transfer). Funnels that require the prospect to switch from digital to physical to complete the purchase (print and sign the form; attend a branch) suffer high abandonment at the switch point.

t: Chapter 20 · 20.9 Vulnerable Customer Management and Inclusive Service Design
x: 20.9.1 Who is a Vulnerable Customer? Vulnerable Customer (NIIRA 2025 / NAICOM Context) A customer who, due to their personal circumstances, is at significantly greater risk of harm from the insurer’s actions or inactions than a typical customer. Vulnerability may be temporary (a bereavement, a sudden illness), cyclical (a mental health condition), or permanent (low literacy, a disability, advanced age with cognitive decline). Vulnerability does not mean the customer is incapable; it means they need adapted service to receive the same standard of outcome as a non-vulnerable customer. Categories of customer vulnerability relevant to Nigerian life insurance: Bereavement: A policyholder’s family member presenting a death claim is, almost by definition, in a state of acute emotional vulnerability. Every claims interaction with a bereaved family must be handled with this awareness. Low financial literacy: A policyholder who does not understand the key terms of their policy — how surrenders work, what the exclusions are, what their beneficiary options are — is at risk of making harmful financial decisions based on incomplete understanding. Low digital literacy: Policyholders who are unable to use digital self-service platforms are excluded from channels that the insurer may be progressively deprioritising relative to physical channels. Elderly customers: Older policyholders may have reduced cognitive capacity for complex financial decisions, be particularly susceptible to pressure-selling tactics, and may have physical limitations that affect their ability to visit branches or use digital interfaces. Financial distress: A policyholder in acute financial hardship who is considering surrendering a long-term policy for its surrender value may not be aware of the paid-up option or other alternatives. An insurer that processes a surrender without proactively presenting alternatives to a financially distressed customer is failing its duty of care. 20.9.2 Identification and Adapted Service Delivery Vulnerable customers are not always identifiable from their policy records. They may reveal their vulnerability in the course of a customer service interaction: a claimant who mentions that the deceased was the sole breadwinner; a policyholder who struggles to understand an agent’s explanation and repeatedly asks for clarification; a caller who is clearly in distress. Contact centre agents and field agents must be trained to: recognise the indicators of vulnerability; record the vulnerability on the customer’s file (with appropriate data protection safeguards); adapt their communication style (simpler language, more time, no sales pressure); and escalate to a specialist vulnerability team or supervisor for cases requiring more intensive support. Adapted service protocols for vulnerable customers: additional time on calls without pressure; written confirmation of all verbal commitments; referral to the insurer’s financial hardship programme where available; third-party advocacy (allowing a family member or community adviser to assist the customer with their interaction); and access to alternative formats for policy documents (larger print, simplified summary in local language). 20.9.3 Inclusive Service Design Inclusive service design is the practice of designing products, processes, and interfaces so that they are accessible and usable by the widest possible range of customers, including those with disabilities, low literacy, or limited digital access. In the Nigerian insurance context, inclusive design addresses: USSD-first interfaces for feature phone users; Yoruba, Hausa, and Igbo language options for non-English-comfortable users; visual and audio-format policy summaries for low-literacy users; and branch accessibility for mobility-impaired customers. Inclusive design is both an ethical obligation and a commercial opportunity. The populations that standard insurance design serves poorly — rural, low-literacy, elderly, informal economy participants — are also the populations where insurance penetration is lowest. Designing for inclusivity expands the addressable market while fulfilling the insurer’s duty of care under NIIRA 2025.

t: Chapter 20 · 20.10 NIIRA 2025: NAICOM Consumer Protection Framework and Complaints Redress
x: 20.10.1 The Consumer Protection Framework NIIRA 2025 consolidates and strengthens the consumer protection obligations that were previously scattered across the Insurance Act 2003, NAICOM market conduct guidelines, and CBN consumer protection frameworks. The NIIRA 2025 consumer protection framework is built around six principles that every licensed insurer must observe in all its dealings with policyholders and prospective customers: Principle 1: Fair Treatment Insurers must treat all customers fairly at all stages of the customer relationship — marketing, product design, sales, servicing, and claims. Unfair treatment includes: applying different standards to customers based on protected characteristics; using terms that are unreasonably difficult to understand; and applying policy conditions in a manner inconsistent with the customer’s reasonable expectations. Principle 2: Transparency and Disclosure All material information about a product — premium, coverage, exclusions, surrender value basis, commission paid to intermediaries — must be disclosed to the customer before the policy is concluded, in plain language, and in a format the customer can reasonably be expected to understand. Principle 3: Product Suitability Products must be sold to customers for whom they are suitable. A complex investment-linked product must not be sold to a customer with no financial sophistication or surplus investable income. The suitability assessment must be documented. Principle 4: Complaints Handling Every insurer must have a written complaints handling policy, a dedicated complaints function, a clear complaints procedure communicated to all customers, and a defined timeline for complaint acknowledgement and resolution. Principle 5: Data Protection Customer data must be collected and processed in accordance with the NDPA 2023. Customers must be informed of how their data is used and must be able to exercise their data rights (access, correction, erasure) without unnecessary obstacle. Principle 6: Vulnerable Customer Protection Insurers must identify and make appropriate accommodations for vulnerable customers, ensuring they receive an equivalent standard of outcome as non-vulnerable customers despite their individual circumstances. 20.10.2 The NAICOM Complaints Redress Mechanism NIIRA 2025 establishes a formal multi-tier complaints redress mechanism for insurance consumers. The mechanism works progressively: the complaint must first be addressed internally by the insurer, and only if the internal resolution process fails or the customer is dissatisfied with the outcome may the complaint be escalated externally. NIIRA 2025: The Three-Tier Complaints Redress Process TIER 1 — INTERNAL INSURER RESOLUTION: The policyholder submits their complaint to the insurer’s designated complaints officer. The insurer must acknowledge the complaint within the prescribed timeframe and resolve it within the SLA timeline. The insurer must communicate the outcome in writing with clear reasons. If the policyholder is satisfied, the process ends. TIER 2 — NAICOM CONSUMER PROTECTION DEPARTMENT: If the policyholder is dissatisfied with the insurer’s internal resolution, or if the insurer fails to respond within the prescribed timeframe, the complaint may be referred to NAICOM’s Consumer Protection Department. NAICOM will review the complaint, request information from the insurer, and issue a finding. NAICOM’s finding may direct the insurer to pay the claim, amend its decision, or provide an explanation. NAICOM’s finding is binding on the insurer. TIER 3 — LEGAL AND ADR: Policyholders retain the right to pursue the matter through the courts or through Alternative Dispute Resolution (ADR) mechanisms, including arbitration and mediation, if they are dissatisfied with the NAICOM resolution process. NIIRA 2025 does not extinguish any policyholder’s right to judicial redress. 20.10.3 NAICOM Enforcement Powers in Respect of Consumer Protection NIIRA 2025 gives NAICOM substantial enforcement powers in response to consumer protection failures. These powers escalate from administrative remedies to existential regulatory consequences: Financial penalties: NAICOM may impose financial penalties on insurers that systematically fail to meet consumer protection obligations — including claims payment failures, non-compliant marketing, and inadequate complaints handling. Public disclosure: NAICOM may publicly name insurers with persistent consumer protection failures in its regulatory bulletins, market conduct reports, and website. Reputational consequences of public naming are a powerful deterrent. Business restrictions: NAICOM may suspend an insurer’s authority to write new business in specific product lines or through specific channels pending remediation of identified consumer protection failures. Management intervention: NAICOM may direct the removal or replacement of the Head of Customer Experience, Customer Service Director, or other responsible officers where NAICOM has determined that management failure is the root cause of the consumer protection problem. Licence revocation: In cases of systematic, serious, and unresolved consumer protection failure, NAICOM may revoke the insurer’s operating licence. This is the most extreme sanction and is reserved for the most serious cases.

t: Chapter 20 · 20.11 Advisory: Building a Customer Experience Function for a Nigerian Life Insurer
x: A customer experience function that genuinely transforms the policyholder’s experience requires more than a renamed customer service department. It requires organisational commitment, management accountability, technology investment, and a cultural shift toward customer-centricity that must be led from the top. Advisory: The Customer Experience Maturity Ladder for Nigerian Life Insurers Most Nigerian life insurers currently sit at Level 1 or 2 of the following CX maturity ladder. The NIIRA 2025 regulatory environment and competitive pressures are driving the need to reach Level 3 and 4: LEVEL 1 — REACTIVE: Customer service is treated as a complaint-handling function. No proactive communication with policyholders between premium collection and claims. No formal SLAs. No CX metrics tracked. Contact centre staffed primarily for inbound complaint management. LEVEL 2 — OPERATIONAL: Formal SLAs exist and are tracked. A complaints handling policy is documented. Contact centre handles standard queries. Annual statements are sent. There is no proactive lapse management programme. Customer feedback is collected sporadically. LEVEL 3 — CUSTOMER-CENTRIC: NPS is measured and tracked. Customer journey maps are documented. A proactive lapse management programme operates. Conservation and revival programmes run regularly. Cross-sell is managed systematically. Vulnerable customer protocols are documented and trained. Digital self-service covers 70%+ of routine transactions. LEVEL 4 — CX-LED GROWTH: CX metrics are Board-level KPIs. The Head of Customer Experience is an Executive Committee member. NPS is >30. Claims storytelling is a central marketing activity. The referral programme generates 20%+ of new business. Customer effort scores drive operational improvement priorities. The insurer is known in the market for the quality of its claims experience. The Single Most Impactful CX Investment for a Nigerian Life Insurer If an insurer can only make one investment in customer experience, it should be in the claims experience. This is true for every life insurer globally, but it is especially true in Nigeria, where the trust deficit is primarily driven by claims payment failures and the fear of them. Specifically: invest in a proactive claims communication system that sends an automated update to every claimant every 5 business days while their claim is open. This single process change — which requires only a modest technology implementation and a modest increase in contact centre capacity — will reduce complaint rates, improve NPS, generate more claimant testimonials, and create a claims experience that policyholders actually talk about positively. In a market where the fear of ‘they won’t pay’ is the primary purchase barrier, an insurer that demonstrably communicates throughout the claims process is not just providing good service — it is rewriting the industry narrative.

Customer Experience (CX) Every interaction a policyholder has with an insurer across the full relationship lifecycle — from awareness through purchase, in-force servicing, and claims — and the cumulative impression those interactions create. Customer Journey Map A structured representation of every significant interaction a customer has with the insurer, documenting the customer’s goals, emotional state, pain points, and the insurer’s moments of truth at each stage. Moment of Truth A specific customer interaction at which the customer forms a definitive impression of the organisation that either builds or destroys their trust. The claim payment is the ultimate moment of truth in insurance. Service Level Agreement (SLA) A commitment by the insurer to deliver a defined standard of service within a defined timeframe. SLAs convert subjective service quality into measurable, manageable performance targets. Net Promoter Score (NPS) A customer loyalty metric calculated as the percentage of Promoters (those scoring 9–10 on a recommendation likelihood question) minus the percentage of Detractors (those scoring 0–6). Customer Satisfaction Score (CSAT) A transaction-level metric measuring customer satisfaction with a specific interaction, typically on a 1–5 or 1–10 scale administered immediately after the interaction. Customer Effort Score (CES) A metric measuring how easy it was for a customer to complete an interaction, rated on a scale from ‘strongly disagree’ to ‘strongly agree’ with the statement ‘the company made it easy to handle my issue.’ First Contact Resolution (FCR) The proportion of customer queries resolved in the first interaction, without the customer needing to call back or escalate. A measure of both service quality and operational efficiency. Lapse Management The systematic process of identifying at-risk policies (those with missed premiums), diagnosing the cause, and intervening before the policy moves from active to lapsed status. Conservation Programme A structured set of interventions designed to retain policyholders who are considering or have initiated a surrender or cancellation, by presenting alternatives and ensuring the customer has full information to make a genuinely informed decision. Policy Revival The reinstatement of a lapsed policy, typically involving repayment of overdue premiums and satisfying any re-underwriting requirements. Revival campaigns target lapsed policyholders with incentives to reinstate. Cross-Selling The sale of a different insurance product to an existing policyholder, based on their existing relationship with the insurer and the expanded coverage need identified from their known financial profile. Upselling Increasing the coverage amount or adding riders to an existing policy, expanding the policyholder’s protection and the insurer’s premium income from the existing relationship. Referral Programme A structured incentive that rewards existing policyholders for introducing new customers, leveraging social proof and personal endorsement as acquisition tools. Affinity Group A defined population sharing a common characteristic or institutional membership to whom insurance is offered at group rates or with simplified underwriting, using the institutional relationship as a distribution and trust pathway. Vulnerable Customer A customer who, due to personal circumstances (bereavement, illness, low literacy, financial distress, advanced age), is at greater risk of harm from the insurer’s actions or inactions than a typical customer. Inclusive Service Design The practice of designing products, processes, and interfaces to be accessible and usable by the widest possible range of customers, including those with disabilities, low literacy, or limited digital access. Phygital Model A hybrid service delivery model combining physical presence (agent, branch) with digital enablement (app, USSD, WhatsApp), providing human interaction where needed and digital efficiency for routine transactions.
