The 'ultimate moment of truth' in a life insurance customer's experience is generally considered to be: The moment the policyholder receives their first annual benefit statement. The first premium collection by direct debit. The claim payment, which tests whether the insurer's promise was genuine. The product presentation by the insurance agent. (C) The claim payment, which tests whether the insurer's promise was genuine. Why (C) is Correct The 'moment of truth' concept in service management identifies the interactions that most powerfully define a customer's perception of a service provider. In life insurance, the claim payment is the definitive test: the policyholder (or their beneficiary) has paid premiums for years in exchange for a promise. The claim is the moment when that promise is either honoured or broken. Every other interaction (policy issuance, annual statements, premium receipts) is subordinate — it is the claim that determines whether the customer (or their family) was wise to trust the insurer. Why the Others Are Wrong (A) The annual benefit statement confirms the policy is in force and reports accumulated values — an important servicing interaction but not the definitive trust test.(B) The first premium collection confirms the payment mechanism is working — an administrative milestone, not a trust-testing moment.(D) The product presentation is the acquisition moment — trust has not yet been established. It is the beginning of the relationship, not its defining test.

The Net Promoter Score (NPS) is calculated by: Subtracting the percentage of dissatisfied claimants from the percentage of satisfied claimants. Subtracting the percentage of Detractors (scoring 0–6) from the percentage of Promoters (scoring 9–10). Averaging all customer satisfaction scores collected in the relevant period. Dividing the number of referred new customers by the total number of existing policyholders. (B) Subtracting the percentage of Detractors (those scoring 0–6 on the recommendation question) from the percentage of Promoters (those scoring 9–10). Why (B) is Correct NPS is calculated from a single question: 'How likely are you to recommend [Insurer Name] to a friend or family member?' scored 0–10. Respondents are classified:• Promoters: scored 9–10 (loyal enthusiasts who actively recommend)• Passives: scored 7–8 (satisfied but not enthusiastic — excluded from the NPS calculation)• Detractors: scored 0–6 (unhappy customers who may actively warn others against the insurer) NPS = % Promoters − % Detractors. A score of +30 indicates significantly more Promoters than Detractors. Nigerian life insurers typically have negative NPS scores — more people warn others against them than recommend them. Under NIIRA 2025's three-tier complaints redress mechanism, if a policyholder is dissatisfied with the insurer's internal resolution, the next step is: To file a claim in the Federal High Court. To refer the complaint to NAICOM's Consumer Protection Department. To contact the insurer's Board of Directors directly. To notify the Nigerian Insurers Association (NIA) of the dispute. (B) To refer the complaint to NAICOM's Consumer Protection Department. Why (B) is Correct NIIRA 2025 establishes a three-tier complaints resolution framework:Tier 1: Internal resolution — the insurer's own complaints team attempts to resolve within a defined period (typically 15 working days).Tier 2: NAICOM Consumer Protection Department — if the insurer's resolution is unsatisfactory, the policyholder escalates to NAICOM. NAICOM investigates and issues a finding. This is the regulatory escalation stage.Tier 3: The courts — if NAICOM's finding is not accepted or does not resolve the matter, litigation in the courts is available as the final recourse. A policyholder calls to update their beneficiary. The agent cannot resolve it immediately and promises to call back within 24 hours. When the agent does not call back and the policyholder calls again the following day, this represents a failure of: The insurer's reinsurance management obligations. The First Contact Resolution principle and the Service Level Agreement for callback commitments. The insurer's NIIRA 2025 mandatory policy filing requirement. The policyholder's duty of disclosure under the policy contract. (B) The First Contact Resolution principle and the Service Level Agreement for callback commitments. Why (B) is Correct First Contact Resolution (FCR) is the principle that customer queries are resolved at the first point of contact wherever possible, without requiring the customer to call back or follow up. In this case, FCR was not achieved — the beneficiary update required a callback promise. The agent's failure to call back within 24 hours is a Service Level Agreement (SLA) breach: the insurer's contact centre SLA defines the maximum response time for different interaction types and callback commitments are binding service obligations. The policyholder's need to call back represents both a customer experience failure and an SLA failure. Why the Others Are Wrong (A) Reinsurance management obligations relate to the insurer's cession of risk to reinsurers — entirely unrelated to a contact centre callback failure.(C) Policy filing requirements relate to NAICOM product approval — also unrelated.(D) The duty of disclosure is the insured's pre-contract obligation

x: Learning Objectives On completing this chapter, the reader should be able to: Describe the CIIN Code of Ethics, identify its core principles, and explain how the Code’s obligations apply to insurance practitioners at all levels — agents, brokers, underwriters, claims officers, and senior managers. Explain the concept of ‘treating customers fairly’ (TCF) in insurance, describe its six outcomes, and apply the TCF framework to evaluate the conduct of insurance intermediaries and insurers in the Nigerian market. Define mis-selling in the insurance context, identify its principal forms in Nigerian life insurance practice, and describe the legal consequences and regulatory sanctions available to NAICOM in response to proven mis-selling. Describe the duty of care owed to customers by insurance practitioners, with specific attention to the heightened duty applicable in dealings with vulnerable customers, and identify the circumstances in which the duty of care creates legal liability for insurance companies and their intermediaries. Explain the Know Your Customer (KYC) obligations and Anti-Money Laundering (AML) requirements that apply to insurance practitioners in Nigeria, including the identification of Politically Exposed Persons, the reporting of suspicious transactions, and the Money Laundering (Prevention and Prohibition) Act 2022 obligations. t: Chapter 21 · 21.1 Introduction: Ethics and Conduct as Competitive Advantage
x: Market conduct — the behaviour of insurance companies and intermediaries in their dealings with customers — is the bridge between the insurance contract on paper and the insurance experience in practice. An industry whose contracts are technically sound but whose conduct is ethically deficient produces outcomes that are indefensible: premiums collected, claims denied on technicalities, vulnerable customers misled, complaints ignored, and the regulatory framework circumvented rather than complied with. Nigeria’s insurance sector has been characterised by conduct failures that go beyond individual cases of bad practice into structural patterns: systematic under-disclosure of product terms, commission-driven pressure selling, non-payment and delayed payment of valid claims, and the use of KYC and AML procedures as bureaucratic barriers rather than genuine compliance disciplines. These patterns are the proximate cause of the trust deficit examined in Chapter 19. They are also the target of NIIRA 2025’s most significant regulatory interventions. This chapter treats market conduct as both a regulatory compliance obligation and a professional identity issue. The CIIN Code of Ethics, the treating customers fairly framework, and the duty of care are not externally imposed constraints on a practitioner’s commercial freedom — they are the professional standards that distinguish a qualified insurance practitioner from a commission-motivated sales person. Internalising these standards is what makes the difference between a profession and a trade. The chapter addresses the full landscape of market conduct obligations: the professional ethics framework, the treatment of customers (including the vulnerable), the AML/KYC compliance regime, data protection, the premium collection discipline, and the professional indemnity obligation. Together, these form the compliance architecture within which every licensed insurance practitioner in Nigeria must operate.

t: Chapter 21 · 21.2 The CIIN Code of Ethics and Professional Standards
x: 21.2.1 The CIIN’s Role in Professional Standards The Chartered Insurance Institute of Nigeria (CIIN) is the statutory professional body for the insurance industry in Nigeria, established by Act No. 22 of 1993. One of its primary functions is to set and enforce the professional standards and code of ethics that govern the conduct of insurance practitioners. Membership of CIIN, and compliance with its Code of Ethics, are conditions of professional practice: an insurance practitioner who violates the Code faces CIIN disciplinary proceedings that can result in suspension or expulsion from the profession. The CIIN Code of Ethics draws on the global principles of the International Federation of Insurance Associations and reflects the professional standards of the CII (UK), the CIIN’s international counterpart. It establishes the minimum ethical standards expected of all insurance practitioners — not merely a negative prohibition list, but a positive statement of the professional values that CIIN members commit to uphold. 21.2.2 The Core Principles of the CIIN Code Integrity CIIN members must be honest, trustworthy, and straightforward in all professional dealings. They must not engage in deception, fraud, or dishonest conduct in any professional or personal capacity that brings the profession into disrepute. Competence CIIN members must maintain the professional knowledge and skill required to perform their role to a high standard. They must not offer advice or services outside their competence, and they must engage in Continuing Professional Development to keep their knowledge current. Duty to the client Members must act in the best interest of their clients at all times, placing the client’s interest above their own financial or commercial interest. This principle is the professional foundation of the broker’s fiduciary duty and the agent’s duty not to mis-sell. Fair dealing Members must deal fairly with all parties — clients, insurers, reinsurers, and colleagues — without deception, manipulation, or the exploitation of information advantages. Regulatory compliance Members must comply with all applicable laws, regulations, and professional rules, including NAICOM regulations, NIIRA 2025, the NDPA 2023, and the AML/CFT framework. Regulatory compliance is a professional obligation, not merely a legal one. Confidentiality Members must protect the confidentiality of client information obtained in the course of their professional duties. They must not disclose or use client information for any purpose other than the performance of their professional functions, unless required by law or with the client’s consent. Professional development Members must commit to continuous learning and development, completing the CPD requirements set by CIIN annually, and sharing professional knowledge with colleagues and the wider profession. Professionalism Members must conduct themselves in a manner that maintains and enhances the reputation of the insurance profession. This includes avoiding conduct that is dishonest, illegal, or brings the profession into disrepute, whether in their professional or personal capacity. 21.2.3 CIIN Disciplinary Procedures Where a CIIN member is alleged to have violated the Code of Ethics, the CIIN’s disciplinary procedure is activated. The procedure involves: receipt of a complaint (from a client, employer, regulator, or colleague); initial assessment for prima facie merit; investigation by the CIIN’s professional standards committee; a formal hearing before the CIIN Disciplinary Panel if the case is substantiated; and a finding with a defined sanction. Sanctions available to the CIIN Disciplinary Panel range from a formal reprimand (a recorded finding of professional misconduct, short of suspension) through suspension of membership for a defined period to expulsion from the Institute — the professional equivalent of disbarment. Expulsion is recorded in the public register of CIIN members and is reported to NAICOM; NAICOM may then revoke the individual’s agent or broker registration as a consequence. The linkage between CIIN discipline and NAICOM registration means that the most serious professional misconduct findings can effectively end a career in insurance.

t: Chapter 21 · 21.3 Treating Customers Fairly: Principles and Application
x: 21.3.1 The TCF Framework Treating Customers Fairly (TCF) is a regulatory and professional standard originating in the UK’s Financial Conduct Authority framework and adopted as the guiding principle of NAICOM’s market conduct supervision under NIIRA 2025. TCF is not a checklist of prohibited behaviours; it is a outcomes-based framework: the test of whether an insurer or intermediary is treating customers fairly is not whether they have followed specified procedures, but whether the customer is actually receiving fair outcomes. The TCF framework identifies six core consumer outcomes that fair treatment should deliver. Each outcome can be assessed both as a standard for individual conduct and as a metric for measuring an insurer’s overall market conduct performance: TCF Outcome Description Conduct Implications Key Indicator of Failure 1. Culture and governance Consumers can be confident they are dealing with insurers where the fair treatment of customers is central to the corporate culture. Board oversight of market conduct; TCF as a management KPI; conduct reporting to Board Risk Committee. High complaint volumes; NAICOM market conduct findings; low NPS. 2. Products designed for target market Products and services marketed and sold in the retail market are designed to meet the needs of the customers they are directed at. Target market definition in product filings; suitability assessment tools for agents; no complex products sold to financially unsophisticated customers. High early lapse rates; customer complaints about product suitability; claims disputes arising from misunderstood coverage. 3. Clear information before and after sale Consumers are provided with clear information and are kept appropriately informed before, during, and after the point of sale. Plain language policy documents; benefit illustrations in prescribed format; annual statements; proactive communication about material policy changes. Policyholder complaints of confusion about policy terms; claims disputes based on coverage misunderstanding. 4. Advice meeting customers’ needs Where consumers receive advice, it is suitable and takes account of their individual circumstances. Fact-find documentation; suitability assessment for each recommendation; documented rationale for product recommendation. Mis-selling complaints; unsuitable product recommendations; high surrender rates shortly after sale. 5. Products perform as firms have led consumers to expect Consumers are provided with products that perform as the firm has led them to expect. Accurate benefit illustrations; no misleading return projections; product performance monitoring by actuarial function. Claims below illustrated expectations; bonus declaration significantly below projection; high surrender post-maturity. 6. No post-sale barriers Consumers do not face unreasonable post-sale barriers imposed by firms to change product, switch provider, submit a claim, or make a complaint. No excessive documentation for straightforward transactions; fair surrender value basis; complaint handling within SLA. Claims obstruction; excessive documentation demands; unreasonable lapse-prevention pressure; complaint dismissal without investigation. 21.3.2 TCF in Practice: Application to Common Scenarios The TCF framework becomes operational when applied to the specific scenarios that arise in day-to-day Nigerian insurance practice. The following illustrates how TCF applies to four common conduct situations: Agent pressure selling: An agent who pressures a policyholder to purchase a product without adequate explanation of the terms, exclusions, or surrender value basis — driven by the need to hit a production target before month end — is violating TCF Outcomes 3 and 4. The customer has not received clear information, and the advice is not based on a proper assessment of their needs. Bancassurance product substitution: A bank relationship manager who recommends a specific life insurance product because it generates the highest commission for the bank, rather than because it is most suitable for the customer, is violating TCF Outcome 4 (advice meeting customers’ needs) and potentially the NCRIB/CIIN conflict of interest duty. Misleading benefit illustration: An insurer that presents a participating endowment policy’s maturity projection using an unrealistically high investment return assumption, without adequate disclosure that the projection is not guaranteed, is violating TCF Outcome 5 (products performing as led to expect). Claims obstruction: An insurer that demands extensive documentation for a straightforward death claim, delays assessment without adequate communication, or invokes obscure policy conditions to reduce or avoid payment of a claim that is substantively valid is violating TCF Outcome 6 (no post-sale barriers).

21.4.1 Definition and Forms of Mis-Selling Mis-Selling The sale of an insurance product to a customer through conduct that is dishonest, misleading, or otherwise contrary to the customer’s interests. Mis-selling may involve a positive misrepresentation (making a false claim about the product), an omission (failing to disclose a material term or exclusion), unsuitable advice (recommending a product that does not meet the customer’s needs), or the use of pressure or manipulation to overcome the customer’s informed resistance to purchase. The most common forms of mis-selling encountered in Nigerian life insurance practice are: Return misrepresentation: Describing a participating endowment or unit-linked product as offering a ‘guaranteed’ return when the return is explicitly non-guaranteed, or using benefit illustrations that project unrealistically high returns without adequate risk disclosure. Coverage misrepresentation: Describing a term assurance as covering ‘all causes of death’ without disclosing the suicide exclusion, the pre-existing condition exclusion, or war exclusions. The customer relies on the agent’s representation and buys a product believing it covers risks it does not. False urgency and pressure tactics: Creating artificial urgency (‘this offer is only available until the end of the month’ for a product with no genuine time limit) or using emotional pressure, particularly around the prospect’s family’s vulnerability to loss, to overcome the customer’s hesitation without providing full information. Product substitution for commission: Recommending a higher-premium or higher-commission product when a lower-cost product would equally meet the customer’s needs, without disclosing the agent’s commission interest. Identity fraud and phantom policies: An agent who collects premiums from a customer (which the Act prohibits: s.38(2)) and issues a false policy document, without actually placing the policy with the insurer. This is both mis-selling and criminal fraud. Target market violation: Selling a product outside its NAICOM-approved target market — for example, selling a complex investment-linked product to a low-income customer who lacks the financial literacy to understand it and the risk tolerance to bear the investment risk. 21.4.2 Legal Consequences and Regulatory Sanctions for Mis-Selling Legal and Regulatory Consequences of Mis-Selling under NIIRA 2025 Proven mis-selling exposes the insurer, the intermediary, and the individual practitioner to consequences across four legal and regulatory dimensions: NAICOM ADMINISTRATIVE SANCTIONS: Financial penalties as the Commission may impose (inducing a contract by a misleading statement is also an offence under s.209, punishable by at least ₦500,000, or two years’ imprisonment, or both); suspension of the right to sell the mis-sold product; public disclosure of the insurer’s name and the specific market conduct finding on NAICOM’s website and in its published reports. For systemic mis-selling (affecting a significant proportion of the policyholder base), NAICOM may require the insurer to conduct a customer remediation programme. INDIVIDUAL PRACTITIONER CONSEQUENCES: An agent or broker who mis-sells may have their NAICOM registration revoked, terminating their ability to conduct insurance business in Nigeria. CIIN disciplinary proceedings may result in expulsion from the Institute. These consequences are personal and are not mitigated by the employer taking over responsibility for the mis-selling. CIVIL LIABILITY: The mis-sold customer has a civil cause of action against the insurer or intermediary for damages arising from the mis-sale. Potential damages include: the premiums paid; the investment return the customer would have received if appropriately advised; the cost of replacing the unsuitable product with a suitable one; and consequential losses (e.g., a customer who cancelled a previous valid policy on the agent’s advice to ‘switch’ to the mis-sold product). CRIMINAL LIABILITY: Where mis-selling involves fraudulent misrepresentation (deliberate false statements of fact), false pretences (obtaining money by deception), or forgery of policy documents, criminal charges under the Criminal Code Act may be brought against the individual practitioner and, in cases of systemic fraud, the insurer’s directors. 21.4.3 The Suitability Assessment Obligation The regulatory response to mis-selling is the suitability assessment obligation: before recommending any insurance product to a customer, the practitioner must conduct a documented assessment of the customer’s needs, financial circumstances, and risk tolerance to establish that the recommended product is genuinely suitable. For life insurance, the minimum suitability assessment covers: the customer’s current life insurance coverage and any gaps; the financial consequences for their dependants of their death or disability; their premium affordability (ensuring the premium does not create financial hardship that will lead to early lapse); and their financial literacy and understanding of the product type (particularly important for complex products like unit-linked insurance). The suitability assessment must be documented in a fact-find document that is signed by both the customer and the agent, retained in the customer’s file, and available for inspection by NAICOM.

t: Chapter 21 · 21.5 Duty of Care and Vulnerable Customers
x: 21.5.1 The Duty of Care in Insurance The duty of care is the legal obligation to exercise reasonable care and skill in the performance of professional services, such that the customer does not suffer harm as a result of the practitioner’s negligence. In insurance, the duty of care applies across the full range of professional activities: the broker’s advice on coverage; the agent’s representation of product terms; the underwriter’s assessment of the risk; the claims officer’s investigation and assessment of a claim; and the customer service representative’s handling of a complaint. The duty of care is not absolute: it is a duty to exercise the standard of care that a reasonably competent insurance professional in the relevant role would exercise in the same circumstances. A newly qualified agent who makes a genuine and understandable error of product knowledge has not necessarily breached the duty of care; an experienced senior broker who fails to identify a material coverage gap in a complex programme they are advising on most likely has. Breach of the duty of care creates liability in tort (negligence) for the resulting harm. For insurance intermediaries, the most common negligence claims arise from: failure to place the insurance as instructed; failure to advise on a material coverage gap; failure to disclose material policy terms before the customer commits to purchase; and failure to assist with a claim that falls within the policy’s coverage but is disputed by the insurer. 21.5.2 Heightened Duty of Care for Vulnerable Customers Chapter 20 addressed the identification and service adaptation required for vulnerable customers. From a market conduct and legal perspective, the heightened duty of care for vulnerable customers is a critical additional obligation: the standard of care owed to a vulnerable customer is higher than the standard owed to a financially sophisticated, fully informed customer. The rationale is that the potential for harm is greater when a practitioner deals with a person whose ability to protect their own interests is impaired. Specific duty of care obligations in dealings with vulnerable customers include: ensuring that the customer genuinely understands the product they are buying (which may require additional explanation time, simpler language, or the involvement of a trusted third party); not using sales tactics that exploit the customer’s vulnerability (fear, bereavement, financial distress) to accelerate a purchase decision; proactively presenting all relevant alternatives before processing a surrender request by a customer who may not understand the long-term implications of surrendering; and escalating to a supervisor where the agent has reason to believe the customer is being influenced or pressured by a third party.

t: Chapter 21 · 21.6 Know Your Customer and Anti-Money Laundering Obligations
x: 21.6.1 The AML/CFT Framework for Insurance in Nigeria The Money Laundering (Prevention and Prohibition) Act 2022 (MLPPA 2022) classifies insurance as a designated business sector and imposes AML/CFT (Anti-Money Laundering and Counter-Financing of Terrorism) obligations on all licensed insurers, brokers, and insurance agents. These obligations are supplemented by NAICOM’s AML/CFT Guidelines for Insurance Institutions, which translate the MLPPA 2022’s general requirements into insurance-specific operational requirements. The AML/CFT framework is grounded in the recognition that life insurance is a financial product with money laundering exposure. Large single-premium policies, single-premium annuities, investment-linked products, and credit life arrangements involving significant premium flows can all, if not properly managed, be used as vehicles for placing, layering, or integrating proceeds of crime. The AML/CFT obligations are designed to prevent this misuse without creating disproportionate compliance burdens for legitimate customers. 21.6.2 KYC Requirements Know Your Customer (KYC) is the process of identifying, verifying, and understanding the customer and the source of the funds they use to pay insurance premiums. For Nigerian life insurance, the minimum KYC requirements are: Identity verification: Full legal name; date of birth; residential address; National Identity Number (NIN); government-issued photo ID (NIN slip, international passport, driver’s licence, or permanent voter’s card). For corporate policyholders: company name, registration number (CAC), registered address, and the identity of all directors and beneficial owners with 10%+ shareholding. Source of funds verification: For large single-premium transactions (typically above defined thresholds), the customer must provide evidence of the source of the funds used to pay the premium: payslips, bank statements, sale proceeds, or business income documentation. Politically Exposed Person (PEP) screening: All customers must be screened against PEP lists maintained by the insurer or a third-party screening provider. A PEP is a person who holds or has held a senior public position — including heads of state, government ministers, senior civil servants, military officers, senior judges, and senior political party officials. PEP transactions require enhanced due diligence and senior management approval. Sanctions screening: All customers must be screened against the UN Consolidated Sanctions List, OFAC (US) Specially Designated Nationals List, and NAICOM’s local sanctions list, which includes names designated by the EFCC and the Office of the National Security Adviser. Beneficial ownership identification: For policies held by trusts, companies, or other legal entities, the insurer must identify the natural person(s) who are the ultimate beneficial owners of the entity. Policies held by entities whose beneficial ownership cannot be determined must not be accepted. 21.6.3 Enhanced Due Diligence Standard KYC procedures apply to the majority of insurance customers. Enhanced Due Diligence (EDD) is required for higher-risk customers: PEPs: Enhanced identity verification; source of wealth documentation (not merely source of funds for the specific transaction); senior management approval before policy acceptance; ongoing monitoring of PEP policy activity. High-premium transactions: Any single premium above a defined threshold (NAICOM specifies the threshold in AML guidelines) requires EDD, including detailed source of funds documentation and income corroboration. High-risk jurisdictions: Customers from FATF (Financial Action Task Force) grey-listed or black-listed countries require EDD and, in some cases, specific NAICOM notification. Unusual transaction patterns: A customer who purchases multiple policies simultaneously, pays single premiums in round numbers, or requests early surrender shortly after policy issuance requires EDD and, if suspicion is not resolved, a suspicious transaction report. 21.6.4 Suspicious Transaction Reporting Where an insurer or its employee has reason to suspect that a transaction involves the proceeds of crime or is connected to terrorist financing, the insurer’s Money Laundering Reporting Officer (MLRO) must be notified. The MLRO assesses the suspicion and, where not resolved, files a Suspicious Transaction Report (STR) with the Nigerian Financial Intelligence Unit (NFIU), which is the national FIU responsible for receiving and analysing STRs. The obligation to file an STR arises on reasonable suspicion — it does not require certainty that a crime is being committed. An employee who suspects but fails to report faces personal criminal liability under the MLPPA 2022. This means that every insurance practitioner who handles customer transactions — agents, brokers, claims officers, underwriters, and contact centre staff — must be trained to recognise AML red flags and know the internal escalation process. AML Red Flags in Insurance Transactions The following indicators should trigger escalation to the MLRO: Customer insists on paying a premium in cash or via an untraceable payment method. Premium amount is substantially inconsistent with the customer’s declared income or occupation. Policy is purchased and a surrender request is made within a short period, without a plausible explanation. Customer is unable or unwilling to provide standard KYC documentation. Customer is on a sanctions list or identified as a PEP without prior approval. Multiple policies are purchased simultaneously by different individuals with the same address or bank account. Premium is paid by a third party with no evident relationship to the policyholder or insurable interest in the risk. The policy’s stated purpose (e.g., ‘investment’) is inconsistent with the customer’s financial profile.

t: Chapter 21 · 21.7 Consumer Protection Framework under NIIRA 2025
x: The NIIRA 2025 consumer protection framework was addressed in Chapter 20 from a customer experience management perspective. This section addresses its market conduct and compliance dimensions — specifically, the obligations it creates for insurance practitioners and the regulatory enforcement architecture NAICOM uses to monitor and sanction compliance. 21.7.1 NAICOM’s Market Conduct Inspection Powers NIIRA 2025 gives NAICOM extensive inspection powers to monitor market conduct compliance. These include: On-site inspections: NAICOM inspectors may visit an insurer’s premises at any time (with or without notice for cause-based inspections) to review sales records, agent qualification certificates, complaint files, premium accounting records, claims files, and marketing materials. On-site inspection findings are the most powerful evidence in market conduct enforcement proceedings. Mystery shopping: NAICOM may conduct mystery shopping exercises — sending trained investigators posing as customers through the insurer’s sales process — to identify mis-selling, inadequate disclosure, pressure tactics, and qualification failures in real-time sales interactions. Thematic reviews: Industry-wide reviews of specific market conduct issues (e.g., compliance with benefit illustration standards; treatment of claims for specific product types) in which NAICOM requests data and documentation from all licensed insurers and compares compliance across the market. Complaint pattern analysis: NAICOM analyses the complaint data submitted by insurers in their regulatory returns to identify patterns suggesting systemic market conduct issues. A single high-frequency complaint type at a specific insurer triggers a targeted inspection. 21.7.2 The Market Conduct Sanctions Regime NIIRA 2025 establishes a tiered sanctions regime for market conduct violations, calibrated to the severity and systemic nature of the breach. The sanctions available to NAICOM include: Sanction Trigger Amount / Scope Private warning Minor, isolated breach; first occurrence; mitigating circumstances. Formal notice to the insurer’s Board; remediation plan required within 30 days; not publicly disclosed. Financial penalty (individual breach) Proven specific market conduct violation: mis-selling, product marketing without approval, claims delay, non-disclosure failure. Up to ₦5,000,000 per proven individual breach. Financial penalty (systemic breach) Pattern of market conduct violations affecting a significant number of policyholders or continuing over a sustained period. Up to ₦50,000,000 for systemic breaches; NAICOM may direct additional policyholder remediation. Regulatory order Continuing breach requiring immediate management action. Directions to cease specific marketing or distribution activities; directions to review and remediate claims files; directions to conduct specific training. Product suspension Specific product found to involve systematic mis-selling or to be materially non-compliant with NAICOM filing. Suspension of the insurer’s authority to write new business under the specific product until remediation is completed and approved by NAICOM. Public disclosure (naming) Significant breach where public awareness is in the consumer interest. Publication of the insurer’s name, the specific breach, and the sanction imposed on NAICOM’s website and in its quarterly market conduct report. Business restriction Serious or repeated market conduct failure. Restriction on writing new business in one or more product lines or distribution channels; may affect all life business. Licence revocation Systematic, serious, and unresolved market conduct failure; fraud; criminal conviction. Revocation of the insurer’s operating licence. The most extreme sanction; subjects in-force policies to run-off management by NAICOM or transfer to a solvent insurer.

t: Chapter 21 · 21.8 The NAICOM Complaints Redress Mechanism
x: The complaints redress mechanism was described structurally in Chapter 20 from a customer experience perspective. This section addresses the compliance obligations it creates for insurers and the market conduct consequences of inadequate complaints management. From a market conduct compliance perspective, the complaints function is not merely a customer service operation — it is an early warning system for conduct failures. An insurer that receives 150 complaints about the same agent’s mis-selling conduct in a month and does not act on that pattern is accumulating the evidence for NAICOM’s most serious enforcement action. The compliance obligation is not just to handle individual complaints within SLA timelines; it is to analyse complaint data for systemic indicators and remediate the underlying conduct failures that are generating them. Compliance Obligation Requirement Documentation Required Complaints policy Written, Board-approved complaints handling policy, accessible to all policyholders, describing the complaints process and the customer’s escalation rights. Published in policy documents; posted on insurer’s website; available at all branches. Complaints officer A designated senior officer responsible for overseeing the complaints function and ensuring compliance with SLA standards. Complaints officer’s name and contact details in all policy documentation. Acknowledgement Written acknowledgement to the complainant within the prescribed timeframe (24 hours internal; NAICOM specifies the maximum). Dated acknowledgement letter or email on file. Investigation and resolution Substantive investigation with a written outcome communicated within the SLA period. Outcome must include reasons for the decision and details of escalation rights. Investigation file; decision letter with reasons; escalation options clearly stated. Regulatory reporting Monthly or quarterly complaint statistics submitted to NAICOM in the prescribed format as part of the insurer’s regulatory returns. NAICOM complaint return; complaint register. Pattern analysis Monthly analysis of complaint data by category, agent, product line, and channel to identify systemic conduct issues requiring management action. Complaint analysis report to CX Director and COO; Board summary quarterly.

t: Chapter 21 · 21.9 Data Protection: NDPA 2023 in the Insurance Context
x: 21.9.1 Overview of the NDPA 2023 The Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023 (NDPA 2023), signed by President Bola Tinubu on 12 June 2023, is Nigeria’s first comprehensive statutory data protection law. It establishes the legal framework for the collection, processing, storage, and transfer of personal data in Nigeria, aligned with international standards including the EU’s General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). The National Data Protection Commission (NDPC) is the regulatory body responsible for enforcing the NDPA 2023. Life insurers are expressly categorised as ‘Data Controllers of Major Importance’ under the NDPA 2023 — a designation that triggers enhanced compliance obligations, including mandatory registration with the NDPC, the appointment of a Data Protection Officer (DPO), and the mandatory conduct of Data Protection Impact Assessments (DPIAs) for high-risk processing activities. The General Application and Implementation Directive (GAID) issued by the NDPC in September 2025 provides the operational guidance for implementing the NDPA 2023’s requirements. 21.9.2 Lawful Bases for Processing Customer Data Insurance companies process significant volumes of personal data in the course of their business: names, addresses, NINs, health information, financial details, and beneficiary information. Each processing activity must have a lawful basis under the NDPA 2023. The most relevant lawful bases for insurance processing are: Contract performance: Processing is necessary for the performance of the insurance contract with the data subject — the most fundamental basis, covering the collection of proposer information for underwriting, premium processing, and claims assessment. Legal obligation: Processing required to comply with a legal obligation — covers AML/KYC data collection (MLPPA 2022 obligation), NAICOM reporting, and data retention under regulatory requirements. Legitimate interests: Processing necessary for the insurer’s legitimate interests, provided these are not overridden by the data subject’s rights and interests. Covers fraud detection analytics, portfolio experience analysis, and market conduct monitoring. Consent: Where no other lawful basis is available, processing requires the data subject’s informed, specific, and freely given consent. Consent is the required basis for: direct marketing communications; sharing data with third-party marketers; processing sensitive personal data (health information) in circumstances beyond what is strictly necessary for the insurance contract. 21.9.3 Sensitive Personal Data in Insurance Health data is classified as ‘sensitive personal data’ under the NDPA 2023 and attracts the highest level of protection. For life insurance underwriting — which necessarily involves the collection and processing of health information (medical examination results, APS reports, HIV status, disability information) — the NDPA 2023 creates specific obligations: Explicit consent for health data: The insurer must obtain explicit, informed consent from the proposer before collecting or processing any health data. The standard proposal form consent clause must be updated to meet the NDPA 2023’s explicit consent standard — a general ‘I agree to the terms’ signature is not sufficient. Data minimisation: The insurer may only collect the health data that is strictly necessary for the underwriting decision. Collecting health information ‘for future reference’ or for marketing purposes beyond underwriting is a data protection breach. Access restriction: Health data must be accessible only to personnel with a genuine need for it (underwriters, medical officers, the statutory actuary’s function). Marketing staff, distribution managers, and other functions must not have access to individual health records. HIV data protection: HIV status is specifically protected under both the NDPA 2023 and NIIRA 2025’s HIV non-discrimination provisions. HIV status data must be protected with the highest available security controls and must not be disclosed to any person other than those directly involved in the underwriting assessment. 21.9.4 Data Subject Rights The NDPA 2023 grants data subjects (insurance customers) the following rights, all of which the insurer must be able to fulfil within the prescribed timeframes: Right of access The data subject may request a copy of all personal data the insurer holds about them. The insurer must respond within 72 hours (NDPC interpretation). Right to rectification The data subject may request correction of inaccurate data. Relevant for policy records, beneficiary details, and address information. Right to erasure (‘right to be forgotten’) The data subject may request deletion of their personal data where the processing is no longer necessary. Limited in insurance by legal retention obligations (NAICOM requires retention of policy records for a minimum period after the policy terminates). Right to data portability The data subject may request their data in a portable format for transfer to another controller (e.g., a new insurer). Relevant for policy information and medical records. Right to object The data subject may object to processing based on legitimate interests, including direct marketing. An opt-out from marketing communications must be honoured immediately. Right to withdraw consent Where processing is based on consent, the data subject may withdraw consent at any time. Withdrawal does not affect the lawfulness of prior processing. 21.9.5 Data Breach Notification A personal data breach is a security incident that results in the accidental or unlawful destruction, loss, alteration, unauthorised disclosure of, or access to, personal data. Insurance companies, as Data Controllers of Major Importance, are subject to mandatory breach notification obligations under the NDPA 2023: NDPC notification: Notify the NDPC of the breach within 72 hours of becoming aware of it, using the NDPC’s prescribed breach notification form. Notification is required unless the breach is unlikely to result in any risk to the rights and freedoms of the affected data subjects. Affected individual notification: Where the breach is likely to result in a high risk to the rights and freedoms of affected data subjects, the insurer must also notify those individuals directly, without undue delay, describing the nature of the breach and the steps taken to mitigate its impact. Internal investigation: All breaches must be investigated internally and documented in a breach register, whether or not they meet the threshold for NDPC notification. The breach register is subject to NDPC inspection.

t: Chapter 21 · 21.10 Premium Collection and the ‘No Premium, No Cover’ Rule
x: 21.10.1 The No Premium, No Cover Principle No Premium, No Cover The fundamental insurance contract principle that an insurer’s obligation to pay a benefit does not arise unless the policyholder has paid the agreed premium. A policy for which no premium has been received is not in force and creates no enforceable coverage obligation. Coverage commences from the date the first premium is received and the policy is formally accepted by the insurer. This principle has several important practical implications for insurance practitioners: An agent cannot bind the insurer to coverage by issuing a receipt without having actually received and remitted the premium. A proposal form, even if completed and submitted, does not create coverage. The risk begins only when the insurer issues a policy schedule or a cover note and the premium is paid. A premium that is collected by the agent but not remitted to the insurer does not create valid coverage: the insurer has not received the premium and the policy has not been formally issued. A renewed policy for which the renewal premium is not paid before the renewal date lapses and provides no coverage from the lapse date, subject to the grace period provisions. 21.10.2 Temporary Cover An exception to the strict no premium, no cover rule is the grant of temporary cover (also called a cover note). A temporary cover note extends coverage to the risk being insured for a defined short period (typically 30–60 days) while the formal underwriting and policy issuance process is completed. Temporary cover may be issued where: the insurer has received the completed proposal form; there is a genuine risk of loss in the period before the policy can be formally issued; and the proposer has paid the first premium or entered into a binding payment commitment. In Nigerian life insurance, temporary cover is less common than in general insurance (where the risk of loss is more immediate and unpredictable). Group life temporary cover notes are sometimes issued for new employer schemes that have been accepted in principle by the insurer while the full member census is being compiled and the master policy is being prepared. The cover note must be specific about: the covered risks; the sum assured; the effective date; and the expiry date on which full formal coverage commences. 21.10.3 Premium Receipts and Proof of Payment A premium receipt is the documentary evidence that a specific premium payment has been made and received by the insurer (or its authorised collecting agent). The receipt is important for: Establishing the in-force date of the coverage (premiums are due in advance; the coverage period runs from the date the premium is due, not from the date the insurer physically receives the funds, where there is an authorised debit mandate in place). Resolving disputes about the policy’s in-force status at the date of a claim. Providing the policyholder with evidence for tax deduction purposes (where life insurance premiums are deductible under Nigerian income tax law for qualifying products). The insurer must issue a premium receipt for every premium payment received. An agent who collects a premium (prohibited by s.38(2)) and issues an informal handwritten receipt that does not match the insurer’s formal receipt system is creating a dangerous gap in the evidence chain: if the premium is not remitted to the insurer, the policyholder holds a receipt but has no valid coverage. This is the mechanism by which the phantom policy fraud discussed in Section 21.4 operates.

t: Chapter 21 · 21.11 Professional Indemnity Insurance for Intermediaries
x: 21.11.1 What is Professional Indemnity Insurance? Professional Indemnity Insurance (PII) is insurance that protects a professional practitioner (a broker, an IFA, an employee benefit consultant, or other insurance professional) against claims by clients alleging that the practitioner’s negligence, error, or omission in the performance of their professional services caused the client a financial loss. For insurance intermediaries, PII is essential because the financial losses that can arise from a professional error are potentially very large: a broker who fails to place adequate group life coverage for a large employer, and an employee dies without adequate coverage as a result, faces a claim equivalent to the full benefit the deceased’s family would have received under a correctly structured policy. Without PII, such a claim could be catastrophic for the broker’s business. 21.11.2 PII Requirements for Different Intermediary Categories Intermediary Category NAICOM/NCRIB PII Requirement Minimum Indemnity Limit Key Coverage Areas Licensed insurance broker (all categories) Mandatory; evidence required at annual licence renewal with NAICOM and NCRIB. Set by NAICOM; typically ₦50m–₦200m depending on portfolio size. Negligent advice; failure to place as instructed; failure to disclose policy terms; claims advocacy failures. Reinsurance broker Mandatory; higher minimum due to larger premium volumes. Set by NAICOM; typically ₦200m+. Treaty design errors; premium accounting errors; failure to notify reinsurer of claims within treaty terms. Independent Financial Adviser (IFA/independent agent) Recommended (CIIN guidelines); not always mandatory for individual agents. Minimum ₦20m recommended. Unsuitable advice; product misrepresentation; failure to disclose material terms. Employee Benefit Consultant (EB) Recommended where providing advice on pension, health, and life benefit design. Minimum ₦50m; higher for large corporate portfolios. EB programme design errors; pension cross-selling advice; tax planning advice on benefits. 21.11.3 PII Policy Design for Insurance Intermediaries Key design considerations when placing PII for an insurance intermediary: Claims-made vs occurrence basis: Most PII policies are written on a ‘claims-made’ basis: the policy responds to claims made during the policy period, regardless of when the alleged negligence occurred. An ‘occurrence’ basis policy responds to errors that occurred during the policy period, regardless of when the claim is made. For insurance intermediaries, claims-made coverage with an adequate retroactive date (extending back to the firm’s inception) is the appropriate form. Retroactive date: A claims-made PII policy should have a retroactive date as early as possible — ideally from the inception of the firm. A retroactive date of only one or two years exposes the firm to uncovered claims for professional errors committed before the retroactive date, even if the claim is made during the current policy period. Run-off coverage: Where the firm ceases operations or a partner retires, run-off PII coverage is required to protect against claims that arise after the firm has closed, relating to advice given during its operating life. PII does not automatically continue after a firm ceases operations; run-off coverage must be specifically arranged. Regulatory defence costs: PII should cover the cost of defending regulatory investigations by NAICOM or NCRIB, not just the cost of compensating clients. Regulatory investigation costs can be substantial even where no client claim is ultimately proven.

t: Chapter 21 · 21.12 Advisory: Building a Market Conduct Compliance Culture
x: Regulatory compliance and ethical conduct are not the same thing. An insurer can meet the minimum technical requirements of every NAICOM regulation while conducting its business in ways that systematically harm customers, distort competition, and erode public trust. A genuine market conduct culture goes beyond compliance checklists to the internalization by every employee and intermediary of the values that the CIIN Code and TCF framework describe. Advisory: Five Practices That Build a Genuine Market Conduct Culture PRACTICE 1: TONE FROM THE TOP — BUT MEASURED AT THE BOTTOM. The Board and CEO must visibly and consistently communicate that ethical conduct is a non-negotiable organisational value — not a compliance function. But tone from the top is empty without measurement at the bottom: the insurer must measure how agents, contact centre staff, and claims officers actually behave with customers, through mystery shopping, call recording review, complaint analysis, and field observation. The gap between the CEO’s speech and the agent’s sales pitch is the market conduct risk. PRACTICE 2: CONSEQUENCE MANAGEMENT. Conduct violations must have genuine consequences. An insurer that dismisses an agent for a qualification breach but retains a top-producing agent who mis-sells has communicated that production outweighs conduct. The opposite message — that mis-selling terminates the relationship regardless of production volume — changes agent behaviour faster than any training programme. PRACTICE 3: CONDUCT METRICS IN EVERY PERFORMANCE REVIEW. Every agent’s performance review must include conduct metrics alongside production metrics: persistency rate (low persistency is a leading indicator of mis-selling); complaint rate attributable to the agent; NIGO (not-in-good-order) application rate; and qualification status. An agent whose production is excellent but whose persistency is 45% and whose complaint rate is 3x the branch average is a conduct risk, not a high performer. PRACTICE 4: MAKE DOING THE RIGHT THING EASIER THAN DOING THE WRONG THING. Many mis-selling incidents occur not because agents are deliberately dishonest, but because the correct process (conducting a full suitability assessment, completing a detailed fact-find, explaining all product exclusions) is more time-consuming than the shortcut (presenting the benefit and asking for a signature). Investing in tools that streamline compliance — a digital fact-find that auto-populates from the proposal form, an exclusion disclosure tool that requires the customer to confirm each exclusion before the form is submitted — removes the friction from compliant behaviour. PRACTICE 5: TREAT COMPLAINTS AS INTELLIGENCE, NOT EMBARRASSMENTS. Every complaint is data. An insurer whose complaints function exists primarily to close complaints within SLA timelines, rather than to understand what the complaints reveal about systemic conduct failures, is wasting the most valuable conduct monitoring tool available. Monthly complaint root-cause analysis, reported to the Board, with management actions tracked to completion, is the single most powerful market conduct intelligence function an insurer can build.

CIIN Code of Ethics The professional standards document published by the Chartered Insurance Institute of Nigeria that establishes the ethical obligations of all CIIN members, covering integrity, competence, duty to the client, fair dealing, regulatory compliance, and confidentiality. Treating Customers Fairly (TCF) An outcomes-based regulatory standard requiring that insurance companies and intermediaries ensure customers receive fair outcomes across six dimensions: culture, product design, information, advice, product performance, and absence of post-sale barriers. Mis-Selling The sale of an insurance product to a customer through dishonest, misleading, or unsuitable conduct, including misrepresentation of product terms, omission of material exclusions, unsuitable product recommendation, or use of pressure tactics. Suitability Assessment A documented assessment of a customer’s needs, financial circumstances, and risk tolerance conducted before recommending an insurance product, to establish that the recommended product is genuinely suitable for the customer. Duty of Care The legal obligation to exercise the standard of care that a reasonably competent professional in the relevant role would exercise, such that the customer does not suffer harm from the practitioner’s negligence. Know Your Customer (KYC) The process of identifying, verifying, and understanding the insurance customer and the source of the funds used to pay premiums, as required by the Money Laundering (Prevention and Prohibition) Act 2022 and NAICOM AML/CFT guidelines. Anti-Money Laundering (AML) The regulatory framework and operational practices designed to prevent insurance products from being used to launder proceeds of crime or finance terrorism. Politically Exposed Person (PEP) A person who holds or has held a prominent public function, including government ministers, senior civil servants, and senior military officers. PEP transactions require enhanced due diligence. Money Laundering Reporting Officer (MLRO) The designated senior officer responsible for receiving internal suspicious transaction reports, assessing them, and filing Suspicious Transaction Reports (STRs) with the Nigerian Financial Intelligence Unit (NFIU). Suspicious Transaction Report (STR) A formal report filed by the MLRO with the NFIU where the insurer has reason to suspect that a transaction involves the proceeds of crime or is connected to terrorist financing. Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023 (NDPA 2023) Nigeria’s comprehensive statutory data protection law, establishing the legal framework for the collection, processing, and protection of personal data, administered by the National Data Protection Commission (NDPC). Data Controller of Major Importance A category of data controller under the NDPA 2023, including life insurance companies, that is subject to enhanced compliance obligations: mandatory NDPC registration, Data Protection Officer appointment, and Data Protection Impact Assessments. Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA) A structured assessment of the data protection risks associated with a high-risk data processing activity, required under the NDPA 2023 for activities involving sensitive personal data or large-scale processing. No Premium, No Cover The fundamental insurance principle that coverage does not exist until the premium has been paid and the policy has been formally issued by the insurer. Temporary Cover / Cover Note A short-term insurance coverage document issued while the formal underwriting and policy issuance process is completed, confirming that the risk is covered for a defined period. Professional Indemnity Insurance (PII) Insurance covering an insurance intermediary against claims by clients alleging that the intermediary’s professional negligence, error, or omission caused the client a financial loss. Claims-Made Policy (PII) A PII policy that responds to claims made during the policy period, regardless of when the alleged negligence occurred, provided it was after the retroactive date. Enhanced Due Diligence (EDD) A more intensive level of KYC and AML assessment applied to higher-risk customers: PEPs, high-premium transactions, customers from high-risk jurisdictions, or unusual transaction patterns.

An insurance agent who recommends a higher-commission product when a lower-cost product would equally meet the customer's needs, without disclosing the commission interest, is most likely in violation of which CIIN Code of Ethics principle? Regulatory compliance. Confidentiality. Duty to the client and fair dealing. Professional development. (C) Duty to the client and fair dealing. Why (C) is Correct The CIIN Code of Ethics places the client's interest at the heart of the professional's obligation. Recommending a more expensive product for personal financial gain, without disclosing the commission incentive, violates the duty of fair dealing — the agent is using the client relationship to benefit themselves at the client's expense. This is precisely the conflict-of-interest conduct that NIIRA 2025's remuneration disclosure requirements are designed to prevent. Why the Others Are Wrong (A) Regulatory compliance is a CIIN Code principle but describes compliance with legal and regulatory requirements. The specific issue here is the undisclosed conflict of interest — a fair dealing failure rather than a pure regulatory breach.(B) Confidentiality governs the agent's obligation to protect client information — not relevant to product recommendation conflicts.(D) Professional development covers the agent's obligation to maintain their knowledge and skills — also not directly relevant to a commission conflict situation.

Under the NDPA 2023, life insurance companies are classified as 'Data Controllers of Major Importance.' Which is NOT one of the enhanced obligations this classification triggers? Mandatory registration with the NDPC. Appointment of a Data Protection Officer (DPO). Mandatory purchase of cyber insurance to cover data breaches. Conducting Data Protection Impact Assessments (DPIAs) for high-risk processing activities. (C) Mandatory purchase of cyber insurance to cover data breaches. Why (C) is Correct Answer to 'Which is NOT' The NDPA 2023 does not require Data Controllers of Major Importance to purchase cyber insurance. Data breach risk management is required through technical and organisational security measures — encryption, access controls, incident response planning — but the specific mechanism of managing residual risk (including whether to purchase cyber insurance) is left to the controller's discretion. Why the Others Are Genuine DCPMI Obligations (A) Mandatory NDPC registration is a DCPMI requirement under the NDPA 2023 and GAID 2025.(B) Appointment of a qualified DPO is explicitly required for DCPMIs — the DPO monitors compliance, advises on DPIAs, and is the contact point for the NDPC.(D) DPIAs are required before undertaking high-risk personal data processing activities — including health data processing (which life insurers do routinely in underwriting) and large-scale profiling.

The 'no premium, no cover' principle means: An insurer may refuse to pay a claim if the premium has not been received within 24 hours of the due date. An insurance contract is not in force and the insurer has no coverage obligation until the agreed premium has been paid. An insurance agent may not discuss product terms before the first premium is paid. The insurer may cancel any policy for which the premium is not paid by the due date, without a grace period. (B) An insurance contract is not in force and the insurer has no coverage obligation until the agreed premium has been paid. Why (B) is Correct NIIRA 2025 codifies the no-premium-no-cover principle as a statutory rule applicable to all insurance contracts at inception: the insurer's obligation to cover the risk does not arise until the premium is received. This prevents the historic practice of agents issuing cover notes or confirming coverage before premium collection, which exposed insurers to unfinanced claims liabilities. The principle applies to policy inception; after a policy is in force, the grace period stated in the policy conditions governs premium payment. Whenever a customer requests to pay a premium in cash, regardless of the amount. When the insurer has reason to suspect that a transaction involves the proceeds of crime or is connected to terrorist financing, based on reasonable suspicion, not certainty. Only by the insurer's managing director personally, not by a delegated MLRO. (C) When the insurer has reason to suspect that a transaction involves the proceeds of crime or is connected to terrorist financing, based on reasonable suspicion, not certainty. Why (C) is Correct The STR threshold under the MLPPA 2022 is reasonable suspicion — a standard deliberately set below certainty or proof. If financial institutions were required to have firm evidence of money laundering before filing an STR, almost no reports would ever be made (money launderers are sophisticated at concealing evidence). Reasonable suspicion means the reporting officer has identified facts or circumstances that, considered together, suggest a possible connection to criminal activity — even if the officer cannot prove it definitively. Critically evaluate whether an outcomes-based market conduct standard is more effective than a rules-based standard in protecting Nigerian insurance consumers, with reference to: the structural limitations of rules-based compliance in a market where the spirit of the rules is systematically circumvented while the letter is technically observed; the organisational and measurement challenges of implementing an outcomes-based standard in an insurer with diverse distribution channels and large agent forces; the role of NAICOM’s market conduct inspection and enforcement powers in making the TCF standard credible; and the evidence from other markets where TCF or equivalent outcome-based standards have been implemented.
