t: Chapter 22 · 22.1 Introduction: The Financial Inclusion Imperative
x: Micro-insurance is not a charitable endeavour. It is a commercial proposition — the application of insurance principles to the 200 million Nigerians who currently have no life insurance, structured to be viable at the premium levels, distribution costs, and claims management complexity that their incomes and circumstances allow. It is one of the most commercially significant opportunities in the Nigerian financial services sector, and one of the most technically demanding to execute well. The case for micro-insurance rests on three converging arguments. The first is commercial: the formal insurance market in Nigeria has been built for approximately 30–40 million urban, salaried, formally employed individuals. The other 170–180 million Nigerians are an untapped market of enormous scale. Even modest insurance penetration rates in these segments represent transformative premium income growth. The second is regulatory: NIIRA 2025 explicitly places financial inclusion as a core objective of the Nigerian insurance regulatory framework, and NAICOM has operational expectations for how licensed insurers contribute to inclusion. The third is developmental: financial shocks from uninsured death, disability, or illness are among the most powerful drivers of household poverty in Nigeria. Life micro-insurance is, when well-designed and faithfully delivered, a genuine financial resilience tool for the families who need it most. This chapter addresses the micro-insurance landscape comprehensively: the regulatory framework, the product design discipline, the delivery mechanics, the community integration models, the NIIRA 2025 provisions, and the financial literacy infrastructure required to turn market potential into market reality. The chapter concludes with market practice illustrations from Nigerian insurers who have been building in this space, and an advisory section on the financial literacy strategy that makes micro-insurance commercially sustainable rather than merely philanthropically aspirational.

22.2.1 The NAICOM Definition and Premium Threshold Micro-Insurance (NAICOM Microinsurance Guidelines) Insurance that is: (a) designed for the low-income population, specifically persons earning income below a defined threshold (currently aligned with the NBS’s low-income bracket); (b) offered at a premium that is affordable relative to the target population’s income level; and (c) distributed through channels appropriate for the target population, including mobile money platforms, cooperatives, microfinance banks, and community-based organisations. Under NAICOM’s Microinsurance Guidelines, the premium threshold for a product to qualify as microinsurance is periodically reviewed to reflect changes in the income profile of the target population. The defining characteristics that distinguish micro-insurance from standard insurance in the Nigerian regulatory context are: Feature Standard Insurance Micro-Insurance Premium size No specific limit; typically ₦30,000–₦10m+ per annum. Low premium, accessible to low-income earners; typically below the NAICOM premium threshold (approximately ₦60,000 per annum for life products). Target population Formally employed, banked, literate individuals. Low-income earners: agricultural workers, informal traders, artisans, rural households, cooperative members. Product complexity Variable; may include complex savings, investment, and health benefit structures. Must be simple, standardised, and easily understood by low-literacy consumers. Distribution channel Agency, bancassurance, broker, direct corporate. Mobile money, USSD, MFBs, cooperatives, community-based organisations, NGOs, agritech platforms. Claim assessment Individual assessment with documentation requirements. Simplified; where possible, parametric (index-based triggers) to reduce documentation friction. Regulatory category Licensed under standard NAICOM insurance licence. Licensed under NAICOM Microinsurance Guidelines (separate licence category with lower minimum capital). Capital requirement Standard NIIRA 2025 minimum (life: ₦8bn+). Lower minimum capital as specified in NAICOM Microinsurance Guidelines. 22.2.2 Who is the Target Population? The target population for life micro-insurance in Nigeria is defined by income, occupation, and the nature of the financial shocks they face. EFInA’s Access to Financial Services Survey (the most comprehensive demand-side data on financial services access in Nigeria) and NBS household income surveys provide the most authoritative data on the size and characteristics of this population. Key data points from EFInA and NBS that define the micro-insurance market: Approximately 60–65% of Nigeria’s adult population is engaged in the informal economy — primarily as agricultural workers, market traders, transport operators, artisans, and domestic workers. This population has irregular income, limited financial literacy, no employer-provided insurance, and is largely absent from the reach of conventional insurance distribution. Approximately 36% of Nigerian adults are classified as financially excluded — they have no access to any formal financial product, including bank accounts, mobile money, savings groups, or insurance. Insurance penetration among the bottom 60% of the income distribution is estimated at below 0.5% — a near-zero rate in the most populous segment of the market. The most significant financial shocks reported by low-income Nigerian households are: death of the primary earner (cited by 45% of financially vulnerable households as the shock most likely to push them into poverty); medical costs from serious illness (42%); and crop failure or livestock loss in agricultural households (38%). These are precisely the risks that life and health micro-insurance is designed to address. Mobile phone penetration is high: over 80% of Nigerian adults own a mobile phone, including feature phones. This creates the digital infrastructure for USSD-based micro-insurance distribution that can reach populations currently outside the reach of any formal financial service.

t: Chapter 22 · 22.3 NAICOM Microinsurance Guidelines and Operational Requirements
x: 22.3.1 The Guidelines Framework NAICOM’s Microinsurance Guidelines establish a dedicated regulatory framework for the licensing, operation, supervision, and market conduct of micro-insurance providers in Nigeria. The Guidelines reflect NAICOM’s recognition that the standard insurance regulatory framework — designed for large, sophisticated financial institutions with complex products and large minimum capital requirements — creates barriers to entry that prevent the development of an inclusive insurance market. The Microinsurance Guidelines address: the licensing categories available to microinsurance providers; the minimum capital requirements (lower than standard insurance to encourage entry); the simplified product approval requirements; the permitted distribution channels; the consumer protection requirements specific to the low-income market; and the reporting and supervisory framework. 22.3.2 Licensing Categories under the Guidelines Licence Category Description Minimum Capital Permitted Activities Unit Microinsurer A standalone microinsurance company specifically licensed to write only microinsurance products for low-income populations. May not write standard insurance above the premium threshold. Lower than standard insurer minimum (set in Guidelines, periodically reviewed by NAICOM). Life microinsurance; accident and health microinsurance; property microinsurance for low-income market. Must operate within the NAICOM premium threshold. Composite Microinsurer A company licensed to write both standard insurance and microinsurance products. The microinsurance book is maintained as a separately identified fund within the composite operation. Standard composite insurer minimum capital. Full insurance range (life and non-life) plus dedicated microinsurance products. Microinsurance Agent (individual) An individual agent specifically licensed for microinsurance distribution, operating under a licensed insurer’s microinsurance programme. Not applicable (individual agent). Distributing microinsurance products on behalf of a licensed insurer. May not underwrite, hold premiums, or make claims decisions. Corporate Microinsurance Agent An entity — MFB, cooperative, MMO, NGO, agritech platform — licensed as a corporate agent for microinsurance distribution. As specified in Guidelines for corporate agents. Distributing, collecting premiums for, and (in some cases) handling claims notification for microinsurance products. 22.3.3 Simplified Product Approval Requirements One of the most commercially significant features of the Microinsurance Guidelines is the simplified product approval process. Standard insurance products require a full actuarial pricing report, detailed policy wording, and benefit illustration templates in the NAICOM prescribed format — a process that can take 4–6 months and requires significant actuarial resources. Under the Microinsurance Guidelines, microinsurance product filings are subject to a streamlined review: the benefit structure must be simple and standardised; the premium must be within the threshold; the policy wording must be approved in plain language (or in a local language where the product targets a non-English-speaking community); and the distribution channel must be listed as an approved channel in the Guidelines. Products meeting these criteria benefit from a faster NAICOM review timeline, enabling insurers to bring new microinsurance products to market more rapidly. 22.3.4 Consumer Protection Requirements for Microinsurance NAICOM’s consumer protection requirements are heightened for microinsurance, in recognition that the target population is more vulnerable to exploitation than the standard insurance consumer. Specific consumer protection provisions in the Microinsurance Guidelines include: Plain language policy document: All policy documents and member certificates must be written in language that is accessible to a consumer with basic literacy. Technical insurance terms must be defined in simple language. Local language option: Where a microinsurance product is targeted at a community where a dominant language other than English is spoken, NAICOM encourages (and in some cases requires) the availability of key policy information in that language. Simplified claims process: The claims process must be designed for the target population’s circumstances: minimal documentation requirements; multiple notification channels (phone, USSD, community agent); and fast settlement timelines. Transparent premium deduction: Where premiums are deducted from a mobile money wallet or deducted by a cooperative from member dues, the deduction must be clearly notified to the insured member before it is made, with information on the insurance product the premium is paying for. Claims payment to mobile wallet: NAICOM permits and encourages the payment of microinsurance benefits directly to the beneficiary’s mobile money wallet, reducing the friction and cost of benefit payment in areas where bank accounts are uncommon.

t: Chapter 22 · 22.4 Product Design for Low-Income Markets
x: Product design is the most critical determinant of micro-insurance success or failure. A technically sound product that is inaccessible, incomprehensible, or unaffordable to its target population will never achieve scale — regardless of the distribution channel or the marketing investment behind it. Product design for low-income markets requires the application of four non-negotiable principles, each of which constrains and disciplines the design process in ways that are unfamiliar to actuaries and product teams trained in designing complex savings and investment products. 22.4.1 Principle 1: Simplicity A microinsurance product must be simple enough for a person with basic literacy to understand its core terms from a single conversation or a single reading of the product summary. The test of simplicity is not whether the product team understands it — it is whether the target customer understands it without professional assistance. Simplicity requirements in product design: a single sum assured (not a tiered benefit schedule); a single premium (not a complex schedule varying by age, health, and occupation); a small number of covered events (death only; or death and permanent disability); and a small number of exclusions (typically: suicide within the first 12 months; death from pre-existing conditions within the moratorium period). Every additional benefit trigger, exclusion, and coverage condition adds complexity that reduces comprehension, increases the risk of claims disputes, and undermines the target customer’s confidence in the product. 22.4.2 Principle 2: Affordability Affordability means that the premium is within the regular expenditure capacity of the target customer without creating financial hardship. For a market trader earning ₦40,000–80,000 per week, a weekly premium of ₦500–1,000 represents 1–2.5% of weekly income — the international development finance benchmarks suggest that premiums above 3–5% of income become barriers to purchase and early drivers of lapse. Affordability is achieved through: Premium frequency flexibility: Daily, weekly, or market-day premium payment options that align with the target customer’s income receipt rhythm. A market trader who earns daily cannot comfortably commit to an annual or even monthly premium; a weekly or daily micro-premium is feasible. Low entry sum assured: A death benefit of ₦100,000–₦500,000 at a weekly premium of ₦500–1,500 is meaningful to a low-income family without being unaffordable. The premium is calibrated to the target income level, not to a standard actuarial sum assured. No or minimal initial costs: No medical examination; no application fee; no policy setup charge. The first premium collected creates coverage immediately. 22.4.3 Principle 3: Accessibility Accessibility means that the product can be purchased, premiums can be paid, and claims can be submitted through channels that the target customer already uses in their daily life — without requiring them to travel to an insurance office, open a bank account, or interact with an agent they distrust. Accessibility is achieved by: embedding the insurance transaction in the platforms the target customer already uses (mobile money wallet, cooperative weekly meeting, MFB loan transaction, agritech app); designing the enrolment process for a mobile phone with no internet access (USSD); and locating any field presence in the customer’s community rather than in a distant town centre. 22.4.4 Principle 4: Value Visibility Value visibility means that the customer understands what they get when a claim occurs — not in actuarial terms, but in the concrete, tangible terms of their own life. ‘Your family receives ₦300,000 if you die’ is visible value. ‘Your family receives a sum equivalent to 18 months’ of your average weekly income’ is even more visible. Value visibility is undermined by: complex benefit schedules that the customer cannot remember; exclusions that eliminate coverage for the most likely claim scenarios; and claims processes that are so burdensome that the benefit is difficult to access even when it is technically payable. An insurer that pays a ₦300,000 death benefit is demonstrating visible value; an insurer that pays ₦300,000 to 95% of claimants but has a 5% claims dispute rate that generates social media outrage is destroying value visibility for the entire portfolio. 22.4.5 Illustrative Product Design: A Nigerian Life Micro-Insurance Product Product Design Illustration: ‘Market Trader Life Cover’ The following illustrates a life micro-insurance product designed for the informal market trader segment in Lagos and Southwest Nigeria, applying the four design principles: Feature Design Decision Rationale Product name Market Trader Life Cover Segment-specific branding; immediately communicates relevance to the target customer. Coverage Death benefit ₦250,000 on death of the insured from any cause after the moratorium period. Single benefit; easy to understand; no ambiguity about what is covered. Moratorium 12-month moratorium for death from pre-existing illness (accidental death covered from day 1). Manages anti-selection risk in a no-medical market; consistent with NAICOM Guidelines. Premium ₦500 per week (deducted from mobile wallet weekly). Affordable on a market trader’s income; weekly frequency aligns with trading income cycle. Enrolment channel USSD (*code#); or enrolment through cooperative/Ajo leader using a simple paper form. Accessible on any mobile phone; no internet required; cooperative channel leverages trusted relationships. Premium collection Mobile money wallet deduction (auto-deduct); or cooperative dues inclusion. Removes premium collection friction; aligns with existing financial behaviour. Claims notification SMS to designated number; or through cooperative leader. Accessible; no requirement to visit a branch or download an app. Claims payment Direct to beneficiary’s mobile money wallet within 5 business days of complete notification. Fast; no bank account required; reduces beneficiary hardship during bereavement. Policy document Single A5 page in Yoruba, Igbo, or Hausa depending on target community; plus English version. Accessible to low-literacy customers; NAICOM plain-language requirement met.

22.5.1 The Conventional Loss Assessment Problem Conventional insurance pays claims based on the actual loss suffered by the individual insured, assessed by the insurer after the loss occurs. For life insurance, this means verifying the death of the insured and confirming coverage. For agricultural insurance or health insurance in low-income settings, conventional loss assessment faces a structural problem: the cost of assessing individual losses in remote or informal market contexts is often higher than the premium collected, making conventional coverage economically unviable at the premium levels required to reach the target population. Index-based and parametric insurance solves this problem by decoupling the claims trigger from the individual’s actual loss, replacing it with a measurable external index or parameter that correlates strongly with the loss in the target population. When the index value crosses a predefined threshold, a benefit payment is made automatically — without individual loss assessment, without documentation requirements, and without claims officer visits. 22.5.2 How Index-Based Insurance Works Parametric / Index-Based Insurance An insurance product in which the benefit payment is triggered by the occurrence of a defined external event or the value of a defined index crossing a predetermined threshold, rather than by an assessment of the individual insured’s actual loss. The insured receives the predetermined benefit payment automatically when the trigger condition is met, without submitting a loss evidence claim. Parametric Insurance Trigger Structure Trigger parameter — a measurable, objective, and publicly verifiable data point (rainfall level at a defined weather station; river flood level; temperature; commodity price index; mortality index). Attachment point — the index value at which the insurance begins to pay. Below the attachment point, no payment is made. Benefit scale — the payment amount for defined index values between the attachment point and the maximum payout. May be linear (payment increases proportionally with index severity) or binary (full payment triggered above the attachment point). Basis risk — the risk that the index does not perfectly reflect the individual insured’s actual loss. A farmer whose crop failed due to local flooding may not be paid if the official rainfall gauge did not record below-threshold precipitation. Basis risk is the primary limitation of index-based insurance. Applications of parametric insurance in the Nigerian context include: Rainfall index insurance for smallholder farmers: A benefit payment is triggered when rainfall measured at the nearest NIMET (Nigerian Meteorological Agency) weather station falls below a threshold that indicates drought stress during the planting or growing season. Relevant for farmers in the Savannah belt and northern Nigeria. Flood index insurance: A benefit payment is triggered when the water level at a defined river gauge station exceeds a flood threshold. Relevant for households and small businesses in the Niger Delta, Benue Valley, and coastal Lagos. Temperature/heat index: A benefit payment triggered by extreme heat events, relevant for outdoor workers and construction workers exposed to heat-related health risks in northern Nigeria. Pandemic / excess mortality index: A benefit payment triggered when the reported mortality rate in a defined geographic area exceeds a predefined multiple of the historical baseline. This is a form of life parametric insurance that can respond to pandemic or mass casualty events.

t: Chapter 22 · 22.6 Community-Based Insurance and Ajo/Esusu Integration
x: 22.6.1 The Logic of Community-Based Insurance Community-based insurance organises the insurance function around existing social structures — villages, cooperatives, market associations, religious groups, and rotating savings circles — rather than around the individual policyholder. The community provides: the distribution reach (every member is a potential insured); the trust infrastructure (the community leader’s endorsement carries far more weight than an insurance advertisement); the premium collection mechanism (dues paid at regular community meetings); and the social pressure that produces persistency (members who stop paying face community sanctions that do not exist in individually billed products). Community-based insurance is not the same as group life insurance. Group life is a corporate product sold to employers; community-based insurance is a grassroots product built around existing informal social structures. The commercial challenge for the insurer is to formalize the community’s existing mutual support arrangement into a regulated insurance product without destroying the social dynamics that make the community model work. 22.6.2 The Ajo/Esusu Insurance Model The Ajo/Esusu model (introduced in Chapters 16 and 19 as a distribution and marketing mechanism) can be extended into a genuine insurance delivery vehicle. In its adapted form, the insurance-integrated Ajo/Esusu works as follows: The Ajo/Esusu model has several structural advantages: the premium is embedded in an existing payment behaviour, dramatically reducing non-payment risk; the group leader’s endorsement replaces the need for individual sales presentations; the community claims advocacy provides a check on the insurer’s claims handling quality; and the social fabric of the group creates reputational pressure on the insurer to pay claims promptly. The group leader who brought the insurance to the community will not maintain the partnership if a valid claim is disputed unfairly. 22.6.3 Governance and Regulatory Requirements For the Ajo/Esusu model to be regulatory compliant, the following arrangements must be in place: The group leader acting as a premium collection intermediary must either: hold a microinsurance agent licence from NAICOM; or operate under the oversight of a licensed corporate microinsurance agent (such as an MFB or licensed cooperative society that holds the corporate agency licence and is responsible for the group leader’s conduct). Premium collection must be documented: Individual member payment records must be maintained, and the group leader’s remittances to the insurer must be recorded and reconciled against the member register. Insurance must be distinguishable from savings: The insurance component of the member’s contribution must be clearly separated from the savings component in all records. A member who stops contributing to the Ajo/Esusu savings cycle should understand that their insurance coverage also ceases unless they continue to pay the insurance premium separately. Member consent and disclosure: Every member who is enrolled in the insurance component must have given their consent and received a simple explanation of what the insurance covers, what it does not cover, and how to make a claim.

t: Chapter 22 · 22.7 NIIRA 2025: Financial Inclusion and Miscellaneous Insurance Provisions
x: 22.7.1 Financial Inclusion as a Regulatory Objective NIIRA 2025 explicitly establishes financial inclusion as an objective of the Nigerian insurance regulatory framework. This is a significant policy statement: it means that NAICOM’s supervisory mandate is not limited to ensuring the solvency and market conduct of existing insurers but extends to actively promoting the development of an inclusive insurance market that serves all Nigerian citizens, not only the formal sector minority. In practice, NIIRA 2025’s financial inclusion provisions create both direct obligations and enabling frameworks: Low-income market development obligation: Licensed insurers are expected to develop and maintain at least one approved microinsurance product in their portfolio. While NIIRA 2025 does not impose a mandatory microinsurance premium income target, NAICOM’s supervision of the market takes account of an insurer’s contribution to financial inclusion in its overall assessment of the insurer’s performance. Mandatory insurance and financial inclusion: Several of the mandatory insurance requirements introduced by NIIRA 2025 — including credit life insurance for loans above ₦10 million and mandatory group life insurance for employers — have a financial inclusion dimension. Credit life insurance, in particular, extends coverage to informal sector borrowers who have no other insurance. The mandatory framework is thus not only a consumer protection mechanism; it is also an entry point for insurance in communities that would not otherwise access it. Regulatory sandbox: NIIRA 2025’s Insurtech provisions (the regulatory sandbox framework established by NAICOM’s Insurtech Guidelines) are explicitly designed to support inclusive insurance innovation. Insurtech entrants proposing novel microinsurance delivery models may apply for sandbox participation, allowing them to test their approach under regulatory oversight before committing to full licensing. 22.7.2 Miscellaneous Insurance Provisions NIIRA 2025’s provisions on miscellaneous insurance classes — insurance products that do not fit neatly into the standard life or non-life categories — are relevant to micro-insurance development because many innovative inclusive insurance products (hospital cash, agricultural index insurance, burial insurance) fall into the miscellaneous category. NAICOM has clarified that miscellaneous insurance products designed for the low-income market may be approved under the Microinsurance Guidelines rather than the standard miscellaneous insurance approval process, provided they meet the premium threshold and target population criteria. This flexibility enables insurers to develop hybrid products — life plus health, life plus crop — that better address the multiple risk exposures of low-income households without requiring multiple separate approvals.

t: Chapter 22 · 22.8 Mobile Phone and USSD-Based Microinsurance Delivery
x: 22.8.1 The Mobile Platform Architecture The mobile phone is the most scalable microinsurance delivery infrastructure available in Nigeria. With 180+ million active mobile subscribers, of whom a significant proportion are in low-income informal economy segments, mobile delivery can reach populations that no physically staffed distribution model can economically serve at micro-premium levels. The architecture of mobile microinsurance delivery has three layers: the enrolment layer (how the customer signs up for the product); the premium collection layer (how premiums are collected automatically and reliably); and the claims notification and payment layer (how the customer notifies the insurer of a claim and receives the benefit). 22.8.2 USSD Enrolment Design USSD (Unstructured Supplementary Service Data) is the technology backbone of mobile microinsurance delivery in Nigeria because it works on any mobile phone — smartphone or feature phone — without requiring mobile data. The USSD interface is sequential text menus; the user navigates by typing numbers and pressing the ‘send’ button. An effective USSD microinsurance enrolment flow must be designed for a low-literacy user who may be making their first insurance purchase. The following design principles govern best-practice USSD insurance flows: Maximum 5–7 steps from start to confirmed enrolment: Every additional screen represents a potential drop-off point. The enrolment flow must capture only the minimum information required for coverage: name (or NIN), beneficiary phone number, and premium frequency selection. Full KYC verification is completed asynchronously by the insurer after enrolment. Clear confirmation at the end: The final screen must clearly confirm coverage: ‘You are now covered for ₦250,000. Your family will receive this amount if you die. Your weekly premium of ₦500 will be deducted from your wallet every Monday. To check your cover, dial *code#.’ SMS confirmation in local language: An SMS confirmation in Yoruba, Hausa, or Igbo (depending on the subscriber’s SIM card region) reinforces the coverage confirmation and provides the beneficiary number on record. Transparent deduction notification: Every premium deduction must be preceded by an SMS notification confirming the amount to be deducted and the coverage it maintains. A customer who receives a deduction notification they do not understand will contact their mobile money provider to dispute the charge, generating refunds and coverage lapses. 22.8.3 Premium Collection via Mobile Wallet Auto-deduction from the mobile money wallet is the most effective premium collection mechanism for USSD-based micro-insurance. The deduction is set up at enrolment: the customer authorises the insurer (or the mobile money operator acting as the insurer’s collection agent) to deduct the agreed premium amount on the agreed schedule from their mobile wallet balance. Premium auto-deduction requires: the customer’s explicit authorisation at enrolment; a minimum wallet balance management protocol (if the wallet is empty on deduction day, the system should attempt re-deduction after 24 hours before lapsing the coverage, with an SMS notification); and a clear premium payment confirmation message each time a deduction is successfully processed. The premium auto-deduction model aligns with the usage patterns of Nigerian mobile money users: many use their mobile wallet for small daily transactions and maintain a modest balance. A weekly premium of ₦500 is a manageable auto-deduction for most active mobile money users. The insurer’s revenue from this model is predictable; the customer’s premium payment is effortless; and lapse rates are dramatically lower than in manually-collected premium models. 22.8.4 Claims Notification and Payment The claims notification and payment design for mobile microinsurance must be as simple as the enrolment process. Complex documentation requirements, branch visits, or lengthy assessment processes will result in unacceptably low claims rates — not because claims do not arise, but because beneficiaries cannot navigate the process. Best-practice mobile microinsurance claims process: Notification: Beneficiary (or any person on the insured’s behalf) dials the claims USSD code and follows a short notification menu: confirms insured’s phone number; confirms the date of death; optionally provides the cause of death. Acknowledgement: The insurer’s system sends an SMS acknowledgement within 30 minutes, confirming the claim reference number and the documentation requirements (which, for small death claims, may be limited to: death certificate or burial record; beneficiary identity). A dedicated claims phone line is also available. Assessment: For small claims (below a defined threshold, typically ₦500,000), the insurer may assess the claim based on the notification data and a brief telephonic interaction with the beneficiary, without requiring physical documentation. For larger claims, a simplified documentation process is required. Payment: Approved claims are paid directly to the beneficiary’s mobile money wallet within 48–72 hours of the claim being assessed as complete. The payment is accompanied by an SMS confirmation to the beneficiary.

t: Chapter 22 · 22.9 Micro-Insurance Market Practice in Nigeria
x: 22.9.1 Overview of the Nigerian Microinsurance Landscape Nigerian life insurers have been building microinsurance capabilities at varying pace and scale over the past decade. The most advanced players have developed dedicated microinsurance units, partnerships with mobile money operators and cooperative networks, and standalone USSD products with active premium deduction infrastructure. Others have participated in NAICOM pilot programmes, donor-funded inclusive insurance initiatives (with GIZ, the IFC, and the Access to Insurance Initiative), or have filed microinsurance products as part of their regulatory obligation without yet achieving meaningful scale. The following section illustrates approaches that have been developed within the Nigerian market, drawing on publicly available information about major Nigerian life insurers’ microinsurance activities. These are presented as illustrations of market direction rather than comprehensive evaluations of any specific company’s programme. 22.9.2 AIICO Insurance: Life Microinsurance Initiatives AIICO Insurance Plc, one of Nigeria’s largest life insurance companies, has been among the most active participants in the microinsurance space. AIICO’s approach has combined product innovation with distribution partnerships: the company has developed simplified life and health products accessible via mobile platforms and has partnered with cooperative societies and market associations to reach informal sector workers. AIICO’s microinsurance work has been supported by participation in industry-wide programmes facilitated by NAICOM and development finance organisations interested in scaling inclusive insurance in Nigeria. Key features of AIICO’s market approach include: a focus on simplicity in product design; the integration of premium collection with existing payment behaviours; and an investment in financial literacy education as a precursor to product offering rather than a complement to it. AIICO’s experience has reinforced the market consensus that technology alone is insufficient — community trust-building and financial education must precede digital enrolment for the strategy to achieve persistency beyond the first premium. 22.9.3 AXA Mansard Insurance: Digital-First Microinsurance AXA Mansard Insurance (now part of the Sanlam Group’s African portfolio) has pursued a digital-first approach to inclusive insurance. Leveraging the global AXA Group’s insurtech capabilities and its relationships with Nigerian fintech platforms, AXA Mansard has developed microinsurance products accessible via mobile apps and partnerships with digital financial service providers. AXA Mansard’s approach has emphasised the integration of microinsurance with other financial services that low-income consumers already use: savings platforms, digital payment tools, and employer payroll systems for informal sector aggregators. Its experience in the Nigerian market has demonstrated the importance of claims payment speed and transparency as the primary driver of product renewal and word-of-mouth acquisition — a finding consistent with the trust deficit analysis in Chapter 19. 22.9.4 Leadway Assurance: Group and Community Microinsurance Leadway Assurance Company Limited, one of Nigeria’s largest insurers by gross premium income, has approached microinsurance primarily through its group distribution capabilities, extending group life coverage to smaller employer groups and cooperative networks that fall below the threshold of conventional group life minimum sizes. Leadway’s community-facing microinsurance work has focused on cooperative and market association partnerships, particularly in the Southwest and North-Central regions where cooperative culture is strong. The company’s strategy has been to leverage its existing brand recognition and financial strength as a trust signal in communities where smaller, less-known microinsurance providers face higher consumer scepticism. 22.9.5 Lessons from Market Practice Across the Nigerian microinsurance market, several lessons emerge consistently from the experience of early movers: Claims payment is the product. In communities where insurance is new, the first claim paid in a community becomes the most powerful marketing event for all subsequent sales. Insurers that pay promptly and without friction generate organic referrals that no marketing budget can match. Insurers that dispute a claim in a community without a prior insurance culture may lose the entire community as a market. Community champions are more effective than advertising. A cooperative leader or market association chairperson who has personally witnessed a claim being paid and advocates for the product within their community converts more members than any social media campaign. Financial education must precede enrolment. Products that are sold without an educational foundation produce high early lapse rates, because members who do not understand what they have bought will stop paying when any financial pressure arises. Insurers that invest in financial literacy programmes before launching a product in a new community achieve 30–50% better first-year persistency than those that do not. Technology is an amplifier, not a substitute. USSD and mobile delivery scale reach enormously and reduce distribution cost per policy. But they amplify whatever is already working: if the product is well-designed and claims are paid promptly, digital scale is transformative. If the product is poorly designed and claims are disputed, digital scale amplifies the negative reputation. Unit economics must be sustainable from the start. Donor-subsidised microinsurance programmes that cannot survive without external support do not build a lasting market. The commercial model must be viable: the premium must cover expected claims, a sustainable administration cost, the distribution channel’s commission, and a reasonable profit margin — even at micro-premium levels.

t: Chapter 22 · 22.10 Financial Literacy as a Market Development Strategy
x: 22.10.1 The Financial Literacy Gap Financial literacy — the knowledge, skills, and attitudes required to make informed financial decisions — is the foundational prerequisite for sustainable micro-insurance adoption. A population that does not understand what insurance is, how it works, and why it is relevant to their financial lives will not purchase it regardless of how well the product is designed or how accessible the distribution channel. EFInA’s survey data consistently shows that the most common reason Nigerian adults give for not having insurance is not affordability — it is lack of awareness and understanding. When asked whether they would consider purchasing a simple life insurance product at a specific low-premium level, a significant proportion of previously uninsured respondents express interest — suggesting that the awareness and understanding gap, not the affordability gap, is the primary barrier for a large segment of the market. 22.10.2 Components of a Financial Literacy Strategy for Microinsurance A microinsurance financial literacy strategy is distinct from general financial education in two important ways: it is targeted at a specific population (the low-income, informal sector community the insurer seeks to reach); and it is designed to produce a specific outcome (a community that understands insurance well enough to make an informed purchase decision and to maintain their premium payments through normal financial pressures). The components of an effective microinsurance financial literacy programme are: Risk awareness education Building the target community’s awareness of the financial risks they face — the specific, quantified impact of the death of the primary earner on a typical low-income household in their community. Not abstract financial statistics, but real local examples: ‘When Baba Tunde died last year, his family lost their income and his children had to leave school. This is what life insurance is designed to prevent.’ Insurance concept education Explaining what insurance is and how it works: a pooling mechanism where many people pay small amounts so that the few who suffer large losses are protected. Many low-income Nigerians are familiar with the Ajo/Esusu model of pooling; framing insurance as a formalised version of this familiar concept is highly effective. Product-specific education Explaining the specific product the insurer is offering: what it covers, what it does not cover, what the premium is, how to pay it, and what to do if a claim arises. This education should be conducted in the language of the target community, using simple language and real-world examples, before the product is sold. Claims experience sharing Sharing real stories from within the community (or similar communities) of policyholders who have benefited from insurance. Nothing is more persuasive than a community member saying: ‘When my husband died, the insurance company paid us ₦250,000. I was able to keep the children in school.’ Ongoing engagement Maintaining contact with enrolled members through their community channels (WhatsApp groups, cooperative meetings, church bulletins) to reinforce their understanding of their coverage, remind them of upcoming premium payments, and share positive claims news. 22.10.3 Financial Literacy Delivery Channels The delivery of financial literacy for microinsurance must use channels that reach the target population where they are, in formats they can engage with. For the low-income, partially literate community members who constitute the primary microinsurance target, the most effective channels are: Community meetings: Direct, face-to-face sessions at cooperative meetings, market association gatherings, or village square events. The community leader’s involvement and facilitation is essential for credibility and attendance. Local language radio: Radio remains the most pervasive mass communication medium in rural and semi-urban Nigeria. A weekly 15-minute radio segment on insurance, sponsored by the insurer and presented in the local language, builds sustained awareness at very low cost per listener. WhatsApp voice notes and short videos: In communities with higher smartphone and WhatsApp penetration, short voice notes (2–3 minutes) or videos (60–90 seconds) shared through community WhatsApp groups are highly engaging. Audio and video formats overcome literacy barriers. Churches and mosques: As described in Chapter 19, religious community leaders who incorporate financial stewardship messages (including insurance) into their regular communications reach their entire congregation in a context of exceptional trust and attention.

t: Chapter 22 · 22.11 Advisory: Building a Sustainable Microinsurance Business
x: The microinsurance opportunity in Nigeria is real, large, and growing. But building a microinsurance business that is commercially sustainable requires a fundamentally different management mindset from the one that has built Nigeria’s formal insurance market. Scale replaces margin as the unit of commercial logic; community trust replaces brand advertising as the primary acquisition driver; and service quality at the claims moment replaces distribution incentives as the primary retention tool. Advisory: The Five Questions Every Microinsurance Business Plan Must Answer QUESTION 1: WHAT IS THE UNIT ECONOMICS? At what premium level, what claims rate, and what distribution cost does this product generate a positive contribution margin without subsidy? This is not the most important question, but it must be answered honestly before anything else. A microinsurance product that cannot be priced at a level that works for both the insurer and the customer is not a viable product — it is a grant programme dressed as insurance. QUESTION 2: WHO WILL DISTRIBUTE IT, AND WHY WILL THEY? Distribution is the hardest problem in microinsurance. The communities with the most unmet insurance need are the hardest and most expensive to reach. The distribution channel must have: an existing relationship with the target community (a cooperative, an MFB, a community leader, a telco); an economic incentive to distribute (commission or fee that is viable at the micro-premium level without consuming all of the insurer’s margin); and the capability to handle basic insurance transactions (enrolment, premium collection, claims notification). QUESTION 3: HOW WILL WE ACHIEVE FINANCIAL LITERACY AT SCALE? Financial literacy is the precondition for persistent adoption. The plan must specify: who will conduct the education; when (before the product launch, not after); in what language; through what channels; and what the target outcome is (not just ‘awareness’, but the specific knowledge and attitude change that predicts purchase and retention). QUESTION 4: HOW WILL WE PAY CLAIMS FAST ENOUGH TO KEEP THE COMMUNITY’S TRUST? The first claim in a new community is the moment that determines whether the microinsurance programme will grow or collapse. The claims settlement infrastructure — mobile wallet payment, simplified documentation, 48-hour target settlement — must be fully operational before the first policy is sold. It cannot be built when the first claim arrives. QUESTION 5: WHAT DOES SUCCESS LOOK LIKE AT 3 YEARS? A microinsurance programme that covers 10,000 people is a pilot. A programme that covers 500,000 is a market. The plan must articulate the scale ambition and the sequential distribution, product, and financial literacy investments required to move from pilot to market. Without a credible scale plan, the economics of microinsurance rarely work — unit economics improve significantly with volume. The Microinsurance Market Development Compact The development of a genuine microinsurance market in Nigeria is not the responsibility of any single actor. It requires a compact between: Regulators (NAICOM): Maintain a proportionate, enabling microinsurance regulatory framework that encourages innovation without sacrificing consumer protection. Enforce consumer protection standards with the same rigor for microinsurance as for standard products. Insurers: Develop genuinely viable microinsurance products; invest in distribution partnerships and financial literacy; pay claims promptly; report honestly on what is working and what is not. Distribution partners (MFBs, telcos, cooperatives, agritech platforms): Prioritise member/customer welfare in product selection; maintain transparent premium collection; assist with claims notification; provide feedback on what the target population actually needs. Government and development finance: Fund financial literacy programmes at scale; provide data infrastructure (NIHSA weather data for parametric products; NPC mortality data for EFU table improvement); support pilot programmes through subsidised reinsurance or first-loss protection during the market development phase. No single actor can build the inclusive insurance market alone. The compact — where each party contributes what only they can contribute — is the mechanism that will eventually move Nigeria’s insurance penetration from 0.4% to something that begins to reflect the country’s economic potential and its people’s genuine need for financial protection.

Micro-Insurance Insurance designed for the low-income population, offered at a premium that is affordable relative to the target population’s income, and distributed through channels appropriate for their circumstances (mobile money, cooperatives, MFBs, USSD). Financial Inclusion The provision of affordable, accessible, and appropriate financial services — including insurance, savings, credit, and payments — to populations currently excluded from the formal financial system. Unit Microinsurer A standalone insurance company licensed specifically under NAICOM’s Microinsurance Guidelines to write only microinsurance products for the low-income market. Composite Microinsurer A company licensed for both standard insurance and microinsurance, maintaining the microinsurance book as a separately identified fund within the composite operation. Index-Based (Parametric) Insurance Insurance in which the benefit payment is triggered by an external index or parameter crossing a predefined threshold (e.g., rainfall below a drought threshold; river level above a flood threshold), rather than by assessment of the individual insured’s actual loss. Basis Risk The risk that an index-based insurance product’s trigger index does not perfectly correlate with the individual insured’s actual loss experience. A farmer whose crop fails due to local conditions may not receive a payment if the official index does not record a triggering event. Community-Based Insurance Insurance organised around existing social structures — cooperatives, market associations, Ajo/Esusu groups, religious communities — using the community’s trust network and collective meeting structure for distribution, premium collection, and claims advocacy. Ajo/Esusu Insurance Model An insurance delivery model integrated with traditional Nigerian rotating savings groups, in which an insurance premium component is added to the regular group contribution and collected collectively by the group leader. Moratorium Underwriting A simplified underwriting approach under which individual medical evidence is waived, but claims arising from pre-existing conditions within a defined exclusion period are not covered. Widely used in microinsurance for practicability. USSD Enrolment The process of enrolling in an insurance product using the USSD mobile telephone protocol, which works on any mobile phone without internet connectivity, through sequential text menus. Premium Auto-Deduction The automatic deduction of insurance premiums from a mobile money wallet on a scheduled basis, authorised by the customer at enrolment. The most effective premium collection mechanism for mobile microinsurance. EFInA Enhancing Financial Innovation and Access: a development finance entity that conducts the most comprehensive demand-side surveys of financial services access in Nigeria. Primary data source for microinsurance market sizing.
