t: Chapter 23 · 23.1 Introduction: The Investment Function in Life Insurance
x: A life insurance company is simultaneously an insurance business and an investment business. When a policyholder pays a premium, most of that money does not immediately flow back out as claims — it is held for months, years, or decades until the policy matures, the insured dies, or the policyholder surrenders. During this holding period, the insurer invests the premium, and the investment return generated is a fundamental component of the insurer’s commercial model. For a participating endowment policy with a 20-year term, the investment return earned on the accumulated reserve over the full 20 years contributes a significant portion of the maturity benefit. For an annuity product, the insurer must earn investment returns sufficient to fund the guaranteed income payments for the full lifetime of the annuitant, which may extend for 20–30 years or more beyond the annuity commencement date. For a whole life policy, the insurer invests premiums for the entire active duration of the policy, which may be 40–50 years. The investment function is therefore not peripheral to a life insurer’s business — it is central. The return assumption embedded in product pricing, the interest rate used to discount policy reserves in the actuarial valuation, and the yield on the investment portfolio are three expressions of the same underlying reality: the life insurer’s financial health depends critically on earning adequate, reliable, and sustainable investment returns over very long time horizons. In the Nigerian context, the investment function operates under conditions that are unusually challenging: high nominal interest rates (which generate attractive short-term yields but create asset-liability duration mismatch risk when rates inevitably fall); a domestic bond market that lacks the depth and duration required for long-term liability matching; an equity market that is volatile and relatively illiquid for large institutional holdings; and a regulatory framework that has historically lagged the sophistication of the investment management challenge. NIIRA 2025 represents a significant step toward a more rigorous investment governance regime, introducing new admissible asset criteria, NAICOM investment reporting requirements, and ALCO governance obligations.

t: Chapter 23 · 23.2 The Investment Mandate of a Life Insurer
x: 23.2.1 Investment Objectives The investment mandate of a life insurance company is the set of objectives, constraints, and guidelines that govern how the investment portfolio is managed. Unlike a hedge fund (whose mandate may be to maximise absolute return regardless of volatility) or a pension fund (whose mandate is to maximise the probability of meeting future pension payments), the life insurer’s investment mandate must balance several objectives simultaneously: Capital preservation The insurer must not lose the policyholder’s premium. Capital preservation is the primary obligation: the investment portfolio must not be managed in a way that puts the principal at material risk. This means that speculative, highly leveraged, or illiquid investment strategies are inconsistent with the insurance investment mandate. Liability matching The investment portfolio must be structured to generate cash flows that align with the timing and amount of the insurer’s expected policy liability outflows. A 20-year endowment creates a liability that matures in 20 years; the investment portfolio should include assets with 20-year maturities to match this liability. Adequate return on assets The investment portfolio must earn a return at least equal to the investment return assumption embedded in the pricing of the insurer’s products. If the pricing assumes a 12% p.a. investment return and the portfolio only earns 9%, the pricing assumption is violated and the product will be unprofitable. Liquidity management The insurer must have sufficient liquid assets to meet unexpected cash demands: a surge in claims (pandemic or catastrophe scenario), a wave of policy surrenders, or a regulatory capital requirement increase. Investing exclusively in long-duration illiquid assets (property, private placements) creates liquidity risk that is inconsistent with the insurance mandate. Regulatory compliance The investment portfolio must comply with NAICOM’s admissible asset requirements, concentration limits, and fund separation rules at all times. Non-compliant investments do not count toward the insurer’s regulatory capital base. Risk management The investment portfolio must be managed within the risk limits set by the Board in the investment policy statement, including limits on market risk, credit risk, liquidity risk, and currency risk. The investment function is a key component of the ERM framework (Chapter 15). 23.2.2 The Asset-Liability Management Committee (ALCO) NIIRA 2025 requires every life insurer to establish an Asset-Liability Management Committee (ALCO) as the governance body responsible for overseeing the investment function and ensuring that the investment strategy remains consistent with the liability profile. The ALCO is typically chaired by the CFO or CIO and includes the Statutory Actuary, the Chief Risk Officer, the Head of Investment, and senior representatives from the product and underwriting functions. The ALCO’s mandate includes: approving the investment policy statement; setting and monitoring asset-liability duration gap limits; reviewing the investment portfolio’s compliance with NAICOM admissible asset requirements quarterly; approving any deviation from the investment policy limits; and reporting investment performance and ALM metrics to the Board on a quarterly basis. The ALCO is the organisational interface between the investment function and the risk management framework, ensuring that investment decisions are made with full awareness of their impact on the insurer’s liability obligations.

t: Chapter 23 · 23.3 Statutory Separation of Life and Non-Life Funds
x: 23.3.1 The Fund Separation Requirement Nigerian insurance law — rooted in the Insurance Act 2003 and reinforced by NIIRA 2025 — requires that a composite insurer (one licensed to write both life and non-life insurance) must maintain completely separate, identifiable funds for its life insurance business and its non-life insurance business. The life insurance fund consists of all premiums, investment income, and other receipts attributable to life policies, and it must be used exclusively to meet life policy obligations. It cannot be drawn upon to meet non-life insurance claims, operating expenses of the non-life business, or shareholder dividends beyond the amount actuarially available for distribution. Statutory Life Insurance Fund The separate fund maintained by a life insurer (or the life insurance subsidiary of a composite group) into which all life insurance premiums, investment income attributable to life assets, and other life insurance receipts are paid. The assets of the statutory life insurance fund are held in trust for the benefit of life policyholders and may not be applied to meet non-life obligations or distributed to shareholders without the prior approval of NAICOM and the concurrence of the Statutory Actuary. The rationale for statutory fund separation is policyholder protection: life insurance policyholders make long-term financial commitments to a company based on the expectation that the premiums they pay are segregated and protected for their benefit. Without fund separation, the life fund’s assets could be raided to meet the obligations of a failing non-life book, leaving life policyholders exposed to a solvency deficit arising from risks they did not knowingly take. 23.3.2 Fund Separation in Practice In practice, fund separation requires: Separate accounting: The life fund and the non-life fund must be separately accounted for in the insurer’s books, with all income, expense, and asset movements attributed to the correct fund. Separate investment portfolios: The assets backing the life fund must be physically identified and segregated from the assets backing the non-life fund and the shareholders’ fund. Separate custody: Ideally (and for large portfolios, practically required), the life fund’s investment assets are held in separate custody accounts, clearly designated as life fund assets. Actuarial certification: The Statutory Actuary must annually certify that the assets of the life fund are at least equal to the total life insurance liabilities, confirming that the life fund is solvent on a standalone basis. 23.3.3 NIIRA 2025 Penalties for Fund Commingling NIIRA 2025: Consequences of Life and Non-Life Fund Commingling Fund commingling — the mixing of life insurance fund assets with non-life or shareholders’ fund assets — is a serious regulatory breach under NIIRA 2025: Financial penalty of up to ₦50,000,000 for an insurer that fails to maintain the required statutory fund separation. NAICOM may direct the insurer to restore the fund separation within a defined remediation period. Failure to restore separation within the directed period may result in appointment of a special examiner. The Statutory Actuary who certifies the insurer’s accounts when fund commingling is present faces personal professional liability under the Insurance Act and may be reported to the actuarial professional body. Directors of the insurer are personally liable where fund commingling is found to have been deliberate and to have prejudiced policyholder interests.

t: Chapter 23 · 23.4 Admissible Assets and Investment Restrictions
x: 23.4.1 The Admissible Asset Framework Admissible assets are the classes of investment that NAICOM recognises as qualifying assets for the purposes of meeting the life fund’s liabilities and the insurer’s regulatory capital requirements under the RBC framework. An investment in a non-admissible asset does not count toward the insurer’s regulatory solvency position: from NAICOM’s perspective, the asset effectively does not exist for solvency purposes. The admissible asset framework serves two purposes: it protects policyholders by limiting the investment of life fund assets to instruments with defined quality, liquidity, and risk characteristics; and it creates a common, verifiable basis for NAICOM’s supervisory assessment of insurer solvency. An insurer that invests its life fund in non-admissible assets may appear technically solvent on a gross balance sheet basis while being insolvent on the regulatory basis that counts. 23.4.2 Principal Admissible Asset Classes and Limits Asset Class Admissibility Status NAICOM Limit (Indicative) Risk Profile for Life Insurer Federal Government of Nigeria (FGN) Bonds Fully admissible. The highest-quality domestic fixed-income instrument. No specific concentration limit; typically the largest single asset class. Low credit risk (sovereign); interest rate risk (price falls when rates rise); long-duration bonds available for liability matching. FGN Treasury Bills (T-Bills) Fully admissible. Short-term (91–364 days) sovereign instruments. No specific concentration limit. Minimal credit risk; excellent liquidity; short duration creates reinvestment risk for long-term liabilities. State and Local Government Bonds Admissible with limitations. Sub-sovereign credit quality; varies by issuing state. Concentration limits apply; typically limited to a percentage of the life fund. Higher credit risk than FGN; lower liquidity; useful for yield enhancement. Corporate Bonds (investment grade) Admissible with limits. Must be listed on the FMDQ or approved exchange; minimum credit rating required. Typically limited to 25–30% of the life fund. Higher yield than FGN bonds; credit risk from issuer default; useful for liability matching if long-dated bonds are available. Listed Nigerian Equities (NGX) Admissible with limits. Must be listed on the Nigerian Exchange Group. Typically limited to 25–35% of the life fund. Higher expected return over the long term; significant capital volatility; not suitable for liability matching due to unpredictable cash flows. Real Estate (direct property) Admissible with limits. Must be professionally valued; location and asset quality restrictions. Typically limited to 25–30% of the life fund; single property concentration limit. Inflation protection; income yield; very long duration aligns with long-term liabilities; illiquid. Money Market Instruments (call accounts, placements with approved banks) Admissible. Banks must meet NAICOM’s approved counterparty criteria. Concentration limits per counterparty (typically 10–15% of fund per bank). Liquidity; no duration; yield below longer-term instruments; useful for short-term cash management. Foreign Currency Assets Admissible within CBN limits; subject to NAICOM restrictions on foreign currency proportions of the life fund. Typically limited to 15–20% of the life fund; subject to CBN repatriation rules. Currency risk (Naira devaluation is a two-edged sword: gains in Naira terms on foreign assets; cost increases for foreign-currency-denominated liabilities). Infrastructure Bonds / Green Bonds Admissible; encouraged under NAICOM guidelines for long-term investment. Concentration limits apply; overlap with corporate bond limits. Long duration; well-matched to long-term life liabilities; developing market in Nigeria. Policy Loans Admissible. Loans to policyholders secured against the surrender value of the policy. Subject to specific policy loan accounting within the life fund. Very low default risk (secured); self-liquidating; reduces NAR (and therefore mortality risk) of the policy. Note: Specific limits are determined by NAICOM’s Investment Guidelines, which are periodically updated. Insurers should refer to the most current NAICOM investment guidelines for exact limits. The above reflects approximate market practice under the current framework. 23.4.3 Non-Admissible Assets Assets that are not admissible for the life fund include: unlisted private company equity; speculative derivatives (options, futures used for speculation rather than hedging); unsecured personal loans; assets outside Nigeria without CBN and NAICOM approval; cryptocurrencies and digital assets; and any investment that creates a direct conflict of interest with the insurer’s directors or major shareholders (related-party investments require specific NAICOM approval and are subject to strict limitations).

23.5.1 The ALM Concept Asset-Liability Matching (ALM) The investment management discipline of structuring the insurer’s investment portfolio so that the cash flows generated by the assets (interest, dividends, and maturing principal) correspond in timing and amount to the cash flows required to meet policy liabilities (claims, maturities, and expenses) as they fall due. Perfect ALM eliminates interest rate risk and liquidity risk from the insurer’s balance sheet; imperfect ALM (a mismatch between asset and liability profiles) creates risks that can materially affect solvency. ALM is the central discipline of insurance investment management. An insurer that invests 20-year endowment policy reserves in 91-day Treasury bills has a severe duration mismatch: it must reinvest the T-bill proceeds every 91 days, accepting whatever interest rate the market offers at each reinvestment date. If rates fall from 22% to 10% over the course of the 20-year policy, the T-bill investment strategy will generate far less than the return assumed in the pricing — producing losses and policyholder benefit shortfalls. An insurer that matches its 20-year liability with a 20-year FGN bond locks in the investment return for the full liability duration, eliminating this reinvestment risk. 23.5.2 Duration Matching Duration (Modified Duration / Macaulay Duration) A measure of the interest rate sensitivity of a fixed-income instrument or a portfolio. Specifically, modified duration expresses the approximate percentage change in the price of a bond or portfolio for a 1% change in interest rates. A bond with modified duration of 8 years will fall in price by approximately 8% if interest rates rise by 1%. Duration is the primary ALM metric: by matching the duration of the asset portfolio to the duration of the liability portfolio, the insurer minimises the net impact of interest rate movements on its surplus. Duration Matching Condition Duration(Assets) ≈ Duration(Liabilities) When asset duration equals liability duration, a parallel shift in interest rates affects the value of assets and liabilities by approximately the same amount, leaving the surplus (assets minus liabilities) unchanged. When asset duration is shorter than liability duration (a positive duration gap), rising interest rates improve the surplus (asset values fall less than liability values). When asset duration is longer than liability duration (a negative duration gap), rising interest rates destroy surplus. Duration Gap = Duration(Assets) − Duration(Liabilities). Target: Duration Gap close to zero. NAICOM/ALCO typically sets a tolerance band (e.g., gap between −1 and +1 year). Worked Example 23.1 — Duration Gap Analysis A Nigerian life insurer has the following asset and liability portfolio (simplified for illustration): Portfolio Market Value (₦bn) Duration (years) Contribution to Weighted Duration ASSETS: FGN Bonds (20-year) 25 14.2 14.2 × 25/70 = 5.07 ASSETS: FGN T-Bills (90-day) 20 0.25 0.25 × 20/70 = 0.07 ASSETS: Corporate Bonds (5-year) 15 4.3 4.3 × 15/70 = 0.92 ASSETS: Equities (NGX) 10 n/a n/a TOTAL ASSETS 70 — Portfolio Duration ≈ 6.06 years LIABILITIES: Endowment Reserves (15-year average) 55 10.5 10.5 × 55/70 = 8.25 LIABILITIES: Annuity Reserves (20-year) 15 13.0 13.0 × 15/70 = 2.79 TOTAL LIABILITIES 70 — Liability Duration ≈ 11.04 years Duration Gap = 6.06 − 11.04 = −4.98 years. The asset portfolio is significantly shorter in duration than the liability portfolio. This is a POSITIVE duration gap problem from the insurer’s perspective: if interest rates FALL (which is the medium-term risk in Nigeria’s high-rate environment), the liabilities will increase in value (as the discount rate falls) by more than the assets, destroying surplus. ALCO action required: extend asset duration by purchasing longer-dated FGN bonds; reduce T-bill allocation. 23.5.3 Cash Flow Matching Cash flow matching is a more precise (and more conservative) ALM approach than duration matching. Rather than managing the aggregate duration of the portfolio, cash flow matching involves constructing the asset portfolio so that the specific cash flows generated by assets on specific future dates are sufficient to meet the specific liability cash flows due on those dates. For a life insurer with a large annuity book, cash flow matching might involve purchasing a sequence of bonds that mature (or generate coupon payments) in each future year, with the maturity or coupon proceeds exactly equal to the annuity payments due in that year. This approach eliminates both reinvestment risk (no need to reinvest maturing proceeds at uncertain future rates) and liquidity risk (cash is available exactly when needed) but is operationally complex and may not be achievable in the Nigerian bond market where long-dated bonds are limited in availability.

t: Chapter 23 · 23.6 Principal Investment Classes for Nigerian Life Insurers
x: 23.6.1 Government Securities: FGN Bonds and Treasury Bills Federal Government of Nigeria (FGN) bonds are the highest-quality, most liquid domestic fixed-income instrument available to Nigerian life insurers. They are issued by the Debt Management Office (DMO) and traded on the FMDQ Securities Exchange. They carry sovereign credit risk — which, while not zero, is the lowest available in the Nigerian market. Maturities range from 2 to 30 years, providing the duration options necessary for liability matching. The Nigerian bond market has grown significantly since 2000, and long-dated FGN bonds (15–30 year maturities) are increasingly available. These are the most important instruments for ALM in Nigerian life insurance: they provide long-duration, sovereign-quality assets whose coupon payments and maturities can be aligned with long-term life insurance liabilities. However, the market for very long-dated bonds remains thinner than in mature markets, and large institutional purchases can move prices. FGN Treasury Bills (T-Bills) are short-term (91–364 day) discount instruments. They are fully liquid, near-zero credit risk, and earn the shortest-maturity segment of the sovereign yield curve. For life insurers, T-bills are appropriate for: the liquidity reserve (the portion of the portfolio held to meet unexpected cash demands); and short-term investment of premium income received while long-term investment decisions are being made. Their limitation is duration: a portfolio dominated by T-bills creates severe reinvestment risk for long-term liabilities. 23.6.2 Nigerian Equities Listed Nigerian equities — traded on the Nigerian Exchange Group (NGX) — offer higher expected returns over the long term than fixed-income instruments, reflecting the equity risk premium that compensates investors for bearing the higher volatility and residual claim priority of equities relative to bonds. For long-term life insurance portfolios, a measured allocation to equities is consistent with maximising long-term returns, provided the allocation is within NAICOM’s admissible limits and the portfolio does not create liquidity risk. The characteristics of the Nigerian equity market that define its suitability for life insurance investment include: Market breadth: The NGX lists over 150 companies across banking, consumer goods, oil and gas, industrial goods, and financial services sectors. The market capitalisation is dominated by a small number of large-cap names (MTN Nigeria, Dangote Cement, Airtel Africa, GTCO, Zenith Bank), creating concentration risk for large institutional portfolios. Liquidity: Daily trading volumes on the NGX are relatively low compared to larger African exchanges. A life insurer with a large equity portfolio may find it difficult to liquidate positions quickly without moving market prices, creating liquidity risk in stress scenarios. Valuation and dividend income: Nigerian listed equities have historically provided substantial dividend income as well as capital appreciation. Dividend yields on many blue-chip Nigerian companies have been comparable to fixed-income yields, providing income that supports the insurance portfolio’s cash flow needs. Currency and macroeconomic sensitivity: Nigerian equity market performance is strongly influenced by macroeconomic conditions — oil price movements, currency depreciation, and interest rate policy. A portfolio with a significant equity allocation must be managed with awareness of these macro sensitivities. 23.6.3 Real Estate Real estate is an important investment class for Nigerian life insurers, offering several characteristics that align well with long-term life insurance liabilities: it is a real (inflation-linked) asset; it generates regular rental income; it has a long economic life that matches long-duration liabilities; and it provides diversification from the financial market correlation of bonds and equities. Nigerian commercial and residential property has delivered strong returns in Naira terms over the past two decades, driven by urbanisation, population growth, and the expansion of Nigeria’s middle class. However, real estate investment carries material risks for life insurers: illiquidity (large property positions cannot be liquidated quickly without significant discount to market value); valuation uncertainty (professional valuations are required but may not fully reflect market clearing prices); and concentration risk (a large property portfolio in Lagos commercial real estate is exposed to the specific demand conditions of that market). NAICOM’s admissible asset rules require that real estate investments in the life fund be professionally valued at least annually by a NAICOM-approved valuer, and that the valuation methodology be consistent, documented, and auditable. Properties with disputed ownership, pending litigation, or unusual occupancy structures may not qualify as fully admissible. 23.6.4 Money Market Instruments Money market instruments — call account deposits, fixed deposits with approved banks, commercial paper, and banker’s acceptances — are the liquidity component of the life insurance investment portfolio. They mature within one year, carry low credit risk where the counterparty is a well-rated bank, and provide instant or very short-notice liquidity. In Nigeria’s high interest rate environment, money market instruments have historically offered attractive nominal yields relative to their very low credit risk. However, for life insurance ALM purposes, they should represent only the portion of the portfolio needed for operational liquidity and short-term premium receipt investment. An excessive allocation to money market instruments creates the reinvestment risk scenario described in Section 23.5: yield rates that are attractive today may be unavailable on reinvestment, creating a mismatch between the pricing assumption and the actual portfolio yield.

t: Chapter 23 · 23.7 Portfolio Theory Applied to Insurance Investment
x: 23.7.1 Diversification and Correlation Modern Portfolio Theory (MPT), developed by Harry Markowitz in the 1950s, demonstrates that combining assets whose returns are less than perfectly correlated produces a portfolio whose risk (measured by return volatility) is lower than the weighted average risk of its individual components. This is the principle of diversification: spreading investment across multiple asset classes and instruments reduces the impact of any single adverse event on the portfolio’s overall value. For a Nigerian life insurer, the key correlation relationships that drive diversification benefit are: Bonds and equities: In most market environments, bond prices and equity prices move in opposite directions (negative or low positive correlation): when economic conditions deteriorate, equity prices fall but sovereign bond prices rise as investors seek safety. A portfolio combining bonds and equities therefore has lower volatility than either asset class alone. Fixed income and real estate: Real estate prices are less correlated with bond price movements than equities, providing additional diversification. Both generate income; real estate provides inflation protection that bonds do not. Naira and foreign currency assets: Where the insurer holds a defined allocation to foreign currency assets (within NAICOM limits), these provide a hedge against Naira depreciation scenarios that would reduce the real value of Naira-denominated assets relative to the insurer’s foreign currency liabilities. 23.7.2 The Efficient Frontier and the Insurance Investment Constraint The efficient frontier is the set of investment portfolios that maximise expected return for a given level of risk (or minimise risk for a given expected return). A portfolio on the efficient frontier is fully diversified in the Markowitz sense: no other combination of assets offers a better risk-return trade-off. For a life insurer, the efficient frontier cannot be the only guide to portfolio construction because the insurer faces constraints that a pure return-maximiser does not: the regulatory admissible asset limits constrain the feasible portfolio space; the ALM obligation requires that the portfolio’s duration profile reflects the liability profile, not merely the return-risk optimum; and the liquidity requirement forces a minimum allocation to liquid instruments that may not be on the unconstrained efficient frontier. In practice, the insurance investment team constructs a ‘constrained efficient frontier’ that represents the best achievable risk-return combinations within all regulatory and ALM constraints. The ALCO approves the portfolio allocation within this constrained frontier, balancing the competing objectives of maximum return, adequate ALM performance, regulatory compliance, and sufficient liquidity.

t: Chapter 23 · 23.8 The Nigerian Capital Market and SEC Regulation
x: 23.8.1 Capital Market Infrastructure Institution Role Relevance to Insurance Investment Nigerian Exchange Group (NGX) The primary stock exchange for equity listing and trading in Nigeria. Operates the Main Board (large-cap equities), Premium Board (top-tier equities), and Growth Board (smaller companies). The primary market for the insurance portfolio’s equity allocation. Insurance portfolio managers trade NGX-listed equities through SEC-registered stockbrokers. FMDQ Securities Exchange Nigeria’s principal fixed income and currency derivatives market. Primary market for FGN bonds, T-bills, commercial paper, and corporate bonds. Also hosts the foreign exchange spot and derivatives market. The primary market for the insurance portfolio’s fixed-income allocation. FGN bonds, corporate bonds, and T-bills are all primarily traded on FMDQ. Insurance companies are significant participants. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) The apex capital market regulator. Registers and supervises capital market operators, approves listed securities, and enforces capital market laws. Insurance companies managing their own investment portfolios must comply with SEC regulations. Insurance asset managers must be registered with SEC. Insider trading restrictions and disclosure obligations apply. Debt Management Office (DMO) Issues and manages FGN bonds and T-bills on behalf of the Federal Government. Primary issuer of the sovereign bonds that constitute the largest asset class in Nigerian life insurance portfolios. Central Securities Clearing System (CSCS) The central depository, clearing, and settlement system for capital market transactions in Nigeria. All equity and bond trades are settled through CSCS. Insurance portfolio managers must have CSCS accounts (through their custodian banks) to hold and trade listed securities. Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN) Regulates the money market, foreign exchange market, and banking sector. Issues OMO (Open Market Operations) bills and regulates bank deposits. CBN policy directly affects insurance investment: monetary policy rate (MPR) determines the reference rate for money market instruments and influences the yield curve on FGN bonds. CBN foreign exchange regulations govern cross-border holdings. 23.8.2 Insurance Investment and SEC Compliance Insurance companies that manage their own investment portfolios (rather than delegating to an SEC-registered asset manager) must comply with SEC’s regulations for institutional investors. Key SEC compliance obligations for insurance portfolio managers include: Insider trading prohibition: Insurance investment team members who receive material non-public information in the course of their business relationships (e.g., information about a listed company obtained through a corporate insurance client relationship) must not use that information in investment decisions. Insurance companies must maintain information barriers between their business functions and their investment function. Large shareholder disclosure: An insurance company that acquires more than 5% of the outstanding shares of any single listed company must disclose the holding to the NGX and SEC. Acquisition of 10% or more may trigger additional regulatory requirements. Investment management registration: Where the insurance company delegates investment management to an external asset manager, that manager must be registered with SEC as an investment adviser or portfolio manager.

t: Chapter 23 · 23.9 Foreign Currency Assets and Cross-Border Holdings
x: 23.9.1 The Regulatory Framework for Foreign Currency Investment Nigerian life insurers face a complex dual-regulatory framework for foreign currency investment: NAICOM’s admissible asset rules set the maximum proportion of the life fund that may be invested in foreign currency instruments; and the CBN’s foreign exchange management regulations govern the mechanics of converting Naira to foreign currency for investment and repatriating foreign currency proceeds. NAICOM’s admissible asset guidelines permit life insurers to hold a defined percentage of the life fund in foreign currency assets (typically up to 15–20%), subject to: the assets being held with approved custodians in approved jurisdictions; the assets meeting quality standards comparable to Nigerian admissible assets (investment-grade rated, listed on approved exchanges); and the foreign currency holdings being reported to NAICOM in the quarterly investment return. 23.9.2 Currency Risk in Life Insurance Foreign currency assets create currency risk in the life insurance portfolio: if the Naira appreciates against the foreign currency in which the assets are denominated, the Naira value of the foreign currency assets declines, reducing the portfolio’s market value. Conversely, if the Naira depreciates (as it did significantly in 2023 and 2024), the Naira value of foreign currency assets rises, generating mark-to-market gains. The currency risk management challenge for Nigerian life insurers is asymmetric: policies are denominated in Naira, so liabilities are Naira-denominated. Foreign currency assets provide a partial hedge against Naira depreciation (the Naira value of the assets rises with depreciation) and a source of investment income in a foreign currency that may offer lower nominal yields but more stable real returns than Naira instruments. The insurer must decide, within its investment policy, what proportion of the portfolio to hold in foreign currency as a deliberate currency risk and inflation hedge, balanced against the currency risk this creates when the Naira appreciates.

t: Chapter 23 · 23.10 The Impact of the Interest Rate Environment on Solvency
x: 23.10.1 Nigeria’s Interest Rate Environment Nigeria has historically operated in a high nominal interest rate environment, driven by elevated inflation, currency depreciation expectations, and the CBN’s monetary policy responses. The 12-month Treasury bill rate in Nigeria exceeded 22% in 2024 — a rate that, while attractive in nominal terms for short-duration investment, creates significant actuarial and ALM challenges for life insurers. The challenge is not the high rate itself — high rates generate attractive current investment income. The challenge is the valuation of long-term liabilities: high current rates used to discount future policy obligations reduce the present value of those obligations, making the insurer appear better capitalised than it would be at lower rates. When rates inevitably normalise (fall), the discount rate used in the liability valuation falls, and the present value of long-term liabilities increases dramatically — potentially revealing a solvency deficit that the high-rate environment had concealed. Interest Rate Sensitivity Example A simplified illustration of interest rate sensitivity for a life insurer: Consider a life insurer with a 20-year endowment portfolio with an aggregate nominal maturity value of ₦100 billion, payable in 20 years. Discounted at 22% p.a.: PV of liabilities ≈ ₦4.3 billion. Discounted at 12% p.a.: PV of liabilities ≈ ₦10.4 billion. Discounted at 8% p.a.: PV of liabilities ≈ ₦21.5 billion. A fall in the valuation discount rate from 22% to 8% increases the present value of this liability by ₦17.2 billion — a more than five-fold increase. An insurer whose portfolio earns 22% today but whose liabilities are discounted at 22% (matching) has adequate solvency. An insurer whose discount rate falls to 8% but whose T-bill portfolio can only reinvest at 8% faces a liability explosion that may not be covered by the asset portfolio. 23.10.2 The Reinvestment Risk Problem For Nigerian life insurers that have historically invested predominantly in short-duration instruments (T-bills and money market deposits), the reinvestment risk is severe: when today’s T-bills mature, the insurer must reinvest at whatever rate is available in the market at that time. If rates have fallen from 22% to 12%, the portfolio’s yield is materially lower than the pricing assumption, and the insurer’s ability to meet its long-term benefit obligations is compromised. The structural solution to reinvestment risk is to lock in today’s high rates by purchasing long-dated FGN bonds with maturities that match the liability duration. An insurer that purchases a 20-year FGN bond at 18% today locks in that yield for 20 years, regardless of what happens to short-term rates. This is the core ALM discipline: use today’s high-rate environment to extend asset duration toward the liability duration, rather than riding the high short-term rates and accepting the risk of reinvestment at lower rates in the future.

t: Chapter 23 · 23.11 NIIRA 2025: Investment Obligations and NAICOM Oversight
x: 23.11.1 Investment Policy Statement Requirement NIIRA 2025 requires every licensed life insurer to maintain a written Investment Policy Statement (IPS), approved by the Board of Directors and reviewed at least annually. The IPS must include: the insurer’s investment objectives, risk tolerance, and ALM targets; the approved asset classes and concentration limits; the currency risk management approach; the liquidity management requirements; the ALCO governance structure and meeting frequency; and the investment performance benchmarks against which portfolio managers are evaluated. The IPS is the foundational governance document for the investment function. An investment decision that is inconsistent with the IPS — even if commercially attractive in isolation — is a governance breach that requires Board approval for an IPS amendment or a specific exception. NAICOM may request the IPS as part of its annual supervisory review and may require the insurer to revise provisions that are inconsistent with prudent investment standards. 23.11.2 Investment Reporting to NAICOM NIIRA 2025 requires quarterly investment reporting to NAICOM, using the prescribed return format. The quarterly investment return must include: A full schedule of investments by asset class, instrument, issuer, and market value, with each investment categorised as admissible or non-admissible. The calculated coverage ratio: total admissible assets as a percentage of total life insurance liabilities. NAICOM requires the coverage ratio to be maintained above 100% at all times; a ratio below 100% constitutes a regulatory deficiency requiring immediate remediation. The asset-liability duration gap, calculated using NAICOM’s prescribed methodology. Any changes in investment policy or significant portfolio restructuring since the last quarterly return. Investment income received in the quarter, segmented by asset class. Any investment-related related-party transactions, with disclosure of the nature of the relationship and the basis on which the transaction was assessed as being on arm’s length terms. 23.11.3 NAICOM Supervisory Powers over Investment NIIRA 2025 significantly strengthens NAICOM’s powers in relation to the investment function. These powers include: Directed divestment: NAICOM may direct a life insurer to divest a specific investment within a defined period where NAICOM has determined that the investment is non-admissible, creates an unacceptable concentration risk, or is inconsistent with the insurer’s IPS. The insurer may request a review of the direction, but must comply with the direction pending the review outcome. Investment freeze: NAICOM may freeze the insurer’s investment activities (prevent new investments and restrict asset disposals) where NAICOM has concerns about the solvency of the life fund. An investment freeze is typically accompanied by a special examination of the insurer’s financial position. Appointed investment manager: Where NAICOM determines that the insurer’s investment management is materially deficient and represents a risk to policyholders, NAICOM may require the appointment of a NAICOM-approved investment manager to manage the life fund until the deficiency is remediated. Coverage ratio enforcement: Where the coverage ratio falls below 100%, NAICOM has immediate authority to restrict the insurer from paying dividends, making shareholder distributions, or writing new business until the coverage ratio is restored.

t: Chapter 23 · 23.12 Advisory: Investment Management Best Practices for Nigerian Life Insurers
x: The investment function in Nigerian life insurance is in transition. The historical model — a simple portfolio of T-bills and money market deposits managed by the finance team with minimal actuarial input and no ALCO governance — is being replaced by a more sophisticated, ALM-driven, institutionally managed approach. This transition is driven by NIIRA 2025’s governance requirements, the growing complexity of the insurance liability profile, and the competitive pressure to earn better risk-adjusted returns. Advisory: The Investment Function Transformation Agenda for Nigerian Life Insurers PRIORITY 1: ESTABLISH A FUNCTIONING ALCO. The ALCO is not a reporting committee — it is a decision-making body. An ALCO that meets quarterly to review a spreadsheet of investment positions and minutes that no action was required is not managing the investment function; it is observing it. A functioning ALCO: sets the duration target and monitors the duration gap monthly; challenges the investment team on asset allocation decisions; reviews the coverage ratio against both the regulatory minimum and the insurer’s management target; and escalates to the Board when any parameter is breached. PRIORITY 2: EXTEND DURATION — NOW. The high Nigerian interest rate environment of 2023–2025 is an asset-liability management opportunity that Nigerian life insurers should be exploiting. By purchasing long-dated FGN bonds at today’s yields, insurers can lock in rates that are dramatically above the return assumption embedded in most in-force product pricing. The risk of not acting — continuing to roll short-duration T-bills and accepting tomorrow’s lower reinvestment rate — is far greater than the mark-to-market risk of holding long-dated bonds while rates remain elevated. PRIORITY 3: INVEST IN INVESTMENT TALENT. The investment function of a life insurer is a specialised financial role. It requires professionals who understand fixed income mathematics, portfolio construction, ALM principles, and the Nigerian capital market. Many Nigerian life insurers manage billions of naira in investment assets with insufficient specialist talent. The cost of hiring a qualified CFA charterholder or investment professional with institutional asset management experience is trivial relative to the value of even modest improvements in portfolio yield or risk management. PRIORITY 4: BUILD INVESTMENT GOVERNANCE DOCUMENTATION. An Investment Policy Statement that specifies the insurer’s objectives, constraints, and benchmarks is not optional under NIIRA 2025 — it is mandatory. But beyond compliance, a well-crafted IPS disciplines the investment decision-making process: it prevents ad-hoc concentration in a single asset class; it creates accountability for underperformance; and it provides a clear framework for NAICOM’s supervisory engagement with the investment function. Every insurer should have an IPS that is Board-approved, actuary-reviewed, and genuinely used to guide investment decisions.

Investment Mandate The set of objectives, constraints, and guidelines that govern how a life insurer’s investment portfolio is managed, including return targets, risk tolerance, ALM requirements, admissible asset classes, and regulatory compliance obligations. Statutory Life Insurance Fund The separate fund maintained by a life insurer into which all life insurance premiums and investment income are paid, held in trust for life policyholders and segregated from non-life and shareholder funds. Fund Separation The regulatory requirement that composite insurers maintain completely separate, identifiable funds for life and non-life insurance business, preventing cross-subsidisation between fund types. Admissible Assets Investment instruments recognised by NAICOM as qualifying assets for the purpose of meeting life fund liabilities and regulatory capital requirements under the RBC framework. Asset-Liability Management (ALM) The investment management discipline of structuring the portfolio so that asset cash flows correspond in timing and amount to policy liability cash flows, managing interest rate risk and liquidity risk. Duration (Modified Duration) A measure of a bond or portfolio’s sensitivity to interest rate changes, expressed as the approximate percentage price change for a 1% change in interest rates. Duration Gap The difference between the duration of the investment portfolio (assets) and the duration of the policy liabilities. A positive gap means assets are shorter in duration than liabilities; a negative gap means assets are longer. Cash Flow Matching An ALM approach in which the specific cash flows generated by assets on specific dates are structured to exactly match the specific liability cash flows due on those dates. ALCO (Asset-Liability Management Committee) The governance body responsible for overseeing the investment function and ensuring the investment strategy remains consistent with the liability profile. Required by NIIRA 2025. Coverage Ratio Total admissible assets as a percentage of total life insurance liabilities. NAICOM requires this ratio to be maintained above 100% at all times. Reinvestment Risk The risk that proceeds from maturing short-duration instruments must be reinvested at lower interest rates than originally assumed in pricing, reducing portfolio yield relative to the liability discount rate. Efficient Frontier The set of investment portfolios that maximise expected return for a given level of risk, or minimise risk for a given expected return. The optimal portfolio lies on the efficient frontier, subject to regulatory and ALM constraints. FGN Bond Federal Government of Nigeria bond — a fixed-income instrument issued by the DMO, denominated in Naira, with maturities from 2 to 30 years. The highest-quality domestic fixed-income instrument available to Nigerian life insurers. FMDQ Exchange Nigeria’s primary fixed income and currency derivatives market, where FGN bonds, T-bills, and commercial paper are traded by institutional investors including life insurance companies. Investment Policy Statement (IPS) A Board-approved document specifying the insurer’s investment objectives, risk tolerance, ALM targets, approved asset classes and limits, ALCO governance, and performance benchmarks. Mandatory under NIIRA 2025. Currency Risk The risk of financial loss arising from adverse movements in exchange rates between the Naira and foreign currencies in which the insurer holds assets.
