t: Chapter 24 · 24.1 Introduction: Why Governance Matters More in Insurance
x: Corporate governance is the system by which a company is directed and controlled. It encompasses the structures, processes, rules, and practices through which a company’s Board of Directors ensures accountability to shareholders, policyholders, regulators, and the broader public. Good governance is the institutional foundation of financial reliability: a company with strong governance is more likely to manage risks prudently, report accurately, comply with regulatory obligations, and respond effectively when things go wrong. Governance obligations are particularly stringent in the insurance sector for reasons that are specific to the insurance business model. A life insurance company manages funds that belong not to shareholders, but to policyholders who have paid premiums in exchange for a promise of future benefit. The policyholder has no visibility into how the insurer manages its assets, how it calculates its reserves, or whether it is maintaining adequate capital. The insurer’s governance framework is the primary mechanism through which these information asymmetries are managed: the Board ensures that management acts in the interests of policyholders as well as shareholders; the actuary certifies that reserves are adequate; the auditor verifies the accuracy of financial statements; and NAICOM supervises the entire framework. NIIRA 2025 represents the most comprehensive governance reform of the Nigerian insurance sector since the Insurance Act 2003. Its provisions on Board composition, fit and proper requirements, the RBC solvency framework, IFRS-based financial reporting, dividend restrictions, and the actuarial function create a governance architecture that is significantly more demanding than what existed under the previous regime. This chapter examines each dimension of this architecture in detail, from the composition of the Board of Directors to the mechanics of IFRS 17 measurement, and addresses the practical governance and compliance implications for Nigerian life insurance professionals.

t: Chapter 24 · 24.2 Principles of Insurance Corporate Governance
x: 24.2.1 Core Governance Principles Insurance corporate governance draws on the general principles of corporate governance established in the King Codes (South Africa), the UK Corporate Governance Code, and the OECD Principles of Corporate Governance, adapted for the specific obligations of a financial institution managing public trust funds. The IAIS Insurance Core Principles (ICP 7: Corporate Governance) establishes the international standard that NAICOM’s governance framework reflects. The core principles of insurance corporate governance are: Board accountability The Board of Directors is ultimately accountable to shareholders for the company’s performance and to policyholders and regulators for its solvency, conduct, and compliance. The Board sets strategy, approves risk appetite, oversees management, and ensures that the company’s governance framework is effective. Separation of ownership and control The directors who control the company’s operations must be genuinely independent from the shareholders who own it. This separation is essential for Board decisions on risk-taking, dividend policy, and management remuneration to be made in the interests of all stakeholders, not only the major shareholder. Transparency and disclosure The company must provide accurate, timely, and complete information to regulators, shareholders, policyholders, and the market. This includes financial statements, solvency reports, actuarial valuations, and material risk disclosures. Checks and balances The governance framework must include effective internal checks: internal audit provides independent assurance; the audit committee independently oversees financial reporting; the risk committee independently oversees risk management; and the actuary independently certifies the adequacy of reserves. Fit and proper leadership All persons in positions of governance and senior management authority must be suitable — competent, honest, financially sound, and free from conflicts of interest that would compromise their ability to act in the best interests of the company and its policyholders. Proportionality The governance framework must be proportionate to the size, complexity, and risk profile of the insurer. The governance requirements for a small life insurer are different from those of a large composite group, though the core principles apply equally. 24.2.2 The Board’s Specific Responsibilities in Life Insurance The Board of a Nigerian life insurer has specific governance responsibilities that go beyond those of a typical listed company: Policyholder protection: The Board is responsible for ensuring that the company’s management of policyholders’ funds meets the highest standards of prudence and integrity. This includes approving the risk appetite and investment policy; reviewing the Statutory Actuary’s reserving and valuation conclusions; and acting on any management or regulatory concerns about the adequacy of policyholder protection. Capital adequacy oversight: The Board is responsible for ensuring that the company maintains adequate capital above the RBC minimum at all times. This requires the Board to understand the RBC calculation, to review the ORSA results, and to have a capital contingency plan that specifies the actions to be taken if the solvency ratio deteriorates. Regulatory relationship management: The Board is the principal interface with NAICOM from a governance perspective. NAICOM’s prudential correspondence is directed to the Board; NAICOM’s supervisory findings and directives must be addressed by the Board; and the Board’s tone and responsiveness in its regulatory relationship signals the quality of the governance framework.

t: Chapter 24 · 24.3 Board Composition and Committee Structure
x: 24.3.1 Board Composition Requirements under NIIRA 2025 NIIRA 2025 establishes specific Board composition requirements for licensed life insurers. These requirements are designed to ensure that the Board includes both the industry expertise to govern a complex financial institution and the independence to challenge management effectively. NIIRA 2025: Board Composition Requirements for Life Insurers Minimum Board size: Not fewer than five directors. Independent Non-Executive Directors (INEDs): At least one-third of the Board must be INEDs. An INED is a director who: has not been employed by the company or its affiliates in the past five years; has no material business relationship with the company; is not a major shareholder or the representative of a major shareholder; and is not a close family member of any executive director or senior manager. Board Chairman: The Chairman of the Board must be a Non-Executive Director. The Chairman and the Chief Executive Officer (CEO) must be different persons. The separation of the Chairman and CEO roles is a fundamental governance requirement that NIIRA 2025 makes non-negotiable. Executive Directors: The CEO and (where separately appointed) the Chief Financial Officer (CFO) may be executive directors. Additional executive directors require specific NAICOM approval. Director qualifications: At least one INED must have financial expertise (defined as current or recent senior experience in finance, accounting, actuarial science, or investment management). The Board as a whole must demonstrate collective competence in insurance, finance, law, and general management. NAICOM approval: All Board appointments (executive and non-executive) require NAICOM’s prior approval as part of the fit and proper assessment process. An individual who has not been approved by NAICOM may not act as a director. 24.3.2 Mandatory Board Committees NIIRA 2025 requires life insurers to establish specific Board-level committees with defined terms of reference. The four mandatory committees are: Committee Membership Primary Mandate Key NIIRA 2025 Requirements Board Audit Committee Majority of INEDs; at least one INED with financial expertise as Chair. Oversight of financial reporting quality; internal audit independence; external audit appointment, scope, and findings; compliance with accounting standards. Review and recommend approval of the annual financial statements and actuarial valuation report before Board approval; oversee the external auditor appointment and fees; review internal audit reports; receive whistleblowing reports. Board Risk Committee Majority INEDs; financial risk expertise required. Oversight of risk management framework; review and approval of risk appetite statement; ORSA review; monitoring of KRI breaches. Review and approve the ORSA before NAICOM submission; receive quarterly CRO reports; review investment policy and ALM metrics; approve stress test scenarios. Board Investment Committee May overlap with Risk Committee in smaller companies; investment expertise required. Oversight of investment strategy and portfolio performance; approval of investment policy statement; monitoring of NAICOM investment compliance. Review quarterly investment returns before NAICOM submission; approve investment policy statement; review coverage ratio and duration gap. Board Remuneration Committee Majority INEDs; no executive director may Chair. Setting remuneration policy for executive directors and senior management; ensuring remuneration is aligned with long-term performance, not short-term sales volumes. Ensure remuneration structures do not incentivise excessive risk-taking or mis-selling; review and approve the CEO’s remuneration package.

24.4.1 The Fit and Proper Standard Fit and Proper Requirement The regulatory standard that requires persons in positions of governance and senior management authority in a licensed life insurer to be ‘fit’ (competent, knowledgeable, and experienced for the role) and ‘proper’ (honest, of good character, and free from conflicts of interest or legal/regulatory disqualifications). A person who does not meet the fit and proper standard may not hold a controlled function in a regulated insurance company. NIIRA 2025 applies the fit and proper requirement to a defined set of ‘controlled functions’ — positions that carry material responsibility for the governance, management, or risk oversight of the insurer. These include: all Board directors (executive and non-executive); the CEO; the CFO; the Chief Risk Officer; the Statutory Actuary; the Chief Compliance Officer; the Head of Internal Audit; and the Chief Underwriting Officer. The list of controlled functions may be supplemented by NAICOM guidance. 24.4.2 The Two Dimensions of Fit and Proper Dimension Assessment Criteria Evidence Required Disqualifying Factors FITNESS(Competence) Qualifications relevant to the role; professional experience; technical knowledge; continuing professional development. CV / professional biography; evidence of qualifications; reference checks; prior relevant experience. Material skills gap for the role; lack of relevant qualifications or experience; no evidence of CPD maintenance. PROPERNESS(Character and Integrity) Honesty and integrity; financial soundness; absence of criminal convictions; regulatory record; conflicts of interest. Criminal record check; credit record; regulatory history in previous roles; declaration of conflicts of interest; professional reference checks. Criminal conviction (particularly for fraud, dishonesty, financial crimes); prior regulatory finding of misconduct; personal insolvency; undisclosed conflict of interest; false or misleading statements in the NAICOM application. 24.4.3 NAICOM’s Fit and Proper Assessment Process Before any person may take up a controlled function in a Nigerian life insurer, the insurer must submit a fit and proper application to NAICOM on the prescribed form. The application includes: the individual’s CV and qualifications; a criminal clearance certificate; a financial status declaration; a regulatory history declaration (listing any previous regulatory findings or enforcement actions in any jurisdiction); a declaration of material conflicts of interest; and personal references from persons who can speak to the individual’s professional reputation. NAICOM reviews the application and may: approve the appointment unconditionally; approve with specific conditions (e.g., requiring the appointee to complete a specific qualification within a defined period); or reject the appointment. A rejection must be communicated to the insurer with reasons, and the insurer has a right of appeal. An individual may not take up the controlled function until NAICOM’s approval is confirmed — acting in a controlled function without approval is a regulatory breach by both the individual and the appointing insurer. 24.4.4 Ongoing Fit and Proper Obligations The fit and proper obligation is not a one-time assessment — it is an ongoing requirement. The insurer must notify NAICOM promptly if any controlled function holder experiences a change in circumstances that may affect their fit and proper status: a criminal conviction; a regulatory finding in another jurisdiction; a significant personal financial event (insolvency, CCJ, major undisclosed debt); or a material conflict of interest that arises after appointment. NAICOM may initiate a retrospective fit and proper review of any controlled function holder at any time, particularly where NAICOM’s supervisory activities reveal governance failures or conduct issues that suggest a leadership quality concern. Where NAICOM concludes that a controlled function holder no longer meets the fit and proper standard, NAICOM may direct the insurer to remove the individual from their position within a defined period.

t: Chapter 24 · 24.5 The Risk-Based Capital Framework and the Supervisory Intervention Ladder
x: 24.5.1 Overview of the RBC Framework The Risk-Based Capital (RBC) framework introduced by NIIRA 2025 replaces the previous fixed-minimum solvency requirement with a dynamic, risk-sensitive capital adequacy standard. Under the previous regime, a life insurer was required to maintain a defined absolute amount of capital regardless of the size, composition, or risk profile of its business. Under RBC, the required capital is calculated as a function of the insurer’s specific risk exposures: the more risk the insurer carries, the more capital it is required to hold. The RBC framework was addressed in Chapter 15 (ERM) and Chapter 13 (Actuarial Concepts) in the context of the ORSA and the solvency assessment. This section addresses the RBC framework from the corporate governance perspective: who is responsible for it, how it is reported, and what NAICOM’s supervisory intervention ladder looks like when the solvency ratio deteriorates. 24.5.2 RBC Components and the Solvency Ratio Solvency Ratio Under the NIIRA 2025 RBC Framework Solvency Ratio = Total Available Capital ÷ Total Risk Charge Total Available Capital = Tier 1 Capital (paid-up share capital + retained earnings + share premium + other qualifying equity items) + Tier 2 Capital (subordinated debt + revaluation reserves + other qualifying instruments). NAICOM specifies minimum Tier 1 proportions. Total Risk Charge = f(C1, C2, C3, C4) where: C1 = Insurance Risk Charge (mortality, morbidity, lapse adverse experience); C2 = Market Risk Charge (interest rate, equity, property, currency); C3 = Credit Risk Charge (counterparty default, reinsurer insolvency); C4 = Operational Risk Charge (system failures, fraud, legal risk). The combination formula f(·) applies diversification adjustments: the total risk charge is less than the arithmetic sum of individual charges because risks are not perfectly correlated. NAICOM specifies the diversification methodology in its RBC implementation guidelines. 24.5.3 The Supervisory Intervention Ladder NIIRA 2025 establishes a graduated supervisory intervention framework keyed to the insurer’s solvency ratio. The intervention ladder defines the supervisory actions available to NAICOM at defined solvency ratio thresholds: Solvency Ratio Band Status NAICOM Supervisory Response Insurer Obligations ≥ 130% Strong / Green Zone Normal supervisory engagement; standard reporting cycle. Maintain risk management framework; complete ORSA annually; submit quarterly returns. 110%–129% Adequate / Watch List Enhanced monitoring; increased reporting frequency; NAICOM may request additional information on capital management plan. Submit capital management plan; report any further deterioration within 5 business days; no new significant capital commitments without NAICOM notification. 100%–109% Threshold / Yellow Zone Formal supervisory review; NAICOM meeting with Board and management; capital restoration plan required within 30 days. Submit capital restoration plan; cease dividend payments; cease material new business expansion; report to Board Risk Committee at every meeting. 80%–99% Deficiency / Orange Zone Intensive supervision; NAICOM may appoint a special examiner; major actions require prior NAICOM approval. Immediate NAICOM notification; management action plan within 14 days; suspension of new business writing may be directed; operational restrictions. < 80% Critical / Red Zone NAICOM may take control: appoint administrator; transfer portfolio to a solvent insurer; commence wind-down proceedings. Company is effectively under NAICOM control; directors’ governance powers are suspended for material decisions; policyholder protection measures activated.

t: Chapter 24 · 24.6 Solvency II as Global Benchmark
x: 24.6.1 The Solvency II Framework Solvency II is the European Union’s risk-based insurance regulatory framework, which came into full force in January 2016 for all EU-domiciled insurers. It is widely regarded as the most sophisticated and comprehensive insurance solvency regulation framework in the world, and it has served as the primary international benchmark for insurance regulatory reform globally, including in Nigeria. Solvency II is structured around three pillars: Pillar 1: Quantitative Requirements The technical provisions (equivalent to the actuarial reserve) and the Solvency Capital Requirement (SCR) — the risk-sensitive capital charge — and the Minimum Capital Requirement (MCR) — the absolute floor below which licence revocation is triggered. All are calculated on a market-consistent basis. This pillar is the direct precursor to NIIRA 2025’s RBC framework. Pillar 2: Governance and Risk Management Qualitative requirements covering corporate governance, the ORSA, internal controls, the actuarial function, the risk management system, the compliance function, and the internal audit function. NIIRA 2025’s governance requirements for the Board, the ALCO, the CRO, and the ORSA are directly aligned with Solvency II’s Pillar 2. Pillar 3: Reporting and Disclosure Public disclosure requirements (the Solvency and Financial Condition Report — SFCR) and supervisory reporting requirements (the Regular Supervisory Report — RSR). NIIRA 2025’s expanded regulatory reporting obligations reflect Pillar 3’s transparency agenda. 24.6.2 The Nigerian Adaptation NIIRA 2025’s RBC framework adapts the Solvency II model for the Nigerian market’s specific characteristics. The principal adaptations are: the risk factors in the RBC risk charges are calibrated to Nigerian (rather than European) mortality, investment, and operational risk experience; the minimum capital thresholds (absolute floors) reflect the Nigerian insurance market’s scale; the implementation timeline is phased to allow Nigerian insurers to build the actuarial, risk management, and IT infrastructure required for full compliance; and the proportionality principle — smaller insurers face less onerous Pillar 2 and 3 requirements than large composite groups — is adapted to the size distribution of the Nigerian market. The most significant gap between Solvency II and the current NIIRA 2025 framework is in the market-consistency of the liability valuation: Solvency II requires technical provisions to be calculated on a market-consistent basis using risk-free discount rates, producing liability values that are highly sensitive to market interest rate movements. NIIRA 2025 has not yet fully adopted this market-consistent valuation approach, retaining elements of the historical actuarial basis while moving toward IFRS 17’s current-value measurement for financial reporting purposes.

t: Chapter 24 · 24.7 Financial Reporting Obligations under NIIRA 2025
x: 24.7.1 IFRS-Based Reporting Requirement NIIRA 2025 requires all licensed Nigerian life insurers to prepare their financial statements in accordance with International Financial Reporting Standards (IFRS) as adopted in Nigeria by the Financial Reporting Council of Nigeria (FRC). This requirement aligns Nigerian insurance financial reporting with global best practice and ensures that the financial statements of Nigerian life insurers are prepared on a basis that is comparable with international peers. The principal IFRS standards relevant to Nigerian life insurance financial reporting are: IFRS 17 (Insurance Contracts — addressed in Section 24.9); IFRS 9 (Financial Instruments — governing the measurement of the investment portfolio); IAS 19 (Employee Benefits — covering staff pension obligations); IAS 36 (Impairment of Assets); and IFRS 16 (Leases). The introduction of IFRS 17 represents the most significant change in insurance financial reporting in the history of the industry, and its implementation is a major strategic and operational project for Nigerian life insurers. 24.7.2 Mandatory Actuarial Investigation NIIRA 2025 requires every licensed life insurer to commission a mandatory annual actuarial investigation of its financial condition, to be conducted by or under the oversight of the Statutory Actuary and reported to NAICOM within four months of the financial year end. The mandatory actuarial investigation is distinct from — though closely related to — the annual IFRS 17 liability measurement: IFRS 17 measurement: Produces the liability figures used in the insurer’s published IFRS financial statements, prepared on a market-consistent, current-value basis for the purpose of financial reporting comparability. Statutory actuarial investigation: Produces the Statutory Actuary’s professional opinion on the adequacy of the insurer’s provisions to meet all future policyholder obligations, prepared on a prudent actuarial basis for the purpose of regulatory solvency assessment. The Statutory Actuary’s certificate, attesting to the adequacy of reserves, is a required component of the NAICOM annual return. The Statutory Actuary has a direct reporting obligation to NAICOM and must report material concerns about the adequacy of the insurer’s financial condition directly to NAICOM, independently of management, where necessary. 24.7.3 Dividend Restrictions under NIIRA 2025 NIIRA 2025: Dividend Payment Restrictions A Nigerian life insurer may not pay a dividend to its shareholders without first satisfying the following conditions: The solvency ratio (as calculated under the RBC framework) must be at or above the NAICOM minimum threshold after the proposed dividend payment. The Statutory Actuary must have issued an unqualified actuarial certificate confirming that the policy reserves are adequate. The external auditor must have issued an unqualified (or qualified only for non-material matters) audit report on the financial statements. NAICOM approval must be obtained before a dividend is paid where: the insurer’s solvency ratio is below 130%; the insurer has received any NAICOM supervisory direction or finding in the relevant year; or the proposed dividend exceeds a defined percentage of the insurer’s distributable profits (NAICOM specifies the threshold in its guidelines). Prohibition on dividend payment: A life insurer may not pay any dividend if: its solvency ratio is below 100%; it has received a NAICOM direction requiring it to improve its capital position; or the Statutory Actuary has issued a qualified or adverse actuarial certificate. Rationale: Dividend restrictions ensure that policyholders’ funds are not returned to shareholders when the insurer needs capital to meet its future obligations. The requirement for NAICOM approval above the minimum threshold creates a supervisory checkpoint that catches situations where the insurer is technically solvent but its solvency margin is insufficient to bear the proposed dividend withdrawal.

t: Chapter 24 · 24.8 Quarterly and Annual Regulatory Returns
x: 24.8.1 Overview of the Reporting Cycle Nigerian life insurers are required to submit a comprehensive suite of regulatory returns to NAICOM on defined timelines. These returns are the primary mechanism through which NAICOM monitors the financial condition, solvency, market conduct, and operational performance of each licensed insurer. The accuracy, completeness, and timeliness of regulatory returns is both a compliance obligation and a governance indicator: insurers with consistently late, incomplete, or inaccurate returns attract enhanced supervisory attention. Return Frequency Filing Deadline Key Contents Quarterly Financial Returns Quarterly 45 days after quarter end Unaudited income statement; balance sheet; premium and claims statistics by product class; solvency ratio update; investment schedule and coverage ratio. Quarterly Investment Return Quarterly 45 days after quarter end Full investment schedule by asset class and instrument; admissibility classification; coverage ratio; duration gap calculation; related-party investment disclosures. Quarterly Market Conduct Return Quarterly 45 days after quarter end Complaint statistics by category; claims settlement time performance; agent licensing compliance; any NAICOM findings and remediation status. Annual Report and Accounts Annual 4 months after financial year end (or as extended by FRC) Audited IFRS financial statements; Directors’ report; Corporate governance report; Actuarial certificate. Annual NAICOM Return Annual 4 months after financial year end Comprehensive financial return in NAICOM’s prescribed format; actuarial valuation report and certificate; ORSA report; investment policy compliance report. Annual AML/CFT Return Annual As specified by NAICOM and NFIU KYC compliance statistics; STR filings; PEP transactions; training completion rates for AML/CFT. ORSA Report Annual (minimum) 6 months after financial year end Own Risk and Solvency Assessment as described in Chapter 15: risk profile, stress tests, capital projections, management actions. Material Event Notification Ad hoc Immediately (within 24–48 hours) Any material event: solvency ratio breach; large single loss; significant litigation; director resignation or misconduct; data breach; regulatory action in another jurisdiction. 24.8.2 Consequences of Late or Inaccurate Filing NIIRA 2025: Penalties for Non-Compliance with Regulatory Reporting Late filing, incomplete filing, or materially inaccurate filing of NAICOM regulatory returns attracts the following consequences under NIIRA 2025: Financial penalty: Fines of up to ₦500,000 per day for each day a required return is outstanding beyond the filing deadline. Escalated supervision: Persistent late filing triggers placement on NAICOM’s enhanced supervision list, requiring more frequent engagement and potentially a special examination. Director liability: Where late or inaccurate filing is found to have been deliberate — particularly where inaccurate returns misrepresented the insurer’s solvency position — directors responsible for the filing may face personal sanctions. Licence implications: Systemic or serious reporting failures are a factor in NAICOM’s licence renewal assessment. An insurer with a persistent reporting compliance deficit risks non-renewal.

t: Chapter 24 · 24.9 IFRS 17 Insurance Contracts: Implications for Nigerian Life Insurers
x: 24.9.1 From IFRS 4 to IFRS 17 IFRS 4 (Insurance Contracts), which preceded IFRS 17, was widely regarded as an interim standard — it permitted insurers to continue using their existing national accounting methods for insurance liabilities, producing financial statements that were not comparable across jurisdictions or even across insurers within the same market. This lack of comparability was a significant concern for investors, analysts, and regulators who needed to assess and compare insurance company financial strength. IFRS 17, effective for annual periods beginning on or after 1 January 2023 (with a one-year deferral to 2024 for some insurers), replaces IFRS 4 with a comprehensive, current-value-based measurement standard that applies consistently to all insurance contracts globally. Under IFRS 17, insurance liabilities are no longer measured at their original pricing basis (as under IFRS 4) but at the present value of all future cash flows, discounted using current market-consistent rates, with a risk adjustment for non-financial risk and a Contractual Service Margin (CSM) representing deferred unearned profit. 24.9.2 The IFRS 17 Measurement Models IFRS 17 provides three measurement models for insurance contracts, applied depending on the nature of the contracts: Model Applicable To Key Features Nigerian Life Insurance Application General Measurement Model (GMM) / Building Block Approach (BBA) All insurance contracts as the default model. Three building blocks: (1) Present Value of Future Cash Flows (PVFCF); (2) Risk Adjustment (RA) for non-financial risk; (3) Contractual Service Margin (CSM). Total carrying value = PVFCF + RA + CSM. Applicable to all individual life, group life, and annuity contracts that do not qualify for a simpler model. Requires full actuarial cash flow modelling for each policy cohort. Premium Allocation Approach (PAA) Short-duration contracts where the coverage period is one year or less. Simplified approach: liability for remaining coverage = unearned premium; liability for incurred claims = best estimate of claims obligations. Analogous to the approach used for general insurance. Applicable to annual renewable term assurance and group life with one-year coverage periods. Significantly simpler to implement than BBA. Variable Fee Approach (VFA) Direct participating contracts — products where policyholders have a substantial share of a clearly identified pool of underlying items. Contractual Service Margin adjusts for changes in the fair value of the underlying items. Reflects the policyholder’s right to participate in investment returns. Applicable to participating endowment and whole life products where the policyholder’s benefit is directly linked to the with-profit fund’s investment performance. 24.9.3 The Contractual Service Margin (CSM) The CSM is one of the most distinctive features of IFRS 17 and represents a fundamental change in how insurance profit is recognised. Under IFRS 4, profit on a life insurance contract could be recognised immediately at inception (the ‘day one gain’) even though the insurance services had not yet been provided. Under IFRS 17, any profit embedded in the contract at inception is deferred into the CSM and released into income progressively over the coverage period as insurance services are provided. The CSM has the following characteristics: it is calculated at contract inception as the amount that, when added to the PVFCF and the RA, makes the total opening liability equal to the premium received (no day one gain is recognised); it is updated each period for changes in estimates of future cash flows that relate to future service; it is released into income as the insurer provides insurance coverage (based on coverage units); and a negative CSM (which would arise if the contract is onerous from inception) is recognised immediately in the income statement as a loss. The CSM is a key metric for analysing an insurer’s embedded profitability: a growing CSM indicates profitable new business is being written and retained; a shrinking CSM indicates the opposite. For Nigerian life insurers, the CSM provides a more transparent and forward-looking measure of the value of the in-force book than the traditional embedded value metrics previously used. 24.9.4 IFRS 17 Implementation Challenges for Nigerian Life Insurers The implementation of IFRS 17 is a multi-year transformation programme for most Nigerian life insurers. The principal implementation challenges are: Data quality: IFRS 17 requires granular, cohort-level policy data going back to the inception of every in-force contract. Many Nigerian insurers have legacy data in formats, systems, and paper records that are not IFRS 17-ready. Data remediation — the process of cleaning, reconstructing, and validating historical policy data — is often the longest and most expensive component of IFRS 17 implementation. Actuarial modelling capability: The PVFCF calculation under BBA requires a full actuarial cash flow model for every product group, incorporating current-value assumptions for mortality, lapses, expenses, and investment returns. This is a significant step up in actuarial modelling sophistication from the traditional prospective reserve calculation. Systems and technology: IFRS 17 calculations produce volumes of data — per-cohort PVFCF, RA, CSM, and their components — that cannot be managed in Excel-based models. A dedicated IFRS 17 calculation engine (either a commercial actuarial system or a custom-built platform) is required for any insurer above a minimal size. Finance and actuarial integration: Under IFRS 4, the finance and actuarial functions operated largely independently: the actuary calculated reserves; the finance team incorporated the reserve figure into the accounts. Under IFRS 17, the two functions must work on a single, integrated model that produces both the IFRS financial statements and the actuarial liability assessments simultaneously.

24.10.1 The Anti-Fraud Governance Framework Insurance fraud is addressed in Chapter 12 from a claims management perspective. From a corporate governance perspective, the Board is responsible for ensuring that the insurer has an adequate anti-fraud framework that addresses all categories of fraud risk: external fraud (policyholders, claimants, and third parties); internal fraud (employees and agents); and management fraud (manipulation of financial results, misappropriation of premium income, or deliberate misrepresentation to NAICOM). The anti-fraud governance framework in a Nigerian life insurer comprises: Anti-fraud policy: A Board-approved policy that defines fraud, sets out the insurer’s zero-tolerance approach, specifies the controls in place to prevent and detect fraud, and outlines the consequences of fraud (including criminal referral). Anti-fraud controls: Segregation of duties in premium collection, claims payment, and investment management; dual authorisation for significant transactions; independent audit of high-risk processes; automated exception reporting for anomalous transactions. Fraud risk assessment: An annual fraud risk assessment conducted by the internal audit or risk function, identifying the insurer’s most significant fraud exposures and assessing the adequacy of existing controls. Special Investigations Unit (SIU): A dedicated investigation function for claims fraud and internal fraud cases, operating independently of the claims approval and finance functions. Fraud reporting to the Board: Quarterly fraud statistics — claims fraud detected, internal fraud incidents, investigation outcomes, and financial losses — reported to the Board Audit Committee. Material fraud events (above a defined financial threshold or involving senior staff) are reported to the full Board. 24.10.2 Whistleblowing Framework Whistleblowing The act of reporting by a person (an employee, agent, contractor, or other insider) of suspected wrongdoing, illegal activity, unethical conduct, or regulatory non-compliance within the organisation to an appropriate internal or external authority. A whistleblowing framework is the institutional system that: enables such reporting; protects the reporter from retaliation; ensures reports are investigated; and ensures that NAICOM is notified where required. NIIRA 2025 requires licensed Nigerian life insurers to establish a formal whistleblowing framework, including: Multiple reporting channels: At least one anonymous reporting channel (a dedicated whistleblowing hotline, an online reporting portal, or an independent third-party reporting service) that does not require the reporter to identify themselves. Non-retaliation guarantee: A formal commitment by the Board that employees, agents, and contractors who make good-faith reports of suspected wrongdoing will not face retaliation (dismissal, demotion, harassment, or any other adverse consequence). Retaliation against a whistleblower is a serious governance failure and, under NIIRA 2025, a regulatory breach. Independent investigation: All whistleblowing reports must be independently investigated — not by the person or function implicated in the report. The Board Audit Committee must receive summaries of all material whistleblowing reports and their investigation outcomes. NAICOM notification: Where a whistleblowing investigation reveals a material regulatory breach (a significant misrepresentation in a NAICOM return, fraud by a senior officer, or a material consumer protection failure), the insurer is required to notify NAICOM even if the matter has been remediated internally. A whistleblowing culture in which employees are genuinely comfortable reporting concerns is one of the most effective early warning systems available to the Board and to NAICOM. Many of the most serious governance failures in financial institutions globally — misrepresented solvency positions, concealed investment losses, claims fraud by senior management — were known to junior employees long before they came to the attention of the Board or the regulator. An effective whistleblowing system is the channel through which this knowledge travels upward before irreversible harm is done.

t: Chapter 24 · 24.11 Advisory: Building a Governance-First Culture in Nigerian Life Insurance
x: Corporate governance is not a compliance exercise. It is the foundation of the institutional trust on which the entire insurance business model rests. A Board that treats governance as a regulatory obligation to be minimally satisfied — appointing INEDs who ask no difficult questions, commissioning actuarial reports that are never read, filing regulatory returns that are completed without understanding — is not governing a life insurance company. It is providing a veneer of governance while exposing policyholders and the institution to unmanaged risks. Advisory: The Governance Health Checklist for a Nigerian Life Insurance Board The following questions should be asked by every Board member of a Nigerian life insurer at every Board meeting. A Board that cannot answer all these questions with current, specific data is not governing effectively: What is our current solvency ratio, and how has it changed since the last Board meeting? What is the trend over the past four quarters? Has the Statutory Actuary raised any concerns or qualifications in the most recent actuarial report? What was the Board’s response? What is the current duration gap between our asset portfolio and our liability portfolio, and is it within the tolerance approved in our investment policy? How many customer complaints did we receive last quarter? What are the top three complaint categories, and what management actions are being taken? What is our 13-month persistency rate by product and channel, and how does it compare to our pricing assumptions? What actions is management taking on any channels below target? Have there been any material regulatory findings, NAICOM correspondence, or NAICOM meeting requests in the past quarter? What is the status of any required responses? Has the whistleblowing framework received any reports in the past quarter? What were the outcomes of investigations? What is the status of the IFRS 17 implementation programme? Are we on schedule for the next reporting milestone? The Single Most Important Governance Investment for a Nigerian Life Insurer If a Board can make only one governance investment, it should invest in the quality and independence of its Board Audit Committee and in the direct access of the Statutory Actuary and the Chief Audit Executive to that committee. The most serious governance failures in insurance — concealed solvency deterioration, misrepresented reserves, fraudulent financial statements — invariably involve the circumvention of the Audit Committee’s independent oversight. An Audit Committee whose INED members genuinely understand insurance financial reporting; whose actuary presents independently (not through the CEO); whose internal auditor reports directly to the committee chair rather than to management; and whose external auditor is questioned rigorously on valuation assumptions is the most powerful deterrent to management fraud and financial misrepresentation available in the governance framework.

Corporate Governance The system of structures, processes, rules, and practices by which a company is directed and controlled, ensuring accountability to shareholders, policyholders, regulators, and the broader public. Independent Non-Executive Director (INED) A Board director who is independent of management and major shareholders, having no material business relationship with the company and no employment or family ties to executive directors or senior managers. INEDs provide objective challenge and oversight. Fit and Proper Requirement The regulatory standard requiring persons in controlled functions to be competent (‘fit’) and of good character (‘proper’). Applied by NAICOM to all Board directors, the CEO, CFO, CRO, Statutory Actuary, and other key function holders. Controlled Function A senior management or governance role in a licensed insurer that carries material responsibility and is therefore subject to NAICOM’s fit and proper assessment before appointment. Risk-Based Capital (RBC) A capital adequacy framework in which the required capital is calculated as a function of the insurer’s specific risk exposures, rather than as a fixed absolute amount. Introduced for Nigerian life insurers by NIIRA 2025. Solvency Ratio Total Available Capital divided by the Total Risk Charge under the RBC framework. A ratio above 100% indicates solvency; the supervisory intervention ladder defines escalating NAICOM responses as the ratio falls. Supervisory Intervention Ladder A graduated framework of NAICOM supervisory actions keyed to defined solvency ratio bands, from enhanced monitoring at 110–129% through NAICOM taking operational control below 80%. Solvency II The European Union’s comprehensive risk-based insurance regulatory framework, effective January 2016, structured around three pillars (quantitative capital requirements, governance and risk management, reporting and disclosure). Serves as the primary international benchmark for NIIRA 2025’s RBC framework. IFRS 17 (Insurance Contracts) The International Financial Reporting Standard that replaced IFRS 4 for insurance contract accounting, effective January 2023. Requires insurance liabilities to be measured at current value using three measurement models: BBA/GMM, PAA, and VFA. General Measurement Model (GMM / BBA) The default IFRS 17 measurement model, comprising three building blocks: Present Value of Future Cash Flows (PVFCF), Risk Adjustment (RA), and Contractual Service Margin (CSM). Contractual Service Margin (CSM) Under IFRS 17, the deferred profit embedded in an insurance contract at inception, released into income progressively over the coverage period as insurance services are provided. A growing CSM indicates profitable new business. Premium Allocation Approach (PAA) The simplified IFRS 17 measurement model applicable to short-duration contracts (annual renewable term, group life), analogous to the unearned premium reserve approach used for general insurance. Variable Fee Approach (VFA) The IFRS 17 measurement model for direct participating contracts where policyholders share in the returns of a clearly identified pool of underlying items. CSM adjusts for changes in the fair value of the underlying items. Mandatory Actuarial Investigation The annual review of a life insurer’s financial condition required by NIIRA 2025, conducted by the Statutory Actuary, producing a prudent-basis assessment of reserve adequacy and the actuarial certificate. Whistleblowing The reporting by an insider of suspected wrongdoing, illegal activity, or regulatory non-compliance. NIIRA 2025 requires a formal whistleblowing framework including anonymous reporting channels and a non-retaliation guarantee. IFRS 9 (Financial Instruments) The IFRS standard governing the measurement of investment portfolios: classification and measurement of financial assets and liabilities; impairment; and hedge accounting. Affects how insurance investment portfolios are valued in IFRS financial statements.

Under NIIRA 2025, the minimum proportion of the Board of a Nigerian life insurer that must be Independent Non-Executive Directors is: One-quarter. One-third. Half. Two-thirds. (B) One-third of the Board. Why (B) is Correct NIIRA 2025 and the NAICOM Corporate Governance Guidelines require that at least one-third of the Board of a licensed insurer must be Independent Non-Executive Directors (INEDs). INEDs are directors who: have no material financial relationship with the insurer beyond their director's fees; were not previously employed by the insurer within the past 3 years; are not connected to the insurer's significant shareholders; and exercise independent judgment. This minimum proportion is designed to ensure that the Board has sufficient independent challenge to management. Why the Others Are Wrong (A) One-quarter would be insufficient to ensure genuine independent oversight — a minority this small can be consistently outvoted by executive and non-independent directors.(C) Half is higher than the NIIRA 2025 minimum — some jurisdictions (e.g., UK corporate governance code) do apply this higher standard, but the Nigerian mandatory minimum is one-third.(D) Two-thirds would effectively require a Board dominated by INEDs — which is not the NIIRA 2025 standard and would be unusual in most insurance governance frameworks globally.

A Nigerian life insurer's solvency ratio is currently 95%. Under NIIRA 2025's supervisory intervention ladder, this ratio places the insurer in: The Green Zone, requiring no specific NAICOM response. The Yellow Zone (Threshold), requiring NAICOM formal supervisory review and a capital restoration plan within 30 days. The Orange Zone (Deficiency), requiring intensive supervision and potentially a NAICOM-appointed special examiner. The Red Zone (Critical), meaning NAICOM may take control of the company. (C) The Orange Zone (Deficiency), requiring intensive supervision and potentially a NAICOM-appointed special examiner. Why (C) is Correct NIIRA 2025's supervisory intervention ladder has four zones:• Green Zone: Solvency ratio ≥ 150% — no specific regulatory action required.• Yellow Zone (Threshold): Solvency ratio 100–149% — NAICOM formal review; capital restoration plan required.• Orange Zone (Deficiency): Solvency ratio 75–99% — intensive NAICOM supervision; special examiner possible; restrictions on new business writing; dividend ban.• Red Zone (Critical): Solvency ratio <75% — NAICOM may appoint an administrator or initiate resolution. At 95%, the insurer is in the Orange Zone — below the minimum solvency ratio of 100% but above the critical threshold. Note: Specific zone boundaries may vary from the above — candidates should confirm the precise thresholds from the NIIRA 2025 implementing regulations. The question as stated expects (C) based on the Orange Zone description most consistent with a 95% solvency ratio below 100%.

The Contractual Service Margin (CSM) under IFRS 17 represents: The present value of future cash flows expected to be received from policyholders. The risk adjustment for non-financial risk in the insurance contract measurement. The deferred profit in an insurance contract at inception, released into income progressively as insurance services are provided. The minimum capital charge required under the RBC framework for insurance risk. (C) The deferred profit in an insurance contract at inception, released into income progressively as insurance services are provided. Why (C) is Correct Under IFRS 17, when an insurance contract is measured at inception and the fulfilment cash flows (present value of future claims and expenses, less present value of future premiums) produce a net gain, this gain is not recognised as immediate profit — it is deferred as the CSM. The CSM is then released into profit as the insurer provides insurance coverage over the coverage period. The CSM is effectively the insurer's deferred new business profit — it represents the economic value of the insurance services the insurer has committed to provide. A positive CSM indicates profitable new business; a negative CSM (which is an onerous contract loss) is recognised immediately in profit. Under NIIRA 2025, a Nigerian life insurer may NOT pay a dividend to shareholders if: The insurer's annual gross written premium income is below a threshold set by NAICOM. Its solvency ratio is below 100%, or the Statutory Actuary has issued a qualified or adverse actuarial certificate. The insurer has not obtained a specific NAICOM licence endorsement for dividend payment. The dividend amount exceeds 50% of the insurer's annual investment income. (B) Its solvency ratio is below 100%, or the Statutory Actuary has issued a qualified or adverse actuarial certificate. Why (B) is Correct NIIRA 2025 imposes two conditions that independently prohibit dividend payment:1. Solvency ratio below 100%: If the insurer's admissible assets are below its total policy liabilities, paying dividends would further reduce the policyholder-backing assets — directly harming life policyholders. The prohibition protects life fund adequacy.2. Qualified/adverse actuarial certificate: If the Statutory Actuary is unable to certify that the life fund's policy liabilities are fully covered by admissible assets, the same policy protection rationale applies — dividends cannot be paid when the actuary has raised material solvency concerns. Why the Others Are Wrong (A) There is no GWP threshold for dividend eligibility under NIIRA 2025.(C) NAICOM does not require a separate licence endorsement for dividend payment — the conditions are solvency-based, not licence-endorsement-based.(D) A 50% investment income cap on dividends does not exist as a NIIRA 2025 rule — the standard is the solvency ratio and actuarial

Solvency II's three-pillar structure covers, in order: Capital requirements; corporate governance and risk management; reporting and disclosure. Actuarial standards; customer conduct; corporate governance. Premium setting; investment management; reinsurance. Financial reporting; taxation; regulatory capital. (A) Capital requirements; corporate governance and risk management; reporting and disclosure. Why (A) is Correct Solvency II's three-pillar structure (which has influenced NIIRA 2025's design) is:Pillar 1: Quantitative capital requirements — the calculation of technical provisions and the Solvency Capital Requirement (SCR) and Minimum Capital Requirement (MCR) using prescribed models.Pillar 2: Governance and risk management — the ORSA, the governance requirements (Board composition, risk management function, actuarial function, internal audit), and supervisory review of the insurer's risk management quality.Pillar 3: Reporting and disclosure — regulatory reporting to the supervisor (RSR) and public disclosure of solvency and financial condition (SFCR). Why the Others Are Wrong (B), (C), and (D) describe topics that appear in insurance regulation but are not the Solvency II three-pillar framework description.
