t: Chapter 25 · 25.1 Introduction: Life Insurance Within the Personal Financial Plan
x: A life insurance policy in isolation is a financial instrument. A life insurance policy within a personal financial plan is a solution. The distinction matters: an instrument sells features (sum assured, premium, maturity benefit); a solution addresses a specific financial risk or objective that the client has identified as a priority. Insurance practitioners who understand personal financial planning can have profoundly different — and far more valuable — conversations with clients than those who understand only insurance products. Personal financial planning is the structured process of helping an individual or family: identify their financial goals and the timeline for each; understand the financial risks that could prevent them from reaching those goals; design a strategy — using savings, insurance, investment, debt management, and tax planning — to address each goal and risk; and implement and regularly review that strategy as life circumstances evolve. Life insurance occupies a specific and irreplaceable niche in the personal financial plan: it is the instrument that addresses the financial consequences of premature death and serious disability — events that savings and investment alone cannot prepare for, because they may occur before the savings have been accumulated. A 30-year-old professional with a young family and a ₦250,000 mortgage cannot save enough in the next two years to replace 20 years of future income if they die. A ₦50,000-per-annum term assurance premium can. This is the insurance gap: the period during which the individual’s financial obligations exceed their accumulated assets, and where life insurance is the only affordable solution. This chapter addresses the full scope of personal financial planning for a Nigerian client: the analytical frameworks for quantifying insurance needs; the planning strategies for protection, savings, retirement, education, and estate; the tax considerations; and the professional role of the financial adviser who coordinates this planning. The chapter is structured to be directly applicable to the financial adviser’s client-facing practice as well as to the examinations that test this knowledge at CIIN level.

t: Chapter 25 · 25.2 Quantifying the Life Insurance Need
x: 25.2.1 The Human Life Value Approach Human Life Value (HLV) The present value of the future stream of income that an individual is expected to generate over their remaining working life, net of their personal consumption and the expenses of earning the income. The HLV represents the financial value of the individual to their dependants — the amount that, if received today in the form of an insurance payout, would make the dependants financially indifferent to the individual’s death. Human Life Value Formula HLV = PV of [Annual Income − Personal Consumption − Income Tax] over remaining working years Where: Annual Income = gross employment or business income; Personal Consumption = the individual’s own share of household expenditure (not the family’s total); Income Tax = estimated tax payable on the income; remaining working years = years to planned retirement age; PV = discounted at an appropriate rate (typically the risk-free rate or an inflation-adjusted rate). Limitation: HLV is a theoretical maximum — the insurable limit of the individual’s economic value. In practice, life insurance sum assureds are calibrated to the family’s specific financial needs (the FNA approach) rather than the gross HLV, which may produce excessively large sums that are unaffordable to insure. Worked Example 25.1 — Human Life Value Calculation Adaeze is 35 years old, earns ₦6,000,000 gross per year, plans to retire at 60, and estimates her personal consumption at 25% of her income. Her effective income tax rate is 15%. The discount rate is 12% p.a. Net contribution to family per year = ₦6,000,000 × (1 − 0.25 − 0.15) = ₦6,000,000 × 0.60 = ₦3,600,000 Remaining working years = 60 − 35 = 25 years HLV = PV of ₦3,600,000/year for 25 years at 12% = ₦3,600,000 × 7.843 = approximately ₦28,234,800 Adaeze’s HLV is approximately ₦28.2 million. This represents the theoretical maximum life cover she could justify on a HLV basis. Her actual insurance need, calculated via FNA, may be lower, reflecting the specific liabilities and obligations of her household. 25.2.2 The Financial Needs Analysis Approach The Financial Needs Analysis (FNA) approach quantifies the insurance requirement by analysing the specific financial obligations that the insured’s dependants would face in the event of their death. Unlike the HLV (which asks ‘what is this person’s total economic value?’), the FNA asks ‘what specific financial needs would this death create, and how much capital would be needed to meet them?.’ The FNA typically produces a more operationally useful insurance sum assured because it is grounded in the client’s specific circumstances. The FNA framework for an individual life insurance client covers: Immediate needs Funeral and final expenses (typically ₦500,000–1,500,000 in the Nigerian market); estate administration costs; outstanding short-term debts (credit cards, overdrafts). Debt clearance needs Outstanding mortgage balance; vehicle finance; personal loans; business loans for which the individual is personally liable. A family that loses its breadwinner should not simultaneously face outstanding debt obligations. Income replacement needs The annual income the family would need to maintain their current standard of living, multiplied by the number of years until the youngest child is financially independent (or until the surviving spouse reaches retirement age, whichever is longer). Typically the largest component of the insurance need. Education funding needs The full cost of each dependent child’s education from the current point to the end of tertiary education, allowing for educational inflation. Particularly significant in the Nigerian context where private secondary and university education is a major expenditure item. Special needs Any specific obligations the insured has: supporting an elderly parent; funding a sibling’s education; providing for a dependent with a disability; a charitable commitment. Existing resources Existing life insurance cover (employer group life, personal policies); savings and investments; property that could be sold or leveraged; CPF pension RSA balance; other anticipated inheritances. Existing resources are deducted from the gross insurance need to determine the net coverage gap. Worked Example 25.2 — Financial Needs Analysis Chukwuemeka, 40, married to Ngozi, 37, two children (ages 8 and 5). He earns ₦9,600,000/year net. Family monthly expenditure is ₦600,000. Mortgage outstanding: ₦18,000,000. Car loan: ₦2,500,000. University cost per child (today’s value): ₦4,000,000 each. His employer provides 3× salary group life (₦28,800,000). He has ₦5,000,000 in savings. Need Category Calculation Amount (₦) Funeral / immediate expenses Estimated 1,200,000 Debt clearance Mortgage + car loan 20,500,000 Income replacement ₦7,200,000/yr (family expenditure × 12) for 18 years (to youngest child age 23) at 10% discount rate: PV = ₦7,200,000 × 8.201 = ₦59,047,200 59,047,200 Education funding 2 × ₦4,000,000 (today’s value, inflated) 10,000,000 Total Gross Need 90,747,200 Less: Group life cover −28,800,000 −28,800,000 Less: Existing savings −5,000,000 −5,000,000 NET INSURANCE GAP 56,947,200 Chukwuemeka’s net insurance gap is approximately ₦57 million. He requires approximately ₦57 million of additional life cover — primarily via a long-term term assurance or whole life policy — to fully protect his family.

t: Chapter 25 · 25.3 Protection Needs: Death, Disability, and Critical Illness
x: 25.3.1 Life Cover: The Foundation of the Personal Financial Plan The life cover need — the sum payable on death — is calculated through the FNA described above. The appropriate product vehicle depends on the nature and duration of the need: Term assurance: The most cost-efficient protection vehicle. Fixed sum assured payable on death within the policy term; no maturity benefit. Appropriate for covering time-limited needs (mortgage balance, income replacement during child-rearing years, business loan cover). Decreasing term assurance is appropriate where the liability being covered declines over time (a repayment mortgage). Whole life assurance: Provides permanent death cover without a policy term. More expensive than term due to the certainty of eventual payment. Appropriate for permanent estate planning needs (providing a fixed sum for estate equalisation or legacy) and for clients who need lifelong dependant support (a child with a disability). Endowment with protection: Combines savings accumulation with life cover. The death benefit provides protection during the savings accumulation period; the maturity benefit delivers the savings objective. Appropriate where the client has both a protection need and a savings goal that can be achieved within the same timeframe. 25.3.2 Disability Cover: Total and Permanent Disability Disability — the loss of the ability to earn income through illness or injury — is statistically a more likely financial risk for most working-age individuals than premature death. Yet disability insurance is dramatically under-purchased relative to life cover in the Nigerian market. The financial impact of a total and permanent disability (TPD) is, in many respects, worse than death from a financial planning perspective: the disabled individual can no longer earn income but still has living expenses, potentially significant medical costs, and may require ongoing care. Total and Permanent Disability (TPD) cover pays a lump sum if the insured is permanently and totally unable to work, typically meeting the same FNA-based need calculation as the life cover (income replacement, debt clearance, and ongoing care costs). The premium for TPD cover is typically offered as a rider to a life policy or as a standalone disability policy. In calculating the disability insurance need, the financial adviser must also consider: whether the employer provides any disability income continuation; the availability of group disability cover; the insured’s savings that could partially fund a disability period; and, for self-employed clients, the impact of disability on the business (which may require separate business interruption or keyman cover). 25.3.3 Critical Illness Cover Critical illness (CI) cover pays a lump sum on the diagnosis of one of a defined list of serious medical conditions: typically cancer, heart attack, stroke, organ failure, and other major conditions. The CI benefit is paid regardless of the insured’s ability to work — unlike income protection insurance, it does not require a loss of earnings test. It is designed to fund the additional costs associated with serious illness: private medical treatment, home modifications, convalescence costs, and the financial burden of extended sick leave. In the Nigerian context, CI cover has a compelling case. Private medical treatment for cancer, cardiac surgery, or organ transplantation can cost tens of millions of Naira; government health infrastructure cannot reliably provide these services; and medical evacuation for specialist treatment abroad — a common recourse for affluent Nigerians with serious illness — is extremely expensive. A CI benefit of ₦10–20 million can be the difference between receiving potentially life-saving treatment and forgoing it.

25.4.1 The Role of Insurance in Savings Planning For many Nigerian clients — particularly those without access to sophisticated investment platforms — savings-linked insurance products represent an accessible, disciplined, and professionally managed savings vehicle. The endowment policy and the whole life policy (with its accumulating cash value) offer the client a combination of contractual savings discipline (the premium payment obligation acts as a forced saving), death protection, and professional investment management. The financial adviser’s role in savings planning is to ensure that the client understands the trade-offs between different savings vehicles: the guaranteed maturity benefit of a participating endowment versus the higher potential returns of a direct equity investment; the surrender value of an endowment if the client needs liquidity before maturity; and the cost of the protection element of a combination product versus a pure savings account. The recommendation must be genuinely suited to the client’s risk tolerance, time horizon, and liquidity needs — not driven by the commission structure of the product. 25.4.2 Comparing Insurance Savings Products with Other Vehicles Vehicle Key Features Best Suited For Main Limitation Participating endowment Contractual savings with guaranteed sum assured; reversionary and terminal bonus; death cover throughout the term. Clients who need forced savings discipline and simultaneous death protection; medium-risk tolerance; defined savings goal (education, retirement supplementation). Surrender value is typically poor in the early years; lower expected return than pure equity investment; long-term commitment. Unit-linked insurance plan (ULIP) Premium split between insurance cost and investment in a unit-linked fund; returns depend on fund performance. Clients with higher risk tolerance seeking market-linked returns with incidental insurance cover; medium-to-long savings horizon. Mortality and expense charges reduce net investment; complexity; performance risk. Fixed deposit / money market fund Short-term interest-bearing account; liquid; no insurance element. Emergency fund; short-term savings goals (1–3 years); low-risk clients. No protection element; inflation erosion of real value; subject to reinvestment risk. Direct equity investment (shares/ETFs) Market-linked capital growth and dividends; high potential return; high volatility. Long-term wealth accumulation; clients with high risk tolerance and investment knowledge; no insurance need. No protection element; high volatility; requires investment sophistication. Treasury bills / FGN bonds Sovereign-guaranteed return; predictable cash flow; no capital growth. Conservative clients; wealth preservation; ALM for clients approaching retirement. No protection element; low real return in high-inflation environment. Real estate investment Capital appreciation and rental income; inflation protection. Wealthy clients with a long time horizon and large lump-sum capital. Illiquid; significant management burden; large minimum investment.

t: Chapter 25 · 25.5 Retirement Planning and the Annuity Decision
x: 25.5.1 The Nigerian Retirement Planning Framework The retirement planning framework for formally employed Nigerians is structured around the Contributory Pension Scheme (CPS) established under the Pension Reform Act 2014. Under the CPS, every employee in the private sector with three or more employees — and all federal public servants — is required to participate in a pension plan funded by contributions from both the employer and the employee. The RSA holder accumulates contributions throughout their working life and draws retirement benefits at or after the age of 50. The CPS is a defined-contribution scheme: the retirement benefit is not guaranteed by the employer or the government, but depends on the accumulated fund value at retirement, which reflects the total contributions made and the investment returns earned by the Pension Fund Administrator (PFA) managing the RSA. This structure places the investment risk squarely on the RSA holder, making the financial adviser’s guidance on retirement income planning critically important. 25.5.2 The Income Replacement Ratio Target Income Replacement Ratio (IRR) The proportion of pre-retirement income that a retiree needs to maintain their desired standard of living in retirement. The IRR is typically lower than 100% because some working-life expenses (mortgage payments that will be cleared by retirement, commuting costs, pension contributions) do not continue in retirement. A commonly targeted IRR in financial planning is 70–80% of final salary, though the appropriate target varies significantly by individual circumstances. For Nigerian professionals, the retirement planning process involves several analytical steps: Project the RSA balance at retirement: Using the current RSA balance, the projected annual contributions (employer + employee contributions = minimum 18% of monthly emoluments under the Pension Reform Act), an assumed net investment return, and the years to retirement, project the likely RSA balance at retirement age. Determine the retirement income need: Apply the IRR target to the client’s current or projected final salary to determine the annual retirement income required. Allow for inflation between today and retirement to express this in future-value terms. Calculate the retirement income gap: Compare the income the projected RSA balance can generate (as a Retirement Life Annuity) with the target retirement income. The gap — if any — is the additional savings required. Design the supplementary savings strategy: If a gap exists, design a savings and investment strategy using voluntary pension contributions (Voluntary Contribution is allowed under the PRA), endowment savings plans, and other investment vehicles to close the gap. 25.5.3 The Annuity Decision at Retirement At retirement, an RSA holder above the defined threshold has two primary benefit options under the Pension Reform Act 2014: a Retirement Life Annuity (RLA) from a NAICOM-licensed life insurer; or a Programmed Withdrawal (PW) from their PFA. The annuity decision is one of the most consequential financial decisions a Nigerian professional will ever make, because it is typically irreversible. The key dimensions of the annuity choice are: Single life vs joint life: A single life annuity pays income for the annuitant’s lifetime only; a joint life annuity continues (at a reduced rate) to the surviving spouse. Married clients should almost always choose joint life cover: the income of the surviving spouse after the annuitant’s death is often the most overlooked planning risk. Level vs escalating: A level annuity pays the same nominal income throughout; an escalating annuity increases annually at a fixed rate or in line with inflation. Given Nigeria’s historical inflation experience, an escalating annuity that maintains real purchasing power is generally preferable to a level annuity that declines in real value over a 20–30 year retirement. Guarantee period: A guarantee period (typically 5–10 years) ensures that if the annuitant dies shortly after commencement, payments continue to the nominated beneficiary for the balance of the guarantee period. Without a guarantee period, the insurer retains the full fund if the annuitant dies in year one. Enhanced annuity: A higher-than-standard annuity rate available to annuitants with diagnosed health conditions that reduce life expectancy (cancer, heart disease, diabetes). An enhanced annuity rate compensates the annuitant for their statistically shorter life expectancy, increasing the monthly income relative to a standard healthy annuity. Many Nigerian retirees who would qualify for enhanced rates are unaware this option exists.

25.6.1 The Education Funding Challenge in Nigeria Education is one of the highest-priority financial objectives for Nigerian parents across all income levels. The cost of quality education in Nigeria — from private secondary school through university, whether domestic or international — is significant and has increased substantially faster than general inflation over the past decade. For a Nigerian parent with a child aged 5, funding a quality secondary and university education requires planning that begins immediately. The specific education funding challenge has three components. The first is the funding adequacy problem: accumulating sufficient capital to pay education fees when they fall due. The second is the death risk: the parent who dies before the child reaches school age has left the education fund entirely unfunded unless insurance is in place. The third is the disability risk: a parent who is seriously disabled and cannot earn income may be unable to continue funding the education savings plan even if they survive. 25.6.2 Designing an Education Funding Strategy A comprehensive education funding strategy for a Nigerian parent integrates: An education endowment policy: A savings-plus-protection product specifically designed for education funding: the policy matures at the projected date of the child’s secondary or university enrolment; if the parent dies or is permanently disabled before maturity, the full maturity benefit is paid immediately (or premiums are waived and the policy continues to maturity). This is the foundational product for education financial planning because it addresses both the savings and the risk objectives simultaneously. A waiver of premium rider: An add-on to the education endowment that waives all future premiums if the parent becomes totally and permanently disabled, while the policy continues to maturity at the original projected benefit. Addresses the disability risk at typically modest additional cost. A supplementary investment account: For parents with surplus savings capacity, a direct investment in Treasury bills, bonds, or a low-cost equity fund to augment the endowment benefit and hedge against educational inflation. Foreign currency component: For parents planning to send their child abroad for university, a portion of the education fund should be held in foreign currency (USD or GBP), either in a foreign currency savings account or through foreign-denominated investments, to hedge against Naira depreciation between today and the date of enrolment.

t: Chapter 25 · 25.7 Tax Treatment of Life Insurance in Nigeria
x: 25.7.1 Premium Tax Treatment Under the Personal Income Tax Act (PITA) as amended, life insurance premiums paid by an individual on a policy insuring their own life or the life of their spouse may be deductible from taxable income, subject to specific qualifying conditions. The key conditions for premium deductibility are: the policy must be a qualifying life insurance policy (a term assurance or endowment — not a pure investment bond); the policyholder must be the insured or the insured’s spouse; and the deduction is subject to a maximum limit. PITA Premium Deduction: Key Conditions Under PITA, life insurance premium payments may be deductible subject to the following conditions: The policy is a qualifying life insurance contract — term assurance, endowment, or annuity; not a pure investment vehicle. The policyholder is paying premiums on a policy insuring their own life or their spouse’s life. The deduction applies to the protection element of the premium; the savings or investment element may not be deductible. The maximum annual deduction amount is set by FIRS; practitioners should confirm the current limit with the FIRS or a tax adviser, as the limit is periodically revised. Practitioner note: Tax legislation is subject to change; the financial adviser must always refer clients to a qualified tax adviser for specific tax guidance. This section provides an overview for planning awareness, not definitive tax advice. 25.7.2 Benefit Tax Treatment The tax treatment of life insurance benefits received by a policyholder or beneficiary in Nigeria is broadly favourable: Death benefit: A death benefit paid to a named beneficiary under a life insurance policy is generally not subject to income tax in the hands of the beneficiary. The benefit is treated as an insurance payout rather than income. However, if the death benefit forms part of the deceased’s estate (i.e., no beneficiary is nominated and the benefit falls into the estate), it may be subject to estate administration and distribution rules. Maturity benefit: The tax treatment of an endowment maturity benefit may depend on whether the policy meets PITA’s qualifying policy criteria. For a qualifying policy held for the full term, the maturity benefit (including accumulated bonuses) is typically received tax-free. Practitioners should advise clients that early surrender of a qualifying policy may affect the tax treatment of the proceeds. Annuity income: Regular annuity payments received under a Retirement Life Annuity are treated as income for tax purposes and are subject to income tax at the annuitant’s applicable marginal rate. The annuitant should be aware that their retirement income, while generally lower than their working income, may still attract income tax above the minimum threshold.

t: Chapter 25 · 25.8 Estate Planning: Wills, Trusts, and Life Insurance
x: 25.8.1 The Estate Planning Imperative Estate planning — the process of arranging the management and distribution of one’s assets during life and at death in accordance with one’s intentions — is a critically important but widely neglected component of personal financial planning in Nigeria. The consequences of dying intestate (without a will) in Nigeria — where the applicable inheritance law may be customary law, statutory law, or Islamic law depending on the state and the individual’s background — can be deeply damaging to the financial security of dependants, particularly widows and children from blended family structures. The financial adviser’s role in estate planning is not to draft legal documents (that requires a solicitor) but to help the client understand their estate planning needs, identify the role that life insurance can play in meeting those needs, and refer them to the appropriate professional advisers for legal and tax implementation. 25.8.2 The Will as the Foundation of the Estate Plan A valid will is the foundational document of the estate plan. It specifies: who receives the testator’s assets on their death; who is responsible for administering the estate (the executor); who should be the guardian of minor children; and any specific bequests (charitable, personal, or family-specific). Without a valid will, the distribution of assets is governed by intestacy rules that may not reflect the individual’s intentions and may create protracted legal disputes. The financial adviser’s estate planning checklist includes confirming that the client has a current, valid will that reflects their current family circumstances (particularly important after marriage, divorce, birth of a child, or acquisition of significant assets); that the will is held by a trusted solicitor or the client’s family members; and that the executors named in the will are willing and capable of administering the estate. 25.8.3 Life Insurance and Estate Planning Life insurance plays several specific roles in estate planning: Estate liquidity: A large estate may include significant illiquid assets (property, business shares, investment portfolios) but have insufficient liquid cash to pay estate administration costs, funeral expenses, and inheritance obligations. A life insurance policy, payable promptly on death, provides the liquid capital needed to avoid the forced sale of estate assets. Estate equalisation: Where the testator wishes to leave equal inheritance to multiple children but their assets (a family business, a property) cannot easily be divided, a life insurance policy can provide the balancing payment. For example: the family business is inherited by the eldest child; a life insurance policy provides equivalent value to the other children. Bypass trusts and policy trusts: Where a life insurance benefit is placed in trust rather than paid directly to a beneficiary, the benefit is paid directly to the trust beneficiaries on the insured’s death, bypassing the estate and its associated administration costs, delays, and potential inheritance disputes. Policy trusts are particularly effective for protecting life insurance benefits for minor children — the trustee manages the benefit until the child reaches the age of majority. 25.8.4 Beneficiary Nomination Rules The beneficiary nominated on a life insurance policy is the person or institution entitled to receive the death benefit. Correct beneficiary nomination is one of the simplest and most important estate planning actions available. The key rules governing beneficiary nomination in Nigerian life insurance are: Nomination effectiveness: A valid beneficiary nomination means the death benefit is paid directly to the nominated beneficiary without passing through the insured’s estate. This avoids probate delay and estate administration fees, and protects the benefit from any claims by the insured’s creditors (subject to specific legal exceptions). Updating nominations: Beneficiary nominations should be reviewed and updated after every major life event: marriage, divorce, birth of a child, death of a previously nominated beneficiary. An outdated nomination — naming a deceased parent or an ex-spouse — creates complications that require legal resolution. Minor beneficiaries: A death benefit cannot be paid directly to a minor (a person under 18). Where a minor is nominated, the insurer must pay the benefit to a legal guardian or into a trust. The financial adviser should ensure that the client has specified a trustee or guardian for any minor beneficiaries.

25.9.1 The HNI Planning Context High-Net-Worth Individuals (HNIs) — broadly defined in the Nigerian market as individuals with investable assets above ₦50 million and annual income above ₦20 million — have insurance and financial planning needs that differ materially from those of the standard working professional. The complexity of their asset base, the scale of their obligations, and the sophistication of their financial objectives require planning tools and products that go beyond the standard retail insurance product range. The principal insurance planning needs of Nigerian HNIs are: 25.9.2 Keyman Insurance Keyman insurance protects a business against the financial loss that results from the death or total disability of a key individual — a founder, CEO, major revenue generator, or specialist whose contribution is central to the business’s financial performance. For an HNI who is the primary driver of their business’s revenues, keyman insurance provides the business with the capital needed to: replace the individual; service business debt; fund a business continuity period while a successor is established; or provide for an orderly wind-down. Keyman insurance is taken out by the business as policyholder and beneficiary; the key person is the life assured; and the sum assured is calculated based on a multiple of the person’s contribution to the business (typically 3–5 times annual profit contribution or annual revenue generated). The premium is a deductible business expense, and the benefit is received by the business as ordinary income (subject to income tax in the business’s hands). 25.9.3 Business Succession Planning Business succession planning addresses the transfer of a business from one generation or ownership structure to the next. For an HNI business owner, the largest asset in their estate is frequently their business interest. Without a succession plan backed by financial instruments, the death of the founder can trigger a business valuation and ownership dispute that destroys the business value their dependants were depending on. Buy-sell agreements — contracts between business partners specifying what happens to each partner’s share of the business on their death or disability — are frequently funded by cross-purchase or entity-purchase life insurance arrangements. In a cross-purchase arrangement, each partner takes out a life insurance policy on the other partners; if Partner A dies, Partner B receives the death benefit and uses it to buy out Partner A’s share from Partner A’s estate at the agreed price. This ensures the business continues uninterrupted and Partner A’s family receives fair value. 25.9.4 Estate Equalisation and Large-Sum Personal Cover HNI clients with complex, multi-asset estates — a combination of property, business interests, financial portfolios, and personal assets — often need large-sum whole life insurance specifically for estate equalisation and legacy planning. The sum assured is calibrated to: provide the liquid capital needed for estate administration without forced asset sales; equalise inheritance across multiple beneficiaries when indivisible assets are involved; fund philanthropic legacies; and maintain the lifestyle of a surviving spouse during the estate administration period. For very large sums (above the capacity of a single insurer), HNI life insurance may be placed as a co-insurance arrangement across multiple Nigerian insurers, or with a combination of domestic and international (Lloyd’s) underwriters, through a specialist broker. The placement mechanics for large individual life risks are described in Chapter 18.

t: Chapter 25 · 25.10 The Financial Adviser’s Role in Personal Financial Planning
x: 25.10.1 The Fact-Find Process The fact-find is the structured information-gathering process through which the financial adviser collects all the information needed to understand the client’s financial position, goals, and risk tolerance before making any recommendations. A thorough fact-find is both a professional obligation (the suitability requirement under NIIRA 2025) and the foundation of genuinely useful advice. A comprehensive personal financial planning fact-find collects: Personal data: name, date of birth, marital status, number and ages of dependants, occupation, employer. Financial position: income (from employment, business, investment), expenditure, savings balances, investment portfolio, property values, outstanding debts. Existing insurance cover: life policies (in force, sum assured, beneficiaries), group life from employer, disability cover, health insurance. Financial goals: protection objectives, savings targets, retirement income target, education funding needs, estate planning intentions. Risk tolerance: ability to bear investment risk; attitude to insurance versus self-insurance; experience with financial products. Health status: material health conditions relevant to life and disability underwriting; smoking status; family health history. Tax position: income tax band; any tax-efficient savings already being used. 25.10.2 The Suitability Obligation and the Personal Financial Plan Having collected the fact-find information, the financial adviser’s obligation is to make recommendations that are genuinely suitable for the client’s specific circumstances. The suitability obligation (described in Chapter 21 as a market conduct requirement) is the technical expression of what good financial planning practice requires: recommending what the client needs, not what generates the highest commission. A personal financial plan should be a written document that: summarises the client’s current financial position and the key risks it exposes; sets out the recommended strategy to address each risk and goal; identifies the specific products recommended (with the rationale for each); sets out the associated costs and expected outcomes; and specifies the review schedule. The plan must be signed by both the client and the adviser, and a copy retained in the client file for regulatory inspection purposes. 25.10.3 The Continuing Review Responsibility A personal financial plan is not a one-time transaction. Circumstances change — income increases, children are born, mortgages are paid off, health conditions change, businesses are sold, retirement approaches — and the plan must be reviewed and updated to remain relevant. The financial adviser’s continuing review responsibility includes: an annual review of the client’s financial position against the plan; a re-assessment of the insurance coverage gap; a review of beneficiary nominations; and an update of the savings projections against the retirement and education funding targets. The continuing review relationship is also the primary defence against a mis-selling claim: a client who has received regular, documented, suitability-assessed advice that evolves appropriately as their circumstances change is a satisfied client who refers colleagues and family members. A client who was sold a policy twelve years ago and never heard from the adviser again is a potential complainant and a potential lapsed policyholder.

Personal Financial Planning The structured process of helping an individual or family identify financial goals, understand the risks that could prevent them from reaching those goals, and design and implement a strategy using savings, insurance, investment, debt management, and tax planning to address each goal and risk. Human Life Value (HLV) The present value of the future stream of income an individual is expected to generate over their remaining working life, net of personal consumption and income tax, representing the financial value of the individual to their dependants. Financial Needs Analysis (FNA) An approach to quantifying the life insurance requirement by analysing the specific financial obligations the insured’s dependants would face on their death, including immediate expenses, debt clearance, income replacement, and education funding, less existing resources. Insurance Gap The period during which an individual’s financial obligations exceed their accumulated assets, making life insurance the only affordable way to provide financial security to dependants in the event of premature death. Income Replacement Ratio (IRR) The proportion of pre-retirement income a retiree needs to maintain their desired standard of living in retirement. Typically targeted at 70–80% of final salary. Retirement Life Annuity (RLA) A life annuity purchased with RSA funds under the Contributory Pension Scheme, providing a guaranteed income for the life of the annuitant and optionally a surviving spouse. Enhanced Annuity A life annuity paying a higher-than-standard income to an annuitant with a diagnosed medical condition that reduces life expectancy, compensating for the shorter statistical lifetime. Education Endowment Policy A savings-plus-protection product specifically designed for education funding, maturing at the projected date of the child’s school enrolment and providing the full maturity benefit immediately if the parent dies or is permanently disabled before maturity. Waiver of Premium Rider An add-on to an insurance policy that waives all future premiums if the policyholder becomes totally and permanently disabled, while the policy continues to maturity at the original projected benefit. Keyman Insurance Life or disability insurance taken out by a business on the life of a key individual whose death or disability would materially harm the business, providing the capital to replace the individual, service debt, or fund business continuity. Estate Planning The process of arranging the management and distribution of one’s assets during life and at death in accordance with one’s intentions, using wills, trusts, beneficiary nominations, and life insurance to protect dependants and manage the tax and administrative consequences of death. Estate Equalisation A life insurance strategy used when a testator wishes to leave equal inheritance to multiple children but their assets cannot easily be divided, with the life insurance providing a balancing cash payment to children who do not receive the indivisible asset. Buy-Sell Agreement A legal contract between business partners specifying the terms under which a deceased or disabled partner’s business interest is transferred to the surviving partners, typically funded by cross-purchase or entity-purchase life insurance. Cross-Purchase Life Insurance A buy-sell funding arrangement in which each business partner purchases a life insurance policy on the other partners; on death, the surviving partners use the proceeds to buy out the deceased partner’s share from their estate. Beneficiary Nomination The designation by a policyholder of the person(s) entitled to receive the death benefit, enabling direct payment to the nominee without passing through the insured’s estate. Fact-Find The structured information-gathering process through which a financial adviser collects all information needed to understand a client’s financial position, goals, and risk tolerance before making any recommendations.

In estate planning, the primary advantage of naming a beneficiary on a life insurance policy (rather than leaving the benefit to pass through the estate) is: The death benefit becomes tax-free in all circumstances. The death benefit is paid directly to the beneficiary without passing through the estate, avoiding probate delay and estate administration costs, and protecting the benefit from certain creditor claims. The policyholder can change the beneficiary designation after their death. NAICOM requires all life insurance policies to have a named beneficiary. (B) The death benefit is paid directly to the beneficiary without passing through the estate, avoiding probate delay and estate administration costs, and protecting the benefit from certain creditor claims. Why (B) is Correct A named beneficiary on a life policy means the death benefit passes directly to that beneficiary without being included in the deceased's estate — it does not go through the probate process. This delivers multiple advantages:1. Speed: The beneficiary receives payment within days or weeks of death notification, without waiting for probate (which in Nigeria can take years).2. Cost: Estate administration and legal fees (which can amount to 5–10% of estate value) are not applied to the insurance benefit.3. Privacy: The payment is not part of the public estate record.4. Creditor protection: In most circumstances, life insurance proceeds payable to a named beneficiary are protected from the deceased's creditors — the creditors have a claim against the estate, not against the insurance proceeds.
