t: Chapter 26 · 26.1 Introduction: The Revenue Architecture of a Life Insurer
x: Understanding how a life insurance company generates, manages, and sustains its revenue is fundamental to managing the business strategically. A life insurer is not a single-revenue-stream business: it simultaneously earns premium income, investment income, fee income, and reinsurance recoveries, and each of these streams has its own dynamics, drivers, risks, and management levers. The CEO who understands only premium growth — and not the investment yield, the expense ratio, or the embedded value — is managing a fraction of the business with the tools of a different sector. The concept of revenue architecture describes the complete map of an insurer’s income sources, their relative sizes, their interdependencies, and the management disciplines required to sustain and grow each. For a Nigerian life insurer operating in a market with high nominal yields, strong premium growth potential, but also high expense ratios, agent commission costs, and early lapse rates, the revenue architecture analysis is the starting point for every significant strategic and financial decision. This chapter addresses revenue architecture at the level of detail required for both examination purposes and professional practice. It covers the mechanics of premium income, investment income, fee income, the profit sources framework, embedded value, new business value, financial planning and budgeting, and revenue diversification. Together these provide the financial management foundation for the strategy work addressed in Chapter 27.

26.2.1 Gross Written Premium, Net Written Premium, and Net Earned Premium Gross Written Premium (GWP) The total premium income billed by the insurer to policyholders during the accounting period, before any deduction for reinsurance premiums ceded to reinsurers. GWP is the headline measure of the insurer’s premium generating activity and market share. Under IFRS 17, the concept of GWP is replaced by insurance revenue, but GWP remains widely used for management reporting and market statistics. Reinsurance Premium Ceded The portion of the GWP paid to reinsurers in exchange for their acceptance of a defined share of the insurer’s risk. For a life insurer with a quota share reinsurance treaty at 40%, 40% of every premium received is ceded to the reinsurer. Reinsurance cessions reduce the insurer’s net premium income but also reduce its net claims liability. Net Written Premium (NWP) GWP minus reinsurance premium ceded. Represents the portion of the written premium that the insurer retains for its own account. NWP is the premium income base on which the insurer’s own financial performance is assessed. Unearned Premium Reserve (UPR) The portion of written premium that relates to future coverage periods within the policy year. For a 12-month policy for which the annual premium was received on 1 October, 9 months of premium is ‘unearned’ at 31 December. Under IFRS 17’s PAA model, the UPR is called the liability for remaining coverage. Net Earned Premium (NEP) NWP adjusted for the movement in the UPR. NEP represents the premium that has been ‘earned’ by providing coverage during the period. For life products with multi-year coverage, the earned premium concept is central to the technical account. 26.2.2 Premium Income Drivers The premium income of a Nigerian life insurer is driven by four variables that management must track, model, and actively manage: New business premium: The annualised first-year premium (AFYP) on policies issued in the period. New business premium reflects the productivity of the distribution channels, the appeal of the product range, and the effectiveness of marketing. It is the fuel that powers premium income growth. In-force book persistency: The proportion of the existing policy portfolio that remains in force and continues to pay premiums. A persistency rate of 80% at 13 months means that 20% of the policies written 13 months ago have already lapsed, taking their renewal premiums with them. High persistency is the second engine of premium income growth; low persistency is the most insidious premium income destroyer. Renewal premium rate: For annually renewable products (group life, annual term), the premium rate on renewal affects the total renewal premium income. Market competition, claims experience, and investment return changes all affect renewal rates. Portfolio reinsurance programme: The proportion of premium ceded under reinsurance treaties directly determines net written premium. An insurer that cedes 50% of all premiums under a quota share treaty is building a reinsurer’s business as much as its own. 26.2.3 The Technical Account The technical account is the income statement presentation of the insurer’s insurance underwriting result — the profit or loss attributable to the insurance operations before investment income. It is the key internal management report for evaluating whether the underwriting activity (pricing, risk selection, claims management) is generating a positive contribution before the investment return. Illustrative Life Insurance Technical Account Structure The following structure represents a simplified technical account for a Nigerian life insurer (management reporting basis): Line Item Notes (+) Gross Written Premium Total premium billed in the period. (−) Reinsurance premium ceded Premium paid to reinsurers. = Net Written Premium (±) Change in Unearned Premium Reserve Movement in UPR (or liability for remaining coverage under IFRS 17). = Net Earned Premium The base for the underwriting account. (−) Net claims incurred Claims paid + change in outstanding claims reserve, net of reinsurance recoveries. (−) Change in life policy reserves Movement in actuarial reserves; the primary technical account outflow for long-term life products. (−) Commission and distribution expenses Agent FYC, renewal commission, bancassurance commission, broker brokerage. (−) Operating expenses allocated to underwriting Staff costs, IT, office costs, and marketing allocated to the insurance function. = Technical Result (Underwriting Result) Profit or loss from insurance operations before investment income. (+) Investment income attributed to insurance funds Investment income earned on the reserves and other insurance liabilities. = Overall Insurance Operating Result The combined technical and investment result from insurance operations.

26.3.1 Structure of Investment Income Investment income is the second major revenue stream of a life insurer, and for long-term life products (endowments, annuities, whole life), it can exceed premium income in a mature portfolio. Investment income in life insurance has two components: recurring income (interest, dividends, and rental income from the investment portfolio) and capital gains (realised gains on the sale of investment assets and, under IFRS 9, unrealised fair value movements on certain asset classes). Component Source Nature Management Lever Coupon / interest income FGN bonds, corporate bonds, money market deposits, policy loans. Recurring; predictable; contractual. Portfolio duration; credit quality; reinvestment strategy; yield enhancement through credit selection. Dividend income Listed equities (NGX). Variable; linked to corporate earnings and payout policy. Equity selection; portfolio concentration management; dividend reinvestment policy. Rental income Direct property investments. Recurring; contractual (subject to tenancy terms); inflation-linked over time. Property selection; tenant management; occupancy rate; rent review timing. Realised capital gains Sale of investments above book value. Non-recurring; triggered by portfolio rebalancing or liquidity needs. Active portfolio management; timing of disposals; tax-efficient realisation. Unrealised fair value gains (IFRS 9) Mark-to-market movements on fair-value-through-profit-or-loss (FVTPL) assets. Volatile; driven by market prices; reversed when prices fall. Asset allocation; portfolio volatility management; hedging. Policy loan interest Interest on loans against the surrender value of in-force policies. Recurring; at rates set in the policy terms. Policy loan pricing; management of outstanding loan balances. 26.3.2 The Investment Yield and its Drivers Portfolio Investment Yield The total investment income generated by the investment portfolio as a proportion of the average invested assets during the period. The investment yield is the primary measure of the portfolio’s income-generating efficiency and is the key parameter monitored against the pricing assumption embedded in the insurer’s product pricing. Investment Yield Calculation Investment Yield = Total Investment Income ÷ Average Invested Assets × 100% Example: A life insurer has an investment portfolio with average assets of ₦180bn during the year. Total investment income (interest + dividends + rental) is ₦24bn. Investment yield = 24/180 = 13.3% p.a. The yield must be compared against the pricing assumption: if the pricing assumed a 15% annual investment return but the portfolio only earns 13.3%, the pricing assumption is being violated and product profitability is eroded. This reinforces the critical importance of ALM and duration extension discussed in Chapter 23. The principal drivers of the portfolio investment yield for a Nigerian life insurer are: Asset allocation: A portfolio heavily weighted toward long-dated FGN bonds will have a different yield profile than one dominated by T-bills, equities, or real estate. The asset allocation decision, set within NAICOM’s admissible asset framework, is the most powerful lever available to management for managing the portfolio yield. Duration and reinvestment: In a high-rate environment, extending duration by purchasing long-dated bonds locks in the current high yield. Short-duration strategies require frequent reinvestment at whatever rate the market offers at reinvestment date, introducing yield volatility. Credit quality: Higher-yielding assets (sub-sovereign bonds, corporate bonds, property in secondary markets) offer yield enhancement relative to pure FGN bond portfolios, but at the cost of higher credit risk. The investment function must calibrate the yield/credit risk trade-off within the IPS risk limits. Cash management: Investment income is earned on invested assets, not on idle cash. Premium income that sits in current accounts rather than being promptly invested generates no return. The speed with which new premium receipts are invested is a management discipline that affects the portfolio yield at the margin.

t: Chapter 26 · 26.4 Fee Income and Ancillary Revenue Streams
x: 26.4.1 Categories of Fee Income Fee income represents the insurer’s earnings for services rendered beyond the pure risk transfer, typically in connection with savings, investment management, and advisory functions embedded in or adjacent to the insurance product. Fee income is less capital-intensive than underwriting income (it does not require the insurer to hold reserves and capital against risk) and is therefore disproportionately valuable as a contribution to return on equity. Policy fee income Fixed charges levied on each policy per payment period (typically annually or monthly) to recover the administrative cost of maintaining the policy. For example, a ₦5,000 per-policy annual administration fee on a portfolio of 200,000 policies generates ₦1 billion per year in fee income irrespective of the premium level. Policy fees are disclosed in the policy document and must meet NAICOM’s maximum fee guidelines. Fund management charge (FMC) An annual charge as a percentage of the fund value on unit-linked or investment-linked policies, covering the cost of managing the investment element of the policy. The FMC is the primary revenue source for the insurer’s investment management function on linked products. Typical FMC range: 1–2.5% p.a. of fund value. NAICOM’s product approval framework limits the FMC to prevent excessive charges to policyholders. Surrender / alteration fees Charges for processing policy alterations (sum assured changes, premium frequency changes, beneficiary updates) and for processing policy surrenders, particularly early surrenders within the penalty period. These fees recover the administrative cost of the transaction and create a minor financial deterrent to unnecessary early surrenders. Annuity management fee For Retirement Life Annuity products, an annual management fee applied to the annuity fund to recover the ongoing administration and actuarial costs of managing the longevity risk. Bancassurance service fee Fees charged by the insurer to the bank for providing product training, marketing materials, compliance oversight, and claims support under the bancassurance distribution agreement. In addition to brokerage paid to the bank, the insurer may charge a service fee to the bank for administrative and regulatory support. Claims administration fee Charged in specific group or worksite products where the insurer provides a managed claims administration service beyond the standard claims assessment function. More common in the group health and employee benefit space than in pure life insurance. 26.4.2 Regulatory Constraints on Fee Income NIIRA 2025 and NAICOM’s product approval process impose disclosure and maximum fee requirements on all charges levied on policyholders. The key regulatory constraints on fee income are: Full disclosure: Every fee and charge that affects the policyholder must be disclosed in the policy document and in the benefit illustration before the policy is sold. Hidden fees — charges that appear only in the policy fine print or that are not mentioned in the sales presentation — constitute a market conduct breach. NAICOM maximum charge limits: NAICOM sets maximum permissible rates for FMC and certain policy fees as part of the product approval process. Products with charges above the NAICOM maximum will not receive product approval. Insurers that charge fees above approved levels are in breach of their product filing. Value for money requirement: Under NIIRA 2025’s treating customers fairly framework, product charges must represent value for money for the target market. A product that levies charges so high that the policyholder cannot reasonably expect to receive value relative to the cost fails the TCF standard.

t: Chapter 26 · 26.5 Expense Management and the Expense Ratio
x: 26.5.1 The Expense Base of a Life Insurer The expenses of a life insurer fall into four broad categories: acquisition expenses (the costs of bringing new business onto the books, primarily agent commissions and distribution costs); maintenance expenses (the costs of administering in-force policies, including contact centre, claims, IT, and actuarial functions); investment management expenses (the cost of managing the investment portfolio); and overheads (general management, governance, regulatory compliance, and corporate centre costs). Of these, acquisition expenses are by far the most significant in the short term: the commission paid on a new life policy is typically 35–40% of the first-year premium, paid in the same month the policy is issued, while the premium income from that policy will be received over the next 10–30 years. This creates a structural cash flow deficit in the first year of a new policy: the insurer’s first-year costs (commission + reserve establishment) significantly exceed its first-year income, and the policy becomes profitable only if it persists through the subsequent years when renewal premiums are received at negligible acquisition cost. 26.5.2 The Expense Ratio Expense Ratio The total operating expenses of the insurer’s insurance operations (excluding claims and reserve changes) as a percentage of net earned premium. The expense ratio measures the operational efficiency of the insurer’s business: the proportion of every naira of premium income consumed by the cost of running the business before claims and reserves are considered. Expense Ratio Expense Ratio = (Acquisition Expenses + Maintenance Expenses) ÷ Net Earned Premium × 100% A life insurer with net earned premium of ₦50bn and total operating expenses (excluding claims) of ₦20bn has an expense ratio of 40%. Nigerian life insurance market average expense ratios have historically been high relative to mature markets, reflecting: high first-year commission rates; small portfolio sizes that cannot absorb fixed overheads efficiently; significant investment in distribution infrastructure; and the cost of compliance with an evolving regulatory framework. Benchmark: A well-managed Nigerian life insurer should target an expense ratio below 35–40% of NEP. An expense ratio persistently above 50% indicates a structural cost problem that is impairing the insurer’s ability to price competitively and generate acceptable returns. 26.5.3 Expense Allocation and Profitability by Product Line Aggregate expense ratios are a starting point, not an endpoint. The strategic management of an insurance portfolio requires understanding how expenses are distributed across product lines and distribution channels, so that management can identify which products and channels are generating the best risk-adjusted returns on the capital and expense investment they require. A product-level profitability analysis allocates expenses to product lines using a defined cost allocation methodology: direct costs (agent commission, underwriting costs, claims staff) are allocated directly to the relevant product; indirect costs (IT platforms, contact centre, actuarial function) are allocated on a proportional basis (e.g., proportion of policy count, premium income, or direct staff time). The resulting product-level contribution statements enable management to identify: Products generating positive contribution: Those where premium income, fee income, and investment income exceed the allocated claims, reserve change, commission, and expense burden. These are the products to scale. Products generating negative contribution: Those where the allocated costs exceed the income. These products are either repricing candidates (if the market will support it) or exit candidates (if they cannot be made profitable at a scale the insurer can realistically achieve). Distribution channels with high CAC relative to policyholder lifetime value: A distribution channel that generates high-volume, low-persistency business may appear productive in headline premium terms but be unprofitable on a lifetime value basis.

26.6.1 The Four Sources of Profit in Life Insurance Traditional life insurance profit analysis identifies four primary sources from which an insurer’s profit emerges, each arising from the difference between the assumption embedded in the product pricing and the actual experience during the policy’s lifetime. Understanding these four profit sources is essential for product management, pricing, and the interpretation of the insurer’s financial results. Profit Source Definition Positive (Gain) Scenario Negative (Loss) Scenario Management Lever Mortality Profit (C1) The difference between the mortality rate assumed in pricing and the actual mortality experienced. Actual deaths are fewer than the pricing assumed (a mortality gain). The insurer paid fewer death claims than it reserved for. Actual deaths exceed pricing assumptions (a mortality loss). The insurer paid more death claims than reserved. May indicate adverse selection, underwriting failure, or an external event (epidemic, pandemic). Underwriting quality; risk selection; reinsurance retention limits; catastrophe cover; ongoing mortality experience monitoring. Interest Profit (C2) The difference between the investment return assumed in pricing and the actual return earned on the investment portfolio. The actual portfolio yield exceeds the pricing assumption (an interest gain). The insurer earned more investment income than it credited to policyholders. The actual portfolio yield falls below the pricing assumption (an interest loss). The insurer earned less investment income than required to fund the guaranteed interest credited to policyholders. Portfolio yield management; ALM; duration extension; avoidance of reinvestment risk. Expense Profit (C3) The difference between the expense loading assumed in pricing and the actual expenses incurred. Actual expenses are lower than the loading (an expense gain). The insurer operated more efficiently than it priced for. Actual expenses exceed the loading (an expense loss). Operational inefficiency or unplanned cost growth is consuming margin that the pricing assumed would not exist. Expense ratio management; scale efficiency; technology investment; overhead cost control. Lapse Profit (C4) The difference between the lapse rate assumed in pricing and the actual lapse experience. (Note: the direction of the lapse profit depends on the product design and whether higher or lower lapses are more favourable.) For products where reserves exceed surrender values: fewer lapses than assumed (persistency gain). Policyholders retain their policies longer, reducing the gain from lapses at reserve-to-surrender-value differential. Higher lapses than assumed for products where the surrender charge does not fully recover the acquisition cost deficit. The insurer recovers less of the acquisition cost front-loading than the pricing assumed. Persistency management; distribution incentive design; conservation programmes; product design (surrender value basis). 26.6.2 Applying the Profit Sources Framework to Product Analysis The profit sources framework provides a structured diagnostic for understanding why a product is performing above or below expectation. A product that is generating disappointing profits may be suffering from any combination of the four sources: adverse mortality (claims worse than expected); interest loss (yields below the pricing assumption); expense overrun (costs higher than loaded in pricing); or excess lapses (persistency below the pricing assumption). A well-managed insurer conducts an annual profit source analysis for each major product line, quantifying the profit or loss arising from each of the four sources. The results directly inform: pricing updates (if a specific source is consistently generating losses, the pricing assumption for that source must be updated); product management decisions (a product with a structural interest loss due to long-duration liabilities is a candidate for repricing or redesign); and operational management actions (an expense loss requires investigation of cost allocation accuracy and operational efficiency).

t: Chapter 26 · 26.7 Embedded Value and New Business Value
x: 26.7.1 Embedded Value: Measuring the Intrinsic Worth of the Business Embedded Value (EV) The present value of the shareholders’ interest in the life insurance business, comprising the Adjusted Net Asset Value (ANAV) plus the Value of In-Force Business (VIF). EV provides a forward-looking measure of the value of the existing business that is more informative for strategic decision-making than the book value of the insurer’s equity. Embedded Value Components Embedded Value = Adjusted Net Asset Value (ANAV) + Value of In-Force Business (VIF) Adjusted Net Asset Value (ANAV) = The market value of the insurer’s net assets, adjusted for the difference between the market value and the book value of investments, and net of the required capital that must be held within the business to meet regulatory requirements. Value of In-Force Business (VIF) = The present value of future after-tax shareholder profits expected to emerge from the in-force policy portfolio, discounted at the risk discount rate. The VIF reflects the economic value of the policies already on the books — the future profits that will be generated by existing policyholders if they persist to maturity. 26.7.2 EV Movement Analysis The movement in EV between reporting periods is a key management information tool. EV movement can be decomposed into its component parts, enabling management to understand the sources of value creation and destruction: Expected return on EV The return that EV was expected to generate at the start of the period based on the opening assumptions — the ‘expected’ profit. This is the risk discount rate applied to the opening EV. New business value (NBV) The value created by the new policies written during the period. If the insurer wrote profitable new business, the EV increases by the NBV. If the new business was written at a loss (NBV negative), the EV is reduced. Operating variances The difference between actual experience and the assumptions underlying the EV: mortality experience better or worse than assumed; expenses higher or lower than projected; lapses higher or lower than the EV assumption. Each variance creates a positive or negative EV impact. Economic variances The impact of changes in the economic environment: changes in interest rates (affecting the discount rate and the asset values); changes in equity or property valuations; currency movements. Assumption changes Where the insurer updates the assumptions underlying the EV (new mortality tables, revised lapse rate assumptions, updated expense projections), the change in EV from the assumption update is separately disclosed. Capital movements Dividends paid out of the insurer reduce EV (the ANAV decreases); capital injections increase EV. 26.7.3 New Business Value and New Business Margin New Business Value (NBV) The present value of future after-tax shareholder profits expected from policies written in the current period, calculated at the point of sale using the pricing assumptions, the economic assumptions at the date of sale, and the cost of required capital. NBV is positive for profitable new business (the profit exceeds the acquisition cost) and negative for loss-making new business (the acquisition cost exceeds the present value of expected future profits). New Business Margin New Business Margin (NBM) = New Business Value (NBV) ÷ Present Value of New Business Premium (PVNBP) × 100% PVNBP = the present value of all expected future premiums on new business written in the period, calculated at the risk discount rate. NBM expresses the new business profit as a percentage of the total premium value of the new business. Example: An insurer writes new business with PVNBP of ₦120bn and achieves NBV of ₦12bn. NBM = 12/120 = 10%. A positive NBM means new business is creating value. An NBM below the risk discount rate means new business is being written at an economic loss. The NBM is one of the most important strategic metrics for a life insurer. It enables management to compare the profitability of new business across: product lines (which products generate the highest per-premium profit?); distribution channels (which channels deliver the highest-margin business?); customer segments (which segments are most profitable to serve?); and geographic markets (which regions generate the best new business economics?). A declining NBM over successive reporting periods is an early warning signal that pricing is too competitive, expenses are rising, or the distribution channel mix is shifting toward higher-cost, lower-margin channels.

26.8.1 The Annual Planning Cycle The financial planning and budgeting process of a Nigerian life insurer is a multi-function exercise that translates the strategic plan into specific financial targets for the coming year and beyond. It is not an accounting exercise — it is a management discipline that forces the CEO, CFO, actuary, investment director, and distribution leadership to align on what the business will deliver and how. The annual planning cycle typically runs from October to December for a calendar-year insurer, producing a final approved budget by the end of December for the following year. The process has four principal components: Premium income budget: The AFYP target by product line and distribution channel, based on the projected agent headcount, bancassurance partner performance, broker pipeline, and digital channel conversion rates. The premium budget is tested against the realistic capacity of the distribution infrastructure: does the insurer actually have the agents, bancassurance branches, and digital leads to generate the budgeted AFYP? Investment income projection: A projection of investment income based on the opening portfolio, the expected new premium inflows, the asset allocation strategy, and the yield assumptions for each asset class. In Nigeria’s high-rate environment, the investment income projection must account for the current yield curve and the impact of any planned duration extension on the portfolio’s yield profile. Expense budget: A bottom-up budget of all operating expenses: staff costs by department; IT costs; marketing budget by channel and product; NAICOM levy; office and premises costs; professional fees (actuarial, audit, legal); and compliance costs. The expense budget must be tested against the premium income budget to determine the projected expense ratio. Capital plan: A projection of the solvency ratio through the budget year, incorporating the budgeted premium income growth, the expected reserve growth, the investment portfolio changes, and any planned capital transactions (dividend payments, subordinated debt issuance, potential capital injection). The capital plan must confirm that the solvency ratio will remain above NAICOM’s minimum throughout the budget year under both the base case and a defined stress scenario. 26.8.2 Multi-Year Financial Projections In addition to the annual budget, a Nigerian life insurer’s financial planning process should include a three-to-five year strategic financial projection that shows the trajectory of the key financial metrics under the strategic plan: premium income growth; investment portfolio size and yield; expense ratio improvement (or deterioration); solvency ratio; EV growth; and NBV production. These multi-year projections enable the Board to evaluate whether the strategic plan will deliver adequate returns to shareholders and maintain adequate solvency margins. The multi-year projection is also the foundation for the ORSA (Chapter 15) and for investor communications in the case of publicly listed insurers. An insurer that cannot produce a credible multi-year financial projection linked to its strategic assumptions is not managing the business with the rigour that NIIRA 2025 and good governance require.

Concentration of revenue in a single stream is a strategic risk. A Nigerian life insurer whose revenue is entirely dependent on individual life premium income from a single distribution channel is vulnerable to any shock that affects that channel: a regulatory change affecting agents, a competitor with superior bancassurance terms, a pandemic that reduces the agency force’s productivity, or a macroeconomic downturn that increases lapse rates. Revenue diversification — building multiple income streams that are not perfectly correlated — is a resilience strategy as much as a growth strategy. 26.9.1 Product Range Diversification An insurer that writes only individual term assurance is more vulnerable than one that writes term assurance, endowments, group life, credit life, and annuities. Each product has a different revenue dynamics, cost structure, and sensitivity to economic conditions. A well-diversified product portfolio provides natural offsets: when credit life volumes decline (because lending slows), group life may be growing (because employers are expanding headcount); when individual life persistency falls (in an economic downturn), annuity renewals (which are guaranteed for life) remain stable. The product range diversification strategy must be evaluated against the insurer’s operational capacity: each product category requires specific underwriting, claims management, and actuarial capabilities. An insurer that expands into annuities without the investment management and longevity risk management infrastructure required is diversifying in name only. 26.9.2 Geographic Diversification Within Nigeria Most Nigerian life insurers are heavily concentrated in Lagos, Abuja, and the major commercial centres of the South-West. The northern states — where Takaful products, community-based distribution, and mobile delivery models are most relevant — represent a significantly under-penetrated geographic market. Geographic diversification within Nigeria does not require a foreign currency exposure; it requires distribution infrastructure, localised product design, and language-appropriate marketing in new markets. The geographic diversification case is also a demographic case: Nigeria’s population growth is fastest in the states and cities outside the South-West, and the young professional cohorts in Abuja, Port Harcourt, Kano, and Enugu represent an untapped urban insurance market with characteristics similar to the Lagos market of a decade ago. 26.9.3 Adjacent Financial Services Revenue A life insurer with a large policyholder base has an existing customer relationship that it can leverage to offer adjacent financial services: pension fund administration (through a PFA subsidiary or partnership); health insurance (through a Health Maintenance Organisation subsidiary); investment management (through an SEC-registered asset management subsidiary); and financial planning services (through a fee-based advisory arm). Each of these generates fee income that is not correlated with claims experience, reducing the volatility of the total revenue stream. The regulatory implications of adjacent financial services expansion require careful management: each additional regulated activity requires a separate licence, a separate capital base, and a separate governance framework. An insurer expanding into PFA, HMO, and asset management simultaneously is building a financial services conglomerate that requires the governance and risk management infrastructure of a group — not just an expanded insurance company. 26.9.4 Fee-Based Advisory Revenue The most capital-efficient revenue diversification available to a Nigerian life insurer is the development of a fee-based financial advisory service that generates income from advice rather than from product sales. A fee-based advisory arm charges clients a professional fee for financial planning, retirement planning, employee benefit design, and wealth management advice; it may also place insurance and investment products on the client’s behalf, but the product transaction is separate from the advice fee. Fee-based advisory revenue is highly scalable: the same adviser can serve a larger client base if the advice process is supported by digital tools; the income is recurring (annual retainer fees rather than one-off commissions); and it is higher-margin than pure insurance distribution because it does not bear the same capital and reserve requirements. The challenge is the market development cost: Nigerian clients are not accustomed to paying for financial advice, and building a fee-paying advisory client base requires significant investment in professional credentialing, brand development, and client education.

t: Chapter 26 · 26.10 Advisory: Building Financial Management Discipline in a Nigerian Life Insurer
x: The financial management function in Nigerian life insurance has historically been dominated by premium income reporting and annual account preparation, with limited management use of the richer analytical frameworks — profit source analysis, EV/NBV, product-level contribution analysis, multi-year projections — that characterise financially mature insurance markets. NIIRA 2025’s governance requirements, combined with the competitive pressures of the market, are driving the need for a more sophisticated financial management discipline. Advisory: The Financial Management Transformation Priorities PRIORITY 1: IMPLEMENT PRODUCT-LEVEL PROFITABILITY REPORTING. An insurer that does not know which products are profitable and which are not is making distribution, pricing, and capital allocation decisions without the necessary information. Product-level contribution statements, updated quarterly, should be the cornerstone of management financial reporting. The investment required (a cost allocation methodology, an actuarial model update) is modest relative to the strategic value of the information. PRIORITY 2: ADOPT THE PROFIT SOURCES FRAMEWORK. Decomposing the insurer’s profitability into the four sources (mortality, interest, expense, and lapse) transforms management’s understanding of where the business is performing and where it is not. An insurer suffering from an interest loss can address it through ALM; one suffering from an expense overrun needs operational efficiency work. Without the profit sources lens, both appear simply as ‘underperformance’ with no clear management direction. PRIORITY 3: PRODUCE AN ANNUAL EMBEDDED VALUE REPORT. EV is the strategic currency of insurance management. A Board that evaluates its life insurance business solely on book value profits is missing the forward-looking value creation or destruction that the EV framework reveals. Even a simplified EV calculation — ANAV plus VIF using conservative assumptions — provides a far more useful strategic picture than the historic cost balance sheet. PRIORITY 4: LINK THE BUDGET TO THE STRATEGY. A budget that is built from the bottom up (last year’s numbers plus X%) without reference to the strategic objectives the insurer is trying to achieve is a financial control exercise, not a management tool. The budget process should force every line of the income statement to justify itself against the strategic plan: why are we spending ₦2bn on marketing if the strategy is to grow through bancassurance? Why is the expense ratio still 48% if the strategy is to achieve scale efficiency? These questions, asked in the budget process, produce the management discipline that drives financial improvement. The Single Most Impactful Financial Management Investment If a Nigerian life insurer can make only one financial management investment, it should build the actuarial and financial infrastructure to calculate and report New Business Margin by product line and distribution channel every quarter. NBM is the diagnostic metric that connects every significant business decision — pricing, distribution mix, product design, marketing spend, expense management — to a single number that measures whether the insurer is creating or destroying economic value with each policy it sells. An insurer that tracks NBM quarterly will make better decisions on every dimension of the business than one that tracks only GWP and expense ratios. It is the financial management metric that most acutely measures whether the insurer is building a valuable business or an expensive one.

Revenue Architecture The complete map of an insurer’s income sources, their relative sizes, their interdependencies, and the management disciplines required to sustain and grow each. Gross Written Premium (GWP) The total premium income billed by the insurer to policyholders during the accounting period, before any deduction for reinsurance premiums ceded. Net Earned Premium (NEP) The portion of net written premium that has been earned by providing coverage during the period, adjusted for the movement in the unearned premium reserve. Technical Account The income statement presentation of the insurer’s insurance underwriting result — premium income less claims incurred, reserve changes, and distribution expenses — before investment income is included. Portfolio Investment Yield Total investment income generated by the investment portfolio as a proportion of average invested assets during the period. Policy Fee Income Fixed charges levied on policyholders to recover administrative costs, providing recurring non-underwriting income independent of premium level. Fund Management Charge (FMC) An annual percentage charge on the fund value of unit-linked policies, covering investment management costs and providing fee income to the insurer. Expense Ratio Total operating expenses (excluding claims and reserve changes) as a percentage of net earned premium; measures the operational efficiency of the insurance business. Profit Sources Framework The decomposition of life insurance profit into four components: mortality profit (C1), interest profit (C2), expense profit (C3), and lapse profit (C4), each representing the difference between the pricing assumption and actual experience. Mortality Profit (C1) The profit arising from the difference between assumed and actual mortality experience. A mortality gain arises when fewer deaths occur than assumed in pricing. Interest Profit (C2) The profit arising from the difference between the assumed and actual investment return. An interest gain arises when the portfolio earns more than the pricing assumed. Expense Profit (C3) The profit arising from the difference between assumed and actual expense levels. An expense gain arises when actual expenses are lower than the loading in the product pricing. Lapse Profit (C4) The profit arising from the difference between assumed and actual lapse rates. The direction of the gain or loss depends on the product design and the relationship between reserves and surrender values. Embedded Value (EV) The present value of shareholders’ interest in the life insurance business: Adjusted Net Asset Value (ANAV) plus Value of In-Force Business (VIF). Value of In-Force Business (VIF) The present value of future after-tax shareholder profits expected to emerge from the existing in-force policy portfolio, discounted at the risk discount rate. New Business Value (NBV) The present value of future after-tax shareholder profits expected from policies written in the current period, calculated using pricing and economic assumptions at the point of sale. New Business Margin (NBM) New Business Value divided by the Present Value of New Business Premium, expressed as a percentage. The primary metric of new business profitability.

The Net Earned Premium (NEP) of a life insurer is best described as: The total premiums billed to policyholders before any reinsurance deduction. The net written premium adjusted for the movement in the unearned premium reserve, representing the premium earned by providing coverage during the period. The investment income earned on the premium reserves during the accounting period. The gross written premium minus commission paid to distribution intermediaries. (B) The net written premium adjusted for the movement in the unearned premium reserve, representing the premium earned by providing coverage during the period. Why (B) is Correct NEP = Net Written Premium − (Closing UPR − Opening UPR). The UPR adjustment converts written premium (premiums collected or due) into earned premium (premiums relating to coverage actually provided during the period). Where the closing UPR exceeds the opening UPR, the insurer has collected more premium than it has earned — the excess is deferred to future periods. NEP is the most accurate measure of the revenue the insurer has genuinely earned by bearing risk during the accounting period. Why the Others Are Wrong (A) Premiums billed before reinsurance deduction is the Gross Written Premium — a different metric that includes reinsured risk the insurer has passed on.(C) Investment income on reserves is a separate revenue stream — it is not a component of NEP, which is purely a premium metric.(D) Gross premium minus commission is not a standard metric — commission is an expense deducted below the revenue line, not from the premium calculation it

A Nigerian life insurer's investment portfolio earns total investment income of ₦18bn during the year. The average invested assets during the year were ₦120bn. The investment yield is: 6.7%. 15.0%. 13.3%. 18.0%. (B) 15.0%. Why (B) is Correct Investment yield = Investment income ÷ Average invested assets × 100%= ₦18bn ÷ ₦120bn × 100% = 15.0% Why the Others Are Wrong (A) 6.7% would result from inverting the calculation (₦8bn ÷ ₦120bn) or from a calculation error.(C) 13.3% would result from ₦16bn ÷ ₦120bn — different numerator.(D) 18.0% confuses the investment income figure (₦18bn) with the yield percentage — a category error.

A life insurer's expense ratio of 45% means: 45% of the insurer's gross written premium is paid as claims. 45% of every naira of net earned premium is consumed by operating expenses (excluding claims and reserve changes). The insurer's investment portfolio generates a return of 45% per annum. 45% of the insurer's agent workforce has achieved their monthly production target. (B) 45% of every naira of net earned premium is consumed by operating expenses (excluding claims and reserve changes). Why (B) is Correct The expense ratio is defined as: Total operating expenses (commissions + administration + management costs) ÷ Net Earned Premium × 100%. An expense ratio of 45% means that for every ₦1.00 of NEP, ₦0.45 is consumed by operating expenses before any claim or reserve consideration. A high expense ratio relative to industry peers indicates either cost inefficiency or an insufficiently large premium base to absorb fixed costs — both of which directly compress underwriting profitability. Why the Others Are Wrong (A) The proportion of gross written premium paid as claims is the claims ratio or loss ratio — a different metric.(C) Investment yield is measured separately from the expense ratio — the expense ratio relates exclusively to operating costs against earned premium.(D) Agent workforce production attainment is an agency management metric entirely unrelated to the accounting expense ratio.

In the profit sources framework for a traditional life insurer, an 'interest loss' (C2 loss) arises when: The insurer's claims experience is worse than the mortality table used in pricing. The insurer's actual investment return falls below the return assumption embedded in the product pricing. The insurer's operating expenses exceed the expense loading included in the premium. Policyholders lapse their policies at a higher rate than the pricing assumed. (B) The insurer's actual investment return falls below the return assumption embedded in the product pricing. Why (B) is Correct In the four-source profit model (C1 mortality; C2 interest; C3 expenses; C4 lapses), the C2 component is the profit or loss arising from the difference between the investment return actually earned and the investment return assumption that was built into the pricing. If pricing assumed 14% and the insurer actually earns 11%, the 3-percentage-point shortfall represents an interest loss — the product is not generating the investment income required to fund its obligations at the price charged. Why the Others Are Wrong (A) Claims experience worse than the mortality table creates a C1 (mortality) loss, not a C2 loss.(C) Expenses exceeding the expense loading creates a C3 (expense) loss.(D) Higher-than-assumed lapse rates create a C4 (lapse) result — which may be a gain or a loss depending on whether early lapse is profitable or unprofitable for the specific product.

The New Business Margin (NBM) is calculated as: Total new business premium written in the period divided by total in-force premium. New Business Value divided by the Present Value of New Business Premium, expressed as a percentage. The number of new policies issued divided by the number of agents in the field. New Business Value divided by total operating expenses incurred in acquiring new business. (B) New Business Value divided by the Present Value of New Business Premium, expressed as a percentage. Why (B) is Correct NBM = New Business Value (NBV) ÷ Present Value of New Business Premium (PVNBP) × 100%. The NBM expresses what proportion of the present value of future premium income from new business flows through as actuarial value to the shareholders — after allowing for expected future claims, expenses, and investment returns. A NBM of 12% means that for every ₦100 of present value of new business premiums, the insurer creates ₦12 of actuarial value. It is the key EV-based metric for assessing new business profitability relative to distribution scale. Why the Others Are Wrong (A) New business premium relative to in-force premium is a growth rate metric — unrelated to the NBM calculation.(C) New policies divided by agents is a productivity ratio, not a margin.(D) NBV divided by acquisition expenses would be a return-on-acquisition-investment ratio — not the standard NBM definition.

The embedded value framework provides a richer picture of a life insurance company’s financial performance and strategic progress than traditional IFRS income statement metrics. Critically evaluate this proposition with specific reference to the Nigerian life insurance market.
