AI chatbots for first-level queries; WhatsApp Business automated servicing; self-service portals; predictive outreach for lapse prevention. WhatsApp chatbot for policy status queries; automated premium reminder via SMS.

t: Chapter 28 · 28.3 NAICOM Insurtech Guidelines and the Regulatory Sandbox
x: 28.3.1 Overview of the NAICOM Insurtech Guidelines (August 2025) NAICOM’s Insurtech Guidelines, issued in August 2025, establish the regulatory framework for technology-driven insurance innovation in Nigeria. They address: the licensing requirements for different categories of Insurtech business; the regulatory sandbox framework for innovation testing; the conditions for embedded insurance distribution; the data governance requirements for AI-based underwriting; and the cybersecurity standards applicable to digital insurance operations. The Guidelines reflect NAICOM’s recognition that the standard insurance licensing framework — designed for large, capital-intensive traditional insurers — creates barriers to entry for technology-driven innovators that are not commensurate with the risks they pose. A mobile insurance platform distributing simple microinsurance products does not pose the same systemic risk as a full-service composite insurer; regulating both with the same framework either stifles the innovation that the market needs or creates regulatory arbitrage. The Insurtech Guidelines attempt to solve this by creating proportionate regulatory pathways for different categories of Insurtech activity. 28.3.2 Insurtech Licensing Categories Category Description Licensing Requirement Capital Requirement Full-Stack Digital Insurer A company that holds an insurance licence, underwrites risk on its own balance sheet, and distributes and services exclusively or primarily through digital channels. Full NAICOM insurance licence (life or composite). Same capital requirements as traditional insurers. Standard NIIRA 2025 minimum capital (₦8bn+ for life). Digital Insurance Agent (Individual) An individual agent who distributes insurance products exclusively through digital channels (mobile app, website, WhatsApp), without physical meetings. Standard NAICOM individual agent registration + CIIN qualification. No separate Insurtech licensing category. Not applicable (individual). Digital Corporate Agent (Platform) A company (fintech, agritech, telco, e-commerce) that distributes insurance products on behalf of a licensed insurer through its digital platform, without holding its own insurance licence. Corporate agent licence from NAICOM. Compliance with the Insurtech Guidelines’ specific obligations for digital corporate agents. Minimum capital for corporate agents as specified in NAICOM guidelines (lower than full insurance licence). Insurtech Enabler (B2B) A technology company that provides software, data, analytics, or platform services to licensed insurers but does not itself distribute insurance or bear insurance risk. No insurance licence required. Subject to data protection (NDPA 2023) and cybersecurity requirements if handling policyholder data. Not applicable (no insurance risk). Sandbox Participant A company testing an innovative insurance business model under NAICOM’s regulatory sandbox, before committing to full licensing. Sandbox application approved by NAICOM. Operates under sandbox-specific conditions and limitations (maximum policyholder exposure, defined test period). Reduced capital requirement during sandbox period, as specified in sandbox approval conditions. 28.3.3 The Regulatory Sandbox Framework The regulatory sandbox allows an Insurtech company to test its innovative model in a live market environment with real customers, under NAICOM’s close supervision, without first obtaining a full insurance licence. The sandbox is designed for models that do not fit neatly within existing regulatory categories — a parametric agricultural insurance platform operating through an agritech app, a blockchain-based reinsurance settlement mechanism, an AI underwriting tool that makes decisions without a human underwriter review — where the innovation requires a period of live testing before the appropriate long-term regulatory framework can be determined. NAICOM Sandbox: Entry and Graduation Process STEP 1 — APPLICATION: The applicant submits a sandbox application to NAICOM, describing: the innovative model being tested; the specific regulatory requirement for which an exemption or modification is being sought; the consumer protection safeguards in place; the test parameters (number of policyholders, geographic scope, duration); the exit plan (what happens to policyholders at the end of the test); and the applicant’s plan for obtaining a full licence if the test is successful. STEP 2 — NAICOM REVIEW: NAICOM assesses the application against three criteria: innovation (is the model genuinely novel?); consumer benefit (does the model address a genuine market gap?); and risk management (are the consumer protection safeguards adequate?). NAICOM may request modifications to the proposed test parameters before approval. STEP 3 — SANDBOX OPERATION: The approved participant operates within the sandbox conditions: maximum number of policyholders; geographic limitations; product premium ceiling; reporting obligations (monthly operational updates to NAICOM); and consumer protection requirements identical to those applicable to fully licensed insurers. STEP 4 — ASSESSMENT AND GRADUATION: At the end of the test period (typically 12–24 months), NAICOM assesses the sandbox outcomes: Were consumers adequately protected? Did the model work as proposed? Is there a viable path to full licensing? Successful participants graduate to a full licence; unsuccessful models are wound down in an orderly manner. STEP 5 — FULL LICENCE OR EXIT: Graduated participants apply for the appropriate full insurance or corporate agent licence. The sandbox experience provides a documented operating history that informs the licence application. Participants that cannot meet full licensing requirements exit the market through a supervised run-off process that protects in-force policyholders.

t: Chapter 28 · 28.4 Digital Distribution: Platforms, Virtual Agents, and Unit Economics
x: 28.4.1 Full-Stack Digital Insurers A full-stack digital insurer holds its own insurance licence and manages the complete insurance value chain — product design, underwriting, policy administration, customer service, and claims management — through digital infrastructure rather than physical branches and agent networks. The full-stack model’s commercial logic is scale efficiency: with sufficiently large policy volumes, the fixed cost of the digital platform is spread across a very large number of micro-premium policies, producing a unit economics profile that is unavailable to traditional agent-based distribution. The unit economics challenge for a full-stack digital insurer in Nigeria is acute in the early stages: building a digital platform capable of handling USSD enrolment, mobile wallet deduction, automated underwriting, claims processing, and customer service requires a ₦500 million to ₦2 billion technology investment before the first policy is issued. This investment must be recovered across a portfolio of micro-premium policies generating ₦500–2,000 per week in premium per policy. Achieving the volumes required for viability — typically 500,000 to 2 million active policies — requires aggressive distribution partnerships that make the full-stack model dependent on external platforms for customer acquisition. 28.4.2 Virtual Agent and Digital Intermediary Models The virtual agent model reduces the capital intensity of digital insurance by separating the risk-bearing function (held by a licensed insurer) from the distribution and servicing function (handled by the digital platform). The digital intermediary does not hold an insurance licence; it operates as a corporate agent or licensed broker, distributing products on behalf of one or more licensed insurers. This model is commercially attractive to fintech and platform companies that have large, engaged user bases: they add insurance to their product offering without bearing insurance risk or investing in an insurance licence, while generating referral or commission income on every policy placed. The insurer benefits from the platform’s distribution reach and customer relationship without building those relationships from scratch. The key commercial tension is the commission rate negotiation: a platform with 5 million monthly active users has significant bargaining power over the insurer whose product it distributes, and can threaten to switch to a competitor insurer if commission terms are not favourable. 28.4.3 The CAC Economics of Digital vs. Agent Distribution Digital vs. Agent Distribution: Unit Economics Comparison The following illustrates the unit economics comparison between agent and digital distribution for a simple life microinsurance product (weekly premium ₦500, sum assured ₦250,000): Metric Agent Distribution USSD/Mobile Digital Distribution Premium per policy per year ₦26,000 ₦26,000 First-year commission (40% FYC) ₦10,400 0 (or platform referral fee ₦1,000–2,000) Technology cost per policy (amortised over 2M policies) ₦500–1,000 ₦500–1,000 Onboarding / KYC cost ₦500–1,500 (agent time) ₦200–500 (automated USSD/API) Customer Acquisition Cost (CAC) ₦11,400–12,900 per policy ₦1,700–3,500 per policy Break-even persistency required 3–4 years (to recover CAC) Less than 1 year At-scale unit economics Dependent on persistency; high CAC limits margin Highly scalable; significantly lower margin required per policy to break even The digital model’s 4–7× lower CAC is the economic foundation of mass-market insurance in Nigeria. However, the digital model requires scale (volume) and persistency (low auto-deduction failure rate) that the agent model’s relationship-based retention provides naturally. The optimal model for most Nigerian products is hybrid: digital acquisition with agent-assisted conservation for at-risk policies.

t: Chapter 28 · 28.5 Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning in Underwriting
x: 28.5.1 Automated Underwriting Automated underwriting uses rules-based logic and, increasingly, machine learning models to make underwriting decisions without human intervention. For standard risk profiles — individuals within defined age, health, and lifestyle parameters — an automated underwriting engine can assess the application, approve or decline, and issue a policy in seconds. This eliminates the underwriter’s role in routine cases, reducing processing cost and time while maintaining consistent, auditable risk decisions. The architecture of a Nigerian automated underwriting system for life insurance: Rule-based triage: Immediate automated approval for applications that fall within defined ‘green zone’ parameters (age range, NIN verified, sum assured below simplified underwriting threshold, no medical conditions declared). Approximately 60–70% of standard retail applications in well-designed systems. Refer for additional information: Applications that fall outside green zone parameters but do not meet immediate decline criteria are referred: for additional medical questions (via digital questionnaire), for medical examination, or for additional financial evidence (for large sums assured). Decline or offer modified terms: Applications that meet clear decline criteria (active cancer, very high mortality risk conditions) are automatically declined or offered coverage with an exclusion or premium loading. Automated decline decisions must be reviewable; the applicant must have a right to request human review. 28.5.2 Alternative Data for Risk Scoring Traditional life insurance underwriting relies on data provided by the applicant (health declaration, financial status, occupation) supplemented by third-party medical evidence. In the Nigerian market, where a significant proportion of the target population lacks formal medical records, employment documentation, or a verifiable financial history, traditional data sources are insufficient for underwriting the mass market. Alternative data sources — data generated by the individual’s digital behaviour rather than by formal institutions — offer a potential solution to this data scarcity problem. Research from comparable emerging markets suggests several alternative data signals that correlate with insurance risk outcomes: Mobile money transaction patterns: Regularity and volume of mobile money transactions; consistency of income inflows; pattern of expenditure. High transaction regularity and consistent income patterns correlate with lower lapse risk; irregular or declining income patterns correlate with higher lapse risk. Airtime usage: Duration and frequency of voice calls; data usage patterns. Research in some markets suggests correlations between communication patterns and mortality risk, though the causal mechanism requires careful examination before commercial deployment. Geolocation patterns: Consistent residential and workplace location patterns (via GPS in the mobile app) that verify the applicant’s stated employment and location, reducing anti-selection risk from falsified application information. Ethical and Regulatory Considerations for Alternative Data Underwriting The use of alternative data in underwriting raises significant ethical and regulatory concerns that must be managed before deployment: Proxy discrimination: Alternative data variables that correlate with race, religion, gender, or disability may produce underwriting decisions that discriminate against protected classes even without explicit reference to those characteristics. NAICOM’s Insurtech Guidelines require insurers using AI underwriting to conduct and document bias testing of their models. Transparency: Under NIIRA 2025’s treating customers fairly framework and the NDPA 2023’s right to explanation of automated decisions, applicants who are declined or loaded based on AI/ML models must be able to understand the basis of the decision and challenge it. Consent for data use: Using mobile money or telco data for underwriting purposes requires the applicant’s explicit, informed consent under the NDPA 2023. The consent must be specific to the underwriting use — a general terms and conditions consent is insufficient. Model risk: AI underwriting models trained on historical data may perform poorly in new conditions (economic downturns, new demographics). Models must be monitored continuously against actual claims outcomes and updated when performance degrades.

28.6.1 What is Embedded Insurance? Embedded Insurance The integration of insurance coverage into a non-insurance product, service, or transaction, such that the insurance is purchased as part of the primary transaction rather than as a separate act. The customer buys the insurance as an inherent feature of the primary product, often without a separate sales interaction. Examples: credit life insurance embedded in a digital loan disbursement; travel insurance embedded in an airline ticket purchase; device insurance embedded in a smartphone sale. Embedded insurance is the highest-potential distribution model for Nigerian life insurance at scale, because it resolves the two fundamental barriers to mass-market adoption simultaneously: the trust barrier (the customer is buying insurance from a platform they already trust and use, not from an unfamiliar insurance company) and the friction barrier (the insurance purchase requires no separate action — it is included in something the customer is already doing). The NIIRA 2025 mandatory credit life requirement for loans above ₦10 million is, in effect, a mandate for embedded insurance in the lending market. Every digital lender in Nigeria with a loan portfolio above the threshold must embed credit life in its product — creating a structural, regulatory-enforced embedded insurance market that was not present before the Act. 28.6.2 Principal Embedding Use Cases in Nigeria Embedding Context Insurance Product Embedding Mechanics Scale Potential Digital lending (Carbon, FairMoney, Branch) Credit life insurance Insurance premium added to loan disbursement; cover activated at disbursement; claim triggers automatic loan balance clearance. Very high: millions of digital loans disbursed annually in Nigeria. Mobile money wallet (MTN MoMo, OPay) Personal accident / life cover Monthly or weekly premium auto-deducted from wallet at minimal cost; benefit payable to wallet beneficiary. Very high: 60+ million mobile money accounts. Agricultural input financing (Babban Gona, ThriveAgric) Group credit life / parametric weather insurance Insurance bundled with input financing package; premium included in financing cost. High: millions of smallholder farmers in the formal agritech value chain. Ride-hailing / gig economy (Bolt, Uber, Gokada) Personal accident cover for drivers / riders Daily or trip-based micro-premium; cover active during working hours. Moderate: hundreds of thousands of gig economy workers. E-commerce / retail (Jumia) Device / purchase protection Insurance offered at checkout as add-on to electronics or high-value purchases. Moderate: growing e-commerce market. Savings / investment platforms (Piggyvest, Cowrywise) Term assurance / family protection Insurance offered as a complementary product to savings goals; premium deducted from savings plan. High: 5+ million users on leading platforms. Employer payroll systems (HR software providers) Group life; income protection Annual group life premium calculated and deducted through payroll software integration. High: formal sector employers across Nigeria. 28.6.3 Commercial and Regulatory Requirements A successful embedded insurance programme requires alignment across four dimensions: Commercial alignment: The embedding partner (fintech, agritech, platform) must have a genuine commercial incentive to embed insurance, not merely a regulatory obligation. The insurer’s commercial offer must include an appropriate commission or revenue share that reflects the platform’s customer acquisition contribution, without creating a conflict of interest between the platform’s obligation to recommend suitable insurance and its commission income. Technical integration: The insurance transaction must be seamlessly embedded in the primary product’s digital flow. An embedded credit life programme that requires the borrower to leave the loan app, visit a separate insurance website, and complete a separate application form is not truly embedded — it is merely a cross-sell link with a high abandonment rate. API integration between the lender’s core system and the insurer’s PAS must enable real-time policy issuance within the primary transaction. Regulatory compliance: The embedding partner must hold a NAICOM corporate agent licence or operate under the insurer’s direct supervision as a distribution channel. Consumer disclosure — making clear that the insurance is a separate product, describing its key terms and the claims process — must be embedded in the primary product’s transaction flow, not buried in general terms and conditions. Claims design: The claims process must be as embedded as the enrolment: a borrower who defaults because they have died should have the credit life claim automatically triggered by the lender’s system detecting the default, not by requiring the deceased’s family to navigate the insurer’s standard claims process. API-triggered automatic claims are the operational ideal for embedded insurance.

t: Chapter 28 · 28.7 Blockchain and Distributed Ledger Technology in Insurance
x: 28.7.1 Blockchain Fundamentals for Insurance Professionals A blockchain is a distributed ledger — a database that is simultaneously maintained by multiple participants (nodes) in a network, where each new record (block) is cryptographically linked to the previous one, making the ledger tamper-evident and verifiable without a central authority. In the insurance context, blockchain’s value derives from three properties: immutability (once a record is on the chain, it cannot be altered without the consensus of the network); transparency (all parties to a smart contract can see the same data in real time); and programmability (smart contracts execute automatically when predefined conditions are met, without requiring manual intervention by either party). 28.7.2 Blockchain Applications in Life Insurance The most commercially viable blockchain applications in life and insurance are those where the value of immutability, transparency, and automation is highest: Parametric insurance trigger and payment: A smart contract on a blockchain can be programmed to automatically pay a parametric benefit when an oracle (a trusted external data source, such as a NIMET rainfall gauge feed) delivers data confirming that the trigger condition has been met. The payment is made automatically, without any claims submission, assessment, or human approval. This is the highest-value blockchain application for Nigerian insurance because it eliminates the basis risk and trust deficit associated with conventional claims assessment. Reinsurance settlement: Smart contracts can automate the complex accounting settlements between cedants and reinsurers under proportional treaties, calculating premium cessions, claims recoveries, and commission adjustments in real time based on agreed rules, and executing the corresponding payment instructions without the month-end reconciliation processes that currently introduce delays and disputes. Identity verification and KYC sharing: A blockchain-based digital identity system would allow an individual’s verified identity to be shared across multiple financial institutions (including insurers) without requiring each institution to independently re-verify the same information, reducing the cost and friction of KYC for both the customer and the insurer. Claims fraud prevention: A shared blockchain ledger of insurance claims could identify duplicate claims — the same individual submitting the same loss event to multiple insurers — across the market, without requiring individual insurers to share sensitive policyholder data directly with competitors. 28.7.3 State of Blockchain Insurance Deployment in Africa Blockchain insurance deployment in Africa remains largely in the pilot and proof-of-concept stage. The most advanced deployments are in agricultural parametric insurance, where blockchain smart contracts automate payments triggered by satellite imagery data and weather station readings. Etherisc (a global blockchain insurance protocol) has partnered with African insurers and agritech companies to implement parametric crop insurance programmes in Kenya, Ethiopia, and West Africa. In Nigeria specifically, blockchain insurance pilots have been limited. The barriers to broader deployment include: the absence of a legal framework for smart contract enforceability in the Nigerian context; the limited availability of high-quality, tamper-proof data oracles for Nigerian-specific parametric triggers; the technology infrastructure gap between blockchain-based settlement systems and the legacy core systems of most Nigerian insurers; and regulatory uncertainty about the treatment of blockchain-based insurance contracts under the Insurance Act and NIIRA 2025.

28.8.1 The Data-Driven Insurance Value Chain Data analytics transforms the insurance value chain from a series of largely manual, judgement-based processes into a system of evidence-based, continuously improving decisions. Every stage of the insurance lifecycle generates data; every data point, if collected and analysed, provides information that improves a subsequent decision. An insurer that systematically collects, integrates, and analyses its data will, over time, price risk more accurately, detect fraud more efficiently, target conservation interventions more precisely, and serve customers more personally than an insurer that does not. The specific analytics use cases of highest commercial value for a Nigerian life insurer are: Lead scoring and propensity modelling Using existing policyholder and prospect data to identify which leads are most likely to convert to policies, enabling the distribution team to prioritise their outreach and reducing wasted agent time on low-propensity contacts. Lapse prediction and early intervention Building a model that predicts which in-force policyholders are at highest risk of lapsing in the next 30–90 days, based on payment behaviour, contact recency, financial stress indicators, and product characteristics, enabling targeted conservation outreach before the lapse occurs. Claims fraud detection Using claims data patterns to identify suspicious claims: unusual timing, frequency, amounts, or claimant behaviour that deviates from the insurer’s expected claims distribution. AI fraud detection models can flag cases for investigator review in real time, significantly improving the efficiency of the SIU function. Mortality experience analysis Continuously comparing actual claims against the EFU life table and the insurer’s own pricing assumptions, by age band, gender, occupation, and product, to identify emerging adverse experience trends that should trigger pricing updates. Cross-sell recommendation engine Analysing the existing policyholder’s policy mix, financial behaviour, and lifecycle stage to identify the most relevant next product to offer, personalising the cross-sell approach rather than broadcasting the same product offer to the entire portfolio. Customer lifetime value modelling Calculating the expected future profitability of each policyholder relationship based on their current products, persistency probability, and cross-sell potential, enabling the insurer to allocate service and conservation resources proportionally to relationship value.

t: Chapter 28 · 28.9 Open APIs and Digital Ecosystem Integration
x: 28.9.1 What is an API in the Insurance Context? An Application Programming Interface (API) is a set of protocols and tools that enables two software systems to communicate with each other and exchange data or functionality in real time. In the insurance context, an API allows an external system (a fintech app, a bank’s core system, an agritech platform) to request insurance services (quote generation, policy issuance, premium debit, claims notification) from the insurer’s systems without any human intermediary, in milliseconds. Open APIs — APIs that are published and accessible to third-party developers subject to agreed commercial and technical standards — are the technical foundation of the embedded insurance model. When a digital lender embeds credit life insurance in its loan disbursement, it is typically doing so through an API call to the insurer’s policy issuance system: the lender’s software sends the borrower’s data (name, NIN, loan amount, term) to the insurer’s API; the insurer’s system responds with a policy number, a cover confirmation, and a premium debit instruction; the entire transaction completes in under two seconds, entirely invisible to the borrower except for the line on their loan statement showing the insurance premium. 28.9.2 Building an Insurance API Layer A Nigerian life insurer that wants to enable embedded insurance distribution through the ecosystem of fintech, agritech, e-commerce, and payroll platforms needs to build and maintain an API layer that exposes its core insurance services in a standardised, documented, and reliable format. The key services that a life insurance API layer should expose include: Quotation API: Input: applicant age, sum assured, premium frequency, coverage type. Output: premium quotation, product description, key exclusions. Policy Issuance API: Input: applicant KYC data (name, NIN, date of birth, phone number), beneficiary details, premium payment authorisation. Output: policy number, cover confirmation, policy certificate. Premium Collection API: Input: policy number, premium amount, payment method. Output: payment confirmation, premium receipt. Policy Status API: Input: policy number or NIN. Output: policy status, next premium due date, sum assured, beneficiary details. Claims Notification API: Input: policy number, claimant identity, event date, supporting documents. Output: claim reference number, acknowledgement, documentation checklist.

t: Chapter 28 · 28.10 The Incumbent Insurer’s Insurtech Response Strategy
x: 28.10.1 Build, Buy, or Partner The incumbent life insurer’s strategic response to Insurtech disruption involves a choice among three broad approaches, each with different speed, cost, risk, and control implications. In practice, most successful incumbents pursue a portfolio approach across all three, allocating each capability gap to the most appropriate response mode: Approach Description When Best Suited Key Risks BUILD(internal development) Develop digital capabilities from within, using internal technology teams or specialist consultants, retaining full ownership and control of the resulting system. Core customer-facing infrastructure (app, customer portal) where the insurer’s brand and data are competitive advantages; capabilities that must be customised to the insurer’s specific products and regulatory environment. Slow (internal development timelines are typically 2–3× longer than external builds); expensive; technology team capability gap; risk of building the wrong solution. BUY(acquisition) Acquire an Insurtech company that has already built the capability the incumbent needs, gaining the technology, talent, and customer base in a single transaction. When a proven Insurtech player exists with a complementary capability (a digital distribution platform, a fraud detection system, an alternative data underwriting engine) that would take too long to build internally. Acquisition premium; cultural integration challenges; key talent retention post-acquisition; regulatory approval of ownership change from NAICOM. PARTNER(commercial arrangement) Establish a commercial partnership with an Insurtech company that provides the capability as a service, without the insurer acquiring ownership. Capabilities that are better provided by a specialist (AI fraud detection, telematics analytics, parametric trigger data); capabilities that need to be tested before a build or buy decision; embedding distribution through fintech/agritech platforms. Dependence on the partner’s technology; data sharing with a third party (NDPA 2023 obligations); potential for the partner to switch to a competitor insurer; commercial terms negotiation.

t: Chapter 28 · 28.11 Digital Transformation Risks and Risk Management
x: 28.11.1 Principal Digital Risk Categories Every digital capability the insurer builds or partners for introduces new operational risks that must be managed within the ERM framework. The principal digital risk categories are: Cybersecurity risk: The risk of unauthorised access to the insurer’s systems, data exfiltration, ransomware, or denial-of-service attacks. Cybersecurity risk is the most immediate and potentially most damaging digital risk for an insurer with millions of policyholders’ personal and financial data. NAICOM’s Insurtech Guidelines impose minimum cybersecurity standards; the NDPA 2023 imposes breach notification obligations within 72 hours. Model risk: The risk that an AI or ML model used for underwriting, fraud detection, or lapse prediction produces incorrect outputs due to flawed development, data quality issues, or distribution shift (the real-world conditions have changed since the model was trained). Model risk can be subtle and slow-emerging: a fraud detection model that misses a new fraud typology, or an underwriting model that approves risks that subsequently experience adverse mortality, may not reveal its failure until significant losses have accumulated. Technology dependency and concentration risk: An insurer that depends on a single cloud provider, a single API partner, or a single data vendor for critical operations has a concentration risk: if the provider fails, is hacked, or terminates the relationship, the insurer’s operations are disrupted. Business continuity planning for digital operations must include a scenario in which each critical digital dependency becomes unavailable. Data quality risk: The risk that the data on which underwriting, pricing, and analytics decisions are based is incomplete, inaccurate, or biased. In the Nigerian context, where NIN verification infrastructure is still maturing, mobile money data is fragmented across multiple operators, and historical insurance data is limited, data quality is a pervasive challenge. AI models trained on poor-quality data will produce poor-quality decisions. NDPA 2023 compliance risk: The risk of regulatory enforcement action arising from inadequate data protection practices: insufficient consent mechanisms, data breaches that are not notified within 72 hours, sharing of personal data with third-party Insurtech partners without the required contractual protections, or using personal data for purposes not disclosed to the data subject.

t: Chapter 28 · 28.12 Advisory: Building a Credible Digital Insurance Capability in Nigeria
x: Nigerian life insurers are at very different stages of digital capability development. Some have built functional mobile apps, deployed WhatsApp Business for customer service, and established API integrations with fintech partners. Others are still managing their distribution through paper proposal forms and their customer service through physical branches. The gap between these two groups will widen rapidly over the next three to five years as consumer expectations and competitive dynamics accelerate digital adoption. Advisory: The Digital Insurance Capability Building Agenda: A Sequenced Investment Plan PHASE 1 (Year 1): DIGITAL FOUNDATIONS. Priority investments: (1) Agent app with digital proposal form — eliminate paper applications; (2) Customer self-service portal — policy status, premium payment, beneficiary update; (3) WhatsApp Business integration for customer service; (4) Automated premium reminder system (SMS/WhatsApp). These four investments digitise the most friction-heavy customer interactions without requiring the insurer to rebuild its core systems. Estimated investment: ₦150–350 million. Expected return: 20–30% reduction in NIGO applications; 15–25% reduction in contact centre volume; measurable improvement in NPS. PHASE 2 (Years 2–3): DISTRIBUTION EXPANSION AND ANALYTICS. Priority investments: (1) USSD enrolment platform — enabling product distribution without internet access; (2) API layer for partner integration — enabling embedded insurance with two to three fintech or agritech platform partners; (3) Basic data analytics capability — lapse prediction model, lead scoring for agents; (4) Digital fraud detection model for claims. These investments begin to transform the revenue architecture: adding new premium income from digital channels while improving persistency and claims quality. Estimated investment: ₦400–800 million. Expected return: new digital channel premium income; 10–15% improvement in persistency through targeted conservation. PHASE 3 (Years 3–5): AUTOMATED UNDERWRITING AND PERSONALISATION. Priority investments: (1) Automated underwriting engine for standard retail applications; (2) Alternative data integration for mass-market risk scoring; (3) Personalised product recommendation engine; (4) Sandbox application for specific innovative model. By Phase 3, the insurer is operating a genuinely digital insurance business that supplements its agency distribution rather than replacing it, achieving materially lower CAC for digital-originated business and materially better pricing accuracy for the automated underwriting portfolio. Estimated investment: ₦500 million–1 billion. Expected return: 30–40% of new business applications processed without human underwriter review; measurable improvement in New Business Margin for digital channel. The Single Most Important Digital Investment for a Nigerian Life Insurer If an insurer can only make one digital investment, it should build an API-ready policy issuance and premium collection service that enables at least three embedded insurance partnerships within 18 months of launch. The embedded insurance model has the best CAC economics of any channel, creates recurring premium income through auto-deduction, and reaches populations that agent distribution cannot economically serve. The insurer that builds this API capability first and establishes the strongest embedded partnerships will have a structural distribution advantage that is very difficult to replicate once the key platform relationships are occupied.

Insurtech The use of technology innovations to improve the efficiency, accessibility, and personalisation of insurance products and services across the full value chain. Full-Stack Digital Insurer A company that holds its own insurance licence and operates the complete insurance value chain through digital infrastructure, without physical branches or traditional agent networks. Digital Corporate Agent A company (fintech, agritech, telco, e-commerce platform) holding a NAICOM corporate agent licence that distributes insurance products through its digital platform on behalf of a licensed insurer. Regulatory Sandbox (NAICOM) A controlled regulatory environment established by NAICOM’s Insurtech Guidelines in which Insurtech companies can test innovative insurance models under close NAICOM supervision before committing to full licensing. Embedded Insurance The integration of insurance coverage into a non-insurance product, service, or transaction such that the insurance is purchased as part of the primary transaction without a separate sales interaction. Automated Underwriting A rule-based or AI-powered system that makes underwriting decisions — approve, refer, or decline — without human intervention, for applications that fall within defined risk parameters. Alternative Data Data generated by an individual’s digital behaviour (mobile money transactions, airtime usage, geolocation patterns) rather than by formal institutions, used as a supplement to traditional underwriting data. API (Application Programming Interface) A set of protocols enabling two software systems to communicate and exchange data or services in real time, enabling embedded insurance integration between insurer and platform partner systems. Smart Contract A self-executing programme on a blockchain that automatically implements the terms of an agreement (such as a parametric insurance payment) when predefined conditions are verified, without requiring human approval. Blockchain A distributed, tamper-evident ledger maintained simultaneously by multiple network participants, with new records cryptographically linked to previous ones, providing the immutability and transparency required for smart contract insurance. Model Risk The risk that an AI or ML model used for underwriting, fraud detection, or analytics produces incorrect outputs due to flawed development, data quality issues, or changed real-world conditions. Lapse Prediction Model An AI/ML model that identifies in-force policyholders at high risk of lapsing based on payment behaviour, contact recency, and other signals, enabling targeted conservation interventions. Parametric Trigger The specific index value or event (rainfall below threshold, river level above threshold) that must be observed for a parametric insurance benefit payment to be automatically executed. Oracle (Blockchain) A trusted external data source that delivers real-world data (weather readings, commodity prices, mortality statistics) to a blockchain smart contract to verify whether a parametric trigger condition has been met. Cybersecurity Risk The risk of unauthorised access to the insurer’s systems, data exfiltration, ransomware, or service disruption, which can compromise policyholder data and operational continuity. NDPA 2023 Compliance Risk The regulatory risk arising from inadequate data protection practices — insufficient consent, breach notification failure, unauthorised data sharing — under the Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023.

The integration of insurance coverage into a non-insurance product or transaction, so that the insurance is purchased as an inherent part of the primary transaction without a separate sales interaction. A company testing an innovative insurance model in a controlled environment under NAICOM's close supervision, before committing to full licensing, is operating under: A provisional insurance licence subject to annual review. A special NAICOM exemption from capital requirements for a period of five years. The regulatory sandbox framework. A temporary digital corporate agent licence. (C) The regulatory sandbox framework. Why (C) is Correct NAICOM's Insurtech Guidelines (August 2025) establish the regulatory sandbox as the specific mechanism for testing innovative insurance models under regulatory supervision. Sandbox participants operate under defined parameters: limited customer numbers; constrained product scope; close NAICOM monitoring; and a defined exit path (either to a full licence if the model proves viable, or winding down if it does not). This framework enables innovation without the full capital commitment of a licensed entity. Why the Others Are Wrong (A) A provisional licence is a different regulatory concept — a transitional licence issued to entities in the process of meeting full licensing requirements, not for testing an unproven model.(B) NAICOM does not grant capital requirement exemptions of 5 years — this would create an unregulated insurance market.(D) A digital corporate agent licence enables the distribution of insurance products on behalf of a licensed insurer — it does not enable the testing of the insurer's own model.

Digital distribution generates significantly lower Customer Acquisition Cost (typically 4–7 times lower) due to the elimination or reduction of agent commission. Digital products are not subject to the 'no premium, no cover' rule. Digital distribution allows the insurer to charge higher premiums than NAICOM maximum commission guidelines permit. (B) Digital distribution generates significantly lower Customer Acquisition Cost (typically 4–7 times lower than agent distribution) due to the elimination or reduction of agent commission. Why (B) is Correct For microinsurance products with premiums of ₦500–₦5,000 per week, the agent distribution model is commercially unsustainable: a first-year commission of 30–40% on a ₦26,000 annual premium would generate ₦7,800–₦10,400 in commission per policy, which must be recovered through the small margin available after claims and expenses. Which of the following is NOT one of the principal risks of using AI and alternative data for insurance underwriting? Proxy discrimination — AI models may produce decisions that correlate with protected characteristics without explicitly using them. Model risk — AI models trained on historical data may perform poorly in new or changed conditions. Transparency — applicants may not understand why they were declined based on AI analysis of their mobile data. Investment risk — the insurer's investment portfolio may underperform if too much capital is allocated to AI development. (D) Investment risk — the insurer's investment portfolio may underperform if too much capital is allocated to AI development. Why (D) is the Answer to 'Which is NOT' Investment portfolio performance is driven by asset allocation, market conditions, and ALM management — not by how much capital the insurer allocates to AI development. The amount spent on AI development is a technology capex and operating expense item; it does not affect the investment portfolio's return on invested assets. This is therefore NOT a principal risk of using AI for underwriting. Why the Others Are Genuine AI Underwriting Risks (A) Proxy discrimination: AI models trained on mobile phone data may learn correlations with protected characteristics (gender, ethnicity, location) without those variables being explicitly included — producing discriminatory underwriting outcomes that violate NIIRA 2025's non-discrimination provisions.(B) Model risk: All AI models are trained on historical data that may not represent future conditions.
