t: Chapter 29 · 29.1 Introduction: The PAS as the Insurer’s Operational Core
x: If a life insurance company is a machine for making and keeping promises to policyholders — promising to pay on death, disability, maturity, or retirement — then the Policy Administration System (PAS) is the machine’s engine. Every promise the insurer makes to every policyholder is recorded in the PAS. Every premium the policyholder pays flows through the PAS. Every claim is processed against the PAS record. Every reinsurance cession is calculated from PAS data. Every regulatory return is derived from PAS outputs. When the PAS works well, the insurer works well. When the PAS fails, corrupts data, cannot produce required reports, or cannot support a new product or distribution channel — the insurer’s entire operational capability is compromised. Despite its centrality, the PAS is one of the most underinvested systems in many Nigerian life insurers. The industry historically grew through relationship-based distribution and manual processes, and many companies operate PAS platforms that are decades old, poorly documented, and incapable of supporting the regulatory demands of NIIRA 2025, the IFRS 17 reporting standard, the NDPA 2023 data governance requirements, and the digital channel expectations of a new generation of insurance buyers. This chapter provides a comprehensive treatment of the PAS for Nigerian life insurance practitioners: what it is, what it must do, how to select and implement one, what it must produce, how it integrates with other systems, and how to evaluate whether the current PAS is fit for the demands of the post-NIIRA 2025 market.

t: Chapter 29 · 29.2 What Is a Policy Administration System?
x: Policy Administration System (PAS) The core software system that creates, stores, and manages all insurance policy records across the policy lifecycle — from application and underwriting through issuance, premium management, policy servicing, claims processing, and eventual termination (by lapse, surrender, maturity, or death). The PAS is the system of record for all policyholder obligations and the primary source of data for actuarial reserving, regulatory reporting, financial accounting, and management information. The PAS sits at the centre of a life insurer’s technology ecosystem. It is not the only system the insurer operates — it interfaces with CRM platforms, actuarial systems, financial accounting systems, regulatory reporting tools, and digital customer channels — but it is the authoritative source of truth for the insurer’s policy portfolio. Any data about a policy that conflicts between the PAS and another system should be resolved in favour of the PAS record, unless the PAS record itself is demonstrably in error. The distinction between the PAS and adjacent systems is critical to understand: PAS vs CRM (Customer Relationship Management) The CRM manages the insurer’s relationships with prospects, agents, and policyholders — interactions, leads, activities, and communication history. The PAS manages the actual policy contracts, premium records, and obligation data. In a well-integrated technology stack, a sales agent’s CRM view of a policyholder’s profile draws real-time policy data from the PAS via API. PAS vs Actuarial System The actuarial system uses policy data extracted from the PAS (typically via a data extract or data warehouse) to perform reserving calculations, pricing model validation, and ORSA stress testing. The actuarial system’s outputs (reserve amounts, profit source analysis) feed back into the PAS’s financial reporting modules. The PAS holds the raw data; the actuarial system holds the analytical model. PAS vs Financial Accounting System (ERP) The financial accounting or ERP system records premium income, claims expenditure, commission payments, and investment transactions for financial reporting purposes. The PAS generates the source transactions (premium billings, claims settlements, commission calculations); the ERP records them as financial journal entries. In an integrated stack, PAS-generated transactions flow automatically into the ERP via API or batch interface. PAS vs Digital Customer Portal The digital customer portal (mobile app or web portal) is the customer’s interface — it allows policyholders to view their policy details, pay premiums, submit claims notifications, and update personal information. All of these actions read from or write to the PAS. The portal is the frontend; the PAS is the backend. PAS vs Claims Management System Some larger insurers operate a separate Claims Management System (CMS) that manages the claims workflow — notification, assessment, investigation, approval, and settlement. In most Nigerian life insurers, claims management functionality is embedded within the PAS itself rather than being a separate system.

A fully functional life insurance PAS comprises eight core modules, each managing a distinct stage of the policy lifecycle. Understanding each module’s functions, data inputs, and outputs is essential for both selecting and configuring a PAS, and for evaluating whether an existing PAS is meeting the insurer’s operational and regulatory requirements. 29.3.1 New Business Processing Module The new business module handles the journey from application submission to policy issuance. It captures all proposal form data (personal details, health declarations, benefit selections, beneficiary nominations), routes the application through the underwriting workflow, records the underwriting decision, generates the policy number, and creates the master policy record. Key functions Application capture (manual data entry, digital form intake, API intake from digital channels); underwriting workflow routing (straight-through processing for clean risks, referral queue for complex risks); underwriting decision recording (acceptance, rating, exclusion, decline); policy number generation; policy document production; issuance notification to policyholder and agent. Critical data captured Policyholder identity (NIN, BVN, date of birth, address); life assured health data (medical history, current conditions, test results); benefit structure (product code, sum assured, premium, term, riders); agent / intermediary details; beneficiary nominations; premium payment method and bank account details. NIIRA 2025 / regulatory link All data captured at new business must be sufficient to support the insurer’s regulatory obligations: AML/KYC verification (NIN, BVN, identity documents); NDPA 2023 consent recording; premium basis alignment with NAICOM-approved product; commission calculation at the approved rate. Quality control NIGO (Not In Good Order) detection: the PAS should flag incomplete or inconsistent applications before they enter the underwriting queue, reducing the cycle time for applications that require re-work from the agent. 29.3.2 Policy Issuance Module The policy issuance module generates the formal insurance contract and associated documentation for the policyholder. In a digital-first PAS, this includes automated generation of the policy document (PDF), the welcome letter, the premium payment instructions, and the direct debit mandate. Policy document generation: The PAS populates the approved policy wording template (itself a NAICOM product-approved document) with the policyholder’s specific schedule data to produce a personalised policy document. The document generation must be triggered within the NIIRA 2025 product approval framework — only approved wordings may be issued. Free look period tracking: The PAS must record the policy delivery date and calculate the free look period expiry date. Any cancellation request received within the free look period triggers an automatic premium refund and policy cancellation. Certificate issuance for group life: For group life policies, the PAS generates individual member certificates for each eligible employee, summarising their specific coverage under the master policy. 29.3.3 Premium Collection Module Premium collection is the most operationally complex module in a life insurance PAS, because the consequences of premium management errors are severe: under-collected premiums create financial shortfalls; incorrectly lapsed policies create regulatory exposure (premature lapse without proper grace period management); and unreconciled premium receipts create ghost policies — records that show premiums paid but where the payment cannot be matched to a bank receipt. Premium billing generation The PAS generates a premium billing schedule for each policy at inception, showing every premium due date and amount across the policy term. Premium reminders (SMS, email, WhatsApp) are triggered automatically by the PAS from this schedule. Premium receipt recording Each premium payment received (via direct debit, electronic transfer, mobile money, or cash through an agent) is matched to the policy’s premium schedule by the PAS reconciliation module. Matched receipts update the policy’s premium payment status; unmatched receipts enter a suspense account for manual investigation. Grace period management When a premium is not received on the due date, the PAS automatically enters the grace period (typically 30 days, as stated in the policy conditions). The policy remains in force during the grace period. If payment is received within the grace period, the policy is updated as current. If not, the PAS triggers the lapse workflow. Lapse processing On lapse, the PAS calculates the surrender value (if any), generates the lapse notification letter, removes the policy from the active in-force register, and triggers the conservation workflow (outreach to the policyholder by the customer service or agent team). Premium reconciliation The daily premium reconciliation process matches the PAS’s expected premium income against the insurer’s bank receipts. The reconciliation difference (unmatched debits or credits) must be investigated and cleared within a defined period. Unreconciled premium gaps are a significant audit finding and a potential indicator of premium theft. 29.3.4 Policy Maintenance Module The policy maintenance module handles all changes to an in-force policy after issuance: policyholder address changes, beneficiary nomination changes, premium frequency changes, sum assured alterations, rider additions or removals, policy loans, and reinstatements. Every change must be recorded with an audit trail that captures: who requested the change, who authorised it, when it was effective, and what the previous and new values were. Endorsement processing: Material changes to policy terms are recorded as formal endorsements in the PAS. The endorsement record links to the policy record, creating a complete history of all changes made to the policy since inception. Reinstatement workflow: The PAS manages the reinstatement application process: receiving the reinstatement request, calculating the outstanding premiums and interest due, routing the medical evidence for underwriting review (where required), recording the reinstatement decision, and updating the policy’s lapse status. Policy loan management: Where the product permits policy loans, the PAS calculates the maximum loan available (based on the surrender value), records the loan disbursement, calculates monthly interest, reduces the available surrender value by the outstanding loan balance, and (if applicable) deducts the outstanding loan from any claim payment. 29.3.5 Benefit Calculation Module The benefit calculation module computes the value of benefits payable under each policy at any given point in the policy’s life: the current surrender value, the paid-up value (if premiums were stopped), the death benefit (including any accumulated bonuses for participating policies), and the maturity benefit. These calculations must align precisely with the product’s NAICOM-approved benefit structure and the actuarial assumptions certified by the Statutory Actuary. For participating (with-profits) policies, the benefit calculation module must record the bonus declarations made each year and apply them to each individual policy. The bonus record must be auditable — the Statutory Actuary’s annual investigation will verify that declared bonuses have been correctly applied to all eligible policies. 29.3.6 Claims Processing Module The claims processing module manages the end-to-end claims workflow from notification to settlement. Under NIIRA 2025 (s.210) the insurer must settle valid claims within 60 days of notification; the book also recommends acknowledging claims within 5 business days as an internal service standard. The claims module must be designed to support these statutory timelines through automated workflow, escalation triggers, and SLA monitoring. Claims notification Intake of the claim notification (via phone, email, in-branch, or digital portal). The PAS records the notification date, creates a claim reference number, and initiates the 5-day acknowledgement timer and the 60-day settlement timer. Documentation management Tracking of all required documents (death certificate, proof of identity, medical reports, employer records for group life). The PAS flags outstanding documents and sends automated reminders to the claimant. Claims assessment workflow Routing the claim to the appropriate assessor based on the claim type and amount. For claims above a defined threshold, the PAS routes to senior assessors and, for potential fraud, to the Special Investigation Unit (SIU). All assessment actions and decisions are recorded with timestamps. Settlement calculation Computing the benefit payable: the sum assured less any outstanding policy loan, plus any accumulated bonus (participating policies), less any outstanding premium (where death occurs during grace period). The calculation is driven by the benefit calculation module. Payment processing Generating the payment instruction and transmitting it to the insurer’s bank for electronic transfer to the claimant’s account. The PAS records the payment reference and the payment date. NIIRA 2025 SLA monitoring The claims module must generate a real-time dashboard showing the settlement status of all open claims against the 5-day and 60-day timelines. Claims approaching the deadline trigger escalation alerts to the Claims Manager and, if not resolved, to the COO. A claim that breaches the 60-day deadline triggers a regulatory breach notification workflow. 29.3.7 Reinsurance Cession Module For insurers with reinsurance treaties (the majority of Nigerian life insurers), the PAS must calculate and record reinsurance cessions — the portion of each policy’s risk (and premium) transferred to reinsurers under the treaty. The reinsurance module reads the policy data, applies the treaty terms, computes the cession for each policy, aggregates cessions into treaty statements, and tracks reinsurance recoveries on claims. Automatic treaty processing: The PAS applies the treaty’s cession formula (quota share percentage or surplus line calculation) to each eligible policy automatically at issuance. The treaty’s retention limit, reinsurer’s lines, and cession percentages are configured in the PAS’s reinsurance module. Treaty statement generation: At the treaty accounting period (typically quarterly or annually), the PAS generates the reinsurance treaty statement — a detailed cession schedule listing every policy ceded, the ceded premium, the ceded reserve, and any recoveries on claims — for submission to the reinsurer and the reinsurance broker. Domestic cession compliance (NIIRA 2025): The PAS must track the proportion of each treaty that is ceded to domestic reinsurers (Continental Re, NRC) versus international reinsurers, to demonstrate compliance with NIIRA 2025’s domestic cession requirement. The domestic cession report is a NAICOM statutory return requirement. 29.3.8 Financial Reporting Interface The financial reporting interface generates the data outputs that feed the insurer’s financial accounting system, actuarial reporting, and NAICOM regulatory returns. These outputs include: premium income recognised in the period; claims paid; commission paid; policy reserve movements; lapse income; reinsurance premium ceded; and the in-force policy count and aggregate sum assured (for the NAICOM quarterly return). For IFRS 17 compliance, the financial reporting interface must produce the granular contract group data required for the IFRS 17 measurement models — the contractual service margin (CSM), the risk adjustment, and the liability for remaining coverage — at the level of policy cohorts defined by the insurer’s accounting policy. This is a significantly more complex data output than IFRS 4 required, and many legacy PAS platforms cannot produce it without extensive customisation or a middleware data transformation layer.

t: Chapter 29 · 29.4 Key Management Reports from a Life Insurance PAS
x: A well-configured PAS must produce a defined set of management and operational reports that enable the insurer’s management team to monitor business performance, identify emerging problems, and manage operational compliance. The following reports are the minimum expected from a functional life insurance PAS in the Nigerian market. Their absence — or their production only through manual extraction and manipulation — is a significant operational risk indicator. Report Name Content Primary Users Frequency Regulatory Link In-Force Policy Register A complete list of all active policies: policy number, policyholder name, product, sum assured, premium, commencement date, next premium due date, and payment status. The definitive record of the insurer’s current policyholder obligations. Actuarial (reserving); Finance (income recognition); Operations (servicing); Compliance (NAICOM in-force count) Monthly snapshot; daily for premium management NAICOM quarterly return (in-force count and aggregate sum assured) New Business Summary All policies issued in the period: number of policies, aggregate sum assured, aggregate first-year premium, breakdown by product, distribution channel, and geography. The primary measure of the insurer’s growth. CEO, CMO, Chief Distribution Officer, Finance Weekly/monthly NAICOM quarterly premium report Lapse and Conservation Report All policies lapsed in the period (by product, channel, agent, and cause); 13-month persistency rates by product and channel; policies currently in the grace period and at risk of lapsing; policies in active conservation. The insurer’s primary retention intelligence tool. Chief Distribution Officer, Operations, Actuarial (lapse assumption validation) Weekly/monthly NAICOM market conduct data; ORSA lapse risk quantification Claims Register All open and closed claims in the period: claim reference, policy number, claim type, date of notification, date of complete documentation, settlement date, amount paid, and settlement status against the NIIRA 2025 60-day target. Flags all claims approaching or breaching the regulatory deadline. Head of Claims, COO, Compliance Daily (open claims); monthly summary NAICOM claims settlement report; market conduct inspection data Premium Reconciliation Report Daily comparison of expected premium income (from the PAS billing schedule) against actual receipts (from the insurer’s bank statement). Identifies: matched receipts, unmatched receipts (suspense), expected premiums not received (grace period or overdue). The primary internal control over premium collection integrity. Finance, Operations, Internal Audit Daily Financial audit; premium income recognition for NAICOM returns Reinsurance Cession Statement All policies ceded to each reinsurer in the period: policy data, ceded premium, ceded reserve, and claims recoveries. The basis for treaty settlement with each reinsurer and for NAICOM’s domestic cession compliance report. Finance, Reinsurance team, Actuarial Quarterly / per treaty accounting period NIIRA 2025 domestic cession report; reinsurance treaty settlement Agent Production Report Each agent’s production in the period: new policies written, AFYP, persistency rate of the agent’s book, NIGO rate, and commission earned and paid. The primary sales management and commission verification tool. Chief Distribution Officer, Agency Managers Monthly NAICOM commission compliance; CIIN agent licensing verification Policy Reserve Report Actuarial reserves by product and treaty cohort, calculated by the actuarial system from PAS data. Confirms reserve adequacy for the Statutory Actuary’s annual investigation and IFRS 17 liability measurement. Statutory Actuary, Finance, CFO Monthly (IFRS 17); quarterly for NAICOM return NAICOM statutory return; IFRS 17 financial reporting NDPA Data Access Log A log of all access to policyholder personal data: who accessed what data, when, and for what purpose. The primary evidence of data governance compliance under NDPA 2023. DPO, Compliance, Internal Audit Continuous logging; quarterly review NDPA 2023 accountability obligation; NDPC audit evidence

t: Chapter 29 · 29.5 Cloud vs On-Premise PAS Deployment for Nigerian Insurers
x: The decision whether to deploy a PAS in the cloud (hosted on the infrastructure of a cloud service provider such as AWS, Azure, or a local Nigerian cloud provider) or on-premise (on servers hosted in the insurer’s own data centre) is one of the most consequential technology architecture decisions a Nigerian life insurer can make. It affects cost structure, scalability, data governance, security posture, and regulatory compliance. Dimension Cloud Deployment On-Premise Deployment Capital cost Low upfront investment. Typically subscription-based (pay per user or per policy). Eliminates the large initial server hardware investment. High upfront investment in servers, storage, networking equipment, and data centre infrastructure. Depreciates over 5–7 years. Operating cost Predictable monthly subscription fee plus data egress costs. Scales up as policy count grows (cost advantage). Risk of cost escalation if usage patterns exceed contracted tiers. Lower ongoing licence fees. Internal IT team cost. Risk of underutilisation (over-provisioned hardware capacity). Maintenance and upgrade costs are discrete capital events. Scalability Inherently scalable: cloud infrastructure can be scaled up during peak periods (year-end policy issuance, December claim surges) without hardware procurement. Limited by the hardware capacity installed. Scaling requires hardware procurement lead time of weeks to months. Data localisation (NDPA 2023 / GAID 2025) Nigerian policyholder data must be stored on servers physically located in Nigeria (primary storage). Nigerian cloud providers (Galaxy Backbone, MainOne, 21st Century Technologies) can satisfy this requirement. International cloud providers (AWS Lagos, Azure South Africa) may satisfy the requirement depending on NDPC guidance. By definition compliant: servers are in the insurer’s own data centre on Nigerian soil. No data localisation risk. Cybersecurity Cloud providers typically invest more in security infrastructure than individual insurers can afford. Shared responsibility model: the cloud provider secures the infrastructure; the insurer secures the application and data. Concentration risk: a cloud provider breach affects all customers. Full control over physical security, access controls, and network architecture. Requires significant internal security investment and expertise to match enterprise cloud security standards. Business continuity Cloud providers typically offer built-in redundancy, failover, and disaster recovery across multiple data centres. RTO and RPO targets are contractually guaranteed. Requires separate disaster recovery site, replication, and failover infrastructure — significant additional cost. RTO/RPO depends on the insurer’s own investment. Vendor dependency Dependent on cloud provider availability and pricing. Service disruption or contract termination by the cloud provider can be operationally catastrophic without a migration plan. Complete control over infrastructure. No dependency on cloud provider availability. Hardware obsolescence risk if refresh cycle is not maintained. NAICOM / regulatory posture NAICOM’s Insurtech Guidelines (2025) acknowledge cloud deployment as a legitimate infrastructure model, subject to data localisation compliance and cybersecurity standards. NAICOM may require evidence of the cloud provider’s security certifications (ISO 27001, SOC 2). No specific regulatory advantage over cloud. NAICOM’s inspection of on-premise infrastructure focuses on access controls, backup integrity, and disaster recovery capability. Recommended for Start-up and mid-size insurers; insurers implementing a new PAS; insurers prioritising flexibility and lower capital cost; Standalone Insurtechs. Large established insurers with significant existing on-premise infrastructure investment; insurers with regulatory certainty requirements that cloud cannot currently satisfy; insurers in markets where reliable internet connectivity for cloud access cannot be guaranteed. Advisory: Hybrid Deployment: The Pragmatic Nigerian Solution Many Nigerian life insurers are adopting a hybrid deployment model: the core PAS runs on-premise (preserving data localisation certainty and the existing infrastructure investment), while new digital capabilities — the customer portal, the mobile app, the agent onboarding platform, and the analytics layer — run on cloud infrastructure. This ‘cloud-first for new, on-premise for core’ approach allows the insurer to modernise its customer-facing technology without committing to a full cloud migration of a complex legacy PAS. The risk is integration complexity: the on-premise PAS and cloud-based digital tools must exchange data reliably and securely.

A modern life insurance PAS does not operate in isolation. It is the hub of an integration network connecting multiple operational systems. The quality of these integrations — their reliability, real-time capability, data fidelity, and error handling — determines whether the insurer’s technology ecosystem functions as a coherent operational machine or as a collection of disconnected systems that require expensive manual reconciliation. 29.6.1 API-Based Integration: The Modern Standard Application Programming Interface (API) A defined protocol that enables two software systems to exchange data and trigger actions in real time over a network connection, without human intervention. In insurance, APIs enable a digital customer portal to query the PAS for a real-time policy status; a bancassurance bank system to trigger a new policy application in the PAS; or a claims management workflow tool to update the PAS’s claims status when a payment is authorised. Legacy PAS platforms typically communicate through batch file exchanges — large data files exported from one system and imported into another at defined intervals (overnight, weekly). This approach produces stale data, reconciliation challenges, and an inability to support real-time digital customer experiences. A modern PAS must offer REST or SOAP API connectivity as a standard feature, enabling real-time data exchange with all integrated systems. 29.6.2 Key Integration Interfaces Integration Partner Data Exchanged Direction Business Purpose Nigerian Context Core Banking System (Bancassurance) New policy applications; premium collection mandates; policy status queries; claims payment instructions. Bidirectional: bank to PAS (applications, premium receipts); PAS to bank (policy confirmations, claims payments). Enables bancassurance channel operation: bank customers can apply for insurance through the bank’s internet banking or branch system, with the application flowing directly into the PAS’s new business queue. CBN regulatory requirements on bank data sharing with insurance partners must be satisfied. The bancassurance agreement must specify the API integration standards and data protection obligations. CRM Platform Policyholder contact details; policy portfolio summary; service interaction history; renewal reminders. PAS to CRM (policy data); CRM to PAS (policy updates initiated by service team). Enables agent and customer service teams to see a 360° view of the policyholder’s insurance relationship without logging into the PAS directly. Many Nigerian insurers use local CRM implementations or WhatsApp Business API as a CRM substitute. API integration must work with these lightweight tools as well as enterprise CRM platforms. Actuarial / Valuation System Policy data extract (product, age, benefit, premium, status) for reserve calculation; mortality experience data for assumption setting. PAS to actuarial system (data extract, typically nightly or monthly); actuarial system to PAS (reserve amounts for financial reporting). Enables the Statutory Actuary’s annual investigation and IFRS 17 measurement by providing clean, complete policy data in the format required by the actuarial model. IFRS 17 requires policy-level data on cohort membership, inception date, and liability measurement group. Legacy PAS platforms often cannot produce this granularity without significant data transformation. Financial Accounting / ERP System Premium income transactions; claims payments; commission disbursements; reinsurance premium ceded; reserve movements. PAS to ERP (financial transactions, daily or real-time); ERP to PAS (payment confirmations). Enables automated financial reporting without manual re-keying of PAS financial data into the accounting system. Eliminates a significant source of financial reporting error and reconciliation effort. SAP, Oracle, and Sage are common ERP platforms in Nigerian insurance. The PAS vendor must either provide a pre-built ERP connector or offer an open API for custom integration. NAICOM Regulatory Reporting Portal Quarterly market returns (new business count and premium, in-force register, claims settlement data, solvency margin, domestic cession ratio). PAS to NAICOM portal (quarterly, via NAICOM’s mandated data format). Enables compliance with NAICOM’s statutory reporting requirements without manual extraction and formatting of PAS data. NAICOM’s digital filing portal requires data submission in a specific format (XML or structured CSV). The PAS must generate this output directly. Digital Customer Portal / Mobile App Policy details; premium payment history; premium due dates; claims status; policy documents. Bidirectional: PAS to portal (read-only policy data); portal to PAS (premium payments, service requests, claims notifications). Enables policyholders to self-serve: check their policy status, pay premiums, submit a claim notification, or download their policy document without contacting the insurer. NDPA 2023 consent management: the portal must capture and record policyholder consent for data processing, with consent status stored in the PAS. WhatsApp Business API / USSD Premium reminders; payment confirmations; claims notifications; policy status queries. PAS to WhatsApp/USSD (outbound notifications); WhatsApp/USSD to PAS (inbound queries, triggered by policyholder actions). In the Nigerian market, WhatsApp and USSD are often more reliable and more widely used than mobile apps or email for policyholder communication. PAS integration with these channels is not optional — it is essential for effective policyholder engagement. NAICOM’s USSD insurance distribution guidelines (Log 3A, 2020 Circular) require that USSD-distributed products are properly connected to a NAICOM-approved PAS backend.

t: Chapter 29 · 29.7 PAS Compliance: NIIRA 2025, NDPA 2023, and IFRS 17
x: 29.7.1 NIIRA 2025 PAS Requirements NIIRA 2025 Requirement PAS Implication Claims settlement: 5-day acknowledgement + 60-day settlement timeline The PAS claims module must: timestamp the date and time of every claim notification; calculate the 60-day settlement deadline automatically; generate escalation alerts as the deadline approaches; and produce the NAICOM claims settlement report showing compliance status for every claim. Premium receipt confirmation The no-premium-no-cover principle requires the PAS to block policy activation until a confirmed premium receipt is matched to the new business record. No policy should be shown as ‘in-force’ in the PAS until premium receipt is confirmed. Agent licensing compliance The PAS’s agent module must hold each agent’s CIIN Cert. COP number and licence expiry date. The PAS should block commission payment to an agent whose licence has lapsed and should alert the Agency Manager to unlicensed agent production. Commission compliance Commission calculations in the PAS must be configured at the NAICOM-approved rates for each product. Commission payments above the approved rate are a regulatory breach; the PAS configuration is the primary control against this. Audit trail for governance NIIRA 2025’s three lines of defence framework requires the insurer to demonstrate that risk controls are operating. The PAS must maintain a complete, tamper-evident audit trail of every material action: policy issuance, premium receipt, policy change, claims decision, and commission payment — with user identity, timestamp, and the before/after values for every data change. 29.7.2 NDPA 2023 and GAID 2025 PAS Obligations Data Protection Obligations Embedded in the PAS The PAS is the primary system processing the personal data of Nigerian life insurance policyholders. Every NDPA 2023 obligation applies to how the PAS stores, accesses, and manages this data. • Consent management: The PAS must record the specific consent given by each policyholder at application (for medical data processing, for marketing, for data sharing) and must flag any processing that goes beyond the recorded consent. • Data subject access rights: The PAS must be able to generate a complete data extract for any policyholder who exercises their NDPA 2023 right of access, within 30 days of the request. • Data minimisation: The PAS configuration must limit data capture to what is strictly necessary for the insurance contract. Data fields that are collected ‘just in case’ without a lawful basis violate the NDPA 2023’s data minimisation principle. • Retention and disposal: The PAS must enforce the retention schedule: active policies (retained for the policy term plus 7 years); claims records (retained for 10 years). Records beyond their retention period must be automatically scheduled for deletion. • Access control and data access logging: The PAS must enforce role-based access controls (no user can access data beyond what their role requires) and must log all access to policyholder health and financial data with user identity and timestamp.

t: Chapter 29 · 29.8 PAS Vendors in the African and Nigerian Market
x: The PAS market for African life insurers comprises four broad categories: global enterprise platforms adapted for the African market; regional African-developed platforms; Nigeria-specific local solutions; and bespoke internally developed systems. Each category has different cost profiles, capability ranges, and support models. Vendor Category Representative Platforms Typical Profile of Insurer Key Strengths Key Limitations for Nigerian Market Global Enterprise PAS Oracle Insurance Policy Administration (OIPA); Majesco; EIS Suite; Sapiens; Guidewire. Large composite insurers; subsidiaries of international insurance groups; insurers seeking best-in-class functionality and IFRS 17-native capability. IFRS 17 native; API-ready; scalable to very large policy volumes; strong vendor support; continuous product development. Regional African PAS Jenisys (South Africa); Global Insurance System (GIS, South Africa); BroadPoint Insurance System; Veritech PAS. Mid-size African insurers; regional groups operating across multiple African markets; insurers needing African market regulatory compliance built in. Pre-configured for African market specifics; lower cost than global platforms; often includes Nigerian regulatory modules; local implementation support. Smaller vendor R&D budgets mean slower feature development; IFRS 17 capability may require additional modules; vendor viability risk for smaller providers. Nigeria-Specific Solutions Locally developed platforms by Nigerian software houses; customised versions of ERP systems (Sage, Tally) used as de facto PAS; hybrid spreadsheet-database systems. Start-up insurers; very small insurers; companies with highly bespoke product structures that commercial PAS platforms cannot accommodate. Fully customised for the Nigerian regulatory environment; lower initial cost; responsive local development team. t: Chapter 29 · 29.9 PAS Selection Criteria for Nigerian Life Insurers
x: The selection of a PAS is one of the most consequential and irreversible technology decisions a life insurer can make. A poorly selected PAS will constrain the insurer’s operational capability, regulatory compliance, and digital ambition for a decade or more. The following criteria framework provides the basis for a structured PAS evaluation process. Criterion What to Evaluate Weight (Indicative) Red Flag Functional completeness Does the platform support all eight core PAS modules? Does it handle the specific product types the insurer writes (participating policies, unit-linked, group life, annuities)? Can it be configured for new product structures without custom development? High A platform that requires significant custom development to support the insurer’s existing products is immediately problematic. NIIRA 2025 regulatory compliance Does the platform natively support: NAICOM reporting format; the claims SLA monitoring required by NIIRA 2025; agent licensing compliance checks; commission configuration at NAICOM-approved rates? High (mandatory) A PAS that cannot produce the NAICOM quarterly return in the correct format without manual extraction is non-compliant with regulatory obligations. IFRS 17 readiness Can the platform produce policy-level data in the format required for IFRS 17 CSM calculation? Does it maintain cohort assignment data from policy inception? High (for listed insurers) Many legacy platforms require a complete data transformation layer to produce IFRS 17-compliant outputs. This is a significant hidden cost. NDPA 2023 compliance Does the platform support: role-based access control; data access logging; consent management at the field level; data subject access request data extraction; retention and disposal enforcement? High (mandatory) A PAS with no data access logging capability is structurally non-compliant with NDPA 2023’s accountability obligations. API capability Does the platform offer REST APIs for real-time integration with CRM, digital portals, bancassurance banking systems, and USSD platforms? Is the API documentation publicly available and well-maintained? High A PAS without open API connectivity cannot support digital channel integration and will require expensive batch file workarounds. Scalability Can the platform handle the insurer’s projected 5-year policy count without performance degradation? Has the vendor demonstrated performance at scale in comparable markets? Medium-High A platform that has only been deployed at small insurer scale in similar markets is unproven. Total cost of ownership (TCO) What is the total 5-year cost: licence fees + implementation + customisation + training + ongoing support + upgrade costs? How does this compare to the value of operational improvements? Medium A very low headline licence fee that conceals high implementation and customisation costs is a common PAS procurement trap. Vendor viability and support How long has the vendor been operating? What is their financial position? Do they have an active development roadmap? What is the support model (24/7, local, remote)? What are the SLAs for issue resolution? Medium-High A PAS vendor with no other clients in Nigeria or the West African region will have no local market knowledge and no demonstrated ability to support the regulatory environment. Data migration capability How will historical policy data be migrated from the current system? Has the vendor done comparable migrations? What is the data validation and testing approach? High (if replacing an existing system) A vendor who cannot articulate a credible data migration methodology should not be selected for a PAS replacement project. Cloud deployment option Does the vendor offer a cloud deployment option with Nigerian data localisation capability (data centre in Nigeria)? What is the vendor’s cloud security certification? Medium (depending on deployment preference)

t: Chapter 29 · 29.10 PAS Implementation: Governance, Risk, and Common Failure Modes
x: PAS implementation projects are among the most complex and highest-risk technology initiatives a life insurer can undertake. Policy data migration, regulatory continuity, agent tool disruption, and operational paralysis during the cutover are all genuine risks that have derailed PAS implementations in comparable markets. The following governance framework and failure mode inventory are based on Nigerian and African market implementation experience. PAS Implementation Governance Framework EXECUTIVE SPONSOR: The CEO or COO must own the PAS implementation at ExCo level. A PAS implementation that is managed purely at IT level will fail — the cross-functional decisions required (data migration priorities, product configuration, regulatory reporting requirements, agent tool design) cannot be made without executive authority and cross-departmental coordination. STEERING COMMITTEE: A steering committee comprising the CEO/COO, CFO, Head of Operations, Head of IT, Chief Distribution Officer, and the Statutory Actuary must meet at least fortnightly during implementation. The steering committee resolves escalated issues that the project team cannot resolve within the implementation timeline. PROJECT MANAGEMENT: An experienced implementation project manager (who has delivered at least one life insurance PAS implementation) must lead the project. The insurer’s project manager works alongside the vendor’s implementation team. Project milestones, risk register, and issue log must be reviewed at every steering committee meeting. DATA MIGRATION: The data migration from the old PAS to the new PAS is the highest-risk element of the implementation. All historical policy data must be: extracted from the old system; cleansed and standardised; validated against the old system’s reports; migrated to the new system; and re-validated against the new system’s reports. No cutover should proceed until the data migration validation confirms that the new system’s in-force register matches the old system’s register exactly. USER ACCEPTANCE TESTING (UAT): A structured UAT programme must test every material business scenario before go-live: policy issuance across all product types; premium collection and lapse processing; claims processing and settlement; reinsurance cession calculation; all management reports against expected values; all regulatory report outputs. UAT must be conducted by business users, not IT staff. Sign-off authority for UAT completion rests with the COO and the Statutory Actuary. Common PAS Implementation Failure Modes in the Nigerian Market 1. DIRTY DATA MIGRATION: The most common failure mode. Policy data accumulated over years in a legacy system is frequently inconsistent, incomplete, and inaccurate. Migrating dirty data into a new PAS simply perpetuates the data quality problems in a more expensive system. A data cleansing project must precede migration. 2. UNDERESTIMATING CONFIGURATION COMPLEXITY: Commercial PAS platforms are highly configurable but require significant configuration effort to match a specific insurer’s product structures, commission rules, and regulatory reporting requirements. Insurers that underestimate this effort (and the internal resource required to manage it) consistently overshoot implementation timelines and budgets. 3. PARALLEL RUN SKIPPED: The parallel run — operating both the old and new PAS simultaneously for a defined period (typically 1–3 months), comparing their outputs daily — is the most effective risk mitigation for a PAS go-live. Under pressure to meet a go-live deadline, many implementations skip the parallel run and go directly to cutover. This is the decision most regretted when issues emerge. 4. INADEQUATE CHANGE MANAGEMENT: A new PAS changes the daily working tools of every member of the operations, sales support, claims, and finance teams. Inadequate training, insufficient user involvement in the UAT process, and poor communication about what is changing and when produces a workforce that is demotivated, resistant, and prone to error at go-live. 5. NO REGULATORY CONTINUITY PLAN: The NAICOM quarterly return does not pause for a PAS implementation. The NIIRA 2025 claims settlement timelines do not pause. A PAS implementation that does not include a regulatory continuity plan — ensuring all regulatory obligations continue to be met during the transition period — will generate NAICOM findings for late or incorrect submissions.

t: Chapter 29 · 29.11 Advisory: Evaluating Your Current PAS
x: Most Nigerian life insurers currently operate a PAS that was implemented more than ten years ago, against a regulatory and technology environment that is radically different from today’s. The question is not whether the current PAS needs to change — for most Nigerian insurers, it does — but how urgently, and through what route. Advisory: A PAS Assessment Framework for Nigerian Life Insurers STEP 1: REGULATORY COMPLIANCE AUDIT. Can the current PAS produce every NAICOM statutory return in the correct format, without manual extraction and manipulation? Can it enforce the NIIRA 2025 claims settlement SLAs? Can it produce the NDPA 2023 data access log? If the answer to any of these is NO, the insurer has an immediate regulatory compliance gap that must be closed. STEP 2: MANAGEMENT INFORMATION QUALITY AUDIT. Can the current PAS produce all eight reports listed in Section 29.4 automatically, in a format that management can use directly without re-processing in Excel? Significant manual extraction and manipulation is a symptom of a PAS that the insurer has outgrown. STEP 3: INTEGRATION CAPABILITY AUDIT. Does the current PAS have API connectivity to the insurer’s digital customer portal, bancassurance banking systems, and WhatsApp/USSD customer communication channels? An inability to integrate with digital channels through real-time APIs limits the insurer’s ability to compete with Insurtech entrants. STEP 4: VENDOR VIABILITY AUDIT. Is the current PAS vendor actively investing in the platform? Is the platform being upgraded to meet IFRS 17, NDPA 2023, and NIIRA 2025 requirements? Is there an active user community? A PAS whose vendor has stopped active development is on a path to obsolescence. STEP 5: TOTAL COST OF INACTION. The cost of upgrading or replacing a PAS is significant and visible. The cost of not upgrading — manual workarounds, regulatory findings, the inability to launch new products or distribution channels, IFRS 17 non-compliance — is diffuse and accumulates invisibly until a crisis makes it undeniable. Calculate both before deciding. The Most Important PAS Investment Decision for a Nigerian Life Insurer Invest in a PAS that will not require replacement again within five years. The temptation to choose a lower-cost, partial solution — a system that addresses the immediate regulatory compliance gap but cannot grow with the insurer’s digital ambitions — is a false economy. A well-chosen, well-implemented modern PAS with open API architecture, IFRS 17-native reporting, and NDPA 2023-compliant data governance is a one-generation investment that unlocks the insurer’s ability to compete in the digital insurance market. A cheap PAS that requires replacement in three years will cost more in total than the right PAS implemented once.

Policy Administration System (PAS) The core software system that creates, stores, and manages all insurance policy records across the policy lifecycle, from application through to termination. The system of record for all policyholder obligations. New Business Module The PAS module that handles the journey from application intake through underwriting to policy issuance, capturing all proposal form data and routing the application through the underwriting workflow. Premium Collection Module The PAS module managing premium billing generation, premium receipt recording, grace period tracking, lapse processing, and premium reconciliation. Policy Maintenance Module The PAS module handling all changes to an in-force policy after issuance, including endorsements, reinstatements, policy loans, and beneficiary changes, with complete audit trail. Benefit Calculation Module The PAS module computing policy values: surrender value, paid-up value, death benefit (including bonuses for participating policies), and maturity benefit. Claims Processing Module The PAS module managing the end-to-end claims workflow from notification to settlement, with automated SLA monitoring against the 60-day statutory settlement requirement (NIIRA 2025 s.210) and the insurer’s 5-day acknowledgement standard. Reinsurance Cession Module The PAS module calculating and recording reinsurance cessions under treaty arrangements, generating treaty statements, and tracking reinsurance recoveries on claims. Financial Reporting Interface The PAS component generating data outputs for the financial accounting system, actuarial reporting, and NAICOM regulatory returns. In-Force Policy Register A complete list of all active policies with their key data; the definitive record of the insurer’s current policyholder obligations and the basis for actuarial reserving and NAICOM reporting. Premium Reconciliation The daily process of matching expected premium income (from the PAS billing schedule) against actual bank receipts, with investigation of unmatched items. API (Application Programming Interface) A defined protocol enabling two software systems to exchange data and trigger actions in real time; the modern standard for PAS integration with CRM, digital portals, banking systems, and regulatory reporting tools. Data Localisation The NDPA 2023 / GAID 2025 requirement that personal data of Nigerian data subjects be stored primarily on servers physically located in Nigeria; material to cloud deployment decisions. User Acceptance Testing (UAT) A structured testing programme conducted by business users (not IT staff) to verify that every material business scenario works correctly in the new PAS before go-live. Parallel Run The practice of operating both the old and new PAS simultaneously for a defined period after go-live, comparing daily outputs to identify and resolve discrepancies before decommissioning the old system. Total Cost of Ownership (TCO) The full five-year cost of a PAS, including licence fees, implementation, customisation, training, support, and upgrade costs; the correct basis for PAS financial evaluation. NIGO (Not In Good Order) An application flagged by the PAS as incomplete or inconsistent, returned to the agent for correction before entering the underwriting queue.

Under NIIRA 2025, a life insurer's PAS claims module must automatically track which statutory timelines? A 10-day acknowledgement target and a 90-day settlement target. A 5-day acknowledgement target and a 60-day settlement target from notification of the claim. A 24-hour acknowledgement target and a 14-day settlement target. A 7-day acknowledgement target and a 45-day settlement target. (B) A 5-day acknowledgement target and a 60-day settlement target from notification of the claim. Why (B) is Correct Under NIIRA 2025 (s.210) a valid claim must be settled within 60 days of notification, and the book recommends a 5-business-day written acknowledgement of each claim notification as an internal service standard (no statutory acknowledgement period has been confirmed). The PAS claims module must track both deadlines, alert when a claim nears the acknowledgement deadline without confirmation, and escalate as a claim approaches or breaches the 60-day settlement deadline. The NDPA 2023 data localisation requirement means a Nigerian life insurer deploying a cloud-based PAS must ensure that: All policyholder data is stored exclusively on servers owned by the insurer itself. Policyholder data is encrypted at all times and backed up to at least three separate geographic locations. The primary storage of Nigerian policyholder personal data is on servers physically located in Nigeria. Policyholder data may only be accessed by staff who are physically present in Nigeria. (C) The primary storage of Nigerian policyholder personal data is on servers physically located in Nigeria. Why (C) is Correct NDPA 2023 (and the GAID 2025 implementation directive) requires data controllers to store and process Nigerian citizens' personal data on servers physically located within Nigeria as the primary data store. This data localisation requirement means that a cloud-based PAS must be deployed on Nigerian-domiciled cloud infrastructure (either an AWS Nigeria region, Azure Nigeria region, or a Nigerian data centre) — not on servers in the US, Europe, or Asia, even if these are offered by major cloud providers. Cross-border data transfers to foreign servers are permitted for specific backup or processing purposes but require specific safeguards. Why the Others Are Wrong (A) The insurer does not need to own the servers — it can use cloud infrastructure that is physically located in Nigeria. The daily premium reconciliation report from a life insurance PAS is primarily used to: Calculate the reinsurance cession due to treaty reinsurers for the month. Match expected premium income from the billing schedule against actual bank receipts, identifying unmatched items for investigation. Calculate the surrender values payable on policies presented for cancellation during the period. Verify that agent commission has been paid at the correct NAICOM-approved rate for each policy. (B) Match expected premium income from the billing schedule against actual bank receipts, identifying unmatched items for investigation. Why (B) is Correct The daily premium reconciliation is a financial control process: the PAS generates a billing schedule (all premiums due on that day's anniversary policies); the bank provides a payment file (all receipts credited to the insurer's premium collection accounts that day); and the reconciliation matches the two files. Unmatched items — premiums expected but not received, or receipts that cannot be matched to a specific policy — require investigation. Without daily reconciliation, the insurer cannot accurately track which policies are in force (premiums received) and which are in grace period or lapsed (premiums not received). (B) Data discrepancies between the old and new system, which would have been identified and resolved during the parallel run, may only be discovered after the old system has been decommissioned. Why (B) is Correct A parallel run involves operating both the old and new PAS simultaneously for a defined period (typically 3–6 months), processing all real transactions through both systems and comparing outputs. Differences in policy records, premium calculations, reserve computations, or claims data are identified and resolved while the old system is still available as a reference. Skipping the parallel run and going live directly on the new system means that any data discrepancies — migrated incorrectly, miscalculated by the new system, or simply incompletely transferred — are only discovered when they cause operational failures (a policyholder's coverage is incorrectly terminated; a claim is incorrectly declined; a premium is not correctly applied).
