t: Chapter 31 · 31.1 Introduction: AI in Insurance — Promise, Reality, and the Nigerian Context
x: Artificial intelligence is the most discussed and most misunderstood technology in the contemporary insurance industry. The promise — automated underwriting that prices every risk perfectly, fraud detection that eliminates claims abuse, customer service bots that handle every policyholder query without human involvement — is real but distant for most Nigerian life insurers. The reality for the overwhelming majority of the Nigerian market is that the prerequisites for effective AI — clean, structured, historical data; robust data infrastructure; qualified data scientists; and a culture of evidence-based decision-making — are only partially in place. This chapter takes a deliberately practical stance. It explains what AI, machine learning, and related technologies actually are; describes the specific insurance use cases where AI is generating demonstrable value in markets comparable to Nigeria; identifies the data and infrastructure requirements for each use case; and provides an honest assessment of where Nigerian life insurers are likely to encounter the most significant implementation barriers. It also addresses the regulatory and ethical constraints — NAICOM’s position, NDPA 2023’s automated decision-making provisions, and the AI/ML governance requirements in the NAICOM Insurtech Guidelines — that define the compliance envelope within which AI use in Nigerian insurance must operate.

t: Chapter 31 · 31.2 AI, ML, and Deep Learning: A Primer for Insurance Professionals
x: Term Definition Insurance Analogy Relevance to Nigerian Life Insurance Artificial Intelligence (AI) The broad field of computer science aimed at building systems that perform tasks that would require human intelligence if performed by a person: recognising patterns, understanding language, making decisions, and learning from experience. An underwriting system that can assess a new application and recommend acceptance, rating, or decline — the way an experienced underwriter would. Umbrella term. When practitioners say ‘AI’ in insurance, they almost always mean machine learning or a specific ML application. Machine Learning (ML) A subset of AI in which algorithms learn patterns from data without being explicitly programmed with rules. Given enough labelled examples (‘this application resulted in a good risk’; ‘this claim was fraudulent’), an ML model identifies the patterns that distinguish one from the other and applies them to new cases. A fraud detection model trained on 50,000 historical claims learns that claims filed within 90 days of policy issuance, with a stated cause of accidental death, by beneficiaries with no prior relationship with the insurer, are flagged at a higher rate. It applies this pattern to new claims. The foundation for all practical AI use cases in insurance. Most of the use cases in this chapter are ML applications. Supervised Learning An ML approach in which the model is trained on labelled data: examples where the correct answer is known. The model learns to predict the label for new, unlabelled cases. Training a lapse prediction model on historical policies: for each policy, the training data shows the policyholder’s characteristics at inception and whether the policy lapsed at 13 months. The model learns which characteristics predict lapse. Most high-value insurance ML use cases (fraud detection, lapse prediction, automated underwriting) use supervised learning. Unsupervised Learning An ML approach in which the model finds patterns in unlabelled data without predefined correct answers. Customer segmentation: grouping policyholders by their behaviour patterns (payment timing, servicing contacts, product holdings) without predefined segments. Used for customer analytics and market segmentation in insurance. Deep Learning A subset of ML using neural networks with many layers (‘deep’ networks) to learn representations of complex, high-dimensional data such as images, audio, and text. Requires very large datasets and significant computing power. OCR of handwritten medical reports; voice analysis for claims call centres; image analysis for accident documentation. Currently limited applicability in most Nigerian life insurers due to data volume requirements. NLP (a deep learning application) is the most accessible deep learning use case. Natural Language Processing (NLP) A deep learning application that enables computers to understand, interpret, and generate human language — both text and speech. An NLP system that reads a hospital discharge summary and extracts the diagnosis, treatment, and prognosis as structured data fields for underwriting or claims assessment. Practical application for medical records processing in underwriting and claims. Algorithm A defined set of rules or mathematical operations that an ML model uses to make predictions or decisions. The formula a risk scoring model uses to translate an applicant’s age, health data, and behavioural signals into a mortality risk score. All ML models are built on algorithms. Understanding the algorithm is important for model governance and explainability. Training Data The historical dataset used to train an ML model, containing the input features and the known correct outcomes (labels). Historical policy data (policyholder characteristics, product, premium, lapse/persist outcome) used to train a lapse prediction model. Data quality and volume are the primary constraints on AI implementation for most Nigerian insurers.

t: Chapter 31 · 31.3 Automated Underwriting: Risk Scoring Using Non-Medical Data
x: Automated underwriting uses ML models to assess mortality risk and make underwriting decisions for standard and near-standard individual life applications without requiring human underwriter review. For applications within the non-medical limit (defined in Chapter 11), where no physical examination is required, an automated underwriting model can assess the proposal form data and make an immediate accept/rate/refer decision — reducing issuance time from days to minutes. 31.3.1 Non-Medical Data Sources for Automated Underwriting The traditional life underwriting model is heavily dependent on medical evidence: the proposal form’s health declaration, the medical examination, and clinical reports. AI-powered underwriting expands the data universe to include ‘alternative data’ — behavioural and contextual signals that predict mortality risk without requiring clinical measurement: Data Source What It Signals Nigerian Availability Limitations Mobile money transaction behaviour Income stability; spending patterns consistent with lifestyle declarations; payment regularity (a person who pays all their bills on time is likely to maintain insurance premiums, and is also likely to be financially stable and lower mortality risk). High — M-Pesa/MTN MoMo/OPay transaction data accessible through partnerships with mobile money operators. Requires explicit consent under NDPA 2023. Correlation with mortality is probabilistic, not causal. Airtime top-up patterns Regular, predictable airtime purchase is correlated with stable behaviour patterns. Very erratic patterns may signal financial instability. High — available through telco partnerships. Weak mortality signal on its own; most useful in combination with other features. Bank Verification Number (BVN) data Age, financial activity history, and identity verification. BVN-linked transaction data provides a structured financial behavioural profile. High — BVN is near-universal in the formal sector. NDPA 2023 consent required. CBN data sharing rules govern access. Social media activity (limited) In some markets, social media-derived lifestyle signals (hazardous activity photos, location patterns) are used as supplementary signals. Highly controversial ethically. Low — social media data use in underwriting faces significant ethical and regulatory resistance in the Nigerian market. NDPA 2023 data minimisation principle; NAICOM’s consumer protection framework. Not recommended for Nigerian deployment. Geolocation / address data Residential area correlates with access to healthcare, occupational hazard exposure, and environmental mortality risk factors. Medium — available from mobile data with consent. Must not proxy for protected characteristics (ethnicity, religion) that are prohibited bases for insurance discrimination. 31.3.2 How Automated Underwriting Models Work A typical automated underwriting model for a Nigerian life insurer is a supervised ML classifier trained on the insurer’s historical policy data. The model is trained on policies where the outcome is known (the policy persisted to maturity or resulted in a claim within a defined period) and where the input features at application are available (age, occupation, health declaration responses, premium level, sum assured, channel). The model learns which combinations of features are associated with higher or lower mortality risk and assigns each new application a risk score. The risk score maps to an underwriting decision: scores below a defined threshold are automatically accepted at standard rates (straight-through processing); scores in a middle band are automatically referred to a human underwriter for review; scores above the upper threshold are automatically rated (a premium loading is calculated by the model) or declined and referred. Automated Underwriting Decision Logic Risk Score Band Model Output Human Underwriter Action Issuance Timeline Score 0–40 (Low risk) Automatic accept at standard rates None — straight-through processing Minutes (policy issued immediately) Score 41–65 (Standard-plus) Automatic accept with minor loading or request for specific additional question Review only if loading is queried by agent Same day Score 66–80 (Refer) Referral to human underwriter queue with model rationale Human underwriter reviews model recommendation and makes final decision 1–3 business days Score 81–100 (High risk / decline) Automatic decline recommendation Senior underwriter reviews; may override with justification recorded in audit trail 1–5 business days Important governance principle: No automated underwriting model in Nigerian life insurance should make a final decline decision without human review. NAICOM’s consumer protection framework requires that a declined applicant can receive a human explanation for the decision. An automated decline without human review does not satisfy this requirement.

t: Chapter 31 · 31.4 Predictive Claims: Fraud Detection and Early Intervention
x: Insurance fraud is a significant drain on Nigerian life insurance profitability. While precise market-wide fraud statistics are not published, industry estimates suggest that fraudulent or inflated claims represent 5–15% of total claims expenditure across the Nigerian insurance market. AI-powered fraud detection systems significantly outperform traditional rule-based approaches (which flag claims based on predefined rules) by identifying subtle patterns that experienced human fraud investigators would not detect in routine assessment. 31.4.1 How ML Fraud Detection Works A fraud detection ML model is trained on historical claims data where fraud status is known (claims that were investigated and confirmed as fraudulent, and claims that were validated as genuine). The model learns the patterns associated with fraudulent claims across multiple features simultaneously: Timing signals: Policies claimed within 90 days of issuance; policies with a lapse history followed by reinstatement followed immediately by a claim; policies taken out in multiple names on the same life by the same proposer. Documentation signals: Death certificates from unusual issuing authorities; medical reports with inconsistent clinical terminology; beneficiary identity documents that cannot be verified against NIMC’s NIN database; multiple claims submitted with the same handwriting style in the supporting documents. Network signals: Beneficiary shares a phone number or bank account with the beneficiary of a previous fraudulent claim; the certifying doctor on the death certificate has certified an unusually high number of accidental deaths in the same geographic area. Behavioural signals: The claimant’s interaction with the insurer’s claims portal differs from typical claimant behaviour (unusually fast document upload, access at unusual hours, multiple failed attempts to submit before the successful submission). Avoiding False Positives: The Human Oversight Imperative The most dangerous failure mode of an AI fraud detection system is the false positive: a valid claim incorrectly flagged as potentially fraudulent and subjected to additional investigation or delay. For a bereaved family relying on a life insurance payout, a 30-day delay because a fraud model flagged their claim is not a minor inconvenience — it is a traumatic experience that drives complaints, regulatory attention, and reputational damage. Every claim flagged by an AI fraud model must be reviewed by a human investigator before any delay, additional document request, or SIU referral is triggered. The AI model’s role is to prioritise the human investigator’s attention, not to make the decision. 31.4.2 Early Intervention: Predictive Claims Triage Beyond fraud detection, ML models can predict which incoming claims are likely to be complex, contested, or high-value, enabling the Claims Manager to allocate the most experienced assessors to these cases from day one rather than discovering their complexity mid-process. A claims triage model uses early signals (claim type, policy characteristics, cause of death, beneficiary profile) to predict: expected settlement time; likelihood of documentation dispute; likelihood of legal challenge; and expected settlement value. This intelligence enables better resource allocation and proactive management of claims that would otherwise surprise the team.

t: Chapter 31 · 31.5 Customer Churn Prediction: Lapse Propensity Modelling
x: A lapse propensity model is one of the highest-ROI AI applications available to a Nigerian life insurer. Rather than waiting until a policy lapses (at which point the customer relationship and the premium income are lost), a lapse prediction model identifies policyholders who are at elevated risk of lapsing in the next 30–90 days, enabling targeted conservation interventions while there is still time to retain them. What lapse prediction models use as input features Premium payment behaviour: number of late payments in the past 12 months; trend in payment timing (consistently earlier, trending later, or erratic); most recent payment method change (switching from direct debit to manual payment is a lapse risk signal). Service interaction history: number of complaint records; calls to the contact centre about policy changes; policy loan enquiries; surrender value requests (which strongly predict lapse intent). Policy characteristics: product type; policy age; premium level relative to similar policyholders; sum assured as a multiple of declared income (over-insured policyholders lapse more). Engagement signals: login frequency to the self-service portal; email open rate for premium reminders; response rate to WhatsApp messages. How model outputs are operationalised The model assigns each in-force policy a lapse risk score (typically 0–100) updated weekly. Policies scoring above a defined threshold are automatically assigned to the insurer’s conservation team with a recommended intervention: high-risk policyholders get a personal call from their agent within 3 days; medium-risk policyholders get a personalised WhatsApp message with a reminder of their policy’s value; policyholders who have made a surrender enquiry get a call from a senior financial adviser who can discuss alternatives to surrender (premium holiday, reduced paid-up benefit, policy loan). The model’s intervention recommendations are calibrated to the insurer’s cost per retention and the expected lifetime value of the retained policy. Advisory: Lapse Propensity Modelling: The Data Reality for Nigerian Insurers A lapse prediction model requires clean, structured, historical policy data with well-recorded payment behaviour, interaction history, and lapse outcomes. For Nigerian insurers with legacy PAS platforms that do not systematically record interaction history or have incomplete payment timing data, a lapse model built on poor-quality data will have poor predictive accuracy. Before investing in a lapse prediction model, the insurer should audit the quality of its PAS data against the feature list above. If more than 30% of policies lack reliable payment behaviour data, the model’s ROI will be significantly lower than projected.

A product recommendation engine uses ML to suggest the most relevant insurance products to a specific customer based on their profile, life stage, existing coverage, and behavioural signals. In life insurance, recommendation engines are used in three contexts: by agents to identify cross-sell and upsell opportunities during client reviews; by digital channels to show contextually relevant products on the insurer’s app or website; and in outbound campaigns to target specific customer segments with the most relevant product message. Recommendation Context Data Inputs Recommendation Logic Suitability Safeguard Agent cross-sell tool (during annual review) Policyholder’s existing products; life stage signals (age, family status, declared income); coverage gap analysis (sum assured relative to income replacement benchmark); policyholder’s interaction history. Collaborative filtering: ‘policyholders with similar profiles who have this product also hold these additional products.’ Coverage gap: ‘policyholder’s existing sum assured covers only 4× annual income vs the 10× benchmark; recommend top-up term.’ Agent must complete a suitability assessment before recommending any product. The recommendation engine surfaces opportunities; the agent validates suitability and documents the rationale. NIIRA 2025 suitability requirement applies. Digital channel personalisation (app/portal) Session behaviour (pages visited, products viewed); demographics; existing portfolio; time since last purchase. Real-time personalisation: the app’s product page displays products most likely to be relevant to this user based on their session behaviour and profile, rather than showing all products equally. Products surfaced digitally must meet the insurer’s NAICOM-approved product parameters. No product must be recommended digitally without a clear mechanism for the customer to receive advice or conduct their own needs analysis before purchase. Outbound marketing campaign targeting Policyholder segment membership (based on life stage, coverage gaps, premium capacity); predicted receptivity score (likelihood of responding to a campaign); channel preference. Propensity modelling: identify the segment of customers most likely to respond positively to a specific product campaign and most likely to benefit from the product. Mass marketing campaigns must not target customers with products that are clearly unsuitable for their profile. The NIIRA 2025 TCF obligation applies to marketing communications as well as sales.

t: Chapter 31 · 31.7 Natural Language Processing for Medical Records Review
x: Medical records — hospital discharge summaries, specialist reports, laboratory results, medical examination narratives — are the most information-dense documents in a life insurance company’s document inventory. They are also typically unstructured: free-text written by clinicians, using medical terminology that varies by institution, specialty, and clinical training background. NLP systems can extract structured information from these documents — diagnoses, treatments, test results, prognoses — at a speed and consistency that no human team can match at scale. 31.7.1 Underwriting Applications Medical examination report processing The NLP model reads the medical examiner’s report (typically a structured but partially handwritten document), extracts the key clinical values (blood pressure, BMI, blood glucose, any noted conditions), and populates the corresponding fields in the PAS underwriting screen. The underwriter reviews the extracted values rather than reading the full report. Processing time: from 15–20 minutes per report (manual) to under 2 minutes (NLP-assisted). Doctor’s report analysis For complex applications, the NLP model reads the Confidential Medical Attendant’s Report (CMAR) and identifies: known conditions mentioned; medications listed; prior investigations or procedures; and any language suggesting prognosis uncertainty. The model flags specific statements for the underwriter’s attention, enabling focused review rather than full document reading. Consistency checking The NLP model compares the health information in the medical examination report against the health declaration on the proposal form. Discrepancies (a condition mentioned in the doctor’s report that was not declared on the proposal form) are flagged automatically as potential non-disclosure for underwriter review. 31.7.2 Claims Applications Hospital record review in death claims Where a death claim is supported by hospital records, the NLP model reads the records and identifies: the admission date and cause; the principal diagnosis; any comorbidities; treatments administered; and the stated cause of death. The model cross-references these against the policy exclusions and the cause-of-death on the death certificate, flagging inconsistencies for human assessor review. Medical history extraction for contestability During the contestability period (first 24 months), the claims assessor may need to determine whether a health condition that contributed to the death was known to the deceased at the time of application but not disclosed. NLP can identify all health conditions mentioned in medical records and compare their dates of first diagnosis against the policy commencement date. NLP Accuracy Limitations in the Nigerian Medical Context NLP medical records models are typically trained on large corpora of standardised medical documents, often from Western healthcare systems. Nigerian medical records frequently: use non-standardised abbreviations; mix English, Pidgin, and local language terms; contain handwritten sections that OCR captures imperfectly; and reference locally-specific diagnoses and treatment protocols not well-represented in global training data. The accuracy of a commercial NLP medical records model in the Nigerian context will be lower than in the market for which it was designed. All NLP-extracted medical data must be reviewed by a qualified underwriter or claims assessor before any underwriting decision or claims determination is made on the basis of the extracted content.

t: Chapter 31 · 31.8 AI-Driven Chatbots for Customer Service
x: Chapter 30 introduced rule-based chatbots (which follow fixed decision trees) as the most immediately deployable chatbot technology for Nigerian insurers. This section addresses NLP-powered conversational AI — chatbots that understand natural language queries, reason about the appropriate response, and generate contextually relevant answers without being limited to predefined question-and-answer pairs. NLP chatbot vs rule-based chatbot A rule-based chatbot can answer: ‘What is my next premium due date?’ (if the question matches the defined intent exactly). An NLP chatbot can understand: ‘When do I need to pay again?’, ‘Is my policy still active?’, ‘My husband just died — what do I do?’ and respond appropriately to each. The NLP chatbot handles the variability of real human language; the rule-based chatbot handles only the language patterns it was designed for. Training requirements An NLP insurance chatbot requires: a large corpus of insurance-specific training utterances in Nigerian English (and ideally Pidgin), mapping to defined intents; integration with the PAS for real-time policy data retrieval; and continuous retraining as new query patterns are identified. The training effort for a quality NLP insurance chatbot is significant — typically 3–6 months before deployment-ready accuracy is achieved. Escalation design Every NLP chatbot must have a clear, low-friction escalation path to a human agent when the chatbot’s confidence in its response falls below a threshold, when the customer expresses frustration, or when the query involves a sensitive subject (bereavement, complaint about a declined claim, lapse warning). A chatbot that traps customers in an automated loop when they need human contact generates the most damaging customer experience possible. Regulatory compliance NIIRA 2025’s consumer protection obligations apply to chatbot interactions as they do to human agent interactions. A chatbot that provides incorrect product information, generates an implicit product recommendation without a suitability assessment, or misrepresents claims settlement terms is the insurer’s liability. The chatbot’s responses must be reviewed for regulatory accuracy before deployment.

t: Chapter 31 · 31.9 AI and Big Data in Actuarial Modelling
x: The actuarial profession has always been analytical and data-driven. What AI adds to actuarial practice is the ability to identify patterns in high-dimensional datasets that traditional statistical models cannot capture, to generate predictions at individual policyholder level rather than aggregate group level, and to update models continuously as new experience data accumulates rather than through discrete annual model rebuilds. 31.9.1 Mortality and Morbidity Prediction Traditional life insurance pricing uses mortality tables (like the EFU Nigerian life tables) that group policyholders by age and gender and apply an average mortality rate to each group. An ML-based mortality model can incorporate many more features — occupation class, geographic location, health declaration patterns, sum assured level, payment behaviour — to produce an individual-level mortality prediction that is more accurate for specific risk profiles than the group average. The practical benefit for a Nigerian insurer is more granular pricing: rather than pricing all 35-year-old male non-smokers at the same EFU table rate, the ML model can identify that 35-year-old male non-smokers in specific occupation classes with specific payment behaviour profiles have materially different mortality experience, enabling competitive pricing for low-risk segments and appropriate loading for higher-risk segments within the same demographic. 31.9.2 Lapse Experience Analysis Traditional actuarial lapse analysis groups policies by product and duration and calculates aggregate lapse rates. ML-based lapse analysis identifies the policy and policyholder characteristics that predict lapse at the individual level — providing the actuarial input for both the lapse propensity model (Section 31.5) and for the actuarial assumption setting process (the lapse assumption used in pricing and ORSA stress testing is significantly more accurate if it reflects the specific characteristics of the insurer’s current portfolio rather than industry average rates). 31.9.3 Governance of AI-Assisted Actuarial Models NIIRA 2025 and the NAICOM Insurtech Guidelines impose specific governance requirements on AI models used in regulated actuarial functions. The Statutory Actuary cannot simply outsource their professional certification to an AI model — they must be able to explain and defend every material assumption in the actuarial investigation, including assumptions that were informed by ML model outputs. Model documentation requirement Every AI/ML model used in an actuarial function (reserve calculation, pricing, ORSA stress scenario design) must be documented: the training data used; the model architecture; the validation approach; the out-of-sample performance metrics; and the limitations and uncertainty range of the model’s predictions. Model validation AI-assisted actuarial models must be validated by a qualified actuary (not the model developer) before use in a regulated actuarial function. Validation includes: back-testing against historical data not used in training; comparison against industry benchmarks; and sensitivity analysis showing how the model’s outputs change as input assumptions are varied. Explainability requirement The Statutory Actuary must be able to explain, in actuarially credible terms, why the AI model’s output supports the assumptions used in the annual investigation. ‘The model said so’ is not a sufficient explanation for a Board Risk Committee or for NAICOM’s supervisory review. NAICOM notification Under the NAICOM Insurtech Guidelines 2025, AI models used in regulated actuarial functions must be disclosed to NAICOM on request. NAICOM may require a demonstration of the model’s performance and governance framework.

t: Chapter 31 · 31.10 Regulatory Framework for AI in Nigerian Insurance
x: 31.10.1 NAICOM’s Position on Algorithmic Underwriting NAICOM’s NIIRA 2025 and Insurtech Guidelines acknowledge and permit the use of AI/ML models in insurance underwriting, but subject them to specific governance requirements designed to ensure that automated underwriting does not create unfair consumer outcomes or undermine the insurer’s regulatory accountability: No final automated decline without human review: A prospective policyholder who is declined must be entitled to a human explanation of the decision. An AI model’s decline recommendation must be reviewed and confirmed by a qualified human underwriter before the decline is communicated to the applicant. Prohibited discriminatory features: AI underwriting models may not use protected characteristics (religion, ethnicity, national origin, gender — except where actuarially justified for mortality purposes) as features. Models that use proxy variables that correlate with protected characteristics (e.g., specific geographic areas that proxy for ethnicity) are also prohibited under the TCF framework. Model approval for material changes: Where an AI model is used to generate product pricing (premium calculations), the model is implicitly part of the NAICOM-approved product. Material changes to the model that affect pricing outcomes require NAICOM notification or resubmission under the product approval process. 31.10.2 NDPA 2023 and Automated Decision-Making The Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023 contains specific provisions on automated decision-making that are directly relevant to AI use in insurance: Right not to be subject to solely automated decisions (NDPA 2023 s.35) A data subject (policyholder or applicant) has the right not to be subject to a decision that is based solely on automated processing and that produces legal or similarly significant effects for them. In insurance, an automated underwriting decline or a claims decision based solely on AI outputs without human review likely violates this provision. Right to explanation Where an automated decision has been made, the data subject has the right to obtain an explanation of the logic involved and to express their point of view. This reinforces the NAICOM requirement for human review of automated decline decisions — the underwriter who reviews the AI model’s output must be able to explain the decision to the applicant. Safeguards required Where automated decision-making is used, the data controller (insurer) must: implement suitable safeguards to protect the data subject’s rights; enable the data subject to contest the decision; provide for human review on request; and ensure the decision is not based on special category data (health data) without explicit consent. 31.10.3 NAICOM Insurtech Guidelines: AI/ML Model Governance Requirements The NAICOM Insurtech Guidelines (August 2025) set out the following specific requirements for AI/ML models used in regulated insurance functions by both Insurtech licensees and conventional licensed insurers deploying AI: Documentation: All AI/ML models must be comprehensively documented, covering training data sources, model architecture, validation methodology, performance metrics, and known limitations. Validation before deployment: Models must be validated by a qualified person independent of the model development team before deployment in a regulated function. Validation must include out-of-sample testing and performance assessment against fairness metrics (false positive rate by demographic group). Ongoing monitoring: Deployed models must be monitored continuously for performance degradation (model drift), data quality issues, and emerging bias. Monitoring results must be documented and reviewed quarterly. Bias testing: Models used in underwriting, claims, or pricing decisions must be tested for disparate impact — whether they produce systematically different outcomes for different demographic groups without actuarial justification. Bias testing results must be available for NAICOM inspection. NAICOM notification: Insurers must notify NAICOM before deploying an AI model that makes binding decisions in a regulated function (underwriting acceptance/decline, claims settlement, pricing). NAICOM may require a technical demonstration.

t: Chapter 31 · 31.11 Ethical AI in Insurance: Fairness, Explainability, and Consumer Protection
x: 31.11.1 Fairness An AI model in insurance is fair if it produces outcomes that are consistent with actuarial risk differentiation and are not influenced by characteristics that are irrelevant to risk or that are prohibited bases for insurance discrimination. The fairness challenge in AI insurance models is that the features most predictive of insurance risk (payment behaviour, geographic location, mobile money usage patterns) may correlate with protected characteristics (wealth, religion, ethnicity) through historical patterns of inequality. An AI model trained on historical insurance data will reflect historical disparities in who was insured, who was accepted at standard rates, and who was declined. If low-income urban policyholders historically lapsed at higher rates due to financial instability rather than inherent risk character, a lapse prediction model trained on this data will assign higher lapse risk scores to low-income policyholders not because they are inherently higher-risk but because history correlates income with lapse. This is a data bias problem that produces discriminatory model outputs even if no discriminatory intent existed in the model design. Practical Fairness Safeguards for Nigerian Insurance AI 1. PROHIBITED FEATURES: Explicitly exclude from model training all features that directly proxy for protected characteristics: religious or ethnic identifiers; features with known high correlation with religion or ethnicity at the national level. 2. DISPARATE IMPACT TESTING: After model training, test the model’s outputs across demographic groups. If the model’s decline rate, loading rate, or lapse risk score distribution differs significantly across groups with similar actuarial risk profiles, investigate the cause before deployment. 3. HUMAN OVERRIDE AUDIT: Track the rate at which human underwriters override AI model recommendations, and in which direction (more accepting or more restrictive than the model). A systematic pattern of human overrides in one direction for a specific demographic group indicates a model fairness problem. 31.11.2 Explainability An AI model is explainable if the insurer can provide a clear, non-technical explanation of why it produced a specific output for a specific input. This is both an ethical obligation (under NDPA 2023’s right to explanation) and a business necessity: an underwriter who cannot explain why the model rated a specific applicant at 150% cannot defend the decision to the agent or the applicant. Deep learning models (neural networks) are inherently less explainable than simpler models (logistic regression, decision trees) because their internal calculations involve thousands of weights that do not map to human-understandable reasoning. For insurance underwriting and claims decisions, where explainability is both a regulatory requirement and a commercial necessity, simpler, more interpretable models are often preferable to highly accurate but opaque neural networks.

t: Chapter 31 · 31.12 Advisory: The AI Adoption Roadmap for a Nigerian Life Insurer
x: The question for most Nigerian life insurers is not ‘should we use AI?’ but ‘where should we start, and how?’. The following roadmap provides a sequenced framework for a Nigerian life insurer at a conventional maturity stage (Chapters 29 and 30’s Stage 1 or Stage 2 insurer) to begin and systematically build its AI capability. Advisory: AI Adoption Roadmap: Four Phases PHASE 1 — DATA READINESS (Months 1–6, Before Any Model Building): Conduct a data audit: for each proposed AI use case, identify what data is required, what data exists in the PAS, what its quality level is, and what the gap is. For the highest-priority use cases (lapse prediction, fraud detection), assess whether the historical data has sufficient volume (minimum 10,000–20,000 labelled examples for a supervised learning model), completeness (fewer than 20% missing values on key features), and time range (at least 3–5 years of policy history). Fix the most critical data quality gaps (premium payment timing recording; interaction history capture; claims outcome labelling) before building models. A model built on poor data will not work and will erode confidence in AI. PHASE 2 — FIRST USE CASE (Months 6–12): LAPSE PROPENSITY MODEL Build or partner to develop a lapse propensity model using the insurer’s historical policy data. Why lapse first: it has a clear ROI (every retained policy is quantifiable premium income), uses data the insurer already has (no new data collection required), produces an output that the conservation team can act on immediately, and has relatively low regulatory risk (the model’s output informs retention outreach, not an adverse consumer decision). Deploy the model as a conservation prioritisation tool. Measure lapse rate improvement quarterly for 12 months. PHASE 3 — SECOND USE CASE (Months 12–18): CLAIMS FRAUD DETECTION Build a claims fraud detection model using historical claims data with fraud outcomes. Why fraud second: it requires more complex data (claims documents, beneficiary network data) and involves more sensitive consumer outcomes (a false positive result in a bereavement claim is highly damaging). The insurer’s team will have learned from the lapse model build and be better prepared. Deploy as a triage tool for the SIU, with human review of every flagged claim mandatory. PHASE 4 — SCALING (Months 18–36): Automated underwriting (starting with straight-through processing for clean, low-sum-assured applications); NLP for medical records; customer product recommendation engine. Each use case follows the same governance discipline: document, validate, test for fairness, deploy with human oversight, monitor continuously. The Single Most Important AI Lesson for Nigerian Life Insurers Build the data infrastructure before building the models. The most common AI implementation failure in comparable markets is not a technology failure — it is a data failure: the insurer invests in an AI platform, hires a data scientist, and then discovers that its historical policy data does not contain the features the model needs, that the claims data has not captured fraud outcomes systematically, or that the PAS does not record premium payment timing at the precision required. Fix the data foundation first. An insurer with clean, complete, well-structured historical data and no AI models yet is closer to successful AI deployment than one with AI models and poor data.

Artificial Intelligence (AI) The broad field of computer science aimed at building systems that perform tasks requiring human-like intelligence: pattern recognition, language understanding, and learning from experience. In insurance, typically refers to machine learning applications. Machine Learning (ML) A subset of AI in which algorithms learn patterns from labelled historical data and apply those patterns to make predictions on new, unseen cases. The foundation of all practical AI use cases in insurance. Supervised Learning An ML approach trained on labelled data (examples with known correct answers), used for predictive tasks with defined outcomes: fraud detection, lapse prediction, automated underwriting. Deep Learning A subset of ML using multi-layered neural networks to learn representations of complex, high-dimensional data (text, images, audio). Requires very large datasets; most relevant insurance application is NLP. Natural Language Processing (NLP) AI technology enabling computers to understand and generate human language; applied in insurance for processing medical records, chatbots, and document review. Automated Underwriting The use of ML risk scoring models to make underwriting decisions (accept, rate, refer, decline) for insurance applications without requiring human underwriter review for standard risks. Training Data The historical dataset used to train an ML model, containing input features and labelled outcomes; the primary determinant of model quality. Model Drift The degradation of an AI model’s predictive accuracy over time as the real-world patterns it was trained on change; requires ongoing monitoring and periodic retraining. Lapse Propensity Model An ML model that assigns each in-force policy a probability of lapsing within a defined future period, enabling targeted conservation intervention. False Positive (Claims Fraud) A valid insurance claim incorrectly flagged by a fraud detection model as potentially fraudulent; the most damaging failure mode of a claims AI system. Explainability (AI) The ability of an insurer to provide a clear, non-technical explanation of why an AI model produced a specific output for a specific input; required by NDPA 2023 and NAICOM’s consumer protection framework. Disparate Impact The production by an AI model of systematically different outcomes for different demographic groups without actuarial justification; a fairness violation under NAICOM’s TCF framework. Collaborative Filtering An ML recommendation technique that identifies patterns across similar users (‘customers with your profile also purchased these products’); used in insurance product recommendation engines. NDPA 2023 Automated Decision-Making The NDPA 2023 provision (Section 35) giving data subjects the right not to be subject to decisions based solely on automated processing that produce legal or significant effects; requires human review of AI-driven adverse decisions in insurance. Model Governance The framework of policies, processes, and accountability structures ensuring that AI models are documented, validated, monitored, tested for fairness, and deployed with appropriate human oversight. Alternative Data (Underwriting) Non-traditional data sources (mobile money transactions, airtime behaviour, BVN data, geolocation) used in AI-powered underwriting as predictors of mortality risk in addition to traditional medical and demographic data.

(B) Identify policyholders at elevated risk of lapsing in the next 30–90 days, enabling targeted conservation intervention. The NDPA 2023's provision on automated decision-making (Section 35) is relevant to AI use in insurance because: It requires all insurance companies to use AI-powered underwriting for all new business applications. It gives data subjects the right not to be subject to decisions based solely on automated processing that produce legal or significant effects, requiring human review of adverse automated decisions. It prohibits the use of any AI or machine learning technology in the assessment of insurance claims. It requires insurers to publish their AI model algorithms for public inspection on the NDPC website. (B) It gives data subjects the right not to be subject to decisions based solely on automated processing that produce legal or significant effects, requiring human review of adverse automated decisions. Why (B) is Correct Section 35 of the NDPA 2023 is Nigeria's equivalent of GDPR Article 22 — the automated decision-making provision. It does not prohibit automated decisions; it requires that where such decisions produce legal or similarly significant effects (insurance decline; significant premium loading; claim refusal), the data subject must have the right to obtain human review of the decision. The insurer cannot hide behind the AI model's output as a basis for refusing to explain or review an adverse decision. This provision is the most directly applicable NDPA requirement to AI use in insurance underwriting and claims. An AI model that produces systematically lower credit scores or higher insurance loadings for applicants from a specific geographic area, where that area predominantly reflects a particular ethnic group, is an example of: Actuarially justified risk differentiation, as geographic location is a valid insurance risk factor. Disparate impact — a fairness violation in which an AI model produces systematically different outcomes for different demographic groups without pure actuarial justification. Enhanced underwriting, as location data improves the accuracy of mortality risk prediction. A compliance requirement under NIIRA 2025's product approval process. (B) Disparate impact — a fairness violation in which an AI model produces systematically different outcomes for different demographic groups without pure actuarial justification. Why (B) is Correct Disparate impact (also called indirect discrimination) occurs when a facially neutral criterion (geographic area) produces systematically different outcomes for different demographic groups — in this case, effectively discriminating based on ethnicity through the proxy of location. Even if geographic location has some actuarial validity as a mortality predictor, an AI model that produces ethnic-group-correlated adverse outcomes must be evaluated against the proportionality standard: is the geographic differentiation actuarially necessary and proportionate, or is the location variable primarily serving as an ethnic proxy? If the latter, the model violates both NIIRA 2025's non-discrimination provisions and NDPA 2023's fair processing

AI has the potential to fundamentally transform the Nigerian life insurance industry: enabling accurate risk pricing for previously uninsurable populations using alternative data, eliminating fraudulent claims that currently drain industry profitability, and delivering personalised financial advice through AI-powered chatbots to customers who cannot afford a human financial adviser. However, AI also presents specific risks: discriminatory model outputs that systematically disadvantage certain customer groups, opaque decisions that policyholders cannot understand or contest, and the possibility that AI confidence in insurance decisions outpaces the quality of the underlying data. Critically evaluate the proposition that the transformative potential of AI in Nigerian life insurance outweighs its risks, and design a governance framework that would enable a Nigerian life insurer to realise the benefits while managing the risks responsibly.   Thesis The transformative potential of AI for Nigerian life insurance is genuine — and for specific, well-defined use cases with adequate data, it already outweighs the risks. For other use cases — particularly those involving adverse decisions about individuals, or those that require data quality that Nigerian insurers do not yet possess — the risks currently outweigh the benefits. The question is not whether AI should be used in Nigerian life insurance but which AI, for which purposes, under which governance conditions, in which sequence.
