t: Chapter 32 · 32.1 Introduction: Data Privacy as a Core Compliance Obligation
x: Life insurance is a data-intensive business. From the moment a prospective policyholder completes a proposal form, the insurer begins collecting and processing sensitive personal data: health history, financial circumstances, family composition, employment details, and biometric information. Through the life of the policy, the insurer adds payment behaviour data, service interaction records, claims history, and beneficiary information. When a claim is made, the insurer processes medical records, post-mortem reports, financial evidence, and identity documents relating to the deceased and their family. Few sectors of the Nigerian economy process personal data that is as sensitive, as voluminous, or as consequential for the individuals concerned. Before the Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023 (NDPA 2023), this data was managed under the Nigeria Data Protection Regulation 2019 (NDPR) — a framework that was widely acknowledged as underpowered and inconsistently enforced. The NDPA 2023, assented to by the President on 12 June 2023 and fully operationalised through the General Application and Implementation Directive (GAID 2025) from September 2025, is a fundamentally different instrument. It establishes an independent Data Protection Commission (NDPC) with genuine enforcement powers; creates a comprehensive set of data subject rights; imposes mandatory breach notification within 72 hours; and classifies large-scale processors of sensitive personal data — including all licensed insurers at scale — as ‘Data Controllers and Data Processors of Major Importance’ subject to the highest tier of compliance obligations. For Nigerian life insurers, NDPA 2023 compliance is not merely a legal obligation. It is a direct commercial and operational risk: the penalty for a serious breach can reach 2% of annual gross revenue; NAICOM market conduct inspections now include data protection compliance checks; and the reputational damage of a publicised data breach or NDPC enforcement action in a market where policyholder trust is already fragile is potentially irreversible. This chapter provides the comprehensive data privacy reference every life insurance professional needs.

t: Chapter 32 · 32.2 The Insurer as Data Controller and Data Processor of Major Importance
x: Term NDPA 2023 Definition Insurance Context Data Subject The identified or identifiable natural person to whom personal data relates. Policyholders, prospective applicants, beneficiaries, claimants, and employees of the insurer. Personal Data Any information relating to an identified or identifiable natural person. Name, NIN, BVN, date of birth, address, health history, premium payment records, claims history, beneficiary designation. Special Category Data Personal data revealing health, biometric, genetic, racial or ethnic origin, political opinions, religious beliefs, sexual orientation, or criminal record. Medical underwriting data (health history, test results, clinical reports); claims medical evidence; biometric identity verification data. Data Controller A person or entity that determines the purposes and means of processing personal data. The licensed insurer. When a life insurer decides to collect health data for underwriting purposes, determines what data to collect, how it is stored, and who can access it, it is acting as a Data Controller. Data Processor A person or entity that processes personal data on behalf of a Data Controller. Third parties engaged by the insurer to process policyholder data: TPA (health claims management); cloud service providers; actuarial firms processing policy data; reinsurers receiving cession data. Data Controller/Processor of Major Importance (DCPMI) A Data Controller or Processor that: (a) processes the personal data of more than a defined number of data subjects; (b) processes special categories of personal data at scale; or (c) engages in processing likely to result in high risk to data subjects’ rights. All licensed Nigerian life insurers above a defined premium threshold are expressly classified as DCPMIs under NDPA 2023 and GAID 2025. The consequences: mandatory DPO appointment, mandatory DPCP submission, mandatory biennial data protection audit, enhanced NDPC oversight. DCPMI Classification: What It Means in Practice Being classified as a Data Controller/Processor of Major Importance is not merely a designation — it triggers a specific, mandatory compliance programme: • Appoint a Data Protection Officer (DPO) — a qualified individual with direct access to the Board or ExCo. • Submit a Data Protection Compliance Programme (DPCP) to the NDPC annually. • Conduct a data protection audit every two years by a NDPC-certified data protection auditor. • Maintain a Record of Processing Activities (RoPA) documenting all personal data processing.

t: Chapter 32 · 32.3 Types of Personal Data Processed in Life Insurance
x: Life insurance operations involve a wider range of personal data types than most other sectors. Understanding the classification of each data type — and the specific legal protections that apply — is the foundation of the insurer’s data governance framework. Data Category Examples in Life Insurance NDPA 2023 Classification Key Protection Requirement Basic identity data Name, date of birth, NIN, BVN, residential address, email, telephone number. Personal data — standard category. Lawful basis required; adequate security; retention period limits. Financial data Income declaration; bank account details; premium payment history; surrender value; policy loan balance; BVN-linked transaction patterns. Personal data — standard category (but sensitive in practice). Heightened security for financial data; strict access controls; not to be shared with third parties without lawful basis. Health data Medical history declared on proposal form; medical examination results (blood pressure, BMI, blood glucose, HIV status); clinical reports; hospital records submitted for claims; cause of death. Special category data under NDPA 2023 — requires heightened protection. Explicit consent or another specific permitted ground required; strict access control (need-to-know only); data minimisation principle strictly applied. Biometric data Fingerprint data captured for digital identity verification; facial recognition data used in eKYC onboarding; voice recognition data from contact centre calls. Special category data under NDPA 2023. Explicit consent required; biometric data may only be processed for the specific stated purpose; must not be used to identify individuals in other contexts. Genetic data DNA test results submitted as evidence in paternity disputes affecting beneficiary entitlement; genetic condition disclosures in underwriting. Special category data under NDPA 2023. Explicit consent; strict access controls; cannot be used for underwriting discrimination beyond actuarially justified mortality assessment. Claims data Death certificate; post-mortem report; accident report; beneficiary identity documents; cause of death; medical history relevant to the claim. Mixture of special category (health, cause of death) and standard personal data. Claims data must be retained for the claims record retention period (minimum 10 years per GAID 2025); access restricted to the claims team and authorised auditors. Communication data WhatsApp message content; email correspondence; contact centre call recordings; chatbot interaction logs. Personal data (and potentially special category if content reveals health information). Call recordings and message logs must be disclosed in a data subject access request; retention period must be defined and documented. Employee data Staff HR records; payroll data; performance records; CIIN CPD records; background check results. Personal data — employee category. Employee data processing governed by employment contract and the specific GAID 2025 provisions on employee data.

t: Chapter 32 · 32.4 Lawful Bases for Processing Personal Data
x: Every processing activity involving personal data must rest on a lawful basis. Processing without a lawful basis is unlawful under NDPA 2023 and exposes the insurer to enforcement action. The six lawful bases, with their insurance applications: Lawful Basis Definition Insurance Application Key Limitation Contract Performance (s.25(1)(b)) Processing necessary to perform a contract to which the data subject is party, or to take steps at their request before entering a contract. Processing policy data to administer an in-force life insurance contract: calculating premiums, processing claims, maintaining policy records. This is the primary lawful basis for core insurance operations. Can only be relied on where the processing is genuinely necessary for the contract. Using contract performance as a basis for marketing communications to policyholders is incorrect. Legal Obligation (s.25(1)(c)) Processing necessary to comply with a legal obligation to which the controller is subject. AML/KYC identity verification and transaction monitoring (MLPPA 2022 obligation); NAICOM regulatory reporting; NDPA 2023 data breach notification; employee data processing required by employment legislation. The legal obligation must be a Nigerian legal obligation applicable to the insurer. A foreign legal obligation (e.g., a reinsurer’s home country requirement) does not by itself constitute a legal obligation under NDPA 2023. Vital Interests (s.25(1)(d)) Processing necessary to protect the vital interests of the data subject or another natural person. Extremely narrow in insurance context. Could apply where a policyholder’s life is at immediate risk and sharing their medical data with emergency services is necessary. Not applicable to routine insurance processing. Should not be used as a fallback basis. Legitimate Interest (s.25(1)(f)) Processing necessary for the legitimate interests of the controller or a third party, provided those interests are not overridden by the data subject’s interests or rights. Fraud prevention (processing data to detect fraudulent claims is in both the insurer’s and honest policyholders’ legitimate interest); security monitoring of the insurer’s systems; direct marketing to existing policyholders about similar products. Requires a three-part legitimate interest assessment (LIA): identify the legitimate interest; show the processing is necessary; confirm the interest is not overridden by the data subject’s rights. Cannot be used where consent would be more appropriate. Public Task (s.25(1)(e)) Processing necessary for the performance of a task in the public interest or the exercise of official authority. Limited insurance application. Potentially applicable to insurers acting as agents of mandatory insurance schemes (e.g., processing data as part of mandatory group life compliance reporting). Applicable only where the insurer is exercising a specific public function. Not a general-purpose basis. Consent (s.25(1)(a)) The data subject has given freely, specific, informed, and unambiguous consent to the processing of their personal data for specified purposes. Direct marketing communications to prospective customers; using health data for purposes beyond the specific underwriting assessment; sharing policyholder data with third-party commercial partners; using data for product development research beyond what the contract requires. Consent must be: freely given (not a condition of the contract unless strictly necessary); specific (one purpose, not a general consent to all uses); informed (the purpose must be clearly explained); unambiguous (clear positive action, not pre-ticked boxes). Consent can be withdrawn at any time. Special Category Data: Additional Lawful Basis Required For special category data (health, biometric, genetic), the insurer must satisfy both a standard lawful basis AND one of the specific additional conditions in NDPA 2023 s.30. The most relevant insurance conditions are: (a) Explicit consent of the data subject (the most commonly relied on basis for health data collection at underwriting); (b) Processing necessary for establishing, exercising, or defending legal claims (relevant to claims disputes and contestation); (c) Processing necessary for the purposes of preventive or occupational medicine or medical diagnosis (relevant to medical underwriting activities conducted under a medical examiner’s clinical authority); (d) Substantial public interest (requires specific NDPC authorisation). The practical implication: health data collected at underwriting requires explicit consent documented in the proposal form, and that consent must be specific to the underwriting purpose. Using the same consent for marketing, product research, or AI model training requires separate, additional consent.

NDPA 2023 establishes a comprehensive suite of rights for data subjects — including policyholders, beneficiaries, claimants, and prospective applicants. The insurer must have documented procedures to receive, validate, and respond to data subject requests within the statutory 30-day timeframe. Failure to respond is an enforcement trigger. Right What It Means Insurance Application Insurer’s Response Obligation Right of Access (s.26) The data subject may request a copy of all personal data the controller holds about them, together with information about the purposes, legal bases, retention periods, and third parties it has been shared with. A policyholder requests all data the insurer holds about them: policy records, underwriting notes, health data, premium history, claims records, communications log. Respond within 30 days with a complete Subject Access Request (SAR) response. The insurer must provide data in a portable format. Cannot charge a fee for standard requests. PAS must be capable of generating a complete data export per individual. Right of Rectification (s.27) The data subject may request correction of inaccurate personal data held about them. Policyholder notices their date of birth is incorrectly recorded in the insurer’s system; requests correction. Respond within 30 days. Correct the data in all relevant systems (PAS, CRM, any data warehouse). Where data was shared with third parties (reinsurers, actuarial firms), notify them of the correction. Right of Erasure (s.28) The data subject may request deletion of their personal data in specified circumstances (consent withdrawn, processing no longer necessary, unlawful processing). Former policyholder whose policy lapsed 15 years ago requests deletion of all their data from the insurer’s systems. The right of erasure is qualified: the insurer may decline where processing is necessary for legal obligations (tax records, claims records required by GAID 2025 minimum retention periods) or the establishment of legal claims. The insurer must respond within 30 days and either comply, partially comply, or explain the lawful basis for retention. Right of Portability (s.29) The data subject may request their data in a structured, machine-readable format for transfer to another controller. Policyholder switching insurers requests their claims history and health underwriting data in a format the new insurer’s PAS can import. Applicable only where the lawful basis is consent or contract performance. Respond within 30 days with data in the requested format (CSV, JSON, or XML). This right is particularly relevant for the future of portable insurance data in Nigeria. Right to Restriction (s.31) The data subject may request that processing of their data is restricted while a dispute about accuracy or lawfulness is pending. Policyholder disputes the accuracy of a health underwriting note and requests restriction while the dispute is resolved. Mark the disputed data as restricted in the PAS; do not use it for any further processing until the dispute is resolved. Right to Object (s.32) The data subject may object to processing based on legitimate interest or public task grounds, and to direct marketing. Policyholder objects to receiving marketing communications from the insurer. Stop marketing communications immediately on receipt of objection. Cannot be overridden unless the insurer can demonstrate compelling legitimate grounds that override the data subject’s interests. Right not to be subject to solely automated decisions (s.35) Addressed in Chapter 31 — data subjects have the right to human review of adverse AI-driven decisions in insurance. AI-recommended underwriting decline; AI-flagged fraudulent claim without human review. Ensure human review is always applied before communicating adverse decisions. Provide explanation of the decision logic on request.

Data Protection Officer (DPO) An individual designated by a Data Controller or Processor of Major Importance to oversee and monitor compliance with data protection obligations, provide advice on data protection matters, cooperate with the NDPC, and act as the contact point for data subjects exercising their rights. The DPO must have expert knowledge of data protection law and practice. The DPO must be provided with the resources necessary to carry out their tasks and must be able to act independently, without instructions from management on the exercise of their data protection functions. Appointment requirements Every DCPMI (including all licensed Nigerian life insurers at scale) must appoint a DPO. The DPO may be an employee or an external consultant. If an employee, the DPO role must be clearly separated from other roles that could create a conflict of interest — a DPO who is also the Head of Marketing (which generates most of the data processing compliance challenges) is not independent. The DPO’s appointment must be registered with the NDPC. Qualifications Expert knowledge of NDPA 2023, GAID 2025, and data protection law and practice. Professional certification is not yet mandatory under Nigerian law, but NDPC-recognised data protection certifications (CIPM, CIPP, CDPO) are the accepted professional standard. DPO’s core functions Monitor compliance with NDPA 2023 and internal data protection policies. Advise the insurer on data protection obligations. Advise on DPIAs and monitor their performance. Cooperate with the NDPC and act as the NDPC’s contact point. Respond to data subject requests escalated to the DPO level. Provide data protection training to staff. Reporting line The DPO must report directly to the Board or ExCo — not to any functional head whose activities they may need to challenge. A DPO who reports to the Chief Marketing Officer, the Head of IT, or the Head of Compliance may face undue influence on their independent functions. Resourcing The DPO must be adequately resourced: time, budget for tools and training, access to all data processing activities, and authority to require management to act on compliance findings. A DPO who is given the title but not the resources or authority to function independently is not a DPO — it is a liability, because it creates the appearance of compliance without the substance. Consequences of under-resourcing The NDPC has signalled that nominal DPO appointments — where the individual lacks the expertise, time, or authority to function effectively — will be treated as non-compliance. The insurer that appoints a junior paralegal as DPO and expects them to manage data protection compliance alongside other duties is not meeting its DCPMI obligations.

Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA) A process required by NDPA 2023 and GAID 2025 before commencing a new processing activity likely to result in high risk to data subjects’ rights and freedoms. The DPIA assesses: the nature, scope, context, and purpose of the processing; the necessity and proportionality of the processing; the risks to data subjects; and the measures to address those risks (including safeguards, security measures, and mechanisms to ensure compliance). The DPIA is a governance tool, not merely a paperwork exercise: its purpose is to identify and mitigate risks before they materialise, not to document risks after deployment. GAID 2025 specifies the categories of processing that require a DPIA. The following activities in a Nigerian life insurer’s operations require a DPIA: Processing Activity Why a DPIA Is Required Key DPIA Findings Expected Mitigation Measures Required AI/ML underwriting models Large-scale automated decision-making using special category (health) data with significant effects on data subjects (acceptance, rating, decline). Risk of discriminatory model outputs; risk of incorrect adverse decision without human review; risk of data subjects not understanding the basis for decisions. Human review mandatory before adverse decisions; bias testing before deployment; right to explanation documented; prohibited features list enforced. Biometric identity verification at onboarding Processing of biometric data (fingerprint or facial recognition) for eKYC, which NDPA 2023 classes as special category data. Risk of biometric data breach (biometric data cannot be changed if compromised); risk of function creep (biometric data used beyond stated KYC purpose). Biometric data stored as a hash, not raw biometric image; strict purpose limitation enforced in PAS; right to use an alternative (non-biometric) verification method offered. Large-scale health data processing for underwriting Processing health data from tens of thousands of proposal forms and medical examination reports at scale. Risk of inadequate access controls allowing unauthorised access to health records; risk of data being retained beyond the underwriting purpose. Role-based access controls (underwriting team only); automatic archiving of health data to restricted-access storage after policy issuance; retention and disposal schedule enforced. Sharing policyholder data with reinsurers Transfer of policyholder health and financial data to reinsurers, potentially outside Nigeria. Risk of cross-border transfer without adequate safeguards; risk of reinsurer using data beyond the reinsurance purpose. Data transfer agreement with reinsurer; data minimisation (only data necessary for the reinsurance treaty); NDPC adequacy assessment for the reinsurer’s jurisdiction. Digital behavioural analytics (mobile app usage) Using policyholder app behaviour for lapse prediction or product recommendation. Risk of data subjects not being aware that their behavioural data is being used for predictive analytics; risk of profiling affecting policyholder rights. Clear privacy notice disclosing behavioural analytics; opt-out mechanism for analytics beyond basic service delivery; legitimate interest assessment documented. Contact centre call recording Recording all inbound and outbound calls, creating a large repository of voice recordings that may contain health and financial data. Risk of recordings being accessed for purposes beyond quality monitoring; risk of insufficient retention controls. Clear caller notification that calls are recorded; purpose limitation (quality monitoring and dispute resolution only); retention period (12 months maximum unless subject to active dispute); access controls.

Nigerian life insurance operations regularly involve the transfer of policyholder personal data outside Nigeria: reinsurance data (policyholder details shared with international reinsurers); actuarial outsourcing (policy data sent to actuarial firms in South Africa, the UK, or India for modelling); cloud storage (data stored on servers outside Nigeria); and banking integration (data shared with international bancassurance partner banks). The NDPA 2023 and GAID 2025 impose specific requirements on all such transfers. Data localisation (primary storage) Under GAID 2025, the primary storage of personal data of Nigerian data subjects must be on servers physically located in Nigeria. Secondary backups may be stored outside Nigeria, subject to adequate safeguards. This means a Nigerian life insurer using a cloud PAS on international servers (AWS Ireland, Azure Netherlands) without a Nigerian primary storage instance is potentially non-compliant. Adequacy decisions Transfers to countries that the NDPC has determined provide an adequate level of data protection may proceed without additional safeguards. The NDPC publishes its adequacy list. Most major insurance markets are not yet on the NDPC’s adequacy list, requiring an alternative transfer mechanism. Appropriate safeguards Where no adequacy decision exists, transfers may proceed if supported by: Standard Contractual Clauses (SCCs) approved by the NDPC; Binding Corporate Rules (BCRs) for intragroup transfers; or a code of conduct or certification mechanism approved by the NDPC. For most reinsurance data transfers, SCCs incorporated into the reinsurance data processing agreement are the standard mechanism. Reinsurance data transfers The reinsurance relationship creates a specific data transfer challenge: international reinsurers receive policyholder name, date of birth, health summary, and sum assured for each risk ceded. The reinsurance treaty (Chapter 14) must include a data processing addendum that: identifies the reinsurer as a data processor; specifies the purposes for which the data may be used (reinsurance assessment and pricing only); includes SCCs; and obliges the reinsurer to comply with NDPA 2023-equivalent standards. Actuarial data outsourcing Where actuarial modelling is performed by an external firm (including cross-border), the policy data extract sent to the actuarial firm is a cross-border data transfer to a data processor. The actuarial firm must have a data processing agreement in place, and the data transfer must be covered by SCCs or another approved mechanism. Anonymisation or pseudonymisation of the data extract (removing individual policyholder identity fields and retaining only actuarially relevant data) is the most practical way to reduce the data transfer compliance burden. Cloud storage compliance pathway Insurers using international cloud providers (AWS, Azure, Google Cloud) should: prioritise deployment in the AWS Lagos, Azure South Africa North, or Google Cloud South Africa regions (all physically within Nigeria or the continent); maintain primary storage in Nigeria with international secondary backup; review cloud provider data processing agreements for NDPA 2023 compatibility; and document the legal basis for any residual international storage.

Personal Data Breach A breach of security leading to the accidental or unlawful destruction, loss, alteration, unauthorised disclosure of, or access to personal data transmitted, stored, or otherwise processed. A personal data breach includes: a ransomware attack that encrypts the insurer’s PAS data; a member of staff emailing a policyholder’s medical records to the wrong recipient; a third-party processor suffering a breach affecting the insurer’s data; or the theft of a laptop containing unencrypted policyholder records. The NDPA 2023 establishes a clear breach response framework with specific timelines: NDPA 2023 Data Breach Response: The Four Obligations OBLIGATION 1: DETECTION AND CONTAINMENT (Immediate, within hours) On becoming aware of a potential breach, the insurer must immediately: contain the breach (revoke compromised credentials, isolate affected systems, stop unauthorised data exfiltration); preserve evidence (logs, access records); activate the incident response team (DPO, Head of IT, Head of Legal, CEO where material); and begin documenting the nature, scope, and likely impact of the breach. OBLIGATION 2: NDPC NOTIFICATION (Within 72 hours of becoming aware) The insurer must notify the NDPC within 72 hours of becoming aware of a breach that is likely to result in a risk to data subjects’ rights and freedoms. The notification must include: the nature of the breach; categories and approximate number of data subjects affected; categories and approximate number of personal data records affected; name and contact of the DPO; likely consequences of the breach; and measures taken or proposed to address the breach. If all information is not available within 72 hours, an initial notification must still be made, with subsequent updates as information becomes available. Note: the 72-hour clock runs from when the insurer became aware, not from when the breach occurred. OBLIGATION 3: DATA SUBJECT NOTIFICATION (Without undue delay where high risk) Where a breach is likely to result in high risk to affected data subjects’ rights and freedoms, the insurer must also notify the affected data subjects directly (by their registered contact details) without undue delay. The notification must: clearly describe what happened; identify what data was involved; provide the DPO’s contact details; and describe the likely consequences and the measures taken. Notification to data subjects may be delayed with NDPC agreement where law enforcement investigations would be jeopardised. OBLIGATION 4: DOCUMENTATION (Ongoing, immediately post-breach) All breaches (including those below the notification threshold) must be documented in the insurer’s breach register: date discovered, date of NDPC notification, nature of breach, categories of data affected, remediation actions taken, and outcome. The breach register is a required document for the biennial data protection audit. Breach Notification: What NOT to Do • Do NOT delay notification to conduct a full internal investigation first. The 72-hour clock cannot be extended pending investigation. File an initial notification and update the NDPC as further information becomes available. • Do NOT treat breach notification as a PR exercise. The NDPC notification is a legal obligation. The insurer’s communications team should not manage the NDPC notification — it should be managed by the DPO and Legal. • Do NOT assume small breaches do not require notification. A breach affecting 50 policyholders’ health data may require notification depending on the sensitivity of the data affected and the risk to those individuals. • Do NOT fail to notify because the breach was caused by a third party (reinsurer, cloud provider, TPA). The insurer as Data Controller is responsible for notifying the NDPC even where the breach occurred at a data processor. The processor is obligated to inform the insurer promptly; the insurer is then obligated to notify the NDPC.

t: Chapter 32 · 32.10 NDPC Sector Investigation (August 2025): Implications for Insurance
x: In August 2025, the NDPC conducted a sector-wide investigation into data protection compliance across the Nigerian financial services industry, including licensed insurers. The investigation — which involved both documentary review and on-site inspections at selected companies — identified material compliance gaps across the sector. The NDPC’s published findings and enforcement actions from this investigation are the most relevant regulatory intelligence available to Nigerian insurance compliance teams. Compliance Gap Identified Frequency Across Sector Required Corrective Action Lessons for Life Insurers DPO not appointed or appointment not registered with NDPC Very common — many insurers had no formal DPO or had designated a junior staff member without formal data protection expertise. Appoint a qualified DPO within 30 days; register the appointment with the NDPC; provide evidence of DPO’s qualifications and reporting line to ExCo. DPO appointment is not optional and not a junior function. The NDPC verified qualifications and reporting independence, not just that a name had been provided. No Data Protection Compliance Programme (DPCP) submitted to NDPC Common — many DCPMIs had not submitted their DPCP by the NDPC’s deadline. Submit a compliant DPCP within 60 days; future annual submissions to be made by the NDPC’s published deadline each year. The DPCP is a substantive document describing the insurer’s entire data governance programme; it is not a tick-box form. Late or superficial submissions attract enforcement action. No Record of Processing Activities (RoPA) Very common — insurers could not produce a documented inventory of their personal data processing activities. Produce a complete RoPA within 90 days; maintain it as a living document updated when new processing activities are introduced. The RoPA must cover every personal data processing activity: underwriting, claims, marketing, HR, outsourcing. It is the foundation document for DPIAs and the DPCP. No data subject access request (DSAR) procedure Common — insurers had no documented process for receiving, validating, and responding to data subject requests. Implement a DSAR procedure; designate a DSAR response team; set up a DSAR intake mechanism (email address, web form); ensure PAS can produce a complete individual data export. In the absence of a procedure, DSAR requests will be missed or inadequately responded to, triggering enforcement. Data retention beyond documented retention periods Common — data was routinely retained indefinitely in legacy PAS systems without any systematic deletion or disposal. Conduct a data retention audit; implement automated retention and disposal schedules in the PAS; delete data exceeding documented retention periods within 6 months. GAID 2025 specifies minimum retention periods (not maximums); the insurer must also define maximum retention periods and enforce them. Inadequate lawful basis documentation Widespread — insurers were processing health data for underwriting without documented explicit consent, and marketing to customers without an adequate lawful basis. Document the lawful basis for every material processing activity; update proposal forms to capture explicit consent for health data processing; update marketing consent processes. The most substantive finding: the absence of documented lawful basis for health data processing makes all underwriting data potentially unlawful. No data processing agreements with key processors Very common — key third parties (medical examiners, TPAs, actuarial firms, cloud providers) had no formal data processing agreements. Execute NDPA 2023-compliant data processing agreements with all third parties processing personal data on the insurer’s behalf within 90 days. Third-party processor risk is the insurer’s risk. A breach at an uncontracted medical examiner firm is the insurer’s NDPC notification obligation.

Privacy by Design The principle that data protection is built into the design and architecture of information systems and business practices from the outset, rather than being added as an afterthought. Privacy by Design requires the insurer to consider data protection implications at the design stage of every new system, process, or product, not after deployment. NDPA 2023 and GAID 2025 require Data Controllers of Major Importance to implement data protection by design and by default. Privacy by Design principles applied to the three highest-risk data contexts in Nigerian life insurance: PAS development or upgrade When specifying a new PAS or significant upgrade: define the minimum data fields required for each processing activity before the system is built (data minimisation by design); configure role-based access controls so that each system user can only access the data their role requires (access control by design); configure retention and disposal schedules so that data is automatically archived or deleted at the end of its retention period (retention management by design); ensure the PAS can generate a complete individual data export for DSAR responses (rights management by design); and ensure all data at rest is encrypted (security by design). Digital channel deployment (app, portal, WhatsApp) When designing a new digital channel: collect only the personal data strictly necessary for the channel’s function (data minimisation); privacy notices must be presented at the first point of data collection, in plain language, before data entry (informed consent by design); analytics and tracking should be off by default, with policyholders able to opt in rather than opt out (privacy by default); and the channel’s back-end integration with the PAS must enforce the same data access controls as the PAS itself. Third-party data sharing arrangements When designing a new data sharing arrangement (reinsurance treaty, TPA engagement, bancassurance integration): specify in the data processing agreement the specific data fields to be shared (data minimisation); define the processor’s permitted processing purposes and explicitly prohibit secondary use (purpose limitation by design); specify the data retention period applicable to the processor; and include the right to audit the processor’s data protection compliance.

Administrative penalties (s.48) First offence breach of NDPA 2023: up to 2% of annual gross revenue or ₦10 million, whichever is higher. Repeat or more serious breach: up to 4% of annual gross revenue or ₦20 million, whichever is higher. For a Nigerian life insurer with ₦15 billion gross premium income, a first-offence breach could attract a fine of up to ₦300 million. Criminal liability for individuals (s.49) Officers of a company (directors, the DPO, the CEO) may be personally criminally liable where the breach resulted from their negligence or wilful action. Criminal penalties include fines and, in serious cases, imprisonment. The personal liability provision is designed to prevent companies treating data protection fines as a cost of doing business. NDPC inspection powers (s.43) The NDPC may conduct inspections (announced or unannounced) of any licensed insurer’s data processing operations; require production of any document or data; interview staff; and take copies of records. An insurer that obstructs an NDPC inspection commits a further offence. Enforcement notices (s.44) The NDPC may issue an enforcement notice requiring the insurer to take specified corrective actions within a defined timeframe. Failure to comply with an enforcement notice is a separate, additional breach. Suspension of processing (s.45) In serious cases (ongoing breach causing harm to data subjects), the NDPC may order the insurer to suspend all or specific data processing activities until compliance is achieved. A suspension of core insurance data processing would make the insurer operationally unable to function. NAICOM interaction NAICOM market conduct inspections from 2025 include data protection compliance as an inspection item. A serious NDPC finding against an insurer may trigger a NAICOM market conduct investigation. The combination of NDPC enforcement action and concurrent NAICOM supervisory escalation represents the dual regulatory risk of data protection non-compliance in the insurance sector.

t: Chapter 32 · 32.13 Advisory: Building the Insurance Data Privacy Programme
x: Advisory: The Five Priority Actions for NDPA 2023 Compliance in a Nigerian Life Insurer ACTION 1: DPO APPOINTMENT. Appoint a qualified, resourced, independent DPO with direct Board access and register the appointment with the NDPC. Do not appoint a junior staff member or combine the DPO role with a conflicting functional role. The DPO’s credibility with the NDPC depends on their independence from the functions they oversee. ACTION 2: RECORD OF PROCESSING ACTIVITIES. Build a complete RoPA covering every personal data processing activity. This is the foundation document: without it, the DPCP cannot be completed, DPIAs cannot be properly scoped, and the insurer cannot demonstrate to the NDPC what data it processes and on what basis. ACTION 3: LAWFUL BASIS DOCUMENTATION. Review the lawful basis for every material processing activity in the RoPA. Update proposal forms and digital onboarding to capture explicit consent for health data processing. Review marketing consent processes. Document the legitimate interest assessment for fraud prevention and security monitoring. ACTION 4: DSAR PROCESS AND PAS DATA EXPORT CAPABILITY. Implement a documented DSAR procedure; test the PAS’s ability to generate a complete individual data export; designate a DSAR response team; and publish a clear mechanism for data subjects to submit requests (dedicated email address, form on the insurer’s website). ACTION 5: THIRD-PARTY PROCESSOR AGREEMENTS. Execute NDPA 2023-compliant data processing agreements with all processors: medical examiners, TPAs, reinsurers (data processing addendum to the treaty), actuarial firms, cloud providers, and any other party processing personal data on the insurer’s behalf. No processor should be receiving policyholder data without a signed DPA. The Single Highest Data Privacy Risk for a Nigerian Life Insurer Health data collected at underwriting without documented explicit consent. Every life insurance policy in a Nigerian insurer’s portfolio that was issued after the NDPA 2023’s commencement, where the proposer’s health data was collected on a proposal form that did not contain a specific, informed, explicit consent statement for health data processing, represents a potential NDPA 2023 breach for every piece of health data in that file. For an insurer with 100,000 in-force policies, the aggregate exposure is significant. The corrective action is not to void the policies — it is to update the proposal form going forward and to rely on the contract performance lawful basis for policies already in force, supplemented by a retrospective consent exercise where feasible. This is one of the most complex legacy compliance challenges the NDPA 2023 creates for the insurance sector.

Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023 (NDPA 2023) The primary Nigerian data protection legislation, assented to on 12 June 2023, establishing comprehensive data subject rights, data processing obligations, and the Nigeria Data Protection Commission (NDPC) as the enforcement authority. GAID 2025 (General Application and Implementation Directive) The NDPC’s primary implementation directive under NDPA 2023, effective 19 September 2025, specifying compliance requirements including data localisation, retention periods, and DCPMI obligations. Data Controller/Processor of Major Importance (DCPMI) A classification under NDPA 2023 for organisations that process personal data at scale or process special category data, triggering the highest tier of compliance obligations including mandatory DPO, DPCP, and biennial audit. Special Category Data Personal data in sensitive categories requiring heightened protection: health data, biometric data, genetic data, racial or ethnic origin, political opinions, religious beliefs, sexual orientation, and criminal record data. Data Protection Officer (DPO) A mandatory appointee for DCPMIs responsible for overseeing data protection compliance, advising on processing activities, cooperating with the NDPC, and acting as the contact point for data subject rights. Data Protection Compliance Programme (DPCP) The annual compliance programme document submitted by DCPMIs to the NDPC, describing the organisation’s data governance framework, processing activities, and compliance measures. Record of Processing Activities (RoPA) A mandatory document cataloguing every personal data processing activity: purposes, legal bases, data categories, data subjects, retention periods, security measures, and third parties. Lawful Basis One of the six legal grounds permitting personal data processing under NDPA 2023: consent, contract performance, legal obligation, vital interests, public task, or legitimate interests. Explicit Consent (Special Category Data) A specific, informed, and unambiguous positive act of agreement to processing of special category data; stricter than standard consent; required for health data collected at underwriting. Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA) A mandatory assessment before commencing high-risk processing activities, evaluating the nature and necessity of the processing, risks to data subjects, and required mitigation measures. Data Subject Access Request (DSAR) A request by a data subject for a copy of all personal data held about them, together with information on processing purposes, legal bases, and third parties; must be responded to within 30 days. Personal Data Breach A security incident leading to accidental or unlawful destruction, loss, alteration, unauthorised disclosure of, or access to personal data. 72-Hour Breach Notification The NDPA 2023 obligation to notify the NDPC within 72 hours of becoming aware of a personal data breach likely to result in risk to data subjects’ rights. Privacy by Design The principle that data protection is built into information systems and processes from the outset, not added as an afterthought; required by NDPA 2023 and GAID 2025 for DCPMIs. Standard Contractual Clauses (SCCs) NDPC-approved contractual terms providing adequate safeguards for cross-border data transfers where no adequacy decision exists. Data Localisation The GAID 2025 requirement that primary storage of personal data of Nigerian data subjects be on servers physically located in Nigeria.

Under the Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023, the health data collected by a Nigerian life insurer during the underwriting process is classified as: Standard personal data, requiring only a lawful basis for processing. Special category data, requiring both a lawful basis AND an additional specific condition such as explicit consent. Anonymised data, which falls outside the scope of the NDPA 2023. Regulatory data, processed solely under the insurer's NAICOM licence and exempt from NDPA 2023. (B) Special category data, requiring both a lawful basis AND an additional specific condition such as explicit consent. Why (B) is Correct NDPA 2023 identifies specific categories of personal data as warranting heightened protection — often called 'special category data' or 'sensitive personal data.' These include: health and medical data; genetic data; biometric data; racial or ethnic origin; religious beliefs; and political opinions. Health data collected during life insurance underwriting (medical examination results, HIV test results, GP records, diagnosis history) falls squarely within the special category. Processing this data requires: (1) a lawful basis from the standard list (consent, contract, legal obligation, legitimate interests); AND (2) an additional specific condition — for insurance underwriting, this is typically explicit consent from the data subject or an insurance-specific statutory provision. A data subject (policyholder) submits a data subject access request to a Nigerian life insurer. Under NDPA 2023, the insurer must respond: Within 7 business days. Within 30 days, providing a complete copy of all personal data held, together with information on purposes, legal bases, retention periods, and third parties. Within 60 days, if the volume of data makes a 30-day response impractical. Within 14 days for standard personal data, and within 30 days for special category data. (B) Within 30 days, providing a complete copy of all personal data held, together with information on purposes, legal bases, retention periods, and third parties. Why (B) is Correct NDPA 2023 provides data subjects with the right to access a copy of all personal data held about them by the data controller. The data controller must respond within 30 days of receiving the request. The response must include: (1) a copy of all personal data held; (2) confirmation of the purposes for which each category of data is processed; (3) the legal bases relied upon; (4) the retention period applicable to each category; and (5) the identity of third parties with whom the data has been shared. This is a comprehensive right that requires the insurer to have a good understanding of its own data holdings and processing activities. The NDPA 2023 obligation to notify the NDPC of a personal data breach requires notification: Within 24 hours of the breach being discovered by any member of staff. Within 72 hours of the insurer becoming aware of a breach likely to result in risk to data subjects' rights and freedoms. Within 30 days, consistent with the data subject access request response timeline. Only where the breach affects more than 1,000 policyholders. (B) Within 72 hours of the insurer becoming aware of a breach likely to result in risk to data subjects' rights and freedoms. Why (B) is Correct NDPA 2023 and GAID 2025 impose a 72-hour notification deadline running from the point the data controller becomes aware of the breach — not from when any staff member first noticed it. The notification must be made where the breach is likely to result in risk to the rights and freedoms of data subjects. This is a risk-based threshold — not all breaches require notification, only those that create material risk. For a life insurer, health data exposure almost always meets this threshold. Why the Others Are Wrong (A) 24 hours is not the NDPA 2023 standard — it is shorter than required. The controller also needs adequate time to assess the breach before notification, which a 24-hour window may not provide.(C) 30 days is the data subject access request timeline — not the breach notification timeline. 72 hours is a much tighter deadline.(D) There is no minimum threshold of affected data subjects for breach notification under NDPA 2023 — the test is risk to rights and freedoms, not volume.

Under GAID 2025, a Nigerian life insurer using a cloud-based PAS must ensure that: The entire cloud infrastructure is located in Nigeria. The primary storage of Nigerian policyholder personal data is on servers physically located in Nigeria, with secondary backups subject to adequate safeguards. All data is stored in Nigeria unless the NDPC grants an exemption; no secondary storage outside Nigeria is permitted. Cloud storage of insurance data is prohibited; only on-premise storage satisfies GAID 2025 requirements. (B) The primary storage of Nigerian policyholder personal data is on servers physically located in Nigeria, with secondary backups subject to adequate safeguards. Why (B) is Correct GAID 2025 implements the NDPA 2023 data localisation requirement. The core obligation is that the primary storage of Nigerian citizens' personal data must be on servers physically located in Nigeria. Secondary storage (backup copies, disaster recovery replicas) may be located outside Nigeria provided adequate safeguards are in place — typically a binding Data Transfer Agreement or Standard Contractual Clauses with the foreign storage provider, and a prior NDPC notification. This balanced approach allows cloud-based systems to maintain offshore backup capacity while protecting the primary data within Nigeria's jurisdiction. Privacy by Design in a Nigerian life insurer means: Appointing a DPO who reviews all new product launches before they go to market. Building data protection into the design of information systems, processes, and products from the outset, rather than adding it as an afterthought after deployment. Designing all insurance products so that they do not require the collection of any special category data. Ensuring that the insurer's privacy notices are displayed prominently on all marketing materials. (B) Building data protection into the design of information systems, processes, and products from the outset, rather than adding it as an afterthought after deployment. Why (B) is Correct Privacy by Design is a foundational data protection principle — originating in Ann Cavoukian's seven Privacy by Design principles, now embedded in GDPR Article 25 and reflected in NDPA 2023. It requires that data protection is a default architecture choice at the system and process design stage, not a retrofit added after a compliance review identifies gaps. For a Nigerian life insurer, Privacy by Design means: the new digital claims portal is designed with data minimisation (only collecting fields necessary for the claim) before the first line of code is written; the new underwriting system is designed with access controls for health data before deployment; and the new AI recommendation engine is designed with fairness testing protocols before the first training run.
