t: Chapter 35 · 35.1 Introduction: People as the Insurer’s Primary Asset
x: An insurance company is, at its most fundamental level, a collection of human judgements. The underwriter’s judgement about which risk to accept at what price; the claims assessor’s judgement about whether a claim is valid; the financial adviser’s judgement about which product genuinely serves the client’s needs; the actuary’s judgement about whether the reserves are adequate; the CEO’s judgement about where to invest the business’s capital — these are the decisions that determine whether an insurance company is financially sound, commercially competitive, and genuinely serving its customers. Systems, processes, and governance structures create the framework within which these judgements are made; but the judgements themselves depend on the quality, training, integrity, and motivation of the people making them. For Nigerian life insurers, the human capital challenge is acute in a specific way: the talent market for qualified insurance professionals is thin, competitive, and shrinking relative to the sector’s growing capability requirements. There are fewer than the market needs of CIIN Associates and Fellows, qualified actuaries, experienced underwriters, competent claims managers, and digital transformation specialists. The insurer that attracts, retains, and develops the right people will have a sustainable competitive advantage that products, systems, and marketing campaigns cannot easily replicate. This chapter addresses the complete human capital agenda of a Nigerian life insurer: attracting talent, qualifying it professionally (CIIN requirements), developing it continuously (CPD and training), directing it effectively (performance management and compensation), retaining it through career pathing and succession planning, and anchoring it to the right values through culture and consequence management.

t: Chapter 35 · 35.2 Talent Acquisition in the Nigerian Insurance Market
x: 35.2.1 The Talent Challenge Talent acquisition in the Nigerian insurance market is structurally difficult for three interconnected reasons. First, the industry’s historical reputation — shaped by claim non-payment, mis-selling, and poor service — makes insurance an unattractive career destination for high-calibre graduates who have alternatives. Second, the pipeline of professionally trained insurance graduates from Nigerian universities and polytechnics is insufficient to meet the industry’s growing demand, particularly for actuarial, risk, and investment talent. Third, the global demand for skilled Nigerian professionals (particularly in technology, finance, and risk) means that the insurer is competing not just with other Nigerian insurers but with multinationals, fintech companies, and international employers offering diaspora opportunities. The talent gap is most acute in specific technical roles: Actuarial professionals: Fellowship-qualified actuaries are extremely scarce in Nigeria; most large insurers have fewer than five qualified actuarial staff, and many mid-size insurers have none. The pipeline through the Institute and Faculty of Actuaries (IFoA), the Institute of Actuaries of Nigeria (IAN), and the Casualty Actuarial Society is growing but cannot yet meet demand. Digital and technology specialists: Data scientists, product managers with fintech experience, UX designers, and cybersecurity professionals are in extreme demand across all sectors of the Nigerian economy; the insurance industry competes poorly for this talent without a deliberate digital employer brand. Senior underwriters and claims professionals: Experienced senior underwriters and claims managers are developed internally over many years; there is very limited external supply of ready-made senior talent in these roles. 35.2.2 Talent Pools and Sourcing Strategies Effective talent acquisition requires active management of multiple sourcing channels, not passive dependence on inbound applications: Graduate programmes Partnerships with target universities (University of Lagos, University of Ibadan, Covenant University, Nile University, American University of Nigeria) to recruit talented final-year students into structured graduate trainee programmes. The graduate programme is the insurer’s primary pipeline for future technical and management talent. It must be long enough (12–18 months), structured enough (rotations through key departments), and visible enough (executive mentorship, cohort events, clear conversion path) to attract high-calibre graduates who have competing offers from banking, consulting, and tech. CIIN student membership The CIIN’s student membership database is a direct source of motivated, career-focused insurance professionals. Sponsoring CIIN examination costs for internal candidates and externally sponsoring promising CIIN students who are not yet employed by the insurer creates a visible talent pipeline and a positive industry relationship. Professional association networks The Institute of Actuaries of Nigeria (IAN), the Nigerian Institute of Management (NIM), ICAN, and CIMA member networks are direct sources of experienced financial professionals who may be interested in transitioning to insurance roles, particularly at senior levels. Diaspora return professionals Nigeria’s large diaspora community in the UK, US, Canada, and South Africa includes many insurance, actuarial, and financial services professionals with international experience who may be willing to return for the right opportunity. Targeted diaspora recruitment — through LinkedIn, Nigerian professional networks abroad, and CIIN’s international diaspora engagement — can bring world-class talent that the domestic market cannot supply. Mid-career lateral hiring For senior technical roles, targeted lateral hiring from competitor insurers, reinsurers, and international insurance groups operating in Nigeria. Critically, this talent must be genuine — not poached solely to access client relationships (which constitutes an unfair market practice). Insurtech and fintech sector For digital roles, the fintech and Insurtech community in Lagos, Abuja, and Port Harcourt contains product managers, engineers, and data specialists who understand financial services and may be attracted by the scale and social impact opportunity of a large life insurance platform. 35.2.3 Employee Value Proposition Design Employee Value Proposition (EVP) The total package of benefits, experiences, and opportunities that an employer offers to current and prospective employees in exchange for their skills, capabilities, and commitment. The EVP encompasses not only compensation and benefits but also career development opportunities, workplace culture, purpose and mission alignment, and the quality of management and leadership that employees experience day-to-day. A compelling EVP for a Nigerian life insurer in 2025 must address the specific motivational drivers of the talent segments the insurer is trying to attract. Research from comparable emerging markets identifies several high-salience EVP elements for insurance industry talent: Professional development and CIIN support: Full sponsorship of CIIN examination fees, study leave, and study materials. For actuarial candidates, sponsorship of IFoA/IAN examinations and time allocation for study. The insurer that invests in professional qualification is advertising a commitment to the individual’s career, not just their current role. Career clarity and progression: A visible career framework that shows the path from graduate trainee to team leader to department head, with specific competency milestones at each level. High performers leave companies where the promotion process is opaque or determined by politics rather than merit. Purpose and social impact: The insurance industry’s purpose — protecting families, funding retirement, enabling businesses to take risks — is genuinely meaningful. An insurer that communicates this purpose authentically and connects employees’ daily work to the financial security of Nigerian families is providing a social impact motivation that competing industries (banking, tech) find harder to match. Flexible working and technology: Post-COVID working expectations in the Nigerian professional community have shifted. An insurer that offers hybrid working where roles permit, provides good-quality technology tools, and maintains a modern physical working environment will attract talent that rejects employers with rigid presenteeism cultures and outdated IT infrastructure.

t: Chapter 35 · 35.3 Professional Qualification Requirements Under NIIRA 2025
x: 35.3.1 CIIN Certificate of Proficiency for Agents NIIRA 2025 mandates that every individual who sells, solicits, or negotiates life insurance products in Nigeria must hold a minimum qualification of the CIIN Certificate of Proficiency (Cert. COP) in Insurance. This requirement applies to all tied agents, bancassurance sales staff, digital sales agents, and any individual who makes a product recommendation to a prospective policyholder in a regulated context. CIIN Certificate of Proficiency: Key Requirements under NIIRA 2025 ELIGIBILITY: Any individual of good character without a criminal record relating to financial crimes or dishonesty, holding at minimum a West African Senior School Certificate (WASSCE) or equivalent. EXAMINATION: Three papers covering Insurance Principles and Practice; Life Assurance Products; and Elements of Insurance Law and Regulation. Examinations are conducted by CIIN at least twice per year. LICENSING: On passing the Cert. COP examination, the agent must be licensed by NAICOM (for tied agents) or registered under their insurer’s distribution licence (for bancassurance staff). The licence is renewed annually, subject to evidence of CPD compliance. NIIRA 2025 TRANSITIONAL PROVISION: Agents already in the market at the Act’s commencement date are given a defined transitional period (typically 12–24 months) to qualify. An insurer that allows an unlicensed agent to sell insurance products after the transitional period is in breach of NIIRA 2025 and is liable to regulatory sanction. EMPLOYER OBLIGATION: The insurer bears primary responsibility for ensuring all agents it employs or appoints hold a valid Cert. COP licence before they are permitted to sell. NAICOM’s market conduct inspections routinely check agent licensing compliance. 35.3.2 CIIN Membership Requirements for Key Officers NIIRA 2025 extends the professional qualification requirement beyond field agents to include key management officers within the insurer. Officers responsible for underwriting, claims management, financial planning advice, and certain other regulated functions must hold or be working toward a higher level of CIIN qualification. Role / Function Minimum CIIN Qualification Required Pathway Head of Underwriting / Senior Underwriter Associate of the Chartered Insurance Institute of Nigeria (ACIIN) — Associateship level. Cert. COP → Diploma in Insurance (Dip. CIIN) → Associateship (ACIIN). Typical completion time: 4–7 years with part-time study. Head of Claims / Senior Claims Manager Associate of the Chartered Insurance Institute of Nigeria (ACIIN) — Associateship level. Same pathway as underwriting. Claims management is an equally demanding regulatory function under NIIRA 2025. Financial Adviser / Personal Financial Planner Diploma in Insurance (Dip. CIIN) minimum; Associateship (ACIIN) strongly preferred for practitioners giving full personal financial planning advice. Cert. COP → Dip. CIIN, with specific modules in personal financial planning, life products, and pension. Company Secretary / Compliance Officer Associate of the Chartered Institute of Secretaries (ICSA) or CIIN Associateship or other recognised professional qualification in compliance. NAICOM may accept equivalent professional qualifications from recognised bodies. MD/CEO and Executive Directors NIIRA 2025 fit-and-proper requirement: demonstrated senior insurance or financial services management experience, supplemented by relevant professional qualifications (CIIN, ICAN, CIBN, MBA). CIIN Fellowship (FCIIN) is particularly relevant for the CEO of a life insurer. Experience-based for senior external hires; CIIN qualification pathway for internally promoted executives.

t: Chapter 35 · 35.4 CIIN Continuing Professional Development Framework
x: 35.4.1 CPD Requirements Continuing Professional Development (CPD) The systematic maintenance, improvement, and broadening of the skills and knowledge required for competent performance of a professional role, throughout the professional’s active career. CIIN’s CPD framework ensures that qualified insurance professionals keep their technical knowledge current in a rapidly evolving regulatory, product, and technology environment. The CIIN CPD framework requires qualified members to complete a defined number of CPD hours per year, drawn from a combination of approved structured activities and unstructured learning: Total CPD hours required per year 30 hours for fully qualified members (ACIIN and FCIIN). 20 hours for Diploma-level members in practice. Specific requirements for Cert. COP holders in active sales roles. Structured CPD (minimum 50%) Formal learning activities with documented learning outcomes: CIIN-organised seminars and conferences; approved external training programmes; classroom and e-learning courses; examination preparation courses for higher CIIN qualifications; industry regulator (NAICOM, PenCom) organised training events. Unstructured CPD (maximum 50%) Self-directed learning: reading CIIN publications, industry journals, regulatory updates; attending industry association events; peer learning and knowledge-sharing; mentoring activities (both giving and receiving). CPD recording Each member maintains a CPD record documenting the activities completed, the hours claimed, and the learning outcomes achieved. The CPD record must be available for CIIN audit; members selected for CPD audit must produce documentation within a defined period. Renewal requirement CIIN membership renewal (typically annual) is conditional on CPD compliance. Members who cannot demonstrate the required CPD hours will not have their membership renewed, which is material because it affects the individual’s NIIRA 2025 licensing compliance. 35.4.2 Employer CPD Obligations The insurer, as the employer of CIIN-qualified professionals, has specific obligations in relation to CPD: Facilitating CPD completion: The insurer must provide structured CPD opportunities (in-house training programmes that generate CPD credit hours, funding for approved external courses, time allocation for CIIN examination preparation) that enable staff to meet their annual CPD requirements without having to source all their CPD independently outside working hours. Tracking CPD compliance: The HR function is responsible for maintaining a CPD compliance register that tracks each qualified member’s CPD hours against their annual requirement. The register should be updated quarterly and reviewed by the Head of HR and the Head of Compliance before the CIIN membership renewal period. Regulatory reporting: NAICOM’s market conduct inspections may request evidence of the insurer’s agent and staff qualification and CPD compliance. An insurer that cannot demonstrate systematic CPD tracking for its qualified professionals is in regulatory breach. 35.4.3 Penalties for CPD Non-Compliance CIIN CPD Non-Compliance: Individual and Employer Consequences FOR THE INDIVIDUAL PROFESSIONAL: Membership non-renewal: Failure to complete the required CPD hours results in CIIN membership not being renewed. The individual may no longer represent themselves as an Associate or Fellow of CIIN. Licensing consequences: Under NIIRA 2025, a financial adviser or senior practitioner without current CIIN membership is no longer qualified to hold their regulated role. This may result in loss of their NAICOM individual licence. Career consequences: A lapsed CIIN membership will be visible to future employers performing qualification checks and may significantly damage the individual’s career progression. FOR THE EMPLOYING INSURER: Regulatory sanction: An insurer that knowingly employs unqualified or CPD-non-compliant professionals in regulated roles is in breach of NIIRA 2025 and subject to NAICOM enforcement action, including financial penalties. Market conduct finding: NAICOM’s market conduct inspection may formally find the insurer non-compliant and publish the finding, with reputational consequences in the market.

t: Chapter 35 · 35.5 Building a Compliance and Ethics Culture
x: 35.5.1 What Organisational Culture Is and Why It Matters Organisational Culture The shared values, beliefs, behaviours, and unwritten rules that characterise how work gets done in an organisation. Culture is ‘how we do things here when no one is watching’. It is shaped by the behaviours modelled by leaders, the behaviours that are rewarded and penalised, the stories that are told about past successes and failures, and the rituals and symbols that reinforce shared identity. Culture cannot be dictated by a policy document; it must be embodied in consistent leadership behaviour and embedded in the organisation’s systems and incentives. For a Nigerian life insurer, the most commercially and regulatory significant cultural dimensions are: Compliance culture: The degree to which every employee — from the field agent to the MD/CEO — understands, accepts, and actively applies the regulatory rules that govern their work. In a strong compliance culture, compliance is not a department’s responsibility; it is everyone’s responsibility. Compliance queries are welcomed rather than resented; regulatory findings are addressed with urgency rather than managed as communications challenges. Ethics culture: The degree to which the organisation’s decision-making consistently prioritises doing the right thing for customers, colleagues, and the market, even when it is commercially inconvenient. In a strong ethics culture, a sales agent who knows that a product is unsuitable for a specific customer declines to sell it, even if the commission would be significant. A claims manager who discovers that a claim denial recommendation is technically defensible but morally unjust will escalate rather than simply file the denial. Trust culture: The degree to which employees trust the organisation’s leadership to make fair decisions, to treat them with respect, and to honour the commitments it makes (regarding career development, compensation, and working conditions). An organisation that talks about trust but behaves in ways that betray it — surprise retrenchments, unexplained compensation changes, opaque promotion decisions — will have a cynical workforce that does just enough to get by. 35.5.2 Cultural Pathologies in the Nigerian Insurance Market NIIRA 2025’s consumer protection provisions are in significant part a regulatory response to specific cultural pathologies that have persisted in sections of the Nigerian insurance market: Sales-above-suitability culture: A culture in which sales agents are incentivised to sell as many policies as possible, regardless of whether those policies are genuinely suitable for the buyers. The result is high lapses (customers who bought products they did not need and eventually stop paying premiums), low satisfaction, and an industry-wide reputation for mis-selling. Claims avoidance culture: A culture in which claims managers are incentivised or evaluated on the basis of claims costs reduced rather than claims fairly settled. The result is disputed claims, delayed payments, and the reputational consequence of a market in which ‘insurance doesn’t pay’ is the dominant consumer belief. Non-disclosure culture: A culture in which the disclosure of problems, errors, or regulatory breaches to senior management or the Board is discouraged — either through explicit pressure or through an implicit understanding that bad news travels badly. The result is that small problems become large ones before leadership is aware of them, and regulatory breaches are managed as communications challenges rather than addressed at their source. Regulatory compliance as formality: A culture in which regulatory requirements are treated as bureaucratic formalities to be technically satisfied rather than genuinely implemented. Policy documents are written to satisfy NAICOM inspection; actual practice is governed by different informal rules. This is the most dangerous cultural pathology because it combines regulatory risk with ethical failure. 35.5.3 Tone from the Top: The Board and CEO’s Role in Culture The most powerful determinant of an insurance company’s culture is the behaviour of its most senior leaders. Employees watch what leaders do, not what they say. An MD/CEO who talks about customer centricity but visibly prioritises sales targets over claims settlement quality has communicated the organisation’s real values — and the sales-above-suitability culture will persist regardless of the policy documents in the compliance library. Specific behaviours that demonstrate genuine tone from the top in a Nigerian life insurer: The CEO settles legitimate contested claims personally, when brought to their attention, even against the Claims department’s recommendation, and communicates the decision to the organisation as a statement of values. The Board discusses culture and compliance as substantive agenda items — not as a single slide in a management presentation — at every Board meeting, reviewing complaint data, claims settlement ratios, NAICOM correspondence, and staff conduct cases. Senior leaders are visibly held accountable for conduct violations, including senior salespeople who mis-sell, claims managers who wrongly decline claims, and executives who misrepresent results to the Board. The organisation’s culture is defined by who gets away with what. Compliance-related concerns are welcomed and protected, not penalised. The organisation maintains a whistleblowing mechanism through which staff can raise concerns about misconduct or regulatory breach without fear of retaliation — and the mechanism is actually used and investigated.

35.6.1 The Training Architecture A well-designed training framework for a Nigerian life insurer addresses four distinct learning populations with different needs and different appropriate delivery formats: field agents; technical insurance professionals (underwriters, claims staff, actuarial analysts); management and leadership; and digital and specialist skill areas. A single ‘training department’ that tries to serve all four populations equally well will serve none of them adequately. The Four-Layer Training Architecture LAYER 1: AGENT TRAINING AND CIIN QUALIFICATION Induction (Weeks 1–4): Company introduction, product knowledge, sales process, compliance and ethics, NAICOM regulations, customer needs analysis, and the CIIN Cert. COP examination syllabus. Delivered by in-house trainers supplemented by CIIN study materials. Goal: the agent understands the products, the regulatory rules, and the sales ethics requirements before they make their first customer contact. Ongoing agent development (Months 2–12): Weekly sales team meetings combining performance review with product and skills development; monthly product-specific training sessions; quarterly regulatory updates; periodic sales skills coaching from senior agents and sales managers. Goal: continuous improvement in sales quality, product knowledge, and compliance behaviour. CIIN Cert. COP examination preparation: Structured study programme aligned with CIIN examination dates; in-house mock examinations; study group facilitation; examination fee sponsorship. Goal: 100% of active agents to hold valid Cert. COP within the NIIRA 2025 transitional period. LAYER 2: TECHNICAL INSURANCE ACADEMY The Technical Insurance Academy is the insurer’s internal professional development programme for underwriters, claims assessors, actuarial analysts, and compliance staff. It offers: an Underwriting Fundamentals module (medical underwriting basics, mortality table application, risk assessment, group underwriting); a Claims Management module (claims assessment principles, fraud investigation, medical evidence interpretation, NIIRA 2025 settlement obligations); and an Actuarial Awareness module (non-actuarial staff understanding of pricing, reserving, and ERM). Delivery: classroom with experienced practitioners as faculty; case-based learning using real or anonymised company cases. LAYER 3: MANAGEMENT AND LEADERSHIP DEVELOPMENT A tiered leadership development programme: a New Manager Programme for first-time managers (managing performance, giving feedback, delegation, compliance responsibilities of a people manager); a Senior Manager Programme for department heads (strategic thinking, financial management, executive communication, board interaction); and an Executive Leadership Programme (strategy, governance, stakeholder management) for ExCo members and future ExCo candidates. Delivery: combination of internal facilitation and external executive education partners (Lagos Business School, IESE, Gordon Institute). LAYER 4: DIGITAL AND SPECIALIST SKILLS Digital literacy: data analysis basics, CRM tool proficiency, digital customer servicing. Specialist skills: NDPA 2023 data protection awareness (all staff); AML/KYC compliance training (all client-facing staff); cybersecurity hygiene (all staff). Delivery: online modules with assessments; annual mandatory completion.

35.7.1 The Performance Management Philosophy A well-designed performance management system creates clarity about what is expected of each person in each role, provides a structured mechanism for ongoing performance feedback, links performance to compensation and career progression, and identifies underperformance early enough to be addressed. In the Nigerian insurance market, where commission-driven sales cultures can create distorted incentives, the performance management system must specifically reinforce the distinction between volume performance (how much was sold) and quality performance (how appropriately it was sold). 35.7.2 KPI Frameworks by Role Category Role Category Primary KPIs Quality / Compliance KPIs Review Cadence Tied Agent Annualised First Year Premium (AFYP); number of new policies issued; number of active clients (face-to-face meetings with documented outcomes). 13-month persistency rate; NIGO (Not In Good Order) application rate; client satisfaction score (sampled calls); zero upheld complaints. Weekly sales meeting; monthly performance review with unit manager; annual appraisal. Bancassurance Relationship Manager AFYP through the bank channel; number of bank branches activated; bank staff training completion rate. Persistency rate; NIGO rate; bank staff satisfaction with insurer support; zero regulatory findings on the channel. Monthly review with Distribution Head; quarterly bancassurance partner review; annual appraisal. Underwriter Number of cases processed; turnaround time (proposal to decision); number of cases requiring referral vs. auto-accepted. Accuracy rate (decisions reviewed and overturned by senior underwriter); claims experience vs. accepted risk profile; NAICOM complaint rate attributable to underwriting decisions. Weekly pipeline review; quarterly underwriting experience analysis; annual appraisal. Claims Assessor Number of claims processed per month; average claims settlement time (vs. NIIRA 2025 60-day target). Claims dispute rate; percentage of claims settled within regulatory target; customer satisfaction score (post-claims survey); fraud detection rate. Weekly claims dashboard review; monthly team review; annual appraisal. Financial Adviser (IFA / PAP) Number of financial plans completed; AFYP from financial planning clients; client retention rate. Suitability assessment completion rate; 13-month persistency of advised clients; zero upheld suitability complaints; CPD compliance. Monthly review with line manager; quarterly compliance review; annual appraisal. Department Head Balanced scorecard performance across financial, customer, process, and learning dimensions (Chapter 27 framework); budget adherence; team engagement score. Regulatory compliance record (zero major findings); staff CPD compliance rate; succession plan currency. Monthly ExCo performance review; quarterly Board reporting; annual appraisal by MD/CEO. 35.7.3 The Appraisal Process A well-designed appraisal process for a Nigerian life insurer includes: Goal-setting (beginning of year): Each employee, in dialogue with their line manager, agrees their annual KPI targets and development goals. Targets must be SMART (Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, and Time-bound) and must include both quantitative performance targets and qualitative compliance and development objectives. Mid-year check-in: A structured conversation between the employee and line manager reviewing progress against the annual targets, identifying any barriers to performance, adjusting targets if material circumstances have changed, and setting the priority focus for the second half of the year. Mid-year check-ins are non-negotiable: a culture where the annual appraisal is the only performance conversation is a culture where underperformance festers unaddressed for 12 months. Annual appraisal: A comprehensive review of the year’s performance against all KPIs and development goals; an overall performance rating; a compensation review recommendation; and agreement of the following year’s goals and development plan. The annual appraisal should not contain any surprises — all significant performance issues should have been raised and addressed throughout the year. Calibration: Before final ratings are confirmed, a manager calibration session (all managers in a department reviewing each other’s proposed ratings) ensures consistency across the team and prevents rating inflation (all staff rated ‘excellent’) or rating compression (all staff rated ‘satisfactory’).

35.8.1 Compensation Philosophy The compensation philosophy is the insurer’s explicit, Board-approved statement of how it intends to position its total compensation package relative to the market, what it values and rewards in employee performance, and how it balances fixed and variable pay. A clearly articulated compensation philosophy prevents the ad hoc, reactive compensation decisions that create internal equity problems and drive unwanted turnover. A recommended compensation philosophy for a Nigerian life insurer in 2025: ‘We aim to pay at the median of our relevant talent market for standard performance, and above the median (50th–75th percentile) for sustained high performance. We value both results and conduct: exceptional results achieved through unethical or non-compliant behaviour will not be rewarded. We will be transparent about how compensation is determined and consistent in its application.’ 35.8.2 Agent Commission: Structure and NIIRA 2025 Constraints Agent commission is the dominant variable compensation mechanism for the distribution workforce. Under NIIRA 2025 and NAICOM’s commission guidelines, agent commission rates are subject to maximum limits that vary by product type, designed to prevent commission-driven sales from systematically distorting agent recommendations. NAICOM Commission Guidelines: Key Principles MAXIMUM FIRST-YEAR COMMISSION (FYC): NAICOM’s product approval framework sets maximum first-year commission rates by product category. Individual life term assurance: typically up to 35–40% of first-year premium. Endowment and whole life: typically up to 30–35% of first-year premium. Group life: brokerage capped at defined percentage of annual premium. The insurer must not pay commission above the approved rate. RENEWAL COMMISSION: Typically 5–10% of renewal premium, declining over the policy term. Renewal commission incentivises the agent to service existing clients and maintain persistency, not merely write new business. COMMISSION CLAWBACK: NIIRA 2025 permits (and best practice requires) a commission clawback mechanism: if a policy lapses within a defined period (typically 13 months) of issuance, the insurer may reclaim a proportional amount of the first-year commission from the agent. Clawback directly incentivises the agent to write policies that will persist, not merely close sales. OVERRIDING COMMISSION AND OVERRIDE: Commission paid to unit managers and agency managers on the production of the agents in their unit. Overrides must be within NAICOM’s guidelines and must not create an incentive for managers to encourage agents to write unsuitable business. 35.8.3 Non-Agent Staff Variable Pay For non-agent professional staff, variable pay should be linked to annual performance against the KPI framework described in Section 35.7, reflecting both quantitative performance and qualitative conduct and compliance behaviour. The variable pay pool for non-agent staff is typically determined by the company’s overall financial performance (profit and premium growth) and then allocated to individuals based on their performance rating. Design principles for non-agent variable pay in a Nigerian life insurer: Performance-based, not loyalty-based: Variable pay should reflect performance in the current year, not tenure. A high-performing second-year employee should receive more variable pay than an average-performing fifth-year employee in the same role. Compliance as a qualifier, not an add-on: Any employee with a serious compliance breach in the year (upheld customer complaint, NAICOM finding attributable to their conduct, disciplinary action for misconduct) should have their variable pay significantly reduced or eliminated, regardless of their quantitative performance. Compliance must be a qualifier for variable pay, not merely one of many components. Differentiating the distribution: Best-practice variable pay systems differentiate meaningfully between performance levels. A high performer should receive variable pay of 3–5× that of a standard performer; a zero or near-zero award should be the consequence of below-standard performance. Uniform variable pay across a team creates no performance incentive. 35.8.4 Non-Monetary Recognition Monetary compensation is not the only retention lever. Research consistently shows that recognition, career development opportunity, and quality of management relationships are major drivers of employee engagement and retention, particularly for professional staff who have multiple employment options. Specific non-monetary recognition mechanisms for a Nigerian life insurer: Annual recognition awards: Company-wide recognition of outstanding performance in specific categories: Best Agent (by AFYP and persistency combined); Best Claims Assessor (customer satisfaction and settlement time); Best Team (team-level achievement of financial and quality KPIs); Innovation Award (most impactful process improvement or digital initiative). Awards should be presented publicly, with specific articulation of why the recipient won. Sponsorship and secondment: Sponsored attendance at international insurance conferences (CIIN Annual Conference, African Insurance Organisation conference, NAICOM-organised international study tours) as a recognition and development mechanism for high-potential professionals. CEO recognition letters and calls: A CEO who personally writes a letter or calls an agent who has just settled a major claim with exceptional compassion, or an underwriter who identified and prevented a fraud, is communicating what the organisation values more powerfully than any policy document.

t: Chapter 35 · 35.9 Succession Planning for Critical Roles
x: 35.9.1 Why Succession Planning Matters in Insurance The loss of a Statutory Actuary, a Chief Underwriter, or a Chief Distribution Officer without a ready internal successor creates two simultaneous crises: an operational crisis (the technical work does not stop needing to be done) and a regulatory crisis (NIIRA 2025 requires qualified incumbents in specific roles; a vacancy in a mandated position may trigger NAICOM notification and a compliance response plan). Succession planning — the systematic identification and development of candidates capable of filling critical roles — is the risk management response to this vulnerability. 35.9.2 The Succession Planning Process A well-designed succession planning process for a Nigerian life insurer includes: Critical role identification: Define which roles are so critical to the business’s operation and regulatory compliance that their unplanned vacancy would create immediate operational or regulatory risk. Typically: Statutory Actuary; MD/CEO; Chief Risk Officer; Chief Underwriter; Chief Claims Officer; Chief Distribution Officer; CFO; Head of Legal and Compliance. Successor identification: For each critical role, identify three categories of successor: ‘Ready now’ (could step in immediately with minimal transition support); ‘Ready in 1–2 years’ (needs specific development to be ready); and ‘Potential 3–5 years’ (early-career talent with the potential to reach this level). Development planning: For each identified successor, design a specific development plan: the experience, training, coaching, and exposure required to close the gap between their current capability and the critical role’s requirements. Development plans must be genuinely developmental, not merely aspirational. Board review: Succession plans for the MD/CEO and all ExCo-level roles must be reviewed annually by the Board. NIIRA 2025 specifically requires the Board to satisfy itself that succession plans for regulated roles are in place and credible. External succession fallback: For the most specialised roles (Statutory Actuary, actuarial senior leadership), where internal successors may not be available within the required timeframe, an external succession fallback plan should be maintained: a defined relationship with a specialist recruiter, a list of qualified external candidates who could be approached, and a timeline for emergency external succession.

t: Chapter 35 · 35.10 Consequence Management and Disciplinary Framework
x: 35.10.1 The Principle of Consequence Management An organisation’s culture is defined by what it tolerates as much as by what it rewards. An insurer that articulates high values in its Code of Conduct but fails to take consistent, visible action when those values are breached is communicating that the values are performative rather than real. Consequence management — the consistent application of appropriate consequences for conduct violations, from a minor process error to a serious ethical breach — is the mechanism through which values are enforced rather than merely stated. The fundamental principle of consequence management is proportionality and consistency: the consequence must be proportional to the seriousness of the breach, and similar breaches must attract similar consequences regardless of the seniority of the person involved. An insurer that disciplines a junior claims assessor for a minor documentation error but ignores a senior manager’s deliberate misrepresentation of results to the Board is communicating that rules apply differently at different levels — the most damaging cultural message an organisation can send. 35.10.2 The Disciplinary Framework A well-designed disciplinary framework for a Nigerian life insurer distinguishes between performance issues and conduct issues, and between minor and serious breaches: Category Examples Appropriate Response Escalation Performance issue Missing sales targets; high NIGO rate; slow claims processing speed. Not misconduct — the employee is trying but not achieving the required standard. Verbal coaching; formal performance improvement plan (PIP); targeted training; re-assessment against PIP milestones. If PIP not met after a defined period: formal written warning; role change; or termination if performance cannot be improved. Minor conduct breach Late reporting of a client complaint; failure to complete a required compliance form; minor documentation error in an underwriting file. Verbal warning from line manager; documented in performance file; specific coaching on the requirement. Not a disciplinary matter. Repetition of minor breaches becomes a pattern of conduct requiring formal disciplinary action. Moderate conduct breach Selling an unsuitable product without conducting a proper needs analysis; processing a claim without obtaining required documentation; failing to disclose a conflict of interest. Formal written warning; compliance re-training; supervision period; potential impact on annual variable pay. Repeat occurrence or aggravating circumstances escalates to serious conduct breach. Serious conduct breach Deliberate mis-selling (knowingly selling an unsuitable product for commission); fraudulent claim (submitting false documentation); falsification of performance data; bribery or corruption; deliberate non-disclosure to NAICOM; theft of company or client assets. Immediate suspension pending investigation; full disciplinary investigation; potential termination with notice (or summarily for gross misconduct); referral to NAICOM for regulatory action against individual licence; referral to law enforcement where criminal conduct is suspected. Board notification for senior management serious breaches; NAICOM notification where required by NIIRA 2025.

t: Chapter 35 · 35.11 Advisory: Building a High-Performance Insurance Organisation in Nigeria
x: The most enduring competitive advantage available to a Nigerian life insurer is not its product range, its technology, or its regulatory compliance record. It is its people: the quality of its professionals, the strength of its culture, and the consistency with which both are maintained. Products can be replicated; systems can be copied; regulatory compliance is table stakes. A team of deeply competent, genuinely ethical, highly motivated insurance professionals who are committed to the organisation’s mission is difficult to replicate and extremely difficult to compete against. Advisory: Six Principles for Building a High-Performance Insurance Organisation PRINCIPLE 1: INVEST IN THE GRADUATE PROGRAMME AS A LONG-TERM ASSET. The graduate trainee who joins the insurer at 24 is, if retained and developed, the branch manager at 30, the department head at 36, and a potential ExCo member at 42. An insurer that attracts exceptional graduates, puts them through a demanding development programme, and invests consistently in their CIIN qualification and leadership development is building an organisational capability that takes a decade to develop and will take competitors much longer to replicate. PRINCIPLE 2: PAY FOR PERFORMANCE, NOT FOR PRESENCE. The insurer that pays the same variable pay to its best performers and its average performers — because ‘it’s not fair’ to differentiate, or because the manager lacks the confidence to have a difficult performance conversation — is systematically destroying the incentive for high performance and subsidising mediocrity. Pay differentials for performance are fair; uniform pay for differentiated performance is the unfair outcome. PRINCIPLE 3: MAKE THE COMPLIANCE CULTURE CONCRETE, NOT ASPIRATIONAL. Abstract values statements in the Code of Conduct change nothing. Concrete, visible enforcement of compliance standards changes everything. An MD/CEO who publicly disciplines a senior salesperson for mis-selling — regardless of their production numbers — is communicating the compliance culture more powerfully than any training programme. PRINCIPLE 4: BUILD MANAGEMENT QUALITY AS A CORE CAPABILITY. The most common reason high-performing insurance professionals leave their employers is not pay — it is their direct manager. A manager who does not give feedback, does not advocate for their team, does not develop people, and does not hold underperformers accountable destroys team performance and drives turnover regardless of the insurer’s brand and compensation package. Investing in management quality — through selection, training, coaching, and holding managers accountable for their team’s development outcomes — is the highest-return HR investment available. PRINCIPLE 5: TREAT CIIN QUALIFICATION AS A NON-NEGOTIABLE PROFESSIONAL STANDARD, NOT A COST. Some Nigerian insurers view CIIN examination sponsorship as a cost to be managed. The insurers that treat it as a professional investment — fully sponsoring all relevant staff through CIIN examination, celebrating qualification achievements, and building career progression explicitly around qualification milestones — develop a more professionally competent, more confident, and more loyal workforce than those that leave qualification to individual initiative. PRINCIPLE 6: SUCCESSION PLAN FOR EVERY CRITICAL ROLE, EVERY YEAR. The succession plan is not a document filed in HR and reviewed every five years. It is a living plan, reviewed annually by the Board for ExCo roles and quarterly by the ExCo for critical functional roles. Every critical role should have at least one ‘ready in 1–2 years’ internal candidate whose development plan is actively being executed. An insurer that is consistently surprised by leadership vacancies — because it had no succession plan — is an insurer whose Board has not been doing its governance job. The Most Important Cultural Investment a Nigerian Life Insurer Can Make Build an organisation where delivering a bad claims result to a policyholder, selling an unsuitable product, or misrepresenting information to management are genuinely unacceptable — not because NAICOM is watching, but because every person in the organisation understands that their professional identity is incompatible with those actions. Culture of this quality does not come from training programmes or policy documents. It comes from a decade of consistent leadership behaviour, consistent recognition of the right conduct, and consistent consequence for the wrong conduct, compounding year after year into an organisational character that is genuinely difficult to corrupt. The insurers that build this culture will be the ones that survive and thrive in the next decade of the Nigerian market.

Employee Value Proposition (EVP) The total package of benefits, experiences, and opportunities an employer offers to attract and retain employees, encompassing compensation, career development, culture, purpose, and management quality. CIIN Certificate of Proficiency (Cert. COP) The minimum professional qualification required under NIIRA 2025 for all individuals who sell, solicit, or negotiate life insurance products in Nigeria; obtained through CIIN examinations covering insurance principles, life products, and insurance law. Associate of the Chartered Insurance Institute of Nigeria (ACIIN) The Associateship qualification required of key management officers including Heads of Underwriting, Claims, and Financial Planning under NIIRA 2025. Fellow of the Chartered Insurance Institute of Nigeria (FCIIN) The highest CIIN qualification, representing distinguished achievement and typically required of or strongly preferred for CEO and senior leadership roles in licensed Nigerian insurers. Continuing Professional Development (CPD) The systematic maintenance, improvement, and broadening of skills and knowledge throughout a professional career; CIIN members must complete a defined number of CPD hours annually as a condition of membership renewal. Structured CPD Formal learning activities with documented outcomes (CIIN-organised seminars, approved training programmes, e-learning) that count toward the minimum 50% structured component of the CIIN CPD requirement. Organisational Culture The shared values, beliefs, behaviours, and unwritten rules that characterise how work gets done in an organisation, shaped primarily by the behaviours modelled and rewarded by senior leaders. Tone from the Top The principle that senior leadership behaviour — the actions, decisions, and priorities of the Board and CEO — is the most powerful determinant of an organisation’s culture, outweighing policy documents and training programmes. Sales-above-Suitability Culture A cultural pathology in which agents are incentivised to maximise sales volume regardless of product suitability for the buyer; a primary target of NIIRA 2025’s consumer protection provisions. Claims Avoidance Culture A cultural pathology in which claims staff are evaluated on claims costs minimised rather than claims fairly settled, resulting in delayed and disputed claims and industry-wide reputational damage. KPI (Key Performance Indicator) A specific, measurable metric used to evaluate an individual’s, team’s, or organisation’s performance against defined targets. Commission Clawback A mechanism through which an insurer reclaims a proportional amount of first-year commission from an agent if the policy they sold lapses within a defined early period, incentivising the sale of persistent business. Succession Planning The systematic identification and development of candidates capable of filling critical roles, so that leadership vacancies do not create operational or regulatory crises. Consequence Management The consistent application of appropriate consequences for conduct violations, from minor process errors to serious ethical breaches; the mechanism through which organisational values are enforced. Performance Improvement Plan (PIP) A formal, time-bound plan agreed between an employee with performance deficiencies and their line manager, specifying the improvement targets and support required, with defined consequences if targets are not met. Calibration (Performance Management) A process in which managers review each other’s proposed performance ratings to ensure consistency across the team, preventing rating inflation or compression.

Under NIIRA 2025, every individual who sells, solicits, or negotiates life insurance products in Nigeria must hold a minimum qualification of: The CIIN Diploma in Insurance. The CIIN Certificate of Proficiency (Cert. COP) in Insurance. The Associate of the Chartered Insurance Institute of Nigeria (ACIIN) qualification. A university degree in insurance, economics, or a related discipline. (B) The CIIN Certificate of Proficiency (Cert. COP) in Insurance. Why (B) is Correct NIIRA 2025 prescribes the CIIN Cert. COP as the minimum qualification for any individual who sells, solicits, or negotiates life insurance products in Nigeria — whether as a tied agent, an independent agent, a bank staff member in a bancassurance arrangement, or any other selling intermediary. This is the statutory minimum: a two-part qualification covering insurance fundamentals (Part 1) and life insurance or general insurance (Part 2). It can be attained in 3–6 months of study. Without it, selling insurance is a criminal offence under NIIRA 2025. Why the Others Are Wrong (A) The CIIN Diploma is a more advanced professional qualification — required for professional roles (underwriters, claims managers) but above the minimum required for sales agents.(C) The ACIIN is the full Associate designation — significantly more advanced than the Cert. COP and required for senior technical professionals, not the minimum for sales agents.(D) A university degree in insurance is not required by NIIRA 2025 — the Cert. COP is the prescribed standard regardless of educational background.

The CIIN CPD framework requires fully qualified CIIN members (ACIIN and FCIIN) to complete how many CPD hours per year? 10 hours, all structured. 20 hours, at least 50% structured. 30 hours, at least 50% structured. 40 hours, all approved by the CIIN examinations board. (C) 30 hours, at least 50% structured learning. Why (C) is Correct The CIIN's CPD framework requires ACIIN and FCIIN members to complete 30 CPD hours per year — of which at least 50% (15 hours) must be structured learning (formal courses, workshops, seminars, or webinars with a defined learning outcome). The remaining 50% (up to 15 hours) may be unstructured learning (self-directed reading, on-the-job learning, research). CPD records must be maintained by the member and are subject to CIIN audit. Failure to meet CPD requirements can result in CIIN membership suspension. Why the Others Are Wrong (A) 10 hours all-structured is below the required standard for ACIIN/FCIIN members.(B) 20 hours at 50% structured is also below the required 30-hour standard.(D) 40 hours all-approved-by-examinations-board does not reflect the CIIN CPD framework — 30 hours with the structured/unstructured split is the correct standard.

An organisation's culture is most powerfully shaped by: The content of the company's Code of Conduct and annual compliance training. The behaviours modelled by senior leaders, and which behaviours are consistently rewarded and penalised. The number of NAICOM market conduct inspections the company passes without a finding. The company's employee satisfaction survey results. (B) The behaviours modelled by senior leaders, and which behaviours are consistently rewarded and penalised. Why (B) is Correct Organisational culture research consistently shows that culture is defined by observable behaviour — specifically, what leaders do (not what they say), and what the organisation consistently rewards and penalises. A company can have an impressive Code of Conduct and an annual compliance training programme — but if the senior leaders visibly cut ethical corners, if agents who write high volume but low-persistency business are celebrated while those who write less but maintain excellent persistency are ignored, and if staff who raise concerns are subsequently marginalised — the culture is shaped by those observable realities, not by the Code of Conduct. Why the Others Are Wrong (A) A Code of Conduct and compliance training are cultural inputs — they signal what the organisation says it values. But culture is determined by what the organisation does, not what it documents.(C) NAICOM inspection passes reflect regulatory compliance at a point in time — not the underlying culture that determines how staff behave on every day between inspections.(D) Employee satisfaction surveys measure

A commission clawback mechanism in agent compensation is designed to: Allow NAICOM to reclaim excessive commission paid in breach of the commission guidelines. Incentivise agents to write persistently sold policies by allowing the insurer to reclaim a proportion of first-year commission if the policy lapses early. Reduce the overall agent commission bill by applying a standard deduction to all commission payments. Enable the insurer to transfer commission payments from unproductive agents to agents who exceed their targets. (B) Incentivise agents to write persistently sold policies by allowing the insurer to reclaim a proportion of first-year commission if the policy lapses early. Why (B) is Correct Commission clawback is an incentive design mechanism — its purpose is to align the agent's financial interest with policy persistency. Under a clawback arrangement, if a policy lapses within a defined period (typically 12–24 months), the insurer reclaims a defined proportion of the first-year commission previously paid to the agent. This creates a direct financial consequence for the agent when their policies lapse early — reducing the incentive to sell to customers who cannot sustain the premiums, and encouraging agents to conduct proper suitability assessments and target customers who will maintain their policies. Why the Others Are Wrong (A) NAICOM does not claim commission payments from agents — any NAICOM enforcement action would be against the insurer for market conduct violations, not a direct commission reclaim from agents.(C) A standard deduction from all commission pay

Succession planning for critical roles in a Nigerian life insurer is primarily a responsibility of: The HR department, which maintains the succession register independently. The MD/CEO and the Board, who review succession plans annually for ExCo-level roles, with NIIRA 2025 specifically requiring Board engagement on succession for regulated positions. NAICOM, which prescribes the minimum succession planning requirements for each licensed insurer. The Remuneration Committee, which approves succession-linked retention bonuses. (B) The MD/CEO and the Board, who review succession plans annually for ExCo-level roles, with NIIRA 2025 specifically requiring Board engagement on succession for regulated positions. Why (B) is Correct Succession planning for critical leadership roles — particularly regulated positions (Statutory Actuary, CRO, Compliance Officer) — is explicitly a Board-level governance responsibility under NIIRA 2025. The Board must ensure that: (1) succession plans exist for all regulated positions; (2) potential successors are identified and their development is actively supported; and (3) emergency succession plans are in place for unplanned vacancies. HR maintains the mechanics; the MD/CEO proposes succession candidates; but the Board approves and monitors the succession framework.
