How to Use This Chapter This chapter is the companion examination guide to the main body of this book. It is designed to serve three groups of readers: • Students preparing for CIIN Foundation, Diploma, or Associateship examinations who want to understand how the content of this book maps to the CIIN syllabus. • Practitioners who hold CIIN qualifications and are fulfilling their CPD requirements, seeking a structured development framework. • Employers and training managers designing qualification pathways and study programmes for insurance staff.

t: Chapter 38 · 38.1 Introduction: The CIIN Qualification as Professional Credential and Regulatory Requirement
x: The Chartered Insurance Institute of Nigeria (CIIN) qualification framework is simultaneously a professional credential and a regulatory requirement. Under the Nigerian Insurance Industry Reform Act 2025 (NIIRA 2025), a valid CIIN qualification is required for every individual who sells insurance products in Nigeria (minimum: the Certificate of Proficiency), for key management officers including Heads of Underwriting, Claims, and Financial Planning (minimum: Associateship), and is a strong expectation for senior leadership. The qualification is therefore not optional for a serious insurance career in Nigeria — it is the professional floor. But the CIIN qualification is also more than a compliance requirement. The knowledge embedded in the CIIN examination syllabus — insurance principles, underwriting, claims management, reinsurance, actuarial concepts, distribution, regulation, corporate governance — is the professional knowledge required to do the job well, not merely to satisfy a licensing threshold. A claims manager who understands the principles behind the claims management framework makes better decisions than one who knows only the procedures. An agent who understands why insurers need accurate disclosure makes more credible conversations with prospects than one who simply follows the proposal form prompts. This chapter sets out the complete examination preparation framework: the qualification structure, examination formats, examination technique, the syllabus mapping to this book’s chapters, the highest-frequency examination topics, model answers to representative questions, and the CPD framework that continues professional development after qualification is achieved.

38.2.1 Overview of the Three Levels Level Qualification Title Designatory Letters Primary Purpose Regulatory Significance under NIIRA 2025 Foundation Certificate of Proficiency (Cert. COP) and Certificate in Insurance (Cert. CIIN) Cert. COP / Cert. CIIN Entry-level professional qualification confirming basic insurance knowledge, product understanding, and regulatory awareness. Cert. COP is specifically designed for insurance sales agents; Cert. CIIN is the broader certificate qualification. NIIRA 2025 mandates that every agent selling insurance in Nigeria holds a valid Cert. COP. This is the minimum licensing requirement for insurance distribution. Diploma Diploma in Insurance (Dip. CIIN) Dip. CIIN Intermediate professional qualification covering the technical core of insurance practice: underwriting, claims, reinsurance, distribution, and risk management at a level appropriate for supervisory and specialist roles. Required for individuals progressing toward regulated functional head roles. A strong expectation for agents seeking to move into management, underwriting, or claims assessment roles. Associateship Associate of the Chartered Insurance Institute of Nigeria (ACIIN) ACIIN The primary professional designation in Nigerian insurance. Demonstrates comprehensive mastery of insurance practice across all domains — technical, commercial, regulatory, and governance. Required for Heads of Underwriting, Claims, and Financial Planning under NIIRA 2025. NIIRA 2025 specifies Associateship (or equivalent) as the minimum professional qualification for key functional heads in licensed Nigerian insurers. Fellowship Fellow of the Chartered Insurance Institute of Nigeria (FCIIN) FCIIN The highest CIIN designation, recognising distinguished achievement in the insurance profession. Awarded on completion of the Fellowship examination or by distinction to practitioners of exceptional professional standing. Strongly preferred for MD/CEO and Board-level roles in licensed Nigerian insurers. Marks a practitioner as a leader of the profession, not merely a qualified member. 38.2.2 Progression and Prerequisites The CIIN qualification pathway is sequential: each level builds on the knowledge base of the preceding level. A candidate cannot sit Diploma papers before completing the Foundation level, and cannot sit Associateship papers before completing the Diploma level. This sequential structure ensures that each level’s examination tests not merely the specific syllabus content of that level but the candidate’s ability to integrate prior knowledge with new material. Typical completion timeframes (for a motivated, employed candidate studying part-time): Certificate of Proficiency (Cert. COP): 3–6 months of part-time study; one to two examination sittings. Certificate in Insurance (Cert. CIIN): 6–12 months of part-time study; sequential papers over two to three sittings. Diploma in Insurance (Dip. CIIN): 12–24 months of part-time study following Foundation completion; four to six papers over multiple sittings. Associateship (ACIIN): 24–36 months of part-time study following Diploma completion; four to six advanced papers. Fellowship (FCIIN): Typically 12–18 months of advanced study following Associateship; two to three senior-level papers or special assessment.

t: Chapter 38 · 38.3 Examination Diets, Registration, and Logistics
x: 38.3.1 Examination Sitting Schedule CIIN examinations are conducted in defined ‘diets’ — scheduled sitting periods throughout the year. CIIN typically conducts at least two major examination diets per year, with a possible third for specific papers: May/June Diet The primary mid-year examination sitting. Most papers across all qualification levels are available. Results are typically published 6–8 weeks after the examination date. October/November Diet The primary end-year examination sitting. All papers available. Results published in December or January. This is often the preferred sitting for candidates who began studying in the first half of the year. March Diet (Selected Papers) CIIN sometimes schedules a March sitting for selected Foundation and Diploma papers to provide an additional opportunity for candidates who missed the May/June diet or who are on accelerated pathways. Registration Deadlines and Examination Logistics REGISTRATION DEADLINE: Typically 8–10 weeks before the examination date. Late registration may be permitted with a surcharge, but closes 4 weeks before the sitting. Candidates registering late risk not receiving study materials in time for adequate preparation. EXAMINATION CENTRES: CIIN conducts examinations at approved examination centres in Lagos, Abuja, Port Harcourt, Kano, Enugu, and other state capitals. Candidates select their preferred centre at registration. International centres may be available for diaspora candidates on request. EXAMINATION DAY REQUIREMENTS: Valid government-issued identification (NIN slip, international passport, or national ID card); CIIN candidate number; approved stationery. Electronic devices (including mobile phones and calculators unless specifically permitted) are prohibited. RESULTS AND TRANSCRIPTS: Results are published on the CIIN portal (ciin.org.ng) within the stated result release period. Official transcripts and certificates are issued by the CIIN Examinations department on request. Employers requiring verification of qualifications should request a CIIN verification letter directly from CIIN.

CIIN examinations use three primary question formats across the qualification levels. Understanding the format of each paper — and the specific skills each format tests — is essential to effective preparation. A candidate who prepares comprehensively for the content but does not understand the format of the examination they are sitting will underperform relative to their actual knowledge level. 38.4.1 Multiple Choice Questions (MCQ) MCQ papers are used primarily at the Foundation (Cert. COP and Cert. CIIN) level and for some Diploma papers. Each question presents a stem (the question or incomplete statement) followed by four options (A, B, C, D), of which exactly one is correct. The remaining three options are distractors — plausible but incorrect answers designed to identify candidates with imprecise or incomplete knowledge. How MCQ Distractors Work: An Example Question: The doctrine of utmost good faith (uberrimae fidei) in insurance requires: (A) The insurer to pay all claims within 60 days of notification. (B) Both parties to the insurance contract to disclose all material facts honestly and completely. (C) The policyholder to pay premiums on time without a grace period. (D) The insurer to provide coverage for all risks disclosed at application. Analysis: (B) is correct. (A) describes a regulatory claims settlement requirement, not the uberrimae fidei doctrine. (C) confuses premium payment obligations with the disclosure duty. (D) inverts the doctrine — disclosure does not create an obligation to cover all disclosed risks. All three distractors contain a kernel of insurance truth, making them plausible to a candidate with superficial knowledge. MCQ examination technique: read the stem carefully before reading the options; answer the question in your head before looking at the options to avoid being influenced by plausible distractors; eliminate options you know are wrong before selecting from the remaining options; do not leave any question unanswered (there is no penalty for incorrect answers in most CIIN MCQ formats — confirm this at registration); manage time to complete all questions (allow approximately 1.5 minutes per MCQ question). 38.4.2 Short-Answer and Structured Questions At Diploma level, CIIN papers typically use structured questions requiring written answers of defined length — from one-sentence definitions to multi-paragraph explanations. Structured questions may be subdivided into parts (a), (b), (c) with different command words and mark allocations. The mark allocation for each part should guide the length and depth of the response: a 2-mark question requires a 2-sentence answer; a 10-mark question requires a substantive response across several paragraphs. Structured question technique: read the full question before starting to write; note the mark allocation for each part and apportion your time accordingly; use the command word (define, describe, explain, identify, distinguish) as a guide to the required format; use brief subheadings or clear paragraph breaks to make your structure visible to the examiner; do not write more than the marks justify. 38.4.3 Essay Questions At Associateship level, CIIN papers include extended essay questions requiring a sustained, well-structured analytical response. Essay questions typically use higher-order command words: ‘critically evaluate’, ‘analyse’, ‘assess’, ‘compare and contrast’, ‘to what extent’. These command words signal that the examiner is looking not merely for knowledge recall but for analytical thinking, evidence-based argument, and the ability to take and defend a position. Anatomy of a High-Scoring Associateship Essay Answer INTRODUCTION (10–15% of response): Frame the question in your own words. Define key terms. State the argument or position you will develop. Do not pad the introduction with general statements that add no analytical value. BODY (70–80% of response): Develop the argument in clearly structured paragraphs, each with a clear topic sentence. Use specific examples, regulatory provisions, and data where available to support each point. Address both sides of an evaluative question — an essay that argues only one side of a ‘critically evaluate’ question will score in the middle range even if technically accurate. CONCLUSION (10–15% of response): Summarise the key argument without merely repeating the body’s points. State a clear, evidence-based conclusion. For evaluative questions, state your overall judgement and the principal reasons for it. WHAT MARKS ARE AWARDED FOR: Knowledge and understanding of relevant concepts (typically 40% of marks); analysis and application to the specific question (typically 35%); evaluation, judgement, and conclusion (typically 25%). Candidates who demonstrate knowledge but do not apply it to the specific question consistently score in the 45–55% range, regardless of their technical knowledge level. 38.4.4 Case Study Questions (Associateship) At Associateship level, some papers include case study questions presenting a detailed description of a company, situation, or problem, followed by several related sub-questions that require the candidate to apply their knowledge to the specific case. Case study questions require a different approach from pure essay questions: Read the case carefully before reading the questions, making brief notes on the key facts, issues, and characteristics of the case as you read. Identify the specific facts in the case that are relevant to each sub-question — case study marks are awarded for applying knowledge to the specific case facts, not for describing general principles without reference to the case. Organise your answer to follow the sub-question structure exactly; do not write a single discursive essay that addresses all sub-questions without clearly identifying which part of your answer corresponds to which sub-question. Use the mark allocation to guide the depth of each sub-answer; a 5-mark sub-question within a case study requires a shorter response than a 20-mark sub-question.

The command word is the most important word in any examination question. It tells the candidate exactly what type of response is expected. The most common failure mode in CIIN examinations is to provide the wrong type of response — typically, a descriptive response to an evaluative question, or a general response to a specific application question. The following command word guide should be memorised: Command Word What It Requires Qualification Level Common Mistake Define A precise, concise statement of the meaning of a term. Typically 1–2 sentences maximum. Foundation, Diploma Describing rather than defining. Giving an example instead of a definition. Identify List or name the specified items without extended explanation. Bullet points are appropriate. Foundation, Diploma Writing explanatory paragraphs when a list is sufficient. Identifying fewer items than requested. Describe A detailed account of a concept, process, product, or characteristic. More depth than ‘identify’; full sentences required. Foundation, Diploma, Associateship Listing without description (treating ‘describe’ as ‘identify’). Describing only partially. Explain A clear, logical account of how or why something works, happens, or is significant. Cause-and-effect reasoning is expected. Diploma, Associateship Describing without explaining why. Providing a definition without the logical mechanism. Distinguish Identify the differences (and sometimes similarities) between two or more terms or concepts. Diploma, Associateship Describing each item separately without explicitly stating the difference between them. Analyse Break the topic into its component parts and examine each in detail, exploring the relationships between parts. Associateship Describing without analysing. Failing to examine how components interact. Assess / Evaluate Make a reasoned judgement about the value, importance, effectiveness, or implications of something, based on evidence. Associateship Describing rather than evaluating. Listing points without taking a position. One-sided evaluation. Critically Evaluate As ‘evaluate’, but explicitly requires examination of both supporting and opposing evidence before reaching a balanced, evidence-based conclusion. Associateship Arguing only one side. Failing to reach a clear conclusion. Treating as ‘describe’. Compare and Contrast Identify both similarities and differences between two or more items in a structured way. Diploma, Associateship Addressing only differences and ignoring similarities, or vice versa. Discuss A balanced consideration of multiple aspects or perspectives on a topic, typically arriving at a conclusion. Diploma, Associateship Presenting only one perspective. Listing points without developing them into a discussion. Outline A structured summary without full detail; more than ‘identify’ but less depth than ‘describe’. Foundation, Diploma Writing as much as a ‘describe’ answer (wasting time) or as little as an ‘identify’ list. Recommend / Advise Make and justify a specific course of action based on the facts of the question; your recommendation must be reasoned, not merely stated. Diploma, Associateship Describing options without making a clear recommendation. Recommending without justification.

t: Chapter 38 · 38.7 High-Frequency Examination Topics by Level
x: Based on the structure of the CIIN syllabus and the core knowledge requirements at each level, the following topics appear most frequently in examination papers and carry the highest aggregate mark weight. Candidates should ensure they have deep and reliable knowledge of these topics before turning to lower-frequency areas. 38.7.1 Foundation Level — Highest-Frequency Topics Cert. COP / Cert. CIIN: Must-Know Topics INSURANCE PRINCIPLES: Insurable interest (definition, examples in life insurance); utmost good faith (mutual obligation on both parties); disclosure and non-disclosure (what constitutes a material fact; consequences of non-disclosure); indemnity (why life insurance is not an indemnity contract); the distinction between pure risk and speculative risk. LIFE ASSURANCE PRODUCTS: Term assurance (level, decreasing, convertible, renewable); whole life (participating and non-participating); endowment (savings and protection combination); unit-linked products (investment risk lies with policyholder); group life (employer obligation under PRA 2014, free cover limit, census); annuities (immediate vs. deferred, level vs. escalating). REGULATORY FRAMEWORK: NAICOM’s role and powers under NIIRA 2025; CIIN qualification requirements for agents; the no-premium-no-cover principle; mandatory insurance (group life 3× annual salary under PRA 2014, TPMI); NDPA 2023 data protection basics for insurance. DISTRIBUTION AND AGENCY: The role of the tied agent; the role of the insurance broker (acts for the client, not the insurer); the NIGO (Not In Good Order) application and its consequences; NIIRA 2025 commission guidelines; the persistency rate and its significance. ETHICS AND MARKET CONDUCT: The suitability requirement; mis-selling (definition, consequences, prevention); the duty of confidentiality to policyholders; the treating customers fairly (TCF) principle; AML/KYC obligations for agents. 38.7.2 Diploma Level — Highest-Frequency Topics Advisory: Dip. CIIN: Must-Know Topics UNDERWRITING: The underwriting process for individual and group life; the free cover limit and its actuarial rationale; types of evidence required (medical examination, blood tests, HIV testing thresholds); premium loading and exclusion as alternatives to decline; the reinsurance retention limit and its relationship to underwriting capacity; financial underwriting and over-insurance prevention. CLAIMS MANAGEMENT: The NIIRA 2025 mandatory claims settlement timeline; the claims documentation requirements for death claims, disability claims, and critical illness claims; fraudulent claims indicators and the Special Investigation Unit; the difference between repudiation and contestation; handling competing beneficiary claims. REINSURANCE: Quota share vs. surplus treaty (proportional); excess of loss — risk and catastrophe (non-proportional); the domestic cession requirement under NIIRA 2025; facultative vs. automatic treaty placement; reinsurance commission; the retention limit and its determinants. RISK MANAGEMENT: The Enterprise Risk Management framework; the four insurance risk categories (mortality, morbidity, longevity, lapse); the ORSA and its components; the three lines of defence model; stress testing and scenario analysis. CORPORATE GOVERNANCE: Board composition under NIIRA 2025; Board committee structure (Audit, Risk, Investment, Remuneration); the Delegation of Authority; the three lines of defence; the Statutory Actuary’s role and independence requirement; solvency margin and Risk-Based Capital. 38.7.3 Associateship Level — Highest-Frequency Topics Associateship: Must-Know Topics for Essay and Case Study Questions STRATEGY AND COMPETITIVE DYNAMICS: Porter’s Five Forces applied to the Nigerian insurance market; the Balanced Scorecard framework; the product innovation six-gate process; competitive intelligence methods and ethical limits; embedded value and its components (ANAV, VIF, NBV); profit source analysis (C1–C4). NIIRA 2025 ADVANCED PROVISIONS: The Risk-Based Capital framework; Insurtech licensing (Partnering Insurtech ₦10m; Standalone Insurtech ₦1–1.5bn); the regulatory sandbox; the enhanced consumer protection framework; product approval requirements; market conduct inspection powers. DIGITAL AND INSURTECH: The full-stack vs. partnering Insurtech model distinction; embedded insurance (legal ownership, distribution, claims); parametric insurance trigger design; AI/ML model risk in underwriting; NDPA 2023 compliance for data-driven insurance; the regulatory sandbox testing framework. ALM AND INVESTMENT: Asset-liability matching for long-duration life and annuity business; duration gap management; NAICOM admissible asset framework; investment policy statement governance; the ALCO structure and decision-making process. HUMAN CAPITAL AND ORGANISATION: The three-lines-of-defence model in practice; the Statutory Actuary’s board independence requirement; the CRO’s governance role; performance management KPIs by role; succession planning for regulated roles; CIIN CPD requirements and employer obligations.

t: Chapter 38 · 38.8 Model Answers to Representative Questions
x: The following model answers demonstrate the standard expected at each CIIN level. They are ‘model’ answers in the sense that they represent a high-quality response — not necessarily a perfect maximum-marks answer, which may require more detail. Candidates should study these answers for structure and approach, not to memorise the content verbatim. 38.8.1 Foundation Level — MCQ Analysis Foundation MCQ — Analysis of Correct and Incorrect Options Question: Under the Pension Reform Act 2014, an employer with 10 or more employees must provide group life insurance for each employee at a minimum sum assured of: (A) 2× the employee’s annual basic salary. (B) 3× the employee’s total annual emoluments. (C) ₦5,000,000, regardless of the employee’s salary level. (D) The employee’s total annual emoluments, including all allowances. Correct Answer: (B) Why (B) is correct: Section 4 of the Pension Reform Act 2014 requires a minimum group life benefit of 3× the employee’s total annual emoluments (which is broader than ‘basic salary’ alone, including allowances). This is a mandatory requirement that has been a significant driver of the Nigerian group life market. Why (A) is wrong: 2× is the wrong multiplier, and ‘basic salary’ is the wrong base — the Act specifies total annual emoluments. Why (C) is wrong: The Act does not specify a fixed sum; the benefit is salary-linked. Why (D) is wrong: 1× total annual emoluments is insufficient; the Act requires 3×. 38.8.2 Diploma Level — Structured Question Model Answer Examination Question (Diploma Level, 20 marks) A life insurance company is reviewing its underwriting process for individual life policies. (a) Explain the difference between a standard risk and a substandard risk in life insurance underwriting. (4 marks) (b) Describe three types of evidence an underwriter may request from an applicant presenting a substandard health history. (6 marks) (c) For each of the three evidence types in (b), explain what the evidence reveals to the underwriter that enables an informed acceptance decision. (10 marks) Model Answer (Diploma Level — structured question) (a) Standard risk vs. substandard risk (4 marks): A standard risk is an applicant whose mortality risk profile falls within the normal parameters assumed in the insurer’s standard premium rates. The underwriter accepts the application without loading or exclusion. A substandard risk is one whose mortality risk is higher than standard due to health conditions, occupation, lifestyle, or other factors, and who must be accepted at a higher premium rate (rated), with specific exclusions, or declined. The distinction determines the terms on which the insurer will provide coverage. (b) Three evidence types for substandard health history (6 marks): 1. Confidential Medical Attendant’s Report (CMAR): A report from the applicant’s own doctor providing their medical history, current conditions, treatment, and the doctor’s clinical opinion on the applicant’s health status. 2. Medical Examination: A clinical examination by a NAICOM-approved medical examiner, including blood pressure, height/weight (BMI), urine analysis, and other clinical measurements relevant to the underwriting assessment. 3. Specialist’s Report: A report from a specialist physician (cardiologist, oncologist, neurologist) providing a detailed clinical assessment of the specific condition disclosed, its severity, treatment, prognosis, and expected impact on life expectancy. (c) What each evidence type reveals to the underwriter (10 marks): 1. CMAR: Reveals the complete medical history the applicant’s own doctor has recorded, potentially including conditions not mentioned on the proposal form. The CMAR provides an independent verification of the applicant’s self-reported health history and may reveal treatment records, hospital admissions, or previous diagnoses that contradict the proposal form’s disclosures. It also provides the GP’s clinical opinion on current health status and the likelihood of the condition affecting life expectancy. 2. Medical Examination: Enables the underwriter to assess the applicant’s current physical condition objectively — not through self-report but through clinical measurement. Blood pressure readings indicate cardiovascular risk; BMI reveals obesity-related mortality risk; urine analysis may indicate diabetes or kidney disease. The medical examination catches conditions that the applicant may not know they have or may have failed to disclose. 3. Specialist’s Report: Provides the specific clinical detail required to apply the actuarial mortality tables’ substandard rating tables for the disclosed condition. For example, a cardiologist’s report on an applicant with previous heart disease would quantify the current cardiac function, describe the treatment received, state the prognosis, and enable the underwriter to apply the appropriate extra mortality loading or exclusion to the policy. Without a specialist’s report, the underwriter cannot distinguish between a well-controlled low-risk condition and an uncontrolled high-risk one. 38.8.3 Associateship Level — Essay Question Model Answer Examination Question (Associateship Level, Essay) NIIRA 2025’s introduction of Risk-Based Capital (RBC) represents a fundamental shift in the Nigerian insurance regulatory framework, replacing the traditional fixed-percentage solvency margin approach. Critically evaluate whether RBC is likely to strengthen the long-term financial soundness of Nigerian life insurers, or whether the reform’s benefits will be undermined by the industry’s current implementation capacity constraints. Model Answer (Associateship Level — essay, approximately 45 minutes) INTRODUCTION: The transition from a fixed-percentage solvency margin to Risk-Based Capital (RBC) under NIIRA 2025 represents the most significant change in Nigerian insurance solvency regulation since the recapitalisation exercise of the mid-2000s. Under RBC, an insurer’s minimum capital requirement is linked to its specific risk profile rather than to a fixed percentage of premium income, incentivising better risk management and more efficient capital allocation. This essay evaluates both the theoretical case for RBC’s contribution to financial soundness and the practical implementation challenges that may limit those benefits in the Nigerian context. THE CASE FOR RBC’S STRENGTHENING EFFECT: The theoretical basis for RBC’s superiority over fixed-percentage solvency margins is well-established in insurance regulation globally. Fixed margins treat all insurers identically regardless of their risk profile: an insurer writing conservative long-term endowment policies requires the same regulatory capital percentage as one writing high-sum-assured medical products with significant catastrophe exposure, which is actuarially unsound. RBC addresses this by aligning the capital requirement to the actual risk — insurance risk, market risk, credit risk, operational risk — that each specific insurer carries. In principle, this creates three reinforcing benefits: insurers with well-managed risk profiles face lower capital costs, incentivising better risk management; the industry’s aggregate capital is more efficiently allocated; and systemic risks — concentrations of undercapitalised risk — are more visible to the regulator. IMPLEMENTATION CAPACITY CONSTRAINTS: Against these theoretical benefits must be weighed the implementation realities of the Nigerian market. RBC requires each insurer to develop internal risk models that quantify their specific risk exposures with actuarial precision — a capability that many Nigerian insurers, particularly smaller and mid-size companies, currently lack. The shortage of qualified actuaries in Nigeria is acute: the market requires far more actuarial capability than the IAN and IFoA pipelines are currently supplying. An insurer without a competent actuarial team cannot develop a credible internal risk model, meaning that NAICOM’s standardised RBC formula — rather than an insurer-specific model — will in practice determine the capital requirement for most Nigerian companies. A standardised RBC formula, while better than a fixed percentage, does not capture the risk-specificity that is RBC’s primary advantage. ADDITIONAL CONSTRAINTS: Data quality is a second constraint. RBC models depend on historical loss data, market risk data, and operational risk data to calibrate the risk factors. Many Nigerian insurers have incomplete or unreliable historical data — a legacy of inadequate record-keeping systems and policy lapses that make portfolios difficult to analyse. Without reliable data, even a well-designed RBC model produces unreliable capital requirements. Third, NAICOM’s own supervisory capacity to validate internal models and assess the appropriateness of RBC calculations is still developing; the risk is that RBC compliance becomes a paperwork exercise rather than a genuine reflection of each insurer’s risk position. CONCLUSION: RBC is a structurally superior framework to fixed-percentage solvency margins and, in the long term, is likely to strengthen Nigerian life insurers’ financial soundness. However, the benefits will not be immediate or uniform. Larger insurers with actuarial resources and good data will benefit from more efficient capital allocation relatively quickly. Smaller insurers constrained by the standardised formula, poor data quality, and limited actuarial capability will achieve compliance without achieving the risk-management quality improvement that RBC is designed to drive. The pace at which NIIRA 2025’s RBC provisions strengthen the Nigerian market will therefore depend critically on parallel investments in actuarial talent development, data infrastructure, and NAICOM’s supervisory capacity — none of which are addressed by the regulatory provision itself.

t: Chapter 38 · 38.10 Continuing Professional Development (CPD): Requirements and Recording
x: The CIIN qualification is not the end of professional development — it is its beginning. The CPD framework ensures that qualified insurance professionals maintain and expand their knowledge throughout their active careers in a rapidly changing regulatory, product, and technology environment. CPD compliance is both a professional obligation and, under NIIRA 2025, a regulatory requirement: NAICOM market conduct inspections review CPD compliance records for key staff. 38.10.1 CPD Requirements by Qualification Level ACIIN and FCIIN (Associateship / Fellowship) 30 CPD hours per year. Minimum 15 hours (50%) must be structured CPD from approved activities. Maximum 15 hours may be unstructured CPD (self-directed reading, peer learning, mentoring). Dip. CIIN in active practice 20 CPD hours per year. Minimum 10 hours structured. Maximum 10 hours unstructured. Cert. COP (Active Licensed Agent) Specific CPD hours as determined by CIIN for the annual licence renewal cycle. Confirm current requirements at registration. CPD recording period The CPD year typically runs from 1 January to 31 December. CPD records must be maintained for a minimum of 3 years and must be available for production within 30 days of a CIIN audit request. 38.10.2 Structured CPD: Approved Activity Categories CIIN Annual Conference Attendance at the CIIN Annual Conference and any CIIN-organised seminars, workshops, or webinars. CPD hours are confirmed on the CIIN Certificate of Attendance issued to each participant. Approved External Training Programmes Attendance at training programmes from providers approved by CIIN for CPD purposes. The training must have a defined learning outcome relevant to insurance practice. Classroom and E-Learning Courses Formal insurance or professional skills courses with documented learning objectives and an assessment component. CIIN-accredited online learning platforms are a primary source. CIIN Examination Preparation Structured study for CIIN examinations at a higher level than already held qualifies as structured CPD — it is documented, outcome-focused professional development. Regulator-Organised Events NAICOM, PenCom, NHIA, and CBN-organised industry training events and regulatory briefings relevant to insurance practice. Speaking at Approved Events Delivering a technical presentation at a CIIN event, an NIA committee meeting, or another approved forum qualifies as structured CPD (typically half of the presentation duration). 38.10.3 Recording and Verifying CPD The CPD record is the member’s personal responsibility. The CIIN provides a standard CPD record template (available on the CIIN portal) which each member must complete for each CPD activity: Date, venue, and name of the CPD activity. The learning provider and the CPD category (structured or unstructured). Duration in hours (rounded to the nearest half-hour). A brief statement of the learning outcome — what the member learned or applied as a result of the activity. Documentary evidence reference: the certificate of attendance number, the training provider’s registration, or the programme brochure. Employer CPD Facilitation: Best Practice Employers are not directly responsible for their employees’ CIIN membership or CPD compliance — these are individual professional obligations. However, best-practice employers actively facilitate CPD through: full sponsorship of CIIN examination fees; payment for approved external training programmes; designation of specific time for CIIN Annual Conference attendance; a mandatory internal training calendar that generates structured CPD credit hours; and a quarterly CPD status check conducted by the HR function. An employer whose professional staff consistently fail to meet CPD requirements is an employer that is not investing in professional development. The resulting competence gap is a commercial risk — underqualified staff make poorer underwriting, claims, and advisory decisions — as well as a regulatory risk under NIIRA 2025.

t: Chapter 38 · Quick Reference: Examination Preparation Checklist
x: Pre-Examination Preparation Checklist ☐ Confirmed the examination paper format (MCQ, structured, essay, case study) and total examination time. ☐ Completed all chapters in the study plan relevant to the paper’s syllabus coverage. ☐ Reviewed all high-frequency topics for the relevant examination level (Section 38.7). ☐ Memorised the command word guide (Section 38.5) and practised writing answers to different command words. ☐ Completed at least one full timed mock examination under examination conditions. ☐ Reviewed the Chapter 37 Glossary for all key terms in the relevant examination domain. ☐ Confirmed CIIN registration, examination centre, and candidate number. ☐ Prepared examination day materials: valid ID, candidate number, approved stationery. ☐ For Associateship candidates: prepared and reviewed at least three full essay plans on the highest-frequency topics, covering both sides of the evaluative argument. The Single Most Important Examination Preparation Habit Write. Not read, not highlight, not summarise into notes. Write full answers to past questions under timed conditions, then compare your response to the model answer and identify the specific gaps. A candidate who has read every chapter of this book but has never written a timed examination answer under conditions approximating the real examination will underperform relative to their knowledge level. The examination rewards the ability to retrieve, organise, and apply knowledge under time pressure — a skill that reading develops only partially. Writing develops it fully. — End of Chapter 38 — The final chapter of this work — Chapter 39: Regulatory Reference Index and Bibliography — follows.

t: Chapter 39 · 39.1 Nigerian Insurance Industry Reform Act 2025 (NIIRA 2025)
x: Primary Instrument Details Full Title Nigerian Insurance Industry Reform Act, 2025 Act Number Act No. 2 of 2025 Commencement Signed 6 August 2025. Came into force on assent except where specific provisions set a later commencement date for specific requirements (e.g., transitional capital compliance timelines). Repeals Repeals and replaces the Insurance Act, Cap I17, Laws of the Federation of Nigeria 2004 (originally the Insurance Act 2003). Provisions of the repealed Act inconsistent with NIIRA 2025 are extinguished; regulations and guidelines made under the repealed Act that are not inconsistent remain in force until replaced. Primary Regulator National Insurance Commission (NAICOM) — established under the NAICOM Act 1997, which continues in force, with NIIRA 2025 expanding NAICOM’s powers and mandate. Access Federal Republic of Nigeria Official Gazette; naicom.gov.ng; National Assembly of Nigeria (nassnigeria.gov.ng). NIIRA 2025: Topic-Referenced Section Index The following index maps the principal subject-matter areas of NIIRA 2025 to the parts and sections of the Act most relevant to each topic, with cross-references to the chapters of this book where each topic is discussed in depth. Section numbers are indicative based on the Act’s published structure; practitioners should verify against the official Gazette version. Subject Area Relevant NIIRA 2025 Provisions Cross-Reference (this book) Licensing of insurers and capital requirements Part II and Part IV: Licensing provisions; capital thresholds in s.15: life ₦10 billion, non-life ₦15 billion, reinsurance ₦35 billion (or risk-based capital if higher). The Act provides no composite insurer licence (s.6); Takaful and Insurtech thresholds come from NAICOM regulation. Chapters 21, 24 Risk-Based Capital (RBC) framework Part III: Solvency and capital adequacy. RBC replaces the fixed-percentage minimum solvency margin. Insurers must maintain RBC at or above the NAICOM-prescribed ratio. ORSA required annually. Chapters 15, 24 Product approval Part IV: All new products and material modifications must be submitted to NAICOM for approval before marketing. Grounds for NAICOM to withhold approval; timelines for response. Chapters 10, 21 No-premium-no-cover Part IV: The statutory codification of the principle that coverage does not commence until the first premium is received by the insurer. Chapter 11 Mandatory life insurance Part V: Mandatory group life at a minimum of 3× annual emoluments for employers with qualifying workforce (cross-references PRA 2014). Mandatory credit life for qualifying loans. Chapters 21, 30 Disclosure and policyholder protection Consumer protection provisions: duty of disclosure and the s.65 limits on repudiation, s.17 policy-document delivery and s.209 misleading statements are in the Act; the TCF mandate, complaint rights, cooling-off period and plain-language requirement come from NAICOM regulation and guidelines. Chapters 11, 20, 21 Claims settlement Part VI: Settlement of valid claims within 60 days of notification (s.210), with compound interest for each month of delay and administrative sanctions. [Verify: a 5-business-day acknowledgement period is not confirmed in the Act.] Chapter 12 Intermediaries: agents and brokers Part VI and Part VIII: Licensing of agents (s.37: certificate of proficiency, 10 years’ underwriting experience) and brokers; s.38 agents may not collect premium; s.62 maximum commission rates (group life 9%, single-premium annuity 3%). Chapters 16, 17, 18, 21 Insurtech licensing Part VIII: Two licensing tracks — Partnering Insurtech (₦10 million capital) and Standalone Insurtech (₦1–1.5 billion capital, depending on product class). Regulatory sandbox provisions. Cybersecurity requirements for Insurtech licensees. Chapter 28 Takaful window and standalone Takaful Part IX: Requirements for conventional insurers to establish Takaful windows; separate fund maintenance; Shari’ah Supervisory Board requirement; standalone Takaful licensing. Chapter 29 Reinsurance and domestic cession Part X: Obligation to offer a defined proportion of reinsurance to domestic reinsurers before international placement. Life and non-life domestic cession percentages. NAICOM approval for international facultative placements above threshold. Chapter 14 Corporate governance Part XI: Board composition (minimum 5 directors, NED majority, minimum 2 independent directors, Chair/CEO separation). Fit and proper requirements. Board committees. Statutory Actuary independence. Three lines of defence. Chapters 24, 34 Investment and ALM Part XII: NAICOM admissible asset framework. Restrictions on connected-party investments. ALM requirements for long-duration life and annuity business. Investment Policy Statement approval. Chapter 23 AML/CFT obligations Part XIII: Insurance sector AML/CFT obligations; KYC requirements; suspicious activity reporting to the Financial Intelligence Unit; MLPPA 2022 compliance. Chapter 21 Data protection Part XIV: Insurers as data controllers under NDPA 2023. Obligations consistent with the Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023 and GAID 2025. Data breach notification. Policyholder data rights. Chapters 21, 28 NAICOM enforcement powers Part XV: NAICOM powers to inspect, investigate, impose administrative fines, suspend or revoke licences, appoint receivers, and disqualify directors. Market conduct inspection framework. Whistleblower protection. Chapter 21 Dispute resolution Part XVI: Internal dispute resolution requirements. NAICOM Consumer Protection Bureau complaint handling. Insurance Ombudsman framework. Escalation to courts. Chapters 20, 21 Transitional provisions Part XVII: Transitional timelines for recapitalisation compliance, agent qualification under Cert. COP, and other provisions requiring lead time for implementation. Chapters 21, 24, 35

Full Title NAICOM Guidelines for Technology-Driven Insurance Operations in Nigeria (Insurtech Guidelines), 2025 Effective Date 1 August 2025 (preceding the formal commencement of NIIRA 2025 by days, co-ordinated for simultaneous practical effect). Legal Status Subsidiary regulation issued by NAICOM under powers conferred by NIIRA 2025. Legally binding on all licensed insurers and Insurtech licensees. Scope Applies to: (1) Licensed insurers operating digital insurance platforms or partnering with technology companies; (2) Partnering Insurtech licensees (₦10m capital); (3) Standalone Insurtech licensees (₦1–1.5bn capital depending on product class); (4) Companies seeking regulatory sandbox admission. Access naicom.gov.ng (regulatory circulars and guidelines section). Guideline Topic Key Provisions Cross-Reference Partnering Insurtech licensing Minimum capital: ₦10 million (NAICOM Insurtech guidelines; not in the Act). Partnering Insurtechs must partner with a fully licensed insurer that retains the insurance risk. The Insurtech performs distribution, technology, or processing functions only. Cannot assume underwriting risk on own account. Chapter 28 Standalone Insurtech licensing Minimum capital: ₦1 billion to ₦1.5 billion (NAICOM Insurtech guidelines; not in the Act). May hold the insurance licence and assume risk on own account. Subject to all NIIRA 2025 capital, solvency, governance, and product approval requirements that apply to conventional licensed insurers. Chapter 28 Regulatory sandbox admission Applications for sandbox admission: purpose, scope, timeline (maximum 24 months), consumer protection safeguards required, reporting obligations during sandbox period, exit pathway to full licensing. Chapter 28 Cybersecurity requirements All Insurtech and digital insurance operations must implement: encryption standards for policyholder data; multi-factor authentication; penetration testing (minimum annual); incident response plan; data breach notification to NAICOM and affected policyholders within 72 hours. Chapters 21, 28 Impermissible activities Insurtechs may not: make binding underwriting decisions without licensed insurer involvement; pay claims directly from operating accounts (claims funds must be segregated); conduct unsolicited direct marketing without valid consent under NDPA 2023; apply algorithmic pricing based on protected characteristics. Chapter 28 AI/ML model governance AI and ML models used in underwriting, pricing, or claims must be: documented (model development, training data, validation); validated by a qualified actuary or risk professional before deployment; monitored for drift and bias on a defined schedule; approved for use in regulated functions by NAICOM on request. Chapter 28 Embedded insurance provisions The licensed insurer (not the embedding partner) is responsible for product approval, claims obligations, and policyholder communication. Embedding agreements must be disclosed to NAICOM. Policyholders must receive clear disclosure of the insurer’s identity. Chapters 16, 28 USSD and mobile insurance USSD-based and mobile-distributed insurance products must comply with product approval requirements. Premium collection through mobile money platforms requires documented reconciliation controls. Chapter 28

t: Chapter 39 · 39.3 Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023 (NDPA 2023) and GAID 2025
x: NDPA 2023 Full Title Nigeria Data Protection Act, 2023 NDPA 2023 Assent Date Signed 12 June 2023 by President Bola Tinubu. Regulatory Body Nigeria Data Protection Commission (NDPC) — established by the Act as the independent data protection authority. Insurance Relevance Licensed insurers are expressly classified as ‘Data Controllers and Data Processors of Major Importance’ due to the volume and sensitivity of personal health, financial, and biometric data they process. GAID 2025 Full Title General Application and Implementation Directive 2025 (GAID) — the primary implementation directive under the NDPA 2023. GAID 2025 Effective Date 19 September 2025. Access ndpc.gov.ng; Federal Republic of Nigeria Official Gazette. NDPA 2023 / GAID 2025 Provision Insurance-Specific Application Cross-Reference Lawful basis for processing (NDPA 2023 s.25) Insurers must identify a lawful basis for each category of personal data processed: contract necessity (policy administration); legal obligation (AML/KYC); legitimate interest (fraud prevention); consent (marketing communications). Consent must be specific, informed, freely given, and revocable. Chapters 21, 28 Special categories of data (NDPA 2023 s.30) Health data collected for underwriting and claims purposes is a ‘special category’ requiring heightened protection. Must be processed under explicit consent or another specific permitted ground. Strict access controls required. Chapters 11, 12, 28 Data subject rights (NDPA 2023 Part IV) Policyholders have rights to: access their personal data; correct inaccurate data; erasure (‘right to be forgotten’ — subject to legal retention requirements); portability; restriction of processing; objection to direct marketing. Insurers must have documented processes for responding to data subject requests within 30 days. Chapters 20, 21 Data breach notification (NDPA 2023 s.40) Insurers must notify the NDPC within 72 hours of becoming aware of a personal data breach likely to result in risk to data subjects. Notification to affected data subjects required where the breach creates high risk to their rights and freedoms. Chapters 21, 28 Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA) (GAID 2025) Insurers must conduct DPIAs before implementing new high-risk processing activities — specifically including: AI/ML underwriting models; biometric data processing; large-scale health data processing; data sharing with third parties outside Nigeria. Chapter 28 Data localisation (GAID 2025) Personal data of Nigerian data subjects must be stored on servers located in Nigeria (primary storage) unless the Data Commissioner grants an exemption or the transfer is subject to appropriate safeguards. Chapters 21, 28 Retention and disposal (GAID 2025) Insurers must not retain personal data longer than necessary for the purpose for which it was collected. Minimum retention periods for insurance data are specified in GAID 2025 (claims records: minimum 10 years; policy records: 7 years after policy expiry). Chapters 21, 28 Compliance as Data Controller of Major Importance (NDPA 2023) Annual NDPC filing; mandatory appointment of a Data Protection Officer (DPO); mandatory Data Protection Compliance Programme (DPCP) reviewed and submitted to the NDPC; mandatory audit every 2 years. Chapters 21, 34

Full Title Pension Reform Act, 2014 (Cap P4, LFN) Primary Regulator National Pension Commission (PenCom) — pencom.gov.ng Principal Interaction with Life Insurance The PRA 2014 creates the insurance industry’s two most significant mandatory product markets: (1) mandatory group life insurance for employers; and (2) the Retirement Life Annuity (RLA) as one of two CPS decumulation options. The PRA 2014 is therefore the single most important piece of external legislation for life insurance practitioners after NIIRA 2025 itself. Access pencom.gov.ng; National Assembly of Nigeria (nassnigeria.gov.ng). PRA 2014 Provision Key Content Cross-Reference Section 4: Mandatory Group Life Insurance Every employer with 3 or more employees must maintain a minimum group life insurance policy providing a death benefit of not less than 3× the total annual emoluments of each employee. Failure to maintain the group life policy is an offence. The policy must be maintained with a NAICOM-licensed insurer. Chapter 30 Section 7–8: Contributory Pension Scheme (CPS) The mandatory defined-contribution pension system for employees in organisations with 3 or more staff. Employer contribution: minimum 10% of monthly emoluments. Employee contribution: minimum 8%. Contributions must be remitted to the employee’s Retirement Savings Account (RSA) managed by a licensed PFA within 7 working days of salary payment. Chapter 33 Section 12–15: Retirement Savings Account (RSA) Each CPS participant has an individual RSA managed by a PFA of their choice. The RSA is portable across employers. PFAs must provide RSA statements at least quarterly. PFAs invest RSA funds in NAICOM/PenCom-approved asset classes. Chapters 31, 33 Section 16: Retirement Benefits On retirement (or reaching 50 years with reduced capacity), an RSA holder may: (1) withdraw up to 25% of the RSA balance as a lump sum; (2) use the balance to purchase a Retirement Life Annuity from a NAICOM-licensed life insurer; or (3) elect Programmed Withdrawal administered by the PFA. Chapters 31, 33 Section 17: Retirement Life Annuity (RLA) An RLA must provide: a guaranteed lifetime income; an option for joint life coverage for a surviving spouse; inflation protection option. The RLA insurer is required to meet NAICOM’s solvency margin requirements. PenCom and NAICOM jointly regulate the RLA market. Chapter 31 Sections 72–74: Death Benefits On death of an RSA holder before retirement: the accumulated RSA balance is payable to the designated beneficiaries. If the employer’s group life insurance has been maintained, the group life death benefit is paid separately and is in addition to the RSA balance. Chapters 25, 30, 33 Section 86: Penalties Failure by an employer to: deduct and remit employee contributions; maintain mandatory group life; or enrol employees in the CPS — exposes the employer to criminal prosecution, fines, and civil liability for any resulting loss to the employee. Chapters 30, 33 Voluntary Contributions (VCs) CPS members may make additional voluntary contributions to their RSA above the mandatory minimum. VCs are tax-deductible under PITA (Personal Income Tax Act). Insurers offering PPP products may position them as complementary to the VC mechanism. Chapters 25, 33

t: Chapter 39 · 39.5 Other Principal Legislative and Regulatory Instruments
x: 39.5.1 NAICOM Act 1997 (Cap N53, LFN) The NAICOM Act establishes the National Insurance Commission as Nigeria’s apex insurance regulator and sets out its constitution, powers, and functions. Key provisions: NAICOM’s corporate status and governance; the Commissioner for Insurance and the NAICOM Board; NAICOM’s powers of inspection, investigation, and enforcement; the NAICOM Establishment Fund; appeals from NAICOM decisions. The NAICOM Act is read together with NIIRA 2025, which expands NAICOM’s regulatory mandate without replacing the NAICOM Act. 39.5.2 CIIN Act 1993 (Cap C10, LFN) The Chartered Insurance Institute of Nigeria Act establishes CIIN as the professional body for insurance in Nigeria. Key provisions: CIIN’s corporate status; the CIIN Council and its composition; the CIIN’s examination, membership, and disciplinary functions; the power to award qualifications and confer membership grades; the CIIN’s role in setting professional standards for the Nigerian insurance market. NIIRA 2025 cross-references CIIN qualifications as the minimum professional standard for regulated insurance roles. 39.5.3 National Health Insurance Authority Act 2022 (NHIA Act) Commencement Signed 19 May 2022. Repeals and replaces the National Health Insurance Scheme (NHIS) Act 1999. Principal Regulator National Health Insurance Authority (NHIA) — nhia.gov.ng Insurance relevance Establishes the legal framework for universal health coverage in Nigeria; licences and regulates Health Maintenance Organisations (HMOs); sets standards for benefit packages, provider contracting, and claims management in the health insurance market. Key provisions for life insurers Sections 9–15: HMO licensing requirements and conditions. Sections 26–30: Minimum benefit standards and claims processing obligations. Section 41: The NHIA’s enforcement powers including licence suspension and revocation. Section 48: The mandatory health insurance initiative for States, applying the universal health coverage mandate. 39.5.4 Cybercrimes (Prohibition, Prevention, Etc.) Act 2015 (as amended 2024) Commencement 2015 (as amended by the Cybercrimes Act (Amendment) Act 2024). Insurance relevance Criminalises unauthorised access to computer systems (relevant to cyber intrusions targeting insurer policy and claims databases); electronic fraud (relevant to digital insurance fraud, false online claims, identity theft); cyberstalking and harassment (relevant to digital insurance distribution); phishing and social engineering (relevant to insurer customer data protection). Key sections for insurers Section 6: Unlawful access to computer systems — criminalises any access without authorisation to an insurer’s PAS or customer database. Section 14: Identity theft and impersonation using computer systems — relevant to synthetic identity fraud in digital insurance. Section 22: Electronic fraud — covers false online insurance claims. Section 38: The Cybercrimes Advisory Council’s role in national cybersecurity coordination. Interaction with NIIRA 2025 and NDPA 2023 The Cybercrimes Act provides the criminal law overlay for cybersecurity incidents that are separately regulated by NIIRA 2025 (operational risk requirements), the NAICOM Insurtech Guidelines (cybersecurity standards), and the NDPA 2023 (breach notification obligations). 39.5.5 Companies and Allied Matters Act 2020 (CAMA 2020) CAMA 2020 is the primary Nigerian corporate law, applying to all registered companies including life insurers. Key provisions for life insurers: the obligation to maintain company registers (directors, members, charges); directors’ duties (fiduciary, care, skill); the annual general meeting and shareholder rights; requirements for company secretarial compliance; the insolvency and winding-up regime applicable when NAICOM has revoked a licence; the statutory merger and acquisition framework applicable to insurance company consolidations. 39.5.6 Money Laundering (Prevention and Prohibition) Act 2022 (MLPPA 2022) The MLPPA 2022 is the primary AML/CFT legislation applicable to financial institutions including insurers. Key provisions: the duty to conduct customer due diligence (CDD) and enhanced due diligence (EDD) for high-risk customers; the obligation to monitor transactions and report suspicious activities to the Nigerian Financial Intelligence Unit (NFIU); record-keeping obligations (minimum 5 years); the penalties for failure to comply (fines, deregistration, criminal prosecution of directors). NIIRA 2025 cross-references the MLPPA 2022 for all AML/CFT obligations applicable to licensed insurers. 39.5.7 Personal Income Tax Act (PITA) — Selected Insurance Provisions Insurance premium deductibility Life insurance premiums paid by individuals for their own life insurance policies are deductible for PITA purposes up to statutory limits. Employer-paid group life premiums are deductible business expenses. Voluntary pension contributions Voluntary contributions to an RSA under the PRA 2014 are fully tax-deductible under PITA, creating a significant tax incentive for the PPP and VC market. Life assurance benefit taxation Death benefits under a life assurance policy are generally not taxable income in the hands of the beneficiary. Maturity benefits and surrender values from endowment and savings-linked policies may be subject to tax on the gains element — practitioners should advise clients to seek tax advice. Critical illness benefits Lump sum critical illness benefits are generally regarded as capital receipts and not subject to income tax.

t: Chapter 39 · 39.6 Selected NAICOM Circulars and Regulatory Guidance (2020–2025)

Includes the Partnering and Standalone Insurtech licensing tracks, sandbox provisions, cybersecurity requirements, and AI/ML governance. Chapter 28 NAICOM/DPR/GUID/No.XX/2025: Product Filing Guidelines Life insurance product approval Standardised format and content requirements for life insurance product filings. Actuarial pricing certificate requirements. Policyholder benefit illustrations. Plain language policy wording requirements. The statutory rule is NIIRA 2025 s.210 (60 days from notification; compound interest for delay). The 5-business-day acknowledgement is unverified. Chapter 12 NAICOM/DPR/CIR/No.XX/2025: Recapitalisation Directive Minimum capital compliance timeline Phased timeline for compliance with the NIIRA 2025 minimum capital requirements by class. Acceptable routes to recapitalisation (fresh capital injection, merger, acquisition). Consequences of failure to meet timeline milestones. Chapters 24, 34 NAICOM/DPR/CIR/No.XX/2024: Market Conduct Framework Consumer protection and TCF The market conduct inspection framework implementing the TCF principle. Inspection criteria. Market conduct reporting requirements. Consumer complaint handling standards. Chapters 20, 21 NAICOM/DPR/CIR/No.XX/2023: Microinsurance Framework (Revised) Microinsurance regulation Revised regulatory framework for microinsurance products and distribution, including mobile and USSD channels, cooperative society distribution, and simplified underwriting for low-income products. Chapter 22 NAICOM/DPR/GUID/No.XX/2022: RLA Market Guidelines Retirement Life Annuity market Guidelines for life insurers in the RLA market: solvency requirements for annuity writers; mortality assumptions; policyholder information requirements; joint operation with PenCom for RSA-to-RLA conversion. The circular numbers in this section are indicative references to the subject matter; specific circular numbers change each year. Practitioners must access the current and full text of each circular from the NAICOM Circular Register at naicom.gov.ng, which is the authoritative source. This book’s regulatory content is current as of the date of publication; subsequent NAICOM guidance may modify, supplement, or supersede the provisions described.

t: Chapter 39 · 39.7 Selected Nigerian Judicial Decisions on Insurance Contracts
x: Nigerian courts have developed a body of case law interpreting insurance contracts that is essential background for insurance practitioners. The following selected decisions address the principal legal issues arising in insurance practice: the duty of disclosure, insurable interest, claims settlement, exclusion clauses, and the interpretation of policy terms. Cases are cited in the standard Nigerian citation format: [Year] NWLR Part Page or (Year) FWLR Part Page. 39.7.1 Utmost Good Faith and Disclosure Case Name Citation Legal Principle Significance for Practitioners Adesanya v. Royal Exchange Assurance Nigeria Ltd (1986) 3 NWLR (Pt.27) 171 CA The duty of utmost good faith requires the proposer to disclose all material facts, whether asked or not. Non-disclosure of a material fact entitles the insurer to avoid the policy. Establishes the breadth of the disclosure obligation in Nigeria: it is not limited to answering the proposal form’s specific questions but extends to any information a prudent insurer would consider material. African Continental Bank Ltd v. Nigerian General Insurance Co. Ltd (1997) 9 NWLR (Pt.522) 626 CA A misrepresentation in a proposal form, even if innocent, entitles the insurer to avoid the policy if it relates to a material fact. Confirms that the materiality test is objective (would a prudent insurer consider it material?) not subjective (did the proposer consider it important?). Okonkwo v. Nigerian Reinsurance Corporation (2002) 3 NWLR (Pt.754) 468 CA The insurer bears the burden of proving that the undisclosed fact was material and that the non-disclosure induced the making of the contract. Important for claims disputes: the insurer cannot invoke non-disclosure as a defence without demonstrating materiality and inducement. 39.7.2 Insurable Interest Case Name Citation Legal Principle Significance Nigerian Agricultural and Co-operative Bank Ltd v. NICON Insurance Corporation (2000) 6 NWLR (Pt.659) 116 A creditor has an insurable interest in the life of a debtor to the extent of the outstanding debt. Establishes the basis for credit life insurance in Nigerian law: the lender’s insurable interest is limited to the outstanding loan balance, not the full life of the borrower. Chief Omonuwa v. Insurance Company of Nigeria Ltd (1983) 1 SCNLR 1 SC A spouse has an insurable interest in the life of the other spouse. The interest is unlimited in both directions. Foundation case for spousal life insurance in Nigeria. Confirms that husband and wife each have unlimited insurable interest in the other’s life. 39.7.3 Claims Settlement and Policy Interpretation Case Name Citation Legal Principle Significance Leadway Assurance Company Ltd v. Zeco (Nig.) Ltd (2005) 12 NWLR (Pt.938) 1 CA Insurance policies must be read as a whole. Ambiguous terms are construed against the insurer (contra proferentem rule). Affirms the contra proferentem doctrine in Nigerian insurance law: where a policy term is ambiguous, the interpretation least favourable to the insurer (who drafted the document) prevails. IGI Plc v. Kalu Industries Ltd (2012) 16 NWLR (Pt.1326) 411 CA An insurer cannot reject a valid claim on technical grounds unrelated to the substance of the loss. A purported rejection without valid legal basis amounts to wrongful repudiation entitling the insured to damages. Critical for claims management: the case establishes that insurers must have substantive legal grounds for repudiation; technical defences unrelated to the merits of the claim do not justify non-payment. NEM Insurance Company (Nig.) Ltd v. Aderibigbe (2011) 3 NWLR (Pt.1234) 215 CA Notice of claim must be given within the period specified in the policy. Failure to give timely notice may bar recovery where the insurer can demonstrate prejudice from the delay. Establishes the standard for late claim notification: mere delay is not sufficient to bar a claim; the insurer must show that the delay prejudiced its ability to investigate or manage the loss. AIICO Insurance Plc v. Benson (2014) 10 NWLR (Pt.1416) 564 CA A beneficiary designation in a life insurance policy overrides inconsistent instructions in the policyholder’s will. Confirms the primacy of the policy nomination over testamentary disposition for life insurance benefits — critical for financial planning advice and estate planning. FBN Insurance Ltd v. Egbu (2019) 14 NWLR (Pt.1694) 392 CA An insurer that delays settlement of a valid claim beyond the contractual period is liable for the principal sum plus interest at the court’s discretion from the date the claim became due. Post-NIIRA 2025, the 60-day mandatory settlement period supplements this case: an insurer that fails to settle within 60 days faces both NAICOM enforcement and potential court-ordered interest.

About This Work Life Insurance in Nigeria: A Professional Body of Knowledge is the most comprehensive reference work on Nigerian life insurance practice ever compiled. It was developed by MTDL Limited to meet a specific and longstanding gap in the Nigerian insurance professional’s library: a single, authoritative, up-to-date reference that integrates the theory of insurance, the practice of Nigerian life insurance operations, the full requirements of the post-NIIRA 2025 regulatory framework, and the practical professional knowledge expected of candidates at every level of the Chartered Insurance Institute of Nigeria’s qualification pathway. This work is not a study guide in the conventional sense. It does not summarise content for the purpose of passing examinations. It is a professional body of knowledge in the truest sense: the accumulated, structured knowledge that a well-rounded Nigerian life insurance professional should possess — from the foundations of insurance law and the principles of underwriting, through the full range of life insurance products, the complete operational and governance framework of a licensed Nigerian life insurer, and the technology, data, and emerging risk dimensions that will define the industry’s next decade. The work is structured across eight parts and thirty-nine chapters. Its regulatory content is anchored in the Nigerian Insurance Industry Reform Act 2025 (NIIRA 2025), the most comprehensive reform of the Nigerian insurance regulatory framework in more than two decades. All chapters have been updated to reflect NIIRA 2025 in full, including its capital adequacy requirements, consumer protection obligations, Insurtech licensing framework, and Takaful provisions. The data privacy chapters are aligned to the Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023 (NDPA 2023) and the General Application and Implementation Directive 2025 (GAID 2025). The pension interface chapters are aligned to the Pension Reform Act 2014 and PenCom’s RLA market guidelines. Three appendix sets provide reference tools designed for daily professional use: technical reference tables (including an illustrative EFU mortality table extract, NIIRA 2025 capital thresholds, and the CIIN qualification framework); specimen insurance documents annotated for educational purposes; and a comprehensive regulatory instruments log covering NAICOM circulars from 2020 to 2025, the NIIRA 2025 commencement tracker, the recapitalisation compliance timeline, the NDPC enforcement log, and the PenCom-NAICOM interface instruments. Each chapter opens with learning objectives mapped to the examination competency level, and closes with practice questions graded at Foundation, Diploma, and Associateship level. The regulatory chapters (particularly Chapters 4, 21, 24, 28–33) provide the most comprehensive available treatment of the post-NIIRA 2025 regulatory environment for Nigerian life insurers. The technology chapters (29–32) provide the framework for assessing and improving the insurer’s technology capability. The appendix sets provide working tools — the regulatory instruments log, specimen documents, and technical tables — for immediate professional use. Chapter 5 introduces life assurance concepts and terminology; Chapter 6 covers the complete product spectrum (term, whole life, endowment, unit-linked); Chapter 7 group life insurance; Chapter 8 annuities and retirement income products; Chapter 9 Takaful and Islamic insurance in Nigeria; and Chapter 10 life insurance product development and pricing. Part Four: Distribution, Marketing, and Customer Management (Chapters 16–22) The complete distribution and customer management framework. t: Appendix 1 — Technical Reference Tables · Table 1A: EFU Nigerian Life Mortality Table — Illustrative Extract
x: Important: Illustrative Extract Only The EFU (Experience Follows Up) Nigerian Life Tables are based on the mortality experience of Nigerian insured lives, compiled and published periodically by NAICOM in collaboration with the Institute of Actuaries of Nigeria (IAN). The qx values in this appendix are a representative illustrative extract showing the structure and format of the EFU life table. For actual product pricing, reserving, actuarial investigations, and regulatory filings, practitioners must use the current officially endorsed EFU table. Access the current endorsed version from: NAICOM (naicom.gov.ng — actuarial resources section); the Institute of Actuaries of Nigeria (IAN); or through your company’s Statutory Actuary. Do not use this illustrative extract for any live actuarial calculation. The EFU Nigerian Life Table expresses mortality as a probability: qx is the probability that a life aged exactly x will die before reaching age x+1. The complement (px = 1 – qx) is the probability of surviving the year. The lx column shows the number of survivors from a notional cohort of 100,000 lives at age 0; dx shows deaths at each age. The êx column shows the curtate expectation of life — the expected number of complete future years of life remaining. Key concepts for reading the table: qx: Mortality rate at age x. Increases with age. Nigerian insured lives show lower qx than the general population at most ages due to the insurance selection effect. 1,000qx: The mortality rate expressed per 1,000 lives — the more intuitive form used in comparative analysis (e.g., ‘2.3 per 1,000’ at age 30). lx: Number alive at exact age x from a radix of 100,000 (l0 = 100,000). Obtained by l(x+1) = lx × (1 – qx). dx: Deaths in the year of age x to x+1. dx = lx × qx. The total of all dx values equals 100,000 (the radix). êx: Curtate life expectancy at age x — expected number of complete future years. A 35-year-old with ê35 = 38.2 is expected to live, on average, 38 more complete years (to approximately age 73). t: Appendix 1 — Technical Reference Tables · Table 1B: NIIRA 2025 Minimum Paid-Up Capital Thresholds
x: Legislative authority Nigerian Insurance Industry Reform Act 2025 (Act No. 2, 2025), Part II. Regulatory instrument NAICOM Recapitalisation Directive (implementing circular) specifies the phased compliance timeline for existing licensees. Definition of ‘minimum paid-up capital’ The fully paid and non-encumbered share capital that a licensee must maintain at all times. Unpaid subscription, share application money not yet allotted, and deferred shares do not qualify. Verification NAICOM confirms capital adequacy through the annual statutory return. Capital must be maintained continuously, not merely at a single point-in-time measurement. Currency All thresholds are denominated in Nigerian Naira (₦). Thresholds apply to the principal licence; subsidiary licences may have additional requirements. Licence Class NIIRA 2025 Minimum Paid-Up Capital Applicability Key Conditions Life Insurance ₦10,000,000,000 (Ten Billion Naira) Companies carrying on life assurance business only. Must maintain an actuarial reserve equal to or greater than 100% of the minimum capital. Solvency margin (assets over liabilities) must meet the RBC ratio prescribed by NAICOM. General (Non-Life) Insurance ₦5,000,000,000 (Five Billion Naira) Companies carrying on general (non-life) insurance business only. Must maintain a solvency margin based on the greater of: the prescribed minimum; 20% of net earned premium; or the RBC formula output. Composite Insurance ₦18,000,000,000 (Eighteen Billion Naira) Companies carrying on both life and general insurance under a composite licence. NIIRA 2025 requires composite licensees to maintain clearly ring-fenced life and non-life funds. Life and non-life funds must be separately maintained and reported. The combined minimum capital reflects the aggregate of life and general thresholds plus a composite premium. Reinsurance (Life) ₦20,000,000,000 (Twenty Billion Naira) Companies accepting life reinsurance cessions from primary life insurers. Must comply with the domestic cession framework: capacity must be sufficient to absorb domestic cedants’ retention requirements. Reinsurance (General) ₦15,000,000,000 (Fifteen Billion Naira) Companies accepting general (non-life) reinsurance cessions. Continental Reinsurance and NRC are the primary domestic reinsurers. Foreign reinsurers are not required to hold capital in Nigeria but must be approved by NAICOM for domestic cessions. Takaful (Standalone) ₦5,000,000,000 (Five Billion Naira) Companies operating a standalone (full) Takaful business (family and/or general Takaful). Must maintain a Shari’ah-compliant capital structure; Participants’ Risk Account (PRA) and shareholders’ funds must be clearly segregated. SSB required. Takaful Window (within conventional insurer) ₦3,000,000,000 (Three Billion Naira) Conventional insurers establishing a ring-fenced Takaful window within their existing licence. The Takaful window must maintain a separate fund structure (PRA) independently of the conventional fund. A Shari’ah Supervisory Board must be appointed. Partnering Insurtech ₦10,000,000 (Ten Million Naira) Technology companies distributing or processing insurance on behalf of a licensed insurer but not assuming insurance risk. Cannot underwrite risks on own account. Must operate under a formal partnership agreement with a fully licensed insurer. Subject to NAICOM Insurtech Guidelines 2025. Standalone Insurtech (Life) ₦1,000,000,000 (One Billion Naira) Technology companies holding a full insurance licence and assuming life insurance risk on own account through digital channels. Subject to all NIIRA 2025 requirements applicable to conventional life insurers, plus additional Insurtech Guidelines requirements (cybersecurity, sandbox pathway, AI/ML governance). Standalone Insurtech (General) ₦1,500,000,000 (One Billion Five Hundred Million Naira) Technology companies holding a full general insurance licence and assuming risk on own account. Higher capital than life Standalone Insurtech reflects the typically shorter-tail and higher-frequency general insurance risk profile. Microinsurance (Standalone) ₦400,000,000 (Four Hundred Million Naira) Companies specifically licensed to write microinsurance products to low-income policyholders through community, mobile, and cooperative channels. Restricted to products meeting NAICOM’s microinsurance product parameters (simplified terms, low premium, low sum assured). Cannot write conventional insurance without an additional licence. Insurance Broker ₦500,000,000 (Five Hundred Million Naira) plus Professional Indemnity Insurance minimum as prescribed by NAICOM. Companies acting as brokers placing insurance on behalf of clients. Must maintain PI insurance coverage as prescribed. Broker capital is in addition to, not in lieu of, the PI insurance requirement. Insurance Agent (Corporate) ₦10,000,000 (Ten Million Naira) for corporate agents; individual agents do not have a capital requirement but must hold CIIN Cert. COP. Corporate entities appointed to distribute insurance products on behalf of licensed insurers. Corporate agents are not licensed to assume insurance risk. Bancassurance partners are corporate agents of the licenced insurer. Loss Adjuster ₦20,000,000 (Twenty Million Naira) plus Professional Indemnity Insurance. Professional firms appointed to assess and report on insurance claims. PI insurance must be maintained at a minimum indemnity limit prescribed by NAICOM and renewed annually. Transitional Note: Existing licensed companies that do not meet the NIIRA 2025 minimum capital thresholds at commencement have a phased compliance timeline set out in the NAICOM Recapitalisation Directive. Companies that fail to meet interim milestones are subject to NAICOM enforcement action including restrictions on new business, licence suspension, and ultimately licence revocation.
