t: Appendix 1 — Technical Reference Tables · Table 1D: NAICOM Approved Investment Classes and Portfolio Limits
x: Authority NIIRA 2025 Part XII; NAICOM Investment Guidelines (subsidiary regulation). Life and general insurance funds are subject to different limit frameworks. Purpose of investment limits Ensure that insurance funds are invested in assets that are: (1) sufficiently liquid to meet claims obligations; (2) sufficiently diversified to avoid concentration risk; (3) of sufficient credit quality to protect policyholder obligations; and (4) denominated to match policy liabilities. Application Limits apply separately to: (a) the Life Fund (all assets backing life policy reserves); (b) the General Fund (assets backing general insurance reserves); and (c) the Shareholders’ Fund (assets held for shareholders’ account above the technical provisions). Takaful window funds are subject to Shari’ah-compliant investment limits. Admissibility principle Only admissible assets count toward the solvency margin calculation. An asset may be held in the portfolio but excluded from the solvency calculation if it fails the admissibility test (e.g., unlisted shares, connected-party loans, impaired assets). Verification Verify current limits against the most recently published NAICOM Investment Guidelines at naicom.gov.ng. Limits may be updated by NAICOM circular without amendment to NIIRA 2025 itself. Asset Class Description Life Fund Max Limit General Fund Max Limit Admissible for Solvency? Notes Federal Government of Nigeria (FGN) Securities FGN bonds, Treasury bills, FGN Sukuk. Issued by the Debt Management Office (DMO) and traded on FMDQ. No upper limit (unlimited) No upper limit (unlimited) Yes — fully admissible The primary insurance investment asset class in Nigeria. Zero credit risk (sovereign). FGN Sukuk is Shari’ah-compliant for Takaful funds. State Government Securities Bonds issued by state governments and FCT. 20% of Life Fund 15% of General Fund Yes — admissible within limits Credit quality varies across states. NAICOM requires investment-grade state bonds only. Limit per issuing state may apply. Investment-Grade Corporate Bonds Bonds rated investment grade (BBB– or better by an approved rating agency) issued by Nigerian corporates and quoted on NGX or FMDQ. 25% of Life Fund 20% of General Fund Yes — admissible within limits Rating must be current (within 12 months) from a NAICOM-approved rating agency. Unrated bonds are not admissible. Listed Equities (NGX) Ordinary shares of companies listed on the Nigerian Exchange Group. 30% of Life Fund 25% of General Fund Yes — admissible within limits Must be exchange-listed. Unlisted equity stakes are excluded from admissibility. No single issuer to exceed 5% of the fund. Shariah-screened equities only for Takaful funds. Real Estate (Direct) Direct investment in commercial or residential real estate located in Nigeria. 25% of Life Fund 15% of General Fund Yes — admissible within limits (valued by NAICOM-approved valuers) Independent professional valuation required at least every 2 years. Properties under development limited to 10% of the real estate allocation. Real Estate (REITs) Units in NAICOM-approved Real Estate Investment Trusts listed on NGX. 15% of Life Fund 10% of General Fund Yes — admissible within limits Provides more liquid real estate exposure than direct investment. Limits are in addition to (not within) the Direct Real Estate limit. Money Market Instruments Treasury bills, commercial paper, bankers’ acceptances, certificates of deposit with approved Nigerian banks. 20% of Life Fund 30% of General Fund Yes — fully admissible within limits Issuing bank must be a licensed Nigerian bank in good regulatory standing. General funds have higher money market limits reflecting shorter duration liabilities. Policy Loans Loans to policyholders secured against the surrender value of in-force life policies. 10% of Life Fund Not applicable Yes — admissible (secured by policy) Limited to the lower of: the outstanding surrender value or 90% of the policy reserve. Interest rate governed by the policy conditions. Infrastructure Bonds and Funds Bonds and funds financing qualifying infrastructure projects (roads, power, water, telecoms). 20% of Life Fund 10% of General Fund Yes — admissible within limits (where listed or NAICOM-approved) Designed to channel insurance long-term capital into Nigeria’s infrastructure deficit. FGN-backed infrastructure bonds are fully admissible. Mortgages (Residential) First-mortgage loans on residential property in Nigeria. 10% of Life Fund 5% of General Fund Yes — admissible within limits Loan-to-value (LTV) must not exceed 75%. Mortgage must be first-charge security. Duration mismatch risk must be managed within the overall ALM framework. Cash and Bank Deposits Demand deposits and fixed-term deposits with NAICOM-approved Nigerian banks. 15% of Life Fund 25% of General Fund Yes — admissible Bank must be licensed by the CBN and in good regulatory standing. No single bank concentration to exceed 10% of the fund. Foreign Currency Assets Assets denominated in foreign currencies (USD, GBP, EUR, XOF). 10% of Life Fund (where policy liabilities are denominated in foreign currency) 5% of General Fund Yes — admissible (matched currency basis) Foreign currency assets may only be held to match foreign-currency-denominated policy liabilities. Speculative foreign currency positions are not admissible. Connected-Party Investments Investments in companies owned or controlled by the insurer’s shareholders or directors. 5% of Life Fund (strictly limited) 5% of General Fund Limited admissibility — requires NAICOM prior approval NAICOM must approve all connected-party investments above de minimis threshold. Failure to obtain approval results in non-admissibility of the asset. Unlisted / Private Equity Equity stakes in companies not listed on a recognised exchange. 5% of Life Fund (restricted) Not admissible Not admissible for solvency purposes May be held in the portfolio but are excluded from the solvency margin calculation. Subject to annual impairment review. Collective Investment Schemes (Approved) Units in NAICOM-approved mutual funds and collective investment schemes registered with the SEC. 20% of Life Fund 15% of General Fund Yes — admissible (if SEC-registered) The underlying portfolio of the CIS determines the effective asset class exposure; limits apply on a look-through basis. ALM Note: Life insurers writing long-duration business (whole life, endowments, annuities) must specifically manage the duration gap between asset and liability cash flows. FGN bonds (the longest-dated admissible fixed-income instrument) are the primary duration-matching tool in the Nigerian market. For annuity writers, the lack of very long-dated (30+ year) FGN bonds creates a residual reinvestment risk that must be managed through the ORSA stress testing framework.

Life Insurance in Nigeria: A Professional Body of Knowledge Appendix Set Two: Specimen Documents Contents of This Appendix This appendix contains five specimen insurance documents, each accompanied by annotation notes explaining the function, regulatory basis, and practical significance of key provisions. These documents are for educational and professional reference purposes. They are not legally binding instruments and must not be used as actual policy documents, proposal forms, or quotations without adaptation by qualified legal and actuarial professionals. • Document 2A: Individual Term Life Assurance Policy — Specimen (Annotated) • Document 2B: Life Assurance Proposal Form with Guidance Notes • Document 2C: Group Life Insurance Master Policy — Selected Clauses (Annotated) • Document 2D: Retirement Life Annuity Quotation Template • Document 2E: Life Insurance Claims Notification Form Specimen Document Disclaimer All documents in this appendix are specimen templates for educational purposes only. Company names, policy numbers, and any personal details shown are fictitious. No reliance should be placed on these documents in any commercial, legal, or regulatory context. Actual insurance policies, proposal forms, and quotations used with policyholders must be: (1) approved by NAICOM under the product approval process required by NIIRA 2025; (2) reviewed by qualified legal counsel; (3) actuarially certified where required. The annotation notes in this appendix are provided to illuminate the purpose and regulatory basis of each document clause — they form part of the educational text of this book, not part of any insurance contract. DOCUMENT 2A — SPECIMEN: INDIVIDUAL TERM LIFE ASSURANCE POLICY Annotated specimen for educational and professional reference. Not a legally binding instrument. APEX LIFE INSURANCE COMPANY LIMITED RC 123456 · Licensed by NAICOM (Licence No. LIC/L/2025/001) · Member, Nigerian Insurers Association 1 Insurance Avenue, Victoria Island, Lagos, Nigeria · info@apexlife.ng · +234 (0) 800 APEX LIFE TERM LIFE ASSURANCE POLICY POLICY SCHEDULE Schedule Item Particulars Policy Number ALI-TL-2025-004872 Policyholder Name Mr. Adewale Chukwuemeka Okafor Policyholder Address 14 Palm Grove Estate, Lekki Phase 1, Lagos State, Nigeria Date of Birth (Policyholder) 12 March 1988 (Age at Entry: 37 years) Life Assured Mr. Adewale Chukwuemeka Okafor (same as policyholder) Product Name Apex ProtectSure Term 20 Policy Commencement Date 1 September 2025 Policy Expiry Date 31 August 2045 (20-year policy term) Sum Assured ₦50,000,000.00 (Fifty Million Naira) Premium Amount ₦189,450.00 per annum (paid monthly: ₦15,787.50) Premium Frequency Monthly, due on the 1st of each calendar month Grace Period 30 days from each premium due date Nominated Beneficiary Mrs. Ngozi Beatrice Okafor (Spouse) — 100% Policy Currency Nigerian Naira (₦) Date of Issue 1 September 2025 NAICOM Product Approval Reference NAICOM/PA/L/2024/0089 Annotation: The Policy Schedule The Policy Schedule is the personalised part of the policy — it contains the specific details that distinguish this policy from every other. Together with the Policy Conditions (below), it forms the complete insurance contract. Key points: • NAICOM Product Approval Reference: All life insurance products must be approved by NAICOM before marketing. The approval reference confirms the product’s regulatory standing. [Chapter 21] • Nominated Beneficiary: The person entitled to receive the death benefit. Under AIICO Insurance Plc v. Benson (2014), the policy nomination overrides a conflicting instruction in the policyholder’s will. The nomination should be reviewed after life events (marriage, divorce, birth of children). [Chapters 12, 25] • Grace Period: Most Nigerian life policies allow a grace period of 30 days (15 days for monthly premiums) for premium payment before a policy lapses; the period is set by the policy conditions and is not a minimum fixed by NIIRA 2025. During the grace period, the policy remains in force and a claim would be payable (though the outstanding premium would be deducted from any benefit). [Chapter 11] OPERATIVE CLAUSE APEX LIFE INSURANCE COMPANY LIMITED (hereinafter “the Company”) agrees, in consideration of the payment of the premium set out in the Policy Schedule and in reliance on the statements made in the Proposal Form dated 28 July 2025 (which form the basis of this contract), to pay the Sum Assured specified in the Policy Schedule to the nominated beneficiary or the legal representative of the Life Assured upon the occurrence of the Death of the Life Assured during the Policy Term, provided that: All premiums due have been paid and no premium is outstanding beyond the Grace Period at the date of death; The death does not arise from an Excluded Cause as set out in the Exclusions clause of this Policy; and The claim is notified to the Company within twelve (12) months of the date of death, accompanied by the documents specified in the Claims Procedure clause. Annotation: The Operative Clause The operative clause is the insurer’s primary contractual promise. It creates the enforceable obligation to pay. Note the three provisos: premium payment, no exclusion, and timely notification. The doctrine of utmost good faith means the insurer’s promise is conditional on the accuracy of the proposal form (‘in reliance on the statements made’). A material misrepresentation in the proposal form can void the policy. [Chapters 11, 12; Adesanya v. Royal Exchange (1986)] DEFINITIONS ‘Death’ The cessation of all biological functions of the Life Assured, certified by a registered medical practitioner and evidenced by a Certificate of Death issued by a competent authority in Nigeria or, where death occurs outside Nigeria, by the equivalent authority in the relevant jurisdiction. ‘Grace Period’ The period of thirty (30) days following the due date of each premium during which the premium may be paid without the Policy lapsing. The Policy remains in force during the Grace Period, but the Company may deduct any outstanding premium from any benefit payable. ‘Lapse’ The termination of this Policy by reason of non-payment of a premium within the Grace Period. A lapsed Policy provides no benefit unless reinstated in accordance with the Reinstatement condition. ‘Proposal Form’ The application completed by the Policyholder dated 28 July 2025, together with any supplementary questionnaires and medical evidence provided to the Company before this Policy was issued. ‘Policy Term’ The period from the Commencement Date to the Expiry Date as specified in the Policy Schedule, being twenty (20) years. ‘Sum Assured’ The amount specified in the Policy Schedule as the Sum Assured, being the benefit payable on the death of the Life Assured during the Policy Term. ‘Excluded Cause’ Any cause of death described in the Exclusions clause of this Policy. POLICY CONDITIONS 1. Payment of Premium The premium specified in the Policy Schedule shall be paid by the Policyholder to the Company on or before the due date in each period. Payment may be made by direct debit, electronic funds transfer, mobile money, or any other method approved by the Company in writing. The Company shall issue a receipt for each premium payment, which shall constitute evidence of payment. Payment to an agent shall not be deemed payment to the Company, because an insurance agent may not collect premium (s.38(2) NIIRA 2025). Premium collected by a licensed broker is deemed paid to the Company (s.60(2) NIIRA 2025). 2. Free Look Period The Policyholder has the right to cancel this Policy within twenty-one (21) days of the date of receipt of the Policy document (the ‘Free Look Period’) by returning the Policy document to the Company’s registered office with a written notice of cancellation. Upon receipt of a valid cancellation notice within the Free Look Period, the Company shall refund the full premium paid without deduction. No claim may be made under this Policy after a Free Look cancellation notice has been submitted. 3. Lapse and Reinstatement If the premium is not paid within the Grace Period, this Policy shall lapse and no benefit shall be payable. A lapsed Policy may be reinstated within twelve (12) months of the lapse date, subject to: (a) payment of all outstanding premiums with interest at the Company’s prevailing rate; (b) production of evidence of continued insurability satisfactory to the Company; and (c) payment of a reinstatement fee, if applicable. The Company reserves the right to decline reinstatement or to modify the terms of reinstatement. Reinstatement shall not be permitted after twelve (12) months from the lapse date. 4. Incontestability After this Policy has been in force for a continuous period of two (2) years from the Commencement Date, the Company shall not contest its validity on the ground of misrepresentation or non-disclosure in the Proposal Form, except in the case of fraudulent misrepresentation or fraudulent non-disclosure. This incontestability clause does not apply to any Excluded Cause, which shall remain excluded regardless of the period for which the Policy has been in force. 5. Nomination of Beneficiary The Policyholder may nominate one or more beneficiaries to receive the Sum Assured on the death of the Life Assured. A nomination made in the Policy Schedule or by written notice to the Company shall take effect from the date of receipt of the notice by the Company. The Policyholder may change the nomination at any time during the Policy Term by written notice to the Company. In the absence of a valid nomination, or where all nominated beneficiaries have predeceased the Life Assured, the Sum Assured shall be paid to the legal representative of the estate of the Life Assured. 6. Assignment This Policy may be assigned as security for a loan or other obligation with the written consent of the Company. An assignment must be executed in writing and registered with the Company before it takes effect. An assigned Policy may not be further assigned without the prior written consent of the assignee. Assignment does not affect the Exclusions applicable to this Policy. 7. Dispute Resolution Any dispute arising under or in connection with this Policy shall be referred in the first instance to the Company’s internal complaints resolution process. If the dispute is not resolved within forty-five (45) days of formal complaint, the Policyholder or claimant may refer the matter to the NAICOM Consumer Protection Bureau or to the courts of the Federal Republic of Nigeria. This Policy is governed by the laws of the Federal Republic of Nigeria. EXCLUSIONS No benefit is payable under this Policy if the death of the Life Assured is directly or indirectly caused by or arises out of any of the following: Suicide or intentional self-inflicted injury, within twenty-four (24) months of the Commencement Date of this Policy or, where the Policy has been reinstated, within twenty-four (24) months of the date of reinstatement; War (whether declared or undeclared), invasion, act of foreign enemy, civil war, rebellion, insurrection, or military coup, where the Life Assured is an active participant; Participation in any criminal act or the commission of any indictable offence; The use of or addiction to any prohibited substance under the Dangerous Drugs Act or any successor legislation, unless the substance was administered by or on the direction of a registered medical practitioner for legitimate medical treatment; Aviation, other than as a fare-paying passenger on a scheduled commercial airline service. Annotation: Exclusions Exclusions are among the most litigated provisions in life insurance. Key points for practitioners: • Suicide exclusion: The 24-month suicide exclusion is standard in the Nigerian market to prevent adverse selection by individuals contemplating suicide. After 24 months, suicide is covered. This is a material fact the proposer need not disclose at application (it is a post-inception risk, not a pre-existing condition). • Burden of proof: Under Leadway Assurance v. Zeco (2005), ambiguous exclusion clauses are construed contra proferentem — against the insurer. The insurer bears the burden of proving that a death falls within an exclusion. • Aviation exclusion: The standard aviation exclusion covers the insured as crew or private pilot. The exception for scheduled commercial passenger flights is standard — routine air travel by an insured is not excluded. Life Insurance in Nigeria: A Professional Body of Knowledge Appendix Set Three: Regulatory Instruments Log Contents of This Appendix This appendix is a structured regulatory reference log covering the five principal regulatory instrument categories relevant to Nigerian life insurance practice. It is designed as a living reference: the structure and methodology are permanent, but practitioners are expected to update the entries as new instruments are issued. Each section includes guidance on where to find current information. • Log 3A: NAICOM Circulars and Directives (2020–2025) — Chronological register by year and subject • Log 3B: NIIRA 2025 Commencement Tracker — Provision-by-provision implementation status • Log 3C: Recapitalisation Compliance Timeline — Phased milestones and acceptable routes • Log 3D: NDPC Insurance Sector Enforcement Log — Data protection enforcement relevant to insurers • Log 3E: PenCom-NAICOM Interface Instruments — The regulatory instruments governing pension-insurance intersection How to Maintain This Log This regulatory instruments log reflects the Nigerian insurance regulatory landscape as at the date of publication of this work. NAICOM, NDPC, and PenCom issue new instruments continuously — often multiple times per year. Practitioners using this appendix should: • Check naicom.gov.ng (circulars register) at least monthly for new NAICOM instruments. • Check ndpc.gov.ng (enforcement section) quarterly for NDPC enforcement actions. • Subscribe to the NIA member circular distribution list to receive NAICOM communications promptly. LOG 3A: NAICOM CIRCULARS AND DIRECTIVES 2020–2025 Chronological register of principal NAICOM regulatory instruments. Access current register at naicom.gov.ng Primary source NAICOM Circular Register — naicom.gov.ng/circulars Format of citations Circulars are cited as: NAICOM/DPR/CIR/[Number]/[Year] for circulars; NAICOM/DPR/GUID/[Number]/[Year] for guidelines; NAICOM/DPR/DIR/[Number]/[Year] for directives. Numbers in this log are indicative reference categories; verify exact numbers from the official register. Scope of this log Principal instruments affecting life insurance, Takaful, Insurtech, consumer protection, capital, and data governance. The NAICOM circular register contains additional instruments on non-life insurance, market conduct inspections, and administrative matters not included here. 2020 — Principal Instruments Reference Category Subject Matter Key Content Life Insurance Impact Book Reference Market Conduct Circular, 2020 Claims Settlement Obligations (pre-NIIRA) Mandatory timelines for claims acknowledgement and settlement under the Insurance Act 2003 framework. Precursor to NIIRA 2025’s statutory settlement requirements. NAICOM directed all insurers to submit quarterly claims settlement reports. Established the market’s expectation of timely settlement before NIIRA 2025 codified the 60-day rule. Insurers building their claims culture should treat the NIIRA 2025 timeline as confirming a pre-existing regulatory expectation. Ch. 12 Consumer Protection Circular, 2020 Policyholder Complaint Handling Required all licensed insurers to establish and publicise an internal complaints procedure. Minimum standards for complaint acknowledgement (5 days), investigation (30 days), and resolution. Required quarterly complaints data submission to NAICOM. Established the minimum consumer protection infrastructure that NIIRA 2025’s consumer protection framework now formalises. Insurers must maintain complaint registers going back to the effective date of this circular. Ch. 20, 21 Investment Circular, 2020 Investment Guidelines Update Updated the admissible asset classes and portfolio limits for life and general insurance funds. Introduced infrastructure bonds as an admissible asset class for the first time. Revised the connected-party investment limit downward. Significant for ALM: the addition of infrastructure bonds gave life insurers access to a longer-duration fixed-income asset that improves the duration match for long-tail life and annuity liabilities. Ch. 23 Digital Insurance Circular, 2020 Digital Distribution Guidance First NAICOM guidance on digital insurance distribution, USSD-based products, and mobile-distributed microinsurance. Established data protection expectations for digital channels ahead of the formal NDPA 2023. Marked the beginning of NAICOM’s digital insurance regulatory framework, subsequently expanded by the 2025 Insurtech Guidelines. Ch. 22, 28 AML/CFT Circular, 2020 Insurance Sector AML/CFT Guidelines Updated AML/CFT requirements for licensed insurers, brokers, and agents. Introduced the requirement for a designated AML Compliance Officer. Enhanced due diligence (EDD) triggers for high-value single-premium policies and annuity purchases. All life insurers must maintain EDD procedures for single-premium policies above threshold. The AML Compliance Officer role must be adequately resourced and independent. Ch. 21 2021 — Principal Instruments Reference Category Subject Matter Key Content Life Insurance Impact Book Reference Risk Management Circular, 2021 ERM Framework Requirements Formalised the three lines of defence model for Nigerian insurers. Required all licensed insurers above a specified premium threshold to appoint a Chief Risk Officer (CRO). Established the Own Risk and Solvency Assessment (ORSA) as an annual Board obligation. The CRO requirement is the structural foundation for the NIIRA 2025 governance provisions. Insurers that complied with this circular in 2021 had a material implementation head start over those that treated it as aspirational guidance. Ch. 15, 34 Group Life Circular, 2021 Group Life Mandatory Compliance Strengthened enforcement of the mandatory group life requirement under PRA 2014. Required insurers to report all group life policy cancellations for non-payment to PenCom. Established the Group Life Compliance Certificate as a required document for employer statutory filings. Group life underwriters must maintain records of all cancellations for non-payment and submit quarterly non-compliance reports to NAICOM and PenCom. Employers discovered to be without mandatory group life face joint NAICOM/PenCom enforcement. Ch. 30 Microinsurance Circular, 2021 Microinsurance Framework (First Edition) Published the first comprehensive microinsurance regulatory framework: product parameters (maximum premium, maximum sum assured, simplified terms), approved distribution channels (mobile, USSD, cooperative societies), and simplified underwriting requirements. Established the regulatory foundation for mobile insurance, cooperative-distributed products, and embedded microinsurance in Nigeria. The 2023 revision updated the framework for Insurtech-facilitated distribution. Ch. 22 Capital Adequacy Circular, 2021 Solvency Margin Reporting Enhancement Updated the format and frequency of solvency margin reporting. Required quarterly solvency filings (previously annual only). Introduced the solvency dashboard as a NAICOM supervisory tool for early identification of capital-stressed insurers. Quarterly solvency reporting significantly increases the CFO and Statutory Actuary’s compliance workload. Insurers must maintain an actuarial reserve calculation process capable of producing quarterly outputs. Ch. 24 Takaful Circular, 2021 Takaful Window Framework Published detailed requirements for conventional insurers seeking to establish Takaful windows: SSB composition and independence standards; fund segregation requirements; Wakalah fee disclosure; surplus distribution mechanism. Preceded the NIIRA 2025 Takaful window licensing provisions. Key transition document for insurers currently operating Takaful windows under informal arrangements. NIIRA 2025’s Takaful provisions build directly on this circular’s framework. Ch. 29 2022 — Principal Instruments Reference Category Subject Matter Key Content Life Insurance Impact Book Reference Recapitalisation Directive, 2022 Recapitalisation Framework (Phase 1) Published the first phase of the recapitalisation programme in anticipation of the new Insurance Act. Set interim capital floors and phased timelines. Required all licensees to submit a Recapitalisation Plan to NAICOM by a specified date. The 2022 recapitalisation directive established the framework that NIIRA 2025 later formalised. Insurers that submitted credible plans in 2022 had a more constructive relationship with NAICOM during the NIIRA 2025 transition. Ch. 24 Data Protection Circular, 2022 Insurance Sector Data Governance (pre-NDPA) Issued in anticipation of the NDPA 2023. Required insurers to: document all personal data processing activities; establish a data governance committee; initiate a data protection compliance programme; and appoint a data protection focal point (formalised as DPO under NDPA 2023). Insurers that acted on this circular promptly were substantively compliant with NDPA 2023’s core requirements at the Act’s commencement. Those that did not have faced a steeper NDPA 2023 catch-up. Ch. 21, 28 RLA Market Circular, 2022 Retirement Life Annuity Market Guidelines Published detailed guidelines for the RLA market: solvency requirements specific to annuity writers (higher than standard life); mandatory joint life option availability; mortality assumption standards; policyholder information requirements at quotation; PenCom-NAICOM RSA transfer protocol. The most operationally significant regulatory instrument for life insurers participating in the annuity market. All RLA writers must comply with the mortality assumption standards; non-compliance risks NAICOM price intervention. Ch. 31 Market Conduct Inspection Framework, 2022 TCF and Consumer Protection Inspections Published the market conduct inspection methodology: inspection triggers (complaint rate, solvency stress, product approval issues); inspection team composition; inspector powers; post-inspection remediation timelines; publication of material findings. The TCF inspection framework is the enforcement mechanism behind NIIRA 2025’s consumer protection provisions. Insurers with high complaint rates or poor claims settlement records are prioritised for inspection. Ch. 20, 21 IFRS 17 Preparation Circular, 2022 IFRS 17 Transition Guidance Published NAICOM’s guidance on the transition from IFRS 4 to IFRS 17 for listed Nigerian insurers. Set the expected effective date for Nigerian listed insurers; required gap analysis submissions; specified the actuarial and accounting resource requirements. IFRS 17 implementation is a major actuarial and accounting challenge. The circular signalled NAICOM’s expectation that all listed insurers would be IFRS 17 compliant from the specified effective date. Ch. 24 2023 — Principal Instruments Reference Category Subject Matter Key Content Life Insurance Impact Book Reference NDPA Implementation Circular, 2023 Insurance Sector NDPA 2023 Compliance Following the NDPA 2023’s assent in June 2023, NAICOM issued sector-specific guidance on insurers’ compliance obligations as Data Controllers of Major Importance. Specified the DPO appointment timeline, the DPCP submission deadline, and the data audit requirement. Every licensed insurer must have appointed a Data Protection Officer and submitted a Data Protection Compliance Programme to the NDPC by the NDPC’s specified deadline. Ch. 21, 28 Microinsurance Framework Revision, 2023 Updated Microinsurance Guidelines Revised the 2021 microinsurance framework to accommodate Insurtech-facilitated distribution, embedded insurance through non-insurance platforms, and USSD-based parametric products. Updated the maximum premium and sum assured thresholds for inflation. The revised framework opened the mobile-embedded microinsurance market more formally. Insurers working with fintech distribution partners should use this circular as the primary product design reference. Ch. 22 Corporate Governance Directive, 2023 Enhanced Governance Standards (Pre-NIIRA) Strengthened Board independence requirements ahead of NIIRA 2025. Required all life insurers above a premium threshold to: convene at least four full Board meetings annually; establish a standalone Risk Committee (not combined with Audit); and formally adopt a Board-approved Risk Appetite Statement. Insurers that implemented the Risk Committee and Risk Appetite Statement in 2023 were substantively NIIRA 2025-compliant on these governance provisions before the Act’s commencement. Ch. 24, 34 Cybersecurity Circular, 2023 Insurance Sector Cybersecurity Standards Issued cybersecurity minimum standards for all licensed insurers: encryption requirements for policyholder data at rest and in transit; multi-factor authentication for all systems accessing policyholder data; mandatory annual penetration testing; incident response plan; 72-hour cyber breach notification to NAICOM. These cybersecurity standards were incorporated verbatim into the 2025 Insurtech Guidelines and apply to all insurers, not only Insurtechs. Compliance is a market conduct inspection item. Ch. 28 AML/CFT Update Circular, 2023 MLPPA 2022 Implementation Published the insurance sector’s implementation guidance for the Money Laundering (Prevention and Prohibition) Act 2022. Updated the KYC thresholds, the suspicious activity reporting format, and the EDD triggers for high-risk customers. The MLPPA 2022 AML/CFT obligations are now the primary AML regulatory standard for Nigerian insurers, superseding earlier NAICOM AML circulars. The 2023 circular is the reference implementation document. Ch. 21 2024 — Principal Instruments Reference Category Subject Matter Key Content Life Insurance Impact Book Reference NIIRA 2025 Consultation Draft, 2024 Pre-Publication Industry Consultation NAICOM circulated the draft of what became NIIRA 2025 for industry consultation. NIA submitted formal comments. The consultation period ran for 60 days. Several provisions were modified between the draft and the final Act. Insurers that participated in the 2024 consultation had early visibility of NIIRA 2025’s provisions and were able to begin implementation planning before the Act’s commencement. Regulatory engagement as an intelligence tool. Ch. 21, 36 Recapitalisation Phase 2 Directive, 2024 Recapitalisation Interim Milestone Set interim recapitalisation milestones for licensees below the target capital thresholds: minimum percentage of target capital to be reached by specified dates. Required all licensees to submit updated recapitalisation progress reports. Critical for insurers below the NIIRA 2025 capital thresholds. Non-compliance with interim milestones triggers NAICOM supervisory escalation including restrictions on new business writing. Ch. 24 GAID 2025 Preparation Circular, 2024 GAID 2025 Insurance Implementation Guidance Issued in anticipation of the GAID 2025 (effective September 2025). Required insurers to prepare data processing records, DPIAs for high-risk processing, data localisation plans, and retention/disposal schedules aligned with GAID 2025 requirements. The data localisation requirement — primary storage of policyholder data on Nigeria-based servers — was the most operationally complex GAID 2025 obligation for insurers using cloud services with non-Nigerian data centres. Ch. 21, 28 Product Filing Circular, 2024 Standardised Product Approval Format Published the revised standardised format for life insurance product filings: actuarial pricing certificate requirements; policyholder benefit illustration standards; plain language policy wording requirements; digital product filing portal launch. Significantly streamlined the product approval process for insurers with compliant actuarial teams. The digital filing portal reduced approval timelines for straightforward products from several months to 6–8 weeks. Ch. 10, 21 Insurtech Licensing Consultation, 2024 Draft Insurtech Guidelines Consultation Published the draft Insurtech Guidelines for industry comment, ahead of the August 2025 formal issuance. Established the Partnering/Standalone Insurtech distinction. Consulted on AI/ML governance, sandbox criteria, and cybersecurity standards. First formal signal of the Insurtech licensing structure that NIIRA 2025 subsequently enacted. Insurtech companies and conventional insurers building digital partnerships used this consultation draft to begin compliance design. Ch. 28 2025 — Principal Instruments Reference Category Subject Matter Key Content Life Insurance Impact Book Reference Insurtech Guidelines, August 2025 Insurtech Licensing Framework (Final) Published as formal subsidiary regulation simultaneously with NIIRA 2025’s practical commencement. Final Partnering Insurtech and Standalone Insurtech licensing requirements; sandbox criteria; AI/ML governance; cybersecurity mandates; impermissible activities list. The primary reference instrument for all digital insurance operations. Supersedes the 2024 consultation draft. All Insurtechs and conventional insurers with digital distribution partnerships must comply. Ch. 28 Recapitalisation Implementation Directive, 2025 NIIRA 2025 Capital Thresholds — Implementation Published the definitive recapitalisation timeline under NIIRA 2025: milestone dates, acceptable routes (fresh capital, merger, acquisition), documentation required at each milestone, NAICOM’s decision-making process for non-compliant licensees. The definitive compliance reference for all licensees below the NIIRA 2025 capital thresholds. See Log 3C for the detailed timeline. Ch. 24 Claims settlement circular — UNVERIFIED (existence not confirmed) NIIRA 2025 Claims Timelines — Implementation Placeholder entry: no NAICOM circular on claims timelines has been verified. The statutory rule is NIIRA 2025 s.210 — valid claims settled within 60 days of notification, with compound interest for each month of delay. The 5-business-day acknowledgement described in Chapter 12 is also unverified. The consequences of late settlement are the most important new element: compound interest on the outstanding amount for each month of delay (s.210), a ₦500,000 penalty (s.210(7)), the claimant’s right to ask NAICOM to pay from the insurer’s statutory deposit (s.210(2)), and, for compulsory insurances only, compensation for unreasonable delay (s.210(8)). No per-day penalty matrix for late claims has been verified. Ch. 12, 21 Corporate Governance Guidelines, 2025 NIIRA 2025 Governance — Implementation Detailed governance implementation guidance: Board composition assessment process; fit and proper evaluation form; Board committee terms of reference templates; three lines of defence documentation requirements; Statutory Actuary independence assessment. Provides the operational detail behind NIIRA 2025’s governance provisions. The fit and proper evaluation form is required for all new director appointments and annual re-certification. Ch. 24, 34 GAID 2025 Commencement Notification, September 2025 GAID 2025 Effective Date Confirmation NAICOM confirmed the GAID 2025 effective date (19 September 2025) and provided insurance-sector specific implementation notes. Confirmed data localisation obligations, DPO reporting lines, and breach notification protocol. From 19 September 2025, full GAID 2025 compliance is required. Insurers not yet compliant with data localisation, DPCP submission, or DPO appointment are in breach of both NDPA 2023 and NAICOM’s sector guidance. Various — per NAICOM implementing directives LOG 3C: RECAPITALISATION COMPLIANCE TIMELINE NIIRA 2025 minimum capital requirements — phased implementation for existing licensees Governing instrument NIIRA 2025 Part II (capital thresholds); Part XVII (transitional provisions); NAICOM Recapitalisation Implementation Directive 2025 Applies to All licensed insurers, reinsurers, brokers, and agents whose current paid-up capital is below the NIIRA 2025 minimum threshold for their licence class. New licensees Must meet NIIRA 2025 capital thresholds from the date of licence application. No transitional period for new entrants. Acceptable recapitalisation routes 1. Organic capital accumulation (retained earnings). 2. Fresh equity capital injection (new shares issued to existing or new shareholders). 3. Rights issue to existing shareholders. 4. Merger or acquisition with another licensed insurer (combined capital must meet the threshold). 5. Portfolio transfer to a sufficiently capitalised insurer, with the transferring insurer converting its licence. NAICOM must approve all merger and acquisition routes before execution. Monitoring mechanism Quarterly capital adequacy report to NAICOM; annual audited financial statements confirming capital position; formal Board resolution at each milestone confirming compliance status and Recapitalisation Plan progress. Phase 1: Recapitalisation Plan Submission Milestone Requirements NAICOM Response Consequence of Non-Compliance Board Approval of Recapitalisation Plan The Board must formally approve a Recapitalisation Plan that: identifies the route to compliance; specifies the quantum and timing of each capital injection or transaction; identifies the source of capital; and is certified by the CFO and the external auditor as achievable. NAICOM acknowledges receipt of Board resolution confirming plan adoption. A licensee that fails to adopt a Board-approved Recapitalisation Plan is in immediate regulatory breach and subject to supervisory escalation. Plan Submission to NAICOM Submit the Board-approved Recapitalisation Plan to NAICOM within 60 days of NIIRA 2025 commencement, using the standard NAICOM submission format. Include: Board resolution; audited latest capital position; proposed route; transaction documents (term sheets, MoUs) for any external capital or M&A route; and Board declaration that the plan is achievable. NAICOM reviews the plan and either: approves it; requests modifications; or rejects it with reasons. A rejected plan must be resubmitted within 30 days. Failure to submit within the 60-day window triggers supervisory action. NAICOM may restrict new business writing pending a compliant plan submission. Phase 2: Interim Milestone Compliance Interim Milestone Capital Target Reporting Requirement NAICOM Action if Missed Milestone 1 (12 months from commencement) Minimum 25% of the gap between current capital and NIIRA 2025 threshold must be closed. (Example: life insurer currently at ₦6bn, target ₦10bn — gap is ₦4bn — must reach ₦7bn by Milestone 1.) Quarterly capital adequacy report showing capital position; auditor’s letter confirming the capital injection or retained earnings have been recognised in the accounts. Formal warning notice. Public disclosure of breach. Restriction on writing new policies in specific product lines until next milestone is met. Milestone 2 (24 months from commencement) Minimum 50% of gap closed. (Continuing example: ₦8bn) Same as Milestone 1. Suspension of certain regulated activities (specified by NAICOM). Appointment of NAICOM-nominated independent director to Board until compliance is achieved. Milestone 3 (36 months from commencement) Minimum 75% of gap closed. (Continuing example: ₦9bn) Same as Milestone 1, plus a revised plan for final 25% if not on track. Imposition of a run-off plan if the remaining 25% is not credibly achievable. Restriction on distribution of dividends or other capital returns. Final Compliance Deadline (48 months from commencement) 100% of gap closed. Full NIIRA 2025 minimum capital achieved. (Continuing example: ₦10bn) Audited financial statements confirming full compliance. NAICOM compliance certification letter issued on confirmation. Licence revocation or compulsory merger / portfolio transfer ordered by NAICOM. Any remaining policyholders’ obligations to be transferred to a compliant insurer. Merger and Acquisition Route: Key Steps Step Action Required Timing NAICOM Involvement 1. Strategic decision Board resolves to pursue merger/acquisition as the recapitalisation route. Engages financial and legal advisers. Month 1–3 Informal engagement with NAICOM recommended before public announcement. 2. Target identification and LOI Identify merger partner or acquirer. Execute Letter of Intent (LOI) or Memorandum of Understanding (MoU). Disclose to NAICOM. Month 2–6 NAICOM no-objection required before execution of binding documents. 3. Due diligence Full financial, actuarial, legal, and regulatory due diligence on the target/partner. Month 3–8 NAICOM may participate in or observe due diligence on request. 4. NAICOM formal approval application Submit merger/acquisition application to NAICOM with: draft Scheme of Merger; independent actuary’s report on policyholder interests; post-merger capital position; combined governance structure. Month 6–10 NAICOM reviews and approves or rejects within 90 days of complete application. 5. Court sanction (if scheme of merger) Apply to the Federal High Court or the relevant State High Court for sanction of the Scheme of Merger under CAMA 2020. Month 9–14 NAICOM’s approval letter is filed with the court application. 6. Effective date and NAICOM notification Merger becomes effective on the court order date. Notify NAICOM of effective date. Submit post-merger capital confirmation. Month 12–18 NAICOM issues revised licence reflecting the merged entity’s new name and capital position. 7. NAICOM licence update Merged entity operates under single licence. Combined capital confirmed to meet NIIRA 2025 threshold. Old licensee certificates surrendered. Post-effective date NAICOM may conduct a post-merger inspection within 6 months. LOG 3D: NDPC INSURANCE SECTOR DATA PROTECTION ENFORCEMENT LOG Nigeria Data Protection Commission — enforcement actions relevant to the insurance sector and financial institutions Primary source NDPC Enforcement Notices — ndpc.gov.ng/enforcement. The NDPC publishes enforcement decisions and penalty notices on its website. Insurance sector status The NDPA 2023 came into force in June 2023 and its implementing GAID 2025 from September 2025. The NDPC’s insurance sector enforcement activity is in its early stages as at the date of publication of this work. This log will become increasingly material as the NDPC’s regulatory capacity grows. Monitoring obligation Insurers should monitor the NDPC enforcement log quarterly. A penalty notice against another insurer is a signal that the NDPC is actively scrutinising the sector and that the relevant compliance gap may exist in other organisations. Penalty range under NDPA 2023 For Data Controllers of Major Importance (the category that includes all licensed insurers at scale): up to 2% of annual gross revenue or ₦10 million (whichever is higher) for first offences; up to 4% of annual gross revenue or ₦20 million for repeat breaches. Directors of non-compliant organisations may face personal liability. Known Enforcement Actions — Financial Services and Adjacent Sectors Date (Approximate) Organisation (Category) Breach Type Outcome Insurance Sector Lesson 2023 (post-NDPA assent) Major commercial bank (not insurance) Unauthorised sharing of customer financial data with a third-party marketing company without consent. Customer financial profiles used for targeted commercial credit offers from a related entity. NDPC issued enforcement notice requiring cessation of the data sharing. Administrative fine and mandatory DPCP submission within 60 days. Insurance sector parallel: insurers must not share policyholder health or financial data with related entities (bancassurance bank parents, sister companies) for marketing without explicit policyholder consent. Data sharing agreements must be NDPA 2023-compliant. 2024 (NDPA 2023 enforcement period) Telecommunications company (data controller of major importance) Failure to appoint a Data Protection Officer within the NDPC deadline. Failure to submit a Data Protection Compliance Programme. Processing of customer location data beyond the stated purpose. Enforcement notice; mandatory DPO appointment within 30 days; DPCP submission within 60 days; administrative fine. Insurance sector parallel: DPO appointment and DPCP submission are not optional. Every licensed insurer is a Data Controller of Major Importance and must meet these obligations. The telco enforcement confirms the NDPC will penalise process failures, not just data breaches. 2024 (NDPA 2023 enforcement period) Fintech company (data processor) Retention of customer data for a period significantly beyond the stated retention period in the privacy notice. Failure to respond to 17 data subject access requests within the statutory 30-day period. Enforcement notice requiring data deletion audit; mandatory response to all outstanding DSARs within 15 days; administrative fine; mandatory staff data protection training. Insurance sector parallel: insurers must have documented retention and disposal schedules. GAID 2025 specifies minimum retention periods (claims: 10 years; policies: 7 years post-expiry); maximum retention beyond these periods requires documented justification. DSAR response processes must be operationally functional. 2025 (GAID 2025 period) Insurance broker (financial services) Data breach: unauthorised access to broker’s client database by a former employee using unrevoked access credentials. 4,200 client records (name, contact, policy details) accessed. Breach not reported to NDPC within 72 hours. Enforcement notice; mandatory incident response plan revision; administrative fine (breach notification failure); mandatory penetration testing and access control audit. Insurance sector lesson: access credential management and prompt revocation on employee departure are critical controls. The 72-hour breach notification obligation to the NDPC is non-negotiable — the penalty for late notification was applied even though the breach was caused by a former employee, not a current one. Insurance Sector Data Protection Compliance Checklist (NDPA 2023 / GAID 2025) ☐ Data Protection Officer (DPO) appointed; appointment registered with NDPC; DPO has direct access to the Board or ExCo. ☐ Data Protection Compliance Programme (DPCP) drafted, Board-approved, and submitted to NDPC. ☐ Record of Processing Activities (RoPA) completed and current: documents every category of personal data processed, its purpose, lawful basis, retention period, and third-party recipients. ☐ Data Subject Access Request (DSAR) process operational: designated team, 30-day response target, tracking system. ☐ Data localisation: policyholder data primary storage confirmed on Nigeria-based servers (or NDPC exemption obtained). ☐ Retention and disposal schedule: documented and implemented. Claims records: minimum 10 years. Policy records: minimum 7 years post-expiry. ☐ Breach notification protocol: incident response plan includes NDPC 72-hour notification step and policyholder notification template. ☐ DPIAs completed for all high-risk processing activities (AI/ML underwriting models; biometric data; large-scale health data; third-party data sharing). ☐ Third-party data processor agreements: all processors engaged by the insurer have signed NDPA 2023-compliant data processing agreements. ☐ Annual NDPC data protection audit completed; findings reported to Board; remediation actions tracked. LOG 3E: PENCOM-NAICOM INTERFACE INSTRUMENTS Regulatory instruments governing the pension-insurance intersection. Both PenCom and NAICOM exercise authority. The dual regulatory challenge The intersection of pension and life insurance is the most complex regulatory environment in the Nigerian financial services sector. PenCom regulates the Contributory Pension Scheme, the PFAs, and the RSA accumulation phase. NAICOM regulates the RLA (the primary pension decumulation product) and the mandatory group life insurance obligation. An insurer operating in the RLA market is simultaneously subject to both regulators — and must manage the requirements of both. Primary PenCom source pencom.gov.ng — Regulations, guidelines, and circulars section. Primary NAICOM source naicom.gov.ng — Circulars and guidelines section. Joint instruments PenCom and NAICOM occasionally issue joint circulars on matters affecting both regulators’ mandates. These are published on both regulators’ websites simultaneously. Primary Interface Instruments Instrument Issuing Body Subject Matter Key Insurance Provisions Book Reference Pension Reform Act 2014 (PRA 2014), Section 4 National Assembly / PenCom enforcement Mandatory group life insurance obligation for qualifying employers Every employer with 3+ employees must maintain group life at minimum 3× total annual emoluments. Policy must be with a NAICOM-licensed insurer. PenCom may verify compliance at its pension audits. NAICOM may receive non-compliance referrals from PenCom. Chapters 30, 33 PRA 2014, Section 16–17 National Assembly / PenCom and NAICOM joint enforcement RSA decumulation — RLA and Programmed Withdrawal options On retirement, RSA holders may purchase an RLA from a NAICOM-licensed life insurer using their RSA balance. The insurer must be on PenCom’s approved RLA insurer register. PenCom regulates the RSA transfer; NAICOM regulates the annuity product. Chapters 31, 33 PenCom Regulation on RSA Transfers to Annuity Providers PenCom The process for transferring RSA funds from a PFA to an approved RLA insurer Specifies: the election process for the RSA holder; the documentation required; the PFA’s obligation to facilitate the transfer within 5 business days of a valid election; the NAICOM-licensed insurer’s obligation to issue the annuity contract within 30 days of fund receipt. Chapter 31 NAICOM RLA Market Guidelines (2022) NAICOM Product and solvency standards for RLA writers Annuity writers must: maintain a separate ‘Annuity Fund’ with assets duration-matched to liability cash flows; apply NAICOM-approved mortality tables; make available a joint life option for married annuitants; provide clear pre-purchase illustrations; comply with enhanced solvency margin requirements for the annuity book. Chapters 23, 31 PenCom Approved RLA Insurer Register PenCom The list of NAICOM-licensed life insurers approved by PenCom to receive RSA transfers for RLA purchase Only insurers on the PenCom Approved Register may receive RSA fund transfers for annuity purchase. Approval requires: NAICOM life licence; minimum capital (typically above the standard NIIRA 2025 life threshold); NAICOM RLA Guidelines compliance certification; submission to PenCom of the insurer’s actuarial and financial data. Chapters 31, 33 PenCom-NAICOM Joint Circular on Group Life Compliance (Periodic) PenCom and NAICOM (joint) Coordinated enforcement of the mandatory group life obligation Periodic joint circulars address gaps in employer group life compliance identified during PenCom’s pension audits. Specify the data-sharing protocol between PenCom and NAICOM on non-compliant employers. Confirm that both regulators may independently enforce the Section 4 obligation. Chapter 30 PenCom Regulation on Voluntary Contributions (VCs) PenCom The framework for RSA holders and self-employed individuals making above-minimum contributions Life insurers offering Personal Pension Plans (PPPs) should understand the VC framework as a complementary or alternative vehicle. PPP positioning relative to VCs is a key financial planning advisory issue. Chapters 25, 33 NAICOM Circular on Bancassurance and Pension Integration NAICOM Guidance on bancassurance arrangements that include pension-linked insurance products Bancassurance partnerships offering RLA quotations, PPPs, or group life products through bank branches must comply with both the bancassurance regulatory framework (NAICOM) and any relevant PenCom licensing requirements (where the bank is also a licensed PFA or PFC). Chapters 16, 31, 33 PenCom Annual Report (published annually) PenCom The comprehensive annual report on the CPS including RLA market data Key life insurance intelligence: total RSA balance (the total pool of funds eligible for RLA conversion); number of RSA holders approaching retirement (the pipeline of potential annuitants); RLA market size and growth rate; average annuity purchase price; PFA market share. Chapters 31, 33, 36 PITA (Personal Income Tax Act) — Insurance and Pension Provisions Federal Inland Revenue Service (FIRS) Tax treatment of insurance premiums, pension contributions, and benefits Life insurance premiums: deductible up to statutory limits. Voluntary pension contributions: fully tax-deductible under PRA 2014. Group life premiums: deductible business expense. Death and disability benefits: not taxable in the beneficiary’s hands. Gains on endowment/savings policies: may be assessable. Chapter 25 The RLA Regulatory Workflow: PenCom and NAICOM Roles Step RSA Holder Action PFA Obligation NAICOM-Licensed Insurer Obligation Regulator 1. Retirement election RSA holder reaches retirement age (or 50 with reduced capacity) and elects to take an RLA (or PW, or combination). — — PenCom (retirement eligibility) 2. Lump sum election (if applicable) RSA holder elects to withdraw up to 25% as a lump sum. Submits election form to PFA. PFA processes the 25% withdrawal and pays to RSA holder’s bank account within 5 business days. — PenCom 3. RLA quotation request RSA holder (or their financial adviser) requests RLA quotations from multiple NAICOM-licensed insurers on the PenCom Approved Register. — Insurer must provide quotation within 5 business days of quotation request. Quotation must comply with NAICOM RLA Guidelines (mortality assumptions, option availability, illustration format). NAICOM (product) 4. Insurer selection RSA holder selects preferred insurer and submits election to PFA. PFA validates that selected insurer is on PenCom Approved Register. — PenCom (validation) 5. Fund transfer RSA holder signs annuity application form. PFA transfers the RSA balance (less 25% lump sum, if elected) to the selected insurer’s designated annuity fund account within 5 business days of confirmed election. Insurer must notify PFA of receipt of funds within 2 business days. PenCom (transfer); NAICOM (receipt confirmation) 6. Annuity contract issuance — — Insurer issues the Annuity Policy document to the annuitant within 30 days of fund receipt. The policy must meet NAICOM RLA Guidelines requirements. NAICOM (policy issuance standards) 7. Income commencement — — First monthly annuity payment made to annuitant’s designated bank account on the payment date specified in the annuity contract. NAICOM (product compliance) 8. Death of annuitant Nominated beneficiary notifies insurer. — Where a guarantee period or joint life option is in force, insurer continues payments to beneficiary or surviving spouse. Issues formal cessation notice to PenCom on annuity termination.
